Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa

Homage to the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.

Saṃyuttanikāye

In the Saṃyutta Nikāya

Nidānavagga-aṭṭhakathā

The Commentary to the Nidāna Vagga

1. Nidānasaṃyuttaṃ

1. The Connected Discourses on Causation

1. Buddhavaggo

1. The Buddha Chapter

1. Paṭiccasamuppādasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Explanation of the Discourse on Dependent Origination

1. Evaṃ [V 2.0001][P 2.0001][M 2.0001] me sutanti – nidānavagge paṭhamaṃ paṭiccasamuppādasuttaṃ. Tatrāyaṃ anupubbapadavaṇṇanā – tatra kho bhagavā bhikkhū āmantesīti, ettha tatrāti desakālaparidīpanaṃ. Tañhi “yaṃ samayaṃ viharati, tatra samaye, yasmiñca jetavane viharati, tatra jetavane”ti dīpeti. Bhāsitabbayutte vā desakāle dīpeti. Na hi bhagavā ayutte dese kāle ca dhammaṃ bhāsati. “Akālo [V 2.0002] kho tāva bāhiyā”tiādi (udā. 10) cettha sādhakaṃ. Khoti padapūraṇamatte, avadhāraṇe ādikālatthe vā nipāto. Bhagavāti lokagarudīpanaṃ. Bhikkhūti kathāsavanayuttapuggalavacanaṃ. Apicettha “bhikkhakoti bhikkhu, bhikkhācariyaṃ ajjhūpagatoti bhikkhū”tiādinā (pārā. 45; vibha. 510) nayena vacanattho veditabbo. Āmantesīti ālapi, abhāsi, sambodhesi, ayamettha attho. Aññatra pana ñāpanepi hoti. Yathāha – “āmantayāmi [M 2.0002] vo, bhikkhave, paṭivedayāmi vo, bhikkhave”ti. Pakkosanepi. Yathāha – “ehi tvaṃ, bhikkhu, mama vacanena sāriputtaṃ āmantehī”ti (a. ni. 9.11). Bhikkhavoti āmantanākāradīpanaṃ. Tañca bhikkhanasīlatādiguṇayogasiddhattā vuttaṃ. Bhikkhanasīlatāguṇayuttopi [P 2.0002] hi bhikkhu, bhikkhanadhammatāguṇayuttopi bhikkhane sādhukāritāguṇayuttopīti saddavidū maññanti. Tena ca tesaṃ bhikkhanasīlatādiguṇayogasiddhena vacanena hīnādhikajanasevitavuttiṃ pakāsento uddhatadīnabhāvaniggahaṃ karoti. “Bhikkhavo”ti iminā ca karuṇāvipphārasommahadayanayananipātapubbaṅgamena vacanena te attano abhimukhe karonto teneva kathetukamyatādīpakena nesaṃ vacanena sotukamyataṃ janeti, teneva ca sambodhanatthena sādhukaṃ manasikārepi niyojeti. Sādhukaṃ manasikārāyattā hi sāsanasampatti.

1. Thus have I heard—in the Nidāna Vagga, the first is the Discourse on Dependent Origination. Herein is the sequential explanation of the terms. In the passage, 'There, the Blessed One addressed the monks,' the word 'there' indicates the location and time. For it explains: 'At whatever time he was dwelling, at that time; and in whichever Jeta's Grove he was dwelling, in that Jeta's Grove.' Or it indicates the appropriate place and time for speaking. Indeed, the Blessed One does not teach the Dhamma in inappropriate places or at inappropriate times. The phrase, 'It is not the time now, Bāhiya,' etc., is evidence here. 'Kho' is a particle used merely as an expletive, or for emphasis, time, and so on. 'Bhagavā' indicates one revered by the world. 'Bhikkhū' is a term for individuals suitable for hearing the discourse. Moreover, here the meaning of the term should be understood according to the method in texts such as the Pārājika and the Vibhaṅga: 'one who begs is a bhikkhu; one who has undertaken the practice of alms-gathering is a bhikkhu,' etc. 'Āmantesi' means he called, he spoke, he made aware—this is the meaning here. Elsewhere, it can also mean informing, as in, 'I inform you, monks, I declare to you, monks.' It can also mean summoning, as in, 'Come, monk, by my word, summon Sāriputta.' 'Bhikkhavo' indicates the mode of address. And this term is used because it is established by their association with qualities such as the habit of alms-seeking. For those skilled in words consider a bhikkhu as one endowed with the quality of the habit of alms-seeking, one endowed with the quality of the nature of alms-seeking, or one endowed with the quality of being proficient in alms-seeking. And by that word, which is established through their association with qualities such as the habit of alms-seeking, he, by revealing the conduct practiced by both inferior and superior persons, subdues haughtiness and dejection. And by this word 'Bhikkhavo'—which is preceded by a gaze from a gentle heart suffused with an outpouring of compassion—he, by turning them towards himself, thereby arouses their desire to listen through that very word that indicates his desire to speak; and by virtue of its meaning of awakening, he also enjoins them to pay careful attention. For the accomplishment of the teaching depends on careful attention.

Aparesupi devamanussesu vijjamānesu kasmā bhikkhūyeva āmantesīti ce? Jeṭṭhaseṭṭhāsannasadāsannihitabhāvato. Sabbaparisasādhāraṇā hi bhagavato dhammadesanā, parisāya jeṭṭhā bhikkhū paṭhamaṃ uppannattā, seṭṭhā anagāriyabhāvaṃ ādiṃ katvā satthucariyānuvidhāyakattā sakalasāsanapaṭiggāhakattā ca, āsannā tattha nisinnesu satthusantikattā, sadāsannihitā satthusantikāvacarattāti. Apica te dhammadesanāya bhājanaṃ yathānusiṭṭhaṃ paṭipattisabbhāvato. Visesato ca ekacce bhikkhūyeva sandhāya ayaṃ desanāpīti evaṃ āmantesi.

If it is asked: 'Even when other gods and humans were present, why did he address only the monks?' Because they are the eldest, the best, the nearest, and constantly in attendance. For the Blessed One’s teaching of the Dhamma is common to all assemblies, but in the assembly the monks are the eldest because they arose first; they are the best because, having taken homelessness as their starting point, they follow the Teacher’s conduct and are the upholders of the entire Dispensation; they are the nearest because, among those sitting there, they are close to the Teacher; and they are constantly in attendance because they are always in the Teacher’s presence. Moreover, they are vessels for the Dhamma teaching, owing to their good practice in accordance with the instruction. And specifically, this teaching is also with reference to certain monks; for this reason too, he addressed them.

Kimatthaṃ pana bhagavā dhammaṃ desento paṭhamaṃ bhikkhū āmantesi, na dhammameva desesīti? Satijananatthaṃ. Bhikkhū aññaṃ cintentāpi vikkhittacittāpi dhammaṃ paccavekkhantāpi kammaṭṭhānaṃ manasikarontāpi nisinnā honti. Te anāmantetvā dhamme desiyamāne “ayaṃ desanā kiṃnidānā kiṃpaccayā katamāya aṭṭhuppattiyā desitā”ti sallakkhetuṃ asakkontā duggahitaṃ vā gaṇheyyuṃ, na vā gaṇheyyuṃ, tena nesaṃ satijananatthaṃ bhagavā paṭhamaṃ āmantetvā pacchā dhammaṃ deseti.

Why then did the Blessed One, when teaching the Dhamma, first address the monks and not teach the Dhamma directly? To generate mindfulness. The monks might be sitting there thinking of other things, with distracted minds, reflecting on the Dhamma, or attending to their meditation subject. If the Dhamma were taught without first addressing them, they, being unable to determine, 'What is the basis for this teaching? What is the cause? On what occasion was it taught?', might grasp it incorrectly or not grasp it at all. Therefore, to generate mindfulness in them, the Blessed One first addresses them and then teaches the Dhamma.

Bhadanteti [V 2.0003][P 2.0003] gāravavacanametaṃ, satthuno paṭivacanadānaṃ vā. Apicettha “bhikkhavo”ti vadamāno bhagavā bhikkhū ālapati. “Bhadante”ti vadamānā te bhagavantaṃ paccālapanti. Tathā hi “bhikkhavo”ti bhagavā ābhāsati, “bhadante”ti [M 2.0003] paccābhāsanti. “Bhikkhavo”ti paṭivacanaṃ dāpeti, “bhadante”ti paṭivacanaṃ denti. Te bhikkhūti ye bhagavā āmantesi, te. Bhagavato paccassosunti bhagavato āmantanaṃ patiassosuṃ, abhimukhā hutvā suṇiṃsu sampaṭicchiṃsu paṭiggahesunti attho. Bhagavā etadavocāti, bhagavā etaṃ idāni vattabbaṃ sakalasuttaṃ avoca. Ettāvatā yaṃ āyasmatā ānandena atthabyañjanasampannassa buddhānaṃ desanāñāṇagambhīrabhāvasaṃsūcakassa imassa suttassa sukhāvagāhaṇatthaṃ kāladesadesakaparisāpadesappaṭimaṇḍitaṃ nidānaṃ bhāsitaṃ, tassa atthavaṇṇanā samattā.

'Bhadante' (Venerable Sir) is a term of respect, or it is the giving of a response to the Teacher. Furthermore, here, the Blessed One, saying 'Bhikkhavo,' addresses the monks. They, saying 'Bhadante,' respond to the Blessed One. Thus, with 'Bhikkhavo,' the Blessed One initiates the address; with 'Bhadante,' they respond. With 'Bhikkhavo,' he elicits a response; with 'Bhadante,' they give the response. 'Te bhikkhū' means those monks whom the Blessed One addressed. 'Bhagavato paccassosuṃ' (They responded to the Blessed One) means they listened attentively to the Blessed One's address, facing him; they received it and accepted it—this is the meaning. 'Bhagavā etadavoca' (The Blessed One said this) means the Blessed One spoke this entire sutta that was now to be spoken. Thus far is concluded the explanation of the meaning of the introduction spoken by the venerable Ānanda—an introduction adorned with indications of the time, place, speaker, and assembly, for the purpose of easy comprehension of this sutta, which is complete in meaning and phrasing and indicative of the profundity of the Buddhas’ teaching-knowledge.

Idāni paṭiccasamuppādaṃ votiādinā nayena bhagavatā nikkhittassa suttassa saṃvaṇṇanāya okāso anuppatto. Sā panesā suttavaṇṇanā yasmā suttanikkhepaṃ vicāretvā vuccamānā pākaṭā hoti, tasmā suttanikkhepaṃ tāva vicāressāma. Cattāro hi suttanikkhepā – attajjhāsayo, parajjhāsayo, pucchāvasiko, aṭṭhuppattikoti. Tattha yāni suttāni bhagavā parehi anajjhiṭṭho kevalaṃ attano ajjhāsayeneva katheti, seyyathidaṃ – dasabalasuttantahārako candopama-vīṇopama-sammappadhāna-iddhipāda-indriyabala-bojjhaṅgamaggaṅga-suttantahārakoti evamādīni, tesaṃ attajjhāsayo nikkhepo.

Now the occasion has arrived for the commentary on the discourse set forth by the Blessed One in the manner beginning, 'Paṭiccasamuppādaṃ vo…'. Since this commentary on the discourse becomes clear when it is spoken after first examining the laying down of the discourse, we shall therefore first examine the laying down of the discourse. For there are four ways of laying down a discourse: through one's own inclination, through the inclination of others, in response to a question, and based on a specific incident. Among these, the discourses that the Blessed One teaches unrequested by others, solely from his own inclination—such as the collection of suttas on the ten powers; the simile of the moon, the simile of the lute, the right strivings, the bases of power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the factors of the path, and so on—the laying down of these is through one's own inclination.

Yāni pana “paripakkā kho rāhulassa vimuttiparipācanīyā dhammā. Yaṃnūnāhaṃ rāhulaṃ uttariṃ āsavānaṃ khaye vineyya”nti (saṃ. ni. 4.121; ma. ni. 3.416) evaṃ paresaṃ ajjhāsayaṃ khantiṃ nijjhānakkhamaṃ manaṃ abhinīhāraṃ bujjhanabhāvañca apekkhitvā parajjhāsayavasena kathitāni, seyyathidaṃ [P 2.0004] – cūḷarāhulovādasuttaṃ, mahārāhulovādasuttaṃ, dhammacakkappavattanaṃ, anattalakkhaṇasuttaṃ, āsīvisopamasuttaṃ, dhātuvibhaṅgasuttanti, evamādīni, tesaṃ parajjhāsayo nikkhepo.

On the other hand, those suttas that were taught by considering others' intention, inclination, fitness for contemplation, mind, aspiration, and potential for awakening, thinking, 'The qualities conducive to the maturation of Rāhula’s deliverance are indeed ripe. It would be good if I were to train Rāhula further in the destruction of the taints'—such as the Cūḷarāhulovāda Sutta, the Mahārāhulovāda Sutta, the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, the Anattalakkhaṇa Sutta, the Āsīvisopama Sutta, and the Dhātuvibhaṅga Sutta, and other such suttas—the exposition of these is the exposition based on the intention of others.

Bhagavantaṃ pana upasaṅkamitvā catasso parisā cattāro vaṇṇā nāgā supaṇṇā gandhabbā asurā yakkhā mahārājāno tāvatiṃsādayo devā mahābrahmāti evamādayo “bojjhaṅgā bojjhaṅgāti, bhante, vuccanti – (saṃ. ni. 5.202) nīvaraṇā nīvaraṇāti, bhante, vuccanti [V 2.0004] – ime nu kho, bhante, pañcupādānakkhandhā, kiṃsūdha vittaṃ purisassa seṭṭha”ntiādinā (saṃ. ni. 1.246; su. ni. 183) nayena pañhaṃ pucchanti. Evaṃ puṭṭhena bhagavatā yāni [M 2.0004] kathitāni bojjhaṅgasaṃyuttādīni, yāni vā panaññānipi devatāsaṃyutta, mārasaṃyutta, brahmasaṃyutta, sakkapañha, cūḷavedalla, mahāvedalla, sāmaññaphalaāḷavaka, sūciloma, kharalomasuttādīni, tesaṃ pucchāvasiko nikkhepo.

Furthermore, having approached the Blessed One, the four assemblies, the four castes, nāgas, supaṇṇas, gandhabbas, asuras, yakkhas, great kings, devas such as those of Tāvatiṃsa, and great brahmās, and other such beings, ask questions in this and other ways: 'Venerable sir, they are called "factors of enlightenment, factors of enlightenment"... Venerable sir, they are called "hindrances, hindrances"... Venerable sir, are these the five aggregates of clinging? What here is a person's best wealth?' and so forth. Those suttas taught by the Blessed One when thus questioned, such as the Connected Discourses on the Factors of Enlightenment and so forth, or also others such as the Devatā Saṃyutta, Māra Saṃyutta, Brahmā Saṃyutta, Sakkapañha Sutta, Cūḷavedalla Sutta, Mahāvedalla Sutta, Sāmaññaphala Sutta, Āḷavaka Sutta, Sūciloma Sutta, and Kharaloma Sutta, and so forth—the exposition of these is the exposition based on a question.

Yāni pana tāni uppannaṃ kāraṇaṃ paṭicca kathitāni, seyyathidaṃ – dhammadāyādaṃ. Cūḷasīhanādasuttaṃ puttamaṃsūpamaṃ dārukkhandhūpamaṃ aggikkhandhūpamaṃ pheṇapiṇḍūpamaṃ pāricchattakūpamanti evamādīni, tesaṃ aṭṭhuppattiko nikkhepo.

And those teachings that were spoken in dependence on an arisen cause, such as the Dhammadāyāda Sutta, the Cūḷasīhanāda Sutta, the Puttamaṃsūpama Sutta, the Dārukkhandhūpama Sutta, the Aggikkhandhūpama Sutta, the Pheṇapiṇḍūpama Sutta, and the Pāricchattakūpama Sutta, and other such suttas—the exposition of these is the exposition based on an occasion.

Evametesu catūsu nikkhepesu imassa paṭiccasamuppādasuttassa parajjhāsayo nikkhepo. Parapuggalajjhāsayavasena hidaṃ bhagavatā nikkhittaṃ. Katamesaṃ puggalānaṃ ajjhāsayavasenāti? Ugghaṭitaññūnaṃ. Cattāro hi puggalā ugghaṭitaññū vipañcitaññū neyyo padaparamoti. Tattha yassa puggalassa saha udāhaṭavelāya dhammābhisamayo hoti, ayaṃ vuccati puggalo ugghaṭitaññū. Yassa puggalassa saṃkhittena bhāsitassa vitthārena atthe [P 2.0005] vibhajiyamāne dhammābhisamayo hoti, ayaṃ vuccati puggalo vipañcitaññū. Yassa puggalassa uddesato paripucchato yoniso manasikaroto, kalyāṇamitte sevato, bhajato, payirupāsato, anupubbena dhammābhisamayo hoti, ayaṃ vuccati puggalo neyyo. Yassa puggalassa bahumpi suṇato, bahumpi dhārayato, bahumpi vācayato na tāya jātiyā dhammābhisamayo hoti, ayaṃ vuccati puggalo padaparamo. Iti imesu catūsu puggalesu ugghaṭitaññūpuggalānaṃ ajjhāsayavasena idaṃ suttaṃ nikkhittaṃ.

Thus, among these four expositions, the exposition of this Paṭiccasamuppāda Sutta is the exposition based on the inclination of others. For this was expounded by the Blessed One in connection with the inclinations of other individuals. In connection with the inclinations of which individuals? Of those of quick understanding. For there are four individuals: the one of quick understanding, the one who understands through elaboration, the one to be guided, and the one limited to the words. Among them, the individual for whom there is a penetration of the Dhamma at the very moment of utterance is called one of quick understanding. The individual for whom there is a penetration of the Dhamma when the meaning of what has been spoken briefly is analyzed in detail is called one who understands through elaboration. The individual for whom there is a gradual penetration of the Dhamma through instruction, questioning, wise attention, and associating with, frequenting, and revering good friends, that individual is called one to be guided. The individual for whom there is no penetration of the Dhamma in that very life, despite hearing much, retaining much, and reciting much, that individual is called one limited to the words. Thus, among these four individuals, this sutta was expounded in connection with the inclinations of individuals of quick understanding.

Tadā kira pañcasatā janapadavāsikā bhikkhū sabbeva ekacarā dvicarā ticarā catucarā pañcacarā sabhāgavuttino dhutaṅgadharā āraddhavīriyā yuttayogā vipassakā saṇhaṃ sukhumaṃ suññataṃ paccayākāradesanaṃ patthayamānā sāyanhasamaye bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā, vanditvā, rattakambalasāṇiyā parikkhipamānā viya desanaṃ paccāsīsamānā parivāretvā nisīdiṃsu. Tesaṃ ajjhāsayavasena bhagavā idaṃ suttaṃ ārabhi. Yathā hi cheko cittakāro aparikammakatabhittiṃ labhitvā, na āditova rūpaṃ samuṭṭhāpesi, mahāmattikalepādīhi pana bhittiparikammaṃ tāva katvā[V 2.0005], kataparikammāya [M 2.0005] bhittiyā rūpaṃ samuṭṭhāpeti, kataparikammaṃ pana bhittiṃ labhitvā, bhittiparikammabyāpāraṃ akatvā, raṅgajātāni yojetvā, vaṭṭikaṃ vā tūlikaṃ vā ādāya rūpameva samuṭṭhāpeti, evameva bhagavā akatābhinivesaṃ ādikammikakulaputtaṃ labhitvā nāssa āditova arahattapadaṭṭhānaṃ saṇhaṃ sukhumaṃ suññataṃ vipassanālakkhaṇaṃ ācikkhati, sīlasamādhikammassakatādiṭṭhisampadāya pana yojento pubbabhāgapaṭipadaṃ tāva ācikkhati. Yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ –

It is said that at that time, five hundred monks from the countryside—all of them dwelling alone, in pairs, in threes, in fours, or in fives, living a common life, observing the ascetic practices, exerting vigorous effort, engaged in the practice, practicing insight, and seeking the gentle, subtle teaching on dependent origination which is voidness—approached the Blessed One in the evening. Having paid homage, they sat down surrounding him, as if enclosing him with a red woolen curtain, eagerly awaiting the teaching. In connection with their inclination, the Blessed One began this discourse. For just as a skilled painter, having obtained a wall not yet prepared, does not immediately create an image, but first prepares the wall with a layer of plaster and so forth; only then, on the prepared wall, does he create the image. But if, having obtained a prepared wall, without doing the work of preparing it, he mixes the colors, takes a brush, and just creates the image. Similarly, the Blessed One, having encountered a clansman who is a beginner and has not yet formed a fixed adherence, does not immediately teach him the characteristic of insight—gentle, subtle, and voidness—which is the basis for attaining Arahantship. Instead, he first instructs him in the preliminary practice, engaging him in the accomplishment of virtue, concentration, and the right view of ownership of action. In reference to which it was said:

“Tasmātiha tvaṃ, bhikkhu, ādimeva visodhehi kusalesu dhammesu. Ko cādi kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ? Sīlañca suvisuddhaṃ diṭṭhi ca ujukā. Yato kho te, bhikkhu, sīlañca suvisuddhaṃ bhavissati diṭṭhi ca ujukā. Tato tvaṃ, bhikkhu, sīlaṃ nissāya sīle patiṭṭhāya cattāro satipaṭṭhāne tividhena bhāveyyāsi. Katame cattāro? Idha [P 2.0006] tvaṃ, bhikkhu, ajjhattaṃ vā kāye kāyānupassī viharāhi ātāpī sampajāno satimā vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ. Bahiddhā vā kāye…pe… ajjhattabahiddhā vā kāye…pe… dhammesu dhammānupassī viharāhi ātāpī sampajāno satimā vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ. Yato kho tvaṃ, bhikkhu, sīlaṃ nissāya sīle patiṭṭhāya ime cattāro satipaṭṭhāne evaṃ tividhena bhāvessasi, tato tuyhaṃ, bhikkhu, yā ratti vā divaso vā āgamissati, vuddhiyeva pāṭikaṅkhā kusalesu dhammesu, no parihānī”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.369).

Therefore, bhikkhu, here you should first of all purify the wholesome states. And what is the beginning of wholesome states? Well-purified virtue and an upright view. When, bhikkhu, your virtue is well-purified and your view is upright, then, bhikkhu, relying on virtue, established in virtue, you should develop the four foundations of mindfulness in three ways. Which four? Here, bhikkhu, dwell contemplating the body in the body internally—ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in the world. Or dwell contemplating the body in the body externally… or dwell contemplating the body in the body both internally and externally… or dwell contemplating phenomena in phenomena—ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in the world. When, bhikkhu, relying on virtue, established in virtue, you have thus developed these four foundations of mindfulness in three ways, then, bhikkhu, whatever night or day comes, only growth in wholesome states is to be expected, not decline.

Evaṃ ādikammikakulaputtassa sīlakathāya parikammaṃ kathetvā, arahattapadaṭṭhānaṃ saṇhaṃ sukhumaṃ suññataṃ vipassanālakkhaṇaṃ ācikkhati.

Thus, having delivered the preliminary instruction by way of the discourse on virtue for the clansman who is a beginner, He explains the characteristic of insight—the proximate cause for the fruit of Arahantship, gentle, subtle, and indicative of voidness.

Parisuddhasīlaṃ pana āraddhavīriyaṃ yuttayogaṃ vipassakaṃ labhitvā, nāssa pubbabhāgapaṭipadaṃ ācikkhati, ujukameva pana arahattapadaṭṭhānaṃ saṇhaṃ sukhumaṃ suññataṃ vipassanālakkhaṇaṃ ācikkhati. Ime pañcasatā bhikkhū pubbabhāgapaṭipadaṃ parisodhetvā ṭhitā sudhantasuvaṇṇasadisā suparimajjitamaṇikkhandhasannibhā, eko lokuttaramaggova nesaṃ anāgato. Iti tassāgamanatthāya satthā tesaṃ ajjhāsayaṃ apekkhamāno idaṃ suttaṃ ārabhi.

Furthermore, having found an insight practitioner who is pure in virtue, with energy aroused, and endowed with exertion, He does not teach him the preliminary practice. Rather, He teaches directly the characteristic of insight, which is the proximate cause for the fruit of Arahantship, gentle, subtle, and indicative of voidness. These five hundred monks, having thoroughly purified the preliminary practice, were established like newly refined, pure gold, like a well-polished block of ruby; for them, only the one supramundane path had not yet arrived. Thus, for the purpose of its arrival, the Teacher, observing their disposition, began this discourse.

Tattha [V 2.0006][M 2.0006] paṭiccasamuppādanti paccayākāraṃ. Paccayākāro hi aññamaññaṃ paṭicca sahite dhamme uppādeti. Tasmā paṭiccasamuppādoti vuccati. Ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthāro pana visuddhimaggato gahetabbo.

Therein, 'paṭiccasamuppāda' means the causal mode. Indeed, the causal mode, by depending on one another, produces co-arisen phenomena. Therefore, it is called 'paṭiccasamuppāda'. This is the summary here; as for the detailed explanation, it should be understood from the Visuddhimagga.

Voti ayaṃ vo-saddo paccatta-upayogakaraṇa-sampadāna-sāmivacana-padapūraṇesu dissati. “Kacci pana vo anuruddhā samaggā sammodamānā”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.326; mahāva. 466) hi paccatte dissati. “Gacchatha, bhikkhave, paṇāmemi vo”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 2.157) upayoge. “Na vo mama santike vatthabba”ntiādīsu (ma. ni. 2.157) karaṇe. “Vanapatthapariyāyaṃ vo, bhikkhave, desessāmī”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.190) sampadāne. “Sabbesaṃ vo, sāriputta, subhāsita”ntiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.345) sāmivacane. “Ye hi vo ariyā parisuddhakāyakammantā”tiādīsu [P 2.0007] (ma. ni. 1.35) padapūraṇamatte. Idha panāyaṃ sampadāne daṭṭhabbo. Bhikkhaveti patissavena abhimukhībhūtānaṃ puna ālapanaṃ. Desessāmīti desanāpaṭijānanaṃ. Taṃ suṇāthāti taṃ paṭiccasamuppādaṃ taṃ desanaṃ mayā vuccamānaṃ suṇātha.

The word 'vo' is seen in the senses of the nominative, accusative, instrumental, dative, genitive, and as a mere expletive. For instance, in passages such as, 'I hope, Anuruddhas, that you are united and harmonious,' it is seen in the nominative sense. In passages such as, 'Go, monks, I dismiss you,' it is in the accusative sense. In passages such as, 'You should not stay near me,' it is in the instrumental sense. In passages such as, 'Monks, I will teach you the discourse on dwelling in the forest,' it is in the dative sense. In passages such as, 'Sāriputta, all of you have spoken well,' it is in the genitive sense. In passages such as, 'For those of you who are noble, with purified bodily conduct,' it is seen as a mere expletive. Here, however, this word should be understood in the dative sense. 'Bhikkhave' is a repeated address to the monks who have turned towards Him in respectful response. 'Desissāmi' is a declaration of the teaching. 'Taṃ suṇātha' means: listen to that teaching on dependent origination, to that teaching being spoken by me.

Sādhukaṃ manasi karothāti ettha pana sādhukaṃ sādhūti ekatthametaṃ. Ayañca sādhusaddo āyācana-sampaṭicchana-sampahaṃsana-sundara-daḷhīkammādīsu dissati. “Sādhu me, bhante, bhagavā saṃkhittena dhammaṃ desetū”tiādīsu (a. ni. 4.257; saṃ. ni. 4.65; 5.381) hi āyācane dissati. “Sādhu, bhanteti kho so bhikkhu bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinanditvā anumoditvā”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 3.86) sampaṭicchane. “Sādhu sādhu, sāriputtā”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 3.349) sampahaṃsane.

Now, in the phrase 'Sādhukaṃ manasi karotha' (attend closely), 'sādhukaṃ' and 'sādhu' have the same meaning. And this word 'sādhu' is seen in the senses of requesting, accepting, rejoicing, excellence, and making firm, among others. For instance, it is seen in the sense of requesting in passages such as, 'It would be good, venerable sir, if the Blessed One were to teach me the Dhamma in brief.' It is seen in the sense of accepting in passages such as, 'That monk, saying, "Very well, venerable sir," having delighted and rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words...' It is seen in the sense of rejoicing in passages such as, 'Excellent, excellent, Sāriputta.'

“Sādhu dhammarucī rājā, sādhu paññāṇavā naro;

Sādhu mittānamaddubbho, pāpassa akaraṇaṃ sukha”nti. –

Excellent is a king who delights in the Dhamma,

excellent is a person endowed with wisdom;

Excellent is not betraying friends,

the non-doing of evil is happiness.

Ādīsu (jā. 2.18.101) sundare. “Tena hi, brāhmaṇa, sādhukaṃ suṇāhī”tiādīsu (a. ni. 5.192) sādhukasaddoyeva daḷhīkamme āṇattiyantipi vuccati. Idha panāyaṃ ettheva daḷhīkamme āṇattiyā ca attho veditabbo, sundaratthepi vaṭṭati. Daḷhīkaraṇatthena hi “daḷhaṃ [V 2.0007] imaṃ dhammaṃ suṇātha, suggahitaṃ gaṇhantā”, āṇattiatthena “mama āṇattiyā suṇātha” sundaratthena “sundaramimaṃ bhaddakaṃ dhammaṃ suṇāthā”ti [M 2.0007] etaṃ dīpitaṃ hoti. Manasi karothāti āvajjetha. Samannāharathāti attho. Avikkhittacittā hutvā nisāmetha, citte karothāti adhippāyo.

In passages such as in the Ummadantī Jātaka, it is seen in the sense of 'excellence'. In passages such as, 'Therefore, brahmin, listen well,' the word 'sādhukaṃ' itself is said to be in the sense of making firm and also in the sense of command. Here, however, its meaning should be understood as making firm and as command, and it is also suitable in the sense of 'excellence'. For, with the meaning of making firm, it is shown thus: 'Listen to this Dhamma firmly, grasping it well.' With the meaning of command, it is shown thus: 'Listen by my command.' With the meaning of 'excellence', it is shown thus: 'Listen to this excellent, auspicious Dhamma.' 'Manasi karotha' means: 'attend,' 'apply the mind well.' The intention is: 'Having become undistracted in mind, listen; establish it in the mind.'

Idānettha taṃ suṇāthāti sotindriyavikkhepanivāraṇametaṃ. Sādhukaṃ manasi karothāti manasikāre daḷhīkammaniyojanena manindriyavikkhepanivāraṇaṃ. Purimañcettha byañjanavipallāsagāhanivāraṇaṃ, pacchimaṃ atthavipallāsagāhanivāraṇaṃ. Purimena ca dhammassavane niyojeti, pacchimena sutānaṃ dhammānaṃ dhāraṇūpaparikkhāsu. Purimena ca “sabyañjano ayaṃ dhammo, tasmā savanīyo”ti [P 2.0008] dīpeti, pacchimena “sāttho, tasmā manasi kātabbo”ti. Sādhukapadaṃ vā ubhayapadehi yojetvā, “yasmā ayaṃ dhammo dhammagambhīro ca desanāgambhīro ca, tasmā suṇātha sādhukaṃ. Yasmā atthagambhīro ca paṭivedhagambhīro ca, tasmā sādhukaṃ manasi karothā”ti evaṃ yojanā veditabbā. Bhāsissāmīti desessāmi. “Taṃ suṇāthā”ti ettha paṭiññātaṃ desanaṃ saṃkhittatova na desessāmi, apica kho vitthāratopi naṃ bhāsissāmīti vuttaṃ hoti. Saṅkhepavitthāravācakāni hi etāni padāni. Yathāha vaṅgīsatthero –

Now, herein, 'Listen to that' is for the prevention of distraction of the ear-faculty. 'Attend closely' is for the prevention of distraction of the mind-faculty by enjoining firmness in attention. Furthermore, the former phrase is for the prevention of wrongly grasping the letter, while the latter is for the prevention of wrongly grasping the meaning. And by the former, one is enjoined in listening to the Dhamma; by the latter, in retaining and investigating the teachings that have been heard. By the former, it is shown: 'This Dhamma is complete with the letter, therefore it should be heard.' By the latter: 'It is complete with the meaning, therefore it should be attended to.' Alternatively, connecting the word 'sādhukaṃ' with both phrases, the construction should be understood thus: 'Because this Dhamma is profound in text and profound in teaching, therefore listen well. Because it is profound in meaning and profound in penetration, therefore attend well.' 'Bhāsissāmi' means 'I will teach.' In 'Listen to that,' it is said that the declared teaching will not be taught merely in brief, but rather, 'I will speak it also in detail.' For these words are indicators of both the concise and the detailed, as the Elder Vaṅgīsa said:

“Saṃkhittenapi deseti, vitthārenapi bhāsati;

Sāḷikāyiva nigghoso, paṭibhānaṃ udīrayī”ti. (saṃ. ni. 1.214; theragā. 1241);

He teaches also in brief, and He speaks also in detail; like the sound of the Sāḷikā bird, He uttered inspired speech.

Evaṃ vutte ussāhajātā hutvā evaṃ, bhanteti kho te bhikkhū bhagavato paccassosuṃ satthu vacanaṃ sampaṭicchiṃsu, paṭiggahesunti vuttaṃ hoti.

When this was said, those monks, becoming filled with enthusiasm, listened in respectful assent to the Blessed One, saying, 'Very well, venerable sir.' They accepted the Teacher's word; they received it. Thus it is said.

Atha nesaṃ bhagavā etadavoca – etaṃ idāni vattabbaṃ “katamo ca, bhikkhave, paṭiccasamuppādo”tiādiṃ sakalaṃ suttaṃ avoca. Tattha katamo ca, bhikkhave, paṭiccasamuppādoti kathetukamyatāpucchā. Pañcavidhā hi pucchā adiṭṭhajotanāpucchā diṭṭhasaṃsandanāpucchā vimaticchedanāpucchā anumatipucchā kathetukamyatāpucchāti, tāsaṃ idaṃ nānattaṃ –

Then the Blessed One said this to them—he spoke the entire sutta, which is now to be set forth, beginning with ‘And what, bhikkhus, is dependent origination?’ Here, ‘And what, bhikkhus, is dependent origination?’ is a question asked out of a desire to speak. For there are five kinds of questions: a question asked to illuminate what has not been seen; a question asked to compare what has been seen; a question asked to cut off doubt; a question asked for the sake of agreement; and a question asked out of a desire to speak. This is their distinction.

Katamā [V 2.0008] adiṭṭhajotanā pucchā (mahāni. 150; cūḷani. puṇṇakamāṇavapucchāniddesa 12)? Pakatiyā lakkhaṇaṃ aññātaṃ hoti adiṭṭhaṃ atulitaṃ atīritaṃ avibhūtaṃ avibhāvitaṃ. Tassa ñāṇāya dassanāya [M 2.0008] tulanāya tīraṇāya vibhūtāya vibhāvanatthāya pañhaṃ pucchati. Ayaṃ adiṭṭhajotanāpucchā.

What is the question that illuminates what has not been seen? By nature, a characteristic is unknown, unseen, unweighed, unjudged, unmanifest, and unclarified. One asks a question for the purpose of knowing it, seeing it, weighing it, judging it, making it manifest, and clarifying it. This is the question that illuminates what has not been seen.

Katamā diṭṭhasaṃsandanāpucchā? Pakatiyā lakkhaṇaṃ ñātaṃ hoti diṭṭhaṃ tulitaṃ tīritaṃ vibhūtaṃ vibhāvitaṃ. So aññehi paṇḍitehi saddhiṃ saṃsandanatthāya pañhaṃ pucchati. Ayaṃ diṭṭhasaṃsandanāpucchā.

What is the question asked to compare what has been seen? By nature, a characteristic is known, seen, weighed, judged, manifest, and clarified. One asks a question for the sake of comparison with other wise people. This is the question asked to compare what has been seen.

Katamā vimaticchedanāpucchā? Pakatiyā saṃsayapakkhando hoti vimatipakkhando dveḷhakajāto – “evaṃ nu kho, na nu kho, kathaṃ nu kho”ti, so vimaticchedanatthāya [P 2.0009] pañhaṃ pucchati, ayaṃ vimaticchedanāpucchā.

What is the question that cuts off doubt? By nature, one is prone to doubt, inclined to uncertainty, and has become twofold in mind—"Is it thus? Is it not thus? How can it be thus?" To cut off doubt, one asks a question; this is the question that cuts off doubt.

Katamā anumatipucchā? Bhagavā bhikkhūnaṃ anumatiyā pañhaṃ pucchati – “taṃ kiṃ maññatha, bhikkhave, rūpaṃ niccaṃ vā aniccaṃ vā”ti, aniccaṃ, bhante. Yaṃ panāniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vā taṃ sukhaṃ vāti, dukkhaṃ, bhante. Yaṃ panāniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vipariṇāmadhammaṃ, kallaṃ nu taṃ samanupassituṃ – “etaṃ mama esohamasmi eso me attā”ti, no hetaṃ bhanteti (saṃ. ni. 3.79). Ayaṃ anumatipucchā.

What is the question asked for the sake of agreement? The Blessed One asks the bhikkhus a question for the sake of their agreement: "What do you think, bhikkhus, is form permanent or impermanent?" "Impermanent, venerable sir." "And what is impermanent, is that suffering or happiness?" "Suffering, venerable sir." "And what is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change, is it fitting to regard it thus: 'This is mine, this I am, this is my self'?" "No, venerable sir, it is not." This is the question asked for the sake of agreement.

Katamā kathetukamyatāpucchā? Bhagavā bhikkhūnaṃ kathetukamyatāya pañhaṃ pucchati – “cattārome, bhikkhave, satipaṭṭhānā. Katame cattāro”ti? Ayaṃ kathetukamyatāpucchāti.

What is the question asked out of a desire to speak? The Blessed One asks the bhikkhus a question out of a desire to speak: "Bhikkhus, there are these four establishments of mindfulness. What are the four?" This is the question asked out of a desire to speak.

Tattha buddhānaṃ purimā tisso pucchā natthi. Kasmā? Buddhānañhi tīsu addhāsu kiñci saṅkhataṃ addhāvimuttaṃ vā asaṅkhataṃ adiṭṭhaṃ ajotitaṃ atulitaṃ atīritaṃ avibhūtaṃ avibhāvitaṃ nāma natthi. Tena nesaṃ adiṭṭhajotanāpucchā natthi. Yaṃ pana bhagavatā attano ñāṇena paṭividdhaṃ, tassa aññena samaṇena vā brāhmaṇena vā devena vā mārena vā brahmunā vā saddhiṃ saṃsandanakiccaṃ natthi. Tenassa diṭṭhasaṃsandanāpucchā natthi. Yasmā panesa akathaṃkathī tiṇṇavicikiccho [V 2.0009] sabbadhammesu vihatasaṃsayo. Tenassa vimaticchedanāpucchā natthi. Itarā pana dve pucchā bhagavato atthi. Tāsu ayaṃ kathetukamyatā pucchāti veditabbā.

Here, the first three questions do not exist for the Buddhas. Why? Because for the Buddhas, in the three periods of time, there is nothing conditioned, or unconditioned and liberated from time, that is unseen, unillumined, unweighed, unjudged, unmanifest, or unclarified. Therefore, they have no question that illuminates what has not been seen. Moreover, what the Blessed One has penetrated by his own knowledge has no need for comparison with another ascetic, brahmin, god, Māra, or Brahmā. Thus, he has no question asked to compare what has been seen. Furthermore, since he is free from perplexity, has overcome doubt, and has dispelled uncertainty regarding all phenomena, he has no question that cuts off doubt. However, the other two questions do exist for the Blessed One. Among these, this is to be understood as the question asked out of a desire to speak.

Idāni tāva pucchāya puṭṭhaṃ paccayākāraṃ vibhajanto avijjāpaccayā, bhikkhave, saṅkhārātiādimāha. Ettha ca yathā nāma “pitaraṃ kathessāmī”ti āraddho [M 2.0009] “tissassa pitā soṇassa pitā”ti paṭhamataraṃ puttampi katheti, evameva bhagavā paccayaṃ kathetuṃ āraddho “avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā”tiādinā nayena saṅkhārādīnaṃ paccaye avijjādidhamme kathento paccayuppannampi kathesi. Āhāravaggassa pana pariyosāne “paṭiccasamuppādañca vo, bhikkhave, desessāmi [P 2.0010] paṭiccasamuppanne ca dhamme”ti (saṃ. ni. 2.20) ubhayaṃ ārabhitvā ubhayampi kathesi. Idāni avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārātiādīsu pana avijjā ca sā paccayo cāti avijjāpaccayo. Tasmā avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā sambhavantīti iminā nayena attho veditabbo. Ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthārena pana sabbākārasampannā anulomapaṭiccasamuppādakathā visuddhimagge kathitā, tasmā sā tattha kathitavaseneva gahetabbā.

Now, explaining the mode of conditionality that was asked about by that question, he said, “With ignorance as condition, bhikkhus, formations arise,” and so on. Here, just as one who has set out to speak of a father might first mention the son (e.g., ‘Tissa’s father,’ ‘Soṇa’s father’), even so the Blessed One, having set out to explain the condition, in explaining the conditions for formations and so on—ignorance and other phenomena—in the manner beginning “with ignorance as condition, formations arise,” also explained the conditionally arisen phenomena. However, at the end of the Āhāra Vagga, he said: “Bhikkhus, I will teach you dependent origination and dependently arisen phenomena,” and having begun with both, he explained both. Now, in passages such as “with ignorance as condition, formations arise,” ‘avijjāpaccayo’ means ‘it is ignorance, and that is a condition.’ Therefore, the meaning should be understood in this way: “Formations arise because of that condition which is ignorance.” This is the summary here. The comprehensive discourse on the forward sequence of dependent origination, complete in all aspects, has been given in the Visuddhimagga; therefore, it should be understood just as it is explained there.

Paṭilomakathāyaṃ pana avijjāya tvevāti avijjāya tu eva. Asesavirāganirodhāti virāgasaṅkhātena maggena asesanirodhā. Saṅkhāranirodhoti saṅkhārānaṃ anuppādanirodho hoti. Evaṃnirodhānaṃ pana saṅkhārānaṃ nirodhā viññāṇādīnañca nirodhā nāmarūpādīni niruddhāniyeva hontīti dassetuṃ saṅkhāranirodhā viññāṇanirodhotiādīni vatvā, evametassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa nirodho hotīti āha. Tattha kevalassāti sakalassa, suddhassa vā, sattavirahitassāti attho. Dukkhakkhandhassāti dukkharāsissa. Nirodho hotīti anuppādo hoti. Iti bhagavā anulomato dvādasahi padehi vaṭṭakathaṃ kathetvā tameva vaṭṭaṃ vinivaṭṭetvā paṭilomato dvādasahi padehi vivaṭṭaṃ kathento arahattena desanāya kūṭaṃ gaṇhi. Desanāpariyosāne te pañcasatā āraddhavipassakā ugghaṭitaññūpuggalā sūriyarasmisamphuṭṭhāni paripākagatāni padumāni viya saccāni bujjhitvā arahattaphale patiṭṭhahiṃsu.

In the reverse discourse, however, ‘avijjāya tveva’ means ‘avijjāya tu eva’ (of ignorance itself). ‘Asesavirāganirodhā’ means ‘through the remainderless cessation by means of the path known as dispassion.’ ‘Saṅkhāranirodho’ means there is the non-arising cessation of formations. To show that with the cessation of formations that have thus ceased, and with the cessation of consciousness and so on, name-and-form and the rest are indeed ceased, he said, “With the cessation of formations, there is the cessation of consciousness,” and so on, and then said, “Thus there is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.” Here, ‘kevalassa’ means ‘of the whole,’ or ‘of the mere,’ or ‘that which is devoid of a being.’ ‘Dukkhakkhandhassa’ means ‘of the mass of suffering.’ ‘Nirodho hoti’ means ‘there is non-arising.’ Thus the Blessed One, having explained the discourse on the cycle in forward order with twelve terms, reversed that very cycle and, explaining the un-cycling in reverse order with twelve terms, took the teaching to its pinnacle with Arahantship. At the conclusion of the discourse, those five hundred practitioners of insight, individuals of quick understanding, awakened to the truths and became established in the fruit of Arahantship, just as a cluster of fully ripened lotuses touched by the sun’s rays would blossom.

Idamavoca bhagavāti idaṃ vaṭṭavivaṭṭavasena sakalasuttaṃ bhagavā avoca. Attamanā te bhikkhūti tuṭṭhacittā te pañcasatā khīṇāsavā bhikkhū. Bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinandunti karavīkarutamañjunā [V 2.0010] kaṇṇasukhena paṇḍitajanahadayānaṃ amatābhisekasadisena brahmassarena bhāsato bhagavato [M 2.0010] vacanaṃ abhinandiṃsu, anumodiṃsu ceva sampaṭicchiṃsu cāti attho. Tenetaṃ vuccati –

"Idamavoca bhagavā" means: The Blessed One spoke this entire discourse concerning the round of existence and the ending of the round. "Attamanā te bhikkhū" means: Those five hundred monks whose cankers were destroyed were delighted in mind. "Bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinandunti" means: They greatly rejoiced in, approved of, and accepted the word of the Blessed One, who spoke with a sublime voice that was melodious like the song of the karavīka bird, pleasing to the ear, and like an anointing with the deathless for the hearts of the assembly of the wise. This is the meaning. Therefore, it is said:

“Subhāsitaṃ sulapitaṃ, sādhu sādhūti tādino;

Anumodamānā sirasā, sampaṭicchiṃsu bhikkhavo”ti.

"The monks, rejoicing in the well-spoken, well-uttered word of the Such-One, saying, 'Excellent, excellent!', accepted it with their heads."

Paṭhamapaṭiccasamuppādasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the First Discourse on Dependent Origination is completed.

2. Vibhaṅgasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Vibhaṅga Sutta

2. Dutiyepi [P 2.0011] vuttanayeneva suttanikkhepo veditabbo. Ayaṃ pana viseso – paṭhamaṃ ugghaṭitaññūpuggalānaṃ vasena saṅkhepato dassitaṃ, idaṃ vipañcitaññūnaṃ vasena vitthāratoti. Imasmiñca pana sutte catasso vallihārakapurisūpamā vattabbā, tā visuddhimagge vuttā eva. Yathā hi vallihārako puriso valliyā aggaṃ disvā tadanusārena mūlaṃ pariyesanto taṃ disvā valliṃ mūle chetvā ādāya kamme upaneyya, evaṃ bhagavā vitthāradesanaṃ desento paṭiccasamuppādassa aggabhūtā jarāmaraṇā paṭṭhāya yāva mūlabhūtaṃ avijjāpadaṃ, tāva desanaṃ āharitvā puna vaṭṭavivaṭṭaṃ desento niṭṭhapesi.

2. In the second sutta as well, the exposition of the sutta should be understood by the very method already stated. This, however, is the distinction: the first was shown briefly for the sake of persons of swift understanding, whereas this one was shown in detail for the sake of persons who understand through explanation. And in this sutta, four similes of the man who gathers vines are to be spoken of; they are indeed spoken of in the Visuddhimagga. For just as a man who gathers vines, having seen the tip of a vine and, following it, searching for the root, sees it, cuts the vine at the root, takes it and would apply it to his work; so too the Blessed One, when teaching the detailed exposition, starting from aging-and-death, which is the tip of dependent origination, brought the teaching as far as the term ignorance, which is the root, and then again, teaching the round and the ending of the round, brought it to a conclusion.

Tatrāyaṃ jarāmaraṇādīnaṃ vitthāradesanāya atthanicchayo – jarāmaraṇaniddese tāva tesaṃ tesanti ayaṃ saṅkhepato anekesaṃ sattānaṃ sādhāraṇaniddesoti viññātabbo. Yā devadattassa jarā, yā somadattassāti evañhi divasampi kathentassa neva sattā pariyādānaṃ gacchanti. Imehi pana dvīhi padehi na koci satto apariyādinno hoti. Tasmā vuttaṃ, “ayaṃ saṅkhepato anekesaṃ sattānaṃ sādhāraṇaniddeso”ti. Tamhi tamhīti ayaṃ gatijātivasena anekesaṃ sattanikāyānaṃ sādhāraṇaniddeso. Sattanikāyeti sādhāraṇaniddesena niddiṭṭhassa sarūpanidassanaṃ. Jarā jīraṇatātiādīsu pana jarāti sabhāvaniddeso. Jīraṇatāti ākāraniddeso. Khaṇḍiccantiādayo tayo kālātikkame kiccaniddesā, pacchimā dve pakatiniddesā. Ayañhi jarāti iminā padena sabhāvato dīpitā, tenassāyaṃ sabhāvaniddeso[M 2.0011]. Jīraṇatāti iminā ākārato, tenassāyaṃ ākāraniddeso. Khaṇḍiccanti iminā kālātikkame dantanakhānaṃ khaṇḍitabhāvakaraṇakiccato. Pāliccanti iminā kesalomānaṃ palitabhāvakaraṇakiccato. Valittacatāti iminā maṃsaṃ [V 2.0011] milāpetvā tacavalibhāvakaraṇakiccato dīpitā. Tenassā ime khaṇḍiccantiādayo tayo kālātikkame kiccaniddesā. Tehi imesaṃ vikārānaṃ dassanavasena [P 2.0012] pākaṭībhūtā pākaṭajarā dassitā. Yatheva hi udakassa vā vātassa vā aggino vā tiṇarukkhādīnaṃ saṃbhaggapalibhaggatāya vā jhāmatāya vā gatamaggo pākaṭo hoti, na ca so gatamaggo tāneva udakādīni, evameva jarāya dantādīsu khaṇḍiccādivasena gatamaggo pākaṭo, cakkhuṃ ummīletvāpi gayhati na ca khaṇḍiccādīneva jarā. Na hi jarā cakkhuviññeyyā hoti.

2. Herein, this is the determination of the meaning of the detailed exposition of aging-and-death and so on. First, in the exposition of aging-and-death, "of such and such beings" (tesaṃ tesaṃ) should be understood as a brief, common designation for many beings. For if one were to speak all day, saying, "The aging of Devadatta, the aging of Somadatta," the beings would never be exhausted. But by these two terms, no being is left unincluded. Therefore it was said, "This is a brief, common designation for many beings." "In such and such" (tamhi tamhi) is a common designation for many groups of beings according to destiny and birth. "Groups of beings" (sattanikāye) is an illustration of the intrinsic nature of what is indicated by the common designation. Now, in "aging, decrepitude" (jarā jīraṇatā), and so on, "aging" (jarā) is a designation of intrinsic nature. "Decrepitude" (jīraṇatā) is a designation of mode. The three terms beginning with "brokenness of teeth" (khaṇḍiccaṃ) are designations of function in the passing of time. The last two are designations of nature. For this aging is shown by its intrinsic nature through the term "jarā"; therefore, this is its designation of intrinsic nature. Through "jīraṇatā," it is shown by its mode; therefore, this is its designation of mode. Through "khaṇḍiccaṃ," it is shown in the passing of time by the function of causing the state of brokenness in teeth and nails. Through "pāliccaṃ," by the function of causing the state of grayness in head-hair and body-hair. Through "valittacatā," it is shown by the function of withering the flesh and causing the state of wrinkledness in the skin. Therefore, these three beginning with "khaṇḍiccaṃ" are its designations of function in the passing of time. Through them, manifest aging, which has become manifest by seeing these alterations, is shown. For just as the path taken by water, wind, or fire is made manifest by the shattering and breaking of grass, trees, and so on, or by their being scorched, yet that path taken is not the water itself, etc.; even so, the path taken by aging is made manifest in the teeth, etc., by way of brokenness and so on. It is grasped even by opening the eye, yet brokenness and so on are not aging itself. For aging is not cognizable by the eye.

Āyuno saṃhāni indriyānaṃ paripākoti imehi pana padehi kālātikkameyeva abhibyattāya āyukkhaya-cakkhādiindriya-paripākasaññitāya pakatiyā dīpitā. Tenassime pacchimā dve pakatiniddesāti veditabbā. Tattha yasmā jaraṃ pattassa āyu hāyati, tasmā jarā “āyuno saṃhānī”ti phalūpacārena vuttā. Yasmā ca daharakāle suppasannāni sukhumampi attano visayaṃ sukheneva gaṇhanasamatthāni cakkhādīni indriyāni jaraṃ pattassa paripakkāni āluḷitāni avisadāni, oḷārikampi attano visayaṃ gahetuṃ asamatthāni honti, tasmā “indriyānaṃ paripāko”ti phalūpacāreneva vuttā.

But with these terms—"the diminishing of the life-span" and "the ripening of the faculties"—aging is shown by its nature, which is designated as the decay of the life-span and the ripening of the faculties such as the eye, and which becomes fully manifest only in the passing of time. Therefore, these last two should be known as designations of nature. Herein, because the life-span diminishes for one who has reached aging, aging is called "the diminishing of the life-span" by a figurative expression based on the result. And because the faculties such as the eye—which in youth are very clear and capable of easily grasping even a subtle object in their own range—become, for one who has reached aging, over-ripe, confused, unclear, and incapable of grasping even a coarse object in their own range, therefore it is called "the ripening of the faculties," also by a figurative expression based on the result.

Sā panāyaṃ evaṃ niddiṭṭhā sabbāpi jarā pākaṭā paṭicchannāti duvidhā hoti. Tattha dantādīsu khaṇḍādibhāvadassanato rūpadhammesu jarā pākaṭajarā nāma, arūpadhammesu pana jarā tādisassa vikārassa adassanato paṭicchannajarā nāma. Tattha yvāyaṃ khaṇḍādibhāvo dissati, so tādisānaṃ dantādīnaṃ suviññeyyattā vaṇṇoyeva, taṃ cakkhunā disvā manodvārena cintetvā “ime dantā jarāya pahaṭā”ti jaraṃ jānāti udakaṭṭhāne baddhāni gosīsādīni oloketvā heṭṭhā udakassa atthibhāvaṃ jānanaṃ viya. Puna [M 2.0012] avīci savīcīti evampi duvidhā hoti. Tattha maṇi-kanaka-rajata-pavāḷacandasūriyādīnaṃ viya mandadasakādīsu pāṇīnaṃ viya ca pupphaphalapallavādīsu ca apāṇīnaṃ viya antarantarā vaṇṇavisesādīnaṃ duviññeyyattā jarā avīcijarā nāma, nirantarajarāti attho. Tato aññesu pana yathāvuttesu antarantarā vaṇṇavisesādīnaṃ suviññeyyattā jarā savīcijarā nāmāti veditabbā.

Furthermore, all this aging, thus described, is of two kinds: manifest and concealed. Herein, the aging in material phenomena is called manifest aging, because of seeing the state of brokenness and so on in teeth and the like. But the aging in immaterial phenomena is called concealed aging, because such an alteration is not seen. Herein, this state of brokenness and so on that is seen is merely the visible form, due to the easy cognizability of such things as teeth. Having seen that with the eye and reflected on it through the mind-door, one knows aging, thinking: "These teeth have been afflicted by aging." This is like knowing the presence of water below by observing cow-skulls and so on tied at a watering place. Again, it is also of two kinds: uninterrupted and interrupted. Herein, aging is called uninterrupted aging because the distinctions of color and so on are difficult to cognize from interval to interval, as with gems, gold, silver, coral, the moon, the sun, and so on; and as with living beings in the slow decades and so on; and as with non-living things such as flowers, fruits, and shoots. The meaning is continuous aging. But in other cases, as mentioned, aging should be known as interrupted aging, because the distinctions of color and so on are easy to cognize from interval to interval.

Ito paraṃ tesaṃ tesantiādi vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Cuti cavanatātiādīsu pana cutīti cavanakavasena vuccati, ekacatupañcakkhandhasāmaññavacanametaṃ. Cavanatāti bhāvavacanena lakkhaṇanidassanaṃ[V 2.0012]. Bhedoti cutikkhandhānaṃ [P 2.0013] bhaṅguppattiparidīpanaṃ. Antaradhānanti ghaṭasseva bhinnassa bhinnānaṃ cutikkhandhānaṃ yena kenaci pariyāyena ṭhānābhāvaparidīpanaṃ. Maccu maraṇanti maccusaṅkhātaṃ maraṇaṃ, tena samucchedamaraṇādīni nisedheti. Kālo nāma antako, tassa kiriyā kālakiriyā. Evaṃ tena lokasammutiyā maraṇaṃ dīpeti.

Henceforth, the passage beginning with 'tesaṃ tesaṃ' should be understood in the way already stated. However, in the passage beginning with 'cuti cavanatā,' the term 'cuti' is spoken of by way of passing away; this is a term common to the aggregates of one, four, and five constituents. By the abstract noun 'cavanatā,' a characteristic is indicated. By 'bheda' is meant the clarification of the aggregates of passing away reaching the moment of dissolution. By 'antaradhāna' is meant the clarification of the absence of any standing place whatsoever for the destroyed aggregates of passing away, just as for a broken pot. 'Maccu maraṇa' is death designated as 'maccu'; by that term, the Blessed One negates annihilation-death and so on. 'Kāla' is the end; its action is 'kālakiriyā.' Thus, by that term, he explains death by way of worldly convention.

Idāni paramatthena dīpetuṃ khandhānaṃ bhedotiādimāha. Paramatthena hi khandhāyeva bhijjanti, na satto nāma koci marati. Khandhesu pana bhijjamānesu satto marati, bhinnesu matoti vohāro hoti. Ettha ca catupañcavokāravasena khandhānaṃ bhedo, ekavokāravasena kaḷevarassa nikkhepo. Catuvokāravasena ca khandhānaṃ bhedo, sesadvayavasena kaḷevarassa nikkhepo veditabbo. Kasmā? Bhavadvayepi rūpakāyasaṅkhātassa kaḷevarassa sabbhāvato. Atha vā yasmā cātumahārājikādīsu khandhā bhijjanteva, na kiñci nikkhipati, tasmā tesaṃ vasena khandhānaṃ bhedo, manussādīsu kaḷevarassa nikkhepo. Ettha ca kaḷevarassa nikkhepakāraṇato maraṇaṃ “kaḷevarassa nikkhepo”ti vuttanti evamattho daṭṭhabbo. Iti ayañca jarā idañca maraṇaṃ, idaṃ vuccati, bhikkhaveti idaṃ ubhayampi ekato katvā jarāmaraṇanti kathīyati.

Now, to explain death in the ultimate sense, the Blessed One spoke the words beginning with 'the breaking up of the aggregates.' For in the ultimate sense, it is only the aggregates that break up; no being whatsoever dies. But when the aggregates are breaking up, it is conventionally said 'a being dies'; and when they have broken up, the convention 'is dead' arises. And here, the breaking up of the aggregates should be understood by way of the four- and five-constituent existences, and the casting off of the corpse by way of the one-constituent existence. And the breaking up of the aggregates should be understood by way of the four-constituent existence, and the casting off of the corpse by way of the remaining two existences. Why? Because in both the one- and five-constituent existences, there is the actual existence of a corpse, which is called the physical body. Alternatively, because in the Cātumahārājika realm and so on, the aggregates just break up and nothing is cast off, therefore, in their case, the breaking up of the aggregates should be understood. And because among humans and so on, there is the casting off of a corpse, therefore, among them, the casting off of a corpse should be understood. And here, the meaning should be understood thus: death is called 'the casting off of the corpse'—this is said figuratively, because it is the cause for the casting off of the corpse. Thus, 'this is aging and this is death... this is called, bhikkhus'—these two, taken together as one, are spoken of as 'aging-and-death'.

Jātiniddese [M 2.0013] jāti sañjātītiādīsu jāyanaṭṭhena jāti, sā aparipuṇṇāyatanavasena yuttā. Sañjāyanaṭṭhena sañjāti, sā paripuṇṇāyatanavasena yuttā. Okkamanaṭṭhena okkanti, sā aṇḍajajalābujavasena yuttā. Te hi aṇḍakosañca vatthikosañca okkamantā pavisantā viya paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhanti. Abhinibbattanaṭṭhena abhinibbatti, sā saṃsedajaopapātikavasena yuttā. Te hi pākaṭāyeva hutvā nibbattanti. Ayaṃ tāva vohāradesanā.

In the exposition of birth, in the passage beginning with 'jāti sañjāti': 'jāti' is in the sense of being born; it is suitable by way of beings with incomplete sense bases. 'Sañjāti' is in the sense of being fully born; it is suitable by way of beings with complete sense bases. 'Okkanti' is in the sense of descending; it is suitable by way of egg-born and womb-born beings. For they, descending into the eggshell and the womb, take rebirth-linking as if entering. 'Abhinibbatti' is in the sense of clearly coming into being; it is suitable by way of moisture-born and spontaneously born beings. For they are born, having become clearly manifest. This, for now, is the conventional teaching.

Idāni paramatthadesanā hoti. Khandhāyeva hi paramatthato pātubhavanti, na satto. Tattha ca khandhānanti ekavokārabhave ekassa, catuvokārabhave catunnaṃ, pañcavokārabhave pañcannampi gahaṇaṃ veditabbaṃ. Pātubhāvoti uppatti. Āyatanānanti ettha tatra tatra uppajjamānāyatanavasena saṅgaho veditabbo. Paṭilābhoti santatiyaṃ pātubhāvoyeva. Pātubhavantāneva [P 2.0014] hi tāni paṭiladdhāni nāma honti. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, jātīti iminā padena vohārato paramatthato ca desitāya jātiyā nigamanaṃ karotīti.

Now there is the ultimate teaching. For indeed, in the ultimate sense, it is only the aggregates that become manifest, not a being. And there, by the term 'aggregates,' the taking of one in the one-constituent existence, of four in the four-constituent existence, and of five in the five-constituent existence should be understood. 'Manifestation' is arising. Here, in the term 'sense bases,' the inclusion should be understood by way of the sense bases that are arising in those respective existences. 'Acquisition' is just the manifestation in the continuity. For only when they are manifesting are those sense bases called 'acquired.' By this phrase, 'This is called, bhikkhus, birth,' the Blessed One draws a conclusion to the teaching on birth that was delivered both conventionally and ultimately.

Bhavaniddese [V 2.0013] kāmabhavoti kammabhavo ca upapattibhavo ca. Tattha kammabhavo nāma kāmabhavūpagakammameva. Tañhi tattha upapattibhavassa kāraṇattā “sukho buddhānaṃ uppādo (dha. pa. 194) dukkho pāpassa uccayo”tiādīni (dha. pa. 117) viya phalavohārena bhavoti vuttaṃ. Upapattibhavo nāma tena kammena nibbattaṃ upādiṇṇakkhandhapañcakaṃ. Tañhi tattha bhavatīti katvā bhavoti vuttaṃ. Sabbathāpi idaṃ kammañca upapattiñca ubhayampetamidha “kāmabhavo”ti vuttaṃ. Esa nayo rūpārūpabhavesūti.

In the exposition of becoming, 'sensual becoming' comprises both kamma-becoming and rebirth-becoming. Therein, kamma-becoming is precisely the kamma that leads to sensual existence. For since it is the cause of rebirth-becoming in that realm, it is called 'becoming' by the convention of its result, as in passages such as, 'Happy is the arising of the Buddhas, painful is the accumulation of evil.' Rebirth-becoming is the set of five aggregates produced by that kamma and grasped by clinging. For because it 'becomes' (bhavati) there, it is called 'becoming.' In every way, both this kamma and this rebirth, this pair, are here called 'sensual becoming.' This is the method in the form and formless becomings.

Upādānaniddese kāmupādānantiādīsu vatthukāmaṃ upādiyanti etena, sayaṃ vā taṃ upādiyatīti kāmupādānaṃ, kāmo ca so upādānañcāti kāmupādānaṃ. Upādānanti daḷhaggahaṇaṃ vuccati. Daḷhattho hi ettha upasaddo upāyāsaupakaṭṭhādīsu viya. Pañcakāmaguṇikarāgassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Ayamettha saṅkhepo. Vitthārato panetaṃ, “tattha katamaṃ kāmupādānaṃ? Yo kāmesu kāmacchando”ti (dha. sa. 1220; vibha. 938) vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ.

In the exposition of clinging, in the passage beginning with 'sensual clinging': it is called 'sensual clinging' (kāmupādāna) because by this, beings cling to objective sensual pleasures, or because it itself clings to them. Or, it is both sensual desire (kāma) and it is clinging (upādāna). 'Clinging' (upādāna) is said to be strong grasping. For here the prefix 'upa,' as in words like 'upāyāsa' and 'upakaṭṭha,' has the meaning of 'strong.' This is a designation for the lust that has the five strands of sensual pleasure as its object. This is the summary here. But in detail, it should be understood in the way stated: 'Herein, what is sensual clinging? It is the sensual desire for sensual pleasures...'

Tathā [M 2.0014] diṭṭhi ca sā upādānañcāti diṭṭhupādānaṃ. Atha vā diṭṭhiṃ upādiyati, upādiyanti vā etena diṭṭhinti diṭṭhupādānaṃ. Upādiyati hi purimadiṭṭhiṃ uttaradiṭṭhi, upādiyanti ca tāya diṭṭhiṃ. Yathāha – “sassato attā ca loko ca idameva saccaṃ moghamañña”ntiādi (ma. ni. 3.27). Sīlabbatupādānaattavādupādānavajjassa sabbadiṭṭhigatassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthārato panetaṃ, “tattha katamaṃ diṭṭhupādānaṃ? Natthi dinna”nti (dha. sa. 1221) vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ.

Similarly, it is both a view and it is clinging, thus it is 'view-clinging.' Alternatively, it is called 'view-clinging' because it clings to a view, or because by means of it, beings cling to a view. For a later view clings to a former view, and by means of that later view, beings cling to the former view. As was said: 'The self and the world are eternal; this alone is true, all else is false,' and so on. This is a designation for all wrong views, with the exception of the clinging to rites and observances and the clinging to a doctrine of self. This is the summary here; but in detail, it should be understood in the way stated: 'Herein, what is view-clinging? "There is nothing given..."'

Tathā sīlabbatamupādiyanti etena, sayaṃ vā taṃ upādiyati, sīlabbatañca [P 2.0015] taṃ upādānañcāti vā sīlabbatupādānaṃ. Gosīlagovatādīni hi “evaṃ suddhī”ti (dha. sa. 1222; vibha. 938) abhinivesato sayameva upādānānīti. Ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthārato panetaṃ, “tattha katamaṃ sīlabbatupādānaṃ? Ito bahiddhā samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ sīlena suddhī”ti vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ.

Similarly, it is 'clinging to rites and observances' because by this, one clings to rites and observances; or because it itself clings to that; or because it is both rites and observances and it is clinging. For, due to the adherence 'Purity comes thus' to practices such as the cow-practice and the cow-vow, these things themselves are clingings. This is the summary here; but in detail, it should be understood in the way stated: 'Herein, what is clinging to rites and observances? It is the view of recluses and brahmins outside of this dispensation that purity comes through rites...'

Idāni vadanti etenāti vādo, upādiyanti etenāti upādānaṃ, kiṃ vadanti upādiyanti vā? Attānaṃ. Attano vādupādānaṃ attavādupādānaṃ. Attavādamattameva vā attāti [V 2.0014] upādiyanti etenāti attavādupādānaṃ. Vīsativatthukāya sakkāyadiṭṭhiyā etaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthārato panetaṃ, “tattha katamaṃ attavādupādānaṃ? Idha assutavā puthujjano ariyānaṃ adassāvī”ti vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ.

Now, 'they speak by this,' thus it is 'doctrine' (vādo); 'they cling by this,' thus it is 'clinging' (upādānaṃ). What do they speak of or cling to? The self. The doctrine and clinging concerning the self is 'doctrine-clinging to self' (attavādupādānaṃ). Or, 'by this they cling to the mere doctrine of self as "self",' thus it is 'doctrine-clinging to self.' This is a designation for the personality-view with its twenty bases. This is the summary here. But in detail, it should be understood by the method spoken of thus: 'Therein, what is doctrine-clinging to self? Here, an uninstructed worldling, who has not seen the noble ones...'

Taṇhāniddese rūpataṇhā…pe… dhammataṇhāti etaṃ cakkhudvārādīsu javanavīthiyā pavattāya taṇhāya “seṭṭhiputto brāhmaṇaputto”ti evamādīsu pitito nāmaṃ viya pitisadisārammaṇato nāmaṃ. Ettha ca rūpārammaṇā taṇhā, rūpe taṇhāti rūpataṇhā. Sā kāmarāgabhāvena rūpaṃ assādentī pavattamānā kāmataṇhā, sassatadiṭṭhisahagatarāgabhāvena “rūpaṃ niccaṃ dhuvaṃ sassata”nti evaṃ assādentī pavattamānā bhavataṇhā, ucchedadiṭṭhisahagatarāgabhāvena “rūpaṃ ucchijjati vinassati pecca na bhavatī”ti evaṃ assādentī pavattamānā vibhavataṇhāti rūpataṇhā evaṃ tividhā hoti. Yathā ca rūpataṇhā, tathā saddataṇhādayopīti evaṃ tāni aṭṭhārasa taṇhāvicaritāni honti. Tāni ajjhattarūpādīsu aṭṭhārasa, bahiddhārūpādīsu aṭṭhārasāti chattiṃsa. Iti atītāni chattiṃsa, anāgatāni chattiṃsa, paccuppannāni [M 2.0015] chattiṃsāti evaṃ aṭṭhasataṃ taṇhāvicaritāni honti. “Ajjhattikassa upādāya asmīti hoti, itthasmīti hotī”ti (vibha. 973) vā evamādīni ajjhattikarūpādinissitāni aṭṭhārasa, “bāhirassa upādāya iminā asmīti hoti, iminā itthasmīti hotī”ti (vibha. 975) vā evamādīni bāhirarūpādinissitāni aṭṭhārasāti [P 2.0016] chattiṃsa, iti atītāni chattiṃsa, anāgatāni chattiṃsa, paccuppannāni chattiṃsāti evampi aṭṭhasataṃ taṇhāvicaritāni honti. Puna saṅgahe kariyamāne rūpādīsu ārammaṇesu chaḷeva taṇhākāyā tissoyeva kāmataṇhādayo hontīti. Evaṃ –

In the exposition of craving, for the craving that occurs by way of the impulsion-process in the eye-door and so on, this name 'craving for forms... (etc.)... craving for mental phenomena' was shown by the Blessed One by way of an object similar to the father, just as in such cases as 'son of a merchant' or 'son of a brahmin,' a name is given based on the father. And here, craving that has form as its object, that is, 'craving in regard to form,' is 'craving for form.' That craving, occurring while savoring form with the nature of sensual lust, is sensual craving. Occurring while savoring form with the nature of lust accompanied by the view of eternalism, thinking, 'Form is permanent, stable, eternal,' it is craving for becoming. Occurring while savoring form with the nature of lust accompanied by the view of annihilationism, thinking, 'Form is annihilated, it perishes, it does not exist after death,' it is craving for non-becoming. Thus, craving for form is threefold. And just as craving for form is threefold, so too are craving for sounds and the rest. In this way, there are eighteen courses of craving. Those are eighteen in regard to internal forms, etc., and eighteen in regard to external forms, etc., making thirty-six. Thus, there are thirty-six past, thirty-six future, and thirty-six present, so in this way there are one hundred and eight courses of craving. Or, 'On account of the internal, there is "I am," there is "I am thus"' and so on—these are the eighteen dependent on internal forms, etc. 'On account of the external, there is "by this I am," there is "by this I am thus"' and so on—these are the eighteen dependent on external forms, etc., making thirty-six. Thus, there are thirty-six past, thirty-six future, and thirty-six present; in this way also there are one hundred and eight courses of craving. Again, when a summary is made, in regard to objects such as forms, there are just six bodies of craving, and just the three, sensual craving and so on. Thus—

“Niddesatthena niddesa, vitthārā vitthārassa ca;

Puna saṅgahato taṇhā, viññātabbā vibhāvinā”ti.

An exposition is for the purpose of exposition, and there are expansions because expansion is also possible; again, craving should be understood in brief by the wise one.

Vedanāniddese vedanākāyāti vedanāsamūhā. Cakkhusamphassajā vedanā…pe… manosamphassajāvedanāti etaṃ “cakkhusamphassajāvedanā atthi kusalā, atthi akusalā, atthi abyākatā”ti evaṃ vibhaṅge (vibha. 34) āgatattā cakkhudvārādīsu pavattānaṃ kusalākusalābyākatavedanānaṃ “sāriputto mantāṇiputto”ti evamādīsu mātito nāmaṃ viya mātisadisato [V 2.0015] vatthuto nāmaṃ. Vacanattho panettha – cakkhusamphassahetu jātā vedanā cakkhusamphassajā vedanāti. Eseva nayo sabbattha. Ayaṃ tāvettha sabbasaṅgāhikā kathā. Vipākavasena pana cakkhudvāre dve cakkhuviññāṇāni, dve manodhātuyo, tisso manoviññāṇadhātuyoti etāhi sampayuttavasena vedanā veditabbā. Eseva nayo sotadvārādīsu. Manodvāre manoviññāṇadhātusampayuttāva.

In the exposition of feeling, 'body of feeling' means collections of feeling. Regarding 'feeling born of eye-contact... (etc.)... feeling born of mind-contact,' because it is stated in the Vibhaṅga thus, 'There is feeling born of eye-contact that is wholesome, there is that which is unwholesome, there is that which is indeterminate,' this designation for the wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate feelings that occur in the eye-door and so on is a name derived from the basis which is like a mother, just as in such cases as 'Sāriputta' or 'Mantāṇiputta,' a name is derived from the mother. Herein, the meaning of the word is: 'feeling born because of eye-contact as cause' is 'feeling born of eye-contact.' This is the method everywhere. This, for a start, is the all-encompassing discourse here. But by way of resultants, feeling should be understood by way of association with these: in the eye-door, two eye-consciousnesses, two mind-elements, and three mind-consciousness-elements. This is the method in the ear-door and so on. In the mind-door, it is only that associated with the mind-consciousness-element.

Phassaniddese cakkhusamphassoti cakkhumhi samphasso. Esa nayo sabbattha. Cakkhusamphasso…pe… kāyasamphassoti ettāvatā ca kusalākusalavipākā pañcavatthukā dasa phassā vuttā honti. Manosamphassoti iminā sesabāvīsatilokiyavipākamanasampayuttā phassā.

In the exposition of contact, 'eye-contact' is contact in the eye. This is the method everywhere. By 'eye-contact... (etc.)... body-contact'—by this much, ten contacts that are wholesome and unwholesome resultants and have the five physical bases as their support have been spoken of. By this term 'mind-contact,' the remaining twenty-two contacts associated with mundane resultant mind-consciousness are spoken of.

Saḷāyatananiddese cakkhāyatanantiādīsu yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ visuddhimagge khandhaniddese ceva āyatananiddese ca vuttameva.

In the exposition of the six sense bases, whatever should be said regarding 'eye-base' and so on, that has already been said in the Visuddhimagga in the exposition of the aggregates and in the exposition of the sense bases.

Nāmarūpaniddese [M 2.0016] namanalakkhaṇaṃ nāmaṃ. Ruppanalakkhaṇaṃ rūpaṃ. Vibhajane panassa vedanāti vedanākkhandho, saññāti saññākkhandho, cetanā phasso manasikāroti saṅkhārakkhandho veditabbo. Kāmañca aññepi saṅkhārakkhandhasaṅgahitā dhammā santi, ime pana tayo sabbadubbalesupi cittesu santi, tasmā etesaṃyeva [P 2.0017] vasenettha saṅkhārakkhandho dassito. Cattāro ca mahābhūtāti ettha cattāroti gaṇanaparicchedo. Mahābhūtāti pathavīāpatejavāyānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Yena pana kāraṇena tāni mahābhūtānīti vuccanti, yo cettha añño vinicchayanayo, so sabbo visuddhimagge rūpakkhandhaniddese vutto. Catunnañca mahābhūtānaṃ upādāyāti ettha pana catunnanti upayogatthe sāmivacanaṃ, cattāri mahābhūtānīti vuttaṃ hoti. Upādāyāti upādiyitvā, gahetvāti attho. Nissāyātipi eke. “Vattamāna”nti ayañcettha pāṭhaseso. Samūhatthe vā etaṃ sāmivacanaṃ, catunnaṃ mahābhūtānaṃ samūhaṃ upādāya vattamānaṃ rūpanti ettha attho veditabbo. Evaṃ sabbathāpi yāni ca cattāri pathavīādīni mahābhūtāni, yañca catunnaṃ mahābhūtānaṃ upādāya vattamānaṃ cakkhāyatanādibhedena abhidhammapāḷiyameva vuttaṃ tevīsatividhaṃ rūpaṃ, taṃ sabbampi rūpanti veditabbaṃ.

In the exposition of name-and-form, 'name' has the characteristic of bending towards an object. 'Form' has the characteristic of being afflicted. In its analysis, by 'feeling' the feeling aggregate is to be understood; by 'perception,' the perception aggregate; and by 'volition, contact, and attention,' the formations aggregate is to be understood. Although there are indeed other phenomena included in the formations aggregate, these three are present even in the very weakest minds; therefore, the formations aggregate is shown here by means of these alone. In 'and the four great elements,' 'four' is a delimitation of the count. 'Great elements' is a designation for earth, water, fire, and air. As for the reason why they are called 'great elements,' and whatever other method of determination there is here, all that has been stated by me in the Visuddhimagga in the exposition of the form aggregate. And in 'dependent on the four great elements,' 'of the four' is a genitive case word in the sense of the accusative; it means 'the four great elements.' 'Dependent on' should be understood to mean 'having clung firmly to,' 'having grasped.' Some also say it means 'relying on.' And here, 'existing' is a remainder of the text. Or, this is a genitive case word in the sense of a collection; the meaning here should be understood as 'form that exists dependent on the collection of the four great elements.' Thus, in every way, both the four great elements which are earth, etc., and the twenty-three kinds of form—spoken of only in the Abhidhamma Piṭaka with the classification of eye-base, etc.—that exist dependent on the four great elements, all that should be understood as 'form.'

Viññāṇaniddese [V 2.0016] cakkhuviññāṇanti cakkhumhi viññāṇaṃ, cakkhuto vā jātaṃ viññāṇanti cakkhuviññāṇaṃ. Evaṃ sotaghānajivhākāyaviññāṇāni. Itaraṃ pana manoyeva viññāṇanti manoviññāṇaṃ. Dvipañcaviññāṇavajjitatebhūmakavipākacittassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ.

In the exposition of consciousness, 'eye-consciousness' is consciousness in the eye-base; or, consciousness born from the eye-base is 'eye-consciousness'. In the same way are ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, and body-consciousness. But the other, 'mind-consciousness', is the mind itself as consciousness; this is a designation for the resultant consciousness of the three planes, excluding the two sets of five consciousnesses.

Saṅkhāraniddese abhisaṅkharaṇalakkhaṇo saṅkhāro. Vibhajane panassa kāyasaṅkhāroti kāyato pavattasaṅkhāro. Kāyadvāre copanavasena pavattānaṃ kāmāvacarakusalato aṭṭhannaṃ, akusalato dvādasannanti vīsatiyā kāyasañcetanānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Vacīsaṅkhāroti vacanato pavattasaṅkhāro, vacīdvāre vacanabhedavasena pavattānaṃ vīsatiyā eva vacīsañcetanānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Cittasaṅkhāroti cittato pavattasaṅkhāro, kāyavacīdvāre copanaṃ akatvā raho nisīditvā cintentassa pavattānaṃ lokiyakusalākusalavasena ekūnatiṃsamanosañcetanānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ.

In the exposition of formations, a formation has the characteristic of constructing. But in its analysis, 'bodily formation' is a formation that proceeds from the body. This is a designation for the twenty bodily volitions that arise in the body-door by way of causing agitation, namely, eight from sense-sphere wholesome states and twelve from unwholesome states. 'Verbal formation' is a formation that proceeds from speech; this is a designation for those very twenty verbal volitions that arise in the speech-door by way of causing verbal intimation. 'Mental formation' is a formation that proceeds from the mind; this is a designation for the twenty-nine mental volitions that arise, by way of mundane wholesome and unwholesome states, for one who is thinking while sitting in seclusion, without causing agitation in the body-door and speech-door.

Avijjāniddese [M 2.0017] dukkhe aññāṇanti dukkhasacce aññāṇaṃ, mohassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Esa nayo dukkhasamudaye aññāṇantiādīsu. Tattha catūhi kāraṇehi dukkhe aññāṇaṃ veditabbaṃ antogadhato vatthuto ārammaṇato paṭicchādanato ca. Tathā [P 2.0018] hi taṃ dukkhasaccapariyāpannattā dukkhe antogadhaṃ, dukkhasaccañcassa nissayapaccayabhāvena vatthu, ārammaṇapaccayabhāvena ārammaṇaṃ, dukkhasaccaṃ etaṃ paṭicchādeti tassa yāthāvalakkhaṇapaṭivedhanivāraṇena ñāṇappavattiyā cettha appadānena.

In the exposition of ignorance, 'non-knowledge in regard to suffering' is non-knowledge in regard to the truth of suffering; this is a designation for delusion. This same method applies to 'non-knowledge in regard to the origin of suffering', and so on. There, non-knowledge in regard to suffering should be understood by four reasons: by being included within, by way of basis, by way of object, and by way of concealing. Indeed, because it is included in the truth of suffering, it is included within suffering. And the truth of suffering is its basis by being a support condition, and its object by being an object condition. This non-knowledge conceals the truth of suffering by preventing the penetration of its true characteristic and by not allowing the arising of knowledge in regard to it.

Dukkhasamudaye aññāṇaṃ tīhi kāraṇehi veditabbaṃ vatthuto ārammaṇato paṭicchādanato ca. Nirodhe paṭipadāya ca aññāṇaṃ ekeneva kāraṇena veditabbaṃ paṭicchādanato. Nirodhapaṭipadānañhi paṭicchādakameva aññāṇaṃ tesaṃ yāthāvalakkhaṇapaṭivedhanivāraṇena tesu ca ñāṇappavattiyā appadānena. Na pana taṃ tattha antogadhaṃ tasmiṃ saccadvaye apariyāpannattā, na tassa taṃ saccadvayaṃ vatthu asahajātattā, nārammaṇaṃ, tadārabbha appavattanato. Pacchimañhi saccadvayaṃ gambhīrattā duddasaṃ, na tattha andhabhūtaṃ aññāṇaṃ pavattati. Purimaṃ pana vacanīyattena sabhāvalakkhaṇassa duddasattā gambhīraṃ, tattha vipallāsagāhavasena pavattati.

Non-knowledge in regard to the origin of suffering should be understood by three reasons: by way of basis, by way of object, and by way of concealing. And non-knowledge in regard to cessation and the path should be understood by one reason only: by way of concealing. For non-knowledge only conceals cessation and the path by preventing the penetration of their true characteristic and by not allowing the arising of knowledge in regard to them. But it is not included within them, because it is not comprised in that pair of truths. That pair of truths is not its basis, because they are not co-arisen with it; nor are they its object, because it does not arise taking them as its object. For the latter pair of truths, being profound, are hard to see; non-knowledge, being blind, does not operate there. But the former pair of truths is profound because its own characteristic is hard to see, though it is describable; and there, non-knowledge operates by way of grasping with perversion.

Apica “dukkhe”ti ettāvatā saṅgahato vatthuto ārammaṇato kiccato ca avijjā dīpitā. “Dukkhasamudaye”ti ettāvatā vatthuto ārammaṇato kiccato ca. “Dukkhanirodhe dukkhanirodhagāminiyā [V 2.0017] paṭipadāyā”ti ettāvatā kiccato. Avisesato pana “aññāṇa”nti etena sabhāvato niddiṭṭhāti ñātabbā.

Furthermore, by the words 'in suffering,' ignorance is shown by way of inclusion, basis, object, and function. By the words 'in the origin of suffering,' it is shown by way of basis, object, and function. By the words 'in the cessation of suffering' and 'in the path leading to the cessation of suffering,' it is shown by way of function. But generally, by this word 'non-knowledge,' it is indicated by way of its own nature. Thus it should be known.

Iti kho, bhikkhaveti evaṃ kho, bhikkhave. Nirodho hotīti anuppādo hoti. Apicettha sabbeheva tehi nirodhapadehi nibbānaṃ desitaṃ. Nibbānañhi āgamma te te dhammā nirujjhanti, tasmā taṃ tesaṃ tesaṃ nirodhoti vuccati. Iti bhagavā imasmiṃ sutte dvādasahi padehi vaṭṭavivaṭṭaṃ desento arahattanikūṭeneva desanaṃ niṭṭhapesi. Desanāpariyosāne vuttanayeneva pañcasatā bhikkhū arahatte patiṭṭhahiṃsūti.

Thus indeed, monks, 'there is cessation' means there is non-arising. Furthermore, here, by all those terms for cessation, Nibbāna is taught. For, having reached Nibbāna, those various states cease; therefore, it is called their cessation. Thus the Blessed One, while teaching in this discourse the round of existence and the unbinding from the round with twelve terms, concluded the teaching with the very peak of Arahantship. At the conclusion of the teaching, by the very method taught, five hundred monks were established in Arahantship.

Vibhaṅgasuttaṃ dutiyaṃ.

The Discourse on Analysis, the second.

3. Paṭipadāsuttavaṇṇanā

3. The Explanation of the Discourse on the Path.

3. Tatiye [M 2.0018][P 2.0019] micchāpaṭipadanti ayaṃ tāva aniyyānikapaṭipadā. Nanu ca avijjāpaccayā puññābhisaṅkhāropi atthi āneñjābhisaṅkhāropi, so kathaṃ micchāpaṭipadā hotīti. Vaṭṭasīsattā. Yañhi kiñci bhavattayasaṅkhātaṃ vaṭṭaṃ patthetvā pavattitaṃ, antamaso pañcābhiññā aṭṭha vā pana samāpattiyo, sabbaṃ taṃ vaṭṭapakkhiyaṃ vaṭṭasīsanti vaṭṭasīsattā micchāpaṭipadāva hoti. Yaṃ pana kiñci vivaṭṭaṃ nibbānaṃ patthetvā pavattitaṃ, antamaso uḷuṅkayāgumattadānampi paṇṇamuṭṭhidānamattampi, sabbaṃ taṃ vivaṭṭapakkhiyaṃ vivaṭṭanissitaṃ, vivaṭṭapakkhikattā sammāpaṭipadāva hoti. Appamattakampi hi paṇṇamuṭṭhimattadānakusalaṃ vā hotu mahantaṃ velāmadānādikusalaṃ vā, sace vaṭṭasampattiṃ patthetvā vaṭṭanissitavasena micchā ṭhapitaṃ hoti, vaṭṭameva āharituṃ sakkoti, no vivaṭṭaṃ. “Idaṃ me dānaṃ āsavakkhayāvahaṃ hotū”ti evaṃ pana vivaṭṭaṃ patthentena vivaṭṭavasena sammā ṭhapitaṃ arahattampi paccekabodhiñāṇampi sabbaññutaññāṇampi dātuṃ sakkotiyeva, na arahattaṃ appatvā pariyosānaṃ gacchati. Iti anulomavasena micchāpaṭipadā, paṭilomavasena sammāpaṭipadā desitāti veditabbā. Nanu cettha paṭipadā pucchitā, nibbānaṃ bhājitaṃ, niyyātanepi paṭipadāva niyyātitā. Na ca nibbānassa paṭipadāti nāmaṃ, savipassanānaṃ pana catunnaṃ maggānametaṃ nāmaṃ, tasmā pucchāniyyātanehi padabhājanaṃ na sametīti. No na sameti, kasmā? Phalena paṭipadāya dassitattā. Phalena hettha paṭipadā dassitā. “Avijjāya tveva asesavirāganirodhā saṅkhāranirodho”ti [V 2.0018] etaṃ nirodhasaṅkhātaṃ nibbānaṃ yassā paṭipadāya phalaṃ, ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, sammāpaṭipadāti ayamettha attho. Imasmiñca atthe asesavirāganirodhāti ettha virāgo nirodhasseva vevacanaṃ, asesavirāgā asesanirodhāti ayañhettha adhippāyo. Yena vā virāgasaṅkhātena maggena asesanirodho hoti, taṃ dassetuṃ etaṃ padabhājanaṃ vuttaṃ. Evañhi sati sānubhāvā paṭipadā vibhattā hoti. Iti imasmimpi sutte vaṭṭavivaṭṭameva kathitanti. Tatiyaṃ.

3. In the third discourse, regarding the wrong practice: this, first of all, is the practice that does not lead to liberation. Is it not so that conditioned by ignorance, there are meritorious formations and also imperturbable formations? How then can that be a wrong practice? Because it is the head of the cycle of rebirth. Indeed, whatever is brought about by aspiring to the cycle of rebirth, which is described as the three realms of existence—even to the extent of the five higher knowledges or the eight attainments—all of that, being on the side of the cycle and being the head of the cycle, is only the wrong practice because it is the head of the cycle. But whatever is brought about by aspiring to that which is free from the cycle, Nibbāna—even to the extent of a gift of a ladleful of gruel or a gift of a handful of greens—all of that, being on the side of that which is free from the cycle and dependent on it, is only the right practice because it is on the side of that which is free from the cycle.
