Indeed, be it a minor wholesome act, such as the gift of a handful of greens, or a great one, such as the gift of Velāma, if it is wrongly established by aspiring for worldly success within the cycle and by means of depending on the cycle, it is able only to bring about the cycle, not that which is free from it. But if it is rightly established by one aspiring for that which is free from the cycle, by means of that which is free from the cycle, with the thought, 'May this gift of mine bring about the destruction of the taints,' it is indeed able to bestow the fruit of Arahantship, the knowledge of a Paccekabuddha, and the knowledge of omniscience; it does not reach its conclusion without attaining the fruit of Arahantship. Thus, it should be understood that the wrong practice is taught by way of the forward order, and the right practice by way of the reverse order. But is it not so that herein the practice was asked about, Nibbāna was analyzed, and in the conclusion, the practice itself was concluded? And 'practice' is not a name for Nibbāna; rather, it is a name for the four paths together with insight. Therefore, the analysis of terms does not accord with the question and the conclusion. It is not that it does not accord. Why? Because the practice has been shown by way of its fruit. Herein, the practice has been shown by way of its fruit. 'With the complete fading away and cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of formations'—this Nibbāna, called cessation, is the fruit of a certain practice. 'This, monks, is called the right practice'—this is the meaning here. And in this sense, in the phrase 'complete fading away and cessation,' 'fading away' (virāga) is a synonym for 'cessation' (nirodha) itself; 'from complete fading away' means 'from complete cessation'—this is the intention here. Alternatively, this analysis of terms was spoken to show that path, called 'dispassion,' by which complete cessation occurs. For when this is so, the practice is analyzed as being efficacious. Thus, in this discourse also, only the cycle and that which is free from the cycle have been discussed. The third.

4. Vipassīsuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Vipassī Sutta

4. Catutthe [M 2.0019] vipassissāti tassa kira bodhisattassa yathā lokiyamanussānaṃ kiñcideva passantānaṃ parittakammābhinibbattassa kammajapasādassa dubbalattā akkhīni vipphandanti[P 2.0020], na evaṃ vipphandiṃsu. Balavakammanibbattassa pana kammajapasādassa balavattā avipphandantehi animisehi eva akkhīhi passi seyyathāpi devā tāvatiṃsā. Tena vuttaṃ – “animisanto kumāro pekkhatīti kho, bhikkhave, vipassissa kumārassa ‘vipassī vipassī’tveva samaññā udapādī”ti (dī. ni. 2.40). Ayañhettha adhippāyo – antarantarā nimisajanitandhakāravirahena visuddhaṃ passati, vivaṭehi vā akkhīhi passatīti vipassī. Ettha ca kiñcāpi pacchimabhavikānaṃ sabbabodhisattānaṃ balavakammanibbattassa kammajapasādassa balavattā akkhīni na vipphandanti, so pana bodhisatto eteneva nāmaṃ labhi.

4. In the fourth discourse, regarding Vipassī: It is said that the eyes of that Bodhisatta did not flicker as do those of ordinary worldly people when they see something, due to the weakness of the eye-sensitivity produced by karma of little power. Rather, due to the strength of the eye-sensitivity produced by powerful karma, he saw with unwavering, unblinking eyes, just like the Tāvatiṃsa devas. Therefore it was said: 'The prince gazes without blinking. It is for this reason, monks, that for Prince Vipassī the designation “Vipassī, Vipassī” arose.' This is the intention here: because of the absence of darkness produced by intermittent blinking, he sees clearly. Or, he sees with open eyes; therefore, he is Vipassī. And here, although the eyes of all Bodhisattas in their final existence do not flicker due to the strength of the eye-sensitivity produced by powerful karma, that Bodhisatta, however, obtained the name from this very reason.

Apica viceyya viceyya passatīti vipassī, vicinitvā vicinitvā passatīti attho. Ekadivasaṃ kira vinicchayaṭṭhāne nisīditvā atthe anusāsantassa rañño alaṅkatapaṭiyattaṃ mahāpurisaṃ āharitvā aṅke ṭhapayiṃsu. Tassa taṃ aṅke katvā palāḷayamānasseva amaccā sāmikaṃ assāmikaṃ akaṃsu. Bodhisatto anattamanasaddaṃ nicchāresi. Rājā “kimetaṃ upadhārethā”ti āha. Upadhārayamānā aññaṃ adisvā “aṭṭassa dubbinicchitattā evaṃ kataṃ bhavissatī”ti puna sāmikameva sāmikaṃ katvā “ñatvā nu kho kumāro evaṃ karotī”ti? Vīmaṃsantā puna sāmikaṃ assāmikamakaṃsu. Puna bodhisatto tatheva saddaṃ nicchāresi. Atha rājā “jānāti mahāpuriso”ti tato paṭṭhāya appamatto ahosi. Tena vuttaṃ “viceyya viceyya kumāro atthe panāyati ñāyenāti kho, bhikkhave, vipassissa kumārassa bhiyyosomattāya ‘vipassī vipassī’tveva samaññā udapādī”ti (dī. ni. 2.41).

4. Furthermore, 'Vipassī' is one who sees after having investigated again and again; the meaning is one who sees after having scrutinized again and again. It is said that one day, while the king was seated in the hall of justice instructing on matters of state, they brought the Great Being, adorned and prepared, and placed him on his lap. While the king, having placed him on his lap, was delighting in him, the ministers made a rightful owner into a non-owner. The Bodhisatta uttered a sound of displeasure. The king said, 'What is this? Investigate it!' Investigating, and seeing no other reason, they thought, 'This must have been done because the case was badly decided,' and so they again made the rightful owner the owner. Wondering, 'Does the prince indeed know and act thus?' and wishing to test this, they again made the owner a non-owner. Again, the Bodhisatta uttered a sound of displeasure in the very same way. Then the king said, 'The Great Being knows!' From then on, he became heedful. Therefore it was said: 'The prince, having investigated again and again, sees the matter. It is for this very reason, monks, and all the more, that for Prince Vipassī the designation “Vipassī, Vipassī” arose.'

Bhagavatoti [V 2.0019] bhāgyasampannassa. Arahatoti rāgādiarīnaṃ hatattā, saṃsāracakkassa vā arānaṃ hatattā, paccayānaṃ vā arahattā arahāti evaṃ guṇato uppannanāmadheyyassa. Sammāsambuddhassāti sammā nayena hetunā sāmaṃ [P 2.0021] paccattapurisakārena cattāri saccāni buddhassa. Pubbeva sambodhāti [M 2.0020] sambodho vuccati catūsu maggesu ñāṇaṃ, tato pubbeva. Bodhisattasseva satoti ettha bodhīti ñāṇaṃ, bodhimā satto bodhisatto, ñāṇavā paññavā paṇḍitoti attho. Purimabuddhānañhi pādamūle abhinīhārato paṭṭhāya paṇḍitova so satto, na andhabāloti bodhisatto. Yathā vā udakato uggantvā ṭhitaṃ paripākagataṃ padumaṃ sūriyarasmisamphassena avassaṃ bujjhissatīti bujjhanakapadumanti vuccati, evaṃ buddhānaṃ santike byākaraṇassa laddhattā avassaṃ anantarāyena pāramiyo pūretvā bujjhissatīti bujjhanakasattotipi bodhisatto. Yā ca esā catumaggañāṇasaṅkhātā bodhi, taṃ patthayamāno pavattatīti bodhiyaṃ satto āsattotipi bodhisatto. Evaṃ guṇato uppannanāmavasena bodhisattasseva sato. Kicchanti dukkhaṃ. Āpannoti anuppatto. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – aho ayaṃ sattaloko dukkhaṃ anuppattoti. Cavati ca upapajjati cāti idaṃ aparāparaṃ cutipaṭisandhivasena vuttaṃ. Nissaraṇanti nibbānaṃ. Tañhi jarāmaraṇadukkhato nissaṭattā tassa nissaraṇanti vuccati. Kudāssu nāmāti katarasmiṃ nu kho kāle.

The Blessed One (Bhagavā) is one endowed with the six glories. The term 'Arahant' refers to one who has slain the enemies of passion and so forth; or who has destroyed the spokes of the wheel of saṃsāra; or who is worthy to receive the four requisites—thus, it is a name that has arisen from qualities. 'Sammāsambuddha' means one who has understood the four truths correctly, by the right method, by himself, through his own effort. 'Before enlightenment' (pubbeva sambodhā): 'Enlightenment' (sambodha) is said to be the knowledge in the four noble paths; thus, 'before that.' In 'of one who was indeed a Bodhisatta' (bodhisattasseva sato), 'bodhi' here means the knowledge of the Arahant path and omniscience. A being who has bodhi is a Bodhisatta; the meaning is one endowed with knowledge, wisdom, and sagacity. For from the time of making the aspiration at the feet of previous Buddhas, that being was wise, not a blind fool; hence, 'Bodhisatta.' Or, just as a lotus bud that has risen from the water and reached maturity will surely blossom upon contact with the sun’s rays and is thus called a 'blossoming lotus,' so too, because he has received the prediction in the presence of the Buddhas, he will surely awaken after fulfilling the perfections without obstacle, and is thus also called a 'being who will awaken'; hence, 'Bodhisatta.' And there is this bodhi called the knowledge of the four paths; because he fares on while aspiring for it, he is a being attached to bodhi; hence, 'Bodhisatta.' Thus, this is of one who is indeed a Bodhisatta, by way of a name that has arisen from qualities. 'Hardship' (kicchaṃ) means suffering. 'Has fallen into' (āpanno) means has reached. This is what is said: 'Oh, this world of beings has reached suffering!' 'Passes away and is reborn'—this is said by way of successive dying and taking rebirth. 'Escape' (nissaraṇaṃ) means Nibbāna. For because it has escaped from the suffering of aging and death, it is called the escape from that. 'When indeed' (kudāssu nāma) means 'at what time indeed?'

Yoniso manasikārāti upāyamanasikārena pathamanasikārena. Ahu paññāya abhisamayoti paññāya saddhiṃ jarāmaraṇakāraṇassa abhisamayo samavāyo samāyogo ahosi, “jātipaccayā jarāmaraṇa”nti idaṃ tena diṭṭhanti attho. Atha vā yoniso manasikārā ahu paññāyāti yoniso manasikārena ca paññāya ca abhisamayo ahu. “Jātiyā kho sati jarāmaraṇa”nti, evaṃ jarāmaraṇakāraṇassa paṭivedho ahosīti attho. Esa nayo sabbattha.

‘Wise attention’ (yoniso manasikārā) means attention to the method, attention to the cause. ‘There was a breakthrough to realization through wisdom’ (ahu paññāya abhisamayo): together with wisdom, there was a breakthrough to, a conjunction with, and a union with the cause of aging and death; the meaning is that this was seen by him: ‘With birth as condition, there is aging and death.’ Alternatively, ‘from wise attention, there was a breakthrough through wisdom’ (yoniso manasikārā ahu paññāya): by means of wise attention and by means of wisdom, a breakthrough to realization occurred. The meaning is: ‘When there is birth, there is aging and death’; thus, there was the penetration of the cause of aging and death. This is the method in all cases.

Iti hidanti evamidaṃ. Samudayo samudayoti ekādasasu ṭhānesu [P 2.0022] saṅkhārādīnaṃ samudayaṃ sampiṇḍetvā niddisati. Pubbe ananussutesūti “avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārānaṃ samudayo hotī”ti. Evaṃ ito pubbe ananussutesu dhammesu, catūsu vā ariyasaccadhammesu. Cakkhuntiādīni ñāṇavevacanāneva. Ñāṇameva hettha dassanaṭṭhena cakkhu, ñātaṭṭhena ñāṇaṃ, pajānanaṭṭhena paññā, paṭivedhanaṭṭhena vijjā, obhāsanaṭṭhena ālokoti vuttaṃ[M 2.0021]. Taṃ panetaṃ catūsu saccesu lokiyalokuttaramissakaṃ [V 2.0020] niddiṭṭhanti veditabbaṃ. Nirodhavārepi imināva nayena attho veditabbo. Catutthaṃ.

‘Thus this is’ (iti hidaṃ) should be understood as ‘evamidaṃ’ (thus this is). ‘Origin, origin’ (samudayo, samudayo): with this phrase, the Blessed One collectively indicates the origin of formations and so forth in eleven instances. ‘In things not heard before’ (pubbe ananussutesu): ‘With ignorance as condition, the origin of formations occurs.’ Thus, in these phenomena not heard before this time, or in the four noble truths. ‘Eye’ (cakkhuṃ) and so on are simply synonyms for knowledge. Here, knowledge itself is called ‘eye’ (cakkhu) in the sense of directly seeing the cause; ‘knowledge’ (ñāṇaṃ) in the sense of knowing; ‘wisdom’ (paññā) in the sense of understanding in detail; ‘true knowledge’ (vijjā) in the sense of penetrating; and ‘light’ (āloko) in the sense of illuminating. It should be understood that this was pointed out by the Blessed One as pertaining to the four truths, being a mixture of mundane and supramundane. In the section on cessation as well, the meaning should be understood by this very same method. The fourth is finished.

5-10. Sikhīsuttādivaṇṇanā

5-10. Commentary on the Sikhī Sutta and so on

5-10. Pañcamādīsu sikhissa, bhikkhavetiādīnaṃ padānaṃ “sikhissapi, bhikkhave”ti na evaṃ yojetvā attho veditabbo. Kasmā? Ekāsane adesitattā. Nānāṭhānesu hi etāni desitāni, attho pana sabbattha sadisoyeva. Sabbabodhisattānañhi bodhipallaṅke nisinnānaṃ na añño samaṇo vā brāhmaṇo vā devo vā māro vā brahmā vā ācikkhati – “atīte bodhisattā paccayākāraṃ sammasitvā buddhā jātā”ti. Yathā pana paṭhamakappikakāle deve vuṭṭhe udakassa gatamaggeneva aparāparaṃ vuṭṭhiudakaṃ gacchati, evaṃ tehi tehi purimabuddhehi gatamaggeneva pacchimā pacchimā gacchanti. Sabbabodhisattā hi ānāpānacatutthajjhānato vuṭṭhāya paccayākāre ñāṇaṃ otāretvā taṃ anulomapaṭilomaṃ sammasitvā buddhā hontīti paṭipāṭiyā sattasu suttesu buddhavipassanā nāma kathitāti.

In the fifth sutta and so on, the meaning of the words 'of Sikhī, O monks,' etc., should not be understood by connecting them as 'Of Sikhī also, O monks.' Why? Because they were not taught in a single session. Indeed, these were taught in various places, but the meaning is the very same everywhere. For all Bodhisattas seated on the seat of enlightenment, no other ascetic, brahmin, deva, Māra, or Brahmā declares: 'In the past, Bodhisattas, having reflected upon the causal structure, became Buddhas.' Rather, just as when it rains at the beginning of the aeon, subsequent rainwater flows only by the path of the water that has already flowed, so too do the later Bodhisattas follow only by the path trodden by those former Buddhas. Indeed, all Bodhisattas, having emerged from the fourth jhāna based on mindfulness of breathing, direct their insight-knowledge onto the causal structure, and having reflected upon it in forward and reverse order, they become Buddhas. Thus, in sequence, in seven suttas, what is called the insight of the Buddhas has been taught.

Buddhavaggo paṭhamo.

The First Chapter: The Buddha.

2. Āhāravaggo

2. The Chapter on Nutriment

1. Āhārasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Āhāra Sutta

11. Āhāravaggassa paṭhame āhārāti paccayā. Paccayā hi āharanti attano phalaṃ, tasmā āhārāti vuccanti. Bhūtānaṃ vā sattānantiādīsu bhūtāti jātā nibbattā. Sambhavesinoti ye sambhavaṃ jātiṃ nibbattiṃ esanti gavesanti. Tattha catūsu yonīsu aṇḍajajalābujā sattā yāva aṇḍakosaṃ vatthikosañca [P 2.0023] na bhindanti, tāva sambhavesino nāma, aṇḍakosaṃ vatthikosañca bhinditvā bahi nikkhantā bhūtā nāma. Saṃsedajā opapātikā ca paṭhamacittakkhaṇe sambhavesino nāma, dutiyacittakkhaṇato pabhuti bhūtā nāma. Yena vā iriyāpathena [V 2.0021] jāyanti, yāva tato aññaṃ na pāpuṇanti, tāva sambhavesino nāma, tato paraṃ bhūtā nāma. Atha vā bhūtāti jātā abhinibbattā, ye bhūtā abhinibbattāyeva, na puna [M 2.0022] bhavissantīti saṅkhaṃ gacchanti, tesaṃ khīṇāsavānaṃ etaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Sambhavamesantīti sambhavesino. Appahīnabhavasaṃyojanattā āyatimpi sambhavaṃ esantānaṃ sekkhaputhujjanānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Evaṃ sabbathāpi imehi dvīhi padehi sabbasatte pariyādiyati. Vāsaddo cettha sampiṇḍanattho, tasmā bhūtānañca sambhavesīnañcāti ayamattho veditabbo.

In the first sutta of the Chapter on Nutriment, 'nutriment' (āhāra) means condition (paccaya). Because conditions bring forth their own fruit, they are called 'nutriments.' In passages such as 'bhūtānaṃ vā sattānaṃ,' 'bhūtā' means those who are born, who have come into existence. 'Sambhavesino' means those who seek becoming, that is, birth and existence. Therein, among the four modes of birth, egg-born and womb-born beings are called 'sambhavesino' as long as they have not broken the eggshell or the womb; once they have broken out, they are called 'bhūtā.' Moisture-born and spontaneously-born beings are called 'sambhavesino' at the moment of the first consciousness; from the second moment of consciousness onwards, they are called 'bhūtā.' Alternatively, by whichever posture they are born, they are called 'sambhavesino' until they reach another posture; thereafter, they are called 'bhūtā.' Or again, 'bhūtā' means those who are born, who have fully come into existence; this is a designation for the Arahants who have destroyed the taints, who have fully come into existence and will not become again. 'Sambhavesino' means those who seek becoming; this is a designation for trainees and worldlings who, because they have not abandoned the fetter of becoming, will seek becoming in the future as well. Thus, in all ways, with these two terms the Blessed One encompasses all beings. And here, the word 'vā' has the meaning of aggregation; therefore, the meaning should be understood as 'of beings and of those seeking to become.'

Ṭhitiyāti ṭhitatthaṃ. Anuggahāyāti anuggahatthaṃ. Vacanabhedoyeva cesa, attho pana dvinnampi padānaṃ ekoyeva. Atha vā ṭhitiyāti tassa tassa sattassa uppannadhammānaṃ anuppabandhavasena avicchedāya. Anuggahāyāti anuppannānaṃ uppādāya. Ubhopi cetāni “bhūtānaṃ vā ṭhitiyā ceva anuggahāya ca, sambhavesīnaṃ vā ṭhitiyā ceva anuggahāya cā”ti evaṃ ubhayattha daṭṭhabbānīti.

“For their stability” means for the purpose of their continuation. “For their support” means for the purpose of their assistance. This is only a difference in wording, but the meaning of both terms is one and the same. Alternatively, “for their stability” means for the non-interruption, by way of succession, of the arisen phenomena in the continuity of each being. “For their support” means for the arising of unarisen phenomena. Both these terms should be seen in connection with both, thus: “for the stability and support of beings that have come to be, and for the stability and support of those seeking to come to be.”

Kabaḷīkāro āhāroti kabaḷaṃ katvā ajjhoharitabbako āhāro, odanakummāsādivatthukāya ojāyetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Oḷāriko vā sukhumo vāti vatthuoḷārikatāya oḷāriko, sukhumatāya sukhumo. Sabhāvena pana sukhumarūpapariyāpannattā kabaḷīkāro āhāro sukhumova hoti. Sāpi cassa vatthuto oḷārikatā sukhumatā ca upādāyupādāya veditabbā. Kumbhīlānañhi āhāraṃ upādāya morānaṃ āhāro sukhumo. Kumbhīlā kira pāsāṇe gilanti, te ca nesaṃ kucchippattā vilīyanti. Morā sappavicchikādipāṇe khādanti. Morānaṃ pana āhāraṃ upādāya taracchānaṃ āhāro sukhumo. Te kira tivassachaḍḍitāni visāṇāni ceva aṭṭhīni ca khādanti, tāni ca nesaṃ kheḷena temitamattāneva kandamūlaṃ viya mudukāni honti. Taracchānaṃ āhāraṃ upādāya [P 2.0024] hatthīnaṃ āhāro sukhumo. Te hi nānārukkhasākhādayo khādanti. Hatthīnaṃ āhārato gavayagokaṇṇamigādīnaṃ āhāro sukhumo. Te kira nissārāni nānārukkhapaṇṇādīni khādanti. Tesampi āhārato gunnaṃ āhāro sukhumo. Te allasukkhatiṇāni khādanti. Tesaṃ āhārato sasānaṃ āhāro sukhumo. Sasānaṃ āhārato sakuṇānaṃ āhāro sukhumo. Sakuṇānaṃ āhārato paccantavāsīnaṃ āhāro sukhumo. Paccantavāsīnaṃ āhārato gāmabhojakānaṃ āhāro [M 2.0023] sukhumo. Gāmabhojakānaṃ āhārato rājarājamahāmattānaṃ āhāro sukhumo. Tesampi āhārato cakkavattino āhāro sukhumo. Cakkavattino [V 2.0022] āhārato bhummānaṃ devānaṃ āhāro sukhumo. Bhummānaṃ devānaṃ āhārato cātumahārājikānaṃ. Evaṃ yāva paranimmitavasavattīnaṃ āhārā vitthāretabbā. Tesaṃ panāhāro sukhumotveva niṭṭhaṃ patto.

Physical nutriment (kabaḷīkāra āhāra) is nutriment that is to be swallowed after making it into a mouthful (kabaḷa). This is a designation for the nutritive essence (ojā) which has as its physical basis substances such as cooked rice and gruel. As for whether it is coarse or subtle: it is coarse by virtue of the substance's coarseness and subtle by virtue of its subtlety. By its own nature, however, because it is included in subtle matter, physical nutriment is only subtle. And its coarseness and subtlety are to be understood by way of comparison. For instance, compared to the food of crocodiles, the food of peacocks is subtle. It is said that crocodiles swallow stones, which dissolve once they reach their stomachs. Peacocks eat creatures like snakes and scorpions. Compared to the food of peacocks, the food of hyenas is subtle. It is said that they eat antlers and bones discarded for three years, which, merely moistened by their saliva, become soft like a tuberous root. Compared to the food of hyenas, the food of elephants is subtle. For they eat the branches of various trees. Compared to the food of elephants, the food of wild oxen, gokaṇṇa deer, and other deer is subtle. It is said they eat the insubstantial leaves of various trees. Compared to their food, the food of cattle is subtle. They eat fresh and dried grass. Compared to their food, the food of rabbits is subtle. Compared to the food of rabbits, the food of birds is subtle. Compared to the food of birds, the food of border-dwellers is subtle. Compared to the food of border-dwellers, the food of village headmen is subtle. Compared to the food of village headmen, the food of kings and their great ministers is subtle. Compared to their food, the food of a wheel-turning monarch is subtle. Compared to the food of a wheel-turning monarch, the food of the earth-dwelling deities is subtle. Compared to the food of earth-dwelling deities, that of the devas of the Four Great Kings is subtle. In this way, this should be extended up to the food of the Paranimmitavasavattī devas. Their food, however, reaches the conclusion of being only subtle.

Ettha ca oḷārike vatthusmiṃ ojā parittā hoti dubbalā, sukhume balavatī. Tathā hi ekapattapūrampi yāguṃ pīto muhutteneva jighacchito hoti yaṃkiñcideva khāditukāmo, sappiṃ pana pasatamattaṃ pivitvā divasaṃ abhottukāmo hoti. Tattha vatthu kammajatejasaṅkhātaṃ parissayaṃ vinodeti, na pana sakkoti pāletuṃ. Ojā pana pāleti, na sakkoti parissayaṃ vinodetuṃ. Dve pana ekato hutvā parissayañceva vinodenti pālenti cāti.

Herein, in a coarse substance, the nutritive essence is meager and weak; in a subtle one, it is strong. For indeed, one who has drunk even a bowlful of rice-gruel becomes hungry in just a moment, desiring to eat anything whatsoever; but having drunk just a small measure of ghee, one has no desire to eat for a whole day. Therein, the physical substance dispels the affliction known as kamma-generated heat, but it cannot sustain the body. The nutritive essence, however, sustains the body, but it cannot dispel the affliction. The two, however, having come together, both dispel the affliction and sustain the body.

Phasso dutiyoti cakkhusamphassādi chabbidhopi phasso etesu catūsu āhāresu dutiyo āhāroti veditabbo. Desanānayo eva cesa, tasmā iminā nāma kāraṇena dutiyo tatiyo cāti idamettha na gavesitabbaṃ. Manosañcetanāti cetanāva vuccati. Viññāṇanti cittaṃ. Iti bhagavā imasmiṃ ṭhāne upādiṇṇakaanupādiṇṇakavasena ekarāsiṃ katvā cattāro āhāre dassesi. Kabaḷīkārāhāro hi upādiṇṇakopi atthi anupādiṇṇakopi, tathā phassādayo. Tattha sappādīhi gilitānaṃ maṇḍūkādīnaṃ vasena upādiṇṇakakabaḷīkārāhāro daṭṭhabbo. Maṇḍūkādayo hi sappādīhi gilitā antokucchigatāpi kiñci kālaṃ jīvantiyeva. Te yāva upādiṇṇakapakkhe tiṭṭhanti, tāva āhāratthaṃ na sādhenti[P 2.0025]. Bhijjitvā pana anupādiṇṇakapakkhe ṭhitā sādhenti. Tadāpi upādiṇṇakāhāroti vuccantīti. Idaṃ pana ācariyānaṃ na ruccatīti aṭṭhakathāyameva paṭikkhipitvā idaṃ vuttaṃ – imesaṃ sattānaṃ khādantānampi akhādantānampi bhuñjantānampi abhuñjantānampi paṭisandhicitteneva sahajātā kammajā ojā nāma atthi, sā yāvapi sattamā divasā pāleti, ayameva [M 2.0024] upādiṇṇakakabaḷīkārāhāroti veditabbo. Tebhūmakavipākavasena pana upādiṇṇakaphassādayo veditabbā, tebhūmakakusalākusalakiriyavasena anupādiṇṇakā. Lokuttarā pana ruḷhīvasena kathitāti.

In the phrase 'Contact is the second,' the sixfold contact, such as eye-contact, should be understood as the second nutriment among these four nutriments. This is merely the method of exposition; therefore, one should not search here for a reason such as, 'for this reason it is second,' and 'for this reason it is third.' By 'mental volition,' volition itself is meant. By 'consciousness,' mind is meant. Thus, in this context, the Blessed One showed the four nutriments by making them into a single group, without distinguishing by way of appropriated and unappropriated. For physical nutriment exists as both appropriated and unappropriated; likewise for contact and the others. Therein, appropriated physical nutriment should be seen by way of creatures like frogs swallowed by snakes. For frogs and the like, having been swallowed by snakes, even having gone inside their bellies, live for some time. As long as they remain in the appropriated category, they do not accomplish the function of nutriment. But having broken down and being in the unappropriated category, they do accomplish it. Even then, they are called appropriated nutriment, so some say. But this is not agreeable to the teachers, so having rejected this in the commentary itself, this was said: For these beings, whether they are eating or not eating, consuming or not consuming, there exists what is called kamma-born nutritive essence that is co-nascent with the rebirth-linking consciousness. It sustains them for up to the seventh day. This very thing should be understood as appropriated physical nutriment. Appropriated contact and the others, however, should be known by way of the resultants of the three planes; the unappropriated should be known by way of wholesome, unwholesome, and functional actions of the three planes. The supramundane, however, are said to be nutriments by way of established usage.

Etthāha – “yadi paccayaṭṭho āhāraṭṭho, atha kasmā aññesupi sattānaṃ paccayesu vijjamānesu imeyeva cattāro vuttā”ti? Vuccate – ajjhattikasantatiyā visesapaccayattā. Visesapaccayo hi kabaḷīkārāhārabhakkhānaṃ sattānaṃ rūpakāyassa kabaḷīkāro āhāro, nāmakāye [V 2.0023] vedanāya phasso, viññāṇassa manosañcetanā, nāmarūpassa viññāṇaṃ. Yathāha – “seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, ayaṃ kāyo āhāraṭṭhitiko āhāraṃ paṭicca tiṭṭhati, anāhāro no tiṭṭhati (saṃ. ni. 5.183), tathā phassapaccayā vedanā, saṅkhārapaccayā viññāṇaṃ, viññāṇapaccayā nāmarūpa”nti (saṃ. ni. 2.1; vibha. 225).

Here, one might ask: “If the meaning of nutriment is the meaning of condition, then why, when other conditions for beings also exist, were only these four spoken of?” It is answered: Because they are special conditions for the internal continuity. For physical nutriment is a special condition for the material body of beings who consume physical nutriment; in the mental body, contact is a special condition for feeling; mental volition is a special condition for consciousness; and consciousness is a special condition for name-and-form. As it was said: ‘Just as, Bhikkhus, this body is sustained by nutriment, stands depending on nutriment, and without nutriment does not stand, so too feeling is conditioned by contact, consciousness is conditioned by formations, and name-and-form is conditioned by consciousness.’”

Ko panettha āhāro kiṃ āharatīti? Kabaḷīkārāhāro ojaṭṭhamakarūpāni āharati phassāhāro tisso vedanā, manosañcetanāhāro tayo bhave, viññāṇāhāro paṭisandhināmarūpanti.

Herein, which nutriment brings what? Physical nutriment brings the material phenomena with nutritive essence as the eighth. Contact-nutriment brings the three feelings. Mental-volition-nutriment brings the three kinds of existence. Consciousness-nutriment brings rebirth-linking name-and-form.

Kathaṃ? Kabaḷīkārāhāro tāva mukhe ṭhapitamatteyeva aṭṭha rūpāni samuṭṭhāpeti, dantavicuṇṇitaṃ pana ajjhohariyamānaṃ ekekaṃ sitthaṃ aṭṭhaṭṭharūpāni samuṭṭhāpetiyeva. Evaṃ kabaḷīkārāhāro ojaṭṭhamakarūpāni āharati. Phassāhāro pana sukhavedanīyo phasso uppajjamānoyeva sukhaṃ vedanaṃ āharati, dukkhavedanīyo dukkhaṃ, adukkhamasukhavedanīyo adukkhamasukhanti evaṃ sabbathāpi phassāhāro tisso vedanā āharati.

How so? Firstly, physical nutriment, merely upon being placed in the mouth, gives rise to eight material phenomena. But when ground by the teeth and being swallowed, each single morsel gives rise to eight material phenomena each. Thus, physical nutriment brings the material phenomena with nutritive essence as the eighth. As for contact-nutriment, contact associated with pleasant feeling, upon arising, brings pleasant feeling; contact associated with painful feeling brings painful feeling; and contact associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling brings neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. Thus, in every way, contact-nutriment brings the three feelings.

Manosañcetanāhāro kāmabhavūpagaṃ kammaṃ kāmabhavaṃ āharati, rūpārūpabhavūpagāni taṃ taṃ bhavaṃ. Evaṃ sabbathāpi manosañcetanāhāro tayo bhave āharati. Viññāṇāhāro pana ye [P 2.0026] ca paṭisandhikkhaṇe taṃsampayuttakā tayo khandhā, yāni ca tisantativasena tiṃsa rūpāni uppajjanti, sahajātādipaccayanayena tāni āharatīti vuccati. Evaṃ viññāṇāhāro paṭisandhināmarūpaṃ āharatīti. Ettha ca “manosañcetanā tayo bhave āharatī”ti sāsavakusalākusalacetanāva vuttā. “Viññāṇaṃ [M 2.0025] paṭisandhināmarūpaṃ āharatī”ti paṭisandhiviññāṇameva vuttaṃ. Avisesena pana taṃsampayuttataṃsamuṭṭhānadhammānaṃ āharaṇatopete “āhārā”ti veditabbā.

Mental-volition-nutriment: kamma leading to the sense-sphere existence brings the sense-sphere existence; kamma leading to the form and formless existences brings those respective existences. Thus, in every way, mental-volition-nutriment brings the three existences. As for consciousness-nutriment, it is said to bring—by way of conditions such as conascence—both the three aggregates associated with it at the moment of rebirth-linking, and the thirty material phenomena that arise by way of the three continuities. Thus, consciousness-nutriment brings rebirth-linking name-and-form. And here, by 'mental volition brings the three existences,' only wholesome and unwholesome volition connected with the taints is meant. By 'consciousness brings rebirth-linking name-and-form,' only rebirth-linking consciousness is meant. But they should also be known as 'nutriments' because they bring, without distinction, the phenomena associated with them and the phenomena originating from them.

Etesu catūsu āhāresu kabaḷīkārāhāro upatthambhento āhārakiccaṃ sādheti, phasso phusantoyeva manosañcetanā āyūhamānāva, viññāṇaṃ vijānantameva. Kathaṃ? Kabaḷīkārāhāro hi upatthambhentoyeva kāyaṭṭhapanena sattānaṃ ṭhitiyā hoti. Kammajanitopi hi ayaṃ kāyo kabaḷīkārāhārena upatthaddho dasapi vassāni vassasatampi yāva āyuparimāṇā tiṭṭhati. Yathā kiṃ[V 2.0024]? Yathā mātuyā janitopi dārako dhātiyā thaññādīni pāyetvā posiyamāno ciraṃ tiṭṭhati, yathā ca upatthambhena upatthambhitaṃ gehaṃ. Vuttampi cetaṃ –

Among these four nutriments, physical nutriment accomplishes the function of nutriment by supporting; contact, by contacting; mental volition, by accumulating; and consciousness, by cognizing. How so? For physical nutriment, by supporting, serves for the maintenance of beings through the establishment of the body. Indeed, this body, though born of kamma, being supported by physical nutriment, stands for ten years, a hundred years, for as long as the limit of the lifespan. Like what? Just as a child, though born of a mother, stands for a long time when nourished by a wet-nurse who gives him milk and so on to drink; and just as an old house is supported by a prop. And this was also said:

“Yathā, mahārāja, gehe papatante aññena dārunā upatthambhitaṃ santaṃ eva taṃ gehaṃ na patati. Evameva kho, mahārāja, ayaṃ kāyo āhāraṭṭhitiko āhāraṃ paṭicca tiṭṭhatī”ti.

‘Just as, great king, when an old house is collapsing, being supported by another piece of wood, that house does not fall; in the very same way, great king, this body is sustained by nutriment; it stands depending on nutriment.’

Evaṃ kabaḷīkāro āhāro upatthambhento āhārakiccaṃ sādheti.

Thus, physical nutriment, by supporting, accomplishes the function of nutriment.

Evaṃ sādhentopi ca kabaḷīkāro āhāro dvinnaṃ rūpasantatīnaṃ paccayo hoti āhārasamuṭṭhānassa ca upādiṇṇakassa ca. Kammajānaṃ anupālako hutvā paccayo hoti, āhārasamuṭṭhānānaṃ janako hutvāti. Phasso pana sukhādivatthubhūtaṃ ārammaṇaṃ phusantoyeva sukhādivedanāpavattanena sattānaṃ ṭhitiyā [P 2.0027] hoti. Manosañcetanā kusalākusalakammavasena āyūhamānāyeva bhavamūlanipphādanato sattānaṃ ṭhitiyā hoti. Viññāṇaṃ vijānantameva nāmarūpappavattanena sattānaṃ ṭhitiyā hotīti.

Furthermore, even while accomplishing thus, physical nutriment is a condition for two continuities of material form: that which has nutriment as its origin and that which is clung to. For kamma-born matter, it is a condition by being a preserver; for nutriment-born matter, it is a condition by being a generator. But contact, only by contacting an object that is the basis for pleasure and so forth, is for the persistence of beings by causing feelings of pleasure and so forth to arise. Mental volition, only by striving by way of wholesome and unwholesome kamma, is for the persistence of beings by producing the root of existence. Consciousness, only by cognizing, is for the persistence of beings by causing name-and-form to arise.

Evaṃ upatthambhanādivasena āhārakiccaṃ sādhayamānesu panetesu cattāri bhayāni daṭṭhabbāni. Seyyathidaṃ – kabaḷīkārāhāre nikantiyeva bhayaṃ, phasse upagamanameva, manosañcetanāya āyūhanameva, viññāṇe abhinipātoyeva bhayanti. Kiṃ kāraṇā? Kabaḷīkārāhāre hi nikantiṃ [M 2.0026] katvā sītādīnaṃ purakkhatā sattā āhāratthāya muddāgaṇanādikammāni karontā anappakaṃ dukkhaṃ nigacchanti. Ekacce ca imasmiṃ sāsane pabbajitvāpi vejjakammādikāya anesanāya āhāraṃ pariyesantā diṭṭheva dhamme gārayhā honti, samparāyepi, “tassa saṅghāṭipi ādittā sampajjalitā”tiādinā lakkhaṇasaṃyutte (saṃ. ni. 2.218) vuttanayena samaṇapetā honti. Iminā tāva kāraṇena kabaḷīkāre āhāre nikanti eva bhayanti veditabbā.

Furthermore, in these nutriments that accomplish the function of nutriment by way of supporting and so forth, four dangers should be seen. They are as follows: in physical nutriment, delight itself is the danger; in contact, approaching itself is the danger; in mental volition, striving itself is the danger; in consciousness, falling upon an object itself is the danger. For what reason? For beings who, having created delight in physical nutriment and being oppressed by cold and so forth, perform actions such as counting coins for the sake of nutriment, and thereby reach no little suffering. And some, even after going forth in this Dispensation, while seeking nutriment through wrong livelihood such as medical practice, become blameworthy in this very life, and in the next life, in the way stated in the Lakkhaṇa Saṃyutta—'his outer robe is ablaze and burning' and so on—they become ascetic ghosts. For this reason, it should be known that in physical nutriment, delight itself is the danger.

Phassaṃ upagacchantāpi phassassādino paresaṃ rakkhitagopitesu dārādīsu bhaṇḍesu aparajjhanti, te saha bhaṇḍena bhaṇḍasāmikā gahetvā khaṇḍākhaṇḍikaṃ vā chinditvā saṅkārakūṭe chaḍḍenti[V 2.0025], rañño vā niyyādenti. Tato te rājā vividhā kammakāraṇā kārāpeti. Kāyassa ca bhedā duggati tesaṃ pāṭikaṅkhā hoti. Iti phassassādamūlakaṃ diṭṭhadhammikampi samparāyikampi bhayaṃ sabbamāgatameva hoti. Iminā kāraṇena phassāhāre upagamanameva bhayanti veditabbaṃ.

Those who delight in contact, while approaching contact, commit offenses against the guarded and protected goods of others, such as wives. The owners of the goods, having seized them along with the goods, either cut them into pieces and discard them on a rubbish heap, or hand them over to the king. Then the king has them subjected to various punishments. And after the breakup of the body, a bad destination is to be expected for them. Thus, all danger rooted in delighting in contact, both in this very life and in the next, has indeed come about. For this reason, it should be known that in the nutriment of contact, approaching itself is the danger.

Kusalākusalakammāyūhane pana tammūlakaṃ tīsu bhavesu bhayaṃ sabbaṃ āgatameva hoti. Iminā kāraṇena manosañcetanāhāre āyūhanameva bhayanti veditabbaṃ.

Furthermore, with the striving of wholesome and unwholesome kamma, all danger rooted in that striving in the three existences has indeed come about. For this reason, it should be known that in the nutriment of mental volition, striving itself is the danger.

Paṭisandhiviññāṇañca yasmiṃ yasmiṃ ṭhāne abhinipatati, tasmiṃ tasmiṃ ṭhāne paṭisandhināmarūpaṃ gahetvāva nibbattati. Tasmiñca nibbatte sabbabhayāni nibbattāniyeva honti tammūlakattāti iminā kāraṇena viññāṇāhāre abhinipātoyeva bhayanti veditabboti.

And in whatever place rebirth-linking consciousness falls upon, in that very place it arises only after having taken up rebirth-linking name-and-form. And when that has arisen, all dangers indeed arise because of having that as their root. For this reason, it should be known that in the nutriment of consciousness, falling upon an object itself is the danger.

Kiṃnidānātiādīsu nidānādīni sabbāneva kāraṇavevacanāni. Kāraṇañhi yasmā phalaṃ nideti, “handa naṃ gaṇhathā”ti [P 2.0028] appeti viya, tasmā nidānanti vuccati. Yasmā taṃ tato samudeti jāyati pabhavati, tasmā samudayo jāti pabhavoti vuccati. Ayaṃ panettha padattho – kiṃnidānaṃ etesanti kiṃnidānā. Ko samudayo etesanti kiṃsamudayā. Kā jāti etesanti kiṃjātikā. Ko pabhavo etesanti kiṃpabhavā. Yasmā pana tesaṃ taṇhā yathāvuttena atthena nidānañceva samudayo [M 2.0027] ca jāti ca pabhavo ca, tasmā “taṇhānidānā”tiādimāha. Evaṃ sabbapadesu attho veditabbo.

In 'What is their source?' and so on, all the terms such as 'source' are synonyms for 'cause.' For a cause is called a 'source' (nidāna) because it presents (nideti) the result, as if handing it over, saying, 'Here, take it!' Because the result arises well (samudeti), is born (jāti), and has its provenance (pabhavati) from that cause, it is therefore called 'origin' (samudaya), 'birth' (jāti), and 'provenance' (pabhava). Herein, this is the meaning of the words: 'What is their source?' (kiṃnidānaṃ etesaṃ) means 'Of what source are they?' (kiṃnidānā). 'What is their origin?' (ko samudayo etesaṃ) means 'Of what origin are they?' (kiṃsamudayā). 'What is their birth?' (kā jāti etesanti) means 'Of what birth are they?' (kiṃjātikā). 'What is their provenance?' (ko pabhavo etesanti) means 'Of what provenance are they?' (kiṃpabhavā). And since craving is, in the sense explained, their source, origin, birth, and provenance, therefore the Blessed One said, 'They have craving as their source,' and so on. The meaning should be understood in this way in all instances.

Ettha ca ime cattāro āhārā taṇhānidānāti paṭisandhiṃ ādiṃ katvā attabhāvasaṅkhātānaṃ āhārānaṃ purimataṇhānaṃ vasena nidānaṃ veditabbaṃ. Kathaṃ? Paṭisandhikkhaṇe tāva paripuṇṇāyatanānaṃ sattānaṃ sattasantativasena, sesānaṃ tato ūnaūnasantativasena uppannarūpabbhantaraṃ jātā ojā atthi, ayaṃ taṇhānidāno upādiṇṇakakabaḷīkārāhāro. Paṭisandhicittasampayuttā pana phassacetanā sayañca cittaṃ viññāṇanti ime taṇhānidānā upādiṇṇaka-phassamanosañcetanā-viññāṇāhārāti evaṃ tāva purimataṇhānidānā paṭisandhikā āhārā. Yathā ca paṭisandhikā, evaṃ tato paraṃ paṭhamabhavaṅgacittakkhaṇādinibbattāpi veditabbā.

And here, in the statement 'these four nutriments have craving as their source,' the source of the nutriments called 'individual existence' should be understood by way of prior cravings, beginning with rebirth-linking. How? Firstly, at the moment of rebirth-linking, for beings with complete sense bases, by way of seven continuities, and for the remaining beings, by way of respectively lesser continuities than that, there is nutritive essence born within the arisen material form. This is the clung-to physical nutriment that has craving as its source. Furthermore, the contact and volition associated with the rebirth-linking consciousness, and that consciousness itself—these are the clung-to nutriments of contact, mental volition, and consciousness that have craving as their source. Thus, firstly, the nutriments at rebirth-linking have prior craving as their source. And just as with those at rebirth-linking, so too should those arisen from the first life-continuum moment and so on be understood.

Yasmā [V 2.0026] pana bhagavā na kevalaṃ āhārānameva nidānaṃ jānāti, āhāranidānabhūtāya taṇhāyapi, taṇhāya nidānānaṃ vedanādīnampi nidānaṃ jānātiyeva, tasmā taṇhā cāyaṃ, bhikkhave, kiṃnidānātiādinā nayena vaṭṭaṃ dassetvā vivaṭṭaṃ dassesi. Imasmiñca pana ṭhāne bhagavā atītābhimukhaṃ desanaṃ katvā atītena vaṭṭaṃ dasseti. Kathaṃ? Āhāravasena hi ayaṃ attabhāvo gahito.

But since the Blessed One knows not only the source of the nutriments, but also the source of craving, which has become the source of the nutriments, and indeed knows the source of feeling and so forth, which are the sources of craving, therefore, having shown the round by the method of 'Bhikkhus, what is the source of this craving?' and so on, He showed the ending of the round. And furthermore, in this place, the Blessed One, having given a teaching oriented towards the past, shows the round by means of the past. How? For this individual existence is taken up by way of the nutriments.

Taṇhāti imassattabhāvassa janakaṃ kammaṃ, vedanāphassasaḷāyatananāmarūpaviññāṇāni yasmiṃ attabhāve ṭhatvā kammaṃ āyūhitaṃ, taṃ dassetuṃ vuttāni, avijjāsaṅkhārā tassattabhāvassa janakaṃ kammaṃ. Iti dvīsu ṭhānesu attabhāvo, dvīsu tassa janakaṃ kammanti saṅkhepena kammañceva kammavipākañcāti, dvepi dhamme dassentena atītābhimukhaṃ desanaṃ katvā atītena vaṭṭaṃ dassitaṃ.

The term 'craving' refers to the kamma that generates this present individual existence. 'Feeling, contact, the six sense bases, name-and-form, and consciousness' are stated to show that past individual existence in which, having been established, kamma was striven for. 'Ignorance and formations' refer to the kamma that generates that past individual existence. Thus, in two instances individual existence is spoken of, and in two instances the kamma that generates it is spoken of. In brief, by the one showing both phenomena—kamma and the result of kamma—the round was shown by means of the past, after a teaching oriented towards the past had been given.

Tatrāyaṃ [P 2.0029] desanā anāgatassa adassitattā aparipuṇṇāti na daṭṭhabbā. Nayato pana paripuṇṇātveva daṭṭhabbā. Yathā hi cakkhumā puriso udakapiṭṭhe nipannaṃ suṃsumāraṃ disvā tassa parabhāgaṃ olokento gīvaṃ passeyya, orato piṭṭhiṃ, pariyosāne naṅguṭṭhamūlaṃ, heṭṭhā kucchiṃ olokento pana udakagataṃ agganaṅguṭṭhañceva cattāro ca hatthapāde na passeyya, so na ettāvatā “aparipuṇṇo suṃsumāro”ti gaṇhāti, nayato pana paripuṇṇotveva gaṇhāti, evaṃsampadamidaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Therein, this teaching should not be regarded as incomplete on account of the future not being shown. Rather, by way of method, it should be regarded as complete indeed. For instance, just as a man with sight, seeing a crocodile lying on the water's surface, while observing its upper part might see its neck, and behind that its back, and at the end the base of its tail; but while looking at its belly from below, he would not see the tip of its tail and its four limbs which are in the water. He does not, on that account alone, conclude, 'The crocodile is incomplete.' Rather, by way of method, he concludes that it is complete indeed. Thus should this example be understood in its completeness.

Udakapiṭṭhe [M 2.0028] nipannasuṃsumāro viya hi tebhūmakavaṭṭaṃ. Tīre ṭhito cakkhumā puriso viya yogāvacaro. Tena purisena udakapiṭṭhe suṃsumārassa diṭṭhakālo viya yoginā āhāravasena imassattabhāvassa diṭṭhakālo. Parato gīvāya diṭṭhakālo viya imassattabhāvassa janikāya taṇhāya diṭṭhakālo. Piṭṭhiyā diṭṭhakālo viya yasmiṃ attabhāve taṇhāsaṅkhātaṃ kammaṃ kataṃ, vedanādivasena tassa diṭṭhakālo. Naṅguṭṭhamūlassa diṭṭhakālo viya tassattabhāvassa janakānaṃ avijjāsaṅkhārānaṃ diṭṭhakālo. Heṭṭhā kucchiṃ olokentassa pana agganaṅguṭṭhañceva cattāro ca hatthapāde adisvāpi “aparipuṇṇo suṃsumāro”ti agahetvā nayato paripuṇṇotveva gahaṇaṃ viya yattha yattha paccayavaṭṭaṃ pāḷiyaṃ na āgataṃ, tattha tattha “desanā aparipuṇṇā”ti agahetvā nayato paripuṇṇātveva gahaṇaṃ veditabbaṃ. Tattha ca āhārataṇhānaṃ antare eko sandhi, taṇhāvedanānaṃ [V 2.0027] antare eko, viññāṇasaṅkhārānaṃ antare ekoti evaṃ tisandhicatusaṅkhepameva vaṭṭaṃ dassitanti. Paṭhamaṃ.

For the round of existence in the three planes is like a crocodile lying on the water's surface. The yogāvacara is like a man with sight standing on the shore. The time when this individual existence is seen by the yogī through nutriment is like the time when the crocodile on the water's surface is seen by that man. The time when craving, the generator of this individual existence, is seen is like the time when the neck is seen from the upper part. The time when that kamma—which was done in a certain individual existence and is designated as craving—is seen by way of feeling and so on, is like the time when the back is seen. The time when ignorance and formations, the generators of that individual existence, are seen is like the time when the base of the tail is seen. And just as for one looking at the belly from below, even without seeing the tip of the tail and the four limbs, one does not conclude, 'The crocodile is incomplete,' but rather takes it as complete by way of method; so too, wherever the round of conditions is not explicitly stated in the Pāḷi, one should understand that one takes the teaching as complete by way of method, without concluding, 'The teaching is incomplete.' And therein, one connection is between nutriment and craving, one is between craving and feeling, and one is between consciousness and formations; thus the round was shown with just three connections and four sections. The first sutta is concluded.

2. Moḷiyaphaggunasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Moḷiyaphagguna Sutta

12. Dutiye sambhavesīnaṃ vā anuggahāyāti imasmiṃyeva ṭhāne bhagavā desanaṃ niṭṭhāpesi. Kasmā? Diṭṭhigatikassa nisinnattā. Tassañhi parisati moḷiyaphagguno nāma bhikkhu diṭṭhigatiko nisinno. Atha satthā cintesi – “ayaṃ uṭṭhahitvā maṃ pañhaṃ pucchissati, athassāhaṃ vissajjessāmī”ti pucchāya okāsadānatthaṃ desanaṃ niṭṭhāpesi. Moḷiyaphaggunoti [P 2.0030] moḷīti cūḷā vuccati. Yathāha –

12. In the second sutta, the Blessed One concluded the teaching right at this point: '...or for the benefit of those seeking existence.' Why? Because one holding a wrong view was seated there. For in that assembly, a monk named Moḷiyaphagguna, who held a wrong view, was seated. Then the Teacher thought: 'This one will rise and ask me a question, and then I shall answer him.' In order to give an opportunity for the question, he concluded the teaching. Regarding 'Moḷiyaphagguna': a top-knot is called 'moḷi'. As it is said:

“Chetvāna moḷiṃ varagandhavāsitaṃ

Vehāyasaṃ ukkhipi sakyapuṅgavo;

Ratanacaṅkoṭavarena vāsavo,

Sahassanetto sirasā paṭiggahī”ti.

“Having cut off the top-knot scented with choice perfumes, the Sakyan chief tossed it into the sky; Vāsava, the thousand-eyed one, received it on his head with a choice jeweled casket.”

Sā tassa gihikāle mahantā ahosi. Tenassa “moḷiyaphagguno”ti saṅkhā udapādi. Pabbajitampi naṃ teneva nāmena sañjānanti. Etadavocāti desanānusandhiṃ ghaṭento etaṃ “ko nu kho, bhante, viññāṇāhāraṃ [M 2.0029] āhāretī”ti vacanaṃ avoca. Tassattho – bhante, ko nāma so, yo etaṃ viññāṇāhāraṃ khādati vā bhuñjati vāti?

His top-knot was large during his time as a householder. Hence, the designation “Moḷiyaphagguna” arose for him. Even after his ordination, they recognized him by that same name. Connecting the thread of the discourse, he spoke this statement: “Venerable sir, who indeed partakes of the nutriment of consciousness?” The meaning of this is: “Venerable sir, who is it that chews or eats this nutriment of consciousness?”

Kasmā panāyaṃ itare tayo āhāre apucchitvā imameva pucchatīti? Jānāmīti laddhiyā. So hi mahante piṇḍe katvāva kabaḷīkārāhāraṃ bhuñjante passati, tenassa taṃ jānāmīti laddhi. Tittiravaṭṭakamorakukkuṭādayo pana mātusamphassena yāpente disvā “ete phassāhārena yāpentī”ti tassa laddhi. Kacchapā pana attano utusamaye mahāsamuddato nikkhamitvā samuddatīre vālikantare aṇḍāni ṭhapetvā vālikāya paṭicchādetvā mahāsamuddameva otaranti. Tāni mātuanussaraṇavasena na pūtīni honti. Tāni manosañcetanāhārena yāpentīti tassa laddhi. Kiñcāpi therassa ayaṃ laddhi, na pana etāya laddhiyā imaṃ pañhaṃ pucchati[V 2.0028]. Diṭṭhigatiko hi ummattakasadiso. Yathā ummattako pacchiṃ gahetvā antaravīthiṃ otiṇṇo gomayampi pāsāṇampi gūthampi khajjakhaṇḍampi taṃ taṃ manāpampi amanāpampi gahetvā pacchiyaṃ pakkhipati. Evameva diṭṭhigatiko yuttampi ayuttampi pucchati. So “kasmā imaṃ pucchasī”ti na niggahetabbo, pucchitapucchitaṭṭhāne pana gahaṇameva [P 2.0031] nisedhetabbaṃ. Teneva naṃ bhagavā “kasmā evaṃ pucchasī”ti avatvā gahitagāhameva tassa mocetuṃ no kallo pañhotiādimāha.

But why, without inquiring about the other three nutriments, does he ask only about this one? Because of his view, “I know.” For he sees people making large balls of food and consuming physical nutriment, and thus he holds the view, “I know that.” Furthermore, seeing partridges, quails, peacocks, chickens, and so on, being sustained by contact with their mothers, he holds the view, “These are sustained by the nutriment of contact.” Moreover, turtles emerge from the great ocean during their season, lay their eggs amidst the sand on the shore, cover them with sand, and descend back into the great ocean. Those eggs do not rot, by the power of the mother’s remembrance of them. He holds the view, “These are sustained by the nutriment of mental volition.” Although the elder held this view, it was not on account of this view that he asked this question. For one holding a wrong view is like a madman. Just as a madman, taking a basket and going into the street, picks up cow dung, stones, excrement, or pieces of food—whether pleasant or unpleasant—and throws them into his basket, so too does one holding a wrong view ask questions, whether appropriate or inappropriate. He should not be rebuked with, “Why do you ask this?” Rather, in every question asked, the very grasping should be refuted. Therefore, the Blessed One did not say to him, “Why do you ask thus?” but rather, to release him from the very view he had grasped, he said, “This is not a fitting question,” and so forth.

Tattha no kalloti ayutto. Āhāretīti ahaṃ na vadāmīti ahaṃ koci satto vā puggalo vā āhāretīti na vadāmi. Āhāretīti cāhaṃ vadeyyanti yadi ahaṃ āhāretīti vadeyyaṃ. Tatrassa kallo pañhoti tasmiṃ mayā evaṃ vutte ayaṃ pañho yutto bhaveyya. Kissa nu kho, bhante, viññāṇāhāroti, bhante, ayaṃ viññāṇāhāro katamassa dhammassa paccayoti attho. Tatra kallaṃ veyyākaraṇanti tasmiṃ evaṃ pucchite pañhe imaṃ veyyākaraṇaṃ yuttaṃ “viññāṇāhāro āyatiṃ punabbhavābhinibbattiyā paccayo”ti. Ettha ca viññāṇāhāroti paṭisandhicittaṃ. Āyatiṃ punabbhavābhinibbattīti teneva viññāṇena sahuppannanāmarūpaṃ. Tasmiṃ bhūte sati saḷāyatananti tasmiṃ punabbhavābhinibbattisaṅkhāte nāmarūpe jāte sati saḷāyatanaṃ hotīti attho.

Therein, no kallo means 'unsuitable.' The statement Āhāretīti ahaṃ na vadāmi ('I do not say, "one partakes of nutriment"') means: I do not say that any being or person partakes of nutriment. The statement Āhāretīti cāhaṃ vadeyyaṃ ('But if I were to say, "one partakes of nutriment"') means: if I were to say, 'one partakes of nutriment.' The statement Tatrassa kallo pañho ('then the question would be fitting') means: if it were spoken thus by me, this question would be suitable. The question Kissa nu kho, bhante, viññāṇāhāro ('For what, venerable sir, is the nutriment of consciousness?') has this meaning: 'Venerable sir, for what phenomenon is this nutriment of consciousness a condition?' Therein, kallaṃ veyyākaraṇaṃ ('a fitting explanation') means: when the question is asked in this way, this explanation is fitting: 'The nutriment of consciousness is a condition for the future production of renewed existence.' And here, 'nutriment of consciousness' means the relinking-consciousness. 'Future production of renewed existence' means the name-and-form that arises together with that very consciousness. The statement Tasmiṃ bhūte sati saḷāyatanaṃ ('When that has come to be, there is the sixfold sense base') has this meaning: when that name-and-form, designated as the production of renewed existence, has arisen, the sixfold sense base comes to be.

Saḷāyatanapaccayā [M 2.0030] phassoti idhāpi bhagavā uttari pañhassa okāsaṃ dento desanaṃ niṭṭhāpesi. Diṭṭhigatiko hi navapucchaṃ uppādetuṃ na sakkoti, niddiṭṭhaṃ niddiṭṭhaṃyeva pana gaṇhitvā pucchati, tenassa bhagavā okāsaṃ adāsi. Attho panassa sabbapadesu vuttanayeneva gahetabbo. “Ko nu kho, bhante, bhavatī”ti kasmā na pucchati? Diṭṭhigatikassa hi satto nāma bhūto nibbattoyevāti laddhi, tasmā attano laddhiviruddhaṃ idanti na pucchati. Apica idappaccayā idaṃ idappaccayā idanti bahūsu ṭhānesu kathitattā saññattiṃ upagato, tenāpi na pucchati. Satthāpi “imassa bahuṃ pucchantassāpi titti natthi, tucchapucchameva pucchatī”ti ito paṭṭhāya desanaṃ ekābaddhaṃ katvā desesi. Channaṃ tvevāti yato paṭṭhāya desanāruḷhaṃ, tameva gahetvā desanaṃ vivaṭṭento evamāha. Imasmiṃ pana sutte viññāṇanāmarūpānaṃ antare eko sandhi, vedanātaṇhānaṃ antare eko, bhavajātīnaṃ antare ekoti. Dutiyaṃ.

Regarding 'With the six sense bases as condition, contact,' here too the Blessed One, giving an opportunity for a further question, paused the teaching. For one holding a wrong view cannot raise a new question; instead, they grasp what has already been stated and ask about it. Thus, the Blessed One granted him the opportunity. The meaning, however, should be understood in all instances according to the method already explained. Why does he not ask, “Who, venerable sir, comes to be?” Because one holding a wrong view has the belief that a being is real and is indeed produced. Therefore, he does not ask this, which contradicts his own belief. Moreover, since it has been stated in many places, “With this as condition, this comes to be; with this as condition, this comes to be,” he has arrived at this understanding, and for that reason also he does not ask. The Teacher, thinking, “Even if this one asks many questions, there is no satisfaction—he merely asks empty questions,” from this point onward delivered the teaching in a single, continuous flow. Regarding 'Of the six...,' starting from the point where the teaching ascended, he took up that very point and, unfolding the teaching, spoke thus. In this discourse, however, there is one link between consciousness and name-and-form, one between feeling and craving, and one between becoming and birth. The Second.

3. Samaṇabrāhmaṇasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Samaṇabrāhmaṇa Sutta

13. Tatiye [V 2.0029] samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vāti saccāni paṭivijjhituṃ asamatthā bāhirakasamaṇabrāhmaṇā. Jarāmaraṇaṃ nappajānantītiādīsu jarāmaraṇaṃ na jānanti dukkhasaccavasena[P 2.0032], jarāmaraṇasamudayaṃ na jānanti saha taṇhāya jāti jarāmaraṇassa samudayoti samudayasaccavasena, jarāmaraṇanirodhaṃ na jānanti nirodhasaccavasena, paṭipadaṃ na jānanti maggasaccavasena. Jātiṃ na jānanti dukkhasaccavasena, jātisamudayaṃ na jānanti saha taṇhāya bhavo jātisamudayoti samudayasaccavasena. Evaṃ saha taṇhāya samudayaṃ yojetvā sabbapadesu catusaccavasena attho veditabbo. Sāmaññatthaṃ vā brahmaññatthaṃ vāti ettha ariyamaggo sāmaññañceva brahmaññañca. Ubhayatthāpi pana attho nāma ariyaphalaṃ veditabbaṃ. Iti bhagavā imasmiṃ sutte ekādasasu ṭhānesu cattāri saccāni kathesīti. Tatiyaṃ.

3. In the third discourse, 'ascetics or brahmins' refers to external ascetics and brahmins who are incapable of penetrating the truths. In phrases such as 'they do not understand aging and death,' this means: they do not understand aging and death in terms of the truth of suffering; they do not understand the origin of aging and death—that birth, together with craving, is the origin of aging and death—in terms of the truth of origin; they do not understand the cessation of aging and death in terms of the truth of cessation; and they do not understand the path in terms of the truth of the path. They do not understand birth in terms of the truth of suffering; they do not understand the origin of birth—that becoming, together with craving, is the origin of birth—in terms of the truth of origin. In this way, by connecting the origin with craving, the meaning should be understood in all instances in terms of the four truths. Regarding 'the goal of asceticism or the goal of brahminhood,' here the Noble Path is both asceticism and brahminhood. In both cases, however, the goal should be understood as the noble fruit. Thus, in this discourse, the Blessed One taught the four truths in eleven instances. The Third.

4. Dutiyasamaṇabrāhmaṇasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Second Samaṇabrāhmaṇa Sutta

14. Catutthe [M 2.0031] ime dhamme katame dhammeti ettakaṃ papañcaṃ katvā kathitaṃ, desanaṃ paṭivijjhituṃ samatthānaṃ puggalānaṃ ajjhāsayena ime dhamme nappajānantītiādi vuttaṃ. Sesaṃ purimasadisameva. Catutthaṃ.

13. In the fourth discourse, this much was taught with elaboration, such as 'these phenomena, what phenomena?'; and the phrase 'they do not understand these phenomena,' and so on, was spoken in accordance with the disposition of individuals capable of penetrating the teaching. The rest is just like the previous. The Fourth.

5. Kaccānagottasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Kaccānagotta Sutta

15. Pañcame sammādiṭṭhi sammādiṭṭhīti yaṃ paṇḍitā devamanussā tesu tesu ṭhānesu sammādassanaṃ vadanti, sabbampi taṃ dvīhi padehi saṅkhipitvā pucchati. Dvayanissitoti dve koṭṭhāse nissito. Yebhuyyenāti iminā ṭhapetvā ariyapuggale sesamahājanaṃ dasseti. Atthitanti sassataṃ. Natthitanti ucchedaṃ. Lokasamudayanti loko nāma saṅkhāraloko, tassa nibbatti. Sammappaññāya passatoti sammāpaññā nāma savipassanā maggapaññā, tāya passantassāti attho. Yā loke natthitāti saṅkhāraloke nibbattesu dhammesu paññāyantesveva yā natthīti ucchedadiṭṭhi uppajjeyya, sā na hotīti attho. Lokanirodhanti saṅkhārānaṃ bhaṅgaṃ. Yā [V 2.0030] loke atthitāti saṅkhāraloke bhijjamānesu dhammesu paññāyantesveva yā atthīti sassatadiṭṭhi uppajjeyya[P 2.0033], sā na hotīti attho.

15. In the fifth sutta, regarding 'right view, right view,' whatever the wise, gods, and humans call right seeing in various places, the monk Kaccānagotta asks by summarizing all of it with two terms. 'Dependent on two' means dependent on two portions. By 'for the most part,' the Blessed One indicates the great multitude, having set aside the noble individuals. 'It exists' means eternalism. 'It does not exist' means annihilationism. 'The origin of the world': 'world' means the world of formations; its arising. 'Sees with right wisdom': right wisdom means path wisdom accompanied by insight; the meaning is: for one who sees with that. As to 'that which in the world is non-existence,' the meaning is this: regarding conditioned phenomena that have arisen in the world of formations, even as they are perceived as a continuum, whatever annihilationist view, 'it does not exist,' might arise, that view does not arise. 'The cessation of the world' means the dissolution of formations. As to 'that which in the world is existence,' the meaning is this: regarding conditioned phenomena that are disintegrating moment by moment in the world of formations, even as they are perceived, whatever eternalist view, 'it exists,' might arise, that view does not arise.

Apica lokasamudayanti anulomapaccayākāraṃ. Lokanirodhanti paṭilomapaccayākāraṃ. Lokanissaye passantassāpi hi paccayānaṃ anucchedena paccayuppannassa anucchedaṃ passato yā natthīti ucchedadiṭṭhi uppajjeyya, sā na hoti. Paccayanirodhaṃ passantassāpi paccayanirodhena paccayuppannanirodhaṃ passato yā atthīti sassatadiṭṭhi uppajjeyya, sā na hotīti ayampettha attho.

Furthermore, 'the origin of the world' means the teaching of dependent origination in forward order. 'The cessation of the world' means the teaching of dependent origination in reverse order. Indeed, even for one who sees the forward sequence of conditions, which is the dependence of the world, because of seeing the non-cessation of the conditioned phenomena through the non-cessation of the conditions, whatever annihilationist view 'it does not exist' might arise, that view does not arise. And even for one who sees the reverse sequence of conditions, which is the cessation of conditions, because of seeing the cessation of the conditioned phenomena through the cessation of the conditions, whatever eternalist view 'it exists' might arise, that view does not arise. Thus, this too is the meaning to be understood here.

Upayupādānābhinivesavinibandhoti upayehi ca upādānehi ca abhinivesehi ca vinibandho. Tattha upayāti dve upayā taṇhupayo ca diṭṭhupayo ca. Upādānādīsupi eseva nayo. Taṇhādiṭṭhiyo hi yasmā ahaṃ mamantiādīhi ākārehi tebhūmakadhamme upenti upagacchanti, tasmā upayāti [M 2.0032] vuccanti. Yasmā pana te dhamme upādiyanti ceva abhinivisanti ca, tasmā upādānāti ca abhinivesāti ca vuccanti. Tāhi cāyaṃ loko vinibandho. Tenāha “upayupādānābhinivesavinibandho”ti.

'Bound by approaches, clingings, and adherences' means firmly bound by approaches, clingings, and adherences in a way that does not allow for release. Therein, 'approaches' refers to two approaches: the approach that is craving and the approach that is view. This same method applies to 'clingings' and so forth. Indeed, because craving and views approach and go to the phenomena of the three realms with modes such as 'I' and 'mine,' they are therefore called 'approaches.' Furthermore, because they firmly grasp and adhere to those phenomena, they are therefore called 'clingings' and 'adherences.' And by these, this world is firmly bound in a way that does not allow for release. Therefore, He said, 'bound by approaches, clingings, and adherences.'

Tañcāyanti tañca upayupādānaṃ ayaṃ ariyasāvako. Cetaso adhiṭṭhānanti cittassa patiṭṭhānabhūtaṃ. Abhinivesānusayanti abhinivesabhūtañca anusayabhūtañca. Taṇhādiṭṭhīsu hi akusalacittaṃ patiṭṭhāti, tā ca tasmiṃ abhinivisanti ceva anusenti ca, tasmā tadubhayaṃ cetaso adhiṭṭhānaṃ abhinivesānusayanti ca āha. Na upetīti na upagacchati. Na upādiyatīti na gaṇhāti. Nādhiṭṭhātīti na adhiṭṭhāti, kinti? Attā meti. Dukkhamevāti pañcupādānakkhandhamattameva. Na kaṅkhatīti “dukkhameva uppajjati, dukkhaṃ nirujjhati, na añño ettha satto nāma atthī”ti kaṅkhaṃ na karoti. Na vicikicchatīti na vicikicchaṃ uppādeti.

As for 'and this,' this noble disciple [does not approach] that approach and clinging, which are craving and view. 'The mind's foundation' means that which has become a basis for the unwholesome mind. 'Adherence and latent tendency' means that which has become adherence and that which has become a latent tendency. For in craving and views, unwholesome consciousness is established, and they both adhere to and lie latent in it. Therefore, He spoke of that pair as 'the mind's foundation' and 'adherence and latent tendency.' 'Does not approach' means does not approach with the nature of craving and view, such as 'this is mine.' 'Does not grasp' means does not firmly take hold by way of craving and view. 'Does not determine' means does not determine with the grasp of craving and the grasp of view, thinking 'my self.' 'Only suffering' means merely the five aggregates of clinging. 'Does not doubt' means one does not create doubt, thinking: 'Only suffering, which is the aggregates of clinging, arises; suffering, which is the aggregates of clinging, ceases. In these five aggregates of clinging, apart from suffering, there is no being whatsoever.' 'Does not waver' means one does not give rise to wavering.

Aparappaccayāti na parappaccayena, aññassa apattiyāyetvā attapaccakkhañāṇamevassa ettha hotīti. Ettāvatā [P 2.0034] kho, kaccāna, sammādiṭṭhi hotīti evaṃ sattasaññāya pahīnattā ettakena sammādassanaṃ nāma hotīti missakasammādiṭṭhiṃ āha. Ayameko antoti esa eko nikūṭanto [V 2.0031] lāmakanto paṭhamakaṃ sassataṃ. Ayaṃ dutiyoti esa dutiyo sabbaṃ natthīti uppajjanakadiṭṭhisaṅkhāto nikūṭanto lāmakanto dutiyako ucchedoti attho. Sesamettha uttānamevāti. Pañcamaṃ.

'Not dependent on others' means not through faith in another, not by relying on another; for that noble disciple, in this suffering which is the aggregates of clinging, there is only knowledge that is directly experienced by oneself. Regarding 'To this extent, Kaccāna, there is right view': in this way, because of the abandonment of the perception of a being, to this extent there is what is called right seeing. Thus He taught the mixed right view, which is a mixture of mundane and supramundane. In 'This is one extreme': this wrong view, 'everything exists,' is one base, lowly extreme, the first, which is eternalism. In 'This is the second': this wrong view, known as the view 'everything does not exist,' is the second base, lowly extreme, the second, which is annihilationism. This is the meaning. The rest here is clear. The fifth is finished.

6. Dhammakathikasuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Dhammakathika Sutta

16. Chaṭṭhe nibbidāyāti nibbindanatthāya. Virāgāyāti virajjanatthāya. Nirodhāyāti nirujjhanatthāya. Paṭipanno hotīti ettha sīlato paṭṭhāya yāva arahattamaggā paṭipannoti veditabbo. Dhammānudhammappaṭipannoti lokuttarassa nibbānadhammassa anudhammabhūtaṃ paṭipadaṃ paṭipanno. Anudhammabhūtanti anurūpasabhāvabhūtaṃ. Nibbidā virāgā nirodhāti nibbidāya ceva virāgena ca nirodhena ca. Anupādā vimuttoti catūhi upādānehi kiñci dhammaṃ anupādiyitvā vimutto. Diṭṭhadhammanibbānappattoti diṭṭheva dhamme nibbānappatto. Alaṃ vacanāyāti, evaṃ vattabbataṃ arahati, yutto anucchavikoti attho[M 2.0033]. Evamettha ekena nayena dhammakathikassa pucchā kathitā, dvīhi taṃ visesetvā sekkhāsekkhabhūmiyo niddiṭṭhāti. Chaṭṭhaṃ.

16. In the sixth sutta: 'For disenchantment' (nibbidāya) means for the purpose of attaining insight into disenchantment. 'For dispassion' (virāgāya) means for the purpose of attaining insight into dispassion. 'For cessation' (nirodhāya) means for the purpose of attaining insight into cessation. Regarding 'He is one who has entered upon the path' (paṭipanno hoti), here it should be understood that one is called 'one who has entered upon the path' from the time of undertaking virtue up to the path of Arahantship. 'One who has entered upon the path in accordance with the Dhamma' (dhammānudhammappaṭipanno) means one who has entered upon the practice that is suitable for the supramundane Dhamma of Nibbāna. 'Suitable for the Dhamma' (anudhammabhūtaṃ) means being of a nature suitable for the attainment of Nibbāna. 'Disenchantment, dispassion, cessation' (nibbidā virāgā nirodhā) means by insight into disenchantment, which is insight meditation culminating in the emergence from formations; by dispassion, which is the noble path; and by cessation, which is the noble path. 'Liberated without clinging' (anupādā vimutto) means liberated by not grasping any conditioned phenomenon through the four kinds of clinging. 'One who has attained Nibbāna in this very life' (diṭṭhadhammanibbānappatto) means one who has attained Nibbāna in this very existence. 'Fit to be called' (alaṃ vacanāya) means he is worthy of being so called; it is suitable and appropriate. This is the meaning. Thus, here the question about the Dhamma-preacher is explained in one way; and by two further ways, having specified the matter, the planes of the trainee and the adept are pointed out. The sixth is finished.

7. Acelakassapasuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Acelakassapa Sutta

17. Sattame acelo kassapoti liṅgena acelo niccelo, nāmena kassapo. Dūratovāti mahatā bhikkhusaṅghena parivutaṃ āgacchantaṃ dūrato eva addasa. Kiñcideva desanti kiñcideva kāraṇaṃ. Okāsanti pañhabyākaraṇassa khaṇaṃ kālaṃ. Antaragharanti “na pallatthikāya antaraghare nisīdissāmī”ti ettha antonivesanaṃ antaragharaṃ. “Okkhittacakkhu antaraghare gamissāmī”ti ettha indakhīlato paṭṭhāya antogāmo. Idhāpi ayameva adhippeto. Yadākaṅkhasīti [P 2.0035] yaṃ icchasi.

17. In the seventh sutta: 'The unclothed Kassapa' (acelo kassapo) means he was unclothed (acelo, niccelo) by his ascetic characteristic, and Kassapa by name. 'From afar' (dūrato) means he saw him coming from afar, surrounded by a great assembly of monks. 'Some matter' (kiñcideva desaṃ) means some cause. 'An opportunity' (okāsaṃ) means the opportune time for answering a question. 'Within a village' (antaragharaṃ): in the passage, "I will not sit cross-legged (pallatthikāya) within a house," 'antaraghara' means inside a dwelling. In the passage, "With downcast eyes, I will go within a village," 'antaraghara' means inside the village, starting from the threshold. Here too, this latter meaning is intended. 'When you wish' (yadākaṅkhasi) means whatever you desire to ask.

Kasmā pana bhagavā kathetukāmo yāvatatiyaṃ paṭikkhipīti? Gāravajananatthaṃ. Diṭṭhigatikā hi khippaṃ kathiyamāne gāravaṃ na karonti, “samaṇaṃ gotamaṃ upasaṅkamitumpi pucchitumpi sukaraṃ, pucchitamatteyeva kathetī”ti vacanampi na saddahanti. Dve tayo vāre paṭikkhitte pana gāravaṃ karonti, “samaṇaṃ gotamaṃ upasaṅkamitumpi pañhaṃ pucchitumpi dukkara”nti [V 2.0032] yāvatatiyaṃ yācite kathiyamānaṃ sussūsanti saddahanti. Iti bhagavā “ayaṃ sussūsissati saddahissatī”ti yāvatatiyaṃ yācāpetvā kathesi. Apica yathā bhisakko telaṃ vā phāṇitaṃ vā pacanto mudupākakharapākānaṃ pākakālaṃ āgamayamāno pākakālaṃ anatikkamitvāva otāreti. Evaṃ bhagavā sattānaṃ ñāṇaparipākaṃ āgamayamāno “ettakena kālena imassa ñāṇaṃ paripākaṃ gamissatī”ti ñatvāva yāvatatiyaṃ yācāpesi.

But why did the Blessed One, though wishing to speak, refuse up to the third time? To generate reverence. For those holding fixed views, when answered quickly, do not show reverence; thinking, “It is easy to approach the ascetic Gotama and to ask a question; he speaks as soon as he is asked,” they do not even believe his words. But when refused two or three times, they show reverence; thinking, “It is difficult to approach the ascetic Gotama and to ask a question,” they listen well and believe when he speaks after being requested up to the third time. Thus the Blessed One, thinking, “This one will listen well and will believe,” had him request up to the third time and then spoke. Furthermore, just as a skilled physician, while cooking oil or molasses, waits for the proper cooking time for both soft and hard preparations, and takes it off the fire without letting the proper time pass, so too the Blessed One, waiting for the ripening of the knowledge of beings, knowing, “After this much time, this one’s knowledge will reach maturity,” had him request up to the third time.

Mā hevaṃ, kassapāti, kassapa, mā evaṃ bhaṇi. Sayaṃkataṃ dukkhanti hi vattuṃ na vaṭṭati, attā nāma koci dukkhassa kārako natthīti dīpeti. Paratopi eseva nayo. Adhiccasamuppannanti akāraṇena yadicchāya uppannaṃ. Iti puṭṭho samānoti kasmā evamāha? Evaṃ kirassa ahosi – “ayaṃ ‘sayaṃkataṃ dukkha’ntiādinā puṭṭho ‘mā heva’nti vadati, ‘natthī’ti puṭṭho ‘atthī’ti vadati. ‘Bhavaṃ gotamo dukkhaṃ na jānāti na passatī’ti puṭṭho ‘jānāmi khvāha’nti vadati. Kiñci nu kho mayā virajjhitvā pucchito”ti mūlato [M 2.0034] paṭṭhāya attano pucchameva sodhento evamāha. Ācikkhatu ca me, bhante, bhagavāti idha satthari sañjātagāravo “bhava”nti avatvā “bhagavā”ti vadati.

‘Do not say so, Kassapa’ means: Kassapa, do not speak thus. For it is not fit to say, ‘suffering is self-made’; the Blessed One shows that there is no agent called a ‘self’ that is the maker of suffering. In the subsequent cases, this is the same method. ‘Arisen without a cause’ means arisen without a cause, by its own accord. ‘Being asked thus’: why did he speak thus? It seems this occurred to him: “When this one is asked with ‘is suffering self-made?’ and so on, he says, ‘Do not say so.’ When asked, ‘Does it not exist?’ he says, ‘It exists.’ When asked, ‘Does the venerable Gotama not know or see suffering?’ he says, ‘Indeed, I know.’ Have I perhaps asked something erroneously?” Thus, starting from the beginning and clarifying his own question, he spoke thus. ‘And let the Blessed One, venerable sir, explain to me’: here, having generated reverence for the Teacher, instead of saying ‘Venerable Sir,’ he says ‘Blessed One.’

So karotītiādi, “sayaṃkataṃ dukkha”nti laddhiyā paṭisedhanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Ettha ca satoti idaṃ bhummatthe sāmivacanaṃ, tasmā evamattho daṭṭhabbo – so karoti so paṭisaṃvedayatīti kho, kassapa, ādimhiyeva evaṃ sati pacchā sayaṃkataṃ dukkhanti ayaṃ laddhi hoti. Ettha ca dukkhanti vaṭṭadukkhaṃ adhippetaṃ. Iti vadanti etassa purimena ādisaddena anantarena ca sassatasaddena [P 2.0036] sambandho hoti. “Dīpeti gaṇhātī”ti ayaṃ panettha pāṭhaseso. Idañhi vuttaṃ hoti – iti evaṃ vadanto āditova sassataṃ dīpeti, sassataṃ gaṇhāti. Kasmā? Tassa hi taṃ dassanaṃ etaṃ pareti, kārakañca vedakañca ekameva gaṇhantaṃ etaṃ sassataṃ upagacchatīti attho.

The passage beginning with ‘He acts’ was spoken to refute the view that ‘suffering is self-made.’ And here, this word ‘sato’ is a genitive word in the sense of the locative. Therefore, the meaning should be understood thus: Kassapa, when it is the case from the very beginning that ‘he who acts is the one who experiences,’ then afterwards this view arises: ‘suffering is self-made.’ And here, by ‘suffering,’ the suffering of the round of existence is intended. ‘Thus speaking’: this has a connection with the preceding word ‘ādi’ and the immediately following word ‘sassata.’ ‘Shows, grasps’ is the remainder of the text here. For this is what is said: one who speaks thus, from the very beginning shows eternalism, grasps eternalism. Why? Because that view of his leads to this; the meaning is that by taking the agent and the experiencer to be one and the same, it approaches this eternalism.

Añño karotītiādi pana “paraṃkataṃ dukkha”nti laddhiyā paṭisedhanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. “Ādito sato”ti idaṃ pana idhāpi āharitabbaṃ. Ayañhettha attho – añño karoti añño paṭisaṃvediyatīti kho pana, kassapa, ādimhiyeva evaṃ sati, pacchā “kārako idheva ucchijjati, tena kataṃ añño paṭisaṃvediyatī”ti evaṃ uppannāya ucchedadiṭṭhiyā saddhiṃ sampayuttāya [V 2.0033] vedanāya abhitunnassa viddhassa sato “paraṃkataṃ dukkha”nti ayaṃ laddhi hotīti. Iti vadantiādi vuttanayeneva yojetabbaṃ. Tatrāyaṃ yojanā – evañca vadanto āditova ucchedaṃ dīpeti, ucchedaṃ gaṇhāti. Kasmā? Tassa hi taṃ dassanaṃ etaṃ pareti, etaṃ ucchedaṃ upagacchatīti attho.

Now, the passage beginning with ‘Another acts’ was spoken to refute the view that ‘suffering is made by another.’ And this phrase ‘from the beginning, when it is the case’ should be brought forward here as well. For this is the meaning here: Kassapa, when it is the case from the very beginning that ‘one person acts, another experiences,’ then afterwards, for one who is afflicted and pierced by a feeling associated with the annihilationist view that has arisen thus: ‘the agent is annihilated right here, what was done by him is experienced by another,’ this view arises: ‘suffering is made by another.’ The passage beginning with ‘Thus speaking’ should be construed in the way already stated. Therein, this is the construction: and one speaking thus, from the very beginning, shows annihilationism, grasps annihilationism. Why? Because that view of his leads to this; it approaches this annihilationism. This is the meaning.

Ete teti ye sassatucchedasaṅkhāte ubho ante (anupagamma tathāgato dhammaṃ deseti, ete te, kassapa, ubho ante) anupagamma pahāya anallīyitvā majjhena tathāgato dhammaṃ deseti, majjhimāya paṭipadāya ṭhito desetīti attho. Kataraṃ dhammanti ce? Yadidaṃ avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārāti. Ettha hi kāraṇato phalaṃ, kāraṇanirodhena cassa nirodho dīpito, na koci kārako vā vedako vā [M 2.0035] niddiṭṭho. Ettāvatā sesapañhā paṭisedhitā honti. Ubho ante anupagammāti iminā hi tatiyapañho paṭikkhitto. Avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārāti iminā adhiccasamuppannatā ceva ajānanañca paṭikkhittanti veditabbaṃ.

‘These two’ refers to the two extremes known as eternalism and annihilationism. Without approaching these two extremes, the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma. This means that without approaching, having abandoned, and not clinging to these two extremes, Kassapa, the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma by the middle; that is, he teaches the Dhamma while established in the middle path. And what is that Dhamma? It is this: “With ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise.” For herein, the result is shown from the cause, and its cessation through the cessation of the cause is also shown. No doer or experiencer is pointed out. By this much, the remaining questions are refuted. Indeed, by this phrase, “without approaching both extremes,” the third question is rejected. By this phrase, “With ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise,” both uncaused origination and non-knowing should be understood as rejected.

Labheyyanti idaṃ so bhagavato santike bhikkhubhāvaṃ patthayamāno āha. Atha bhagavā yonena khandhake titthiyaparivāso (mahāva. 86) paññatto, yaṃ aññatitthiyapubbo sāmaṇerabhūmiyaṃ ṭhito “ahaṃ, bhante, itthannāmo aññatitthiyapubbo [P 2.0037] imasmiṃ dhammavinaye ākaṅkhāmi upasampadaṃ. Svāhaṃ, bhante, saṅghaṃ cattāro māse parivāsaṃ yācāmī”tiādinā nayena samādiyitvā parivasati, taṃ sandhāya yo kho, kassapa, aññatitthiyapubbotiādimāha. Tattha pabbajjanti vacanasiliṭṭhatāvasena vuttaṃ. Aparivasitvāyeva hi pabbajjaṃ labhati. Upasampadatthikena pana nātikālena gāmappavesanādīni aṭṭha vattāni pūrentena parivasitabbaṃ. Āraddhacittāti aṭṭhavattapūraṇena tuṭṭhacittā. Ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthārato panesa titthiyaparivāso samantapāsādikāya vinayaṭṭhakathāya pabbajjakkhandhakavaṇṇanāyaṃ (mahāva. aṭṭha. 86) vuttanayeneva veditabbo.

“May I obtain”: this he said, aspiring to the state of a bhikkhu in the presence of the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One spoke with reference to the probation for former adherents of other sects that was laid down in the Khandhaka, which a former adherent, while standing in the stage of a novice, undertakes and observes in the following manner: “Venerable sir, I, of such-and-such a name, a former adherent of another sect, desire the higher ordination in this Dhamma and Discipline. I, venerable sir, request a four-month probation from the Saṅgha.” Referring to this, the Blessed One said, “Whoever, Kassapa, was formerly an adherent of another sect,” and so on. Therein, “going forth” is mentioned for the sake of verbal elegance, for one obtains the going forth even without observing the probation. However, one who desires the higher ordination must observe the probation, fulfilling the eight duties, such as entering a village, not too soon. “With pleased minds” means with minds delighted by the fulfillment of the eight duties. This is the summary here. But in detail, this probation for former adherents of other sects should be understood according to the method stated in the commentary on the Pabbajjakkhandhaka in the Samantapāsādikā, the commentary on the Vinaya.

Apica mayāti ayamettha pāṭho, aññattha pana “apica metthā”ti. Puggalavemattatā viditāti puggalanānattaṃ viditaṃ. “Ayaṃ puggalo parivāsāraho, ayaṃ na parivāsāraho”ti idaṃ mayhaṃ pākaṭanti dasseti. Tato kassapo cintesi – “aho acchariyaṃ buddhasāsanaṃ, yattha evaṃ ghaṃsitvā koṭṭetvā yuttameva gaṇhanti, ayuttaṃ chaḍḍentī”ti. Tato suṭṭhutaraṃ pabbajjāya sañjātussāho [V 2.0034] sace, bhantetiādimāha. Atha bhagavā tassa tibbacchandataṃ viditvā “na kassapo parivāsaṃ arahatī”ti aññataraṃ bhikkhuṃ āmantesi – “gaccha, bhikkhu, kassapaṃ nahāpetvā pabbājetvā ānehī”ti. So tathā katvā taṃ pabbājetvā bhagavato santikaṃ agamāsi. Bhagavā gaṇe nisīditvā upasampādesi. Tena vuttaṃ alattha kho acelo kassapo bhagavato santike pabbajjaṃ, alattha upasampadanti. Acirūpasampannotiādi sesaṃ brāhmaṇasaṃyutte (saṃ. ni. 1.187) vuttamevāti. Sattamaṃ.

Herein, the reading is “apica mayā,” but elsewhere it is “apica metthā.” “The diversity of individuals is known” means the difference among individuals is known. He shows: “This is clear to me: ‘This person is worthy of probation; this person is not worthy of probation.’” Then Kassapa thought: “Oh, how wonderful is the Buddha's Teaching, wherein they accept only the suitable and reject the unsuitable after rubbing and striking in this way!” Then, with even greater enthusiasm for the going forth having arisen, he said, “If, venerable sir,” and so on.
