Then the Blessed One, knowing his intense desire, thought, “Kassapa is not deserving of probation,” and addressed a certain bhikkhu: “Go, bhikkhu, bathe Kassapa, give him the going forth, and bring him here.” Having done so, that bhikkhu gave him the going forth and went to the Blessed One. The Blessed One, sitting amidst the assembly, conferred the higher ordination. Therefore it was said: “The naked ascetic Kassapa obtained the going forth in the presence of the Blessed One; he obtained the higher ordination.” The remainder, beginning with “Not long after his higher ordination,” has already been stated in the Brāhmaṇasaṃyutta. The Seventh.

8. Timbarukasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Timbaruka Sutta

18. Aṭṭhame [M 2.0036] sā vedanātiādi “sayaṃkataṃ sukhadukkha”nti laddhiyā nisedhanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Etthāpi satoti bhummattheyeva sāmivacanaṃ. Tatrāyaṃ atthadīpanā – “sā vedanā, so vediyatī”ti kho, timbaruka, ādimhiyeva evaṃ sati “sayaṃkataṃ sukhadukkha”nti ayaṃ laddhi hoti. Evañhi sati vedanāya eva [P 2.0038] vedanā katā hoti. Evañca vadanto imissā vedanāya pubbepi atthitaṃ anujānāti, sassataṃ dīpeti sassataṃ gaṇhāti. Kasmā? Tassa hi taṃ dassanaṃ etaṃ pareti, etaṃ sassataṃ upagacchatīti attho. Purimañhi atthaṃ sandhāyevetaṃ bhagavatā vuttaṃ bhavissati, tasmā aṭṭhakathāyaṃ taṃ yojetvāvassa attho dīpito. Evampāhaṃ na vadāmīti ahaṃ “sā vedanā, so vediyatī”ti evampi na vadāmi. “Sayaṃkataṃ sukhadukkha”nti evampi na vadāmīti attho.

18. In the eighth sutta, the passage beginning “that feeling” was spoken to refute the view that “pleasure and pain are self-made.” Herein also, the word ‘sato’ is a possessive case word used in the sense of the locative. Therein, this is the explanation of the meaning: “That feeling is the self; that one experiences.” When this is so from the very beginning, Timbaruka, this view arises: “pleasure and pain are self-made.” For when this is so, feeling is made by feeling itself. And one speaking thus admits the prior existence of this feeling, proclaims eternalism, and adopts eternalism. Why? Because that view of his approaches this, it approaches this eternalism; this is the meaning. For the Blessed One must have spoken this with reference to the meaning in the previous sutta. Therefore, in the commentary, the meaning of this sutta is explained only by connecting it to that. “I do not say thus” means: I do not say, “That feeling is the self; that one experiences,” nor do I say, “Pleasure and pain are self-made.”

Aññā vedanātiādi “paraṃkataṃ sukhadukkha”nti laddhiyā paṭisedhanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Idhāpi ayaṃ atthayojanā –“aññā vedanā añño vediyatī”ti kho, timbaruka, ādimhiyeva evaṃ sati pacchā yā purimapakkhe kārakavedanā, sā ucchinnā. Tāya pana kataṃ añño vediyatīti evaṃ uppannāya ucchedadiṭṭhiyā saddhiṃ sampayuttāya vedanāya abhitunnassa sato “paraṃkataṃ sukhadukkha”nti ayaṃ laddhi hoti. Evañca vadanto kārako ucchinno, aññena paṭisandhi gahitāti ucchedaṃ dīpeti, ucchedaṃ gaṇhāti. Kasmā? Tassa hi taṃ dassanaṃ etaṃ pareti, etaṃ ucchedaṃ upagacchatīti attho. Idhāpi hi imāni padāni aṭṭhakathāyaṃ āharitvā yojitāneva. Imasmiṃ sutte vedanāsukhadukkhaṃ kathitaṃ. Tañca kho vipākasukhadukkhameva vaṭṭatīti vuttaṃ. Aṭṭhamaṃ.

The passage beginning “Another is feeling” was spoken to refute the view that “pleasure and pain are made by another.” Herein also, this is the application of the meaning: “Another is feeling; another experiences.” When this is so from the very beginning, Timbaruka, then afterwards the agent-feeling of the previous phase is annihilated. Then, for one who is pierced by a feeling associated with the annihilationist view that has arisen—namely, that what is done by one is experienced by another—this view arises: “pleasure and pain are made by another.” And one speaking thus proclaims annihilation and adopts annihilation, saying: “The agent is annihilated; rebirth-linking is taken up by another.” Why? Because that view of his approaches this, it approaches this annihilationism; this is the meaning. Indeed, here too, these words were brought forth and applied in the commentary. In this sutta, the pleasure and pain of feeling was taught. And it is said that this is properly only the pleasure and pain that is resultant. The Eighth.

9. Bālapaṇḍitasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Bālapaṇḍita Sutta

19. Navame [V 2.0035] avijjānīvaraṇassāti avijjāya nivāritassa. Evamayaṃ kāyo samudāgatoti evaṃ avijjāya nivāritattā taṇhāya ca sampayuttattāyeva ayaṃ kāyo nibbatto. Ayañceva kāyoti ayañcassa attano saviññāṇako kāyo. Bahiddhā ca nāmarūpanti bahiddhā ca paresaṃ saviññāṇako kāyo. Attano ca parassa ca pañcahi [M 2.0037] khandhehi chahi āyatanehi cāpi ayaṃ attho dīpetabbova. Itthetaṃ dvayanti evametaṃ dvayaṃ. Dvayaṃ paṭicca phassoti aññattha cakkhurūpādīni dvayāni paṭicca cakkhusamphassādayo vuttā, idha pana ajjhattikabāhirāni [P 2.0039] āyatanāni. Mahādvayaṃ nāma kiretaṃ. Saḷevāyatanānīti saḷeva phassāyatanāni phassakāraṇāni. Yehi phuṭṭhoti yehi kāraṇabhūtehi āyatanehi uppannena phassena phuṭṭho. Aññatarenāti ettha paripuṇṇavasena aññataratā veditabbā. Tatrāti tasmiṃ bālapaṇḍitānaṃ kāyanibbattanādimhi. Ko adhippayāsoti ko adhikapayogo.

19. In the ninth sutta, 'hindered by ignorance' means of one who is hindered by ignorance. 'Thus this body has come to be' means: thus, this body is produced precisely because of being hindered by ignorance and because of being associated with craving. 'This very body' refers to this conscious body of his own. 'And externally, name-and-form' refers to the conscious body of others. This meaning of 'body' should be explained by way of the five aggregates and six sense bases of oneself and of others. 'Thus this duality' means: thus this pair comes to be. As for 'contact dependent on duality': elsewhere, the Blessed One taught eye-contact and so on dependent on the pairs of eye and form, etc., having analyzed them. But here, without analyzing them, he taught eye-contact and so on dependent on the six internal and external sense bases as 'contact dependent on duality'. This is indeed called the 'great duality.' 'The six sense bases' means just the six bases for contact, the causes of contact. 'Touched by which' means touched by the contact that has arisen from those sense bases which have become the cause. 'By one or the other'—here, the state of being 'one or the other' should be understood by way of completeness or incompleteness. 'There' means in that arising of the body, etc., of the foolish and the wise. 'What is the intention?' means what is the additional application.

Bhagavaṃmūlakāti bhagavā mūlaṃ etesanti bhagavaṃmūlakā. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – ime, bhante, amhākaṃ dhammā pubbe kassapasammāsambuddhena uppāditā, tasmiṃ parinibbute ekaṃ buddhantaraṃ añño samaṇo vā brāhmaṇo vā ime dhamme uppādetuṃ samattho nāma nāhosi, bhagavatā pana no ime dhammā uppāditā. Bhagavantañhi nissāya mayaṃ ime dhamme ājānāma paṭivijjhāmāti evaṃ bhagavaṃmūlakā no, bhante, dhammāti. Bhagavaṃnettikāti bhagavā hi dhammānaṃ netā vinetā anunetā, yathāsabhāvato pāṭiyekkaṃ pāṭiyekkaṃ nāmaṃ gahetvā dassetāti dhammā bhagavaṃnettikā nāma honti. Bhagavaṃpaṭisaraṇāti catubhūmakadhammā sabbaññutaññāṇassa āpāthaṃ āgacchamānā bhagavati paṭisaranti nāmāti bhagavaṃpaṭisaraṇā. Paṭisarantīti samosaranti. Apica mahābodhimaṇḍe nisinnassa bhagavato paṭivedhavasena phasso āgacchati “ahaṃ bhagavā kinnāmo”ti? Tvaṃ phusanaṭṭhena phasso nāma. Vedanā, saññā, saṅkhārā, viññāṇaṃ āgacchati “ahaṃ bhagavā kinnāma”nti, tvaṃ vijānanaṭṭhena viññāṇaṃ nāmāti evaṃ catubhūmakadhammānaṃ yathāsabhāvato pāṭiyekkaṃ pāṭiyekkaṃ nāmaṃ gaṇhanto bhagavā dhamme paṭisaratīti bhagavaṃpaṭisaraṇā. Bhagavantaṃyeva paṭibhātūti bhagavatova etassa bhāsitassa attho upaṭṭhātu, tumheyeva no kathetvā dethāti attho.

'Rooted in the Blessed One' means the Blessed One is the root for these dhammas; therefore, they are called 'rooted in the Blessed One'. This is what is said: 'Venerable sir, these dhammas of ours were first produced by Kassapa, the Fully Enlightened One. When he attained final Nibbāna, for a whole Buddha-interval, no other ascetic or brahmin was capable of producing these dhammas. But now, these dhammas have been produced for us by the Blessed One. Relying on the Blessed One, we know and penetrate these dhammas.' Thus, 'Venerable sir, our dhammas are rooted in the Blessed One.' 'Guided by the Blessed One' means the Blessed One is the leader, trainer, and one who guides fittingly of the dhammas. He teaches by taking up the name of each one individually according to its own nature; therefore, the dhammas are called 'guided by the Blessed One'. 'Having the Blessed One as their resort': The dhammas of the four planes, coming into the range of the omniscience-knowledge, converge in the Blessed One; therefore, they are called 'having the Blessed One as their resort'. 'They resort' means they converge. Furthermore, for the Blessed One seated at the site of the great awakening, contact came to him by way of penetration, asking, 'Blessed One, what is my name?' 'You are called 'contact' in the sense of touching.' Feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness came, asking, 'Blessed One, what is my name?' 'You are called 'consciousness' in the sense of cognizing.' Thus, by taking up the name of each of the dhammas of the four planes individually according to its own nature, the Blessed One penetrates the dhammas; for this reason too, they are called 'having the Blessed One as their resort'. 'May it become clear to the Blessed One' means: may the meaning of this utterance become clear to the Blessed One alone; may you yourself explain and give it to us.

Sā [V 2.0036] ceva avijjāti ettha kiñcāpi sā avijjā ca taṇhā ca kammaṃ javāpetvā paṭisandhiṃ ākaḍḍhitvā niruddhā, yathā pana ajjāpi yaṃ hiyyo bhesajjaṃ pītaṃ, tadeva bhojanaṃ bhuñjāti sarikkhakattena tadevāti vuccati, evamidhāpi [P 2.0040] sā ceva avijjā sā ca taṇhāti idampi sarikkhakattena vuttaṃ. Brahmacariyanti [M 2.0038] maggabrahmacariyaṃ. Dukkhakkhayāyāti vaṭṭadukkhassa khayatthāya. Kāyūpago hotīti aññaṃ paṭisandhikāyaṃ upagantā hoti. Yadidaṃ brahmacariyavāsoti yo ayaṃ maggabrahmacariyavāso, ayaṃ bālato paṇḍitassa visesoti dasseti. Iti imasmiṃ sutte sabbopi sapaṭisandhiko puthujjano “bālo”ti, appaṭisandhiko khīṇāsavo “paṇḍito”ti vutto. Sotāpannasakadāgāmianāgāmino pana “paṇḍitā”ti vā “bālā”ti vā na vattabbā, bhajamānā pana paṇḍitapakkhaṃ bhajanti. Navamaṃ.

As for 'And that very ignorance': Here, although that ignorance and that craving, having impelled kamma and having drawn out rebirth-linking, have ceased, yet just as, due to similarity, it is said 'that very thing'—like when one says of the medicine drunk yesterday, 'that very medicine was drunk,' or of the food eaten, 'that very food was eaten'—so too here, this phrase 'that very ignorance, that very craving' was spoken by the Blessed One due to similarity. 'The holy life' means the holy life of the path. 'For the destruction of suffering' means for the purpose of the destruction of the suffering of the round of existence. 'He goes to a body' means he is one who goes to another rebirth-linking body. 'That is, the living of the holy life': this living of the holy life of the path shows the distinction of the wise person from the fool. Thus, in this sutta, every worldling who is subject to rebirth-linking is called a 'fool', and the taint-freed one who is not subject to rebirth-linking is called 'wise'. However, stream-enterers, once-returners, and non-returners should not be called either 'wise' or 'fools'; but in their practice, they follow the side of the wise. The ninth is finished.

10. Paccayasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Discourse on Conditions

20. Dasame paṭiccasamuppādañca vo bhikkhave, desessāmi paṭiccasamuppanne ca dhammeti satthā imasmiṃ sutte paccaye ca paccayanibbatte ca sabhāvadhamme desessāmīti ubhayaṃ ārabhi. Uppādā vā tathāgatānanti tathāgatānaṃ uppādepi, buddhesu uppannesu anuppannesupi jātipaccayā jarāmaraṇaṃ, jātiyeva jarāmaraṇassa paccayo. Ṭhitāva sā dhātūti ṭhitova so paccayasabhāvo, na kadāci jāti jarāmaraṇassa paccayo na hoti. Dhammaṭṭhitatā dhammaniyāmatāti imehipi dvīhi paccayameva katheti. Paccayena hi paccayuppannā dhammā tiṭṭhanti, tasmā paccayova “dhammaṭṭhitatā”ti vuccati. Paccayo dhamme niyameti, tasmā “dhammaniyāmatā”ti vuccati. Idappaccayatāti imesaṃ jarāmaraṇādīnaṃ paccayā idappaccayā, idappaccayāva idappaccayatā. Tanti taṃ paccayaṃ. Abhisambujjhatīti ñāṇena abhisambujjhati. Abhisametīti ñāṇena abhisamāgacchati. Ācikkhatīti katheti. Desetīti dasseti. Paññāpetīti jānāpeti. Paṭṭhapetīti ñāṇamukhe ṭhapeti. Vivaratīti vivaritvā dasseti. Vibhajatīti vibhāgato dasseti. Uttānīkarotīti pākaṭaṃ karoti. Passathāti cāhāti passatha iti ca vadati. Kinti? Jātipaccayā, bhikkhave, jarāmaraṇantiādi.

20. In the tenth discourse, regarding the passage, 'Monks, I will teach you dependent origination and dependently arisen phenomena,' the Teacher, intending, 'In this discourse, I will teach both the conditioning phenomena in their own nature and the phenomena produced by conditions in their own nature,' undertook to teach both. Regarding 'Whether Tathāgatas arise or not...': whether in the arising of Tathāgatas, whether Buddhas have arisen or have not arisen, with birth as condition, there is aging and death; birth itself is the condition for aging and death. Regarding 'That element remains established': that nature of conditionality is established. It is not that birth is sometimes not a condition for aging and death; it is always so. By these two terms, 'the stability of phenomena' and 'the lawfulness of phenomena,' the Blessed One speaks only of the condition. For, dependently arisen phenomena are established by a condition; therefore, the condition itself is called 'the stability of phenomena.' The condition determines the phenomena; therefore, it is called 'the lawfulness of phenomena.' Regarding 'specific conditionality': the conditions for these, such as aging and death, are specific conditions; these very specific conditions are 'specific conditionality.' 'That' means that condition. 'He fully awakens to' means he fully awakens to it with knowledge. 'He comprehends' means he arrives at it with knowledge. 'He declares' means he speaks. 'He teaches' means he shows. 'He makes known' means he causes to know. 'He establishes' means he places it at the forefront of knowledge. 'He reveals' means having opened it up, he shows it. 'He analyzes' means he shows it by way of division. 'He makes it plain' means he makes it manifest. 'And he says, "See!"' means he also says, "See!" What does he say? He says the words beginning with, 'Monks, with birth as condition, there is aging and death...'

Iti [P 2.0041] kho, bhikkhaveti evaṃ kho, bhikkhave. Yā tatrāti yā tesu “jātipaccayā jarāmaraṇa”ntiādīsu. Tathatātiādīni paccayākārasseva vevacanāni. So tehi tehi paccayehi [V 2.0037] anūnādhikeheva tassa tassa dhammassa sambhavato tathatāti, sāmaggiṃ upagatesu paccayesu muhuttampi tato nibbattānaṃ dhammānaṃ asambhavābhāvato avitathatāti, aññadhammapaccayehi [M 2.0039] aññadhammānuppattito anaññathatāti, jarāmaraṇādīnaṃ paccayato vā paccayasamūhato vā idappaccayatāti vutto. Tatrāyaṃ vacanattho – imesaṃ paccayā idappaccayā, idappaccayā eva idappaccayatā, idappaccayānaṃ vā samūho idappaccayatā. Lakkhaṇaṃ panettha saddasatthato veditabbaṃ.

'Thus indeed, monks' means 'Thus indeed, monks.' 'That which is therein' refers to that which is in those statements such as, 'With birth as condition, there is aging and death.' The terms beginning with 'suchness' are indeed synonyms for the mode of conditionality. That mode of conditionality, because of the arising of this or that phenomenon from just those particular conditions, neither less nor more, is called 'suchness' (tathatā). Because, when the conditions have come together, there is no non-arising of the phenomena produced from them even for a moment, it is called 'unfalsifiedness' (avitathatā). Because another phenomenon does not arise from the conditions for a different phenomenon, it is called 'non-otherness' (anaññathatā). It is called 'specific conditionality' (idappaccayatā) by the Blessed One either because it is the condition for aging and death and so on, or because it is the collection of their conditions. Therein, this is the meaning of the word: the conditions for these are specific conditions; specific conditions themselves are specific conditionality; or, the collection of specific conditions is specific conditionality. Here, however, the grammatical rule should be known from the science of grammar.

Aniccanti hutvā abhāvaṭṭhena aniccaṃ. Ettha ca aniccanti na jarāmaraṇaṃ aniccaṃ, aniccasabhāvānaṃ pana khandhānaṃ jarāmaraṇattā aniccaṃ nāma jātaṃ. Saṅkhatādīsupi eseva nayo. Ettha ca saṅkhatanti paccayehi samāgantvā kataṃ. Paṭiccasamuppannanti paccaye nissāya uppannaṃ. Khayadhammanti khayasabhāvaṃ. Vayadhammanti vigacchanakasabhāvaṃ. Virāgadhammanti virajjanakasabhāvaṃ. Nirodhadhammanti nirujjhanakasabhāvaṃ. Jātiyāpi vuttanayeneva aniccatā veditabbā. Janakapaccayānaṃ vā kiccānubhāvakkhaṇe diṭṭhattā ekena pariyāyenettha aniccātiādīni yujjantiyeva. Bhavādayo aniccādisabhāvāyeva.

‘Impermanent’ means impermanent in the sense of non-existence after having come to be. And here, ‘impermanent’ does not mean that aging and death are impermanent in themselves; rather, because it is the aging and death of the aggregates, which have an impermanent nature, it is called ‘impermanent’ by extension. This same method applies to ‘conditioned’ and so on. And here, ‘conditioned’ means made by conditions having come together. ‘Dependently arisen’ means arisen in dependence on conditions. ‘Subject to destruction’ means having the nature of destruction. ‘Subject to vanishing’ means having the nature of passing away. ‘Subject to fading away’ means having the nature of dispassion. ‘Subject to cessation’ means having the nature of ceasing. The impermanence of birth, too, should be understood by the method already stated. Alternatively, because the generative conditions are seen at the moment of their effective function, by one method the terms ‘impermanent,’ and so on, are indeed applicable here. Becoming and so on are, by their very nature, impermanent, etc.

Sammappaññāyāti savipassanāya maggapaññāya. Pubbantanti purimaṃ atītanti attho. Ahosiṃ nu khotiādīsu “ahosiṃ nu kho nanu kho”ti sassatākārañca adhiccasamuppattiākārañca nissāya atīte attano vijjamānatañca avijjamānatañca kaṅkhati. Kiṃ kāraṇanti na vattabbaṃ, ummattako viya bālaputhujjano yathā vā tathā vā pavattati. Kiṃ nu kho ahosinti jātiliṅgupapattiyo nissāya “khattiyo nu kho ahosiṃ, brāhmaṇavessasuddagahaṭṭhapabbajitadevamanussānaṃ aññataro”ti kaṅkhati. Kathaṃ nu khoti [P 2.0042] saṇṭhānākāraṃ nissāya “dīgho nu kho ahosiṃ rassaodātakaṇhapamāṇikaappamāṇikādīnaṃ aññataro”ti kaṅkhati. Keci pana “issaranimmānādīni nissāya ‘kena nu kho kāraṇena ahosi’nti hetuto kaṅkhatī”ti vadanti. Kiṃ hutvā kiṃ ahosinti jātiādīni nissāya “khattiyo hutvā nu kho brāhmaṇo ahosiṃ…pe… devo hutvā manusso”ti attano paramparaṃ kaṅkhati. Sabbattheva pana addhānanti kālādhivacanametaṃ. Aparantanti anāgataṃ antaṃ. Bhavissāmi nu kho nanu khoti sassatākārañca ucchedākārañca nissāya anāgate attano vijjamānatañca avijjamānatañca kaṅkhati. Sesamettha vuttanayameva.

‘With right wisdom’ means with the wisdom of the path that is accompanied by insight. ‘The past end’ means the former, the past; this is the meaning. In passages such as ‘Was I indeed?’, regarding ‘Was I indeed? Was I not indeed?’, one doubts one’s own existence and non-existence in the past, based on the mode of eternalism and the mode of accidental origination. One should not ask, ‘For what reason?’; for the foolish worldling, like a madman, proceeds in any which way. Regarding ‘What, indeed, was I?’, based on birth, characteristics, and rebirth, one doubts, ‘Was I a khattiya, or some other among brahmins, vessas, suddas, householders, renunciants, devas, and humans?’ Regarding ‘How, indeed, was I?’, based on the mode of physical form, one doubts, ‘Was I tall, or some other among the short, fair, dark, of medium size, of immeasurable size, and so on?’ But some say, ‘Based on creation by a lord, and so on, one doubts about the cause, thinking, “For what reason, indeed, did I exist?”’ Regarding ‘Having been what, what was I?’, based on birth and so on, one doubts one’s own succession, thinking, ‘Having been a khattiya, was I a brahmin? … Having been a deva, was I a human?’ In all cases, ‘addhāna’ is a term for time. ‘The future end’ means the future end. Regarding ‘Will I be? Will I not be?’, one doubts one’s own existence and non-existence in the future, based on the mode of eternalism and the mode of annihilationism. The remainder here is by the method already stated.

Etarahi [V 2.0038][M 2.0040] vā paccuppannaṃ addhānanti idāni vā paṭisandhimādiṃ katvā cutipariyantaṃ sabbampi vattamānakālaṃ gahetvā. Ajjhattaṃ kathaṃkathī bhavissatīti attano khandhesu vicikicchī bhavissati. Ahaṃ nu khosmīti attano atthibhāvaṃ kaṅkhati. Yuttaṃ panetanti? Yuttaṃ ayuttanti kā ettha cintā. Apicettha idaṃ vatthumpi udāharanti – cūḷamātāya kira putto muṇḍo, mahāmātāya putto amuṇḍo, taṃ puttaṃ muṇḍesuṃ, so uṭṭhāya “ahaṃ nu kho cūḷamātāya putto”ti cintesi. Evaṃ ahaṃ nu khosmīti kaṅkhā hoti. No nu khosmīti attano natthibhāvaṃ kaṅkhati. Tatrāpi idaṃ vatthu – eko kira macche gaṇhanto udake ciraṭṭhānena sītibhūtaṃ attano ūruṃ macchoti cintetvā pahari. Aparo susānapasse khettaṃ rakkhanto bhīto saṅkuṭito sayi, so paṭibujjhitvā attano jaṇṇukāni dve yakkhāti cintetvā pahari. Evaṃ no nu khosmīti kaṅkhati.

‘Now’ or ‘the present time’ means taking the entire present period, from rebirth-linking as the beginning up to death as the limit. ‘He will be doubtful internally’ means he will be doubtful about his own aggregates. ‘Am I indeed?’ means he doubts his own existence. Is this then appropriate? What consideration is there of appropriate or inappropriate in this? Moreover, in this connection they also cite this story: It is said that the younger mother’s son was bald, while the elder mother’s son was not bald. They shaved that son, and upon arising, he thought, ‘Am I indeed the younger mother’s son?’ Thus the doubt, ‘Am I indeed?’ arises. ‘Am I not indeed?’ means he doubts his own non-existence. In that case too, there is this story: It is said that a certain person, while catching fish, struck his own thigh, which had become cold from standing in the water for a long time, thinking, ‘It is a fish.’ Another person, while guarding a field near a charnel ground, lay down curled up in fear. Upon awakening, he struck his own knees, thinking, ‘They are two yakkhas.’ Thus he doubts, ‘Am I not indeed?’

Kiṃ nu khosmīti khattiyova samāno attano khattiyabhāvaṃ kaṅkhati. Eseva nayo sesesupi. Devo pana samāno devabhāvaṃ ajānanto nāma natthi, sopi pana “ahaṃ rūpī nu kho arūpī nu kho”tiādinā nayena kaṅkhati. Khattiyādayo kasmā na jānantīti ce? Apaccakkhā [P 2.0043] tesaṃ tattha tattha kule uppatti. Gahaṭṭhāpi ca potthalikādayo pabbajitasaññino, pabbajitāpi “kuppaṃ nu kho me kamma”ntiādinā nayena gahaṭṭhasaññino. Manussāpi ca rājāno viya attani devasaññino honti. Kathaṃ nu khosmīti vuttanayameva. Kevalañhettha abbhantare jīvo nāma atthīti gahetvā tassa saṇṭhānākāraṃ nissāya “dīgho nu khosmi rassacaturassachaḷaṃsaaṭṭhaṃsasoḷasaṃsādīnaṃ aññatarappakāro”ti kaṅkhanto kathaṃ nu khosmīti? Kaṅkhatīti veditabbo. Sarīrasaṇṭhānaṃ pana paccuppannaṃ ajānanto nāma natthi. Kuto āgato so kuhiṃ gāmī bhavissatīti attabhāvassa āgatigatiṭṭhānaṃ kaṅkhanto evaṃ kaṅkhati. Ariyasāvakassāti idha sotāpanno adhippeto, itarepi pana tayo avāritāyevāti. Dasamaṃ.

‘What am I indeed?’ means: being a khattiya, he doubts his own state of being a khattiya. This same method should be understood for the others as well. But there is no deva who, being a deva, does not know his state of being a deva; however, he too doubts in the manner of, ‘Am I indeed with form, or am I indeed without form?’ and so on. If it is asked, ‘Why do the khattiyas and others not know?’ It is because their birth in those respective families is not directly perceived. And householders, such as Potaliya and others, have the perception of being renunciants; and renunciants too, in the manner of ‘Is my monastic act corrupt indeed?’ and so on, have the perception of being householders. And humans, like kings, have the perception of being devas in themselves. ‘How am I indeed?’ is just in the manner already stated. Only here, having grasped that ‘there is a so-called soul within,’ and relying on its shape and form, one who doubts, ‘Am I indeed tall, or some other kind among the short, square, six-angled, eight-angled, sixteen-angled, and so on?’—it should be understood that he doubts, ‘How am I indeed?’ But there is no one who does not know the present shape of the body. Doubting the coming, going, and station of his existence—‘From where has this being come? Where will it go?’—he doubts thus. Here, by ‘of a noble disciple,’ a stream-enterer is intended, but the other three are also not excluded. The Tenth.

Āhāravaggo dutiyo.

The Chapter on Nutriment, the Second.

3. Dasabalavaggo

3. The Chapter on the Ten Powers

1. Dasabalasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Explanation of the Discourse on the Ten Powers

21. Dasabalavaggassa [V 2.0039][M 2.0041] paṭhamaṃ dutiyasseva saṅkhepo.

21. The first sutta of the Chapter on the Ten Powers is but a summary of the second.

2. Dutiyadasabalasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Explanation of the Second Discourse on the Ten Powers

22. Dutiyaṃ bhagavatā attano ajjhāsayassa vasena vuttaṃ. Tattha dasabalasamannāgatoti dasahi balehi samannāgato. Balañca nāmetaṃ duvidhaṃ kāyabalañca ñāṇabalañca. Tesu tathāgatassa kāyabalaṃ hatthikulānusārena veditabbaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ porāṇehi –

22. The second was spoken by the Blessed One according to his own inclination. Herein, ‘endowed with the ten powers’ means endowed with the ten powers. And this power is of two kinds: bodily power and power of knowledge. Among these, the bodily power of the Tathāgata should be understood according to the lineage of elephants. For this was said by the ancients:

“Kāḷāvakañca gaṅgeyyaṃ, paṇḍaraṃ tambapiṅgalaṃ;

Gandhamaṅgalahemañca, uposathachaddantime dasā”ti.(ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.148; vibha. aṭṭha. 760); –

“Kāḷāvaka and Gaṅgeyya, Paṇḍara, Tamba, and Piṅgala; Gandha, Maṅgala, and Hema, Uposatha and Chaddanta—these ten.”

Imāni dasa hatthikulāni. Tattha kāḷāvakanti pakatihatthikulaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Yaṃ dasannaṃ purisānaṃ kāyabalaṃ, taṃ ekassa kāḷāvakassa hatthino. Yaṃ dasannaṃ kāḷāvakānaṃ balaṃ, taṃ ekassa gaṅgeyyassa. Yaṃ dasannaṃ [P 2.0044] gaṅgeyyānaṃ, taṃ ekassa paṇḍarassa. Yaṃ dasannaṃ paṇḍarānaṃ, taṃ ekassa tambassa. Yaṃ dasannaṃ tambānaṃ, taṃ ekassa piṅgalassa. Yaṃ dasannaṃ piṅgalānaṃ, taṃ ekassa gandhahatthino. Yaṃ dasannaṃ gandhahatthīnaṃ, taṃ ekassa maṅgalassa. Yaṃ dasannaṃ maṅgalānaṃ, taṃ ekassa hemavatassa. Yaṃ dasannaṃ hemavatānaṃ, taṃ ekassa uposathassa. Yaṃ dasannaṃ uposathānaṃ, taṃ ekassa chaddantassa. Yaṃ dasannaṃ chaddantānaṃ, taṃ ekassa tathāgatassa. Nārāyanasaṅghātabalantipi idameva vuccati. Tadetaṃ pakatihatthigaṇanāya hatthīnaṃ koṭisahassānaṃ, purisagaṇanāya dasannaṃ purisakoṭisahassānaṃ balaṃ hoti. Idaṃ tāva tathāgatassa kāyabalaṃ. “Dasabalasamannāgato”ti ettha pana etaṃ saṅgahaṃ na gacchati. Etañhi bāhirakaṃ lāmakaṃ tiracchānagatānaṃ sīhādīnampi hoti. Etañhi nissāya dukkhapariññā vā samudayappahānaṃ vā maggabhāvanā vā phalasacchikiriyā vā [V 2.0040] natthi. Aññaṃ pana dasasu ṭhānesu akampanatthena upatthambhanatthena ca dasavidhaṃ ñāṇabalaṃ nāma atthi. Taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “dasabalasamannāgato”ti.

These are the ten families of elephants. Therein, the Kāḷāvaka is to be regarded as the ordinary family of elephants. The bodily strength of ten men is that of one Kāḷāvaka elephant. The strength of ten Kāḷāvaka elephants is that of one Gaṅgeyya; of ten Gaṅgeyya, that of one Paṇḍara; of ten Paṇḍara, that of one Tamba; of ten Tamba, that of one Piṅgala; of ten Piṅgala, that of one Gandha elephant; of ten Gandha elephants, that of one Maṅgala; of ten Maṅgala, that of one Hemavata; of ten Hemavata, that of one Uposatha; of ten Uposatha, that of one Chaddanta; of ten Chaddanta, that of one Tathāgata. This is also called Nārāyana's compact strength. This is the strength of a thousand koṭis of ordinary elephants, or by the count of men, the strength of ten thousand koṭis of men. This, for now, is the Tathāgata's bodily strength. However, in the phrase 'endowed with the ten powers,' this is not included. For this is external, inferior, and belongs even to animals such as lions. Relying on this, there is no full understanding of suffering, or abandoning of the origin, or development of the path, or realization of the fruit. But there is another, a tenfold power of knowledge, so called because of its unshakable nature and its supportive nature in ten instances. It is with reference to this that it was said, 'endowed with the ten powers.'

Katamaṃ [M 2.0042] pana tanti? Ṭhānāṭṭhānādīnaṃ yathābhūtaṃ jānanaṃ. Seyyathidaṃ – ṭhānañca ṭhānato aṭṭhānañca aṭṭhānato jānanaṃ ekaṃ, atītānāgatapaccuppannānaṃ kammasamādānānaṃ ṭhānaso hetuso yathābhūtaṃ vipākajānanaṃ ekaṃ, sabbatthagāminipaṭipadājānanaṃ ekaṃ, anekadhātunānādhātulokajānanaṃ ekaṃ, parasattānaṃ parapuggalānaṃ nānādhimuttikatājānanaṃ ekaṃ, tesaṃyeva indriyaparopariyattajānanaṃ ekaṃ, jhānavimokkhasamādhisamāpattīnaṃ saṃkilesavodānavuṭṭhānajānanaṃ ekaṃ, pubbenivāsajānanaṃ ekaṃ, sattānaṃ cutūpapātajānanaṃ ekaṃ, āsavakkhayajānanaṃ ekanti. Abhidhamme pana –

What, then, is this? It is the knowledge of cause and non-cause, etc., as they really are. That is to say: 1. The knowledge of cause as cause and what is not a cause as not a cause, is one. 2. The knowledge of the result of actions undertaken in the past, future, and present, with their conditions and causes, as they really are, is one. 3. The knowledge of the path that leads everywhere, is one. 4. The knowledge of the world with its many and various elements, is one. 5. The knowledge of the various dispositions of other beings and individuals, is one. 6. The knowledge of the superiority and inferiority of the faculties of those same beings, is one. 7. The knowledge of the defilement, purification, and emergence regarding the absorptions, liberations, concentrations, and attainments, is one. 8. The knowledge of previous existences, is one. 9. The knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings, is one. 10. The knowledge of the destruction of the taints, is one. But in the Abhidhamma:

“Idha tathāgato ṭhānañca ṭhānato aṭṭhānañca aṭṭhānato yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti. Yampi tathāgato ṭhānañca ṭhānato aṭṭhānañca aṭṭhānato yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti. Idampi tathāgatassa tathāgatabalaṃ hoti, yaṃ balaṃ āgamma tathāgato āsabhaṃ ṭhānaṃ paṭijānāti[P 2.0045], parisāsu sīhanādaṃ nadati, brahmacakkaṃ pavattetī”ti.

“Here, the Tathāgata understands as it really is cause as cause and what is not a cause as not a cause. In that the Tathāgata understands as it really is cause as cause and what is not a cause as not a cause, this too is a power of the Tathāgata. Relying on this power, the Tathāgata claims the foremost position, utters his lion's roar in the assemblies, and sets rolling the Brahma-wheel.”

Ādinā (vibha. 760) nayena vitthārato āgatāneva. Atthavaṇṇanāpi nesaṃ vibhaṅgaṭṭhakathāyañceva (vibha. aṭṭha. 760) papañcasūdaniyā ca majjhimaṭṭhakathāya (ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.148) sabbākārato vuttā. Sā tattha vuttanayeneva gahetabbā.

These are found in detail by the method beginning with the passage cited (Vibhaṅga 760). The explanation of their meaning has also been stated in all aspects in the Vibhaṅga Commentary (Vibhaṅga-aṭṭhakathā 760) and in the Papañcasūdanī, the Majjhima Nikāya Commentary (Majjhima Nikāya-aṭṭhakathā 1.148). It should be understood in the same way as it is stated there.

Catūhi ca vesārajjehīti ettha sārajjapaṭipakkhaṃ vesārajjaṃ, catūsu ṭhānesu vesārajjabhāvaṃ paccavekkhantassa uppannasomanassamayañāṇassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Katamesu catūsu? “Sammāsambuddhassa te paṭijānato ime dhammā anabhisambuddhā”tiādīsu codanāvatthūsu. Tatrāyaṃ pāḷi –

And 'with the four kinds of fearlessness': Herein, fearlessness (vesārajja) is the opposite of timidity (sārajja). This is a name for the knowledge accompanied by joy that arises for one who reflects on the state of fearlessness in four instances. In which four? In the grounds for accusation such as, 'Though you claim to be a Perfectly Enlightened One, these things have not been fully awakened to by you,' and so on. Herein, this is the Pāli text:

“Cattārimāni, bhikkhave, tathāgatassa vesārajjāni…pe…. Katamāni cattāri? ‘Sammāsambuddhassa te paṭijānato ime dhammā anabhisambuddhā’ti tatra vata maṃ samaṇo vā brāhmaṇo vā devo vā māro vā brahmā vā koci vā lokasmiṃ saha dhammena [V 2.0041] paṭicodessatīti nimittametaṃ, bhikkhave, na samanupassāmi. Etamahaṃ, bhikkhave, nimittaṃ asamanupassanto khemappatto abhayappatto vesārajjappatto viharāmi. ‘Khīṇāsavassa te paṭijānato [M 2.0043] ime āsavā aparikkhīṇā’ti tatra vata maṃ…pe… ‘ye kho pana te antarāyikā dhammā vuttā, te paṭisevato nālaṃ antarāyāyā’ti tatra vata maṃ…pe… ‘yassa kho pana te atthāya dhammo desito, so na niyyāti takkarassa sammā dukkhakkhayāyā’ti tatra vata maṃ samaṇo vā brāhmaṇo vā…pe… vesārajjappatto viharāmī”ti (a. ni. 4.8).

“Monks, there are these four kinds of fearlessness of the Tathāgata... Which four? ‘Though you claim to be a Perfectly Enlightened One, these things have not been fully awakened to by you’—I do not see any ground, monks, on which any ascetic or brahmin or god or Māra or Brahmā or anyone in the world could rightfully challenge me on this. Not seeing any such ground, monks, I dwell having attained security, attained fearlessness, and attained confidence. ‘Though you claim to be one whose taints are destroyed, these taints are not completely destroyed’—... I do not see any ground... ‘Those things declared by you to be obstructions are not able to obstruct one who engages in them’—... I do not see any ground... ‘The Dhamma taught by you for a certain purpose does not lead the one who practices it to the complete destruction of suffering’—I do not see any ground, monks, on which any ascetic or brahmin... could rightfully challenge me on this. Not seeing any such ground, I dwell having attained security, attained fearlessness, and attained confidence.” (Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.8)

Āsabhaṃ ṭhānanti seṭṭhaṭṭhānaṃ uttamaṭṭhānaṃ. Āsabhā vā pubbabuddhā, tesaṃ ṭhānanti attho. Apica gavasatajeṭṭhako usabho, gavasahassajeṭṭhako vasabho, vajasatajeṭṭhako vā usabho, vajasahassajeṭṭhako vasabho, sabbagavaseṭṭho sabbaparissayasaho seto pāsādiko mahābhāravaho asanisatasaddehipi asampakampiyo nisabho, so idha usabhoti adhippeto. Idampi hi tassa pariyāyavacanaṃ. Usabhassa idanti āsabhaṃ. Ṭhānanti catūhi pādehi pathaviṃ uppīḷetvā avaṭṭhānaṃ (ma. ni. 1.150). Idaṃ pana āsabhaṃ viyāti āsabhaṃ. Yatheva hi nisabhasaṅkhāto usabho usabhabalena [P 2.0046] samannāgato catūhi pādehi pathaviṃ uppīḷetvā acalaṭṭhānena tiṭṭhati, evaṃ tathāgatopi dasahi tathāgatabalehi samannāgato catūhi vesārajjapādehi aṭṭhaparisapathaviṃ uppīḷetvā sadevake loke kenaci paccatthikena paccāmittena akampiyo acalaṭṭhānena tiṭṭhati. Evaṃ tiṭṭhamāno ca taṃ āsabhaṃ ṭhānaṃ paṭijānāti upagacchati na paccakkhāti, attani āropeti. Tena vuttaṃ “āsabhaṃ ṭhānaṃ paṭijānātī”ti.

“The bull-like state” means: the foremost state, the supreme state. Or, the previous Buddhas are the ‘bulls’ (āsabhā); the meaning is ‘their state’. Furthermore, the chief of a hundred cows is an usabha; the chief of a thousand cows is a vasabha; or the chief of a hundred herds is an usabha; the chief of a thousand herds is a vasabha. The nisabha is the best of all cattle, enduring all dangers, white, inspiring, bearing great loads, and unshaken even by the sounds of a hundred thunderclaps; that one is intended here by usabha. For this too is a synonym for that. “Belonging to the bull” (usabhassa idaṃ) is āsabhaṃ. “State” (ṭhānaṃ) means standing firm, having pressed down on the earth with four feet. But this is like a bull (āsabhaṃ viya), therefore it is called āsabhaṃ. For just as a bull known as nisabha, endowed with a bull's strength, stands with an unshakeable stance, having pressed down on the earth with four feet, so too the Tathāgata, endowed with the ten Tathāgata-powers, stands with an unshakeable stance, having pressed down on the ‘earth’ of the eight assemblies with the four ‘feet’ of the fearlessnesses, being unshaken by any adversary or enemy in the world with its devas. And standing thus, he claims that bull-like state, attains it, does not reject it, and applies it to himself. Therefore it is said, “He claims the bull-like state.”

Parisāsūti “aṭṭha kho imā, sāriputta, parisā. Katamā aṭṭha? Khattiyaparisā brāhmaṇaparisā gahapatiparisā samaṇaparisā cātumahārājikaparisā tāvatiṃsaparisā māraparisā brahmaparisā”ti, imāsu aṭṭhasu parisāsu. Sīhanādaṃ nadatīti seṭṭhanādaṃ abhītanādaṃ nadati, sīhanādasadisaṃ vā nādaṃ nadati. Ayamattho sīhanādasuttena dīpetabbo. Yathā vā sīho sahanato ceva hananato ca sīhoti vuccati, evaṃ tathāgato lokadhammānaṃ sahanato parappavādānañca hananato sīhoti vuccati. Evaṃ vuttassa sīhassa nādaṃ sīhanādaṃ. Tattha yathā sīho sīhabalena samannāgato sabbattha visārado vigatalomahaṃso sīhanādaṃ [M 2.0044] nadati, evaṃ tathāgatasīhopi tathāgatabalehi samannāgato aṭṭhasu parisāsu visārado vigatalomahaṃso, “iti rūpa”ntiādinā [V 2.0042] nayena nānāvidhadesanāvilāsasampannaṃ sīhanādaṃ nadati. Tena vuttaṃ “parisāsu sīhanādaṃ nadatī”ti.

“In the assemblies” means: in these eight assemblies—“There are, Sāriputta, these eight assemblies. Which eight? The assembly of nobles, the assembly of brahmins, the assembly of householders, the assembly of ascetics, the assembly of the Four Great Kings, the assembly of the Thirty-three, the assembly of Māra, and the assembly of Brahmā.” “He roars the lion's roar” means: he utters the supreme roar, the fearless roar; or, he utters a roar similar to a lion's roar. This meaning should be explained by the Lion's Roar Sutta. Or, just as a lion is called a sīha because of enduring (sahana) and striking (hanana), so too the Tathāgata is called a sīha because of enduring worldly conditions and striking down the doctrines of others. The roar of a lion so described is a lion's roar. Just as a lion, endowed with a lion's strength, is confident everywhere, with hair-raising gone, and utters a lion's roar, so too the Tathāgata-lion, endowed with the Tathāgata-powers, is confident in the eight assemblies, with hair-raising gone, and utters a lion's roar endowed with the grace of manifold teachings, by way of “Thus is form,” and so forth. Therefore it is said, “He roars the lion’s roar in the assemblies.”

Brahmacakkaṃ pavattetīti ettha brahmanti seṭṭhaṃ uttamaṃ, visuddhassa dhammacakkassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Taṃ pana dhammacakkaṃ duvidhaṃ hoti paṭivedhañāṇañca desanāñāṇañca. Tattha paññāpabhāvitaṃ attano ariyaphalāvahaṃ paṭivedhañāṇaṃ, karuṇāpabhāvitaṃ sāvakānaṃ ariyaphalāvahaṃ desanāñāṇaṃ. Tattha paṭivedhañāṇaṃ uppajjamānaṃ uppannanti duvidhaṃ. Tañhi abhinikkhamanato paṭṭhāya yāva arahattamaggā uppajjamānaṃ, phalakkhaṇe uppannaṃ nāma. Tusitabhavanato vā yāva mahābodhipallaṅke arahattamaggā uppajjamānaṃ, phalakkhaṇe uppannaṃ nāma. Dīpaṅkarato vā paṭṭhāya yāva arahattamaggā uppajjamānaṃ[P 2.0047], phalakkhaṇe uppannaṃ nāma. Desanāñāṇampi pavattamānaṃ pavattanti duvidhaṃ. Tañhi yāva aññāsikoṇḍaññassa sotāpattimaggā pavattamānaṃ, phalakkhaṇe pavattaṃ nāma. Tesu paṭivedhañāṇaṃ lokuttaraṃ, desanāñāṇaṃ lokiyaṃ. Ubhayampi panetaṃ aññehi asādhāraṇaṃ buddhānaṃyeva orasañāṇaṃ.

Herein, regarding ‘He sets rolling the Brahma-wheel,’ ‘Brahma’ means supreme, excellent; it is a designation for the immaculate Dhamma-wheel. Now, that Dhamma-wheel is of two kinds: the knowledge of penetration and the knowledge of teaching. Therein, the knowledge of penetration, brought about by wisdom, brings the noble fruit to oneself; the knowledge of teaching, brought about by compassion, brings the noble fruit to the disciples. Therein, the knowledge of penetration is twofold: arising and arisen. For, from the great renunciation up to the path of Arahantship, it is ‘arising’; at the moment of fruition, it is called ‘arisen.’ Or, from the Tusita realm up to the path of Arahantship at the great Bodhi-seat, it is ‘arising’; at the moment of fruition, it is called ‘arisen.’ Or, starting from the time of Dīpaṅkara up to the path of Arahantship, it is ‘arising’; at the moment of fruition, it is called ‘arisen.’ The knowledge of teaching is also twofold: occurring and occurred. For, up to the path of stream-entry of Aññāsi Koṇḍañña, it is ‘occurring’; at the moment of fruition, it is called ‘occurred.’ Among these, the knowledge of penetration is supramundane, and the knowledge of teaching is mundane. But both of these, being unshared with others, are the very innate knowledge of the Buddhas alone.

Idāni yaṃ iminā ñāṇena samannāgato sīhanādaṃ nadati, taṃ dassetuṃ iti rūpantiādimāha. Tattha iti rūpanti idaṃ rūpaṃ ettakaṃ rūpaṃ, ito uddhaṃ rūpaṃ natthīti ruppanasabhāvañceva bhūtupādāyabhedañca ādiṃ katvā lakkhaṇarasapaccupaṭṭhānapadaṭṭhānavasena anavasesarūpapariggaho vutto. Iti rūpassa samudayoti iminā evaṃ pariggahitassa rūpassa samudayo vutto. Tattha itīti evaṃ samudayo hotīti attho. Tassa vitthāro “avijjāsamudayā rūpasamudayo taṇhāsamudayā, kammasamudayā āhārasamudayā rūpasamudayoti nibbattilakkhaṇaṃ passantopi rūpakkhandhassa udayaṃ passatī”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.50) evaṃ veditabbo. Atthaṅgamepi “avijjānirodhā rūpanirodho…pe… vipariṇāmalakkhaṇaṃ passantopi rūpakkhandhassa nirodhaṃ passatī”ti ayaṃ vitthāro.

Now, to show the lion's roar that he, endowed with this knowledge, roars, the Blessed One spoke, beginning with ‘Such is form.’ Herein, by ‘such is form,’ is stated the complete comprehension of form without remainder—meaning, ‘This is form, this much is form; beyond this there is no form’—by way of its characteristic, function, manifestation, and proximate cause, beginning with its nature of being afflicted and its distinction into primary and derived matter. By ‘Such is the arising of form,’ the arising of form thus comprehended is stated. Herein, ‘such’ means ‘in this way it arises.’ Its detailed explanation should be understood thus: ‘From the arising of ignorance, there is the arising of form; from the arising of craving, from the arising of kamma, from the arising of nutriment, there is the arising of form. Thus, one who sees the characteristic of production also sees the arising of the aggregate of form.’ In the case of cessation as well, this is the detailed explanation: ‘From the cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of form… (etc.)… one who sees the characteristic of alteration also sees the cessation of the aggregate of form.’”

Iti vedanātiādīsupi ayaṃ vedanā ettakā vedanā, ito uddhaṃ vedanā natthi, ayaṃ saññā, ime saṅkhārā, idaṃ viññāṇaṃ ettakaṃ viññāṇaṃ[M 2.0045], ito uddhaṃ viññāṇaṃ natthīti vedayitasañjānanaabhisaṅkharaṇavijānanasabhāvañceva sukhādirūpasaññādiphassādicakkhuviññāṇādibhedañca ādiṃ katvā lakkhaṇarasapaccupaṭṭhānapadaṭṭhānavasena anavasesavedanāsaññāsaṅkhāraviññāṇapariggaho [V 2.0043] vutto. Iti vedanāya samudayotiādīhi pana evaṃ pariggahitānaṃ vedanāsaññāsaṅkhāraviññāṇānaṃ samudayo vutto. Tatrāpi itīti evaṃ samudayo hotīti attho. Tesampi vitthāro “avijjāsamudayā vedanāsamudayo”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.50) rūpe vuttanayeneva veditabbo. Ayaṃ pana viseso – tīsu khandhesu “āhārasamudayā”ti avatvā “phassasamudayā”ti vattabbaṃ, viññāṇakkhandhe “nāmarūpasamudayā”ti. Atthaṅgamapadampi tesaṃyeva vasena yojetabbaṃ. Ayamettha saṅkhepo. Vitthārato pana udayabbayavinicchayo sabbākāraparipūro visuddhimagge vutto.

Thus, in such Pali passages as 'iti vedanā' (thus is feeling), this is feeling; feeling is this much; beyond this, there is no feeling. This is perception; these are formations; this is consciousness; consciousness is this much; beyond this, there is no consciousness. In this way, having taken as the starting point the nature of feeling, perceiving, forming, and knowing, as well as the distinctions such as pleasant feeling, perception of form, contact, eye-consciousness, and so on, the comprehension of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness without remainder, by way of characteristic, function, manifestation, and proximate cause, was spoken of. Furthermore, by such passages as 'Thus, the arising of feeling,' the arising of these feelings, perceptions, formations, and consciousnesses that have been thus comprehended was spoken of. Therein, 'iti' means 'in this way the arising occurs.' The detailed explanation of these should also be understood in the very same way as was stated in the section on form: 'Due to the arising of ignorance, there is the arising of feeling.' This, however, is the distinction: for the three aggregates, instead of saying 'due to the arising of nutriment,' it should be said 'due to the arising of contact'; for the consciousness aggregate, 'due to the arising of name-and-form.' The term for cessation should also be connected by way of those very same factors. This is the summary here. But as for the detailed explanation, the determination of arising and passing away, complete in all aspects, was spoken by me in the Visuddhimagga.

Imasmiṃ [P 2.0048] sati idaṃ hotīti ayampi aparo sīhanādo. Tassattho – imasmiṃ avijjādike paccaye sati idaṃ saṅkhārādikaṃ phalaṃ hoti. Imassuppādā idaṃ uppajjatīti imassa avijjādikassa paccayassa uppādā idaṃ saṅkhārādikaṃ phalaṃ uppajjati. Imasmiṃ asati idaṃ na hotīti imasmiṃ avijjādike paccaye asati idaṃ saṅkhārādikaṃ phalaṃ na hoti. Imassa nirodhā idaṃ nirujjhatīti imassa avijjādikassa paccayassa nirodhā idaṃ saṅkhārādikaṃ phalaṃ nirujjhati. Idāni yathā taṃ hoti ceva nirujjhati ca, taṃ vitthārato dassetuṃ yadidaṃ avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārātiādimāha.

When this is, that is—this too is another lion's roar. Its meaning is this: When this condition, such as ignorance, is present, this result, such as formations, comes to be. 'From the arising of this, that arises' means: from the arising of this condition, such as ignorance, this result, such as formations, arises. 'When this is not, that is not' means: when this condition, such as ignorance, is not present, this result, such as formations, does not come to be. 'From the cessation of this, that ceases' means: from the cessation of this condition, such as ignorance, this result, such as formations, ceases. Now, in order to show in detail how that both comes to be and ceases, the Blessed One said that which is 'With ignorance as condition, formations...'

Evaṃ svākkhātoti evaṃ pañcakkhandhavibhajanādivasena suṭṭhu akkhāto kathito. Dhammoti pañcakkhandhapaccayākāradhammo. Uttānoti anikujjito. Vivaṭoti vivaritvā ṭhapito. Pakāsitoti dīpito jotito. Chinnapilotikoti pilotikā vuccati chinnaṃ bhinnaṃ tattha tattha sibbitagaṇṭhitaṃ jiṇṇavatthaṃ, taṃ yassa natthīti aṭṭhahatthaṃ navahatthaṃ vā ahatasāṭakaṃ nivattho, so chinnapilotiko nāma. Ayampi dhammo tādiso. Na hettha kohaññādivasena chinnabhinnasibbitagaṇṭhitabhāvo atthi. Apica khuddakasāṭakopi pilotikāti vuccati, sā yassa natthi, aṭṭhanavahattho mahāpaṭo atthi, sopi chinnapilotiko, apagatapilotikoti attho. Tādiso ayaṃ dhammo. Yathā hi catuhatthaṃ sāṭakaṃ [M 2.0046] gahetvā pariggahaṇaṃ karonto puriso ito cito ca añchanto kilamati, evaṃ bāhirakasamaye pabbajitā attano parittakaṃ dhammaṃ “evaṃ sati evaṃ bhavissatī”ti kappetvā kappetvā vaḍḍhentā kilamanti. Yathā pana aṭṭhahatthanavahatthena pariggahaṇaṃ karonto yathāruci pārupati na kilamati, natthi tattha añchitvā vaḍḍhanakiccaṃ; evaṃ imasmimpi dhamme kappetvā kappetvā vibhajanakiccaṃ natthi, tehi tehi kāraṇehi mayāva ayaṃ dhammo suvibhatto suvitthāritoti idampi sandhāya “chinnapilotiko”ti āha. Apica [P 2.0049] kacavaropi [V 2.0044] pilotikāti vuccati, imasmiñca sāsane samaṇakacavaraṃ nāma patiṭṭhātuṃ na labhati. Tenevāha –

`Evaṃ svākkhāto` (Thus well-expounded) means: thus, by way of the analysis of the five aggregates and so on, it is well declared and spoken. `Dhammo` (the Dhamma) means: the Dhamma of the conditional structure of the five aggregates of clinging. `Uttāno` (made plain) means: not turned upside down. `Vivaṭo` (uncovered) means: laid open after being revealed. `Pakāsito` (illuminated) means: made clear, lit up. `Chinnapilotiko` (without patchwork) means: `pilotikā` is said of old cloth that is torn, rent, and stitched and patched here and there. One for whom that does not exist, who wears an unbleached cloth of eight or nine cubits, is called `chinnapilotiko`. This Dhamma is also like that. For in this Dhamma, there is no state of being torn, rent, stitched, and patched by way of hypocrisy, etc. Moreover, a small cloth is also called `pilotikā`. One for whom that does not exist, but has a large cloth of eight or nine cubits, is also `chinnapilotiko`, meaning `apagatapilotiko` (one who is without a `pilotikā`). This Dhamma is like that. For just as a person who takes a four-cubit cloth and tries to wear it becomes weary pulling it from here and there, so too, those gone forth in outside dispensations become weary expanding their own limited Dhamma by repeatedly speculating, 'If this is so, it will be so.' But just as one who wears an eight- or nine-cubit cloth wraps himself as he likes and does not become weary, as there is no need to expand it by pulling; so too in this Dhamma, there is no need for analysis through repeated speculation. With reference to this meaning also—'For these and those reasons, this Dhamma has been well-analyzed and well-expounded by me alone'—the Blessed One said `chinnapilotiko`. Moreover, rubbish is also called `pilotikā`. And in this Dispensation, so-called ascetic-rubbish does not get to be established. Therefore, he said:

“Kāraṇḍavaṃ niddhamatha, kasambuṃ apakassatha;

Tato palāpe vāhetha, assamaṇe samaṇamānine.

“Expel the rubbish-like monks, drag out the worthless ones! Then winnow away the chaff—those who are not ascetics, yet are conceited that they are.

“Niddhamitvāna pāpicche, pāpaācāragocare;

Suddhā suddhehi saṃvāsaṃ, kappayavho patissatā;

Tato samaggā nipakā, dukkhassantaṃ karissathā”ti. (a. ni. 8.10);

“Having expelled those with evil wishes, whose conduct and resort are evil, you who are pure, being respectful towards one another, should associate with the pure. Then, united and endowed with wisdom, you will make an end to suffering.”

Iti samaṇakacavarassa chinnattāpi ayaṃ dhammo chinnapilotiko nāma hoti.

Thus, because the ascetic-rubbish has been cut off, this Dhamma is also called `chinnapilotiko` (Without Patchwork).

Alamevāti yuttameva. Saddhāpabbajitenāti saddhāya pabbajitena. Kulaputtenāti dve kulaputtā ācārakulaputto jātikulaputto ca. Tattha yo yato kutoci kulā pabbajitvā sīlādayo pañca dhammakkhandhe pūreti, ayaṃ ācārakulaputto nāma. Yo pana yasakulaputtādayo viya jātisampannakulā pabbajito, ayaṃ jātikulaputto nāma. Tesu idha ācārakulaputto adhippeto. Sace pana jātikulaputto ācāravā hoti, ayaṃ uttamoyeva. Evarūpena kulaputtena. Vīriyaṃ ārabhitunti caturaṅgasamannāgataṃ vīriyaṃ kātuṃ. Idānissa caturaṅgaṃ dassento kāmaṃ taco cātiādimāha. Ettha hi taco ekaṃ aṅgaṃ, nhāru ekaṃ, aṭṭhi ekaṃ, maṃsalohitaṃ ekanti. Idañca pana caturaṅgasamannāgataṃ vīriyaṃ adhiṭṭhahantena navasu ṭhānesu samādhātabbaṃ purebhatte pacchābhatte purimayāme majjhimayāme pacchimayāme gamane ṭhāne nisajjāya sayaneti.

`Alameva` means: it is indeed fitting. `Saddhāpabbajitena` means: by one who has gone forth through faith. `Kulaputtena`: there are two sons of good family: the son of good family by conduct and the son of good family by birth. Therein, whoever, having gone forth from whatever family, fulfills the five aggregates of Dhamma such as virtue, this one is called a son of good family by conduct. But whoever, like the son of good family Yasa and others, has gone forth from a family endowed with high birth, this one is called a son of good family by birth. Of these two, the son of good family by conduct is intended here. But if a son of good family by birth is possessed of good conduct, he is indeed the best. By such a son of good family. `Vīriyaṃ ārabhitun` means: to arouse energy endowed with four factors. Now, wishing to show its four factors, the words beginning with 'Willingly, let skin...' were said. Here, skin is one factor, sinews are one factor, bones are one factor, and flesh and blood are one factor. And this energy endowed with four factors, by one who is determined, should be established in nine instances: before the meal, after the meal, in the first watch, in the middle watch, in the last watch, in walking, in standing, in sitting, and in lying down.

Dukkhaṃ[M 2.0047], bhikkhave, kusīto viharatīti imasmiṃ sāsane yo kusīto puggalo, so dukkhaṃ viharati. Bāhirasamaye pana yo kusīto, so sukhaṃ viharati. Vokiṇṇoti missībhūto. Sadatthanti sobhanaṃ vā atthaṃ sakaṃ vā atthaṃ, ubhayenāpi arahattameva adhippetaṃ. Parihāpetīti hāpeti na pāpuṇāti. Kusītapuggalassa hi cha dvārāni aguttāni honti, tīṇi kammāni aparisuddhāni, ājīvaṭṭhamakaṃ sīlaṃ apariyodātaṃ, bhinnājīvo kulūpako hoti. So sabrahmacārīnaṃ akkhimhi patitarajaṃ viya upaghātakaro [P 2.0050] hutvā dukkhaṃ viharati, pīṭhamaddano ceva [V 2.0045] hoti laṇḍapūrako ca, satthu ajjhāsayaṃ gahetuṃ na sakkoti, dullabhaṃ khaṇaṃ virādheti, tena bhutto raṭṭhapiṇḍopi na mahapphalo hoti.

"Monks, the lazy person lives in suffering." Thus, in this Dispensation, whichever person is lazy, that person lives in suffering. ‘Vokiṇṇa’ means intermingled with unwholesome states. ‘Sadattha’ refers to either a beautiful purpose or one's own purpose; by the combination of both phrases, only Arahantship is intended. ‘Parihāpeti’ means he causes it to diminish, he does not attain it. For indeed, for a lazy person, the six doors are unguarded, the three actions are impure, the virtue with livelihood as the eighth is not perfectly pure, and he becomes a frequenter of families with a corrupted livelihood. Being harmful to his fellows in the holy life like dust fallen in the eye, he lives in suffering; he is both a presser of benches and a filler with excrement. He is not able to grasp the Teacher's intention, he misses the rare opportunity, and even the country's almsfood eaten by him is not of great fruit.

Āraddhavīriyo ca kho, bhikkhaveti āraddhavīriyo puggalo imasmiṃyeva sāsane sukhaṃ viharati. Bāhirasamaye pana yo āraddhavīriyo, so dukkhaṃ viharati. Pavivittoti vivitto viyutto hutvā. Sadatthaṃ paripūretīti arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti. Āraddhavīriyassa hi cha dvārāni suguttāni honti, tīṇi kammāni parisuddhāni, ājīvaṭṭhamakaṃ sīlaṃ pariyodātaṃ sabrahmacārīnaṃ akkhimhi susītalañjanaṃ viya dhātugatacandanaṃ viya ca manāpo hutvā sukhaṃ viharati, satthu ajjhāsayaṃ gahetuṃ sakkoti. Satthā hi –

"But, Bhikkhus, one with aroused effort dwells happily in this very Dispensation." In an external school, however, one who has aroused effort dwells in suffering. ‘Pavivitta’ means being secluded and disassociated from unwholesome states. ‘Sadatthaṃ paripūreti’ means he attains Arahantship. For indeed, for one with aroused effort, the six doors are well-guarded, the three actions are completely purified, and the virtue with livelihood as the eighth is perfectly pure. Being dear to his fellows in the holy life like a cooling collyrium for the eye and like sandalwood that captivates the heart, he dwells happily and is able to grasp the Teacher’s intention. For the Teacher—

“Ciraṃ jīva mahāvīra, kappaṃ tiṭṭha mahāmunī”ti –

"Live long, O Great Hero! Remain for an eon, O Great Sage!"

Evaṃ gotamiyā vandito, “na kho, gotami, tathāgatā evaṃ vanditabbā”ti paṭikkhipitvā tāya yācito vanditabbākāraṃ ācikkhanto evamāha –

When venerated thus by Gotamī, the Teacher, having rejected it by saying, "Gotamī, Tathāgatas are not to be venerated in this way," and being requested by her, explained the manner of veneration and spoke thus:

“Āraddhavīriye pahitatte, niccaṃ daḷhaparakkame;

Samagge sāvake passa, esā buddhāna vandanā”ti. (apa. therī 2.2.171);

"O one with aroused effort, O one with mind sent forth, O one ever firm in exertion! Behold the disciples in harmony. This is the veneration of the Buddhas."

Evaṃ āraddhavīriyo satthu ajjhāsayaṃ gahetuṃ sakkoti, dullabhaṃ khaṇaṃ na virādheti. Tassa hi buddhuppādo dhammadesanā saṅghasuppaṭipatti saphalā hoti saudrayā, raṭṭhapiṇḍopi tena bhutto mahapphalo hoti.

Thus, one with aroused effort is able to grasp the Teacher's intention and does not miss the rare opportunity. For such a person, the appearance of a Buddha, the teaching of the Dhamma, and the Sangha's good practice become fruitful and lead to growth. Even the country's almsfood eaten by him is of great fruit.

Hīnena [M 2.0048] aggassāti hīnāya saddhāya hīnena vīriyena hīnāya satiyā hīnena samādhinā hīnāya paññāya aggasaṅkhātassa arahattassa patti nāma na hoti. Aggena ca khoti aggehi saddhādīhi aggassa arahattassa patti hoti. Maṇḍapeyyanti pasannaṭṭhena maṇḍaṃ, pātabbaṭṭhena peyyaṃ. Yañhi pivitvā antaravīthiyaṃ patito visaññī attano sāṭakādīnampi assāmiko hoti, taṃ [V 2.0046] pasannampi na pātabbaṃ, mayhaṃ pana sāsanaṃ [P 2.0051] evaṃ pasannañca pātabbañcāti dassento “maṇḍapeyya”nti āha.

"By what is inferior, the highest": by inferior faith, inferior effort, inferior mindfulness, inferior concentration, and inferior wisdom, the attainment of Arahantship, which is designated as the highest, does not occur. "And by what is highest": by the highest qualities beginning with faith, the attainment of the highest Arahantship occurs. ‘Maṇḍapeyya’: ‘maṇḍa’ in the sense of being clear, ‘peyya’ in the sense of being drinkable. For if, having drunk a certain liquor, one falls down unconscious in the middle of the road and is not even the owner of one's own clothes, such a liquor, even if clear, should not be drunk. But showing that my Dispensation is thus both clear and fit to be drunk, the Blessed One said, "maṇḍapeyya."

Tattha tividho maṇḍo – desanāmaṇḍo, paṭiggahamaṇḍo, brahmacariyamaṇḍoti. Katamo desanāmaṇḍo? Catunnaṃ ariyasaccānaṃ ācikkhanā desanā paññāpanā paṭṭhapanā vivaraṇā vibhajanā uttānīkammaṃ, catunnaṃ satipaṭṭhānānaṃ…pe… ariyassa aṭṭhaṅgikassa maggassa ācikkhanā…pe… uttānīkammaṃ, ayaṃ desanāmaṇḍo. Katamo paṭiggahamaṇḍo? Bhikkhū bhikkhuniyo upāsakā upāsikāyo devā manussā ye vā panaññepi keci viññātāro, ayaṃ paṭiggahamaṇḍo. Katamo brahmacariyamaṇḍo? Ayameva ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo, seyyathidaṃ – sammādiṭṭhi…pe… sammāsamādhi, ayaṃ brahmacariyamaṇḍo. Apica adhimokkhamaṇḍo saddhindriyaṃ, assaddhiyaṃ kasaṭo, assaddhiyaṃ kasaṭaṃ chaḍḍetvā saddhindriyassa adhimokkhamaṇḍaṃ pivatīti maṇḍapeyyantiādināpi (paṭi. ma. 1.238) nayenettha attho veditabbo. Satthā sammukhībhūtoti idamettha kāraṇavacanaṃ. Yasmā satthā sammukhībhūto, tasmā vīriyasampayogaṃ katvā pivatha etaṃ maṇḍaṃ. Bāhirakañhi bhesajjamaṇḍampi vejjassa asammukhā pivantānaṃ pamāṇaṃ vā uggamanaṃ vā niggamanaṃ vā na jānāmāti āsaṅkā hoti. Vejjasammukhā pana “vejjo jānissatī”ti nirāsaṅkā pivanti. Evameva amhākaṃ dhammassāmi satthā sammukhībhūtoti vīriyaṃ katvā pivathāti maṇḍapāne nesaṃ niyojento tasmātiha, bhikkhavetiādimāha. Tattha saphalāti sānisaṃsā. Saudrayāti savaḍḍhi. Idāni niyojanānurūpaṃ sikkhitabbataṃ niddisanto attatthaṃ vā hi, bhikkhavetiādimāha. Tattha attatthanti attano atthabhūtaṃ arahattaṃ. Appamādena sampādetunti appamādena sabbakiccāni kātuṃ. Paratthanti paccayadāyakānaṃ mahapphalānisaṃsaṃ. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti. Dutiyaṃ.

Therein, the ‘maṇḍa’ is threefold: the maṇḍa of teaching, the maṇḍa of reception, and the maṇḍa of the holy life. What is the maṇḍa of teaching? It is the pointing out, teaching, proclaiming, establishing, disclosing, analyzing, and making plain of the Four Noble Truths; the pointing out... making plain of the four foundations of mindfulness... of the Noble Eightfold Path. This is the maṇḍa of teaching. What is the maṇḍa of reception? It is the monks, nuns, male lay followers, female lay followers, gods, humans, or any others who are knowers. This is the maṇḍa of reception. What is the maṇḍa of the holy life? It is this very Noble Eightfold Path, that is: right view... right concentration. This is the maṇḍa of the holy life. Furthermore, the meaning here should also be understood by the method beginning with 'maṇḍapeyya' (as in Paṭisambhidāmagga 1.238): The maṇḍa of conviction is the faith faculty, and faithlessness is the dreg; because one discards the dreg of faithlessness and drinks the maṇḍa of conviction of the faith faculty, it is called 'maṇḍapeyya'. 'The Teacher is present'—this is here a statement of reason. Because the Teacher is present, therefore, having applied effort, drink this maṇḍa. For indeed, when those of other schools drink even a medicinal elixir in the absence of a physician, there is anxiety, thinking, 'We do not know the proper measure, or whether it will cause vomiting or purging.' But in the presence of a physician, they drink without anxiety, thinking, 'The physician will know.' Just so, thinking, 'Our Teacher, the Lord of the Dhamma, is present,' make an effort and drink. Thus, urging them to drink the maṇḍa, the Blessed One said, 'Therefore, O monks,' and so on. Therein, 'fruitful' means 'with benefit.' 'With growth' means 'with increase.' Now, pointing out what should be practiced in accordance with this urging, the Blessed One said, 'For one’s own welfare, O monks,' and so on. Therein, 'one’s own welfare' means Arahantship, which is one’s own benefit. 'To accomplish with diligence' means to do all duties with diligence. 'For the welfare of others' means for the great fruit and benefit of the donors of requisites. The rest is clear in all respects. The second.

3. Upanisasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Discourse on Supporting Conditions

23. Tatiye [M 2.0049][P 2.0052] “jānato aha”ntiādīsu jānatoti jānantassa. Passatoti passantassa. Dvepi padāni ekatthāni, byañjanameva nānaṃ. Evaṃ santepi “jānato”ti ñāṇalakkhaṇaṃ upādāya puggalaṃ niddisati. Jānanalakkhaṇañhi ñāṇaṃ. “Passato”ti ñāṇappabhāvaṃ upādāya. Passanappabhāvañhi ñāṇaṃ, ñāṇasamaṅgīpuggalo cakkhumā viya cakkhunā rūpāni[V 2.0047], ñāṇena vivaṭe dhamme passati. Āsavānaṃ khayanti ettha āsavānaṃ pahānaṃ asamuppādo khīṇākāro natthibhāvoti ayampi āsavakkhayoti vuccati, bhaṅgopi maggaphalanibbānānipi. “Āsavānaṃ khayā anāsavaṃ cetovimutti”ntiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.438; vibha. 831) hi khīṇākāro āsavakkhayoti vuccati. “Yo āsavānaṃ khayo vayo bhedo paribhedo aniccatā antaradhāna”nti (vibha. 354) ettha bhaṅgo.

23. In the third discourse, in passages such as 'for one who knows,' the term 'for one who knows' means for one who is knowing. 'For one who sees' means for one who is seeing. Both terms have the same meaning; only the expression is different. Even so, with the term 'for one who knows,' the Blessed One indicates the person by way of the characteristic of knowledge, for knowledge has the characteristic of knowing. With the term 'for one who sees,' He indicates the person by way of the power of knowledge, for knowledge has the power of seeing. Just as a person with eyes sees forms with the eye, so a person endowed with knowledge sees with knowledge the supramundane dhammas that are the escape from the round of existence. In the phrase 'the destruction of the taints,' this can mean the abandonment of the taints, their non-arising, their state of being destroyed, their non-existence; this is called the destruction of the taints. Also their dissolution, as well as the path, fruition, and Nibbāna, are called thus. For in passages such as 'through the destruction of the taints, the taintless liberation of mind,' the state of being destroyed is called the destruction of the taints. In the passage 'whatever is the destruction, the passing away, the breaking up, the complete breaking up, the impermanence, the disappearance of the taints,' it refers to dissolution.

“Sekkhassa sikkhamānassa, ujumaggānusārino;

Khayasmiṃ paṭhamaṃ ñāṇaṃ, tato aññā anantarā”ti. (itivu. 62); –

“For a disciple in training, who is practicing, following the straight path, knowledge arises first in destruction, then immediately after, final knowledge.” (Itivuttaka 62)

Ettha maggo. So hi āsave khepento vūpasamento uppajjati, tasmā āsavānaṃ khayoti vutto. “Āsavānaṃ khayā samaṇo hotī”ti ettha phalaṃ. Tañhi āsavānaṃ khīṇante uppajjati, tasmā āsavānaṃ khayoti vuttaṃ.

Here, the path of Arahantship is called the destruction of the taints. For it arises destroying and pacifying the taints; therefore, it is called 'the destruction of the taints.' In the phrase 'Through the destruction of the taints, one becomes a recluse,' here fruition is called the destruction of the taints. For that fruition arises at the end of the destruction of the taints; therefore, it is called 'the destruction of the taints.'

“Āsavā tassa vaḍḍhanti, ārā so āsavakkhayā”ti; (Dha. pa. 253) –

“His taints increase; he is far from the destruction of the taints.” (Dhammapada 253)

Ettha nibbānaṃ. Tañhi āgamma āsavā khīyanti, tasmā āsavānaṃ khayoti vuttaṃ. Idha pana maggaphalāni adhippetāni. No ajānato no apassatoti yo pana na jānāti na passati, tassa no vadāmīti attho. Etena ye ajānato apassatopi saṃsārādīhiyeva suddhiṃ vadanti, te paṭikkhittā honti. Purimena padadvayena upāyo vutto, iminā anupāyaṃ paṭisedheti.

Here, Nibbāna is called the destruction of the taints. For having reached it, the taints are destroyed; therefore, it is called 'the destruction of the taints.' Here, however, the path and fruition are intended. 'Not for one who does not know, not for one who does not see' means, 'I do not declare it for one who does not know and does not see.' By this, the views of those who declare purification simply from the round of existence and so on, even without knowing and seeing, are rejected. By the first pair of terms, the means has been stated; by this latter pair, the non-means is rejected.

Idāni [P 2.0053] yaṃ jānato āsavānaṃ khayo hoti, taṃ dassetukāmo kiñca, bhikkhave, jānatoti pucchaṃ ārabhi. Tattha jānanā bahuvidhā. Dabbajātiko eva hi koci bhikkhu chattaṃ kātuṃ jānāti, koci cīvarādīnaṃ aññataraṃ, tassa īdisāni kammāni vattasīse ṭhatvā karontassa sā [M 2.0050] jānanā saggamaggaphalānaṃ padaṭṭhānaṃ na hotīti na vattabbaṃ. Yo pana sāsane pabbajitvā vejjakammādīni kātuṃ jānāti, tassevaṃ jānato āsavā vaḍḍhantiyeva. Tasmā yaṃ jānato passato ca āsavānaṃ khayo hoti, tadeva dassento iti rūpantiādimāha. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, jānatoti evaṃ pañcannaṃ khandhānaṃ udayabbayaṃ jānantassa. Āsavānaṃ khayo hotīti āsavānaṃ khayante jātattā “āsavānaṃ khayo”ti laddhanāmaṃ arahattaṃ hoti.

Now, wishing to show what it is that for one who knows brings about the destruction of the taints, the Blessed One began with the question, 'And what, monks, for one who knows...?' Herein, knowing is of many kinds. For some monk skilled in a craft may know how to make an umbrella, or another may know one of the crafts concerning robes and so on. It should not be said that for one performing such work while established in the foremost of duties, that knowledge is not a proximate cause for heaven, the path, and fruition. But for one who, having gone forth in the Dispensation, knows how to perform medical treatments and the like—for one knowing in this way, the taints only increase. Therefore, showing only that Dhamma, knowing and seeing which the destruction of the taints occurs, the Blessed One said, 'Thus is form,' and so on. 'Thus, monks, for one who knows' means: for one who knows in this way the arising and passing away of the five aggregates. 'The destruction of the taints occurs' means: Arahantship, which has received the name 'destruction of the taints' because it arises at the end of the destruction of the taints, occurs.

Evaṃ arahattanikūṭena [V 2.0048] desanaṃ niṭṭhapetvā idāni khīṇāsavassa āgamanīyaṃ pubbabhāgapaṭipadaṃ dassetuṃ yampissa taṃ, bhikkhavetiādimāha. Tattha khayasmiṃ khayeñāṇanti āsavakkhayasaṅkhāte arahattaphale paṭiladdhe sati paccavekkhaṇañāṇaṃ. Tañhi arahattaphalasaṅkhāte khayasmiṃ paṭhamavāraṃ uppanne pacchā uppannattā khayeñāṇanti vuccati. Saupanisanti sakāraṇaṃ sappaccayaṃ. Vimuttīti arahattaphalavimutti. Sā hissa upanissayapaccayena paccayo hoti. Evaṃ ito paresupi labbhamānavasena paccayabhāvo veditabbo.

Having thus concluded the discourse with the peak of Arahantship, now, in order to show the preliminary practice that leads to the state of one whose taints are destroyed, the Blessed One said, 'And that which for him, monks...' and so on. Therein, 'knowledge in destruction' is the reviewing knowledge that arises when the fruit of Arahantship, known as the destruction of the taints, has been attained. For since that reviewing knowledge arises afterwards, when the destruction—known as the fruit of Arahantship—has arisen for the first time, it is called 'knowledge in destruction.' 'With a supporting condition' means with a cause, with a condition. 'Liberation' is the liberation of the fruit of Arahantship. For that is a condition for this 'knowledge in destruction' by way of decisive support condition. In this way, for the subsequent terms also, the state of being a condition should be understood according to what is applicable.

Virāgoti maggo. So hi kilese virājento khepento uppanno, tasmā virāgoti vuccati. Nibbidāti nibbidāñāṇaṃ. Etena balavavipassanaṃ dasseti. Balavavipassanāti bhayatūpaṭṭhāne ñāṇaṃ ādīnavānupassane ñāṇaṃ muñcitukamyatāñāṇaṃ saṅkhārupekkhāñāṇanti catunnaṃ ñāṇānaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Yathābhūtañāṇadassananti yathāsabhāvajānanasaṅkhātaṃ dassanaṃ. Etena taruṇavipassanaṃ dasseti. Taruṇavipassanā hi balavavipassanāya paccayo hoti. Taruṇavipassanāti saṅkhāraparicchede ñāṇaṃ kaṅkhāvitaraṇe ñāṇaṃ sammasane ñāṇaṃ maggāmagge ñāṇanti catunnaṃ ñāṇānaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Samādhīti [P 2.0054] pādakajjhānasamādhi. So hi taruṇavipassanāya paccayo hoti. Sukhanti appanāya pubbabhāgasukhaṃ. Tañhi pādakajjhānassa paccayo hoti. Passaddhīti darathapaṭippassaddhi. Sā hi appanāpubbabhāgassa sukhassa paccayo hoti. Pītīti balavapīti. Sā hi darathapaṭippassaddhiyā paccayo hoti. Pāmojjanti dubbalapīti. Sā hi balavapītiyā paccayo hoti. Saddhāti aparāparaṃ uppajjanasaddhā. Sā hi dubbalapītiyā paccayo hoti. Dukkhanti vaṭṭadukkhaṃ. Tañhi aparāparasaddhāya paccayo hoti. Jātīti savikārā khandhajāti[M 2.0051]. Sā hi vaṭṭadukkhassa paccayo hoti. Bhavoti kammabhavo. (So hi savikārāya jātiyā paccayo hoti.) Etenupāyena sesapadānipi veditabbāni.

Dispassion is the path. For it arises while making the defilements fade away and destroying them; therefore, it is called dispassion. Revulsion is the knowledge of revulsion. By this is shown strong insight. Strong insight is a designation for four kinds of knowledge: the knowledge of appearance as terror, the knowledge of contemplating drawbacks, the knowledge of the desire for deliverance, and the knowledge of equanimity towards formations. Knowledge and vision of things as they actually are is the vision known as knowing things according to their true nature. By this is shown tender insight. For tender insight is a condition for strong insight. Tender insight is a designation for four kinds of knowledge: the knowledge of delimiting formations, the knowledge of overcoming doubt, the knowledge of comprehension, and the knowledge of the path and not-path. Concentration is the foundational jhāna concentration. For that is a condition for tender insight. Happiness is the happiness of the preliminary stage of absorption. For that is a condition for the foundational jhāna. Tranquility is the calming of distress. For that is a condition for the happiness of the preliminary stage of absorption. Rapture is strong rapture. For that is a condition for the calming of distress. Joy is weak rapture. For that is a condition for strong rapture. Faith is faith that arises again and again. For that is a condition for weak rapture. Suffering is the suffering of the round of existence. For that is a condition for faith that arises again and again. Birth is the birth of the aggregates, which is subject to alteration. For that is a condition for the suffering of the round of existence. Existence is kamma-existence. (For that is a condition for birth which is subject to alteration.) By this method, the remaining terms should also be understood.

Thullaphusitaketi mahāphusitake. Pabbatakandarapadarasākhāti ettha kandaraṃ nāma ‘ka’ntiladdhanāmena udakena dārito udakabhinno pabbatapadeso, yo “nitambo”tipi “nadīkuñcho”tipi vuccati. Padaraṃ nāma aṭṭhamāse deve avassante phalito bhūmippadeso. Sākhāti kusumbhagāminiyo khuddakamātikāyo. Kusobbhāti khuddakaāvāṭā. Mahāsobbhāti mahāāvāṭā. Kunnadiyoti khuddakanadiyo. Mahānadiyoti gaṅgāyamunādikā mahāsaritā. Evameva kho[V 2.0049], bhikkhave, avijjūpanisā saṅkhārātiādīsu avijjā pabbatoti daṭṭhabbā. Abhisaṅkhārā meghoti, viññāṇādivaṭṭaṃ kandarādayoti, vimutti sāgaroti.

Thullaphusitaka means having large raindrops. In the compound Pabbatakandarapadarasākhā: here, kandara is a mountain area split by water, so named from ‘kaṃ’ (water); it is also called ‘nitamba’ and ‘nadīkuñcha’. Padara is an area of land that is cracked when it does not rain for eight months. Sākhā means small channels leading to a kusumbha. Kusobbha means small hollows. Mahāsobbha means large hollows. Kunnadiyo means small rivers. Mahānadiyo means great rivers like the Ganges and Yamuna. Just so, monks, in the passage beginning ‘volitional formations are conditioned by ignorance,’ ignorance should be seen as the mountain. Volitional formations should be seen as the cloud, the round of existence beginning with consciousness as the ravines and so on, and liberation as the ocean.

Yathā pabbatamatthake [P 2.0055] devo vassitvā pabbatakandarādīni pūrento anupubbena mahāsamuddaṃ sāgaraṃ pūreti, evaṃ avijjāpabbatamatthake tāva abhisaṅkhārameghassa vassanaṃ veditabbaṃ. Assutavā hi bālaputhujjano avijjāya aññāṇī hutvā taṇhāya abhilāsaṃ katvā kusalākusalakammaṃ āyūhati, taṃ kusalākusalakammaṃ paṭisandhiviññāṇassa paccayo hoti, paṭisandhiviññāṇādīni nāmarūpādīnaṃ. Iti pabbatamatthake vuṭṭhadevassa kandarādayo pūretvā mahāsamuddaṃ āhacca ṭhitakālo viya avijjāpabbatamatthake vuṭṭhassa abhisaṅkhārameghassa paramparapaccayatāya anupubbena viññāṇādivaṭṭaṃ pūretvā ṭhitakālo. Buddhavacanaṃ pana pāḷiyaṃ agahitampi “idha tathāgato loke uppajjati, agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajatī”ti imāya pāḷiyā vasena gahitamevāti veditabbaṃ. Yā hi tassa kulagehe nibbatti, sā kammabhavapaccayā savikārā jāti nāma. So buddhānaṃ vā buddhasāvakānaṃ vā sammukhībhāvaṃ āgamma vaṭṭadosadīpakaṃ lakkhaṇāhaṭaṃ dhammakathaṃ sutvā vaṭṭavasena pīḷito hoti, evamassa savikārā khandhajāti vaṭṭadukkhassa paccayo hoti. So vaṭṭadukkhena pīḷito aparāparaṃ saddhaṃ janetvā agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajati, evamassa vaṭṭadukkhaṃ aparāparasaddhāya paccayo hoti. So pabbajjāmatteneva asantuṭṭho ūnapañcavassakāle nissayaṃ [M 2.0052] gahetvā vattapaṭipattiṃ pūrento dvemātikā paguṇaṃ katvā kammākammaṃ uggahetvā yāva arahattā nijjaṭaṃ katvā kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā araññe vasanto pathavīkasiṇādīsu kammaṃ ārabhati, tassa kammaṭṭhānaṃ nissāya dubbalapīti uppajjati. Tadassa saddhūpanisaṃ pāmojjaṃ, taṃ balavapītiyā paccayo hoti. Balavapīti darathapaṭippassaddhiyā, sā appanāpubbabhāgasukhassa, taṃ sukhaṃ pādakajjhānasamādhissa. So samādhinā cittakallataṃ janetvā taruṇavipassanāya kammaṃ karoti. Iccassa pādakajjhānasamādhi taruṇavipassanāya paccayo hoti, taruṇavipassanā balavavipassanāya, balavavipassanā maggassa, maggo phalavimuttiyā, phalavimutti paccavekkhaṇañāṇassāti[P 2.0056]. Evaṃ devassa anupubbena sāgaraṃ pūretvā ṭhitakālo viya khīṇāsavassa vimuttisāgaraṃ pūretvā ṭhitakālo veditabboti. Tatiyaṃ.

Just as rain falling on a mountain peak fills the mountain’s caves and crevices and gradually fills the great ocean, the sea, so too, first of all, should the raining of the cloud of formations on the peak of the mountain of ignorance be understood. For the uninstructed, foolish worldling, being ignorant through ignorance and forming a desire through craving, strives in wholesome and unwholesome kamma. That wholesome and unwholesome kamma becomes the condition for rebirth-linking consciousness, and rebirth-linking consciousness and so on for name-and-form and so on. Thus, just as the time when the rain that has fallen on the mountain peak, having filled the ravines and so on, stands having reached the great ocean, so too is the time when the cloud of formations that has rained on the peak of the mountain of ignorance, through a chain of conditions, stands having gradually filled the round of existence beginning with consciousness. However, though this word of the Buddha is not taken up in the Pāḷi text, it should be understood that it is indeed taken up by way of this Pāḷi passage: ‘Here, a Tathāgata arises in the world… he goes forth from the household life into homelessness.’ For his arising in that family home, conditioned by kamma-becoming, is called birth with its alteration. Coming into the presence of the Buddhas or their disciples, he hears a Dhamma-talk that reveals the faults of the round of existence and brings forth its characteristics, and he is tormented by the round. Thus his birth of aggregates with its alteration becomes a condition for the suffering of the round. Tormented by the suffering of the round, he repeatedly generates faith and goes forth from the household life into homelessness. Thus, the suffering of the round becomes the condition for his repeated faith. Not content with mere going forth, having taken dependence when less than five years ordained, fulfilling the duties and observances, making the two Pātimokkhas proficient, learning what is and is not a formal act, and having made himself free from tangles up to Arahantship, taking a meditation subject, dwelling in the forest, he undertakes the work on the earth kasiṇa and so on. Based on his meditation subject, weak joy arises. That is gladness, which has faith as its supporting condition; it is a condition for strong joy. Strong joy is a condition for the calming of distress; that is a condition for the bliss of the preliminary part of absorption; that bliss is a condition for the concentration of the foundational jhāna. With his mind made pliant by concentration, he does the work with initial insight. Thus, his concentration of the foundational jhāna becomes a condition for initial insight; initial insight for strong insight; strong insight for the path; the path for the fruit of liberation; the fruit of liberation for reviewing knowledge. In this way, just as the time when the rain stands, having gradually filled the ocean, so too should be understood the time when the one whose taints are destroyed stands, having filled the ocean of liberation. The Third.

4. Aññatitthiyasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Discourse on Other Sectarians

24. Catutthe [V 2.0050] pāvisīti paviṭṭho. So ca na tāva paviṭṭho, “pavisissāmī”ti nikkhantattā pana evaṃ vutto. Yathā kiṃ? Yathā “gāmaṃ gamissāmī”ti nikkhantapuriso taṃ gāmaṃ appattopi “kahaṃ itthannāmo”ti vutte “gāmaṃ gato”ti vuccati, evaṃ. Atippagoti tadā kira therassa atippagoyeva nikkhantadivaso ahosi, atippagoyeva nikkhantabhikkhū bodhiyaṅgaṇe cetiyaṅgaṇe nivāsanapārupanaṭṭhāneti imesu ṭhānesu yāva bhikkhācāravelā hoti, tāva papañcaṃ karonti. Therassa pana “yāva bhikkhācāravelā hoti, tāva paribbājakehi saddhiṃ ekadvekathāvāre karissāmī”ti cintayato yaṃnūnāhanti etadahosi. Paribbājakānaṃ ārāmoti so kira ārāmo dakkhiṇadvārassa ca veḷuvanassa ca antarā ahosi. Idhāti imesu catūsu vādesu. Kiṃvādī kimakkhāyīti kiṃ vadati kiṃ ācikkhati, kiṃ ettha samaṇassa gotamassa dassananti pucchanti. Dhammassa cānudhammaṃ byākareyyāmāti, bhotā gotamena yaṃ vuttaṃ kāraṇaṃ, tassa anukāraṇaṃ katheyyāma. Sahadhammiko vādānupātoti parehi vuttakāraṇena sakāraṇo hutvā samaṇassa gotamassa vādānupāto vādappavatti viññūhi garahitabbaṃ kāraṇaṃ koci appamattakopi kathaṃ nāgaccheyya? Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – kathaṃ sabbākārenapi samaṇassa gotamassa vāde gārayhaṃ kāraṇaṃ na bhaveyyāti?
