24. In the fourth sutta, 'he entered' means he had entered. But he had not yet entered; rather, he was spoken of thus because he had set out with the thought, 'I will enter.' How so? Just as when a person who has set out with the thought, 'I will go to the village,' though he has not yet reached that village, if asked, 'Where is so-and-so?' he is said to have 'gone to the village,' so it is here. 'Too early' means that at that time, it seems, the elder's day of departure was indeed too early. The monks who had set out too early would engage in proliferation in places like the Bodhi courtyard and the shrine courtyard, until the time for the almsround arrived. But the elder, thinking, 'Until the time for almsround arrives, I will engage in one or two discussions with the wanderers,' reflected, 'Why not?' 'The wanderers' park' means that park, it seems, was located between the southern gate and the Bamboo Grove. 'Here' means in these four views. 'What is his teaching? What does he proclaim?' means they ask, 'What does he say? What does he declare? What is the view of the ascetic Gotama here?' 'We would explain the Dhamma and what is in accordance with the Dhamma' means we would speak the corresponding reason for the reason stated by the venerable Gotama. 'A discussion in accordance with the Dhamma' means, having a reason in line with the reason stated by others, how could any reason, even a minor one, for the ascetic Gotama's discussion or mode of speaking to be censured by the wise, not arise? This is said to mean: how could there not be any reason at all for censuring the ascetic Gotama's teaching in any way?

Iti [M 2.0053] vadanti phassapaccayā dukkhanti evaṃ vadantoti attho. Tatrāti tesu catūsu vādesu. Te vata aññatra phassāti idaṃ “tadapi phassapaccayā”ti paṭiññāya sādhakavacanaṃ. Yasmā hi na vinā phassena dukkhapaṭisaṃvedanā atthi, tasmā jānitabbametaṃ yathā “tadapi phassapaccayā”ti ayamettha adhippāyo.

'Thus they say' means: they say, 'Suffering is conditioned by contact.' 'There' means in those four views. 'Indeed, they say that apart from contact'—this is a statement supporting the assertion 'even that is dependent on contact.' For since there is no experiencing of suffering without contact, therefore it should be understood that 'even that is dependent on contact'—this is the intention here.

Sādhu[P 2.0057], sādhu, ānandāti ayaṃ sādhukāro sāriputtattherassa dinno, ānandattherena pana saddhiṃ bhagavā āmantesi. Ekamidāhanti ettha idhāti nipātamattaṃ, ekaṃ samayanti attho. Idaṃ vacanaṃ “na kevalaṃ sāriputtova rājagahaṃ paviṭṭho, ahampi pāvisiṃ. Na kevalañca tassevāyaṃ vitakko uppanno, mayhampi uppajji. Na kevalañca tasseva sā titthiyehi saddhiṃ kathā jātā, mayhampi jātapubbā”ti dassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ.

'Good, good, Ānanda'—this approval was given to the Elder Sāriputta, but the Blessed One addressed the Elder Ānanda. In 'Ekamidāhaṃ,' 'ida' is merely a particle; the meaning is 'on one occasion.' This was stated by the Blessed One to show: 'Not only did Sāriputta enter Rājagaha, I also entered. And not only did this thought arise in him, this thought also arose in me. And not only did that conversation with the sectarians occur to him, that conversation had occurred to me before.'

Acchariyaṃ [V 2.0051] abbhutanti ubhayampetaṃ vimhayadīpanameva. Vacanattho panettha accharaṃ paharituṃ yuttanti acchariyaṃ. Abhūtapubbaṃ bhūtanti abbhutaṃ. Ekena padenāti “phassapaccayā dukkha”nti iminā ekena padena. Etena hi sabbavādānaṃ paṭikkhepattho vutto. Esevatthoti esoyeva phassapaccayā dukkhanti paṭiccasamuppādattho. Taññevettha paṭibhātūti taññevettha upaṭṭhātu. Idāni thero jarāmaraṇādikāya paṭiccasamuppādakathāya taṃ atthagambhīrañceva gambhīrāvabhāsañca karonto sace maṃ, bhantetiādiṃ vatvā yaṃmūlakā kathā uppannā, tadeva padaṃ gahetvā vivaṭṭaṃ dassento channaṃtvevātiādimāha. Sesaṃ uttānamevāti. Catutthaṃ.

'Wonderful' and 'marvelous'—both these terms are for expressing astonishment. As for the etymological meaning here: because it is suitable for snapping the fingers (`accharaṃ`), it is called `acchariyaṃ` (wonderful). Because what had not occurred before (`abhūtapubbaṃ`) has occurred (`bhūtaṃ`), it is called `abbhutaṃ` (marvelous). 'By one phrase' means by this one phrase: 'Suffering is conditioned by contact.' Indeed, by this, the refutation of all doctrines is stated. 'This is the meaning' means this very meaning of dependent origination: 'Suffering is conditioned by contact.' 'Let it appear only to you here' means let it become manifest only to you. Now the Elder, while making that discourse on dependent origination beginning with aging-and-death both profound in meaning and profound in appearance, having said, 'If I, venerable sir,' and so on, and taking up that very phrase which was the origin of the discourse, wishing to show the rolling back of the cycle, said, 'Of the six...' and so on. The rest is clear. The Fourth is finished.

5. Bhūmijasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Bhūmija Sutta

25-26. Pañcame bhūmijoti tassa therassa nāmaṃ. Sesamidhāpi purimasutte vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Ayaṃ pana viseso – yasmā idaṃ sukhadukkhaṃ na kevalaṃ phassapaccayā uppajjati, kāyenapi kariyamānaṃ karīyati, vācāyapi manasāpi, attanāpi kariyamānaṃ karīyati, parenapi kariyamānaṃ karīyati, sampajānenapi kariyamānaṃ karīyati, asampajānenapi, tasmā tassa aparampi paccayavisesaṃ dassetuṃ kāye vā hānanda, satītiādimāha. Kāyasañcetanāhetūti kāyadvāre uppannacetanāhetu. Vacīsañcetanāmanosañcetanāsupi [P 2.0058] eseva nayo. Ettha ca kāyadvāre kāmāvacarakusalākusalavasena [M 2.0054] vīsati cetanā labbhanti, tathā vacīdvāre. Manodvāre navahi rūpārūpacetanāhi saddhiṃ ekūnatiṃsāti tīsu dvāresu ekūnasattati cetanā honti, tappaccayaṃ vipākasukhadukkhaṃ dassitaṃ. Avijjāpaccayā cāti idaṃ tāpi cetanā avijjāpaccayā hontīti dassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Yasmā pana taṃ yathāvuttacetanābhedaṃ kāyasaṅkhārañceva vacīsaṅkhārañca manosaṅkhārañca parehi anussāhito sāmaṃ asaṅkhārikacittena karoti, parehi kāriyamāno sasaṅkhārikacittenāpi karoti, “idaṃ nāma kammaṃ karoti, tassa evarūpo nāma vipāko bhavissatī”ti, evaṃ kammañca vipākañca jānantopi karoti, mātāpitūsu cetiyavandanādīni karontesu anukarontā dārakā viya kevalaṃ kammameva jānanto “imassa pana kammassa ayaṃ vipāko”ti vipākaṃ ajānantopi karoti, tasmā taṃ dassetuṃ sāmaṃ vā taṃ, ānanda, kāyasaṅkhāraṃ abhisaṅkharotītiādi vuttaṃ.

In the fifth, Bhūmija is the name of that Elder. Here too, the rest should be understood in the way stated in the previous sutta. This, however, is the distinction: because this pleasure and pain does not arise solely conditioned by contact, but what is done is also done by the body, what is done is also done by speech, and by mind; what is done is also done by oneself, what is done is also done by another; what is done is also done with understanding, and without understanding; therefore, to show another specific condition for it, the Blessed One said, 'When there is a body, Ānanda,' and so on. 'On account of bodily volition' means on account of volition arisen at the body-door. This same method applies to verbal volition and mental volition. And here, at the body-door, twenty volitions are found by way of wholesome and unwholesome sense-sphere states; likewise at the speech-door. At the mind-door, together with the nine form-sphere and formless-sphere volitions, twenty-nine volitions are found. Thus, in the three doors there are sixty-nine volitions; resultant pleasure and pain conditioned by them has been shown. And 'conditioned by ignorance' was said to show that those volitions are also conditioned by ignorance. Furthermore, because one performs that bodily formation, verbal formation, and mental formation—distinguished as the volitions stated above—either oneself with an unprompted mind, unurged by others, or, being urged by others, one also performs it with a prompted mind; and one acts knowing both the kamma and its result, thinking, 'One does an action of this name, and its result will be of such a name and form'; and one also acts like children imitating their parents paying homage to a cetiya, knowing only the kamma itself while not knowing its result—that is, not knowing that 'of this kamma, this is the result'; therefore, to show that, it was said, 'Or, Ānanda, one forms that bodily formation oneself,' and so on.

Imesu, ānanda, dhammesūti ye ime “sāmaṃ vā taṃ, ānanda, kāyasaṅkhāra”ntiādīsu catūsu [V 2.0052] ṭhānesu vuttā chasattati dvesatā cetanādhammā, imesu dhammesu avijjā upanissayakoṭiyā anupatitā. Sabbepi hi te “avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā”ti ettheva saṅgahaṃ gacchanti. Idāni vivaṭṭaṃ dassento avijjāya tvevātiādimāha. So kāyo na hotīti yasmiṃ kāye sati kāyasañcetanāpaccayaṃ ajjhattaṃ sukhadukkhaṃ uppajjati, so kāyo na hoti. Vācāmanesupi eseva nayo. Apica kāyoti cetanākāyo, vācāpi cetanāvācā, manopi kammamanoyeva. Dvārakāyo vā kāyo. Vācāmanesupi eseva nayo. Khīṇāsavo cetiyaṃ vandati, dhammaṃ bhaṇati, kammaṭṭhānaṃ manasi karoti, kathamassa kāyādayo na hontīti? Avipākattā. Khīṇāsavena hi kataṃ kammaṃ neva kusalaṃ hoti nākusalaṃ. Avipākaṃ hutvā kiriyāmatte tiṭṭhati, tenassa te kāyādayo na hontīti vuttaṃ.

'In these phenomena, Ānanda' refers to these two hundred and seventy-six volitional phenomena spoken of in the four instances beginning with, 'Or, Ānanda, that bodily formation by oneself.' In these phenomena, ignorance is included in the category of decisive support condition. For indeed, all of them are included right here in 'formations are conditioned by ignorance.' Now, showing the rolling back of the cycle, the Blessed One said, 'With the fading away of ignorance...' and so on. 'That body does not exist' means: the body, which being present, internal pleasure and pain arises conditioned by bodily volition—that body does not exist. This same method applies to speech and mind. Moreover, 'body' is the body of volition; 'speech' is the speech of volition; and 'mind' is the kamma-mind itself. Or, 'body' is the door-body. This same method applies to speech and mind. It might be asked: 'An arahant venerates a cetiya, speaks the Dhamma, and applies the mind to a meditation subject; how is it that for him body, etc., do not exist?' Because of their non-resulting. Indeed, kamma done by an arahant is neither wholesome nor unwholesome. Having become non-result-producing, it stands as mere action. Therefore, it was said that for him, those—body, etc.—do not exist.

Khettaṃ taṃ na hotītiādīsupi viruhanaṭṭhena taṃ khettaṃ na hoti, patiṭṭhānaṭṭhena vatthu na hoti, paccayaṭṭhena āyatanaṃ [P 2.0059] na hoti, kāraṇaṭṭhena adhikaraṇaṃ na hoti. Sañcetanāmūlakañhi ajjhattaṃ sukhadukkhaṃ [M 2.0055] uppajjeyya, sā sañcetanā etesaṃ viruhanādīnaṃ atthānaṃ abhāvena tassa sukhadukkhassa neva khettaṃ, na vatthu na āyatanaṃ, na adhikaraṇaṃ hotīti. Imasmiṃ sutte vedanādīsu sukhadukkhameva kathitaṃ, tañca kho vipākamevāti. Pañcamaṃ.

In the phrases beginning 'That is not a field,' etc.: it is not a `khettaṃ` (field) in the sense of sprouting; it is not a `vatthu` (base) in the sense of a foundation; it is not an `āyatanaṃ` (source) in the sense of a condition; it is not an `adhikaraṇaṃ` (locus) in the sense of a cause. Indeed, internal pleasure and pain rooted in volition would arise; but that volition, due to the absence of these meanings of sprouting, etc., is neither the field, nor the base, nor the source, nor the locus of that pleasure and pain. In this sutta, it is precisely pleasure and pain, such as feeling, that was taught; and that, indeed, was taught as being solely the resultant. The Fifth is finished.

Chaṭṭhaṃ upavāṇasuttaṃ uttānameva. Ettha pana vaṭṭadukkhameva kathitanti. Chaṭṭhaṃ.

The sixth, the Upavāṇa Sutta, is clear. Here, however, only the suffering of the round of existence was taught. The Sixth is finished.

7. Paccayasuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Discourse on Conditions

27-28. Sattame paṭipāṭiyā vuttesu pariyosānapadaṃ gahetvā katamañca, bhikkhave, jarāmaraṇantiādi vuttaṃ. Evaṃ paccayaṃ pajānātīti evaṃ dukkhasaccavasena paccayaṃ jānāti. Paccayasamudayādayopi samudayasaccādīnaṃyeva vasena veditabbā. Diṭṭhisampannoti maggadiṭṭhiyā sampanno. Dassanasampannoti tasseva vevacanaṃ. Āgato imaṃ saddhammanti maggasaddhammaṃ āgato. Passatīti maggasaddhammameva passati. Sekkhena ñāṇenāti maggañāṇeneva. Sekkhāya vijjāyāti maggavijjāya eva. Dhammasotaṃ samāpannoti maggasaṅkhātameva dhammasotaṃ samāpanno. Ariyoti puthujjanabhūmiṃ atikkanto. Nibbedhikapaññoti nibbedhikapaññāya samannāgato. Amatadvāraṃ āhacca [V 2.0053] tiṭṭhatīti amataṃ nāma nibbānaṃ, tassa dvāraṃ ariyamaggaṃ āhacca tiṭṭhatīti. Aṭṭhamaṃ uttānameva. Sattamaaṭṭhamāni.

27-28. In the seventh discourse, taking the concluding phrase from what was stated in sequence, it was said, 'And what, bhikkhus, is aging-and-death?' and so on. Thus, 'he understands the condition' means he knows the condition by way of the truth of suffering. The arising of the condition, and so on, should also be understood by way of the truth of the origin, and so on. 'Endowed with view' means endowed with the path-view. 'Endowed with vision' is a synonym for that. 'Has come to this good Dhamma' means he has come to the good Dhamma of the path. 'He sees' means he sees precisely the good Dhamma of the path. 'With the knowledge of a trainee' means with the path-knowledge itself. 'With the true knowledge of a trainee' means with the path-true-knowledge itself. 'Has entered the stream of the Dhamma' means he has entered the stream of the Dhamma, which is designated as the path. 'Noble' means he has transcended the plane of an ordinary person. 'Possessing penetrative wisdom' means endowed with penetrative wisdom. 'Stands touching the door to the deathless' means: the deathless is called Nibbāna; he stands having reached its door, the noble path. The eighth is self-evident. The seventh and eighth are finished.

9. Samaṇabrāhmaṇasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Discourse on Ascetics and Brahmins

29-30. Navamaṃ akkharabhāṇakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ ajjhāsayena vuttaṃ. Te hi parīti upasaggaṃ pakkhipitvā vuccamāne paṭivijjhituṃ sakkonti. Navamaṃ.

29. The ninth discourse was spoken according to the inclination of the bhikkhus who are reciters of the text. For they are able to penetrate when it is spoken with the prefix 'pari-' inserted. The ninth is finished.

Dasame [P 2.0060] sabbaṃ uttānameva. Imesu dvīsu suttesu catusaccapaṭivedhova kathito. Dasamaṃ.

30. In the tenth discourse, everything is self-evident. In these two discourses, the penetration of the Four Truths alone was taught. The tenth is finished.

Dasabalavaggo tatiyo.

The Third Chapter, the Chapter on the Ten Powers, is finished.

4. Kaḷārakhattiyavaggo

4. The Chapter on Kaḷāra the Khattiya

1. Bhūtasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Discourse on What Has Come to Be

31. Kaḷārakhattiyavaggassa [M 2.0056] paṭhame ajitapañheti ajitamāṇavena pucchitapañhe. Saṅkhātadhammāseti saṅkhātadhammā vuccanti ñātadhammā tulitadhammā tīritadhammā. Sekkhāti satta sekkhā. Puthūti teyeva satta jane sandhāya puthūti vuttaṃ. Idhāti imasmiṃ sāsane. Nipakoti nepakkaṃ vuccati paññā, tāya samannāgatattā nipako, tvaṃ paṇḍito pabrūhīti yācati. Iriyanti vuttiṃ ācāraṃ gocaraṃ vihāraṃ paṭipattiṃ. Mārisāti bhagavantaṃ ālapati. Sekkhānañca saṅkhātadhammānañca khīṇāsavānañca paṭipattiṃ mayā pucchito paṇḍita, mārisa, mayhaṃ kathehīti ayamettha saṅkhepattho.

31. 31. In the first discourse of the Chapter on Kaḷāra the Khattiya: 'The question of Ajita' means in the question asked by the student Ajita. 'Those who have discerned the Dhamma' means: `saṅkhātadhammā` are said to be those who have known the Dhamma, weighed the Dhamma, and crossed over the Dhamma. 'Trainees' means the seven trainees. 'Many' means it was spoken as 'many' in reference to those same seven persons. 'Here' means in this Dispensation. 'Discerning' (nipako): wisdom is called `nepakka`; because he is endowed with that, he is discerning. He requests, 'You are wise, please tell me.' 'Conduct' means way of life, behavior, resort, abiding, and practice. With 'Sir' (mārisa), he addresses the Blessed One. 'O wise one, asked by me, sir, tell me the practice of the trainees, of those who have discerned the Dhamma, and of the worthy ones'—this is the concise meaning here.

Tuṇhī ahosīti kasmā yāva tatiyaṃ puṭṭho tuṇhī ahosi? Kiṃ pañhe kaṅkhati, udāhu ajjhāsayeti? Ajjhāsaye kaṅkhati, no pañhe. Evaṃ kirassa ahosi – “satthā maṃ sekkhāsekkhānaṃ āgamanīyapaṭipadaṃ kathāpetukāmo; sā ca khandhavasena dhātuvasena āyatanavasena paccayākāravasenāti [V 2.0054] bahūhi kāraṇehi sakkā kathetuṃ. Kathaṃ kathento nu kho satthu ajjhāsayaṃ gahetvā kathetuṃ sakkhissāmī”ti? Atha satthā cintesi – “ṭhapetvā maṃ añño pattaṃ ādāya caranto sāvako nāma paññāya sāriputtasamo natthi. Ayampi mayā pañhaṃ puṭṭho yāva tatiyaṃ tuṇhī eva. Pañhe nu kho kaṅkhati, udāhu ajjhāsaye”ti. Atha “ajjhāsaye”ti ñatvā pañhakathanatthāya [P 2.0061] nayaṃ dadamāno bhūtamidanti, sāriputta, passasīti āha.

Regarding 'he was silent': why was he silent, though asked up to a third time? Does he doubt the question, or the intention? He doubts the intention, not the question. It seems this occurred to him: 'The Teacher wishes to have me speak about the practice leading to the state of both trainees and those beyond training; and that can be explained in many ways—by way of the aggregates, by way of the elements, by way of the sense bases, or by way of the causal structure. Explaining in what way will I be able to grasp the Teacher’s intention and then speak?' Then the Teacher reflected: 'Setting me aside, there is no other disciple who wanders, taking up the bowl, who is equal to Sāriputta in wisdom. This one, too, when asked a question by me up to the third time, is silent. Does he doubt the question, or the intention?' Then, knowing, 'He doubts the intention,' and giving a method for the purpose of explaining the question, he said: 'Do you see, Sāriputta, that this has come to be?'

Tattha bhūtanti jātaṃ nibbattaṃ, khandhapañcakassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Iti satthā “pañcakkhandhavasena, sāriputta, imaṃ pañhaṃ kathehī”ti therassa nayaṃ deti. Sahanayadānena pana therassa tīre ṭhitapurisassa vivaṭo ekaṅgaṇo mahāsamuddo viya nayasatena nayasahassena pañhabyākaraṇaṃ upaṭṭhāsi. Atha naṃ byākaronto bhūtamidanti, bhantetiādimāha. Tattha bhūtamidanti idaṃ nibbattaṃ khandhapañcakaṃ. Sammappaññāya passatīti saha vipassanāya maggapaññāya sammā passati. Paṭipanno hotīti sīlato paṭṭhāya yāva arahattamaggā nibbidādīnaṃ [M 2.0057] atthāya paṭipanno hoti. Tadāhārasambhavanti idaṃ kasmā ārabhi? Etaṃ khandhapañcakaṃ āhāraṃ paṭicca ṭhitaṃ, tasmā taṃ āhārasambhavaṃ nāma katvā dassetuṃ idaṃ ārabhi. Iti imināpi pariyāyena sekkhapaṭipadā kathitā hoti. Tadāhāranirodhāti tesaṃ āhārānaṃ nirodhena. Idaṃ kasmā ārabhi? Tañhi khandhapañcakaṃ āhāranirodhā nirujjhati, tasmā taṃ āhāranirodhasambhavaṃ nāma katvā dassetuṃ idaṃ ārabhi. Iti imināpi pariyāyena sekkhasseva paṭipadā kathitā. Nibbidāti ādīni sabbāni kāraṇavacanānīti veditabbāni. Anupādā vimuttoti catūhi upādānehi kañci dhammaṃ agahetvā vimutto. Sādhu sādhūti iminā therassa byākaraṇaṃ sampahaṃsetvā sayampi tatheva byākaronto puna “bhūtamida”ntiādimāhāti. Paṭhamaṃ.

Therein, 'what has come to be' (bhūta) means born, produced; it is a name for the five aggregates. Thus the Teacher gives the elder the method, saying: 'Sāriputta, explain this question by way of the five aggregates.' And with the giving of the method, the explanation of the question appeared to the elder through a hundred methods, through a thousand methods, like the great ocean, open and a single expanse, appears to a man standing on the shore. Then, explaining it, he said, 'Venerable sir, this has come to be,' and so on. Therein, 'this has come to be' means this produced fivefold aggregate. 'One sees with right wisdom' means one sees well with the wisdom of the path together with insight. 'One is practicing' means one is practicing for the sake of disenchantment and so on, starting from virtue up to the path of arahantship. 'It originates from that nutriment'—why was this stated? This fivefold aggregate stands in dependence on nutriment; therefore, to show that it is called 'originating from nutriment,' this was stated. Thus, in this way too, the practice of a trainee is taught. 'With the cessation of that nutriment' means with the cessation of those nutriments. Why was this stated? For that fivefold aggregate ceases with the cessation of nutriment; therefore, to show that it is called 'originating from the cessation of nutriment,' this was stated. Thus, in this way too, the practice of a trainee alone is taught. 'Disenchantment' and so on—all these should be understood as words expressing cause. 'Freed through non-clinging' means freed without grasping any phenomenon by the four kinds of clinging. With 'Good, good!', having gladdened at the elder's explanation, he himself, explaining in the very same way, again said, 'This has come to be,' and so on. The first is finished.

2. Kaḷārasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Kaḷāra Sutta

32. Dutiye kaḷārakhattiyoti tassa therassa nāmaṃ. Dantā panassa kaḷārā visamasaṇṭhānā, tasmā “kaḷāro”ti vuccati. Hīnāyāvattoti hīnassa gihibhāvassa atthāya nivatto. Assāsamalatthāti assāsaṃ avassayaṃ patiṭṭhaṃ na hi nūna alattha, tayo magge tīṇi ca phalāni nūna nālatthāti dīpeti. Yadi hi tāni labheyya, na sikkhaṃ paccakkhāya hīnāyāvatteyyāti [P 2.0062] ayaṃ therassa adhippāyo. Na khvāhaṃ, āvusoti ahaṃ kho, āvuso, “assāsaṃ [V 2.0055] patto, na patto”ti na kaṅkhāmi. Therassa hi sāvakapāramīñāṇaṃ avassayo, tasmā so na kaṅkhati. Āyatiṃ panāvusoti iminā “āyatiṃ paṭisandhi tumhākaṃ ugghāṭitā, na ugghāṭitā”ti arahattappattiṃ pucchati. Na khvāhaṃ, āvuso, vicikicchāmīti iminā thero tattha vicikicchābhāvaṃ dīpeti.

32. In the second sutta, Kaḷārakhattiya is the name of that elder. His teeth, however, were kaḷāra, that is, of an uneven shape; therefore, he is called 'Kaḷāra.' 'He turned back to the low' means he turned back for the sake of the low state of a householder. 'He did not attain assurance' means he surely did not attain assurance, a support, a footing; it indicates that he surely did not attain the three paths and the three fruits. For if he had attained them, he would not have renounced the training and turned back to the low state. This is the elder's intention. 'Indeed, friend, I do not doubt' means: 'Friend, indeed, I do not doubt, "Have I attained assurance, or have I not attained it?"' For the Elder's support is the knowledge of the perfection of a disciple; therefore, he does not doubt. By 'But in the future, friend,' he asks about the attainment of Arahantship, thus: 'In the future, has rebirth been removed for you, or has it not been removed?' By 'Indeed, friend, I have no perplexity,' the elder shows the absence of perplexity in that regard.

Yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamīti “imaṃ sutakāraṇaṃ bhagavato ārocessāmī”ti upasaṅkami. Aññā byākatāti arahattaṃ byākataṃ. Khīṇā jātīti na therena evaṃ byākatā, ayaṃ pana thero tuṭṭho pasanno evaṃ padabyañjanāni āropetvā āha. Aññataraṃ bhikkhuṃ āmantesīti taṃ sutvā satthā cintesi – “sāriputto dhīro gambhīro. Na so kenaci kāraṇena evaṃ byākarissati. Saṃkhittena pana pañho byākato [M 2.0058] bhavissati. Pakkosāpetvā naṃ pañhaṃ byākarāpessāmī”ti aññataraṃ bhikkhuṃ āmantesi.

'He approached the Blessed One' means he approached with the thought, 'I will report this matter that I have heard to the Blessed One.' 'Final knowledge was declared' means Arahantship was declared. 'Destroyed is birth'—it was not declared thus by the Elder Sāriputta; rather, this elder, Kaḷārakhattiya, being pleased and confident, applied these words and phrases and spoke thus. 'He addressed a certain monk'—having heard that, the Teacher considered: 'Sāriputta is wise and of profound wisdom. He would not declare it thus for any reason. The question must have been answered concisely. Having summoned him, I will have him explain the question.' Thus, he addressed a certain monk.

Sace taṃ sāriputtāti idaṃ bhagavā “na esa attano dhammatāya aññaṃ byākarissati, pañhametaṃ pucchissāmi, taṃ kathentova aññaṃ byākarissatī”ti aññaṃ byākarāpetuṃ evaṃ pucchi. Yaṃnidānāvuso, jātīti, āvuso, ayaṃ jāti nāma yaṃpaccayā, tassa paccayassa khayā khīṇasmiṃ jātiyā paccaye jātisaṅkhātaṃ phalaṃ khīṇanti viditaṃ. Idhāpi ca thero pañhe akaṅkhitvā ajjhāsaye kaṅkhati. Evaṃ kirassa ahosi – “aññā nāma taṇhā khīṇā, upādānaṃ khīṇaṃ, bhavo khīṇo, paccayo khīṇo, kilesā khīṇātiādīhi bahūhi kāraṇehi sakkā byākātuṃ, kathaṃ kathento pana satthu ajjhāsayaṃ gahetuṃ sakkhissāmī”ti.

The Blessed One asked this, beginning with 'If, Sāriputta,' with the intention of having him declare final knowledge, thinking: 'This Sāriputta, by his own nature, will not declare final knowledge. I will ask him this question, and while explaining it, he will declare final knowledge.' 'Friend, from what cause is birth?' means: 'Friend, this so-called birth arises from whatever condition; due to the destruction of that condition, when the condition for birth is destroyed, it is known that the result called birth is destroyed.' Here too, the elder, not doubting the question, doubts the Teacher's intention. It seems this thought occurred to him: 'Final knowledge can be declared through many reasons, such as: "craving is destroyed," "the condition is destroyed," "the defilements are destroyed," and so on. But in what way, while explaining, will I be able to grasp the Teacher's intention?'

Kiñcāpi evaṃ ajjhāsaye kaṅkhati, pañhaṃ pana aṭṭhapetvāva paccayākāravasena byākāsi. Satthāpi paccayākāravaseneva byākarāpetukāmo, tasmā esa byākarontova ajjhāsayaṃ gaṇhi. Tāvadeva “gahito me satthu ajjhāsayo”ti aññāsi. Athassa nayasatena nayasahassena pañhabyākaraṇaṃ upaṭṭhāsi. Yasmā pana bhagavā uttari pañhaṃ pucchati, tasmā tena taṃ byākaraṇaṃ anumoditanti veditabbaṃ.

Although he doubted the intention in this way, without setting the question aside, he explained it by way of the causal principle. The Teacher also desired to have it explained only by way of the causal principle; therefore, while explaining, Sāriputta grasped the Teacher's intention. At that very moment, he knew: 'The Teacher's intention has been grasped by me.' Then, the explanation of the question occurred to him in a hundred ways, in a thousand ways. And since the Blessed One asked further questions, it should be understood that he approved of that explanation.

Kathaṃ [P 2.0063] jānato pana teti idaṃ kasmā ārabhi? Savisaye sīhanādaṃ nadāpetuṃ. Thero kira sūkaranikhātaleṇadvāre dīghanakhaparibbājakassa vedanāpariggahasutte kathiyamāne tālavaṇṭaṃ gahetvā [V 2.0056] satthāraṃ bījayamāno ṭhito tisso vedanā pariggahetvā sāvakapāramīñāṇaṃ adhigato, ayamassa savisayo. Imasmiṃ savisaye ṭhito sīhanādaṃ nadissatīti naṃ sandhāya satthā idaṃ pañhaṃ pucchi. Aniccāti hutvā abhāvaṭṭhena aniccā. Yadaniccaṃ taṃ dukkhanti ettha kiñcāpi sukhā vedanā ṭhitisukhā vipariṇāmadukkhā, dukkhā vedanā ṭhitidukkhā vipariṇāmasukhā, adukkhamasukhā ñāṇasukhā aññāṇadukkhā, vipariṇāmakoṭiyā pana sabbāva dukkhā nāma jātā. Viditanti yasmā evaṃ vedanāttayaṃ dukkhanti viditaṃ, tasmā yā tattha taṇhā, sā na upaṭṭhāsīti dasseti.

'But for one knowing in what way?'—why was this begun? To have him utter a lion's roar in his own domain. It is said that the Elder, while standing holding a palm-leaf fan and fanning the Teacher as the Vedanāpariggaha Sutta was being taught to Dīghanakha the wanderer at the entrance of the Sūkarakhatā cave, fully comprehended the three kinds of feelings and attained the knowledge of the perfection of a disciple—this is his domain. The Teacher asked this question with reference to him, thinking: 'Standing in this, his own domain, he will utter a lion's roar.' 'Impermanent' means impermanent in the sense of ceasing to be after having been. In 'What is impermanent, that is suffering,' although pleasant feeling is pleasant while it lasts but suffering in its change, painful feeling is suffering while it lasts but pleasant in its change, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is pleasant with knowledge but suffering with ignorance; yet from the standpoint of change, all are indeed called suffering. 'It is understood' shows that because the triad of feelings is thus known as suffering, therefore whatever craving there is in regard to them did not arise.

Sādhu [M 2.0059] sādhūti therassa vedanāparicchedajānane sampahaṃsanaṃ. Thero hi vedanā ekāti vā dve tisso catassoti vā avuttepi vuttanayena tāsaṃ tissoti paricchedaṃ aññāsi, tena taṃ bhagavā sampahaṃsanto evamāha. Dukkhasminti idaṃ bhagavā iminā adhippāyena āha – “sāriputta, yaṃ tayā ‘iminā kāraṇena vedanāsu taṇhā na upaṭṭhāsī’ti byākataṃ, taṃ subyākataṃ. ‘Tisso vedanā’ti vibhajantena pana te atippapañco kato, taṃ ‘dukkhasmi’nti byākarontenapi hi te subyākatameva bhaveyya. Yaṃkiñci vedayitaṃ, taṃ dukkhanti ñātamattepi hi vedanāsu taṇhā na tiṭṭhati”.

'Excellent, excellent!'—this is a statement of delight at the elder's knowledge in distinguishing the feelings. For the elder, even though it was not stated whether feeling is one, two, three, or four, knew by the taught method their classification as three. Therefore, the Blessed One, delighting in him, spoke thus. The Blessed One said this, 'In suffering,' with this intention: 'Sāriputta, that which you have explained—"For this reason, craving did not arise in regard to feelings"—is well explained. But by analyzing it as "three feelings," you have made it too elaborate. For even by answering "In suffering," it would have been well explained by you. For, merely by knowing "Whatever is felt, that is suffering," craving does not persist in regard to feelings.'

Kathaṃ vimokkhāti katarā vimokkhā, katarena vimokkhena tayā aññā byākatāti attho? Ajjhattaṃ vimokkhāti ajjhattavimokkhena, ajjhattasaṅkhāre pariggahetvā pattaarahattenāti attho. Tattha catukkaṃ veditabbaṃ – ajjhattaṃ abhiniveso ajjhattaṃ vuṭṭhānaṃ, ajjhattaṃ abhiniveso bahiddhā vuṭṭhānaṃ, bahiddhā abhiniveso bahiddhā vuṭṭhānaṃ, bahiddhā abhiniveso ajjhattaṃ [P 2.0064] vuṭṭhānanti. Ajjhattañhi abhinivesitvā bahiddhādhammāpi daṭṭhabbāyeva, bahiddhā abhinivesitvā ajjhattadhammāpi. Tasmā koci bhikkhu ajjhattaṃ saṅkhāresu ñāṇaṃ otāretvā te vavatthapetvā bahiddhā otāreti, bahiddhāpi pariggahetvā puna ajjhattaṃ otāreti, tassa ajjhatta saṅkhāre sammasanakāle maggavuṭṭhānaṃ hoti. Iti ajjhattaṃ abhiniveso ajjhattaṃ vuṭṭhānaṃ nāma. Koci ajjhattaṃ saṅkhāresu ñāṇaṃ otāretvā te vavatthapetvā bahiddhā otāreti, tassa bahiddhā saṅkhāre sammasanakāle maggavuṭṭhānaṃ [V 2.0057] hoti. Iti ajjhattaṃ abhiniveso bahiddhā vuṭṭhānaṃ nāma. Koci bahiddhā saṅkhāresu ñāṇaṃ otāretvā, te vavatthapetvā ajjhattaṃ otāreti, ajjhattampi pariggahetvā puna bahiddhā otāreti, tassa bahiddhā saṅkhāre sammasanakāle maggavuṭṭhānaṃ hoti. Iti bahiddhā abhiniveso bahiddhā vuṭṭhānaṃ nāma. Koci bahiddhā saṅkhāresu ñāṇaṃ otāretvā te vavatthapetvā ajjhattaṃ otāreti, tassa ajjhattasaṅkhāre sammasanakāle maggavuṭṭhānaṃ hoti. Iti bahiddhā abhiniveso ajjhattaṃ vuṭṭhānaṃ nāma. Tatra thero “ajjhattasaṅkhāre pariggahetvā tesaṃ vavatthānakāle maggavuṭṭhānena arahattaṃ pattosmī”ti dassento ajjhattaṃ vimokkhā khvāhaṃ, āvusoti āha.

“How is liberation?” means: Which liberation? By which liberation was final knowledge declared by you? This is the meaning. “Internally liberated” means: Through internal liberation, having comprehended the internal formations, one has attained Arahantship. This is the meaning. Therein, a fourfold classification should be known: internal focusing and internal emergence; internal focusing and external emergence; external focusing and external emergence; and external focusing and internal emergence. For, having focused internally, external phenomena must also be seen; and having focused externally, internal phenomena must also be seen. Therefore, a certain monk, having directed knowledge toward internal formations and determined them, directs it externally; having also comprehended the external, he directs it internally again. For him, the emergence that is the path occurs while contemplating the internal formations. This is called internal focusing and internal emergence. A certain monk, having directed knowledge toward internal formations and determined them, directs it externally. For him, the emergence that is the path occurs while contemplating the external formations. This is called internal focusing and external emergence. A certain monk, having directed knowledge toward external formations and determined them, directs it internally; having also comprehended the internal, he directs it externally again. For him, the emergence that is the path occurs while contemplating the external formations. This is called external focusing and external emergence. A certain monk, having directed knowledge toward external formations and determined them, directs it internally. For him, the emergence that is the path occurs while contemplating the internal formations. This is called external focusing and internal emergence. Therein, the Elder, showing that, “Having comprehended the internal formations, at the time of determining them, I attained Arahantship by means of the emergence that is the path,” said, “Friend, I am liberated by internal liberation.”

Sabbupādānakkhayāti [M 2.0060] sabbesaṃ catunnampi upādānānaṃ khayena. Tathā sato viharāmīti tenākārena satiyā samannāgato viharāmi. Yathā sataṃ viharantanti yenākārena maṃ satiyā samannāgataṃ viharantaṃ. Āsavā nānussavantīti cakkhuto rūpe savanti āsavanti sandanti pavattantīti evaṃ chahi dvārehi chasu ārammaṇesu savanadhammā kāmāsavādayo āsavā nānussavanti nānuppavaḍḍhanti, yathā me na uppajjantīti attho. Attānañca nāvajānāmīti attānañca na avajānāmi. Iminā omānapahānaṃ kathitaṃ. Evañhi sati pajānanā pasannā hoti.

“Through the destruction of all clinging” means through the destruction of all four kinds of clinging. “Thus I dwell mindful” means I dwell endowed with mindfulness in that way. “As one dwelling mindful” means in whatever way I dwell endowed with mindfulness. “The taints do not flow in after” means the taints, such as the taint of sensual desire, whose nature is to flow, ooze, stream, and proceed, do not flow in after and do not increase through the six doors toward the six objects; the meaning is that they do not arise in me. “And I do not despise myself” means I do not despise myself. By this, the abandoning of conceit is stated. For when this is so, understanding becomes clear.

Samaṇenāti buddhasamaṇena. Tesvāhaṃ na kaṅkhāmīti tesu ahaṃ “kataro kāmāsavo, kataro bhavāsavo, kataro diṭṭhāsavo, kataro avijjāsavo”ti evaṃ sarūpabhedatopi, “cattāro [P 2.0065] āsavā”ti evaṃ gaṇanaparicchedatopi na kaṅkhāmi. Te me pahīnāti na vicikicchāmīti te mayhaṃ pahīnāti vicikicchaṃ na uppādemi. Idaṃ bhagavā “evaṃ byākarontenapi tayā subyākataṃ bhaveyya ‘ajjhattaṃ vimokkhā khvāhaṃ, āvuso’tiādīni pana te vadantena atippapañco kato”ti dassento āha.

“By the ascetic” means by the Buddha, the ascetic. “I have no doubt about them” means: I have no doubt about them, either regarding the distinction of their individual nature—such as, “Which is the taint of sensual desire? Which is the taint of existence? Which is the taint of views? Which is the taint of ignorance?”—or regarding the determination of their number as “the taints are four.” “I do not doubt that they are abandoned by me” means: I do not give rise to the doubt, “Have they been abandoned by me?” The Blessed One said this to show: “Even by answering thus, it would have been well-answered by you. However, by your saying, ‘Friend, I am liberated by internal liberation,’ and so on, you have made it excessively elaborate.”

Uṭṭhāyāsanā vihāraṃ pāvisīti paññattavarabuddhāsanato uṭṭhahitvā vihāraṃ antomahāgandhakuṭiṃ pāvisi asambhinnāya eva parisāya. Kasmā? Buddhā hi aniṭṭhitāya desanāya asambhinnāya parisāya uṭṭhāyāsanā gandhakuṭiṃ pavisantā puggalathomanatthaṃ vā pavisanti dhammathomanatthaṃ vā. Tattha puggalathomanatthaṃ pavisanto satthā evaṃ cintesi – “imaṃ mayā saṃkhittena uddesaṃ uddiṭṭhaṃ vitthārena ca avibhattaṃ dhammapaṭiggāhakā bhikkhū uggahetvā ānandaṃ vā kaccāyanaṃ vā upasaṅkamitvā pucchissanti, te mayhaṃ ñāṇena saṃsandetvā kathessanti, tatopi dhammapaṭiggāhakā puna maṃ pucchissanti. Tesamahaṃ ‘sukathitaṃ, bhikkhave, ānandena, sukathitaṃ kaccāyanena, maṃ cepi tumhe etamatthaṃ [V 2.0058] puccheyyātha, ahampi naṃ evameva byākareyya’nti evaṃ te puggale thomessāmi. Tato tesu gāravaṃ janetvā bhikkhū upasaṅkamissanti, tepi bhikkhū atthe ca dhamme ca niyojessanti, te tehi niyojitā tisso sikkhā paripūretvā dukkhassantaṃ karissantī”ti.

“He rose from his seat and entered the dwelling” means: He rose from the excellent Buddha-seat that had been prepared and entered the dwelling, the great perfumed chamber within, while the assembly had not yet dispersed. Why? For the Buddhas, when the teaching is unfinished and the assembly has not dispersed, rising from their seats and entering the perfumed chamber, they enter either for the purpose of praising a person or for the purpose of praising the Dhamma. Therein, the Teacher, entering for the purpose of praising a person, thought thus: “This topic pointed out by me in brief and not analyzed in detail—the monks who are receivers of the Dhamma, having learned it, will approach Ānanda or Kaccāyana and ask them. They will explain it, comparing it with my knowledge, and then the receivers of the Dhamma will ask me again. To them I will say, ‘Well spoken, monks, by Ānanda! Well spoken by Kaccāyana! If you were to ask me this same matter, I too would explain it in just the same way.’ Thus I will praise those individuals. Then, generating reverence for them, the monks will approach them. They, in turn, will establish the monks in the meaning and in the Dhamma. Those monks, having been established by them, will fulfill the three trainings and make an end of suffering.”

Atha [M 2.0061] vā panassa evaṃ hoti – “esa mayi pakkante attano ānubhāvaṃ karissati, atha naṃ ahampi tatheva thomessāmi, taṃ mama thomanaṃ sutvā gāravajātā bhikkhū imaṃ upasaṅkamitabbaṃ, vacanañcassa sotabbaṃ saddhātabbaṃ maññissanti, taṃ tesaṃ bhavissati dīgharattaṃ hitāya sukhāyā”ti dhammathomanatthaṃ pavisanto evaṃ cintesi yathā dhammadāyādasutte cintesi. Tatra hissa evaṃ ahosi – “mayi vihāraṃ paviṭṭhe āmisadāyādaṃ garahanto dhammadāyādañca thomento imissaṃyeva parisati nisinno sāriputto dhammaṃ desessati, evaṃ dvinnampi amhākaṃ ekajjhāsayāya matiyā desitā ayaṃ desanā aggā ca garukā ca bhavissati pāsāṇacchattasadisā”ti.

Or alternatively, it occurs to him thus: “When I have departed, this one will display his own power. Then I too will praise him in that same way. Hearing that praise from me, the monks, with reverence arisen, will think that he should be approached, that his word should be heard and trusted. That will be for their welfare and happiness for a long time.” Entering for the purpose of praising the Dhamma, he thought just as he thought in the Dhammadāyāda Sutta. For there it occurred to him thus: “When I have entered the dwelling, Sāriputta, seated right in this assembly, will teach the Dhamma, censuring the heir of material things and praising the heir of the Dhamma. Thus, this teaching, delivered by the wisdom of both of us with a single intention, will become supreme and weighty, like a stone canopy.”

Idha [P 2.0066] pana āyasmantaṃ sāriputtaṃ ukkaṃsetvā pakāsetvā ṭhapetukāmo puggalathomanatthaṃ uṭṭhāyāsanā vihāraṃ pāvisi. Īdisesu ṭhānesu bhagavā nisinnāsaneyeva antarahito cittagatiyā vihāraṃ pavisatīti veditabbo. Yadi hi kāyagatiyā gaccheyya, sabbā parisā bhagavantaṃ parivāretvā gaccheyya, sā ekavāraṃ bhinnā puna dussannipātā bhaveyyāti bhagavā adissamānena kāyena cittagatiyā eva pāvisi.

Furthermore, here, wishing to exalt, make illustrious, and establish the Venerable Sāriputta, for the purpose of praising the person, He rose from His seat and entered the dwelling. In such instances, it should be understood that the Blessed One, having disappeared right from His seated position, enters the dwelling by the movement of His mind. For if He were to go by way of the body, the entire assembly would follow, having surrounded the Blessed One, and that assembly, once dispersed, would be difficult to reassemble. Therefore, the Blessed One entered with an invisible body, only by the movement of His mind.

Evaṃ paviṭṭhe pana bhagavati bhagavato adhippāyānurūpameva sīhanādaṃ naditukāmo tatra kho āyasmā sāriputto acirapakkantassa bhagavato bhikkhū āmantesi. Pubbe appaṭisaṃviditanti idaṃ nāma pucchissatīti pubbe mayā aviditaṃ aññātaṃ. Paṭhamaṃ pañhanti, “sace taṃ, sāriputta, evaṃ puccheyyuṃ kathaṃ jānatā pana tayā, āvuso sāriputta, kathaṃ passatā aññā byākatā khīṇā jātī”ti imaṃ paṭhamaṃ pañhaṃ. Dandhāyitattanti satthu āsayajānanatthaṃ dandhabhāvo asīghatā. Paṭhamaṃ pañhaṃ anumodīti, “jāti panāvuso sāriputta, kiṃnidānā”ti imaṃ dutiyaṃ pañhaṃ pucchanto, “yaṃnidānāvuso, jātī”ti evaṃ vissajjitaṃ paṭhamaṃ pañhaṃ anumodi.

When the Blessed One had thus entered, the Venerable Sāriputta, wishing to utter a lion’s roar in accordance with the Blessed One’s intention, addressed the monks in that very place not long after the Blessed One had departed. 'Previously unperceived' means: it was unknown, not cognized by me beforehand that He would ask this. 'The first question' means this first question: 'If, Sāriputta, they were to ask you thus: "Friend Sāriputta, knowing in what way, seeing in what way, was final knowledge declared by you: ‘Birth is destroyed’?”' 'Slowness' means: a state of being slow, a lack of quickness, for the purpose of knowing the Teacher’s intention. 'He approved the first question' means: while asking this second question, 'Friend Sāriputta, what is the source of birth?', He approved the first question that had been answered thus: 'Friend, whatever is the source of birth...'

Etadahosīti bhagavatā anumodite nayasatena nayasahassena pañhassa ekaṅgaṇikabhāvena pākaṭībhūtattā [V 2.0059] etaṃ ahosi. Divasampāhaṃ bhagavato etamatthaṃ byākareyyanti sakaladivasampi ahaṃ bhagavato etaṃ paṭiccasamuppādatthaṃ [M 2.0062] puṭṭho sakaladivasampi aññamaññehi padabyañjanehi byākareyyaṃ. Yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamīti evaṃ kirassa ahosi – “thero uḷārasīhanādaṃ nadati, sukāraṇaṃ etaṃ, dasabalassa naṃ ārocessāmī”ti. Tasmā yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami.

As for 'This occurred': When there was the approval of the Blessed One, this occurred because of the question becoming manifest as a single field through a hundred methods, through a thousand methods. As for 'I could explain this matter to the Blessed One all day long': If I were asked by the Blessed One about this meaning of dependent origination for the entire day, I could explain it for the entire day with various synonymous words and phrases. As for 'He approached where the Blessed One was': It seems this thought occurred to him: 'The Elder is uttering a sublime lion’s roar. This is a good reason; I shall inform the One with Ten Powers of it.' Therefore, he approached where the Blessed One was.

Sā hi bhikkhu sāriputtassa dhammadhātūti ettha dhammadhātūti paccayākārassa vivaṭabhāvadassanasamatthaṃ sāvakapāramīñāṇaṃ. Sāvakānañhi sāvakapāramīñāṇaṃ sabbaññutaññāṇagatikameva [P 2.0067] hoti. Yathā buddhānaṃ atītānāgatapaccuppannā dhammā sabbaññutaññāṇassa pākaṭā honti, evaṃ therassa sāvakapāramīñāṇaṃ sabbepi sāvakañāṇassa gocaradhamme jānātīti. Dutiyaṃ.

As for 'That, O monk, is Sāriputta's Dhamma-element': Herein, 'Dhamma-element' is the knowledge of the disciple's perfection, which is capable of showing the open nature of the structure of conditions. Indeed, the knowledge of a disciple's perfection is comparable to the course of the knowledge of omniscience in its own domain. Just as for the Buddhas, phenomena of the past, future, and present are manifest to the knowledge of omniscience, so too the Elder’s knowledge of the disciple's perfection knows all phenomena that are the domain of a disciple's knowledge. The Second Sutta is finished.

3. Ñāṇavatthusuttavaṇṇanā

3. Explanation of the Discourse on the Bases of Knowledge

33. Tatiye taṃ suṇāthāti taṃ ñāṇavatthudesanaṃ suṇātha. Ñāṇavatthūnīti cettha ñāṇameva ñāṇavatthūti veditabbaṃ. Jarāmaraṇe ñāṇantiādīsu catūsu paṭhamaṃ savanamayañāṇaṃ sammasanañāṇaṃ paṭivedhañāṇaṃ paccavekkhaṇañāṇanti catubbidhaṃ vaṭṭati, tathā dutiyaṃ. Tatiyaṃ pana ṭhapetvā sammasanañāṇaṃ tividhameva hoti, tathā catutthaṃ. Lokuttaradhammesu hi sammasanaṃ nāma natthi. Jātiyā ñāṇantiādīsupi eseva nayo. Iminā dhammenāti iminā catusaccadhammena vā maggañāṇadhammena vā.

33. In the third discourse, 'listen to that' means listen to that exposition on the bases of knowledge. Herein, regarding 'the bases of knowledge', it should be understood that knowledge itself is the basis of knowledge. Among the four instances beginning with 'knowledge in aging and death', the first is suitable to be fourfold: knowledge born of hearing, knowledge of comprehension, knowledge of penetration, and knowledge of reviewing. Similarly, the second. The third, however, omitting the knowledge of comprehension, is only threefold; likewise the fourth. For in supramundane states, there is no so-called knowledge of comprehension. This same method applies also to 'knowledge in birth', and so on. 'By this Dhamma' means by this Dhamma of the Four Truths or by the Dhamma of path-knowledge.

Diṭṭhenātiādīsu diṭṭhenāti ñāṇacakkhunā diṭṭhena. Viditenāti paññāya viditena. Akālikenāti kiñci kālaṃ anatikkamitvā paṭivedhānantaraṃyeva phaladāyakena. Pattenāti adhigatena. Pariyogāḷhenāti pariyogāhitena paññāya anupaviṭṭhena. Atītānāgate nayaṃ netīti “ye kho kecī”tiādinā nayena atīte ca anāgate ca nayaṃ neti. Ettha ca na catusaccadhammena vā maggañāṇadhammena vā sakkā atītānāgate nayaṃ netuṃ, catusacce pana maggañāṇena paṭividdhe parato paccavekkhaṇañāṇaṃ nāma hoti. Tena nayaṃ netīti veditabbā. Abbhaññaṃsūti abhiaññaṃsu jāniṃsu. Seyyathāpāhaṃ, etarahīti yathā ahaṃ etarahi catusaccavasena jānāmi. Anvaye ñāṇanti anuaye ñāṇaṃ, dhammañāṇassa anugamane ñāṇaṃ, paccavekkhaṇañāṇassetaṃ [V 2.0060] nāmaṃ. Dhamme ñāṇanti maggañāṇaṃ. Imasmiṃ sutte khīṇāsavassa sekkhabhūmi kathitā hoti. Tatiyaṃ.

Regarding 'seen', and so on: 'seen' means seen with the eye of knowledge. 'Known' means known by wisdom. 'Timeless' means delivering its fruit immediately after penetration, without any lapse of time. 'Attained' means achieved. 'Thoroughly penetrated' means thoroughly grasped and entered into by wisdom. 'Leads to the method regarding past and future' means it leads to the method concerning both past and future by the method beginning with 'whatever beings...'. And herein, it is not possible to lead to the method regarding the past and future by means of the Dhamma of the Four Truths or the Dhamma of path-knowledge; however, when the Four Truths are penetrated by path-knowledge, afterwards there arises the so-called knowledge of reviewing. It should be understood that one leads to the method by means of this. 'They knew' means they fully knew, they understood. 'Just as I do now' means just as I now know by way of the Four Truths. 'Knowledge in consequence' means knowledge in what follows, that is, knowledge that is subsequent to the knowledge of the Dhamma; this is a name for the knowledge of reviewing. 'Knowledge of the Dhamma' means path-knowledge. In this discourse, the trainee-stage of the one who has destroyed the taints is taught. The third is finished.

4. Dutiyañāṇavatthusuttavaṇṇanā

4. Explanation of the Second Discourse on the Bases of Knowledge

34. Catutthe [M 2.0063][P 2.0068] sattasattarīti satta ca sattari ca. Byañjanabhāṇakā kira te bhikkhū, bahubyañjanaṃ katvā vuccamāne paṭivijjhituṃ sakkonti, tasmā tesaṃ ajjhāsayena idaṃ suttaṃ vuttaṃ. Dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇanti paccayākāre ñāṇaṃ. Paccayākāro hi dhammānaṃ pavattiṭṭhitikāraṇattā dhammaṭṭhitīti vuccati, ettha ñāṇaṃ dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇaṃ, etasseva chabbidhassa ñāṇassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Khayadhammanti khayagamanasabhāvaṃ. Vayadhammanti vayagamanasabhāvaṃ. Virāgadhammanti virajjanasabhāvaṃ. Nirodhadhammanti nirujjhanasabhāvaṃ. Sattasattarīti ekekasmiṃ satta satta katvā ekādasasu padesu sattasattari. Imasmiṃ sutte vipassanāpaṭivipassanā kathitā. Catutthaṃ.

34. In the fourth discourse, 'seventy-seven' means seven and seventy. It is said that those monks were reciters of the letter, able to penetrate when taught with many letters; therefore, this discourse was spoken according to their inclination. 'Knowledge of the stability of phenomena' is knowledge in the mode of conditions. For the mode of conditions is called 'the stability of phenomena' because it is the cause for the stability of the occurrence of phenomena; knowledge herein is the knowledge of the stability of phenomena. This is a designation for this very sixfold knowledge. 'Subject to destruction' means having the nature of going to destruction. 'Subject to decay' means having the nature of going to decay. 'Subject to fading' means having the nature of fading away. 'Subject to cessation' means having the nature of ceasing. 'Seventy-seven' means seventy-seven in the eleven sections, by taking seven for each. In this discourse, insight and counter-insight are taught. The fourth is finished.

5. Avijjāpaccayasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Discourse on Things Conditioned by Ignorance

35. Pañcame samudayo hotīti satthā idheva desanaṃ osāpesi. Kiṃkāraṇāti? Diṭṭhigatikassa okāsadānatthaṃ. Tassañhi parisati upārambhacitto diṭṭhigatiko atthi, so pañhaṃ pucchissati, athassāhaṃ vissajjessāmīti tassa okāsadānatthaṃ desanaṃ osāpesi. No kallo pañhoti ayutto pañho. Duppañho esoti attho. Nanu ca “katamaṃ nu kho, bhante, jarāmaraṇa”nti? Idaṃ supucchitanti. Kiñcāpi supucchitaṃ, yathā pana satasahassagghanike suvaṇṇathāle vaḍḍhitassa subhojanassa matthake āmalakamattepi gūthapiṇḍe ṭhapite sabbaṃ bhojanaṃ dubbhojanaṃ hoti chaḍḍetabbaṃ, evameva “kassa ca panidaṃ jarāmaraṇa”nti? Iminā sattūpaladdhivādapadena gūthapiṇḍena taṃ bhojanaṃ dubbhojanaṃ viya ayampi sabbo duppañhova jātoti.

35. In the fifth sutta, with the words 'there is arising,' the Teacher concluded the teaching right there. For what reason? To give an opportunity to one holding wrong views. For in that assembly there was one holding wrong views with a mind intent on censure. He would ask a question, and the Teacher thought, 'Then I will answer him.' To give him that opportunity, He concluded the teaching. 'Not a proper question' means an inappropriate question. 'This is an improper question' is the meaning. But was it not well-asked, 'What, venerable sir, is aging and death?' Although it was well-asked, it is just as when a lump of excrement the size of an emblic myrobalan is placed atop exquisite food served in a golden dish worth a hundred thousand, the entire meal becomes repulsive and must be discarded. In the same way, with the question 'And for whom is this aging and death?', by this phrase—like a lump of excrement—which expresses the doctrine that a being is found, this entire question has also become an improper one.

Brahmacariyavāsoti ariyamaggavāso. Taṃ jīvaṃ taṃ sarīranti yassa hi ayaṃ diṭṭhi, so “jīve ucchijjamāne sarīraṃ ucchijjati, sarīre ucchijjante jīvitaṃ ucchijjatī”ti gaṇhāti. Evaṃ [P 2.0069] gaṇhato sā diṭṭhi “satto ucchijjatī”ti gahitattā ucchedadiṭṭhi nāma hoti[V 2.0061]. Sace pana saṅkhārāva uppajjanti ceva nirujjhanti cāti gaṇheyya, sāsanāvacarā sammādiṭṭhi nāma bhaveyya. Ariyamaggo ca nāmeso vaṭṭaṃ nirodhento vaṭṭaṃ samucchindanto uppajjati[M 2.0064], tadeva taṃ vaṭṭaṃ ucchedadiṭṭhiyā gahitākārassa sambhave sati vināva maggabhāvanāya nirujjhatīti maggabhāvanā niratthakā hoti. Tena vuttaṃ “brahmacariyavāso na hotī”ti.

Dwelling in the holy life is dwelling in the noble path. For one who has the view, 'The life-principle is the same as the body,' holds that 'when the life-principle is annihilated, the body is annihilated; when the body is annihilated, the life-principle is annihilated.' For one who holds this, that view is called the annihilationist view because it is grasped as 'the being is annihilated.' If, however, one were to hold that 'only formations arise and cease,' that would be called right view pertaining to the Dispensation. And this noble path arises while bringing the round to cessation, while utterly cutting off the round. If the state of affairs as grasped by the annihilationist view were to exist, that very round would cease even without the development of the path, and thus the development of the path would be pointless. Therefore, it was said, 'there is no dwelling in the holy life.'

Dutiyanaye aññaṃ jīvaṃ aññaṃ sarīranti yassa ayaṃ diṭṭhi, so “sarīraṃ idheva ucchijjati, na jīvitaṃ, jīvitaṃ pana pañjarato sakuṇo viya yathāsukhaṃ gacchatī”ti gaṇhāti. Evaṃ gaṇhato sā diṭṭhi “imasmā lokā jīvitaṃ paralokaṃ gata”nti gahitattā sassatadiṭṭhi nāma hoti. Ayañca ariyamaggo tebhūmakavaṭṭaṃ vivaṭṭento uppajjati, so ekasaṅkhārepi nicce dhuve sassate sati uppannopi vaṭṭaṃ vivaṭṭetuṃ na sakkotīti maggabhāvanā niratthakā hoti. Tena vuttaṃ “aññaṃ jīvaṃ aññaṃ sarīranti vā bhikkhu diṭṭhiyā sati brahmacariyavāso na hotī”ti.

In the second method, one who has the view, 'The life-principle is one thing, the body another,' holds that 'the body is annihilated right here, but not the life-principle; the life-principle, however, goes wherever it pleases, like a bird from a cage.' For one who holds this, that view is called the eternalist view because it is grasped as 'the life-principle has gone from this world to the next world.' And this noble path arises while turning away from the round of the three planes. If even one formation were permanent, stable, and eternal, that path, even having arisen, would not be able to turn away from the round. Thus, the development of the path would be pointless. Therefore, it was said: '...or when a monk has the view, "The life-principle is one thing, the body another," there is no dwelling in the holy life.'

Visūkāyikānītiādi sabbaṃ micchādiṭṭhivevacanameva. Sā hi sammādiṭṭhiyā vinivijjhanaṭṭhena visūkamiva attānaṃ āvaraṇato visūkāyikaṃ, sammādiṭṭhiṃ ananuvattitvā tassā virodhena pavattanato visevitaṃ, kadāci ucchedassa kadāci sassatassa gahaṇato virūpaṃ phanditaṃ vipphanditanti vuccati. Tālāvatthukatānīti tālavatthu viya katāni, puna aviruhaṇaṭṭhena matthakacchinnatālo viya samūlaṃ tālaṃ uddharitvā tassa patiṭṭhitaṭṭhānaṃ viya ca katānīti attho. Anabhāvaṃkatānīti anuabhāvaṃ katānīti. Pañcamaṃ.

The terms beginning with 'visūkāyikāni' are all just synonyms for wrong view. For that wrong view is called 'visūkāyika' because, like a dart, it obstructs itself from being pierced by right view. It is called 'visevita' because it does not follow right view but proceeds in opposition to it. It is called 'vipphandita' because it is a distorted trembling, grasping at times annihilation and at times eternalism. 'Tālāvatthukatāni' means made like a palm-stump, that is, made unable to grow again like a palm tree with its crown cut off, and also made like the site where a palm tree stood after it has been uprooted. 'Anabhāvaṃkatāni' means made not to exist again. The Fifth.

6. Dutiyaavijjāpaccayasuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Second Discourse on Ignorance as a Condition

36. Chaṭṭhe [P 2.0070] iti vā, bhikkhave, yo vadeyyāti tassaṃ parisati diṭṭhigatiko pañhaṃ pucchitukāmo atthi, so pana avisāradadhātuko uṭṭhāya dasabalaṃ pucchituṃ na sakkoti, tasmā tassa ajjhāsayena sayameva pucchitvā vissajjento satthā evamāha. Chaṭṭhaṃ.

36. In the sixth discourse: Regarding the words beginning with, 'Or, bhikkhus, if someone were to say,' in that assembly, there was one holding a wrong view who wished to ask a question. But he, being of an unconfident nature, was not able to rise and ask the Ten-Powered One. Therefore, the Teacher, understanding his intention, asked the question Himself and, wishing to answer, spoke thus. The sixth is finished.

7. Natumhasuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the 'Not Yours' Sutta

37. Sattame [V 2.0062][M 2.0065] na tumhākanti attani hi sati attaniyaṃ nāma hoti. Attāyeva ca natthi, tasmā “na tumhāka”nti āha. Napi aññesanti añño nāma paresaṃ attā, tasmiṃ sati aññesaṃ nāma siyā, sopi natthi, tasmā “napi aññesa”nti āha. Purāṇamidaṃ, bhikkhave, kammanti nayidaṃ purāṇakammameva, purāṇakammanibbatto panesa kāyo, tasmā paccayavohārena evaṃ vutto. Abhisaṅkhatantiādi kammavohārasseva vasena purimaliṅgasabhāgatāya vuttaṃ, ayaṃ panettha attho – abhisaṅkhatanti paccayehi katoti daṭṭhabbo. Abhisañcetayitanti cetanāvatthuko cetanāmūlakoti daṭṭhabbo. Vedaniyanti vedaniyavatthūti daṭṭhabbo. Sattamaṃ.

37. In the seventh discourse: As for 'not yours,' it is because when a self exists, there is what is called 'belonging to self.' And the self itself does not exist; therefore, He said, 'not yours.' As for 'nor of others,' 'of others' means the self of others. If that existed, there would be what is called 'of others.' That too does not exist; therefore, He said, 'nor of others.' As for 'This, bhikkhus, is old kamma,' this body is not merely old kamma, but rather, this body is produced by old kamma. Therefore, it is spoken of thus by way of designation as a condition. The words beginning with 'fabricated' are spoken by way of the designation of kamma, having a nature similar to the preceding term. But here, this is the meaning: 'fabricated' should be understood as 'made by conditions.' 'Willed' should be understood as 'having volition as its basis, having volition as its root.' 'To be felt' should be understood as 'the basis for feeling.' The seventh is finished.

8. Cetanāsuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Discourse on Volition

38. Aṭṭhame yañca, bhikkhave, cetetīti yaṃ cetanaṃ ceteti, pavattetīti attho. Yañca pakappetīti yaṃ pakappanaṃ pakappeti, pavatteticceva attho. Yañca anusetīti yañca anusayaṃ anuseti, pavatteticceva attho. Ettha ca cetetīti tebhūmakakusalākusalacetanā gahitā, pakappetīti aṭṭhasu lobhasahagatacittesu taṇhādiṭṭhikappā gahitā, anusetīti dvādasannaṃ cetanānaṃ sahajātakoṭiyā ceva upanissayakoṭiyā ca anusayo gahito. Ārammaṇametaṃ hotīti (cetanādidhammajāte sati kammaviññāṇassa uppattiyā avāritattā) etaṃ cetanādidhammajātaṃ paccayo hoti. Paccayo hi idha ārammaṇanti [P 2.0071] adhippetā. Viññāṇassa ṭhitiyāti kammaviññāṇassa ṭhitatthaṃ. Ārammaṇe satīti tasmiṃ paccaye sati. Patiṭṭhā viññāṇassa hotīti tassa kammaviññāṇassa patiṭṭhā hoti. Tasmiṃ patiṭṭhite viññāṇeti tasmiṃ kammaviññāṇe patiṭṭhite. Virūḷheti kammaṃ javāpetvā paṭisandhiākaḍḍhanasamatthatāya nibbattamūle jāte. Punabbhavābhinibbattīti punabbhavasaṅkhātā abhinibbatti.

38. In the eighth discourse: As for, 'And what, bhikkhus, one intends,' this means what volition one intends; the meaning is one brings it into being. As for, 'And what one plans,' this means what plan one plans; the meaning is indeed that one brings it into being. As for, 'And what one harbors as a latent tendency,' this means what latent tendency one harbors; the meaning is indeed that one brings it into being. Herein, by 'intends,' wholesome and unwholesome volitions of the three planes are taken. By 'plans,' plans of craving and views in the eight types of consciousness accompanied by greed are taken. By 'harbors as a latent tendency,' the latent tendency is taken for the twelve volitions by way of co-nascence and by way of decisive support. As for, 'This becomes an object for it,' (when the collection of phenomena beginning with volition exists, because the arising of kamma-consciousness is not prevented) this collection of phenomena beginning with volition becomes a condition. For here 'condition' is intended as 'object.' 'For the stability of consciousness' means for the stability of kamma-consciousness. 'When there is an object' means when that condition exists. 'There is a support for consciousness' means there is a support for that kamma-consciousness. 'When that consciousness is established' means when that kamma-consciousness is established. 'When it has grown' means when, having impelled the kamma, a root has arisen with the capacity to draw forth rebirth-linking. 'The production of renewed existence' means the production designated as renewed existence.

No [M 2.0066] ce, bhikkhave, cetetīti iminā tebhūmakacetanāya appavattanakkhaṇo vutto. No ce pakappetīti iminā taṇhādiṭṭhikappānaṃ appavattanakkhaṇo. Atha ce anusetīti iminā tebhūmakavipākesu parittakiriyāsu rūpeti ettha appahīnakoṭiyā anusayo gahito. Ārammaṇametaṃ [V 2.0063] hotīti anusaye sati kammaviññāṇassa uppattiyā avāritattā etaṃ anusayajātaṃ paccayova hoti.

By the phrase, 'If, bhikkhus, one does not intend,' the moment of non-arising of volition of the three planes is stated. By the phrase, 'And if one does not plan,' the moment of non-arising of plans of craving and views is stated. By the phrase, 'But if one harbors a latent tendency,' the latent tendency is taken by way of the unabandoned aspect with regard to the results of the three planes, sense-sphere functional consciousnesses, and form. As for, 'This becomes an object for it,' when a latent tendency exists, because the arising of kamma-consciousness is not prevented, this collection of latent tendencies becomes a condition indeed.

No ceva cetetītiādīsu paṭhamapade tebhūmakakusalākusalacetanā nivattā, dutiyapade aṭṭhasu cittesu taṇhādiṭṭhiyo, tatiyapade vuttappakāresu dhammesu yo appahīnakoṭiyā anusayito anusayo, so nivatto.

In the passage beginning with, 'If one does not intend,' in the first phrase, wholesome and unwholesome volitions of the three planes have ceased. In the second phrase, craving and views in the eight types of consciousness have ceased. In the third phrase, whatever latent tendency lies latent by way of the unabandoned aspect in the aforementioned kinds of phenomena, that has ceased.

Apicettha asammohatthaṃ ceteti pakappeti anuseti, ceteti na pakappeti anuseti, na ceteti na pakappeti anuseti, na ceteti na pakappeti na anusetīti idampi catukkaṃ veditabbaṃ. Tattha paṭhamanaye dhammaparicchedo dassito. Dutiyanaye cetetīti tebhūmakakusalacetanā ceva catasso ca akusalacetanā gahitā. Na pakappetīti aṭṭhasu cittesu taṇhādiṭṭhiyo nivattā. Anusetīti tebhūmakakusale upanissayakoṭiyā, catūsu akusalacetanāsu sahajātakoṭiyā ceva upanissayakoṭiyā ca anusayo gahito. Tatiyanaye na cetetīti tebhūmakakusalākusalaṃ nivattaṃ, na pakappetīti aṭṭhasu cittesu taṇhādiṭṭhiyo nivattā, anusetīti sutte āgataṃ vāretvā tebhūmakakusalākusalavipākakiriyārūpesu appahīnakoṭiyā upanissayo gahito. Catutthanayo purimasadisova.

Moreover, here, for the sake of non-bewilderment, this tetrad should also be known: one intends, plans, and harbors a latent tendency; one intends, does not plan, and harbors a latent tendency; one does not intend, does not plan, but harbors a latent tendency; and one does not intend, does not plan, and does not harbor a latent tendency. Therein, in the first method, the classification of phenomena is shown. In the second method, by 'intends,' wholesome volitions of the three planes and the four unwholesome volitions are taken. By 'does not plan,' craving and views in the eight types of consciousness have ceased. By 'harbors a latent tendency,' the latent tendency is taken for wholesome states of the three planes by way of decisive support, and for the four unwholesome volitions by way of co-nascence and by way of decisive support. In the third method, by 'does not intend,' the wholesome and unwholesome states of the three planes have ceased. By 'does not plan,' craving and views in the eight types of consciousness have ceased. By 'harbors a latent tendency,' having excluded what is mentioned in the sutta, the decisive support is taken by way of the unabandoned aspect in wholesome, unwholesome, resultant, functional, and material phenomena of the three planes. The fourth method is just like the preceding one.

Tadappatiṭṭhiteti tasmiṃ appatiṭṭhite. Avirūḷheti kammaṃ javāpetvā [P 2.0072] paṭisandhiākaḍḍhanasamatthatāya anibbattamūle. Ettha pana kiṃ kathitanti? Arahattamaggassa kiccaṃ, khīṇāsavassa kiccakaraṇantipi navalokuttaradhammātipi vattuṃ vaṭṭati. Ettha ca viññāṇassa ceva āyatiṃ punabbhavassa ca antare eko sandhi, vedanātaṇhānamantare eko, bhavajātīnamantare ekoti. Aṭṭhamaṃ.

As for 'that not being established,' it means when that consciousness is not established. As for 'not having grown,' it means when, having impelled the kamma, a root with the capacity to draw forth rebirth-linking has not arisen. But here, what is stated? It is fitting to say that the function of the path of arahantship is stated; or that the performance of the function by one whose taints are destroyed is stated; or that the nine supramundane dhammas are stated. And here, there is one connection between consciousness and future renewed existence, one between feeling and craving, and one between becoming and birth. The eighth is finished.

9. Dutiyacetanāsuttavaṇṇanā

9. Explanation of the Second Discourse on Intention.

39. Navame [M 2.0067] viññāṇanāmarūpānaṃ antare eko sandhi, vedanātaṇhānamantare eko, bhavajātīnamantare ekoti. Navamaṃ.

39. In the ninth discourse, there is one connection between consciousness and name-and-form, one between feeling and craving, and one between becoming and birth. The ninth is finished.

10. Tatiyacetanāsuttavaṇṇanā

10. Explanation of the Third Discourse on Intention.

40. Dasame [V 2.0064] natīti taṇhā. Sā hi piyarūpesu rūpādīsu namanaṭṭhena “natī”ti vuccati. Āgati gati hotīti āgatimhi gati hoti, āgate paccupaṭṭhite kamme vā kammanimitte vā gahinimitte vā paṭisandhivasena viññāṇassa gati hoti. Cutūpapātoti evaṃ viññāṇassa āgate paṭisandhivisaye gatiyā sati ito cavanasaṅkhātā cuti, tatthūpapattisaṅkhāto upapātoti ayaṃ cutūpapāto nāma hoti. Evaṃ imasmiṃ sutte natiyā ca āgatigatiyā ca antare ekova sandhi kathitoti. Dasamaṃ.

40. In the tenth discourse, 'nati' is craving. Indeed, it is called 'nati' because of its meaning of inclining towards pleasing objects beginning with forms. 'In the arrival, there is a going' means: when kamma, or a kamma-sign, or a destination-sign, called 'āgati' (arrival), has presented itself, there is a 'gati' (going) of consciousness by way of rebirth-linking. As for 'passing away and reappearance': when, in this way, there is a 'going' of the rebirth-linking consciousness in the object of rebirth-linking that has arisen, the 'passing away' called 'shifting from this present existence' and the 'reappearance' called 'arising there' occur. Thus, this is called 'passing away and reappearance'. In this way, in this discourse, only one connection between 'nati' and 'āgati-gati' was taught. The tenth is finished.

Kaḷārakhattiyavaggo catuttho.

The Kaḷārakhattiya Chapter, the fourth.

5. Gahapativaggo

5. The Householder Chapter

1. Pañcaverabhayasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Explanation of the Discourse on the Five Hostilities and Dangers

41. Gahapativaggassa paṭhame yatoti yadā. Bhayāni verānīti bhayaveracetanāyo. Sotāpattiyaṅgehīti duvidhaṃ sotāpattiyā aṅgaṃ, (sotāpattiyā ca aṅgaṃ,) yaṃ pubbabhāge sotāpattipaṭilābhāya saṃvattati, “sappurisasaṃsevo saddhammassavanaṃ yonisomanasikāro dhammānudhammappaṭipattī”ti (dī. ni. 3.311) evaṃ āgataṃ, paṭiladdhaguṇassa ca sotāpattiṃ patvā ṭhitassa aṅgaṃ, yaṃ sotāpannassa [P 2.0073] aṅgantipi vuccati, buddhe aveccappasādādīnaṃ etaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Idamidha adhippetaṃ. Ariyoti niddoso nirupārambho. Ñāyoti paṭiccasamuppannaṃ ñatvā ṭhitañāṇampi paṭiccasamuppādopi. Yathāha – “ñāyo vuccati paṭiccasamuppādo, ariyopi aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo ñāyo”ti. Paññāyāti aparāparaṃ uppannāya vipassanāpaññāya. Sudiṭṭho hotīti aparāparaṃ uppajjitvā dassanavasena suṭṭhu diṭṭho.

41. In the first discourse of the Householder Chapter, 'yato' means 'yadā' (when). 'Bhayāni verāni' refers to the volitions of fear and hostility. As for 'sotāpattiyaṅgehi' (by the factors of stream-entry): the factor of stream-entry is twofold. There is the factor that occurs in the preliminary stage for the attainment of stream-entry, as stated: 'association with good people, listening to the true Dhamma, wise reflection, and practice in accordance with the Dhamma.' And there is the factor of one who, having attained the quality and reached stream-entry, is established therein, which is also called 'the factor of a stream-enterer.' This is a designation for unwavering confidence in the Buddha, etc. Here, this latter one is intended. 'Ariya' (noble) means faultless, without reproach. 'Ñāya' (method) refers to the knowledge established after knowing dependent origination, and also dependent origination itself. As it is said: 'Dependent origination is called ñāya; the noble eightfold path is also ñāya.' 'Paññāya' (by wisdom) means by the insight-wisdom that has arisen in succession. 'Sudiṭṭho hoti' (it is well seen) means: having arisen in succession, it is well seen by the power of the seeing.

Khīṇanirayotiādīsu [M 2.0068] āyatiṃ tattha anuppajjanatāya khīṇo nirayo mayhanti so ahaṃ khīṇanirayo. Esa nayo sabbattha. Sotāpannoti maggasotaṃ āpanno. Avinipātadhammoti na vinipātasabhāvo[V 2.0065]. Niyatoti paṭhamamaggasaṅkhātena sammattaniyāmena niyato. Sambodhiparāyanoti uttarimaggattayasaṅkhāto sambodhi paraṃ ayanaṃ mayhanti sohaṃ sambodhiparāyano, taṃ sambodhiṃ avassaṃ abhisambujjhanakoti attho.

In the phrases beginning with 'khīṇanirayo' (one for whom hell is exhausted): 'For me, hell is exhausted' means because of the nature of not arising there in the future. Thus, 'I am one for whom hell is exhausted.' This method applies everywhere. 'Sotāpanno' (stream-enterer) means one who has entered the stream of the noble path. 'Avinipātadhammo' (one of a nature not to fall) means one who does not have the nature of falling into states of ruin. 'Niyato' (fixed) means fixed by the right-fixedness designated as the first path. 'Sambodhiparāyano' (one with enlightenment as their destination) means: 'Enlightenment, designated as the three higher paths, is the supreme destination for me'; thus, 'I am one with enlightenment as my destination.' The meaning is that one has the nature of certainly awakening to that enlightenment.

Pāṇātipātapaccayāti pāṇātipātakammakāraṇā. Bhayaṃ veranti atthato ekaṃ. Verañca nāmetaṃ duvidhaṃ hoti bāhiraṃ ajjhattikanti. Ekena hi ekassa pitā mārito hoti, so cintesi “etena kira me pitā mārito, ahampi taṃyeva māressāmī”ti nisitaṃ satthaṃ ādāya carati. Yā tassa abbhantare uppannaveracetanā, idaṃ bāhiraṃ veraṃ nāma. Yā pana itarassa “ayaṃ kira maṃ māressāmīti carati, ahameva naṃ paṭhamataraṃ māressāmī”ti cetanā uppajjati, idaṃ ajjhattikaṃ veraṃ nāma. Idaṃ tāva ubhayampi diṭṭhadhammikameva. Yā pana taṃ niraye uppannaṃ disvā “etaṃ paharissāmī”ti jalitaṃ ayamuggaraṃ gaṇhato nirayapālassa cetanā uppajjati, idamassa samparāyikaṃ bāhiraveraṃ. Yā cassa “ayaṃ niddosaṃ maṃ paharissāmīti āgacchati, ahameva naṃ paṭhamataraṃ paharissāmī”ti cetanā uppajjati, idamassa samparāyikaṃ ajjhattaveraṃ. Yaṃ panetaṃ bāhiraveraṃ, taṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “puggalavera”nti vuttaṃ. Dukkhaṃ domanassanti atthato ekameva. Yathā cettha, evaṃ sesapadesupi “iminā mama bhaṇḍaṃ haṭaṃ[P 2.0074], mayhaṃ dāresu cārittaṃ āpannaṃ, musā vatvā attho bhaggo, surāmadamattena idaṃ nāma kata”ntiādinā nayena veruppatti veditabbā. Aveccappasādenāti adhigatena acalappasādena. Ariyakantehīti pañcahi sīlehi. Tāni hi ariyānaṃ kantāni piyāni. Bhavantaragatāpi ariyā tāni na vijahanti, tasmā “ariyakantānī”ti vuccanti. Sesamettha yaṃ vattabbaṃ siyā, taṃ sabbaṃ visuddhimagge anussatiniddese vuttameva. Paṭhamaṃ.

‘Because of the condition of killing living beings’ means because of the cause of the kamma of killing living beings. ‘Fear’ and ‘hostility’ are one in meaning. And this hostility is of two kinds: external and internal. For instance, one person’s father is killed by another, and he thinks, ‘This one has killed my father; I too will kill him,’ and takes up a sharp weapon and goes about. The volition of vengeful hostility that has arisen within him is called external hostility. But the volition that arises in the other, who thinks, ‘This one is going about intending to kill me; I will kill him first,’ is called internal hostility. For now, both of these pertain only to the present life. But the volition that arises in a hell guard who, seeing one reborn in hell, thinks, ‘I will strike this one,’ and takes up a blazing iron club—this is their external hostility pertaining to the future life. And the volition that arises in that hell-being, who thinks, ‘This one is coming to strike me, though I am innocent; I will strike him first’—this is their internal hostility pertaining to the future life. Now, this external hostility is called ‘personal hostility’ in the commentary. ‘Suffering’ and ‘sorrow’ are one in meaning. Just as here, so too in the remaining phrases, the arising of hostility should be understood by the method beginning with: ‘This one has stolen my property,’ ‘He has transgressed with my wife,’ ‘By speaking falsely, he has destroyed my welfare,’ ‘Under the influence of intoxicants, he did such-and-such.’ ‘With unwavering confidence’ means with attained, unshakeable confidence. ‘Pleasing to the noble ones’ refers to the five precepts. For these are dear and pleasing to the noble ones. Even when they have gone to another existence, the noble ones do not abandon them; therefore, they are called ‘pleasing to the noble ones.’ Whatever else should be said here has all been said in the Visuddhimagga, in the exposition on the recollections. The first is finished.

2. Dutiyapañcaverabhayasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Second Discourse on the Five Kinds of Fear and Hostility

42. Dutiye bhikkhūnaṃ kathitabhāvamattameva viseso. Dutiyaṃ.

42. In the second discourse, the only distinction is that it was spoken to the bhikkhus. The second is finished.

3. Dukkhasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Discourse on Suffering

43. Tatiye [M 2.0069] dukkhassāti vaṭṭadukkhassa. Samudayanti dve samudayā khaṇikasamudayo ca paccayasamudayo [V 2.0066] ca. Paccayasamudayaṃ passantopi bhikkhu khaṇikasamudayaṃ passati, khaṇikasamudayaṃ passantopi paccayasamudayaṃ passati. Atthaṅgamopi accantatthaṅgamo bhedatthaṅgamoti duvidho. Accantatthaṅgamaṃ passantopi bhedatthaṅgamaṃ passati, bhedatthaṅgamaṃ passantopi accantatthaṅgamaṃ passati. Desessāmīti idaṃ vaṭṭadukkhassa samudayaatthaṅgamaṃ nibbattibhedaṃ nāma desessāmi, taṃ suṇāthāti attho. Paṭiccāti nissayavasena ceva ārammaṇavasena ca paccayaṃ katvā. Tiṇṇaṃ saṅgati phassoti tiṇṇaṃ saṅgatiyā phasso. Ayaṃ kho, bhikkhave, dukkhassa samudayoti ayaṃ vaṭṭadukkhassa nibbatti nāma. Atthaṅgamoti bhedo. Evañhi vaṭṭadukkhaṃ bhinnaṃ hoti appaṭisandhiyaṃ. Tatiyaṃ.

43. In the third discourse, ‘of suffering’ means of the suffering of the round of existence. In the word ‘origin,’ there are two origins: momentary origin and conditional origin. A bhikkhu who sees conditional origin also sees momentary origin, and one who sees momentary origin also sees conditional origin. ‘Cessation’ is also twofold: absolute cessation and cessation by breaking up. One who sees absolute cessation also sees cessation by breaking up, and one who sees cessation by breaking up also sees absolute cessation. ‘I will teach’ means: ‘I will teach this, which is called the distinction of arising, namely the arising and cessation of the suffering of the round of existence; listen to that.’ This is the meaning. ‘Dependent on’ means having made it a condition by way of dependence and by way of object. ‘The contact is the union of three’ means contact through the union of the three. ‘This, bhikkhus, is the origin of suffering’ means this is called the arising of the suffering of the round of existence. ‘Cessation’ means breaking up. For in this way, the suffering of the round of existence is destroyed, without rebirth-linking. The third is finished.

4. Lokasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Discourse on the World

44. Catutthe lokassāti saṅkhāralokassa. Ayamettha viseso. Catutthaṃ.

44. In the fourth discourse, ‘of the world’ means of the world of formations. This is the distinction here. The fourth is finished.

5. Ñātikasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Discourse at Ñātika

45. Pañcame [P 2.0075] ñātiketi dvinnaṃ ñātakānaṃ gāme. Giñjakāvasatheti iṭṭhakāhi kate mahāpāsāde. Dhammapariyāyanti dhammakāraṇaṃ. Upassutīti upassutiṭṭhānaṃ, yaṃ ṭhānaṃ upagatena sakkā hoti bhagavato saddaṃ sotuṃ, tattha ṭhitoti attho. So kira gandhakuṭipariveṇasammajjanatthaṃ āgato attano kammaṃ pahāya bhagavato dhammaghosaṃ suṇanto aṭṭhāsi. Addasāti tadā kira bhagavato āditova paccayākāraṃ manasikarontassa “idaṃ iminā paccayena hoti, idaṃ iminā”ti āvajjato yāva bhavaggā ekaṅgaṇaṃ ahosi, satthā manasikāraṃ pahāya vacasā sajjhāyaṃ karonto yathānusandhinā desanaṃ niṭṭhapetvā, “api nu kho imaṃ dhammapariyāyaṃ koci assosī”ti āvajjento taṃ bhikkhumaddasa. Tena vuttaṃ “addasā kho bhagavā”ti.

45. In the fifth discourse, ‘at Ñātika’ means in the village of the two kinsmen. ‘In the Brick Hall’ means in the great mansion made of bricks. ‘An exposition of the Dhamma’ means the cause for the Dhamma. ‘Within earshot’ means a place for listening; a place where, having gone, one is able to hear the Blessed One's voice; he stood in that place, this is the meaning. It is said that bhikkhu, having come to sweep the Perfumed Chamber's enclosure, abandoning his own task, stood listening to the Blessed One's Dhamma-voice. ‘He saw’ means: it is said that at that time, as the Blessed One was attending from the very beginning to the causal structure—reflecting, ‘this comes to be with this as condition; this with this’—it became a single open space for him up to the peak of existence. The Teacher, having ceased his mental application and reciting it by voice, concluded the teaching according to its sequence, and reflecting, ‘I wonder, did anyone hear this exposition of the Dhamma?’ he saw that bhikkhu. Therefore it was said, ‘the Blessed One saw.’

Assosi [M 2.0070] noti assosi nu. Atha vā assosi noti amhākaṃ bhāsantānaṃ assosīti. Uggaṇhāhītiādīsu sutvā tuṇhībhūtova paguṇaṃ karonto uggaṇhāti nāma. Padānupadaṃ ghaṭetvā vācāya paricitaṃ karonto pariyāpuṇāti nāma. Ubhayathāpi paguṇaṃ ādhārappattaṃ karonto dhāreti nāma. Atthasaṃhitoti kāraṇanissito. Ādibrahmacariyakoti maggabrahmacariyassa [V 2.0067] ādi patiṭṭhānabhūto. Iti tīsupi imesu suttesu vaṭṭavivaṭṭameva kathitaṃ. Pañcamaṃ.

‘Did he hear?’ means ‘did he hear?’ Alternatively, ‘did he hear us?’ means ‘did you hear us speaking?’ In passages such as ‘Learn this,’ having heard and while remaining silent, one who makes it proficient is said to ‘learn’ it. By connecting it word by word and making it familiar by voice, one is said to ‘master’ it. By either method, one who makes it proficient and established as a basis is said to ‘bear it in mind.’ ‘Connected with the goal’ means based on the cause. ‘Fundamental to the holy life’ means it is the initial foundation of the holy life of the path. Thus, in these three discourses, only the round of existence and the turning away from it are discussed. The fifth is finished.

6. Aññatarabrāhmaṇasuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Discourse about a Certain Brahmin

46. Chaṭṭhe aññataroti nāmavasena apākaṭo aññataro brāhmaṇo. Chaṭṭhaṃ.

46. In the sixth discourse, ‘aññataro’ means a certain brahmin, unspecified by name. The sixth is finished.

7. Jāṇussoṇisuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Jāṇussoṇi Discourse

47. Sattame jāṇussoṇīti ṭhānantaravasena evaṃladdhanāmo asītikoṭivibhavo mahāpurohito. Sattamaṃ.

47. In the seventh discourse, Jāṇussoṇi, so named according to his rank, was a great chaplain with eighty crores of wealth. The seventh discourse is finished.

8. Lokāyatikasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Explanation of the Lokāyatika Discourse

48. Aṭṭhame [P 2.0076] lokāyatikoti vitaṇḍasatthe lokāyate kataparicayo. Jeṭṭhametaṃ lokāyatanti paṭhamaṃ lokāyataṃ. Lokāyatanti ca lokasseva āyataṃ, bālaputhujjanalokassa āyataṃ, mahantaṃ gambhīranti upadhāritabbaṃ parittaṃ bhāvaṃ diṭṭhigataṃ. Ekattanti ekasabhāvaṃ, niccasabhāvamevāti pucchati. Puthuttanti purimasabhāvena nānāsabhāvaṃ, devamanussādibhāvena paṭhamaṃ hutvā pacchā na hotīti ucchedaṃ sandhāya pucchati.
