Evamettha “sabbamatthi, sabbamekatta”nti imā dvepi sassatadiṭṭhiyo, “sabbaṃ natthi, sabbaṃ puthutta”nti imā dve ucchedadiṭṭhiyoti veditabbā. Aṭṭhamaṃ.

48. In the eighth discourse, ‘lokāyatika’ means one familiar with the Lokāyata, the science of sophistry. This view, 'all exists,' is the first Lokāyata. And ‘Lokāyata’ should be understood as the basis of the world itself, the basis of the world of foolish worldlings; it is a dogmatic view, a limited state, though it is considered to be vast and profound. ‘Ekattaṃ’ means a single nature; he asks if it is precisely an eternal nature. ‘Puthuttaṃ’ means of a different nature from a prior nature; having first existed as gods, humans, and so on, and afterwards not existing, he thus asks with reference to annihilation. Thus, herein, these two views, ‘all exists’ and ‘all is oneness,’ are eternalist views; and these two, ‘all does not exist’ and ‘all is diversity,’ should be known as annihilationist views. The eighth discourse is finished.

9. Ariyasāvakasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Explanation of the Discourse on the Noble Disciple

49. Navame kiṃ nu khoti saṃsayuppattiākāradassanaṃ. Samudayatīti uppajjati. Navamaṃ.

49. In the ninth discourse, ‘kiṃ nu kho’ shows the manner of the arising of doubt. ‘Samudayati’ means arises. The ninth discourse is finished.

10. Dutiyaariyasāvakasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Explanation of the Second Discourse on the Noble Disciple

50. Dasame [V 2.0068][M 2.0071] dvepi nayā ekato vuttā. Idameva purimena nānattaṃ, sesaṃ tādisamevāti. Dasamaṃ.

50. In the tenth discourse, both approaches are stated together. This alone is the difference from the preceding discourse; the rest is just the same. The tenth discourse is finished.

Gahapativaggo pañcamo.

The Chapter on Householders, the Fifth, is finished.

6. Dukkhavaggo

6. The Chapter on Suffering

1. Parivīmaṃsanasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Explanation of the Parivīmaṃsana Discourse

51. Dukkhavaggassa paṭhame parivīmaṃsamānoti upaparikkhamāno. Jarāmaraṇanti kasmā jarāmaraṇaṃ ekameva “anekavidhaṃ nānappakāraka”nti vatvā gahitanti ce? Tasmiṃ gahite sabbadukkhassa gahitattā. Yathā hi cūḷāya gahite purise so puriso [P 2.0077] gahitova hoti, evaṃ jarāmaraṇe gahite sabbadukkhaṃ gahitameva hoti. Tasmā “yaṃ kho idaṃ anekavidhaṃ nānappakārakaṃ dukkhaṃ loke uppajjatī”ti nhatvā ṭhitaṃ purisaṃ viya sabbadukkhaṃ dassetvā taṃ cūḷāya gaṇhanto viya jarāmaraṇaṃ gaṇhi.

51. In the first discourse of the Dukkhavagga, ‘parivīmaṃsamāno’ means examining or scrutinizing. As for ‘jarāmaraṇaṃ’: if it is asked, “Why is aging and death, which is just one thing, taken up after saying it is ‘manifold and diverse’?”—it is because when that is grasped, all suffering is grasped. For just as when a man is seized by his topknot, that man is entirely seized, so too when aging and death are grasped, all suffering is indeed grasped. Therefore, having shown all suffering—like showing a man who has bathed and is standing—by stating, ‘whatever manifold and diverse suffering arises in the world,’ he then grasped aging and death, as if seizing that man by his topknot.

Jarāmaraṇanirodhasāruppagāminīti jarāmaraṇanirodhassa sāruppabhāvena nikkilesatāya parisuddhatāya sadisāva hutvā gāminīti attho. Tathā paṭipanno ca hotīti yathā taṃ paṭipannoti vuccati, evaṃ paṭipanno hoti. Anudhammacārīti nibbānadhammaṃ anugataṃ paṭipattidhammaṃ carati, pūretīti attho. Dukkhakkhayāya paṭipannoti sīlaṃ ādiṃ katvā jarāmaraṇadukkhassa nirodhatthāya paṭipanno. Saṅkhāranirodhāyāti saṅkhāradukkhassa nirodhatthāya. Ettāvatā yāva arahattā desanā kathitā.

‘Jarāmaraṇanirodhasāruppagāminī’ means: leading to, having become similar to the cessation of aging and death through its suitability, its freedom from defilements, and its purity. And ‘one has practiced thus’ means: one has practiced in such a way that one is called ‘one who has practiced’ it. ‘Anudhammacārī’ means: one practices, one fulfills, the practice-Dhamma that is in conformity with the Dhamma of Nibbāna. ‘One has practiced for the destruction of suffering’ means: one has practiced for the sake of the cessation of the suffering of aging and death, having made virtue the beginning. ‘For the cessation of formations’ means: for the sake of the cessation of the suffering of formations. By this much, the teaching has been explained up to Arahantship.

Idāni arahattaphalapaccavekkhaṇaṃ satatavihārañca dassetvā desanā nivattetabbā siyā, tathā akatvā avijjāgatoti idaṃ kasmā gaṇhātīti? Khīṇāsavassa samatikkantavaṭṭadukkhadassanatthaṃ[V 2.0069]. Apica puna vaṭṭaṃ ārabhitvā vivaṭṭe kathiyamāne bujjhanakasatto cettha atthi, tassa ajjhāsayavasenāpi idaṃ gaṇhātīti veditabbo. Tattha avijjāgatoti avijjāya [M 2.0072] gato upagato samannāgato. Purisapuggaloti purisoyeva puggalo. Ubhayenāpi sammutikathaṃ katheti. Buddhānañhi sammutikathā paramatthakathāti dve kathā honti. Tattha “satto naro puriso puggalo tisso nāgo”ti evaṃ pavattā sammutikathā nāma. “Khandhā dhātuyo āyatanānī”ti evaṃ pavattā paramatthakathā nāma. Paramatthaṃ kathentāpi sammutiṃ amuñcitvā kathenti. Te sammutiṃ kathentāpi paramatthaṃ kathentāpi saccameva kathenti. Teneva vuttaṃ –

Now, having shown the reviewing of the fruition of Arahantship and the constant abiding, the teaching should be concluded. But not having done so, why does he take up this passage beginning with ‘avijjāgato’? To show that for one whose taints are destroyed, the suffering of the cycle has been transcended. Furthermore, it should be understood that he also takes this up on account of the inclination of a person present here who is capable of awakening when the talk on the cycle is begun again and the talk on its removal is being explained. Therein, ‘avijjāgato’ means gone to, approached, and possessed of ignorance. ‘Purisapuggalo’ means a person who is a man. With both terms, he speaks conventional speech. For the Buddhas have two kinds of speech: conventional speech and ultimate speech. Therein, speech that proceeds as ‘a being, a man, a person, an individual, Tissa, Nāga’ is called conventional speech. Speech that proceeds as ‘aggregates, elements, sense bases’ is called ultimate speech. Even when speaking of the ultimate, they speak without abandoning convention. Whether they are speaking conventionally or speaking of the ultimate, they speak only what is true. Therefore it is said:

“Duve saccāni akkhāsi, sambuddho vadataṃ varo;

Sammutiṃ paramatthañca, tatiyaṃ nūpalabbhati;

Saṅketavacanaṃ saccaṃ, lokasammutikāraṇaṃ;

Paramatthavacanaṃ saccaṃ, dhammānaṃ bhūtalakkhaṇa”nti.

The Fully Enlightened One, the best of speakers, declared two truths: the conventional and the ultimate; a third is not found. Designated speech, which is the reason for worldly convention, is true. Ultimate speech, which is the true characteristic of phenomena, is true.

Puññaṃ [P 2.0078] ce saṅkhāranti terasacetanābhedaṃ puññābhisaṅkhāraṃ. Abhisaṅkharotīti karoti. Puññūpagaṃ hoti viññāṇanti kammaviññāṇaṃ kammapuññena upagataṃ sampayuttaṃ hoti, vipākaviññāṇaṃ vipākapuññena. Apuññaṃ ce saṅkhāranti dvādasacetanābhedaṃ apuññābhisaṅkhāraṃ abhisaṅkharoti. Āneñjaṃ ce saṅkhāranti catucetanābhedaṃ āneñjābhisaṅkhāraṃ. Āneñjūpagaṃ hoti viññāṇanti kammāneñjena kammaviññāṇaṃ, vipākāneñjena vipākaviññāṇaṃ upagataṃ hoti. Ettha ca tividhassa kammābhisaṅkhārassa gahitattā dvādasapadiko paccayākāro gahitova hoti. Ettāvatā vaṭṭaṃ dassitaṃ.

If one forms a meritorious formation (‘puññaṃ ce saṅkhāraṃ’): this is the meritorious formation divided into thirteen volitions. ‘Forms’ (‘abhisaṅkharoti’) means creates. ‘Consciousness becomes endowed with merit’ (‘puññūpagaṃ hoti viññāṇaṃ’) means: kamma-consciousness becomes endowed with and associated with meritorious kamma, and resultant consciousness with meritorious result. If one forms a demeritorious formation (‘apuññaṃ ce saṅkhāraṃ’): one forms the demeritorious formation divided into twelve volitions. If one forms an imperturbable formation (‘āneñjaṃ ce saṅkhāraṃ’): this is the imperturbable formation divided into four volitions. ‘Consciousness becomes endowed with the imperturbable’ (‘āneñjūpagaṃ hoti viññāṇaṃ’) means: kamma-consciousness becomes endowed with imperturbable kamma, and resultant consciousness with imperturbable result. And here, because the threefold kamma-formation is included, the twelve-factored dependent origination is also included. By this much, the cycle has been shown.

Idāni vivaṭṭaṃ dassento yato kho, bhikkhavetiādimāha. Tattha avijjāti catūsu saccesu aññāṇaṃ. Vijjāti arahattamaggañāṇaṃ. Ettha ca paṭhamameva avijjāya pahīnāya vijjā uppajjati. Yathā pana caturaṅgepi tame rattiṃ padīpujjalena andhakāro pahīyati, evaṃ vijjuppādā avijjāya pahānaṃ veditabbaṃ. Na kiñci loke upādiyatīti loke kiñci dhammaṃ na gaṇhāti na parāmasati. Anupādiyaṃ na paritassatīti anupādiyanto agaṇhanto neva taṇhāparitassanāya, na bhayaparitassanāya paritassati, na taṇhāyati na bhāyatīti attho. Paccattaññevāti sayameva attanāva parinibbāyati, na aññassa ānubhāvena.

Now, wishing to show the state of release from the cycle of existence, he spoke the words beginning with, 'From what, monks...' Herein, ignorance is not knowing regarding the four truths. Knowledge is the knowledge associated with the path of Arahantship. And here, knowledge arises only when ignorance has first been abandoned. Just as in a dark night with four factors, darkness is dispelled simultaneously with the lighting of a lamp, so too, the abandoning of ignorance should be understood to occur with the arising of knowledge. 'He does not cling to anything in the world' means that in the world of aggregates, he does not take up any phenomenon as 'this is mine,' nor does he misapprehend it. 'Not clinging, he is not agitated' means that not clinging, not taking up, he is not agitated by the agitation that is craving or the agitation that is fear; he does not crave, he does not fear—this is the meaning. 'By himself indeed' means he attains Parinibbāna by himself, not through the power of another.

So [V 2.0070][M 2.0073] sukhaṃ ce vedananti idaṃ kasmā ārabhi? Khīṇāsavassa paccavekkhaṇañāṇaṃ dassetvā satatavihāraṃ dassetuṃ ārabhi. Anajjhositāti taṇhāya gilitvā pariniṭṭhapetvā agahitā. Atha dukkhavedanā kasmā vuttā, kiṃ tampi abhinandanto atthīti? Āma atthi. Sukhaṃ abhinandantoyeva hi dukkhaṃ abhinandati nāma dukkhaṃ patvā sukhaṃ patthanato sukhassa ca vipariṇāmadukkhatoti. Kāyapariyantikanti kāyaparicchinnaṃ, yāva pañcadvārakāyo pavattati, tāva pavattaṃ pañcadvārikavedananti attho. Jīvitapariyantikanti jīvitaparicchinnaṃ[P 2.0079]. Yāva jīvitaṃ pavattati, tāva pavattaṃ manodvārikavedananti attho.

Why was this, 'If he feels a pleasant feeling...' begun? It was begun in order to show the reviewing knowledge of one whose taints are destroyed, and having shown that, to show his constant abiding. Why was painful feeling mentioned? Is there someone who also delights in that? This is the question. Yes, there is. Indeed, it is one who delights in pleasant feeling who is said to delight in painful feeling. Why? Because having encountered pain, one longs for pleasure, and because of the suffering due to the changing nature of pleasure. Thus should it be answered. 'Ending with the body' means limited by the body; the meaning is the feeling related to the five doors that occurs for as long as the body at the five doors exists. 'Ending with life' means limited by life; the meaning is the feeling related to the mind door that occurs for as long as life exists.

Tattha pañcadvārikavedanā pacchā uppajjitvā paṭhamaṃ nirujjhati, manodvārikavedanā paṭhamaṃ uppajjitvā pacchā nirujjhati. Sā hi paṭisandhikkhaṇe vatthurūpasmiṃyeva patiṭṭhāti. Pañcadvārikā pavatte pañcadvāravasena pavattamānā paṭhamavaye vīsativassakāle rajjanadussanamuyhanavasena adhimattā balavatī hoti, paṇṇāsavassakāle ṭhitā hoti, saṭṭhivassakālato paṭṭhāya parihāyamānā asītinavutivassakāle mandā hoti. Tadā hi sattā “cirarattaṃ ekato nisīdimhā nipajjimhā”ti vadantepi “na sañjānāmā”ti vadanti. Adhimattānipi rūpādiārammaṇāni “na passāma na suṇāma”, “sugandhaṃ duggandhaṃ vā sāduṃ asāduṃ vā thaddhaṃ mudukanti vā na jānāmā”ti vadanti. Iti nesaṃ pañcadvārikavedanā bhaggā hoti, manodvārikāva pavattati. Sāpi anupubbena parihāyamānā maraṇasamaye hadayakoṭiṃyeva nissāya pavattati. Yāva panesā pavattati, tāva satto jīvatīti vuccati. Yadā nappavattati, tadā mato niruddhoti vuccati.

Among these, the feeling related to the five doors, arising later, ceases first; the feeling related to the mind door, arising first, ceases later. For that mind-door feeling is established only in the physical base at the moment of rebirth-linking. The five-door feeling, occurring in the course of existence by way of the five doors, is exceedingly strong and powerful in the first stage of life, at the age of twenty, by way of passion, aversion, and delusion. At the age of fifty, it is stable. Starting from the age of sixty, it declines, becoming weak at the age of eighty or ninety. For at that time, beings, even when saying, 'We sat together, we lay down together for a long, long time,' say, 'We do not recognize them.' Even with very intense objects such as visible forms, they say, 'We do not see, we do not hear,' and 'We do not know whether it is a good scent or a bad scent, a sweet taste or a bitter taste, or whether it is hard or soft.' Thus, for them, the feeling related to the five doors is impaired; only the feeling related to the mind door occurs. That too, gradually declining, occurs at the time of death depending only on the extremity of the heart-base. As long as this occurs, for so long is a being said to be alive. When it does not occur, then he is said to be dead, ceased.

Svāyamattho vāpiyā dīpetabbo –

This meaning should be illuminated by means of a reservoir—

Yathā hi puriso pañcaudakamaggasampannaṃ vāpiṃ kareyya, paṭhamaṃ deve vuṭṭhe pañcahi udakamaggehi udakaṃ pavisitvā antovāpiyaṃ āvāṭe pūreyya, punappunaṃ deve vassante udakamagge pūretvā gāvutaḍḍhayojanamattaṃ ottharitvā udakaṃ tiṭṭheyya tato tato vissandamānaṃ, atha niddhamanatumbe vivaritvā khettesu kamme kariyamāne udakaṃ nikkhamantaṃ, sassapākakāle (udakaṃ nikkhamantaṃ,) udakaṃ parihīnaṃ “macche gaṇhāmā”ti vattabbataṃ āpajjeyya, tato [M 2.0074] katipāhena āvāṭesuyeva udakaṃ saṇṭhaheyya. Yāva pana taṃ āvāṭesu hoti, tāva “mahāvāpiyaṃ [V 2.0071] udakaṃ atthī”ti saṅkhaṃ gacchati. Yadā pana tattha chijjati, tadā “vāpiyaṃ udakaṃ natthī”ti vuccati, evaṃsampadamidaṃ veditabbaṃ.

For it is as if a man were to build a reservoir equipped with five water channels. When the sky first rains, water would enter through the five channels and fill the pits and hollows inside the reservoir. When the sky rains again and again, having filled the water channels and inundated an area of about a gāvuta or half a yojana, the water would stand, overflowing from here and there. Then, when the drainage outlets are opened and work is being done in the fields, the water flows out. At the time of the ripening of the crops, the water having diminished, it would come to be said, 'Let's catch the fish.' Then, after a few days, water would remain only in the pits and hollows. As long as it is in the pits and hollows, it goes by the designation, 'There is water in the great reservoir.' But when the water there is cut off, it is said, 'There is no water in the reservoir.' This sequence of events should be understood in this way.

Paṭhamaṃ [P 2.0080] deve vassante pañcahi maggehi udake pavisante āvāṭānaṃ pūraṇakālo viya hi paṭhamameva paṭisandhikkhaṇe manodvārikavedanāya vatthurūpe patiṭṭhitakālo, punappunaṃ deve vassante pañcannaṃ maggānaṃ pūritakālo viya pavatte pañcadvārikavedanāya pavattikālo, gāvutaḍḍhayojanamattaṃ ajjhottharaṇaṃ viya paṭhamavaye vīsativassakāle rajjanādivasena tassā adhimattabalavabhāvo, yāva vāpito udakaṃ na niggacchati, tāva pūrāya vāpiyā ṭhitakālo viya paññāsavassakāle tassā ṭhitakālo, niddhamanatumbesu vivaṭesu kammante kariyamāne udakassa nikkhamanakālo viya saṭṭhivassakālato paṭṭhāya tassā parihāni, udake bhaṭṭhe udakamaggesu parittodakassa ṭhitakālo viya asītinavutivassakāle pañcadvārikavedanāya mandakālo, āvāṭesuyeva udakassa patiṭṭhānakālo viya hadayavatthukoṭiṃ nissāya manodvārikavedanāya pavattikālo, āvāṭesu parittepi udake sati “vāpiyaṃ udakaṃ atthī”ti vattabbakālo viya yāva sā pavattati, tāva “satto jīvatī”ti vuccati. Yathā pana āvāṭesu udake chinne “natthi vāpiyaṃ udaka”nti vuccati, evaṃ manodvārikavedanāya appavattamānāya “satto mato”ti vuccati. Imaṃ vedanaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “jīvitapariyantikaṃ vedanaṃ vediyamāno”ti.

Just as the time of the filling of the pits and hollows when the sky first rains and water enters through the five channels, so should be seen the time of the establishment of mind-door feeling in the physical base at the very first moment of rebirth-linking. Just as the time when the five channels are filled when the sky rains again and again, so should be seen the time of the occurrence of five-door feeling in the course of existence. Just as the inundation of an area of a gāvuta or half a yojana, so should be seen its state of being exceedingly strong and powerful in the first stage of life, at the age of twenty, by way of passion and so on. Just as the time when the full reservoir stands as long as water does not flow out of it, so should be seen its stable period at the age of fifty. Just as the time of the water flowing out when the drainage outlets are opened and work is being done, so should be seen its decline starting from the age of sixty. Just as the time when little water remains in the water channels when the water has flowed out, so should be seen the weak period of the five-door feeling at the age of eighty or ninety. Just as the time when water remains only in the pits and hollows, so should be seen the time of the occurrence of mind-door feeling depending on the extremity of the heart-base. Just as the time when it is said, 'There is still water in the reservoir,' when there is even a little water in the pits and hollows, so too, as long as that mind-door feeling occurs, it is said, 'The being is alive.' And just as when the water in the pits and hollows is cut off, it is said, 'There is no water in the reservoir,' so too, when mind-door feeling does not occur, it is said, 'The being is dead.' It was with reference to this feeling that it was said, 'experiencing a feeling that is life-ending.'

Kāyassa bhedāti kāyassa bhedena. Jīvitapariyādānā uddhanti jīvitakkhayato uddhaṃ. Idhevāti paṭisandhivasena parato agantvā idheva. Sītībhavissantīti pavattivipphandadaratharahitāni sītāni appavattanadhammāni bhavissanti. Sarīrānīti dhātusarīrāni. Avasissantīti avasiṭṭhāni bhavissanti.

'With the breakup of the body' means by the destruction of the body. 'After the exhaustion of life' means after the end of life. 'Right here' means right here in this present existence, without going to the next world by way of rebirth. 'Will become cool' means they will become peaceful, devoid of the arising, trembling, and anxiety of formations, and having the nature of non-arising. 'The bodily remains' means the elemental relics. 'Will remain' means they will be what is left over.

Kumbhakārapākāti kumbhakārassa bhājanapacanaṭṭhānato. Paṭisisseyyāti ṭhapeyya. Kapallānīti saha mukhavaṭṭiyā ekābaddhāni kumbhakapallāni. Avasisseyyunti [M 2.0075][P 2.0081] tiṭṭheyyuṃ. Evameva khoti ettha idaṃ opammasaṃsandanaṃ – ādittakumbhakārapāko viya hi tayo bhavā daṭṭhabbā, kumbhakāro viya yogāvacaro, pākato kumbhakārabhājanānaṃ nīharaṇadaṇḍako viya arahattamaggañāṇaṃ, samo bhūmibhāgo viya asaṅkhataṃ nibbānatalaṃ, daṇḍakena uṇhakumbhaṃ ākaḍḍhitvā [V 2.0072] same bhūmibhāge kumbhassa ṭhapitakālo viya āraddhavipassakassa rūpasattakaṃ arūpasattakaṃ vipassantassa kammaṭṭhāne ca paguṇe vibhūte upaṭṭhahamāne tathārūpaṃ utusappāyādiṃ labhitvā ekāsane nisinnassa vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā aggaphalaṃ arahattaṃ patvā catūhi apāyehi attabhāvaṃ uddharitvā phalasamāpattivasena asaṅkhate nibbānatale ṭhitakālo daṭṭhabbo. Khīṇāsavo pana uṇhakumbho viya arahattappattadivaseyeva na parinibbāti, sāsanappaveṇiṃ pana ghaṭayamāno paṇṇāsasaṭṭhivassāni ṭhatvā carimakacittappattiyā upādiṇṇakakkhandhabhedā anupādisesāya nibbānadhātuyā parinibbāti. Athassa kumbhassa viya kapallāni anupādiṇṇakasarīrāneva avasissantīti. Sarīrāni avasissantīti pajānātīti idaṃ pana khīṇāsavassa anuyogāropanatthaṃ vuttaṃ.

'Potter's kiln' means from the potter's place for baking vessels. 'Should set aside' means should place. 'Potsherds' means the potter's potsherds that are bound as one together with their rims. 'Would remain' means they would stay. In the same way, here this is the connection of the simile: Indeed, the three realms of existence are to be seen like a blazing potter's kiln; the meditator is to be seen like the potter; the knowledge of the path to arahantship is to be seen like the pole for taking out the potter's vessels from the kiln; the unconditioned ground of Nibbāna is to be seen like a level portion of ground; the time when a hot pot is dragged out with the pole and placed on level ground is to be seen as the time when a meditator who has undertaken insight—contemplating the sevenfold material and sevenfold immaterial formations, with the meditation subject being proficient, clear, and present—having obtained suitable conditions such as agreeable weather, sitting on a single seat, having developed insight, having reached the supreme fruit, arahantship, having lifted his existence out of the four woeful states, abides on the unconditioned ground of Nibbāna by way of fruition attainment. However, an Arahant, like a hot pot, does not attain parinibbāna on the very day of attaining arahantship. Rather, having established the lineage of the Dispensation for fifty or sixty years, upon reaching the final consciousness, due to the breaking up of the clung-to aggregates, he attains parinibbāna with the Nibbāna-element without residue. Then, just as the potsherds of the pot remain, so too only his non-clung-to bodily relics will remain. This phrase, 'he understands that the bodily relics will remain,' was said for the purpose of applying the inquiry to the Arahant.

Viññāṇaṃ paññāyethāti paṭisandhiviññāṇaṃ paññāyetha. Sādhu sādhūti therānaṃ byākaraṇaṃ sampahaṃsati. Evametanti yadetaṃ tividhe abhisaṅkhāre asati paṭisandhiviññāṇassa appaññāṇantiādi, evameva etaṃ. Adhimuccathāti sanniṭṭhānasaṅkhātaṃ adhimokkhaṃ paṭilabhatha. Esevanto dukkhassāti ayameva vaṭṭadukkhassa anto ayaṃ paricchedo, yadidaṃ nibbānanti. Paṭhamaṃ.

'Consciousness would be known' means rebirth-linking consciousness would be known. With 'Good, good!' he delights in the elders' explanation. 'So it is' means: That which is said, namely, 'in the absence of the threefold formations, there is the non-manifestation of rebirth-linking consciousness,' and so on—it is just so. 'Be resolved' means attain the determination called decision. 'This is the end of suffering' means this very Nibbāna is the end, the limit, of the suffering of the round. The first sutta is finished.

2. Upādānasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Clinging Sutta

52. Dutiye upādāniyesūti catunnaṃ upādānānaṃ paccayesu tebhūmakadhammesu. Assādānupassinoti assādaṃ anupassantassa. Tatrāti tasmiṃ aggikkhandhe. Tadāhāroti taṃpaccayo. Tadupādānoti tasseva vevacanaṃ. Evameva [P 2.0082] khoti ettha aggikkhandho viya hi tayo bhavā, tebhūmakavaṭṭantipi etadeva, aggijaggakapuriso viya vaṭṭanissito bālaputhujjano, sukkhatiṇagomayādipakkhipanaṃ viya assādānupassino puthujjanassa [M 2.0076] taṇhādivasena chahi dvārehi kusalākusalakammakaraṇaṃ. Tiṇagomayādīsu khīṇesu punappunaṃ tesaṃ pakkhipanena aggikkhandhassa vaḍḍhanaṃ viya bālaputhujjanassa uṭṭhāya samuṭṭhāya yathāvuttakammāyūhanena aparāparaṃ vaṭṭadukkhanibbattanaṃ.

52. In the second sutta, 'in things that can be clung to' means in the phenomena of the three realms which are the conditions for the four kinds of clinging. 'For one who repeatedly sees gratification' means for one who repeatedly sees gratification. 'Therein' means in that mass of fire. 'Having that as its fuel' means having that as its condition. 'Having that as its clinging-fuel' is a synonym for that very term. In the same way, here the three existences are indeed like a mass of fire; the cycle of the three realms is just this. The foolish ordinary person who is dependent on the cycle is like the man who tends the fire. The performance of wholesome and unwholesome kamma through the six doors by the power of craving, etc., by an ordinary person who repeatedly sees gratification is like the adding of dry grass, cow-dung, and so on. Just as a mass of fire grows by repeatedly adding fuel like grass and cow-dung when it is exhausted, so too is the arising of the suffering of the cycle, again and again, for the foolish ordinary person who strives and exerts himself by accumulating kamma as described.

Na kālena kālaṃ sukkhāni ceva tiṇāni pakkhipeyyāti tañhi koci atthakāmo evaṃ vadeyya [V 2.0073] – “bho kasmā uṭṭhāya samuṭṭhāya kalāpe bandhitvā sukkhatiṇakaṭṭhānaṃ pacchiyañca pūretvā sukkhagomayāni pakkhipanto etaṃ aggiṃ jālesi? Api nu te atthi itonidānaṃ kāci vaḍḍhīti? Vaṃsāgatametaṃ bho amhākaṃ, itonidānaṃ pana me avaḍḍhiyeva, kuto vaḍḍhi? Ahañhi imaṃ aggiṃ jagganto neva nhāyituṃ na bhuñjituṃ na nipajjituṃ labhāmīti. Tena hi bho kiṃ te iminā niratthakena aggijālanena? Ehi tvaṃ etāni ābhatāni tiṇādīni ettha nikkhipa, tāni sayameva jhāyissanti, tvaṃ pana asukasmiṃ ṭhāne sītodakā pokkharaṇī atthi, tattha nhatvā, mālāgandhavilepanehi attānaṃ maṇḍetvā sunivattho supārutova pādukāhi nagaraṃ pavisitvā pāsādavaramāruyha vātapānaṃ vivaritvā mahāvīthiyaṃ virocamāno nisīda ekaggo sukhasamappito hutvā, tattha te nisinnassa tiṇādīnaṃ khayena sayameva ayaṃ aggi appaṇṇattibhāvaṃ gamissatī”ti. So tathā kareyya. Tatheva ca tattha nisinnassa so aggi upādānakkhayena appaṇṇattibhāvaṃ gaccheyya. Idaṃ sandhāyetaṃ “na kālena kāla”ntiādi vuttaṃ.

'One should not from time to time throw in dry grass...' and so on. For a certain person desiring his welfare would say to him: 'Friend, why do you, having striven and exerted yourself, tying up bundles of dry grass and sticks, and filling a basket with dry cow-dung, light this fire? Is there any growth for you on account of this?' 'Sir, this has come down to us through our lineage. But on account of this, for me there is only decline, whence could there be growth? For I, while tending this fire, get no chance to bathe, to eat, or to lie down.' 'Well then, friend, what use is this useless fire-tending to you? Come, you, throw these grasses and so on that you have brought here; they will burn up by themselves. But you, in such-and-such a place there is a pond with cool water. Having bathed there, adorned yourself with garlands, perfumes, and ointments, being well-dressed and well-covered, having entered the city with sandals, ascended a fine palace, opened a window, sit shining in the great street, being one-pointed and endowed with happiness. While you are sitting there, this fire, with the exhaustion of the fuel like grass, will by itself go to a state of no longer being designated.' He would do so. And just so, while he was sitting there, that fire would go to a state of no longer being designated due to the exhaustion of its fuel. It was with reference to this that the phrase 'not from time to time...' and so on was spoken by the Blessed One.

Evameva khoti ettha pana idaṃ opammasaṃsandanaṃ – cattālīsāya kaṭṭhavāhānaṃ jalamāno mahāaggikkhandho viya hi tebhūmakavaṭṭaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ, aggijagganakapuriso viya vaṭṭasannissitako yogāvacaro, atthakāmo puriso viya sammāsambuddho, tena purisena tassa dinnaovādo viya tathāgatena [P 2.0083] “ehi tvaṃ, bhikkhu, tebhūmakadhammesu nibbinda, evaṃ vaṭṭadukkhā muccissasī”ti tassa tebhūmakadhammesu kammaṭṭhānassa kathitakālo, tassa purisassa yathānusiṭṭhaṃ paṭipajjitvā pāsāde nisinnakālo viya yogino [M 2.0077] sugatovādaṃ sampaṭicchitvā suññāgāraṃ paviṭṭhassa tebhūmakadhammesu vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā anukkamena yathānurūpaṃ āhārasappāyādiṃ labhitvā, ekāsane nisinnassa aggaphale patiṭṭhitakālo, tassa nhānavilepanādīhi sudhotamaṇḍitakāyattā tasmiṃ nisinnassa ekaggasukhasamappitakālo viya yogino ariyamaggapokkharaṇiyaṃ maggañāṇodakena sunhātasudhotakilesamalassa hirottappasāṭake nivāsetvā sīlavilepanānulittassa arahattamaṇḍanena attabhāvaṃ maṇḍetvā vimuttipupphadāmaṃ piḷandhitvā iddhipādapādukā āruyha nibbānanagaraṃ pavisitvā dhammapāsādaṃ āruyha satipaṭṭhānamahāvīthiyaṃ virocamānassa nibbānārammaṇaṃ phalasamāpattiṃ appetvā nisinnakālo. Tassa pana purisassa tasmiṃ nisinnassa tiṇādīnaṃ khayena aggikkhandhassa appaṇṇattigamanakālo viya khīṇāsavassa yāvatāyukaṃ ṭhatvā upādiṇṇakakkhandhabhedena anupādisesāya nibbānadhātuyā parinibbutassa mahāvaṭṭavūpasamo daṭṭhabbo. Dutiyaṃ.

Similarly, here this connection of the simile should be understood: The great mass of fire blazing with forty cartloads of wood should be seen as the round of the three planes. The man tending the fire is like a yogāvacara dependent on the round. The man who desires his welfare is like the Fully Enlightened One. The advice given by that man is like the time when the Tathāgata teaches the meditation subject on the phenomena of the three planes to a bhikkhu, saying, 'Come, bhikkhu, become disenchanted with the phenomena of the three planes; thus you will be freed from the suffering of the round.' The time when that man, having practiced as instructed, is sitting in the palace is like the time when the yogāvacara, having accepted the Well-gone One’s advice, enters an empty dwelling, establishes insight into the phenomena of the three planes, gradually obtains suitable food and other requisites, and, sitting on a single seat, becomes established in the highest fruit. The time when that man, his body well-cleansed and adorned by bathing and anointing, sits there endowed with one-pointed happiness is like the time when the yogāvacara—having been well-bathed with the water of path-knowledge in the pond of the noble path and having his stains of defilements well-cleansed, having put on the garment of conscience and fear of wrongdoing, having anointed himself with the unguent of virtue, having adorned his being with the ornament of Arahantship, having worn the flower garland of liberation, having mounted the sandals of the bases of psychic power, having entered the city of Nibbāna, having ascended the palace of the Dhamma, and shining in the great street of the foundations of mindfulness—sits, having attained the fruition attainment that has Nibbāna as its object. Furthermore, like the time when, as that man is sitting there, the mass of fire reaches a state beyond designation due to the exhaustion of fuel such as grass, so should be seen the great appeasement of the round for one whose taints are destroyed, who, having lived for the remainder of his lifespan, attains Parinibbāna with the Nibbāna-element without residue remaining upon the breakup of the clung-to aggregates. The second.

3. Saṃyojanasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Explanation of the Discourse on the Fetters

53. Tatiye [V 2.0074] saṃyojaniyesūti dasannaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ paccayesu. Jhāyeyyāti jaleyya. Telaṃ āsiñceyya vaṭṭiṃ upasaṃhareyyāti dīpapaṭijagganatthaṃ telabhājanañca mahantañca vaṭṭikapālaṃ gahetvā samīpe niccaṃ ṭhitova tele khīṇe telaṃ āsiñceyya, vaṭṭiyā khīṇāya vaṭṭiṃ upasaṃhareyya. Sesamettha saddhiṃ opammasaṃsandanena purimanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Tatiyaṃ.

53. In the third sutta, ‘saṃyojaniyesu’ means in the conditions for the ten fetters. ‘Jhāyeyya’ means ‘it would burn.’ ‘He should pour oil and bring up the wick’ means that for the purpose of attending to the lamp, having taken a large oil container and a large wick holder, he should stand constantly nearby, and when the oil is depleted, he should pour oil; when the wick is depleted, he should bring up the wick. The rest here, together with the connection of the simile, should be understood in the same way as before. The third.

4. Dutiyasaṃyojanasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Explanation of the Second Discourse on the Fetters

54. Catutthe upamaṃ paṭhamaṃ katvā pacchā attho vutto. Sesaṃ tādisameva. Catutthaṃ.

54. In the fourth sutta, the simile is given first, and the meaning is stated afterwards. The rest is the same. The fourth.

5. Mahārukkhasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Discourse on the Great Tree

55. Pañcame [P 2.0084] uddhaṃ ojaṃ abhiharantīti pathavīrasañca āporasañca upari āropenti. Ojāya āropitattā hatthasatubbedhassa rukkhassa aṅkuraggesu bindubindūni viya hutvā sineho tiṭṭhati. Idaṃ panettha opammasaṃsandanaṃ [M 2.0078] – mahārukkho viya hi tebhūmakavaṭṭaṃ, mūlāni viya āyatanāni, mūlehi ojāya ārohanaṃ viya chahi dvārehi kammārohanaṃ, ojāya abhiruḷhattā mahārukkhassa yāvakappaṭṭhānaṃ viya vaṭṭanissitabālaputhujjanassa chahi dvārehi kammaṃ āyūhantassa aparāparaṃ vaṭṭassa vaḍḍhanavasena dīgharattaṃ ṭhānaṃ.

55. In the fifth sutta, ‘they carry the sap upwards’ means they raise the essence of earth and the essence of water upwards. Because the sap is raised, moisture remains in the tips of the sprouts of a tree a hundred cubits high, like drops. Here, the connection of the simile is as follows: the great tree is like the round of existence in the three planes; the roots are like the sense bases; the rising of the sap from the roots is like the accumulation of kamma through the six doors; and just as the great tree stands for an eon because the sap has risen, so too does the uninstructed worldling, dependent on the round of existence, stand for a long time by accumulating kamma through the six doors, by means of the growth of the round again and again.

Kuddālapiṭakanti kuddālañceva pacchibhājanañca. Khaṇḍākhaṇḍikaṃ chindeyyāti khuddakamahantāni khaṇḍākhaṇḍāni karonto chindeyya. Idaṃ panettha opammasaṃsandanaṃ – idhāpi hi mahārukkho viya tebhūmakavaṭṭaṃ, rukkhaṃ nāsetukāmo puriso viya yogāvacaro, kuddālo viya ñāṇaṃ, pacchi viya samādhi, rukkhacchedanapharasu viya ñāṇaṃ, rukkhassa mūle chinnakālo viya yogino ācariyasantike kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā manasikarontassa paññā, khaṇḍākhaṇḍikaṃ chindanakālo viya saṅkhepato catunnaṃ mahābhūtānaṃ manasikāro, phālanaṃ viya dvecattālīsāya koṭṭhāsesu vitthāramanasikāro, sakalikaṃ sakalikaṃ karaṇakālo viya upādārūpassa ceva rūpakkhandhārammaṇassa viññāṇassa cāti imesaṃ vasena nāmarūpapariggaho, mūlānaṃ upacchedanaṃ viya tasseva nāmarūpassa paccayapariyesanaṃ, vātātape [V 2.0075] visosetvā agginā ḍahanakālo viya anupubbena vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā aññataraṃ sappāyaṃ labhitvā kammaṭṭhāne vibhūte upaṭṭhahamāne ekapallaṅke nisinnassa samaṇadhammaṃ karontassa aggaphalappatti, masikaraṇaṃ viya arahattappattadivaseyeva aparinibbāyantassa yāvatāyukaṃ ṭhita kālo, mahāvāte opunanaṃ nadiyā pavāhanaṃ viya ca upādiṇṇakakkhandhabhedena anupādisesāya nibbānadhātuyā parinibbutassa vaṭṭavūpasamo veditabbo. Pañcamaṃ.

‘Kuddālapiṭaka’ means both the hoe and the basket. ‘He should cut it into pieces’ means he should cut it, making small and large fragments. Here, the connection of the simile is as follows: in this case too, the great tree is like the round of existence in the three planes; the man wishing to destroy the tree is like the meditator; the hoe is like knowledge; the basket is like concentration; the axe for cutting the tree is like knowledge; the time of cutting the tree’s roots is like the meditator’s wisdom when taking up a meditation subject from a teacher and reflecting on it; the time of cutting into pieces is like briefly contemplating the four great elements; the splitting is like the detailed contemplation on the forty-two parts; the time of making it into chips is like the discernment of name-and-form by means of the derived form and the consciousness whose object is the form aggregate; the cutting off of the roots is like the investigation of the conditions for that same name-and-form; the time of drying in wind and sun and burning with fire is like gradually developing insight, attaining a suitable basis, and with the meditation subject vividly present, while seated on a single seat, practicing the ascetic’s duty and attaining the highest fruition; the time of grinding into powder is like the time one remains for as long as life lasts, not attaining final Nibbāna on the very day of attaining Arahantship; and the scattering by a great wind or the carrying away by a river is to be understood as the cessation of the round of existence for one who has attained final Nibbāna with the Nibbāna-element without residue remaining, through the breaking up of the grasped aggregates. The fifth.

6. Dutiyamahārukkhasuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Second Discourse on the Great Tree

56. Chaṭṭhepi [P 2.0085] upamaṃ paṭhamaṃ vatvā pacchā attho vutto, idameva nānattaṃ. Chaṭṭhaṃ.

56. In the sixth sutta too, the simile is stated first, and afterwards the meaning is stated; this is the only difference. The Sixth.

7. Taruṇarukkhasuttavaṇṇanā

7. Explanation of the Discourse on the Young Tree

57-59. Sattame [M 2.0079] taruṇoti ajātaphalo. Palimajjeyyāti sodheyya. Paṃsuṃ dadeyyāti thaddhapharusapaṃsuṃ haritvā mudugomayacuṇṇamissaṃ madhurapaṃsuṃ pakkhipeyya. Vuddhinti vuddhiṃ āpajjitvā pupphūpago pupphaṃ, phalūpago phalaṃ gaṇheyya. Idaṃ panettha opammasaṃsandanaṃ – taruṇarukkho viya hi tebhūmakavaṭṭaṃ, rukkhajaggako puriso viya vaṭṭanissito puthujjano, mūlaphalasantānādīni viya tīhi dvārehi kusalākusalakammāyūhanaṃ, rukkhassa vuḍḍhiāpajjanaṃ viya puthujjanassa tīhi dvārehi kammaṃ āyūhato aparāparaṃ vaṭṭappavatti. Vivaṭṭaṃ vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Aṭṭhamanavamāni uttānatthāneva. Sattamādīni.

57-59. In the seventh discourse, 'young' means not yet bearing fruit. 'Should clear it' means should purify. 'Should add soil' means removing coarse, rough soil and applying sweet soil mixed with soft cow-dung powder. 'Growth' means having attained growth, the flower-bearing tree should bear flowers, the fruit-bearing tree should bear fruit. Herein is the connection by way of simile: a young tree is indeed like the round of the three planes of existence; the man who tends the tree is like an ordinary person dependent on the round; the accumulation of wholesome and unwholesome kamma through the three doors is like the roots, fruits, continuity, and so forth; the tree's attainment of growth is like the ordinary person's accumulating kamma through the three doors, leading to the repeated arising of the round of existence. The unbinding should be understood in the way already stated. The eighth and ninth are of obvious meaning. The seventh and so on.

10. Nidānasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Explanation of the Discourse on the Foundation

60. Dasame kurūsu viharatīti kurūti evaṃ bahuvacanavasena laddhavohāre janapade viharati. Kammāsadhammaṃ nāma kurūnaṃ nigamoti evaṃnāmako kurūnaṃ nigamo, taṃ gocaragāmaṃ katvāti attho. Āyasmāti piyavacanametaṃ garuvacanametaṃ. Ānandoti [P 2.0086] tassa therassa nāmaṃ. Ekamantaṃ nisīdīti cha nisajjadose vivajjento dakkhiṇajāṇumaṇḍalassa abhimukhaṭṭhāne chabbaṇṇānaṃ buddharasmīnaṃ anto pavisitvā pasannalākhārasaṃ vigāhanto viya suvaṇṇapaṭaṃ pārupanto [V 2.0076] viya rattakambalavitānamajjhaṃ pavisanto viya dhammabhaṇḍāgāriko āyasmā ānando nisīdi. Tena vuttaṃ “ekamantaṃ nisīdī”ti.

60. In the tenth discourse, 'dwelling among the Kurus' means dwelling in a country known by the plural designation 'Kurus.' 'Kammāsadhamma is the name of a market town of the Kurus' means there is a market town of the Kurus with this name, and the meaning is that he made it his alms-resort village. 'Venerable' is a term of affection and a term of respect. 'Ānanda' is the name of that Elder. 'Sat down to one side' means: avoiding the six faults of sitting, in the place facing the right kneecap, having entered within the six-colored Buddha-rays, as if plunging into clear lac-dye, as if wrapping himself in a golden cloth, as if entering the midst of a red woolen canopy—thus the Venerable Ānanda, the treasurer of the Dhamma, sat down. Hence it is said, 'sat down to one side.'

Kāya pana velāya kena kāraṇena ayamāyasmā bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamantoti? Sāyanhavelāya paccayākārapañhaṃ pucchanakāraṇena. Taṃ divasaṃ kira ayamāyasmā kulasaṅgahatthāya gharadvāre gharadvāre sahassabhaṇḍikaṃ nikkhipanto viya kammāsadhammaṃ piṇḍāya caritvā piṇḍapātapaṭikkanto satthu vattaṃ dassetvā satthari gandhakuṭiṃ paviṭṭhe satthāraṃ vanditvā attano divāṭṭhānaṃ gantvā antevāsikesu vattaṃ dassetvā paṭikkantesu divāṭṭhānaṃ paṭisammajjitvā cammakkhaṇḍaṃ paññapetvā udakatumbato udakena hatthapāde [M 2.0080] sītalaṃ katvā pallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvā nisinno sotāpattiphalasamāpattiṃ samāpajjitvā. Atha paricchinnakālavasena samāpattito vuṭṭhāya paccayākāre ñāṇaṃ otāresi. So “avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā”tiādito paṭṭhāya antaṃ, antato paṭṭhāya ādiṃ, ubhayantato paṭṭhāya majjhaṃ, majjhato paṭṭhāya ubho ante pāpento tikkhattuṃ dvādasapadaṃ paccayākāraṃ sammasi. Tassevaṃ sammasantassa paccayākāro vibhūto hutvā uttānakuttānako viya upaṭṭhāsi. Tato cintesi – “ayaṃ paccayākāro sabbabuddhehi gambhīro ceva gambhīrāvabhāso cāti kathito, mayhaṃ kho pana padesañāṇe ṭhitassa sāvakassa sato uttāno viya vibhūto pākaṭo hutvā upaṭṭhāti, mayhaṃyeva nu kho esa uttānako viya upaṭṭhāti, udāhu aññesampīti attano upaṭṭhānakāraṇaṃ satthu ārocessāmī”ti nisinnaṭṭhānato uṭṭhāya cammakkhaṇḍaṃ papphoṭetvā ādāya sāyanhasamaye bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkami. Tena vuttaṃ – “sāyanhavelāyaṃ paccayākārapañhaṃ pucchanakāraṇena upasaṅkamanto”ti.

And at what time and for what reason did this venerable one approach the Blessed One? In the evening, for the reason of asking a question about dependent origination. It is said that on that day, this venerable one, as if placing a bundle worth a thousand at every door for the sake of supporting families, went on almsround in Kammāsadhamma. Having returned from his almsround, performed his duties for the Teacher, and paid homage to the Teacher after He had entered the fragrant chamber, he went to his own day-dwelling place. After the resident pupils had performed their duties and departed, he swept the day-dwelling place, prepared a piece of hide, cooled his hands and feet with water from a water pot, sat down with his legs crossed, and entered the fruition attainment of stream-entry. Then, having emerged from the attainment after a determined period of time, he directed his knowledge to dependent origination. Starting from 'With ignorance as condition, volitional formations,' he contemplated the twelve-factored dependent origination three times: from the beginning to the end, from the end to the beginning, from both ends to the middle, and from the middle to both ends. As he was thus contemplating, dependent origination became manifest and appeared to him as if exceedingly plain. Then he thought: 'This dependent origination is said by all Buddhas to be profound and of profound appearance. But to me, a disciple established in partial knowledge, it appears as if shallow, manifest, and evident. Does it appear as if shallow only to me, or to others as well? I shall report the reason for its appearance to the Teacher.' Rising from his seat, he shook out the piece of hide, took it, and approached the Blessed One in the evening. Hence it was said: 'approaching in the evening for the reason of asking a question about dependent origination.'

Yāva gambhīroti ettha yāvasaddo pamāṇātikkame. Atikkamma pamāṇaṃ gambhīro, atigambhīroti attho. Gambhīrāvabhāsoti [P 2.0087] gambhīrova hutvā avabhāsati, dissatīti attho. Ekañhi uttānameva gambhīrāvabhāsaṃ hoti pūtipaṇṇarasavasena kāḷavaṇṇaṃ purāṇaudakaṃ viya. Tañhi jāṇuppamāṇampi sataporisaṃ viya dissati. Ekaṃ gambhīraṃ uttānāvabhāsaṃ hoti maṇibhāsaṃ vippasannaudakaṃ viya. Tañhi sataporisampi jāṇuppamāṇaṃ viya khāyati. Ekaṃ uttānaṃ uttānāvabhāsaṃ hoti pātiādīsu udakaṃ viya. Ekaṃ gambhīraṃ gambhīrāvabhāsaṃ hoti sinerupādakamahāsamudde udakaṃ viya. Evaṃ udakameva cattāri nāmāni labhati. Paṭiccasamuppāde panetaṃ natthi. Ayañhi gambhīro ca gambhīrāvabhāso cāti ekameva nāmaṃ labhati[V 2.0077]. Evarūpo samānopi atha ca pana me uttānakuttānako viya khāyati, tadidaṃ acchariyaṃ, bhante, abbhutaṃ, bhanteti evaṃ attano vimhayaṃ pakāsento pañhaṃ pucchitvā tuṇhībhūto nisīdi.

Here, in 'how profound,' the word 'how' (yāva) is in the sense of exceeding a measure. Exceeding the measure, it is profound; the meaning is 'extremely profound.' 'Of profound appearance' means that, being profound, it so appears, it is so seen. For some water, though shallow, appears profound, like old, black-colored water due to the putrid essence of leaves. Though only knee-deep, it appears a hundred fathoms deep. Some water, though profound, appears shallow, like especially clear water shining like a gem. Though a hundred fathoms deep, it appears only knee-deep. Some water, being shallow, appears shallow, like water in a bowl or the like. Some water, being profound, appears profound, like the water in the great ocean at the foot of Mount Sineru. Thus, water alone obtains four designations. But in dependent origination, this is not so. For this obtains only one designation: 'profound and of profound appearance.' 'Although it is of such a nature, yet to me it appears as if very shallow. This is wonderful, venerable sir, this is amazing, venerable sir!' Thus expressing his astonishment, he asked the question and sat down in silence.

Bhagavā [M 2.0081] tassa vacanaṃ sutvā “ānando bhavaggagahaṇāya hatthaṃ pasārento viya sineruṃ bhinditvā miñjaṃ nīharituṃ vāyamamāno viya vinā nāvāya mahāsamuddaṃ taritukāmo viya pathaviṃ parivattetvā pathavojaṃ gahetuṃ vāyamamāno viya buddhavisayaṃ pañhaṃ attano uttānuttānanti vadati, handassa gambhīrabhāvaṃ ācikkhāmī”ti cintetvā mā hevantiādimāha.

The Blessed One, having heard his words, thought: 'Ānanda speaks of a matter within the Buddha's domain as if it were very shallow, like one stretching out his hand to grasp the summit of existence, or like one striving to split Mount Sineru to extract its marrow, or like one wishing to cross the great ocean without a boat, or like one attempting to turn the earth over to grasp its essence. Well then, I shall explain its profound nature to him.' Having reflected thus, he said, 'Do not say so,' and so on.

Tattha mā hevanti ha-kāro nipātamattaṃ, evaṃ mā bhaṇīti attho. “Mā heva”nti ca idaṃ vacanaṃ bhagavā āyasmantaṃ ānandaṃ ussādentopi bhaṇati apasādentopi. Tattha ussādentopīti, ānanda, tvaṃ mahāpañño visadañāṇo, tena te gambhīropi paṭiccasamuppādo uttānako viya khāyati, aññesaṃ panesa uttānakoti na sallakkhetabbo, gambhīroyeva ca so gambhīrāvabhāso ca.

Herein, in the term 'mā hevaṃ,' the letter 'ha' is merely a particle; the meaning is 'do not say thus.' And this statement, 'Mā hevaṃ,' the Blessed One speaks both to encourage and to admonish the Venerable Ānanda. Therein, as to encouraging: 'Ānanda, you are of great wisdom and clear knowledge; therefore, to you, even the profound Dependent Origination appears as if it were shallow. But it should not be regarded as shallow for others; it is indeed profound and has the appearance of being profound.'

Tattha catasso upamā vadanti – cha māse subhojanarasapuṭṭhassa kira katayogassa mahāmallassa samajjasamaye katamallapāsāṇaparicayassa yuddhabhūmiṃ gacchantassa antarā mallapāsāṇaṃ dassesuṃ. So “kiṃ eta”nti āha. Mallapāsāṇoti. Āharatha nanti. “Ukkhipituṃ na [P 2.0088] sakkomā”ti vutte sayaṃ gantvā “kuhiṃ imassa bhāriyaṭṭhāna”nti vatvā dvīhi hatthehi dve pāsāṇe ukkhipitvā kīḷāguḷe viya khipitvā agamāsi. Tattha mallassa mallapāsāṇo lahukoti na aññesampi lahukoti vattabbo. Cha māse subhojanarasapuṭṭho mallo viya hi kappasatasahassaṃ abhinīhārasampanno āyasmā ānando. Yathā mallassa mahābalatāya mallapāsāṇo lahuko, evaṃ therassa mahāpaññatāya paṭiccasamuppādo uttānoti vattabbo, so aññesaṃ uttānoti na vattabbo.

Therein, they speak of four similes. It is said that to a great wrestler—nourished for six months with excellent, delicious food, who had undertaken training and, at the festival grounds, had become familiar with the wrestler's stone—they showed a wrestler's stone while he was going to the battlefield. He said, 'What is this?' 'A wrestler's stone.' 'Bring it.' When it was said, 'We cannot lift it,' he went himself and, saying, 'Where is the heavy part of this?' he lifted two stones with his two hands, threw them as if they were play-balls, and went on his way. Therein, because the wrestler's stone is light for the wrestler, it should not be said that it is also light for others. Indeed, like the wrestler nourished for six months with excellent, delicious food, the Venerable Ānanda is endowed with the fulfillment of his aspiration for a hundred thousand kappas. Just as the wrestler's stone is light for the wrestler due to his great strength, so it should be said that Dependent Origination is shallow for the Elder due to his great wisdom; but it should not be said that it is shallow for others.

Mahāsamudde ca timi nāma mahāmaccho dviyojanasatiko, timiṅgalo tiyojanasatiko, timirapiṅgalo pañcayojanasatiko, ānando timinando ajjhāroho mahātimīti ime cattāro yojanasahassikā. Tattha timirapiṅgaleneva dīpenti. Tassa kira dakkhiṇakaṇṇaṃ cālentassa pañcayojanasate [V 2.0078] padese udakaṃ calati, tathā vāmakaṇṇaṃ, tathā naṅguṭṭhaṃ, tathā sīsaṃ. Dve pana kaṇṇe cāletvā naṅguṭṭhena [M 2.0082] paharitvā sīsaṃ aparāparaṃ katvā kīḷituṃ āraddhassa sattaṭṭhayojanasate ṭhāne bhājane pakkhipitvā uddhane āropitaṃ viya udakaṃ pakkuthati. Yojanasatamatte padese udakaṃ piṭṭhiṃ chādetuṃ na sakkoti. So evaṃ vadeyya – “ayaṃ mahāsamuddo gambhīroti vadanti, kutassa gambhīratā, mayaṃ piṭṭhimattacchādanampi udakaṃ na labhāmā”ti. Tattha kāyūpapannassa timirapiṅgalassa mahāsamuddo uttānoti aññesañca khuddakamacchānaṃ uttānoti na vattabbo, evameva ñāṇūpapannassa therassa paṭiccasamuppādo uttānoti aññesampi uttānoti na vattabbo. Supaṇṇarājā ca diyaḍḍhayojanasatiko hoti. Tassa dakkhiṇapakkho paññāsayojaniko hoti, tathā vāmapakkho, piñchavaṭṭi ca saṭṭhiyojanikā, gīvā tiṃsayojanikā, mukhaṃ navayojanaṃ, pādā dvādasayojanikā, tasmiṃ supaṇṇavātaṃ [P 2.0089] dassetuṃ āraddhe sattaṭṭhayojanasataṃ ṭhānaṃ nappahoti. So evaṃ vadeyya – “ayaṃ ākāso anantoti vadanti, kutassa anantatā, mayaṃ pakkhavātappattharaṇokāsampi na labhāmā”ti. Tattha kāyūpapannassa supaṇṇarañño ākāso parittoti aññesañca khuddakapakkhīnaṃ parittoti na vattabbo, evameva ñāṇūpapannassa therassa paṭiccasamuppādo uttānoti aññesampi uttānoti na vattabbo.

And in the great ocean, there is a great fish named Timi, two hundred yojanas long; the Timiṅgala is three hundred yojanas long; the Timirapiṅgala is five hundred yojanas long; and Ānanda, Timinanda, Ajjhāroha, and Mahātimi—these four are each a thousand yojanas long. Therein, they illustrate with the Timirapiṅgala. It is said that when it moves its right ear, the water stirs in a region of five hundred yojanas; likewise with its left ear, likewise with its tail, and likewise with its head. But when it begins to play by moving both ears, striking with its tail, and moving its head back and forth, the water in a place of seven or eight hundred yojanas boils up as if put in a pot and placed on a stove. In a region of about a hundred yojanas, the water cannot cover its back. It might say thus: 'They say this great ocean is deep. Where is its depth? I cannot find water even enough to cover my back!' Therein, because the great ocean is shallow for the Timirapiṅgala, which is endowed with a massive body, it should not be said that it is also shallow for other small fish. In the very same way, because Dependent Origination is shallow for the Elder, who is endowed with wisdom, it should not be said that it is also shallow for others. And the king of the Supaṇṇas is one hundred and fifty yojanas tall. His right wing is fifty yojanas, likewise his left wing; his tail is sixty yojanas, his neck is thirty yojanas, his beak is nine yojanas, and his feet are twelve yojanas. When he begins to create the Supaṇṇa-wind, a space of seven or eight hundred yojanas is not enough. He might say thus: 'They say this space is infinite. Where is its infinity? We cannot even find enough space to spread the wind from our wings!' Therein, because space is limited for the king of the Supaṇṇas, who is endowed with a great body, it should not be said that it is also limited for other small birds. In the very same way, because Dependent Origination is shallow for the Elder, who is endowed with wisdom, it should not be said that it is also shallow for others.

Rāhu asurindo pana pādantato yāva kesantā yojanānaṃ cattāri sahassāni aṭṭha ca satāni honti. Tassa dvinnaṃ bāhānaṃ antare dvādasayojanasatikaṃ, bahalattena chayojanasatikaṃ, hatthapādatalāni tiyojanasatikāni, tathā mukhaṃ, ekaṅgulipabbaṃ paññāsayojanaṃ, tathā bhamukantaraṃ, nalāṭaṃ tiyojanasatikaṃ, sīsaṃ navayojanasatikaṃ. Tassa mahāsamuddaṃ otiṇṇassa gambhīraṃ udakaṃ jāṇuppamāṇaṃ hoti. So evaṃ vadeyya – “ayaṃ mahāsamuddo gambhīroti vadanti. Kutassa gambhīratā? Mayaṃ jāṇuppaṭicchādanamattampi udakaṃ na labhāmā”ti. Tattha kāyūpapannassa rāhuno mahāsamuddo uttānoti aññesañca uttānoti na vattabbo. Evameva ñāṇūpapannassa therassa paṭiccasamuppādo uttānoti [M 2.0083] aññesampi uttānoti na vattabbo. Etamatthaṃ sandhāya bhagavā mā hevaṃ, ānanda, mā hevaṃ, ānandāti āha.

Furthermore, the asura king Rāhu, from the soles of his feet to the tips of his hair, is four thousand eight hundred yojanas. The span between his two arms is twelve hundred yojanas, and his thickness is six hundred yojanas. The palms of his hands and the soles of his feet are three hundred yojanas each, and likewise his mouth. Each finger-joint is fifty yojanas, and likewise the space between his eyebrows. His forehead is three hundred yojanas, and his head is nine hundred yojanas. For him, having descended into the great ocean, the deep water is knee-deep. He might say thus: 'They say this great ocean is deep. Where is its depth? We cannot find water even enough to cover our knees.' Therein, because the great ocean is shallow for Rāhu, who is endowed with a great body, it should not be said that it is also shallow for others. In the very same way, because Dependent Origination is shallow for the Elder, who is endowed with wisdom, it should not be said that it is also shallow for others. With reference to this meaning, the Blessed One said, 'Do not say so, Ānanda; do not say so, Ānanda.'

Therassa hi catūhi kāraṇehi gambhīro paṭiccasamuppādo uttānoti upaṭṭhāsi. Katamehi catūhi? Pubbūpanissayasampattiyā titthavāsena sotāpannatāya bahussutabhāvenāti.

Indeed, for the Elder, the profound Dependent Origination appeared as shallow due to four reasons. By which four? Through the fulfillment of a supportive past foundation, by dwelling with the Teacher, by the state of being a stream-enterer, and through the state of great learning.

Ito [V 2.0079] kira satasahassime kappe padumuttaro nāma satthā loke uppajji. Tassa haṃsavatī nāma nagaraṃ ahosi, ānando nāma rājā pitā, sumedhā nāma devī mātā, bodhisatto uttarakumāro nāma ahosi. So puttassa jātadivase mahābhinikkhamanaṃ nikkhamma pabbajitvā padhānamanuyutto anukkamena sabbaññutaṃ patvā, “anekajātisaṃsāra”nti udānaṃ udānetvā sattāhaṃ bodhipallaṅke vītināmetvā “pathaviyaṃ pādaṃ ṭhapessāmī”ti pādaṃ abhinīhari. Atha pathaviṃ bhinditvā [P 2.0090] mahantaṃ padumaṃ uṭṭhāsi. Tassa dhurapattāni navutihatthāni, kesaraṃ tiṃsahatthaṃ, kaṇṇikā dvādasahatthā, navaghaṭappamāṇā reṇu ahosi.

It is said that one hundred thousand aeons from this present aeon, the Teacher named Padumuttara arose in the world. His city was called Haṃsavatī, his father was King Ānanda, his mother was Queen Sumedhā, and the Bodhisatta was the prince named Uttara. On the day his son was born, he undertook the great renunciation, went forth, and devoted himself to striving. Gradually attaining omniscience, he uttered the inspired utterance, 'Through the round of countless births…,' and after spending seven days on the seat of enlightenment, he thought, 'I will place my foot upon the earth,' and extended his foot. Then, splitting the earth, a great lotus arose. Its outer petals were ninety cubits in length, the filaments thirty cubits, the pericarp twelve cubits, and there was pollen equal to the volume of nine water pots.

Satthā pana ubbedhato aṭṭhapaññāsahattho ahosi, tassa ubhinnaṃ bāhānamantaraṃ aṭṭhārasahatthaṃ, nalāṭaṃ pañcahatthaṃ, hatthapādā ekādasahatthā. Tassa ekādasahatthena pādena dvādasahatthāya kaṇṇikāya akkantamattāya navaghaṭappamāṇā reṇu uṭṭhāya aṭṭhapaññāsahatthaṃ padesaṃ uggantvā okiṇṇamanosilācuṇṇaṃ viya paccokiṇṇaṃ. Tadupādāya bhagavā “padumuttaro”tveva paññāyittha. Tassa devilo ca sujāto ca dve aggasāvakā ahesuṃ, amitā ca asamā ca dve aggasāvikā, sumano nāma upaṭṭhāko. Padumuttaro bhagavā pitusaṅgahaṃ kurumāno bhikkhusatasahassaparivāro haṃsavatiyā rājadhāniyā vasati.

The Teacher, for his part, was fifty-eight cubits in height. The space between his two arms was eighteen cubits, his forehead was five cubits, and his hands and feet were eleven cubits. When his eleven-cubit foot merely stepped upon the twelve-cubit pericarp, pollen equal to the volume of nine water pots rose up, ascended to a height of fifty-eight cubits, and was scattered about like powdered red arsenic. On account of this, the Blessed One became known as 'Padumuttara.' His two chief disciples were Devala and Sujāta, his two chief female disciples were Amitā and Asamā, and his attendant was named Sumana. The Blessed One Padumuttara, in order to support his father, dwelt in the royal city of Haṃsavatī, surrounded by one hundred thousand bhikkhus.

Kaniṭṭhabhātā panassa sumanakumāro nāma. Tassa rājā haṃsavatito vīsayojanasate bhogaṃ adāsi. So kadāci āgantvā pitarañca satthārañca passati. Athekadivasaṃ paccanto kupito. Sumano rañño sāsanaṃ pesesi. Rājā “tvaṃ mayā, tāta, kasmā ṭhapito”ti paṭipesesi. So core vūpasametvā “upasanto, deva, janapado”ti rañño pesesi. Rājā tuṭṭho “sīghaṃ mama putto āgacchatū”ti āha. Tassa [M 2.0084] sahassamattā amaccā honti. So tehi saddhiṃ antarāmagge mantesi – “mayhaṃ pitā tuṭṭho sace me varaṃ deti, kiṃ gaṇhāmī”ti? Atha naṃ ekacce “hatthiṃ gaṇhatha, assaṃ gaṇhatha, janapadaṃ gaṇhatha, sattaratanāni gaṇhathā”ti āhaṃsu. Apare “tumhe pathavissarassa puttā, na tumhākaṃ dhanaṃ dullabhaṃ, laddhampi cetaṃ sabbaṃ pahāya gamanīyaṃ, puññameva ekaṃ ādāya gamanīyaṃ, tasmā deve varaṃ dadamāne temāsaṃ padumuttaraṃ bhagavantaṃ upaṭṭhātuṃ varaṃ gaṇhathā”ti. So “tumhe mayhaṃ kalyāṇamittā nāma, mametaṃ cittaṃ [P 2.0091] natthi, tumhehi pana uppāditaṃ, evaṃ karissāmī”ti, gantvā pitaraṃ vanditvā pitarā āliṅgetvā, matthake cumbitvā “varaṃ te, putta, demī”ti vutte “icchāmahaṃ, mahārāja, bhagavantaṃ temāsaṃ [V 2.0080] catūhi paccayehi upaṭṭhahanto jīvitaṃ avañjhaṃ kātuṃ, idaṃ me varaṃ dehī”ti āha. Na sakkā, tāta, aññaṃ varehīti. Deva, khattiyānaṃ nāma dvekathā natthi, etameva me dehi, na mamaññena atthoti. Tāta, buddhānaṃ nāma cittaṃ dujjānaṃ, sace bhagavā na icchissati, mayā dinnampi kiṃ bhavissatīti? “Sādhu, deva, ahaṃ bhagavato cittaṃ jānissāmī”ti vihāraṃ gato.

Now, his younger brother was named Prince Sumana. The king gave him a fiefdom at a distance of one hundred and twenty yojanas from Haṃsavatī. From time to time, he would come to see his father and the Teacher. Then one day, the border region revolted. Sumana sent a message to the king. The king sent a message in return: 'My dear son, for what reason have I appointed you?' He pacified the rebels and sent word to the king: 'The province is at peace, Your Majesty.' The king was pleased and said, 'Let my son come quickly.' He had about a thousand ministers. Along the way, he consulted with them: 'My father is pleased. If he grants me a boon, what should I take?' Then some said to him, 'Take an elephant, take a horse, take a province, take the seven treasures.' Others said, 'You are a son of the ruler of the earth; wealth is not difficult for you to acquire. And even when acquired, all this must be left behind at death. Only merit alone can be taken with you. Therefore, when His Majesty offers a boon, take the boon of attending upon the Blessed One Padumuttara for the three months of the rains.' He said, 'You are indeed my good friends. This thought was not my own, but you have given rise to it. I will do so.' Having gone and paid homage to his father, he was embraced by his father, who kissed his forehead and said, 'I grant you a boon, my son.' When this was said, he replied, 'I wish, great king, to make my life fruitful by attending upon the Blessed One for the three months of the rains with the four requisites. Grant me this boon.' 'That is not possible, my dear. Choose another boon.' 'Your Majesty, for khattiyas there is no second word. Grant me only this; I have no need for another.' 'My dear, the minds of Buddhas are hard to know. If the Blessed One does not consent, what will come of my having granted it?' 'Very well, Your Majesty, I will ascertain the Blessed One’s mind.' And he went to the monastery.

Tena ca samayena bhattakiccaṃ niṭṭhāpetvā bhagavā gandhakuṭiṃ paviṭṭho hoti. So maṇḍalamāḷe sannisinnānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ santikaṃ agamāsi. Te naṃ āhaṃsu – “rājaputta kasmā āgatosī”ti? Bhagavantaṃ dassanāya, dassetha me bhagavantanti. “Na mayaṃ, rājaputta, icchiticchitakkhaṇe satthāraṃ daṭṭhuṃ labhāmā”ti. Ko pana, bhante, labhatīti? Sumanatthero nāma rājaputtāti. So “kuhiṃ bhante thero”ti? Therassa nisinnaṭṭhānaṃ pucchitvā gantvā vanditvā – “icchāmahaṃ, bhante, bhagavantaṃ passituṃ, dassetha me bhagavanta”nti āha. Thero “ehi, rājaputtā”ti taṃ gahetvā gandhakuṭipariveṇe ṭhapetvā gandhakuṭiṃ āruhi. Atha naṃ bhagavā “sumana, kasmā āgatosī”ti āha. Rājaputto, bhante, bhagavantaṃ dassanāya āgatoti. Tena hi bhikkhu āsanaṃ paññapehīti. Thero āsanaṃ paññapesi. Nisīdi bhagavā paññatte āsane. Rājaputto bhagavantaṃ vanditvā paṭisanthāraṃ akāsi, “kadā āgatosi rājaputtā”ti? Bhante, tumhesu gandhakuṭiṃ paviṭṭhesu, bhikkhū pana “na mayaṃ icchiticchitakkhaṇe bhagavantaṃ daṭṭhuṃ labhāmā”ti maṃ therassa santikaṃ pāhesuṃ, thero pana ekavacaneneva dassesi, thero, bhante, tumhākaṃ [M 2.0085] sāsane [P 2.0092] vallabho maññeti. Āma, rājakumāra, vallabho esa bhikkhu mayhaṃ sāsaneti. Bhante, buddhānaṃ sāsane kiṃ katvā vallabho hotīti? Dānaṃ datvā sīlaṃ samādiyitvā uposathakammaṃ katvā, kumārāti. Bhagavā ahampi thero viya buddhasāsane vallabho hotukāmo, temāsaṃ me vassāvāsaṃ adhivāsethāti. Bhagavā, “atthi nu kho gatena attho”ti oloketvā “atthī”ti disvā “suññāgāre kho, rājakumāra, tathāgatā abhiramantī”ti āha. Kumāro “aññātaṃ bhagavā, aññātaṃ sugatā”ti vatvā – “ahaṃ, bhante, purimataraṃ gantvā vihāraṃ kāremi, mayā pesite bhikkhusatasahassena saddhiṃ āgacchathā”ti paṭiññaṃ gahetvā pitu santikaṃ gantvā, “dinnā me, deva, bhagavatā paṭiññā, mayā pahite tumhe bhagavantaṃ peseyyāthā”ti pitaraṃ vanditvā nikkhamitvā yojane yojane vihāraṃ kāretvā vīsayojanasataṃ addhānaṃ gato. Gantvā attano nagare vihāraṭṭhānaṃ vicinanto sobhanassa nāma kuṭumbikassa [V 2.0081] uyyānaṃ disvā satasahassena kiṇitvā satasahassaṃ vissajjetvā vihāraṃ kāresi. Tattha bhagavato gandhakuṭiṃ, sesabhikkhūnañca rattiṭṭhānadivāṭṭhānatthāya kuṭileṇamaṇḍape kārāpetvā pākāraparikkhepaṃ dvārakoṭṭhakañca niṭṭhāpetvā pitu santikaṃ pesesi “niṭṭhitaṃ mayhaṃ kiccaṃ, satthāraṃ pahiṇathā”ti.

And at that time, having finished the meal, the Blessed One had entered the Fragrant Hut. That prince approached the monks who were sitting in the circular hall. They said to him, 'Prince, why have you come?' 'I have come for the sight of the Blessed One; show me the Blessed One.' 'Prince, we do not get to see the Teacher at any moment we wish.' 'Then who, venerable sirs, does?' 'The elder named Sumana, prince.' He asked, 'Venerable sir, where is the elder?' Having inquired about the elder’s sitting place, he went, paid homage, and said, 'Venerable sir, I wish to see the Blessed One; show me the Blessed One.' The elder said, 'Come, prince,' and taking him, placed him in the precincts of the Fragrant Hut and ascended to the Fragrant Hut. Then the Blessed One said to him, 'Sumana, why have you come?' 'Venerable sir, the prince has come to see the Blessed One.' 'In that case, monk, prepare a seat.' The elder prepared a seat. The Blessed One sat on the prepared seat. The prince paid homage to the Blessed One and exchanged courteous greetings. 'When did you arrive, prince?' 'Venerable sir, when you entered the Fragrant Hut, the monks said, "We do not get to see the Blessed One at any moment we wish," and sent me to the elder. The elder, however, showed me with just a single word. Venerable sir, the elder, it seems, is intimate in your dispensation.' 'Yes, prince, this monk is intimate in my dispensation.' 'Venerable sir, in the dispensation of the Buddhas, by doing what does one become intimate?' 'By giving gifts, undertaking virtue, and performing the Uposatha observance, prince.' 'Blessed One, I too, like the elder, wish to become intimate in the Buddha’s dispensation. Please accept my invitation for the rains-residence for three months.' The Blessed One, looking to see, 'Is there benefit in going?', and seeing 'There is,' said, 'Prince, Tathāgatas, indeed, delight in secluded places.' The prince said, 'I understand, Blessed One; I understand, Sugata,' and then, 'Venerable sir, I will go first and have a monastery built. When sent for by me, please come together with one hundred thousand monks.' Taking this promise, he went to his father's presence and said, 'Your Majesty, the Blessed One has given me a promise. When I send for him, you should send the Blessed One.' Having paid homage to his father, he departed and, having monasteries built at every yojana, went a distance of one hundred and twenty yojanas. Having gone to his own city, while searching for a site for a monastery, he saw the park of a householder named Sobhana, bought it for one hundred thousand, and spending one hundred thousand, had the monastery built. There, he had built a Fragrant Hut for the Blessed One, and for the remaining monks, for the purpose of night-time and day-time dwellings, huts, caves, and pavilions. Having completed the surrounding wall and the gatehouse, he sent a message to his father's presence: 'My task is finished. Please send the Teacher.'

Rājā bhagavantaṃ bhojetvā “bhagavā sumanassa kiccaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ, tumhākaṃ āgamanaṃ paccāsīsatī”ti. Bhagavā satasahassabhikkhuparivāro yojane yojane vihāresu vasamāno agamāsi. Kumāro “satthā āgacchatī”ti sutvā yojanaṃ paccuggantvā gandhamālādīhi pūjayamāno vihāraṃ pavesetvā –

The king, having offered a meal to the Blessed One, said, 'Blessed One, Sumana's task is finished; he looks forward to your coming.' The Blessed One, surrounded by a retinue of one hundred thousand monks, proceeded, staying in the monasteries at every yojana. The prince, hearing that the Teacher was coming, went forward a yojana to meet him, and honoring him with perfumes, garlands, and so forth, led him into the monastery.

“Satasahassena me kītaṃ, satasahassena māpitaṃ;

Sobhanaṃ nāma uyyānaṃ paṭiggaṇha, mahāmunī”ti. –

'With a hundred thousand it was bought by me, and with a hundred thousand it was built. This park named Sobhana, please accept it, O Great Sage.'

Vihāraṃ niyyātesi. So vassūpanāyikadivase dānaṃ datvā attano puttadāre ca amacce ca pakkosāpetvā āha –“satthā amhākaṃ santikaṃ dūrato āgato, buddhā ca nāma dhammagarunova, nāmisagarukā. Tasmā ahaṃ imaṃ temāsaṃ dve sāṭake [P 2.0093] nivāsetvā dasa sīlāni samādiyitvā idheva [M 2.0086] vasissāmi, tumhe khīṇāsavasatasahassassa imināva nīhārena temāsaṃ dānaṃ dadeyyāthā”ti.

He dedicated the monastery. On the day of entering the rains-residence, having given alms, he had his wife, children, and ministers summoned and said: 'The Teacher has come to us from afar. Buddhas, by nature, revere the Dhamma; they do not revere material things. Therefore, for these three months, I, wearing two cloths and undertaking the ten precepts, will stay right here. You should give alms in this same manner to the one hundred thousand Arahants for three months.'

So sumanattherassa vasanaṭṭhānasabhāgeyeva ṭhāne vasanto yaṃ thero bhagavato vattaṃ karoti, taṃ sabbaṃ disvā, “imasmiṃ ṭhāne ekantavallabho esa thero, etasseva ṭhānantaraṃ patthetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti cintetvā, upakaṭṭhāya pavāraṇāya gāmaṃ pavisitvā sattāhaṃ mahādānaṃ datvā sattame divase bhikkhūsatasahassassa pādamūle ticīvaraṃ ṭhapetvā bhagavantaṃ vanditvā, “bhante, yadetaṃ mayā magge yojanantarikavihārakārāpanato paṭṭhāya puññaṃ kataṃ, taṃ neva sakkasampattiṃ, na mārabrahmasampattiṃ patthayantena, buddhassa pana upaṭṭhākabhāvaṃ patthentena kataṃ. Tasmā ahampi bhagavā anāgate sumanatthero viya ekassa buddhassa upaṭṭhāko homī”ti pañcapatiṭṭhitena patitvā vanditvā nipanno. Bhagavā “mahantaṃ kulaputtassa cittaṃ, ijjhissati nu kho, no”ti olokento[V 2.0082], “anāgate ito satasahassime kappe gotamo nāma buddho uppajjissati, tasseva upaṭṭhāko bhavissatī”ti ñatvā –

He, staying in a place similar to the Elder Sumana's dwelling, observed all the duties that the elder performed for the Blessed One and reflected, 'This elder is truly intimate in this position; it is fitting to aspire to this very same position.' When the Pavāraṇā day was near, he entered the village, gave a great alms-giving for seven days, and on the seventh day, placed the triple robe at the feet of the one hundred thousand monks. Having paid homage to the Blessed One, he said: 'Venerable sir, whatever merit I have made, starting from having monasteries built at one-yojana intervals on the road—that was not made aspiring for the fortune of Sakka, nor for the fortune of Māra or Brahmā, but was made aspiring for the state of being an attendant to a Buddha. Therefore, Blessed One, may I too, in the future, like the Elder Sumana, become the attendant of a Buddha.' He prostrated himself with the five-point prostration, paid homage, and lay down. The Blessed One, observing, 'Great is the mind of this clansman! Will it succeed or not?', knew: 'In the future, one hundred thousand aeons from now, a Buddha named Gotama will arise, and he will become the attendant of that very one.'

“Icchitaṃ patthitaṃ tuyhaṃ, sabbameva samijjhatu;

Sabbe pūrentu saṅkappā, cando pannaraso yathā”ti. –

'May all that is wished and longed for by you be entirely successful; may all your intentions be fulfilled, like the moon on the fifteenth day.'

Āha. Kumāro sutvā “buddhā nāma advejjhakathā hontī”ti dutiyadivaseyeva tassa bhagavato pattacīvaraṃ gahetvā piṭṭhito piṭṭhito gacchanto viya ahosi. So tasmiṃ buddhuppāde vassasatasahassaṃ dānaṃ datvā sagge nibbattitvā kassapabuddhakālepi piṇḍāya carato therassa pattaggahaṇatthaṃ uttarisāṭakaṃ datvā pūjaṃ akāsi. Puna sagge nibbattitvā tato cuto bārāṇasirājā hutvā aṭṭhannaṃ paccekabuddhānaṃ paṇṇasālāyo kāretvā maṇiādhārake upaṭṭhapetvā catūhi paccayehi dasavassasahassāni upaṭṭhānaṃ akāsi. Etāni pākaṭaṭṭhānāni.

He said. The prince, having heard, thought, 'Indeed, Buddhas do not speak with two voices.' On the very second day, taking the Blessed One’s bowl and robes, he was as if following constantly behind him. In that Buddha-era, for one hundred thousand years, he gave alms and was reborn in the celestial realm. Also, in the time of the Buddha Kassapa, he gave his upper garment to an Elder who was wandering for alms for the purpose of taking his bowl and made an offering. Again, having been reborn in the celestial realm and passing away from there, he became the king of Bārāṇasī. He had leaf-huts made for eight Paccekabuddhas, had jeweled bowl-stands provided, and for ten thousand years, performed attendance with the four requisites. These are the evident instances.

Kappasatasahassaṃ pana dānaṃ dadamānova amhākaṃ bodhisattena saddhiṃ tusitapure nibbattitvā [P 2.0094] tato cuto amitodanasakkassa gehe paṭisandhiṃ gahetvā anupubbena katābhinikkhamano sammāsambodhiṃ patvā paṭhamagamanena kapilavatthuṃ āgantvā tato nikkhamante bhagavati bhagavato parivāratthaṃ [M 2.0087] rājakumāresu pabbajantesu bhaddiyādīhi saddhiṃ nikkhamitvā bhagavato santike pabbajitvā nacirasseva āyasmato puṇṇassa mantāṇiputtassa santike dhammakathaṃ sutvā sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi. Evamesa āyasmā pubbūpanissayasampanno, tassimāya pubbūpanissayasampattiyā gambhīropi paṭiccasamuppādo uttānako viya upaṭṭhāsi.

Furthermore, for one hundred thousand aeons, while giving alms, he was reborn in the Tusita celestial realm together with our Bodhisatta. Having passed away from there, he took rebirth-linking in the house of Amitodana the Sakyan. Successively, when the Blessed One, having made the great renunciation and attained perfect enlightenment, had come to Kapilavatthu on his first journey and was departing from there, and when the princes were going forth to form the Blessed One's retinue, he went forth together with Bhaddiya and the others. Having gone forth in the presence of the Blessed One, not long after, upon hearing a Dhamma discourse in the presence of the Venerable Puṇṇa, son of Mantāṇī, he was established in the fruit of stream-entry. Thus, this venerable one is endowed with past supportive conditions. Because of this endowment with past supportive conditions, even the profound Dependent Origination appeared to him as if shallow.

Titthavāsoti pana garūnaṃ santike uggahaṇasavanaparipucchanadhāraṇāni vuccanti. So therassa ativiya parisuddho. Tenāpissāyaṃ gambhīropi uttānako viya upaṭṭhāsi. Sotāpannānañca nāma paccayākāro uttānako hutvā upaṭṭhāti, ayañca āyasmā sotāpanno. Bahussutānaṃ catuhatthe ovarake padīpe jalamāne mañcapīṭhaṃ viya nāmarūpaparicchedo pākaṭo hoti, ayañca āyasmā bahussutānaṃ aggo. Iti bāhusaccabhāvenapissa gambhīropi paccayākāro uttānako viya upaṭṭhāsi. Paṭiccasamuppādo catūhi gambhīratāhi gambhīro. Sā panassa gambhīratā visuddhimagge vitthāritāva. Sā sabbāpi therassa uttānakā viya upaṭṭhāsi. Tena [V 2.0083] bhagavā āyasmantaṃ ānandaṃ ussādento mā hevantiādimāha. Ayañhettha adhippāyo – ānanda, tvaṃ mahāpañño visadañāṇo, tena te gambhīropi paṭiccasamuppādo uttānako viya khāyati. Tasmā “mayhameva nu kho esa uttānako viya hutvā upaṭṭhāti, udāhu aññesampī”ti mā evaṃ avaca.

Furthermore, 'residence at a ford' (titthavāsa) is the term for learning, listening, questioning, and retaining in the presence of revered teachers. That was exceedingly pure for the Elder. For that reason also, this profound Dependent Origination appeared to him as if shallow. And for stream-enterers, the causal structure appears as if shallow, and this venerable one is a stream-enterer. For those of great learning, in a four-cubit chamber with a lamp burning, the discernment of name-and-form is as evident as a bed and a chair; and this venerable one is the foremost among those of great learning. Thus, also due to his state of great learning, the profound causal structure appeared to him as if shallow. Dependent Origination is profound through four kinds of profundity. Now, its profundity has been explained in detail by me in the Visuddhimagga. All of that profundity appeared to the Elder as if shallow. Therefore, the Blessed One, wishing to extol the Venerable Ānanda, said the words beginning with, 'Do not speak thus, Ānanda...'. Herein, this is the intention: 'Ānanda, you are of great wisdom, of clear knowledge; therefore, to you even the profound Dependent Origination appears as if shallow. Therefore, do not speak thus: "Does this, I wonder, appear as if shallow only to me, or to others as well?"'

Yaṃ pana vuttaṃ “apasādento”ti, tatthāyamadhippāyo – ānanda, “atha ca pana me uttānakuttānako viya khāyatī”ti mā hevaṃ avaca. Yadi hi te esa uttānakuttānako viya khāyati, kasmā tvaṃ attano dhammatāya sotāpanno nāhosi, mayā dinnanaye ṭhatvā sotāpattimaggaṃ paṭivijjhi? Ānanda[P 2.0095], idaṃ nibbānameva gambhīraṃ, paccayākāro pana uttānako jāto, atha kasmā oḷārikaṃ kāmarāgasaṃyojanaṃ paṭighasaṃyojanaṃ oḷārikaṃ kāmarāgānusayaṃ paṭighānusayanti ime cattāro kilese samugghātetvā sakadāgāmiphalaṃ na sacchikarosi, teyeva aṇusahagate cattāro kilese samugghātetvā anāgāmiphalaṃ na sacchikarosi, rūparāgādīni [M 2.0088] pañca saṃyojanāni, mānānusayaṃ bhavarāgānusayaṃ avijjānusayanti ime aṭṭha kilese samugghātetvā arahattaṃ na sacchikarosi? Kasmā vā satasahassakappādhikaṃ ekaṃ asaṅkhyeyyaṃ pūritapāramino sāriputtamoggallānā viya sāvakapāramīñāṇaṃ na paṭivijjhasi, satasahassakappādhikāni dve asaṅkhyeyyāni pūritapāramino paccekabuddhā viya ca paccekabodhiñāṇaṃ na paṭivijjhasi? Yadi vā te sabbathāva esa uttānako hutvā upaṭṭhāsi. Atha kasmā satasahassakappādhikāni cattāri aṭṭha soḷasa vā asaṅkhyeyyāni pūritapāramino buddhā viya sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ na sacchikarosi? Kiṃ anatthikosi etehi visesādhigamehi? Passa yāva ca te aparaddhaṃ, tvaṃ nāma sāvakapadesañāṇe ṭhito atigambhīraṃ paccayākāraṃ “uttānako viya me upaṭṭhātī”ti vadasi. Tassa te idaṃ vacanaṃ buddhānaṃ kathāya paccanīkaṃ hoti. Tādisena nāma bhikkhunā buddhānaṃ kathāya paccanīkaṃ kathetabbanti na yuttametaṃ. Nanu mayhaṃ, ānanda, imaṃ paccayākāraṃ paṭivijjhituṃ vāyamantasseva kappasatasahassādhikāni cattāri asaṅkhyeyyāni atikkantāni. Paccayākārapaṭivijjhanatthāya ca pana me adinnadānaṃ nāma natthi, apūritapāramī nāma natthi. “Ajja paccayākāraṃ paṭivijjhissāmī”ti pana me nirussāhaṃ viya mārabalaṃ vidhamantassa ayaṃ mahāpathavī dvaṅgulamattampi nākampi, tathā paṭhamayāme pubbenivāsaṃ, majjhimayāme dibbacakkhuṃ sampādentassa. Pacchimayāme pana me balavapaccūsasamaye, “avijjā saṅkhārānaṃ navahi ākārehi paccayo hotī”ti diṭṭhamatteyeva dasasahassilokadhātu ayadaṇḍena [V 2.0084] ākoṭitakaṃsathālo viya viravasataṃ viravasahassaṃ muñcamānā vātāhate paduminipaṇṇe udakabindu viya pakampittha. Evaṃ [P 2.0096] gambhīro cāyaṃ, ānanda, paṭiccasamuppādo gambhīrāvabhāso ca, etassa, ānanda, dhammassa ananubodhā…pe… nātivattatīti.

Regarding what was said, 'apasādento,' this is the intended meaning: Ānanda, do not say, 'And yet to me it appears to be exceedingly shallow.' For if this Dependent Origination appeared to you as exceedingly shallow, why then, by your own nature, have you not become a stream-enterer? Have you not penetrated the path of stream-entry, standing in the method I have given? Ānanda, if this Nibbāna alone were profound, and the mode of conditions had become shallow, then why, having uprooted these four coarse defilements—the fetter of sensual desire, the fetter of ill will, the underlying tendency of sensual desire, and the underlying tendency of ill will—do you not realize the fruit of once-returning? Why, having uprooted those same four defilements along with their subtle aspects, do you not realize the fruit of non-returning? Why, having uprooted these eight defilements—the five fetters beginning with lust for form, the underlying tendency of conceit, the underlying tendency of craving for existence, and the underlying tendency of ignorance—do you not realize arahantship? Or why do you not penetrate the knowledge of a disciple’s perfection like Sāriputta and Moggallāna, who fulfilled their perfections over one incalculable eon and a hundred thousand kalpas? And why do you not penetrate the knowledge of a Paccekabuddha like the Paccekabuddhas, who fulfilled their perfections over two incalculable eons and a hundred thousand kalpas? Or if this appeared to you as entirely shallow, then why do you not realize the knowledge of omniscience like the Buddhas, who fulfilled their perfections over four, eight, or sixteen incalculable eons and a hundred thousand kalpas? Do you have no need for these special attainments? See how great your error is! You, standing in the partial knowledge of a disciple, say of the exceedingly profound mode of conditions, 'It appears to me as if it were shallow.' This statement of yours is contrary to the word of the Buddhas. It is not fitting for a monk such as you to speak contrary to the word of the Buddhas. Is it not so, Ānanda, that for me, while striving to penetrate this mode of conditions, four incalculable eons and a hundred thousand kalpas passed? For the sake of penetrating the mode of conditions, there is no gift I have not given, no perfection I have not fulfilled.
