When I was destroying the army of Māra as if without effort, thinking, 'Today I will penetrate the mode of conditions,' this great earth did not tremble even by the measure of two fingerbreadths; likewise, it did not tremble when I was attaining the knowledge of past lives in the first watch, and the divine eye in the middle watch. But in the last watch, at the time of the powerful dawn, as soon as it was seen that 'Ignorance is a condition for formations in nine ways,' the ten-thousandfold world system, emitting hundreds and thousands of roars, shook like a bronze bowl struck by an iron rod, like a drop of water on a lotus leaf struck by the wind. So profound, Ānanda, is this Dependent Origination, and it has the appearance of being profound. Ānanda, it is because of not understanding this Dhamma... that this generation... does not transcend it.

Etassa dhammassāti etassa paccayadhammassa. Ananubodhāti ñātapariññāvasena ananubujjhanā. Appaṭivedhāti tīraṇappahānapariññāvasena appaṭivijjhanā. Tantākulakajātāti tantaṃ viya ākulajātā. Yathā nāma dunnikkhittaṃ mūsikacchinnaṃ pesakārānaṃ tantaṃ tahiṃ tahiṃ ākulaṃ hoti, “idaṃ aggaṃ, idaṃ mūla”nti aggena vā aggaṃ, mūlena vā mūlaṃ samānetuṃ dukkaraṃ hoti. Evameva sattā imasmiṃ paccayākāre khalitā ākulā byākulā honti[M 2.0089], na sakkonti paccayākāraṃ ujuṃ kātuṃ. Tattha tantaṃ paccattapurisakāre ṭhatvā sakkāpi bhaveyya ujuṃ kātuṃ, ṭhapetvā pana dve bodhisatte añño satto attano dhammatāya paccayākāraṃ ujuṃ kātuṃ samattho nāma natthi. Yathā pana ākulaṃ tantaṃ kañjiyaṃ datvā kocchena pahaṭaṃ tattha tattha guḷakajātaṃ hoti gaṇṭhibaddhaṃ, evamime sattā paccayesu pakkhalitvā paccaye ujuṃ kātuṃ asakkontā dvāsaṭṭhidiṭṭhigatavasena guḷakajātā honti gaṇṭhibaddhā. Ye hi keci diṭṭhiyo sannissitā, sabbe te paccayaṃ ujuṃ kātuṃ asakkontāyeva.

By 'this Dhamma' is meant this conditional Dhamma. 'Not comprehending' means not understanding by way of full understanding of the known. 'Not penetrating' means not penetrating by way of full understanding through investigation and full understanding through abandoning. 'Become tangled like a ball of thread' means to become tangled like thread. Just as a weaver's thread that is poorly laid out and gnawed by mice becomes tangled here and there, making it difficult to align end with end or root with root, so too are beings who have stumbled in this mode of conditions tangled and bewildered, unable to straighten out the mode of conditions. In that simile, it might be possible to straighten out the thread by applying individual effort, but apart from the two Bodhisattas, there is no other being who is able to straighten out the mode of conditions by their own nature. And just as a tangled thread, when treated with starch and combed, becomes lumpy and knotted here and there, so too these beings, having stumbled among conditions and being unable to straighten them out, become lumpy and knotted by way of the sixty-two wrong views. For whoever relies on wrong views, all of them are unable to straighten out the conditions.

Kulāgaṇṭhikajātāti kulāgaṇṭhikaṃ vuccati pesakārakañjiyasuttaṃ. Kulā nāma sakuṇikā, tassā kulāvakotipi eke. Yathā hi tadubhayampi ākulaṃ aggena vā aggaṃ, mūlena vā mūlaṃ samānetuṃ dukkaranti purimanayeneva yojetabbaṃ.

Regarding 'kulāgaṇṭhikajātā': a weaver's starched thread is called a 'kulāgaṇṭhika.' 'Kulā' is a small bird, and some say it also refers to its nest, a 'kulāvaka.' Just as both of these are tangled and it is difficult to align end with end or root with root, so should this be applied in accordance with the preceding explanation.

Muñjapabbajabhūtāti muñjatiṇaṃ viya pabbajatiṇaṃ viya ca bhūtā tādisā jātā. Yathā hi tāni tiṇāni koṭṭetvā katarajju jiṇṇakāle katthaci patitaṃ gahetvā tesaṃ tiṇānaṃ “idaṃ aggaṃ, idaṃ mūla”nti aggena vā aggaṃ, mūlena vā mūlaṃ samānetuṃ dukkaraṃ, tampi paccattapurisakāre ṭhatvā sakkā bhaveyya ujuṃ kātuṃ, ṭhapetvā pana dve bodhisatte [P 2.0097] añño satto attano dhammatāya paccayākāraṃ ujuṃ kātuṃ samattho nāma natthi, evamayaṃ pajā paccayaṃ ujuṃ kātuṃ asakkontī diṭṭhigatavasena gaṇṭhikajātā hutvā apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ saṃsāraṃ nātivattati.

By 'Muñjapabbajabhūtā' is meant 'become like muñja grass and pabbaja grass.' Just as with a rope made by pounding those grasses, when it has become old and has fallen somewhere, if one takes it, it is difficult to align the tip with the tip or the root with the root of those grasses. And yet, it might be possible to straighten it by individual effort. However, apart from the two Bodhisattas, there is no other being capable of straightening the mode of conditions by their own nature. In the same way, this generation, unable to straighten out the conditions, becomes knotted by way of wrong views and does not transcend the plane of misery, the bad destination, the lower world, and saṃsāra.

Tattha [V 2.0085] apāyoti nirayatiracchānayonipettivisayaasurakāyā. Sabbepi hi te vaḍḍhisaṅkhātassa ayassa abhāvato “apāyo”ti vuccati, tathā dukkhassa gatibhāvato duggati, sukhasamussayato vinipatitattā vinipāto. Itaro pana –

Therein, 'apāya' refers to hell, the animal realm, the peta-sphere, and the asura-group. Indeed, all of these are called 'apāya' because of the absence of well-being (āya), which is known as prosperity (vaḍḍhi). Similarly, because it is a destination (gati) of suffering, it is called 'duggati'; and because one has fallen away (vinipatita) from the accumulation of happiness, it is called 'vinipāta'. As for the other term—

“Khandhānañca paṭipāṭi, dhātuāyatanāna ca;

Abbhocchinnaṃ vattamānā, saṃsāroti pavuccati”.

"The continuity of the aggregates, and of the elements and sense bases, occurring uninterruptedly, is called 'saṃsāra'."

Taṃ sabbampi nātivattati nātikkamati, atha kho cutito paṭisandhiṃ, paṭisandhito cutinti evaṃ punappunaṃ cutipaṭisandhiyo gaṇhamānā tīsu bhavesu catūsu [M 2.0090] yonīsu pañcasu gatīsu sattasu viññāṇaṭṭhitīsu navasu sattāvāsesu mahāsamudde vātakkhittā nāvā viya yante yuttagoṇo viya ca paribbhamatiyeva. Iti sabbametaṃ bhagavā āyasmantaṃ ānandaṃ apasādento āha. Sesamettha vuttanayamevāti. Dasamaṃ.

One does not transcend or overcome all that. Rather, taking up decease and relinking again and again, one wanders on in the three existences, the four wombs, the five destinations, the seven stations of consciousness, and the nine abodes of beings, like a ship tossed by the wind on the great ocean, and like an ox yoked to a mill. Thus, the Blessed One said all this, reproving the Venerable Ānanda. The remainder here is in the manner already stated. The Tenth.

Dukkhavaggo chaṭṭho.

The Dukkha Chapter, the Sixth.

7. Mahāvaggo

7. The Great Chapter

1. Assutavāsuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Assutavā Sutta

61. Mahāvaggassa paṭhame assutavāti khandhadhātuāyatanapaccayākārasatipaṭṭhānādīsu uggahaparipucchāvinicchayarahito. Puthujjanoti puthūnaṃ nānappakārānaṃ kilesādīnaṃ jananādikāraṇehi puthujjano. Vuttañhetaṃ – “puthu kilese janentīti puthujjanā”ti sabbaṃ vitthāretabbaṃ. Apica puthūnaṃ gaṇanapathamatītānaṃ ariyadhammaparammukhānaṃ nīcadhammasamācārānaṃ janānaṃ antogadhattāpi puthujjano, puthu vā ayaṃ visuṃyeva saṅkhaṃ gato, visaṃsaṭṭho sīlasutādiguṇayuttehi ariyehi janoti puthujjano. Evametehi [P 2.0098] “assutavā puthujjano”ti dvīhipi padehi ye te –

61. In the first sutta of the Mahāvagga, 'uninstructed' means one who is devoid of learning, inquiry, and discernment regarding the aggregates, elements, sense bases, dependent origination, foundations of mindfulness, and so on. 'Worldling' (puthujjana) is so called for reasons such as generating manifold and various defilements. And this was stated: 'They generate manifold defilements, thus they are worldlings.' All this should be elaborated. Moreover, one is also called a 'worldling' because of being included among the many folk who have passed beyond reckoning, who have turned their backs on the Noble Dhamma, and who practice base conduct. Or, this one is counted separately, unassociated with the noble folk endowed with virtues such as morality and learning; thus, a 'worldling'. In this way, by both these terms, 'uninstructed worldling', are meant those who—

“Duve [V 2.0086] puthujjanā vuttā, buddhenādiccabandhunā;

Andho puthujjano eko, kalyāṇeko puthujjano”ti. (mahāni. 94); –

"Two worldlings are spoken of by the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun: one is the blind worldling, and one is the virtuous worldling."

Dve puthujjanā vuttā, tesu andhaputhujjano gahito. Imasminti paccuppannapaccakkhakāyaṃ dasseti. Cātumahābhūtikasminti catumahābhūtakāye catumahābhūtehi nibbatte catumahābhūtamayeti attho. Nibbindeyyāti ukkaṇṭheyya. Virajjeyyāti na rajjeyya. Vimucceyyāti muccitukāmo bhaveyya. Ācayoti vuḍḍhi. Apacayoti parihāni. Ādānanti nibbatti. Nikkhepananti bhedo.

Two worldlings are spoken of; of these, the blind worldling is taken. By 'in this', He indicates the present, directly perceived body. In 'composed of the four great elements', the meaning is: in the body of the four great elements, produced from the four great elements, made of the four great elements. 'One should be disenchanted' means one should be wearied. 'One should become dispassionate' means one should not be attached. 'One should be liberated' means one should desire to be free. 'Accumulation' is growth. 'Decay' is decline. 'Taking up' is arising. 'Laying down' is breaking up.

Tasmāti yasmā ime cattāro vuḍḍhihāninibbattibhedā paññāyanti, tasmā taṃkāraṇāti attho. Iti bhagavā cātumahābhūtike kāye rūpaṃ [M 2.0091] pariggahetuṃ ayuttarūpaṃ katvā arūpaṃ pariggahetuṃ yuttarūpaṃ karoti. Kasmā? Tesañhi bhikkhūnaṃ rūpasmiṃ gāho balavā adhimatto, tena tesaṃ rūpe gāhassa pariggahetabbarūpataṃ dassetvā nikkaḍḍhanto arūpe patiṭṭhāpanatthaṃ evamāha.

'Therefore' means: because these four—growth, decline, arising, and breaking up—are manifest, therefore, for that reason. This is the meaning. Thus the Blessed One, having made form in the body composed of the four great elements unsuitable to be grasped, makes what is formless suitable to be grasped. Why? Because for those monks, the grasping of form was strong and excessive. Therefore, showing that their grasping of form was something to be comprehended, and extracting them from it, He spoke thus for the purpose of establishing them in what is formless.

Cittantiādi sabbaṃ manāyatanasseva nāmaṃ. Tañhi cittavatthutāya cittagocaratāya sampayuttadhammacittatāya ca cittaṃ, mananaṭṭhena mano, vijānanaṭṭhena viññāṇanti vuccati. Nālanti na samattho. Ajjhositanti taṇhāya gilitvā pariniṭṭhapetvā gahitaṃ. Mamāyitanti taṇhāmamattena mama idanti gahitaṃ. Parāmaṭṭhanti diṭṭhiyā parāmasitvā gahitaṃ. Etaṃ mamāti taṇhāgāho, tena aṭṭhasatataṇhāvicaritaṃ gahitaṃ hoti. Esohamasmīti mānagāho, tena nava mānā gahitā honti. Eso me attāti diṭṭhigāho, tena dvāsaṭṭhi diṭṭhiyo gahitā honti. Tasmāti yasmā evaṃ dīgharattaṃ gahitaṃ, tasmā nibbindituṃ na samattho.

'Citta' (mind), and so on, are all names for the mind-base itself. Indeed, it is called 'citta' because it is the basis for variegation, because it has a variegated sphere, and because of the variegation of its associated states. It is called 'mano' in the sense of thinking, and 'viññāṇa' in the sense of cognizing. 'Nālaṃ' means not capable. 'Ajjhositaṃ' (clung to) means seized, having been swallowed and brought to completion by craving. 'Mamāyitaṃ' (appropriated) means seized as 'this is mine' through the possessiveness of craving. 'Parāmaṭṭhaṃ' (misapprehended) means seized after having been wrongly assessed through view. 'This is mine' is the grasping of craving; by this, the one hundred and eight proliferations of craving are included. 'I am this' is the grasping of conceit; by this, the nine conceits are included. 'This is my self' is the grasping of view; by this, the sixty-two views are included. 'Therefore' means: because it has been grasped in this way for a long time, one is not capable of becoming disenchanted.

Varaṃ, bhikkhaveti idaṃ kasmā āha? Paṭhamañhi tena rūpaṃ pariggahetuṃ ayuttarūpaṃ kataṃ, arūpaṃ yuttarūpaṃ, atha “tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ rūpato gāho nikkhamitvā arūpaṃ gato”ti ñatvā taṃ nikkaḍḍhituṃ imaṃ desanaṃ ārabhi. Tattha [P 2.0099] attato upagaccheyyāti attāti gaṇheyya. Bhiyyopīti vassasatato uddhampi. Kasmā pana bhagavā evamāha? Kiṃ atirekavassasataṃ tiṭṭhamānaṃ rūpaṃ nāma atthi? Nanu paṭhamavaye pavattaṃ rūpaṃ majjhimavayaṃ na pāpuṇāti, majjhimavaye pavattaṃ pacchimavayaṃ, purebhatte pavattaṃ pacchābhattaṃ, pacchābhatte pavattaṃ paṭhamayāmaṃ, paṭhamayāme [V 2.0087] pavattaṃ majjhimayāmaṃ, majjhimayāme pavattaṃ pacchimayāmaṃ na pāpuṇāti? Tathā gamane pavattaṃ ṭhānaṃ, ṭhāne pavattaṃ nisajjaṃ, nisajjāya pavattaṃ sayanaṃ na pāpuṇāti. Ekairiyāpathepi pādassa uddharaṇe pavattaṃ atiharaṇaṃ, atiharaṇe pavattaṃ vītiharaṇaṃ, vītiharaṇe pavattaṃ vossajjanaṃ, vossajjane pavattaṃ sannikkhepanaṃ, sannikkhepane pavattaṃ sannirujjhanaṃ na pāpuṇāti, tattha tattheva odhi odhi pabbaṃ pabbaṃ hutvā tattakapāle pakkhittatilā viya paṭapaṭāyantā saṅkhārā bhijjantīti? Saccametaṃ. Yathā pana padīpassa jalato jātā taṃ taṃ vaṭṭippadesaṃ anatikkamitvā tattha tattheva bhijjati, atha ca pana paveṇisambandhavasena sabbarattiṃ jalito padīpoti [M 2.0092] vuccati, evamidhāpi paveṇivasena ayampi kāyo evaṃ ciraṭṭhitiko viya katvā dassito.

Why did the Blessed One say, 'Better, monks...'? For at first, He had made form unsuitable to be grasped and what is formless suitable. Then, knowing, 'The grasping of those monks has departed from form and gone to what is formless,' He began this teaching to extract it. Therein, 'one might approach it as self' means one might take it as 'self'. 'Even more' means even beyond one hundred years. But why did the Blessed One speak thus? Is there such a thing as form that lasts for more than a hundred years? Surely, does not the form that arose in the first stage of life fail to reach the middle stage, the form that arose in the middle stage fail to reach the final stage, the form that arose in the forenoon fail to reach the afternoon, the form that arose in the afternoon fail to reach the first watch of the night, the form that arose in the first watch fail to reach the middle watch, and the form that arose in the middle watch fail to reach the last watch? Likewise, does not the form that arose in walking fail to reach standing, the form that arose in standing fail to reach sitting, and the form that arose in sitting fail to reach lying down? Even within a single posture, does not the form that arose in lifting the foot fail to reach its carrying forward, the form that arose in carrying forward fail to reach its moving aside, the form that arose in moving aside fail to reach its letting down, the form that arose in letting down fail to reach its placing down, and the form that arose in placing down fail to reach its ceasing? Do not the formations break apart right there and then, piece by piece, joint by joint, crackling like sesame seeds thrown on a hot pan? This is true. But just as the flame of a burning lamp, arising, does not go beyond that particular part of the wick but breaks apart right there, and yet, on account of the continuity of the series, it is said, 'The lamp burned all night'; so too here, by way of continuity, this body is shown by the Blessed One as if it were long-lasting.

Rattiyā ca divasassa cāti rattimhi ca divase ca. Bhummatthe hetaṃ sāmivacanaṃ. Aññadeva uppajjati, aññaṃ nirujjhatīti yaṃ rattiṃ uppajjati ca nirujjhati ca, tato aññadeva divā uppajjati ca nirujjhati cāti attho. Aññaṃ uppajjati, anuppannameva aññaṃ nirujjhatīti evaṃ pana attho na gahetabbo. “Rattiyā ca divasassa cā”ti idaṃ purimapaveṇito parittakaṃ paveṇiṃ gahetvā paveṇivaseneva vuttaṃ, ekarattiṃ pana ekadivasaṃ vā ekameva cittaṃ ṭhātuṃ samatthaṃ nāma natthi. Ekasmiñhi accharākkhaṇe anekāni cittakoṭisatasahassāni uppajjanti. Vuttampi cetaṃ milindapañhe –

Of the night and of the day means in the night and in the day. This is a genitive case used in the sense of the locative. One thing arises, another ceases means: the mind that arises and ceases at night is different from the mind that arises and ceases during the day; this is the meaning. Another mind arises, and another that has not yet arisen ceases—this meaning, however, should not be taken. The phrase 'Of the night and of the day' was spoken by the Blessed One by taking a small continuum from the preceding continuum and simply by way of that continuity. However, there is indeed no single mind that is capable of remaining for one whole night or one whole day. For in a single snap of the fingers, many hundreds of thousands of crores of minds arise. And this was also stated in the Milindapañha:

“Vāhasataṃ kho, mahārāja[P 2.0100], vīhīnaṃ, aḍḍhacūḷañca vāhā, vīhisattambaṇāni, dve ca tumbā, ekaccharākkhaṇe pavattassa cittassa ettakā vīhī lakkhaṃ ṭhapīyamānā parikkhayaṃ pariyādānaṃ gaccheyyu”nti.

O great king, indeed, one hundred cartloads (vāha) of paddy, and half of that in lesser cartloads, and seven ambaṇas of paddy, and two tumbas—all these grains of paddy do not amount to the hundredth part, nor the sixteenth part (kalā), nor even a fraction of a sixteenth part of the mind that occurs in the time of a single finger-snap.

Pavaneti mahāvane. Taṃ muñcitvā aññaṃ gaṇhāti, taṃ muñcitvā aññaṃ gaṇhātīti iminā na so gaṇhitabbasākhaṃ alabhitvā bhūmiṃ otarati. Atha kho tasmiṃ mahāvane vicaranto taṃ taṃ sākhaṃ gaṇhantoyeva caratīti ayamattho dassito.

Pavaṇa means a great forest. By this phrase, 'Letting go of one, he grasps another; letting go of that, he grasps yet another,' it is shown that the monkey does not descend to the ground without having obtained a branch fit to grasp. Rather, wandering in that great forest, he moves along only while grasping each and every branch—this is the meaning shown.

Evameva khoti ettha idaṃ opammasaṃsandanaṃ – araññamahāvanaṃ viya hi ārammaṇavanaṃ veditabbaṃ. Tasmiṃ vane vicaraṇamakkaṭo viya ārammaṇavane uppajjanakacittaṃ. Sākhāgahaṇaṃ viya [V 2.0088] ārammaṇe lubbhanaṃ. Yathā so araññe vicaranto makkaṭo taṃ taṃ sākhaṃ pahāya taṃ taṃ sākhaṃ gaṇhāti, evamidaṃ ārammaṇavane vicarantaṃ cittampi kadāci rūpārammaṇaṃ gahetvā uppajjati, kadāci saddādīsu aññataraṃ, kadāci atītaṃ, kadāci anāgataṃ vā paccuppannaṃ vā, tathā kadāci ajjhattaṃ, kadāci bāhiraṃ. Yathā ca so araññe vicaranto makkaṭo sākhaṃ alabhitvā oruyha bhūmiyaṃ nisinnoti na vattabbo, ekaṃ pana paṇṇasākhaṃ [M 2.0093] gahetvāva nisīdati, evameva ārammaṇavane vicarantaṃ cittampi ekaṃ olubbhārammaṇaṃ alabhitvā uppannanti na vattabbaṃ, ekajātiyaṃ pana ārammaṇaṃ gahetvāva uppajjatīti veditabbaṃ. Ettāvatā ca pana bhagavatā rūpato nīharitvā arūpe gāho patiṭṭhāpito, arūpato nīharitvā rūpe.

Even so, here is the connection of the simile: The forest of objects should be understood as a great wilderness. The monkey wandering in that forest is like the mind that arises in the forest of objects. Grasping a branch is like clinging to an object. Just as that monkey, wandering in the wilderness, lets go of one branch and grasps another, so too this mind, wandering in the forest of objects, sometimes arises having grasped a form as object, sometimes a sound or another, sometimes the past, sometimes the future or the present, sometimes internal, sometimes external. And just as that monkey, wandering in the wilderness, cannot be said to descend and sit on the ground without finding a branch, but rather sits only after grasping a single leafy branch, so too the mind, wandering in the forest of objects, cannot be said to arise without finding an object to be grasped; it should be understood to arise only after grasping an object of a single kind. To this extent, the Blessed One has withdrawn the grasping from form and established it in the formless, and withdrawn it from the formless and established it in form.

Idāni taṃ ubhayato nikkaḍḍhitukāmo tatra, bhikkhave, sutavā ariyasāvakoti desanaṃ ārabhi. Ayaṃ panattho āsīvisadaṭṭhūpamāya dīpetabbo – eko kira puriso āsīvisena daṭṭho, athassa visaṃ harissāmīti cheko bhisakko āgantvā vamanaṃ kāretvā heṭṭhā garuḷo, upari nāgoti mantaṃ parivattetvā visaṃ upari āropesi. So yāva akkhippadesā āruḷhabhāvaṃ ñatvā “ito paraṃ abhiruhituṃ na dassāmi, daṭṭhaṭṭhāneyeva ṭhapessāmī”ti [P 2.0101] upari garuḷo, heṭṭhā nāgoti mantaṃ parivattetvā kaṇṇe dhumetvā daṇḍakena paharitvā visaṃ otāretvā daṭṭhaṭṭhāneyeva ṭhapesi. Tatrassa ṭhitabhāvaṃ ñatvā agadalepena visaṃ nimmathetvā nhāpetvā “sukhī hohī”ti vatvā yenakāmaṃ pakkāmi.

Now, wishing to extract it from both sides, he began the teaching with, 'There, O bhikkhus, a learned noble disciple...' This meaning should be illustrated by the simile of one bitten by a venomous snake. It seems a certain man was bitten by a venomous snake. Then a skilled physician came, thinking, 'I will remove the poison from him.' He induced vomiting and, reciting the charm 'Garuḷa below, Nāga above,' he made the poison rise upward. Knowing that it had risen as far as the region of the eyes, he thought, 'I will not let it ascend further than this; I will keep it right at the place of the bite.' Reversing the charm to 'Garuḷa above, Nāga below,' blowing into the man's ears, and striking him with a stick, he made the poison descend and stopped it right at the place of the bite. Knowing it had remained there, he neutralized the poison with an antidote ointment, bathed him, said, 'Be well,' and departed wherever he wished.

Tattha āsīvisena daṭṭhassa kāye visapatiṭṭhānaṃ viya imesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ rūpe adhimattagāhakālo, cheko bhisakko viya tathāgato, mantaṃ parivattetvā upari visassa āropitakālo viya tathāgatena tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ rūpato gāhaṃ nīharitvā arūpe patiṭṭhāpitakālo, yāva akkhippadesā āruḷhavisassa upari abhiruhituṃ adatvā puna mantabalena otāretvā daṭṭhaṭṭhāneyeva ṭhapanaṃ viya satthārā tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ arūpato gāhaṃ nīharitvā rūpe patiṭṭhāpitakālo. Daṭṭhaṭṭhāne ṭhitassa visassa agadalepena nimmathanaṃ viya ubhayato gāhaṃ nīharaṇatthāya imissā desanāya āraddhakālo veditabbo. Tattha nibbindaṃ virajjatīti iminā maggo kathito, virāgā vimuccatīti phalaṃ, vimuttasmintiādinā paccavekkhaṇā. Paṭhamaṃ.

In this simile, the settling of poison in the body of one bitten by a venomous snake is like the time when these bhikkhus excessively grasped at form. The skilled physician is like the Tathāgata. The time when the poison was made to rise upward by reciting a charm is like the time when the Tathāgata withdrew the bhikkhus' grasping from form and established it in the formless. The time when, not allowing the risen poison to go beyond the region of the eyes, he made it descend again by the power of the charm and stopped it right at the place of the bite, is like the time when the Teacher withdrew the bhikkhus' grasping from the formless and established it in form. The subduing of the poison settled at the place of the bite with an antidote ointment is to be understood as the time when this teaching was begun for the purpose of removing the grasp from both. Therein, by 'becoming disenchanted, one becomes dispassionate,' the path is taught. By 'through dispassion, one is liberated,' the fruit is taught. By the passage beginning with 'In the liberated,' reviewing-knowledge is taught. The First [Sutta].

2. Dutiyaassutavāsuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Second Assutavā Sutta

62. Dutiye [V 2.0089] sukhavedaniyanti sukhavedanāya paccayaṃ. Phassanti cakkhusamphassādiṃ. Nanu ca cakkhusamphasso sukhavedanāya paccayo na hotīti? Sahajātapaccayena na hoti, upanissayapaccayena pana javanavedanāya hoti[M 2.0094], taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Sotasamphassādīsupi eseva nayo. Tajjanti tajjātikaṃ tassāruppaṃ, tassa phassassa anurūpanti attho. Dukkhavedaniyantiādi vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Saṅghaṭṭanasamodhānāti saṅghaṭṭanena ceva samodhānena ca, saṅghaṭṭanasampiṇḍanenāti attho. Usmāti uṇhākāro. Tejo abhinibbattatīti aggicuṇṇo nikkhamatīti na gahetabbaṃ, usmākārasseva pana etaṃ vevacanaṃ. Tattha dvinnaṃ kaṭṭhānanti dvinnaṃ araṇīnaṃ. Tattha adhoaraṇī viya vatthu, uttarāraṇī viya ārammaṇaṃ, saṅghaṭṭanaṃ viya phasso, usmādhātu viya vedanā. Dutiyaṃ.

62. In the second [discourse], 'contact giving rise to pleasant feeling' means a condition for pleasant feeling. 'Contact' refers to eye-contact and so on. But is not eye-contact a condition for pleasant feeling? It is not a condition by way of co-nascence, but it is a condition by way of decisive support for the feeling in the javana process—it was said referring to this. The same method applies to ear-contact and so on. 'Corresponding' means of the same kind, suitable for it, appropriate for that contact; this is the meaning. 'Contact giving rise to painful feeling' and so on should be understood in the same way as explained. 'By friction and conjunction' means by friction and also by conjunction, and not by the mere combination of rubbing together. 'Heat' means the state of being hot. 'Fire is produced' should not be taken to mean that sparks fly out; rather, this is just a synonym for the state of being hot. Here, 'of two pieces of wood' means of two fire-sticks. In this, the base is like the lower fire-stick, the object is like the upper fire-stick, contact is like the friction, and the heat element is like feeling. The Second.

3. Puttamaṃsūpamasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Discourse of the Simile of the Son's Flesh

63. Tatiye [P 2.0102] cattārome, bhikkhave, āhārātiādi vuttanayameva. Yasmā panassa aṭṭhuppattiko nikkhepo, tasmā taṃ dassetvāvettha anupubbapadavaṇṇanaṃ karissāmi. Katarāya pana idaṃ aṭṭhuppattiyā nikkhittanti? Lābhasakkārena. Bhagavato kira mahālābhasakkāro uppajji, yathā taṃ cattāro asaṅkhyeyye pūritadānapāramīsañcayassa. Sabbadisāsu hissa yamakamahāmegho vuṭṭhahitvā mahoghaṃ viya sabbapāramiyo “ekasmiṃ attabhāve vipākaṃ dassāmā”ti sampiṇḍitā viya lābhasakkāramahoghaṃ nibbattayiṃsu. Tato tato annapānayānavatthamālāgandhavilepanādihatthā khattiyabrāhmaṇādayo āgantvā, “kahaṃ buddho, kahaṃ bhagavā, kahaṃ devadevo narāsabho purisasīho”ti? Bhagavantaṃ pariyesanti. Sakaṭasatehipi paccaye āharitvā okāsaṃ alabhamānā samantā gāvutappamāṇampi sakaṭadhurena sakaṭadhuraṃ āhacca tiṭṭhanti ceva anuppavattanti ca andhakavindabrāhmaṇādayo viya. Sabbaṃ khandhake tesu tesu suttesu ca āgatanayena veditabbaṃ.

63. In the third discourse, 'These four nutriments, monks,' and so on, is to be understood in the same way as stated earlier. However, since this discourse has a presentation of its occasion of arising, I will explain the subsequent words only after showing that here. By what occasion of arising was this laid down? By gain and honor. Indeed, great gain and honor arose for the Blessed One, as was fitting for one whose accumulation of the perfection of giving had been fulfilled over four incalculable eons. From all directions, as if great twin rain clouds, having arisen, produced a great flood, all his perfections, as if compacted together saying, 'We will give our fruit in this single existence,' produced a great flood of gain and honor. From here and there, khattiyas, brahmins, and others, with food, drink, vehicles, robes, garlands, perfumes, and ointments in hand, came asking, 'Where is the Buddha? Where is the Blessed One? Where is the god of gods, the bull among men, the lion among men?' They searched for the Blessed One. Even bringing hundreds of cartloads of requisites, unable to find an opportunity to offer, they stood all around for a distance of even a gāvuta, with cart-yoke pressing against cart-yoke, and also followed along, like the brahmin of Andhakavinda and others. All this should be understood in the way it is presented in the Khandhakas and in those various suttas.

Yathā bhagavato, evaṃ bhikkhusaṅghassāpi. Vuttañcetaṃ –

As with the Blessed One, so also with the Saṅgha of monks. And it was said:

“Tena [V 2.0090] kho pana samayena bhagavā sakkato hoti garukato mānito pūjito apacito lābhī cīvara-piṇḍapāta-senāsana-gilāna-paccaya-bhesajja-parikkhārānaṃ. Bhikkhusaṅghopi kho sakkato hoti…pe… parikkhārāna”nti (udā. 14; saṃ. ni. 2.70).

“At that time, the Blessed One was honored, respected, revered, venerated, and esteemed, a recipient of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick. The Saṅgha of monks was also honored... a recipient of... requisites.”

Tathā [M 2.0095] “yāvatā kho, cunda, etarahi saṅgho vā gaṇo vā loke uppanno, nāhaṃ, cunda, aññaṃ ekasaṅghampi samanupassāmi evaṃ lābhaggayasaggapattaṃ yatharivāyaṃ, cunda, bhikkhusaṅgho”ti (dī. ni. 3.176).

Similarly: “As far as any Saṅgha or group has arisen in the world today, Cunda, I do not see another single Saṅgha that has attained such a peak of gain and fame as this Saṅgha of monks, Cunda.”

Svāyaṃ bhagavato ca saṅghassa ca uppanno lābhasakkāro ekato hutvā dvinnaṃ mahānadīnaṃ udakaṃ viya appameyyo ahosi. Atha satthā rahogato cintesi – “mahālābhasakkāro atītabuddhānampi evarūpo ahosi, anāgatānampi evarūpo bhavissati[P 2.0103]. Kiṃ nu kho bhikkhū āhārapariggāhakena satisampajaññena samannāgatā majjhattā nicchandarāgā hutvā āhāraṃ paribhuñjituṃ sakkonti, na sakkontī”ti?

This gain and honor that arose for the Blessed One and the Saṅgha, having become one, was immeasurable, like the waters of two great rivers. Then the Teacher, having gone into seclusion, reflected: “Such great gain and honor existed for the Buddhas of the past and will exist for those of the future. But are the monks, endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension that comprehends food, remaining equanimous, free from desire and passion, able to consume food, or are they not?”

So addasa ekacce adhunā pabbajite kulaputte apaccavekkhitvā āhāraṃ paribhuñjamāne. Disvānassa etadahosi – “mayā kappasatasahassādhikāni cattāri asaṅkhyeyyāni pāramiyo pūrentena na cīvarādihetu pūritā, uttamaphalassa pana arahattassatthāya pūritā. Imepi bhikkhū mama santike pabbajantā na cīvarādihetu pabbajitā, arahattasseva pana atthāya pabbajitā. Te idāni asārameva sāraṃ anatthameva ca atthaṃ karontī”ti evamassa dhammasaṃvego udapādi. Tato cintesi – “sace pañcamaṃ pārājikaṃ paññapetuṃ sakkā abhavissa, apaccavekkhitāhāraparibhogo pañcamaṃ pārājikaṃ katvā paññapetabbo bhaveyya. Na pana sakkā evaṃ kātuṃ, dhuvapaṭisevanaṭṭhānañhetaṃ sattānaṃ. Yathā pana kathite pañcamaṃ pārājikaṃ viya naṃ passissanti. Evaṃ dhammādāsaṃ saṃvaraṃ mariyādaṃ ṭhapessāmi, yaṃ āvajjitvā āvajjitvā anāgate bhikkhū cattāro paccaye paccavekkhitvā paribhuñjissantī”ti. Imāya aṭṭhuppattiyā imaṃ puttamaṃsūpamasuttantaṃ nikkhipi. Tattha cattārome, bhikkhave, āhārātiādi heṭṭhā vuttatthameva.

He saw some newly ordained clansmen consuming food without reflection. Seeing this, this thought occurred to him: “By me, fulfilling the perfections for four incalculable eons and a hundred thousand more, they were not fulfilled for the sake of robes and so on, but for the sake of the supreme fruit, Arahantship. These monks too, having gone forth in my presence, did not go forth for the sake of robes and so on, but for the sake of Arahantship itself. Yet now they are treating the essenceless as the essence and what is not the goal as the goal.” Thus a sense of spiritual urgency arose in him. Then he reflected: “If it were possible to lay down a fifth Pārājika offense, the unreflective consumption of food should be laid down as a fifth Pārājika. But it is not possible to do so, for this is a constant practice for beings. However, when it is taught, they will regard it like a fifth Pārājika. In this way, I will establish a mirror of the Dhamma, a restraint, a boundary, reflecting on which again and again, future monks will consume the four requisites with reflection.” For this occasion of arising, he laid down this Discourse on the Simile of the Son's Flesh. Herein, 'These four nutriments, monks,' and so on, has the meaning already explained below.

Cattāro [V 2.0091] pana āhāre vitthāretvā idāni tesu ādīnavaṃ dassetuṃ kathañca, bhikkhave, kabaḷīkāro āhāro daṭṭhabbotiādimāha? Tattha jāyampatikāti jāyā ceva pati ca. Parittaṃ sambalanti puṭabhattasattumodakādīnaṃ aññataraṃ appamattakaṃ pātheyyaṃ. Kantāramagganti kantārabhūtaṃ maggaṃ, kantāre vā maggaṃ. Kantāranti corakantāraṃ vāḷakantāraṃ amanussakantāraṃ nirudakakantāraṃ appabhakkhakantāranti pañcavidhaṃ. Tesu yattha corabhayaṃ atthi[M 2.0096], taṃ corakantāraṃ. Yattha sīhabyagghādayo vāḷā atthi, taṃ vāḷakantāraṃ. Yattha balavāmukhayakkhiniādīnaṃ amanussānaṃ vasena bhayaṃ atthi, taṃ amanussakantāraṃ. Yattha pātuṃ vā nhāyituṃ vā udakaṃ natthi, taṃ nirudakakantāraṃ. Yattha khāditabbaṃ vā bhuñjitabbaṃ vā antamaso kandamūlādimattampi [P 2.0104] natthi, taṃ appabhakkhakantāraṃ nāma. Yattha panetaṃ pañcavidhampi bhayaṃ atthi, taṃ kantārameva. Taṃ panetaṃ ekāhadvīhatīhādivasena nittharitabbampi atthi, na taṃ idha adhippetaṃ. Idha pana nirudakaṃ appabhakkhaṃ yojanasatikakantāraṃ adhippetaṃ. Evarūpe kantāre maggaṃ. Paṭipajjeyyunti chātakabhayena ceva rogabhayena ca rājabhayena ca upaddutā paṭipajjeyyuṃ “etaṃ kantāraṃ nittharitvā dhammikassa rañño nirupaddave raṭṭhe sukhaṃ vasissāmā”ti maññamānā.

Now, having elaborated on the four nutriments, to show the danger in them, the Blessed One said: 'And how, monks, should physical food be regarded?' and so on. Herein, 'a couple' means a wife and a husband. 'A small provision' refers to a meager supply of provisions, such as cooked rice in a leaf-packet, barley flour, or sweets. 'A wilderness road' means a road that has become a wilderness, or a road in a wilderness. The wilderness is of five kinds: a robber-infested wilderness, a wild beast-infested wilderness, a non-human-infested wilderness, a waterless wilderness, and a foodless wilderness. Among these, where there is danger from robbers, that is a robber-infested wilderness. Where there are wild beasts like lions and tigers, that is a wild beast-infested wilderness. Where there is danger from powerful non-humans such as ogres with powerful mouths and demonesses, that is a non-human-infested wilderness. Where there is no water to drink or to bathe in, that is a waterless wilderness. Where there is nothing to chew or to eat, not even so much as roots or tubers, that is called a foodless wilderness. And where all five of these dangers are present, that is a wilderness indeed. However, some of these can be crossed in one, two, or three days, but that is not the intended meaning here. Here, however, a waterless and foodless wilderness of a hundred yojanas is intended. 'They would travel along such a wilderness road' means they would proceed, oppressed by fear of hunger, disease, and the king, thinking, 'Having crossed this wilderness, we will live happily in the just king’s realm, free from danger.'

Ekaputtakoti ukkhipitvā gahito anukampitabbayutto athirasarīro ekaputtako. Vallūrañca soṇḍikañcāti ghanaghanaṭṭhānato gahetvā vallūraṃ, aṭṭhinissitasirānissitaṭṭhānāni gahetvā sūlamaṃsañcāti attho. Paṭipiseyyunti pahareyyuṃ. Kahaṃ ekaputtakāti ayaṃ tesaṃ paridevanākāro.

'An only son' means an only son who is carried and held, worthy of compassion, and frail-bodied. Regarding 'dried meat (`vallūra`) and choice cuts (`soṇḍika`)', the meaning is that `vallūra` is meat taken from the thickest parts, and `soṇḍika` is skewered meat taken from the parts attached to bone and sinew. `Paṭipiseyyuṃ` means they would beat their chests. 'Where, O only son?'—this is the manner of their lamentation.

Ayaṃ panettha bhūtamatthaṃ katvā ādito paṭṭhāya saṅkhepato atthavaṇṇanā – dve kira jāyampatikā puttaṃ gahetvā parittena pātheyyena yojanasatikaṃ kantāramaggaṃ paṭipajjiṃsu. Tesaṃ paññāsayojanāni gantvā pātheyyaṃ niṭṭhāsi, te khuppipāsāturā viraḷacchāyāyaṃ nisīdiṃsu. Tato puriso bhariyaṃ āha – “bhadde ito samantā paññāsayojanāni gāmo vā nigamo vā natthi. Tasmā yaṃ taṃ purisena kātabbaṃ bahumpi kasigorakkhādikammaṃ, na dāni sakkā taṃ mayā kātuṃ, ehi maṃ māretvā upaḍḍhamaṃsaṃ khāditvā upaḍḍhaṃ pātheyyaṃ katvā puttena saddhiṃ kantāraṃ nittharāhī”ti. Puna sāpi taṃ āha – “sāmi mayā dāni yaṃ taṃ itthiyā kātabbaṃ bahumpi suttakantanādikammaṃ, taṃ kātuṃ na sakkā, ehi maṃ māretvā upaḍḍhamaṃsaṃ khāditvā upaḍḍhaṃ pātheyyaṃ katvā puttena saddhiṃ kantāraṃ nittharāhī”ti. Puna sopi taṃ āha – “bhadde mātugāmamaraṇena dvinnaṃ [V 2.0092] maraṇaṃ paññāyati[P 2.0105]. Na hi mando kumāro mātarā vinā [M 2.0097] jīvituṃ sakkoti. Yadi pana mayaṃ jīvāma. Puna dārakaṃ labheyyāma. Handa dāni puttakaṃ māretvā, maṃsaṃ gahetvā kantāraṃ nittharāmā”ti. Tato mātā puttamāha – “tāta, pitusantikaṃ gacchā”ti, so agamāsi. Athassa pitā, “mayā ‘puttakaṃ posessāmī’ti kasigorakkhādīhi anappakaṃ dukkhamanubhūtaṃ, na sakkomi ahaṃ puttaṃ māretuṃ, tvaṃyeva tava puttaṃ mārehī”ti vatvā, “tāta mātusantikaṃ gacchā”ti āha. So agamāsi. Athassa mātāpi, “mayā puttaṃ patthentiyā govatakukkuravatadevatāyācanādīhipi tāva anappakaṃ dukkhamanubhūtaṃ, ko pana vādo kucchinā pariharantiyā? Na sakkomi ahaṃ puttaṃ māretu”nti vatvā “tāta, pitusantikameva gacchā”ti āha. Evaṃ so dvinnamantarā gacchantoyeva mato. Te taṃ disvā paridevitvā vuttanayena maṃsāni gahetvā khādantā pakkamiṃsu.

Herein, this is a concise explanation of the meaning, making the actual story clear from the beginning: Indeed, a husband and wife, taking their son, set out on a hundred-yojana wilderness road with a small amount of provisions. Having traveled fifty yojanas, their provisions ran out, and afflicted by hunger and thirst, they sat down in sparse shade. Then the husband said to his wife: 'Dear, there is no village or town within fifty yojanas around here. Therefore, the many tasks that a man must do, such as plowing and cattle-rearing, I cannot do now. Come, kill me, eat half my flesh, make half of it provisions, and cross the wilderness with our son.' Then she also said to him: 'Husband, the many tasks that a woman must do, such as spinning thread, I cannot do now. Come, kill me, eat half my flesh, make half of it provisions, and cross the wilderness with our son.' Again, he said to her: 'Dear, by the death of a woman, the death of two is implied. For this helpless boy cannot live without his mother. But if we live, we may have another child. Come now, let us kill our son, take his flesh, and cross the wilderness.' Then the mother said to the son: 'Dear, go to your father.' He went. Then his father said: 'Having endured no small amount of hardship through plowing, cattle-rearing, and such work, thinking, "I will raise my son," I cannot kill my son. You yourself kill your son.' Saying this, he said, 'Dear, go to your mother.' He went. Then his mother also said: 'Longing for a son, I endured no small amount of suffering even through vows such as the cow-vow and the dog-vow and praying to deities—what need to mention carrying him in my womb? I cannot kill my son.' Saying this, she said, 'Dear, go back to your father.' Thus, while going back and forth between the two, the boy died. Seeing this, they lamented, took his flesh in the manner described, ate it, and departed.

Tesaṃ so puttamaṃsāhāro navahi kāraṇehi paṭikūlattā neva davāya hoti, na madāya, na maṇḍanāya, na vibhūsanāya, kevalaṃ kantāranittharaṇatthāyeva hoti. Katamehi navahi kāraṇehi paṭikūloti ce? Sajātimaṃsatāya ñātimaṃsatāya puttamaṃsatāya piyaputtamaṃsatāya taruṇamaṃsatāya āmakamaṃsatāya abhogamaṃsatāya aloṇatāya adhūpitatāyāti. Evañhi te navahi kāraṇehi paṭikūlaṃ taṃ puttamaṃsaṃ khādantā na sārattā giddhamānasā hutvā khādiṃsu, majjhattabhāveyeva pana nicchandarāgaparibhoge ṭhitā khādiṃsu. Na aṭṭhinhārucammanissitaṭṭhānāni apanetvā thūlathūlaṃ varamaṃsameva khādiṃsu, hatthasampattaṃ maṃsameva pana khādiṃsu. Na yāvadatthaṃ kaṇṭhappamāṇaṃ katvā khādiṃsu, thokaṃ thokaṃ pana ekadivasaṃ yāpanamattameva khādiṃsu. Na aññamaññaṃ maccharāyantā khādiṃsu, vigatamaccheramalena pana parisuddheneva cetasā khādiṃsu. Na aññaṃ kiñci migamaṃsaṃ vā moramaṃsādīnaṃ vā aññataraṃ khādāmāti sammūḷhā khādiṃsu, piyaputtamaṃsabhāvaṃ pana jānantāva [P 2.0106] khādiṃsu. Na “aho vata mayaṃ punapi evarūpaṃ puttamaṃsaṃ khādeyyāmā”ti patthanaṃ katvā khādiṃsu, patthanaṃ pana vītivattāva hutvā khādiṃsu. Na “ettakaṃ kantāre khāditvā avasiṭṭhaṃ kantāraṃ atikkamma loṇambilādīhi yojetvā khādissāmā”ti sannidhiṃ akaṃsu, kantārapariyosāne pana “pure mahājano passatī”ti bhūmiyaṃ vā nikhaṇiṃsu, agginā [M 2.0098] vā jhāpayiṃsu. Na “koci añño amhe viya evarūpaṃ puttamaṃsaṃ khādituṃ na labhatī”ti mānaṃ vā dappaṃ vā akaṃsu, nihatamānā pana nihatadappā hutvā khādiṃsu. “Kiṃ iminā aloṇena anambilena adhūpitena duggandhenā”ti na hīḷetvā khādiṃsu, hīḷanaṃ pana vītivattā hutvā khādiṃsu[V 2.0093]. Na “tuyhaṃ bhāgo mayhaṃ bhāgo tava putto mama putto”ti aññamaññaṃ atimaññiṃsu. Samaggā pana sammodamānā hutvā khādiṃsu. Imaṃ nesaṃ evarūpaṃ nicchandarāgādiparibhogaṃ sampassamāno satthā bhikkhusaṅghampi taṃ kāraṇaṃ anujānāpento taṃ kiṃ maññatha, bhikkhave, api nu te davāya vā āhāraṃ āhāreyyuntiādimāha. Tattha davāya vātiādīni visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 1.18) vitthāritāneva. Kantārassāti nittiṇṇāvasesassa kantārassa.

For them, that food of their son's flesh was repulsive for nine reasons, and so it was not for sport, not for intoxication, not for adornment, nor for beautification—it was solely for the purpose of crossing the wilderness. If it is asked, 'For which nine reasons was it repulsive?' Because it was flesh of the same species, flesh of a relative, flesh of a son, flesh of a beloved son, tender flesh, raw flesh, flesh unfit for consumption, unsalted flesh, and unsmoked flesh. Thus, eating that repulsive flesh of their son for these nine reasons, they did not consume it with attachment or greedy minds, but rather, abiding in a state of neutrality, their consumption was free from desire and passion. They did not eat only the large, choice pieces after removing what was attached to bones, sinews, and skin, but ate only the flesh that came to hand. They did not eat as much as they wished, filling their throats, but only in small amounts, just enough to sustain themselves for the day. They did not eat it while being stingy toward one another, but with minds purified and free from the stain of stinginess. They did not eat it in delusion, thinking, 'We are eating some other kind of meat, like deer or peacock,' but knowing full well that it was the flesh of their beloved son. They did not eat it with the longing, 'Oh, if only we could eat such flesh again!' but having overcome such longing. They did not store it, thinking, 'After eating this much in the wilderness, we will season the remainder with salt and sour things once we cross,' but at the end of the wilderness, they buried it in the ground or burned it in fire, thinking, 'Lest the populace see it.' They did not eat it with conceit or arrogance, thinking, 'No one else gets to eat such flesh as we do,' but with conceit and arrogance abandoned. They did not eat it with disparagement, thinking, 'What is to be done with this unsalted, unsour, unsmoked, foul-smelling flesh?' but having overcome such disparagement. They did not despise one another, saying, 'This is your share, this is mine; your son, my son,' but ate in harmony and with mutual joy. Seeing this kind of consumption of theirs, free from desire, passion, and so on, the Teacher, wishing to authorize that reason for the community of monks as well, asked, 'What do you think, monks? Would they take that food for sport?' and so on. Here, the terms 'for sport' and so on are explained in detail in the Visuddhimagga. 'Of the wilderness' means of the remaining part of the wilderness that was yet to be crossed.

Evameva khoti navannaṃ pāṭikulyānaṃ vasena piyaputtamaṃsasadiso katvā daṭṭhabboti attho. Katamesaṃ navannaṃ? Gamanapāṭikulyatādīnaṃ. Gamanapāṭikulyataṃ paccavekkhantopi kabaḷīkārāhāraṃ pariggaṇhāti, pariyesanapāṭikulyataṃ paccavekkhantopi, paribhoganidhānaāsayaparipakkāparipakkasammakkhaṇanissandapāṭikulyataṃ paccavekkhantopi, tāni panetāni gamanapāṭikulyatādīni visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 1.294) āhārapāṭikulyatāniddese vitthāritāneva. Iti imesaṃ navannaṃ pāṭikulyānaṃ vasena puttamaṃsūpamaṃ katvā āhāro paribhuñjitabbo.

The meaning of the phrase 'Just so, indeed' is this: food should be regarded as similar to the flesh of a beloved son by way of nine kinds of repulsiveness. Which nine? Those beginning with the repulsiveness of going. Even while reflecting on the repulsiveness of going, one accepts physical food; even while reflecting on the repulsiveness of seeking; and even while reflecting on the repulsiveness of consumption, of the receptacle, of its abode, of what is digested, of what is undigested, of being smeared by it, and of its discharge, one accepts physical food. These kinds of repulsiveness, beginning with the repulsiveness of going, are explained in detail in the Visuddhimagga in the exposition on the repulsiveness in food. Thus, by way of these nine kinds of repulsiveness, food should be consumed using the simile of a son's flesh.

Yathā te jāyampatikā pāṭikulyaṃ piyaputtamaṃsaṃ khādantā na sārattā giddhamānasā hutvā khādiṃsu, majjhattabhāveyeva nicchandarāgaparibhoge ṭhitā khādiṃsu, evaṃ nicchandarāgaparibhogaṃ katvā paribhuñjitabbo. Yathā ca te na aṭṭhinhārucammanissitaṃ apanetvā thūlathūlaṃ varamaṃsameva khādiṃsu, hatthasampattameva [P 2.0107] pana khādiṃsu, evaṃ sukkhabhattamandabyañjanādīni piṭṭhihatthena apaṭikkhipitvā vaṭṭakena viya kukkuṭena viya ca odhiṃ adassetvā tato tato sappimaṃsādisaṃsaṭṭhavarabhojanaṃyeva vicinitvā abhuñjantena sīhena viya sapadānaṃ paribhuñjitabbo.

Just as that husband and wife, while eating the repulsive flesh of their beloved son, did not eat with attachment or with greedy minds, but ate abiding in a state of neutrality, in consumption free from desire and passion, so too should one consume food by practicing consumption free from desire and passion. And just as they did not remove what was attached to bone, sinew, and skin to eat only the large, choice pieces of flesh, but rather ate only what came to hand, so too, one should not push away dry rice, poor curries, and the like with the back of the hand. Not picking and choosing like a quail or a chicken, and not selecting and eating only the choice food mixed with ghee, meat, and so on from here and there, one should consume the food in sequence, like a lion.

Yathā ca te na yāvadatthaṃ kaṇṭhappamāṇaṃ khādiṃsu, thokaṃ thokaṃ pana ekekadivasaṃ yāpanamattameva khādiṃsu, evameva āharahatthakādibrāhmaṇānaṃ aññatarena viya yāvadatthaṃ udarāvadehakaṃ abhuñjantena catunnaṃ pañcannaṃ vā [M 2.0099] ālopānaṃ okāsaṃ ṭhapetvāva dhammasenāpatinā viya paribhuñjitabbo. So kira pañcacattālīsa vassāni tiṭṭhamāno “pacchābhatte ambiluggārasamuṭṭhāpakaṃ katvā ekadivasampi āhāraṃ na āhāresi”nti vatvā sīhanādaṃ nadanto imaṃ gāthamāha –

And just as they did not eat as much as they wished, filling their throats, but ate only a little each day, just enough to sustain themselves, so too, one should not eat one's fill to the point of stuffing the belly, like one of the Āharahatthaka brahmins and so on. Rather, one should eat like the General of the Dhamma, leaving space for four or five mouthfuls. It is said that he, for forty-five years, while abiding, roared a lion's roar, saying, 'I have never, even for a single day, eaten food in such a way as to cause sour eructations after the meal,' and spoke this verse:

“Cattāro [V 2.0094] pañca ālope, abhutvā udakaṃ pive;

Alaṃ phāsuvihārāya, pahitattassa bhikkhuno”ti. (theragā. 983);

“Leaving four or five mouthfuls uneaten, one should drink water; this is sufficient for the comfortable abiding of a monk with a resolute mind.”

Yathā ca te na aññamaññaṃ maccharāyantā khādiṃsu, vigatamalamaccherena pana parisuddheneva cetasā khādiṃsu, evameva piṇḍapātaṃ labhitvā amaccharāyitvā “imaṃ sabbaṃ gaṇhantassa sabbaṃ dassāmi, upaḍḍhaṃ gaṇhantassa upaḍḍhaṃ, sace gahitāvaseso bhavissati, attanā paribhuñjissāmī”ti sāraṇīyadhamme ṭhiteneva paribhuñjitabbo. Yathā ca te na “aññaṃ kiñci mayaṃ migamaṃsaṃ vā moramaṃsādīnaṃ vā aññataraṃ khādāmā”ti sammūḷhā khādiṃsu, piyaputtamaṃsabhāvaṃ pana jānantāva khādiṃsu, evameva piṇḍapātaṃ labhitvā “ahaṃ khādāmi bhuñjāmī”ti attūpaladdhisammohaṃ anuppādetvā “kabaḷīkārāhāro na jānāti ‘cātumahābhūtikakāyaṃ vaḍḍhemī’ti, kāyopi na jānāti ‘kabaḷīkārāhāro maṃ vaḍḍhetī’”ti, evaṃ sammohaṃ pahāya paribhuñjitabbo. Satisampajaññavasenāpi cesa asammūḷheneva hutvā paribhuñjitabbo.

Just as they did not eat being stingy towards each other, but ate with a mind that was indeed pure and free from the stain of stinginess, in this very way, having received almsfood, one should partake without stinginess, established in the qualities that foster concord, thinking: 'To one who takes all of this, I will give all. To one who takes half, I will give half. If there is any remainder after it has been taken, I myself will consume it.' And just as they did not eat being utterly deluded, thinking, 'We are eating some other meat, such as deer meat or peacock meat,' but rather ate knowing it to be the flesh of their beloved son, in this very way, having received almsfood, one should partake without giving rise to the delusion associated with the view of a self, thinking, 'I eat, I consume.' One should partake having abandoned delusion thus: 'The physical nutriment does not know, "I nourish this body made of the four great elements," nor does the body know, "The physical nutriment nourishes me."' And by the power of mindfulness and clear comprehension, this food should be partaken of, being indeed free from delusion.

Yathā ca te na “aho vata mayaṃ punapi evarūpaṃ puttamaṃsaṃ khādeyyāmā”ti patthanaṃ katvā khādiṃsu, patthanaṃ pana vītivattāva hutvā khādiṃsu, evameva paṇītabhojanaṃ [P 2.0108] laddhā ‘aho vatāhaṃ svepi punadivasepi evarūpaṃ labheyyaṃ’, lūkhaṃ vā pana laddhā “hiyyo viya me ajja paṇītabhojanaṃ na laddha”nti patthanaṃ vā anusocanaṃ vā akatvā nittaṇhena –

And just as they did not eat making a wish, 'Oh, would that we might eat such son's flesh again!', but rather ate having overcome that wish; in this very way, having obtained fine food, one should not make a wish, thinking, 'Oh, would that I might obtain such food tomorrow or on another day!' Or, having received coarse food, one should not make a wish or lament, thinking, 'Today I did not receive fine food as I did yesterday,' but without craving—

“Atītaṃ nānusocāmi, nappajappāmināgataṃ;

Paccuppannena yāpemi, tena vaṇṇo pasīdatī”ti. (jā. 2.22.90) –

“I do not grieve for the past, nor do I long for the future; I sustain myself with what is present, therefore my complexion is clear.”

Imaṃ ovādaṃ anussarantena “paccuppanneneva yāpessāmī”ti paribhuñjitabbo.

Remembering this instruction, one should consume food, thinking, 'I shall sustain myself with what is present only.'

Yathā ca te na “ettakaṃ kantāre khāditvā avasiṭṭhaṃ kantāraṃ atikkamma loṇambilādīhi yojetvā khādissāmā”ti sannidhiṃ akaṃsu, kantārapariyosāne [M 2.0100] pana “pure mahājano passatī”ti bhūmiyaṃ vā nikhaṇiṃsu, agginā vā jhāpayiṃsu, evameva –

And just as they did not make a store, thinking, 'Having eaten this much in the wilderness, we will cross the remaining wilderness and eat the rest combined with salt, sour fruits, and other things,' but at the end of the wilderness, thinking, 'Lest the public see it beforehand,' they either buried it in the ground or burned it with fire; in this very way—

“Annānamatho [V 2.0095] pānānaṃ,

Khādanīyānaṃ athopi vatthānaṃ;

Laddhā na sannidhiṃ kayirā,

Na ca parittase tāni alabhamāno”ti. (su. ni. 930); –

“Having obtained food and also drinks, chewables and also clothing, one should not make a store of them, nor be anxious when they are not obtained.”

Imaṃ ovādaṃ anussarantena catūsu paccayesu yaṃ yaṃ labhati, tato tato attano yāpanamattaṃ gahetvā, sesaṃ sabrahmacārīnaṃ vissajjetvā sannidhiṃ parivajjantena paribhuñjitabbo. Yathā ca te na “koci añño amhe viya evarūpaṃ puttamaṃsaṃ khādituṃ na labhatī”ti mānaṃ vā dappaṃ vā akaṃsu, nihatamānā pana nihatadappā hutvā khādiṃsu, evameva paṇītabhojanaṃ labhitvā “ahamasmi lābhī cīvarapiṇḍapātādīna”nti na māno vā dappo vā kātabbo. “Nāyaṃ pabbajjā cīvarādihetu, arahattahetu panāyaṃ pabbajjā”ti paccavekkhitvā nihatamānadappeneva paribhuñjitabbo.

Remembering this instruction, from whatever one obtains among the four requisites, taking only enough for one's own sustenance and relinquishing the rest to one's companions in the holy life, one should consume food while avoiding storing. And just as they did not have pride or arrogance, thinking, 'No one else like us gets to eat such son's flesh,' but ate with pride and arrogance struck down; in this very way, having obtained fine food, one should not have pride or arrogance, thinking, 'I am a recipient of robes, almsfood, and so on.' Having reflected, 'This going forth is not for the sake of robes and so on, but this going forth is for the sake of Arahantship,' one should consume food with pride and arrogance struck down.

Yathā ca te “kiṃ iminā aloṇena anambilena adhūpitena duggandhenā”ti [P 2.0109] hīḷetvā na khādiṃsu, hīḷanaṃ pana vītivattā hutvā khādiṃsu, evameva piṇḍapātaṃ labhitvā “kiṃ iminā assagoṇabhattasadisena lūkhena nirasena, suvānadoṇiyaṃ taṃ pakkhipathā”ti evaṃ piṇḍapātaṃ vā “ko imaṃ bhuñjissati, kākasunakhādīnaṃ dehī”ti evaṃ dāyakaṃ vā ahīḷentena –

And just as they did not eat, despising it and thinking, 'What is this unsalted, unsoured, unflavored, foul-smelling flesh?', but ate having overcome that contempt; in this very way, having received almsfood, one should not despise the almsfood, thinking, 'What is this coarse, tasteless food, like food for horses and oxen? Throw it into the dog's trough!' nor despise the donor, thinking, 'Who will eat this? Give it to the crows and dogs!'—

“Sa pattapāṇi vicaranto, amūgo mūgasammato;

Appaṃ dānaṃ na hīḷeyya, dātāraṃ nāvajāniyā”ti. (su. ni. 718); –

“Wandering with bowl in hand, not mute, though considered as mute; one should not despise a small gift, nor should one look down upon the giver.”

Imaṃ ovādaṃ anussarantena paribhuñjitabbo. Yathā ca te na “tuyhaṃ bhāgo, mayhaṃ bhāgo, tava putto mama putto”ti aññamaññaṃ atimaññiṃsu, samaggā pana, sammodamānā hutvā khādiṃsu, evamevaṃ piṇḍapātaṃ labhitvā yathā ekacco “ko tumhādisānaṃ dassati nikkāraṇā ummāresu pakkhalantānaṃ āhiṇḍantānaṃ vijātamātāpi vo dātabbaṃ na maññati, mayaṃ pana [M 2.0101] gatagataṭṭhāne paṇītāni cīvarādīni labhāmā”ti sīlavante sabrahmacārī atimaññati, yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ –

Remembering this instruction, one should consume the food. And just as they did not look down on each other, thinking, 'Your share, my share; your son, my son,' but ate in harmony, rejoicing together; in this very way, having received almsfood, one should not be like a certain person who looks down upon virtuous companions in the holy life, thinking: 'Who will give to the likes of you, who wander about, stumbling on doorsteps without reason? Even the mother who bore you would not think to give to you. But we, wherever we go, receive fine requisites like robes.' It is with reference to this that it was said—

“So [V 2.0096] tena lābhasakkārasilokena abhibhūto pariyādiṇṇacitto aññe pesale bhikkhū atimaññati. Tañhi tassa, bhikkhave, moghapurisassa hoti dīgharattaṃ ahitāya dukkhāyā”ti (saṃ. ni. 2.161).

“He, overcome by that gain, honor, and fame, his mind seized, looks down upon other amiable bhikkhus. Bhikkhus, that indeed is for the long-term harm and suffering of that foolish man.”

Evaṃ kañci anatimaññitvā sabbehi sabrahmacārīhi saddhiṃ samaggena sammodamānena hutvā paribhuñjitabbaṃ.

Thus, without looking down upon anyone, one should consume food in harmony and rejoicing together with all companions in the holy life.

Pariññāteti ñātapariññā tīraṇapariññā pahānapariññāti imāhi tīhi pariññāhi pariññāte. Kathaṃ? Idha bhikkhu “kabaḷīkārāhāro nāma ayaṃ savatthukavasena ojaṭṭhamakarūpaṃ hoti, ojaṭṭhamakarūpaṃ kattha paṭihaññati? Jivhāpasāde, jivhāpasādo kinnissito? Catumahābhūtanissito. Iti ojaṭṭhamakaṃ jivhāpasādo tassa paccayāni mahābhūtānīti ime dhammā rūpakkhandho nāma, taṃ pariggaṇhato uppannā phassapañcamakā dhammā cattāro arūpakkhandhā. Iti sabbepime pañcakkhandhā saṅkhepato nāmarūpamattaṃ hotī”ti pajānāti. So te dhamme sarasalakkhaṇato vavatthapetvā [P 2.0110] tesaṃ paccayaṃ pariyesanto anulomapaṭilomaṃ paṭiccasamuppādaṃ passati. Ettāvatānena kabaḷīkārāhāramukhena sappaccayassa nāmarūpassa yāthāvato diṭṭhattā kabaḷīkārāhāro ñātapariññāya pariññāto hoti. So tadeva sappaccayaṃ nāmarūpaṃ aniccaṃ dukkhaṃ anattāti tīṇi lakkhaṇāni āropetvā sattannaṃ anupassanānaṃ vasena sammasati. Ettāvatānena so tilakkhaṇapaṭivedhasammasanañāṇasaṅkhātāya tīraṇapariññāya pariññāto hoti. Tasmiṃyeva nāmarūpe chandarāgāvakaḍḍhanena anāgāmimaggena parijānatā pahānapariññāya pariññāto hotīti.

It is fully understood by the three kinds of full understanding: full understanding as knowledge (ñātapariññā), full understanding as investigation (tīraṇapariññā), and full understanding as abandonment (pahānapariññā). How? Here, a bhikkhu understands: ‘This nutriment consisting of morsels of food, in terms of its basis, is form with nutritive essence as the eighth. Where is form with nutritive essence as the eighth encountered? At the tongue sensitivity. What does the tongue sensitivity depend on? It depends on the four great elements. Thus, form with nutritive essence as the eighth, the tongue sensitivity, and its conditions, the great elements—these phenomena are called the form aggregate. For one who comprehends that, the phenomena with contact as the fifth arise—the four immaterial aggregates. Thus, all these five aggregates, in brief, are merely name-and-form,’ he understands. Having determined these phenomena by their individual characteristics, he investigates their condition and sees dependent origination in forward and reverse order. To this extent, by means of nutriment consisting of morsels of food as the starting point, because name-and-form together with its conditions has been seen as it really is, nutriment consisting of morsels of food is fully understood by the full understanding as knowledge. He then comprehends that same name-and-form together with its conditions by applying the three characteristics—impermanent, suffering, and non-self—by means of the seven kinds of contemplation. To this extent, by this bhikkhu, that nutriment is fully understood by the full understanding as investigation, which is known as the knowledge of comprehension through penetrating the three characteristics. By one who fully understands through the path of non-returning, which removes desire and lust for that very name-and-form, it is fully understood by the full understanding as abandonment.

Pañcakāmaguṇikoti pañcakāmaguṇasambhavo rāgo pariññāto hoti. Ettha pana tisso pariññā ekapariññā sabbapariññā mūlapariññāti. Katamā ekapariññā? Yo bhikkhu jivhādvāre ekarasataṇhaṃ parijānāti, tena pañcakāmaguṇiko rāgo pariññātova hotīti. Kasmā? Tassāyeva tattha uppajjanato. Sāyeva hi taṇhā cakkhudvāre uppannā rūparāgo [M 2.0102] nāma hoti, sotadvārādīsu uppannā saddarāgādayo. Iti yathā ekasseva corassa pañcamagge hanato ekasmiṃ magge gahetvā sīse chinne pañcapi maggā khemā honti, evaṃ jivhādvāre rasataṇhāya pariññātāya pañcakāmaguṇiko rāgo pariññāto hotīti ayaṃ ekapariññā nāma.

Lust that arises from the five strands of sensual pleasure is fully understood. Here, there are three kinds of full understanding: full understanding of one (ekapariññā), full understanding of all (sabbapariññā), and full understanding of the root (mūlapariññā). What is the full understanding of one? When a bhikkhu fully understands the single craving for taste at the tongue door, the lust that arises from the five strands of sensual pleasure is thereby fully understood. Why? Because that very craving arises there. Indeed, that same craving, when arisen at the eye door, is called lust for forms; when arisen at the ear door and so on, they are called lust for sounds and so forth. Thus, just as when a single thief who robs on five roads is caught and beheaded on one road, all five roads become safe, so too when craving for tastes is fully understood at the tongue door, the lust that arises from the five strands of sensual pleasure is fully understood. This is called the full understanding of one.

Katamā [V 2.0097] sabbapariññā? Patte pakkhittapiṇḍapātasmiñhi ekasmiṃyeva pañcakāmaguṇikarāgo labbhati. Kathaṃ? Parisuddhaṃ tāvassa vaṇṇaṃ olokayato rūparāgo hoti, uṇhe sappimhi tattha āsiñcante paṭapaṭāti saddo uṭṭhahati, tathārūpaṃ khādanīyaṃ vā khādantassa murumurūti saddo uppajjati, taṃ assādayato saddarāgo. Jīrakādivasagandhaṃ assādentassa gandharāgo, sādurasavasena rasarāgo. Mudubhojanaṃ phassavantanti assādayato phoṭṭhabbarāgo. Iti imasmiṃ āhāre satisampajaññena pariggahetvā nicchandarāgaparibhogena paribhutte sabbopi so pariññāto hotīti ayaṃ sabbapariññā nāma.

What is the full understanding of all? In a single portion of almsfood placed in the bowl, lust connected with the five strands of sensual pleasure is found. How? For one looking at its pure color, lust for form arises. When hot ghee is poured on it, a 'paṭapaṭa' sound arises, or when eating such food a 'murumuru' sound arises; for one delighting in that sound, lust for sound arises. For one savoring the fragrance of spices like cumin, lust for smell arises. By means of the delicious taste, lust for taste arises. For one savoring soft food as having a pleasant touch, lust for tactile sensation arises. Thus, when this food is comprehended with mindfulness and clear comprehension, and consumed with a usage free from desire and lust, all of that lust becomes fully understood. This is called the full understanding of all.

Katamā mūlapariññā? Pañcakāmaguṇikarāgassa hi kabaḷīkārāhāro mūlaṃ. Kasmā? Tasmiṃ sati tassuppattito[P 2.0111]. Brāhmaṇatissabhaye kira dvādasa vassāni jāyampatikānaṃ upanijjhānacittaṃ nāma nāhosi. Kasmā? Āhāramandatāya. Bhaye pana vūpasante yojanasatiko tambapaṇṇidīpo dārakānaṃ jātamaṅgalehi ekamaṅgalo ahosi. Iti mūlabhūte āhāre pariññāte pañcakāmaguṇiko rāgo pariññātova hotīti ayaṃ mūlapariññā nāma.

What is the full understanding of the root? Nutriment consisting of morsels of food is indeed the root of lust connected with the five strands of sensual pleasure. Why? Because when that food exists, that lust arises. It is said that during the danger of Brahmin Tissa, for twelve years, married couples had no thought of gazing at each other with desire. Why? Due to the scarcity of food. But when the danger subsided, the island of Tambapaṇṇi, a hundred yojanas in extent, became as one single festival with the birth celebrations of children. Thus, when food, which is the root, is fully understood, the lust connected with the five strands of sensual pleasure is also fully understood. This is called the full understanding of the root.

Natthi taṃ saṃyojananti tena rāgena saddhiṃ pahānekaṭṭhatāya pahīnattā natthi. Evamayaṃ desanā yāva anāgāmimaggā kathitā. “Ettakena pana mā vosānaṃ āpajjiṃsū”ti etesaṃyeva rūpādīnaṃ vasena pañcasu khandhesu vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā yāva arahattā kathetuṃ vaṭṭatīti. Paṭhamāhāro (niṭṭhito).

That fetter does not exist: because it is abandoned, sharing the same state of abandonment with that passion, it does not exist. Thus, this teaching has been explained up to the path of non-returning. But thinking, 'Let them not come to a conclusion with just this much,' it is fitting, having developed insight into the five aggregates by means of these very forms and so on, to speak up to Arahantship. The discourse on the first nutriment is concluded.

Dutiye [M 2.0103] niccammāti khurato paṭṭhāya yāva siṅgamūlā sakalasarīrato uddālitacammā kiṃsukarāsivaṇṇā. Kasmā pana aññaṃ hatthiassagoṇādiupamaṃ agahetvā niccammagāvūpamā gahitāti? Titikkhituṃ asamatthabhāvadīpanatthaṃ. Mātugāmo hi uppannaṃ dukkhavedanaṃ titikkhituṃ adhivāsetuṃ na sakkoti, evameva phassāhāro abalo dubbaloti dassanatthaṃ sadisameva upamaṃ āhari. Kuṭṭanti silākuṭṭādīnaṃ aññataraṃ. Kuṭṭanissitā pāṇā nāma uṇṇanābhisarabūmūsikādayo. Rukkhanissitāti uccāliṅgapāṇakādayo. Udakanissitāti macchasuṃsumārādayo. Ākāsanissitāti ḍaṃsamakasakākakulalādayo. Khādeyyunti luñcitvā khādeyyuṃ. Sā tasmiṃ tasmiṃ ṭhāne taṃ taṃṭhānasannissayamūlikaṃ pāṇakhādanabhayaṃ sampassamānā neva attano [V 2.0098] sakkārasammānaṃ, na piṭṭhiparikammasarīrasambāhanauṇhodakāni icchati, evameva bhikkhu phassāhāramūlakaṃ kilesapāṇakakhādanabhayaṃ sampassamāno tebhūmakaphassena anatthiko hoti.

In the second, 'skinless' means having the skin flayed from the entire body, from the hooves up to the root of the horns, having a color like that of a Kiṃsuka flower. But why was the simile of a skinless cow used, instead of another simile of an elephant, horse, ox, or the like? It was used to show the state of being unable to endure. Indeed, a woman is not able to endure and bear painful feeling that has arisen; in the same way, to show that the nutriment of contact is weak and feeble, a similar simile was brought forth. 'Wall' means one among stone walls and the like. 'Creatures dependent on the wall' are creatures such as spiders, house-lizards, and mice. 'Dependent on trees' means small creatures called uccāliṅga. 'Dependent on water' means water creatures such as fish and porpoises. 'Dependent on the sky' means creatures such as gadflies, mosquitoes, crows, and hawks. 'Would devour' means they would pull off and eat. That cow, seeing in each and every place the danger of being eaten by creatures whose root is dependence on that particular place, desires neither honor nor respect for herself, nor back-rubbing, body-massaging, or warm water. In the same way, a bhikkhu, seeing the danger of being eaten by the creatures of the defilements, which is rooted in the nutriment of contact, has no desire for contact belonging to the three planes.

Phasse, bhikkhave, āhāre pariññāteti tīhi pariññāhi pariññāte. Idhāpi tisso pariññā. Tattha “phasso saṅkhārakkhandho[P 2.0112], taṃsampayuttā vedanā vedanākkhandho, saññā saññākkhandho, cittaṃ viññāṇakkhandho, tesaṃ vatthārammaṇāni rūpakkhandho”ti evaṃ sappaccayassa nāmarūpassa yāthāvato dassanaṃ ñātapariññā. Tattheva tilakkhaṇaṃ āropetvā sattannaṃ anupassanānaṃ vasena aniccādito tulanaṃ tīraṇapariññā. Tasmiṃyeva pana nāmarūpe chandarāganikkaḍḍhano arahattamaggo pahānapariññā. Tisso vedanāti evaṃ phassāhāre tīhi pariññāhi pariññāte tisso vedanā pariññātāva honti tammūlakattā taṃsampayuttattā ca. Iti phassāhāravasena desanā yāva arahattā kathitā. Dutiyāhāro.

“When contact as nutriment, monks, is fully comprehended,” means when it is fully comprehended by the three kinds of full comprehension. Here too, there are three kinds of full comprehension. Among them, the seeing of name-and-form together with its cause as it really is—thus: ‘contact is the aggregate of formations; the feeling associated with it is the aggregate of feeling; perception is the aggregate of perception; consciousness is the aggregate of consciousness; their bases and objects are the aggregate of form’—is full comprehension as knowledge. Applying the three characteristics to that very name-and-form and weighing it as impermanent and so forth by way of the seven contemplations is full comprehension by scrutiny. Furthermore, in that very name-and-form, the path of Arahantship, which eradicates desire and passion, is full comprehension by abandonment. As for ‘the three feelings’: when contact as nutriment is thus fully comprehended by the three kinds of full comprehension, the three feelings are also fully comprehended, because they are rooted in it and associated with it. Thus, by way of contact as nutriment, the teaching has been spoken up to Arahantship. The second nutriment is finished.

Tatiye aṅgārakāsūti aṅgārānaṃ kāsu. Kāsūti rāsipi vuccati āvāṭopi.

In the third, `aṅgārakāsu` means a pit of embers. `Kāsu` is said to be a heap and also a pit.

“Aṅgārakāsuṃ [M 2.0104] apare phuṇanti,

Narā rudantā paridaḍḍhagattā;

Bhayañhi maṃ vindati sūta disvā,

Pucchāmi taṃ mātali devasārathī”ti. (jā. 2.22.462); –

“Others sift a heap of embers, men weeping with their bodies scorched. Having seen this, O charioteer, fear indeed seizes me. I ask you, O Mātali, divine charioteer.”

Ettha rāsi “kāsū”ti vutto.

Here, a heap is called `kāsu`.

“Kinnu santaramānova, kāsuṃ khanasi sārathī”ti? (Jā. 2.22.3). –

“Why, O charioteer, being in such a hurry, do you dig a pit?”

Ettha āvāṭo. Idhāpi ayameva adhippeto. Sādhikaporisāti atirekaporisā pañcaratanappamāṇā. Vītaccikānaṃ vītadhūmānanti etenassa mahāpariḷāhataṃ dasseti. Jālāya vā hi dhūme vā sati vāto samuṭṭhāti, pariḷāho mahā na hoti, tadabhāve vātābhāvato pariḷāho mahā hoti. Ārakāvassāti dūreyeva bhaveyya.

Here, it means a pit. Here too, this very meaning is intended. `Sādhikaporisā` means more than a person's height, the measure of five cubits. By `vītaccikānaṃ vītadhūmānaṃ` [without flame, without smoke], its great heat is shown. For when there is flame or smoke, wind arises, and the heat is not great; in their absence, due to the absence of wind, the heat is great. `Ārakāvassā` means it should be far away indeed.

Evameva [V 2.0099] khoti ettha idaṃ opammasaṃsandanaṃ – aṅgārakāsu viya hi tebhūmakavaṭṭaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Jīvitukāmo puriso viya vaṭṭanissito bālaputhujjano. Dve balavanto purisā viya kusalākusalakammaṃ. Tesaṃ taṃ purisaṃ nānābāhāsu gahetvā aṅgārakāsuṃ upakaḍḍhanakālo viya [P 2.0113] puthujjanassa kammāyūhanakālo. Kammañhi āyūhiyamānameva paṭisandhiṃ ākaḍḍhati nāma. Aṅgārakāsunidānaṃ dukkhaṃ viya kammanidānaṃ vaṭṭadukkhaṃ veditabbaṃ.

“Even so”: here, this is the application of the simile. The round of existence in the three planes should be seen as like the pit of embers. The foolish ordinary person who is dependent on the round should be seen as like a man who wishes to live. Wholesome and unwholesome kamma should be seen as like two strong men. The time of an ordinary person's accumulation of kamma should be seen as like the time when those two men, having seized that man by his various arms, drag him towards the pit of embers. Indeed, kamma, while it is being accumulated, is what is called 'drawing one to rebirth'. The suffering of the round, which has kamma as its cause, should be understood as like the suffering which has the pit of embers as its cause.

Pariññāteti tīhi pariññāhi pariññāte. Pariññāyojanā panettha phasse vuttanayeneva veditabbā. Tisso taṇhāti kāmataṇhā bhavataṇhā vibhavataṇhāti imā pariññātā honti. Kasmā? Taṇhāmūlakattā manosañcetanāya. Na hi hetumhi appahīne phalaṃ pahīyati. Iti manosañcetanāhāravasenapi yāva arahattā desanā kathitā. Tatiyāhāro.

“Is fully comprehended” means when it is fully comprehended by the three kinds of full comprehension. Here, the application of full comprehension should be understood in the same way as stated for contact. As for “the three cravings”: sensual craving, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence—these are fully comprehended. Why? Because mental volition has craving as its root. Indeed, when the cause is not abandoned, the effect is not abandoned. Thus, by way of mental volition as nutriment also, the teaching has been spoken up to Arahantship. The third nutriment is finished.

Catutthe āgucārinti pāpacāriṃ dosakārakaṃ. Kathaṃ so purisoti so puriso kathaṃbhūto, kiṃ yāpeti, na yāpetīti pucchati? Tatheva deva jīvatīti yathā pubbe, idānipi tatheva jīvati.

In the fourth, `āgucāriṃ` means one who does evil, a wrongdoer. By “How is that man?” it is asked: What is that man like? How does he fare? Does he not fare well? “Just so, lord, he lives” means: just as he lived before, so he lives now.

Evameva [M 2.0105] khoti idhāpi idaṃ opammasaṃsandanaṃ – rājā viya hi kammaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ, āgucārī puriso viya vaṭṭasannissito bālaputhujjano, tīṇi sattisatāni viya paṭisandhiviññāṇaṃ, āgucāriṃ purisaṃ “tīhi sattisatehi hanathā”ti raññā āṇattakālo viya kammaraññā vaṭṭasannissitaputhujjanaṃ gahetvā paṭisandhiyaṃ pakkhipanakālo. Tattha kiñcāpi tīṇi sattisatāni viya paṭisandhiviññāṇaṃ, sattīsu pana dukkhaṃ natthi, sattīhi pahaṭavaṇamūlakaṃ dukkhaṃ, evameva paṭisandhiyampi dukkhaṃ natthi, dinnāya pana paṭisandhiyā pavatte vipākadukkhaṃ sattipahaṭavaṇamūlakaṃ dukkhaṃ viya hoti.

“Even so”: here too, this is the application of the simile. Kamma should be seen as like a king. The foolish ordinary person dependent on the round should be seen as like a criminal. Rebirth-consciousness should be seen as like three hundred spears. The time when the king of kamma, having seized the ordinary person dependent on the round, casts him into rebirth should be seen as like the time when the king gives the command, “Strike this criminal with three hundred spears!” There, although rebirth-consciousness is like three hundred spears, there is no suffering in the spears themselves; suffering is rooted in the wound made by the spears. Just so, in rebirth itself there is no suffering; but once rebirth is given, in the course of existence, the suffering of the result occurs, like the suffering rooted in the wound made by the spears.

Pariññāteti tīheva pariññāhi pariññāte. Idhāpi pariññāyojanā phassāhāre vuttanayeneva veditabbā. Nāmarūpanti viññāṇapaccayā nāmarūpaṃ. Viññāṇasmiñhi pariññāte taṃ pariññātameva hoti tammūlakattā sahuppannattā ca. Iti viññāṇāhāravasenapi yāva arahattā desanā kathitāti. Catutthāhāro. Tatiyaṃ.

“Is fully comprehended” means when it is fully comprehended by the three kinds of full comprehension. Here too, the application of full comprehension should be understood in the same way as stated for contact as nutriment. “Name-and-form” means name-and-form conditioned by consciousness. Indeed, when consciousness is fully comprehended, that name-and-form is also fully comprehended, because it has that as its root and arises together with it. Thus, by way of consciousness as nutriment also, the teaching has been spoken up to Arahantship. The fourth nutriment. The third.

4. Atthirāgasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Explanation of the Discourse on the Existence of Lust

64. Catutthe [V 2.0100][P 2.0114] rāgotiādīni lobhasseva nāmāni. So hi rañjanavasena rāgo, nandanavasena nandī, taṇhāyanavasena taṇhāti vuccati. Patiṭṭhitaṃ tattha viññāṇaṃ virūḷhanti kammaṃ javāpetvā paṭisandhiākaḍḍhanasamatthatāya patiṭṭhitañceva virūḷhañca. Yatthāti tebhūmakavaṭṭe bhummaṃ, sabbattha vā purimapurimapade etaṃ bhummaṃ. Atthi tattha saṅkhārānaṃ vuddhīti idaṃ imasmiṃ vipākavaṭṭe ṭhitassa āyativaṭṭahetuke saṅkhāre sandhāya vuttaṃ. Yattha atthi āyatiṃ punabbhavābhinibbattīti yasmiṃ ṭhāne āyatiṃ punabbhavābhinibbatti atthi.

64. In the fourth discourse, terms such as 'lust' (rāga) are simply names for greed (lobha). For it is called 'lust' by way of attachment, 'delight' by way of delighting, and 'craving' by way of thirsting. 'Consciousness, established there, grows' means: consciousness as kamma, having impelled the process, becomes both established and grown through its capability of drawing in rebirth-linking. 'Where' refers to the locative case in the sense of the three-realm round of existence; or, in all such cases, this locative refers to the preceding term. 'There is growth of formations there'—this was said with reference to the formations that are the cause of the future round for one who is established in this present resultant round. 'Where there is future rebirth-manifestation' means: when there is a cause, there is the arising of future rebirth-manifestation.

Evameva khoti ettha idaṃ opammasaṃsandanaṃ – rajakacittakārā viya hi sahakammasambhāraṃ kammaṃ, phalakabhittidussapaṭā viya tebhūmakavaṭṭaṃ. Yathā rajakacittakārā parisuddhesu phalakādīsu rūpaṃ samuṭṭhāpenti, evameva sasambhārakakammaṃ bhavesu rūpaṃ samuṭṭhāpeti. Tattha yathā akusalena cittakārena samuṭṭhāpitaṃ rūpaṃ virūpaṃ hoti dussaṇṭhitaṃ amanāpaṃ, evameva ekacco [M 2.0106] kammaṃ karonto ñāṇavippayuttena cittena karoti, taṃ kammaṃ rūpaṃ samuṭṭhāpentaṃ cakkhādīnaṃ sampattiṃ adatvā dubbaṇṇaṃ dussaṇṭhitaṃ mātāpitūnampi amanāpaṃ rūpaṃ samuṭṭhāpeti. Yathā pana kusalena cittakārena samuṭṭhāpitaṃ rūpaṃ surūpaṃ hoti susaṇṭhitaṃ manāpaṃ, evameva ekacco kammaṃ karonto ñāṇasampayuttena cittena karoti, taṃ kammaṃ rūpaṃ samuṭṭhāpentaṃ cakkhādīnaṃ sampattiṃ datvā suvaṇṇaṃ susaṇṭhitaṃ alaṅkatapaṭiyattaṃ viya rūpaṃ samuṭṭhāpeti.

Similarly, here is the application of the simile: kamma together with its requisites is like dyers and painters, and the three-realm round of existence is like a board, a wall, or a cloth. Just as dyers and painters produce a form on a clean board and so on, even so, kamma with its requisites produces form in states of existence. Therein, just as a form produced by an unskilled painter is deformed, misshapen, and unpleasing, even so, a certain person, when doing kamma, does it with a mind dissociated from wisdom; that kamma, when producing form, without giving the perfection of the eye and so forth, produces a form that is of bad color and misshapen. But just as a form produced by a skilled painter is beautiful, well-shaped, and pleasing, even so, a certain person, when doing kamma, does it with a mind associated with wisdom; that kamma, when producing form, giving the perfection of the eye and so forth, produces a form that is of good color, well-shaped, as if adorned and prepared.

Ettha ca āhāraṃ viññāṇena saddhiṃ saṅkhipitvā āhāranāmarūpānaṃ antare eko sandhi, vipākavidhiṃ nāmarūpena saṅkhipitvā nāmarūpasaṅkhārānaṃ antare eko sandhi, saṅkhārānañca āyatibhavassa ca antare eko sandhīti veditabbo.

And here, it should be understood that by grouping nutriment together with consciousness, there is one connection between nutriment and name-and-form; by grouping the process of result with name-and-form, there is one connection between name-and-form and formations; and there is one connection between formations and future becoming.

Kūṭāgāranti ekakaṇṇikaṃ gāhāpetvā kataṃ agāraṃ. Kūṭāgārasālāti dve kaṇṇike gahetvā katasālā. Evameva khoti ettha khīṇāsavassa kammaṃ sūriyarasmisamaṃ [P 2.0115] veditabbaṃ. Sūriyarasmi pana atthi, sā kevalaṃ patiṭṭhāya abhāvena appatiṭṭhā nāma jātā, khīṇāsavassa kammaṃ natthitāya eva appatiṭṭhaṃ. Tassa hi kāyādayo atthi, tehi pana katakammaṃ kusalākusalaṃ [V 2.0101] nāma na hoti, kiriyamatte ṭhatvā avipākaṃ hoti. Evamassa kammaṃ natthitāya eva appatiṭṭhaṃ nāma jātanti. Catutthaṃ.

A 'peaked house' is a house made by having a single pinnacle installed. A 'peaked hall' is a hall made by taking two pinnacles. Similarly, here the kamma of one whose cankers are destroyed should be understood as being like the sun's rays. The sun's rays exist, but they become called 'unestablished' simply because of the absence of a support. The kamma of one whose cankers are destroyed is 'unestablished' precisely because of its non-existence. For them, the body and so forth exist, but kamma done by these is not called wholesome or unwholesome; remaining in the state of mere action, it is without result. Thus, their kamma becomes called 'unestablished' precisely because of its non-existence. The fourth.

5. Nagarasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Explanation of the Discourse on the City

65. Pañcame nāmarūpe kho sati viññāṇanti ettha “saṅkhāresu sati viññāṇa”nti ca “avijjāya sati saṅkhārā”ti ca vattabbaṃ bhaveyya, tadubhayampi na vuttaṃ. Kasmā? Avijjāsaṅkhārā hi tatiyo bhavo, tehi saddhiṃ ayaṃ vipassanā na ghaṭīyati. Mahāpuriso hi paccuppannapañcavokāravasena abhiniviṭṭhoti.

65. In the fifth discourse, regarding “when there is name-and-form, there is consciousness”—here, it should be said, “when there are formations, there is consciousness,” and “when there is ignorance, there are formations.” But neither of these is stated. Why? Because ignorance and formations are the third becoming, and this insight does not connect with them. For the Great Being was focused on the present five-constituent existence.

Nanu ca avijjāsaṅkhāresu adiṭṭhesu na sakkā buddhena bhavitunti. Saccaṃ na sakkā, iminā pana te bhavaupādānataṇhāvasena diṭṭhāva. Tasmā yathā nāma godhaṃ anubandhanto puriso taṃ kūpaṃ paviṭṭhaṃ disvā otaritvā paviṭṭhaṭṭhānaṃ khaṇitvā godhaṃ gahetvā pakkameyya, na parabhāgaṃ khaneyya[M 2.0107], kasmā? Kassaci natthitāya.
