Evaṃ mahāpurisopi godhaṃ anubandhanto puriso viya bodhipallaṅke nisinno jarāmaraṇato paṭṭhāya “imassa ayaṃ paccayo, imassa ayaṃ paccayo”ti pariyesanto yāva nāmarūpadhammānaṃ paccayaṃ disvā tassapi paccayaṃ pariyesanto viññāṇameva addasa. Tato “ettako pañcavokārabhavavasena sammasanacāro”ti vipassanaṃ paṭinivattesi, parato tucchakūpassa abhinnaṭṭhānaṃ viya avijjāsaṅkhāradvayaṃ atthi, tadetaṃ heṭṭhā vipassanāya gahitattā pāṭiyekkaṃ sammasanūpagaṃ na hotīti na aggahesi.

But is it not so that if ignorance and formations are unseen, one cannot become a Buddha? Truly, one cannot. However, by this one, they were indeed seen by way of becoming, clinging, and craving. Therefore, just as a man pursuing a monitor lizard, seeing it enter a burrow, would descend, dig where it entered, catch the monitor lizard, and depart, not digging in the other part—why? Because there is nothing to be done there. So too the Great Being, seated on the Bodhi-throne, like the man pursuing the monitor lizard, starting from aging and death and searching, “This is the condition for this,” saw the condition for the phenomena of name-and-form, and searching for its condition, saw only consciousness. Then, thinking, “This much is the range of contemplation by way of the five-constituent existence,” he turned back the insight. Beyond that, like the undug part of an empty burrow, the pair of ignorance and formations exists; but because it was grasped by insight previously, he did not take it up, thinking, ‘It does not become subject to separate contemplation.’

Paccudāvattatīti paṭinivattati. Katamaṃ panettha viññāṇaṃ paccudāvattatīti? Paṭisandhiviññāṇampi vipassanāviññāṇampi. Tattha paṭisandhiviññāṇaṃ paccayato paṭinivattati, vipassanāviññāṇaṃ ārammaṇato. Ubhayampi nāmarūpaṃ nātikkamati, nāmarūpato paraṃ na gacchati. Ettāvatā jāyetha vātiādīsu viññāṇe nāmarūpassa paccaye honte, nāmarūpe viññāṇassa paccaye honte, dvīsupi aññamaññapaccayesu [P 2.0116] hontesu ettakena jāyetha vā upapajjetha vā. Ito hi paraṃ kimaññaṃ jāyetha vā upapajjetha vā, nanu etadeva jāyati ca upapajjati cāti?

“It turns back” means it returns. What consciousness turns back here? Both rebirth-linking consciousness and insight consciousness. Therein, rebirth-linking consciousness turns back from its condition, and insight consciousness turns back from its object. Both do not transcend name-and-form; they do not go beyond name-and-form. In such phrases as, “To this extent one might be born,” the meaning is: with consciousness being a condition for name-and-form, and name-and-form being a condition for consciousness, when both are mutual conditions, by this much one might be born or come into existence. For beyond this, what else would be born or come into existence? Is it not so that just this is what is born and comes into existence?

Evaṃ [V 2.0102] saddhiṃ aparāparacutipaṭisandhīhi pañca padāni dassetvā puna taṃ ettāvatāti vuttamatthaṃ niyyātento yadidaṃ nāmarūpapaccayā viññāṇaṃ, viññāṇapaccayā nāmarūpanti vatvā tato paraṃ anulomapaccayākāravasena viññāṇapaccayā nāmarūpamūlakaṃ āyatijarāmaraṇaṃ dassetuṃ nāmarūpapaccayā saḷāyatanantiādimāha.

Thus, having shown the five terms together with successive deaths and rebirth-linkings, then, while delivering the meaning stated as “to this extent”—that is, having again said, “with name-and-form as condition, consciousness comes to be; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form comes to be”—he then, by way of the conditional structure in forward order, in order to show future aging-and-death which is rooted in name-and-form conditioned by consciousness, said, “with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases come to be,” and so on.

Añjasanti maggasseva vevacanaṃ. Uddhāpavantanti āpato uggatattā uddhāpanti laddhavohārena pākāravatthunā samannāgataṃ. Ramaṇīyanti samantā catunnaṃ dvārānaṃ abbhantare ca nānābhaṇḍānaṃ sampattiyā ramaṇīyaṃ. Māpehīti mahājanaṃ pesetvā vāsaṃ kārehi. Māpeyyāti vāsaṃ kāreyya. Kārento ca paṭhamaṃ aṭṭhārasa manussakoṭiyo pesetvā “sampuṇṇa”nti pucchitvā “na tāva sampuṇṇa”nti vutte aparāni pañcakulāni peseyya. Puna pucchitvā “na tāva sampuṇṇa”nti vutte aparāni pañcapaññāsakulāni peseyya. Puna pucchitvā “na tāva sampuṇṇa”nti vutte aparāni tiṃsa [M 2.0108] kulāni peseyya. Puna pucchitvā “na tāva sampuṇṇa”nti vutte aparaṃ kulasahassaṃ peseyya. Puna pucchitvā “na tāva sampuṇṇa”nti vutte aparāni ekādasanahutāni kulāni peseyya. Puna pucchitvā “na tāva sampuṇṇa”nti vutte aparāni caturāsītikulasahassāni peseyya. Puna “sampuṇṇa”nti pucchite, “mahārāja, kiṃ vadesi? Mahantaṃ nagaraṃ asambādhaṃ, iminā nayena kulāni pesetvā na sakkā pūretuṃ, bheriṃ pana carāpetvā ‘amhākaṃ nagaraṃ imāya ca imāya ca sampattiyā sampannaṃ, ye tattha vasitukāmā, yathāsukhaṃ gacchantu, imañcimañca parihāraṃ labhissantī’ti nagarassa ceva vaṇṇaṃ lokassa ca parihāralābhaṃ ghosāpethā”ti vadeyya. So evaṃ kareyya. Tato manussā nagaraguṇañceva parihāralābhañca sutvā sabbadisāhi samosaritvā nagaraṃ pūreyyuṃ. Taṃ aparena samayena [P 2.0117] iddhañceva assa phītañca. Taṃ sandhāya tadassa nagaraṃ aparena samayena iddhañceva phītañcātiādi vuttaṃ.

The word `añjasa` is a synonym for `magga` (path). The word `uddhāpavanta` refers to something endowed with a rampart, so called by common usage because it is raised up from the water [of a moat]. `Ramaṇīya` means delightful due to the abundance of various goods both inside and around the four gates. `Māpehi` means: sending the populace, have them establish a dwelling. `Māpeyya` means: one should establish a dwelling. And in so doing, he would first send eighteen crores of people and ask, “Is it full?” When told, “Not yet full,” he would send another five families. Again asking, and when told, “Not yet full,” he would send another fifty-five families. Again asking, and when told, “Not yet full,” he would send another thirty families. Again asking, and when told, “Not yet full,” he would send another thousand families. Again asking, and when told, “Not yet full,” he would send another eleven nahutas (110,000) of families. Again asking, and when told, “Not yet full,” he would send another eighty-four thousand families. When asked again, “Is it full?” they would say, “O great king, what are you saying? The city is great and not crowded. It is not possible to fill it by sending families in this way. Rather, have a drum beaten and proclaim: ‘Our city is endowed with this and that prosperity. Whoever wishes to dwell there, let them go as they please. They will receive this and that privilege.’ Thus, announce the city’s quality and the people’s gain of privilege.” He would do so. Then, hearing of the city’s quality and the gain of privilege, people would gather from all directions and fill the city. In time, it would become prosperous and flourishing. With reference to this, it was said: ‘That city in time became prosperous and flourishing,’ and so on.

Tattha iddhanti samiddhaṃ subhikkhaṃ. Phītanti sabbasampattīhi pupphitaṃ. Bāhujaññanti bahūhi ñātabbaṃ, bahujanānaṃ hitaṃ vā. “Bahujana”ntipi pāṭho. Ākiṇṇamanussanti manussehi ākiṇṇaṃ nirantaraṃ phuṭṭhaṃ. Vuḍḍhivepullappattanti vuḍḍhippattañceva vepullappattañca, seṭṭhabhāvañceva vipulabhāvañca pattaṃ, dasasahassacakkavāḷe agganagaraṃ jātanti attho.

Therein, `iddha` means prosperous and well-supplied with food. `Phīta` means flourishing with all kinds of prosperity. `Bāhujañña` means known by many, or beneficial to many people. There is also the reading `bahujana`. `Ākiṇṇamanussa` means crowded with people, continuously filled and teeming. `Vuḍḍhivepullappatta` means having attained growth and expansion, having reached both an excellent state and an extensive state; the meaning is that it became the chief city in the ten-thousandfold world-system.

Evameva [V 2.0103] khoti ettha idaṃ opammasaṃsandanaṃ – araññapavane caramānapuriso viya hi dīpaṅkarapādamūlato paṭṭhāya pāramiyo pūrayamāno mahāpuriso daṭṭhabbo, tassa purisassa pubbakehi manussehi anuyātamaggadassanaṃ viya mahāsattassa anupubbena bodhipallaṅke nisinnassa pubbabhāge aṭṭhaṅgikassa vipassanāmaggassa dassanaṃ, purisassa taṃ ekapadikamaggaṃ anugacchato aparabhāge mahāmaggadassanaṃ viya mahāsattassa uparivipassanāya ciṇṇante lokuttaramaggadassanaṃ, purisassa teneva maggena gacchato purato nagaradassanaṃ viya tathāgatassa nibbānanagaradassanaṃ, bahinagaraṃ panettha aññena diṭṭhaṃ, aññena manussavāsaṃ kataṃ, nibbānanagaraṃ satthā sayameva passi, sayaṃ vāsamakāsi. Tassa purisassa catunnaṃ dvārānaṃ diṭṭhakālo viya tathāgatassa catunnaṃ maggānaṃ diṭṭhakālo, tassa catūhi dvārehi nagaraṃ paviṭṭhakālo viya tathāgatassa catūhi maggehi [M 2.0109] nibbānaṃ paviṭṭhakālo, tassa nagarabbhantare bhaṇḍavavatthānakālo viya tathāgatassa paccavekkhaṇañāṇena paropaṇṇāsakusaladhammavavatthānakālo. Nagarassa agārakaraṇatthaṃ kulapariyesanakālo viya satthu phalasamāpattito vuṭṭhāya veneyyasatte volokanakālo, tena purisena yācitassa rañño ekaṃ mahākuṭumbikaṃ diṭṭhakālo viya mahābrahmunā yācitassa bhagavato aññāsikoṇḍaññattheraṃ diṭṭhakālo, rañño mahākuṭumbikaṃ pakkosāpetvā “nagaravāsaṃ karohī”ti pahitakālo [P 2.0118] viya bhagavato ekasmiṃ pacchābhatte aṭṭhārasayojanamaggaṃ gantvā āsāḷhipuṇṇamadivase bārāṇasiyaṃ isipatanaṃ pavisitvā theraṃ kāyasakkhiṃ katvā dhammaṃ desitakālo, mahākuṭumbikena aṭṭhārasa purisakoṭiyo gahetvā nagaraṃ ajjhāvuṭṭhakālo viya tathāgatena dhammacakke pavattite therassa aṭṭhārasahi brahmakoṭīhi saddhiṃ sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhitakālo, evaṃ nibbānanagaraṃ paṭhamaṃ āvāsitaṃ, tato sampuṇṇaṃ nagaranti pucchitvā na tāvāti vutte pañca kulāni ādiṃ katvā yāva caturāsītikulasahassapesanaṃ viya tathāgatassa pañcamadivasato paṭṭhāya anattalakkhaṇasuttādīni desetvā pañcavaggiye ādiṃ katvā yasapamukhā pañcapaṇṇāsa kulaputtā, tiṃsa bhaddavaggiyā, sahassapurāṇajaṭilā, bimbisārapamukhāni ekādasapurisanahutāni, tirokuṭṭānumodane caturāsītisahassānīti ettakassa janassa ariyamaggaṃ otāretvā nibbānanagaraṃ pesitakālo, atha tena nayena nagare apūriyamāne bheriṃ carāpetvā nagarassa vaṇṇaghosanaṃ kulānaṃ parihāralābhaghosanaṃ viya ca māsassa aṭṭha divase tattha tattha nisīditvā dhammakathikānaṃ nibbānavaṇṇassa ceva nibbānappattānaṃ jātikantārādinittharaṇānisaṃsassa ca ghosanaṃ, tato sabbadisāhi āgantvā manussānaṃ nagarasamosaraṇaṃ viya tattha tattha dhammakathaṃ sutvā [V 2.0104] tato tato nikkhamitvā pabbajjaṃ ādiṃ katvā anulomapaṭipadaṃ paṭipannānaṃ aparimāṇānaṃ kulaputtānaṃ nibbānasamosaraṇaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ.

In the same way, here is the connection of the simile. Just as a man wandering in a forest wilderness should be seen as the Great Being fulfilling the perfections starting from the feet of the Buddha Dīpaṅkara, so too should the following be seen: the sight of the path followed by previous people for that man is like the sight of the eight-factored path of insight for the Great Being seated gradually on the Bodhi-throne in his earlier stage; the sight of the great path for that man following that single-footpath in his later stage is like the sight of the supramundane path for the Great Being at the culmination of practicing with higher insight; the sight of the city ahead for that man traveling by that very path is like the sight of the city of Nibbāna for the Tathāgata. However, in this simile, the outer city was seen by another, and the human settlement was made by another, but the city of Nibbāna was seen by the Teacher himself; he himself made it his dwelling. The time when that man saw the four gates is like the time when the Tathāgata saw the four paths. The time when that man entered the city through the four gates is like the time when the Tathāgata entered Nibbāna through the four paths. The time when that man determined the goods inside the city is like the time when the Tathāgata determined the more than fifty wholesome qualities through reviewing knowledge. The time when that man sought families for building houses in the city is like the time when the Teacher, having emerged from fruition attainment, surveyed beings fit to be taught. The time when that man saw a great householder of the king who had been requested by him is like the time when the Blessed One, who had been requested by Mahā Brahmā, saw the Elder Aññāsikoṇḍañña. The time when the king summoned the great householder and sent him, saying, “Establish the city’s settlement,” is like the time when the Blessed One, after traveling eighteen yojanas in one afternoon, entered Isipatana in Bārāṇasī on the full moon day of Āsāḷha and, making the Elder a bodily witness, taught the Dhamma. The time when the great householder, having taken eighteen crores of men, inhabited the city is like the time when, after the Tathāgata set the Wheel of Dhamma in motion, the Elder became established in the fruit of stream-entry along with eighteen crores of Brahmās. Thus, the city of Nibbāna was first inhabited. Then, when asked whether the city was full, and it was said, “Not yet,” the sending of up to eighty-four thousand families, beginning with five families, is like the time when the Tathāgata, starting from the fifth day, taught the Anattalakkhaṇa Sutta and others, beginning with the group of five, then fifty-five clansmen led by Yasa, the thirty Bhaddavaggiyā, the thousand former matted-hair ascetics, eleven myriads of men led by Bimbisāra, and eighty-four thousand beings during the dedication of merit of the Tirokuṭṭa Sutta, and having guided such a multitude to the noble path, sent them to the city of Nibbāna. Then, when the city was still not filled in that way, having a drum beaten to proclaim the city’s renown and the gain of privileges for the families is like the proclamation by the Dhamma-preachers, sitting in various places on the eight days of the month, of the praise of Nibbāna and the benefit of crossing over the wilderness of birth, etc., for those who have attained Nibbāna. Thereafter, the gathering of people in the city, having come from all directions, is like the gathering in Nibbāna of immeasurable clansmen who, after hearing the Dhamma talk in various places, went forth from those various places, beginning with ordination, and undertook the progressive practice. This is how it should be seen.

Purāṇaṃ magganti ariyaṃ aṭṭhaṅgikaṃ maggaṃ. Ayañhi ariyamaggo pavāraṇasutte (saṃ. ni. 1.215) avattamānakaṭṭhena “anuppannamaggo”ti vutto, imasmiṃ sutte avaḷañjanaṭṭhena “purāṇamaggo”ti. Brahmacariyanti sikkhattayasaṅgahaṃ sakalasāsanaṃ. Iddhanti jhānassādena [M 2.0110] samiddhaṃ subhikkhaṃ. Phītanti abhiññābharaṇehi pupphitaṃ. Vitthārikanti vitthiṇṇaṃ. Bāhujaññanti bahujanaviññeyyaṃ. Yāva devamanussehi [P 2.0119] suppakāsitanti yāva dasasahassacakkavāḷe devamanussehi paricchedo atthi, etasmiṃ antare suppakāsitaṃ sudesitaṃ tathāgatenāti. Pañcamaṃ.

‘The ancient path’ means the Noble Eightfold Path. Indeed, this Noble Path is called ‘the unarisen path’ in the Pavāraṇā Sutta (Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.215) in the sense of not being in operation, while in this sutta it is called ‘the ancient path’ in the sense of not being used. ‘The holy life’ means the entire teaching, which is comprised of the threefold training. ‘Flourishing’ means it is prosperous and has abundant provisions through the taste of jhāna. ‘Thriving’ means it is blossomed with the ornaments of the higher knowledges. ‘Widespread’ means extensive. ‘Known by many’ means knowable by many people. ‘Well-proclaimed among devas and humans’ means that insofar as there is a demarcation of devas and humans in the ten-thousandfold world system, within that realm it is well-proclaimed and well-taught by the Tathāgata. Fifth.

6. Sammasasuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Sammasa Sutta

66. Chaṭṭhe āmantesīti kasmā āmantesi? Yasmāssa sukhumā tilakkhaṇāhatā dhammadesanā upaṭṭhāsi. Tasmiṃ kira janapade manussā sahetukā paññavanto. Siniddhāni kirettha bhojanāni, tānisevato janassa paññā vaḍḍhati, te gambhīraṃ tilakkhaṇāhataṃ dhammakathaṃ paṭivijjhituṃ samatthā honti. Teneva bhagavā dīghamajjhimesu mahāsatipaṭṭhānāni (dī. ni. 2.372 ādayo) mahānidānaṃ (dī. ni. 2.95 ādayo), āneñjasappāyaṃ (ma. ni. 3.66 ādayo), saṃyuttake cūḷanidānādisuttanti evamādīni aññāni gambhīrāni suttāni tattheva kathesi. Sammasatha noti sammasatha nu. Antaraṃ sammasanti abbhantaraṃ paccayasammasanaṃ. Na so bhikkhu bhagavato cittaṃ ārādhesīti paccayākāravasena byākārāpetukāmassa bhagavato tathā abyākaritvā dvattiṃsākāravasena byākaronto ajjhāsayaṃ gahetuṃ nāsakkhi.

66. In the sixth, regarding ‘he addressed them’: why did he address them? Because a subtle Dhamma discourse, marked by the three characteristics, presented itself to him. It is said that in that region, the people were endowed with a wholesome cause and were wise. The food there was rich, and for the people who partook of it, wisdom grew, and they became capable of penetrating profound Dhamma talks marked by the three characteristics. For this very reason, the Blessed One taught there other profound suttas such as, in the Dīgha and Majjhima Nikāyas: the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna (Dīgha Nikāya 2.372 ff.), the Mahānidāna (Dīgha Nikāya 2.95 ff.), the Āneñjasappāya (Majjhima Nikāya 3.66 ff.); and in the Saṃyutta Nikāya: the Cūḷanidāna Sutta and others. ‘Sammasatha no’ means ‘sammasatha nu’ (Do you examine?). ‘Examine internally’ means the internal examination of conditions. ‘That monk did not please the Blessed One’s mind’ means: because the Blessed One wished to have it explained in terms of conditionality, that monk, without explaining it in that way, explained it in terms of the thirty-two parts of the body and was not able to grasp his intention.

Etadavocāti desanā yathānusandhiṃ na gatā, desanāya yathānusandhigamanatthaṃ etadavoca. Tenahānanda, suṇāthāti idaṃ tepiṭake buddhavacane asambhinnapadaṃ. Aññattha hi evaṃ vuttaṃ nāma natthi. Upadhinidānanti khandhupadhinidānaṃ. Khandhapañcakañhettha upadhīti adhippetaṃ. Uppajjatīti jāyati. Nivisatīti punappunaṃ pavattivasena patiṭṭhahati.

‘Etadavoca’ (He said this): The discourse did not proceed according to its sequence; to make the discourse proceed according to its sequence, this was said. ‘Tenāhānanda, suṇātha’ (Therefore, Ānanda, listen): This is an uninterrupted phrase in the word of the Buddha in the Tipiṭaka. Indeed, a statement spoken in this way is not found elsewhere. ‘Upadhinidānaṃ’ (With upadhi as condition): The condition is the upadhi of the aggregates. For here, the five aggregates are intended as ‘upadhi’. ‘Uppajjati’ (It arises): It is born. ‘Nivisati’ (It settles): It is established by way of occurring again and again.

Yaṃ kho loke piyarūpaṃ sātarūpanti yaṃ lokasmiṃ piyasabhāvañceva madhurasabhāvañca. Cakkhuṃ loketiādīsu [V 2.0105] lokasmiñhi cakkhādīsu mamattena abhiniviṭṭhā sattā sampattiyaṃ patiṭṭhitā attano cakkhuṃ ādāsādīsu nimittaggahaṇānusārena vippasannapañcapasādaṃ suvaṇṇavimāne ugghāṭitamaṇisīhapañjaraṃ viya maññanti, sotaṃ rajatapanāḷikaṃ viya pāmaṅgasuttaṃ [P 2.0120] viya [M 2.0111] ca maññanti, tuṅganāsāti laddhavohāraṃ ghānaṃ vaṭṭetvā ṭhapitaharitālavaṭṭiṃ viya maññanti, jivhaṃ rattakambalapaṭalaṃ viya mudusiniddhamadhurarasadaṃ maññanti, kāyaṃ sālalaṭṭhiṃ viya suvaṇṇatoraṇaṃ viya ca maññanti, manaṃ aññesaṃ manena asadisaṃ uḷāraṃ maññanti.

‘That in the world which is pleasing and agreeable’ means whatever in the world has the nature of being dear and the nature of being sweet. Regarding ‘the eye in the world,’ etc., beings in the world, attached to the eye and other senses with possessiveness and established in their attainments, regard their own eye—a very clear sense faculty, according to their grasping of signs in mirrors and so forth—like an opened jeweled lion-window in a golden mansion. They regard the ear like a silver tube or a plumb line. The nose, which has received the designation ‘high-bridged,’ they regard like a stick of orpiment that has been rounded and placed. The tongue, which gives a soft, smooth, and sweet taste, they regard like a surface of red wool blanket. The body they regard like a sal tree trunk or a golden archway. The mind they regard as incomparable with the minds of others, and lofty.

Niccato addakkhunti niccanti addasaṃsu. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo. Na parimucciṃsu dukkhasmāti sakalasmāpi vaṭṭadukkhā na parimucciṃsu. Dakkhissantīti passissanti. Āpānīyakaṃsoti sarakassa nāmaṃ. Yasmā panettha āpaṃ pivanti, tasmā “āpānīyo”ti vuccati. Āpānīyo ca so kaṃso cāti āpānīyakaṃso. Surāmaṇḍasarakassetaṃ nāmaṃ. “Vaṇṇasampanno”tiādivacanato pana kaṃse ṭhitapānameva evaṃ vuttaṃ. Ghammābhitattoti ghammena abhitatto. Ghammaparetoti ghammena phuṭṭho, anugatoti attho. Pivato hi kho taṃ chādessatīti pivantassa taṃ pānīyaṃ vaṇṇādisampattiyā ruccissati, sakalasarīraṃ vā pharitvā tuṭṭhiṃ uppādayamānaṃ ṭhassati. Appaṭisaṅkhāti apaccavekkhitvā.

‘Niccato addakkhuṃ’ (They saw as permanent): They saw it as permanent. The same method applies to the remaining phrases. ‘Na parimucciṃsu dukkhasmā’ (They were not freed from suffering): They were not freed from all the suffering of the cycle of existence. ‘Dakkhissanti’ (They will see): They will perceive. ‘Āpānīyakaṃso’: This is the name for a small drinking cup. Because they drink water (āpaṃ) here, it is called ‘āpānīya’. It is both a drinkable (āpānīya) and a bowl (kaṃso), thus it is ‘āpānīyakaṃso’. This is the name for a small cup of clear liquor. However, from the statement ‘endowed with color,’ etc., it is the liquor mixed with poison standing in the bronze bowl that is spoken of thus. ‘Ghammābhitatto’ (Afflicted by heat): Afflicted by heat. ‘Ghammapareto’ (Overcome by heat): Touched by heat, followed by it; this is the meaning. ‘Pivato hi taṃ chādessati’ (For one who drinks, it will be pleasing): For the one who drinks, it will be pleasing due to its perfection of color, etc., or it will stand pervading the entire body, causing satisfaction. ‘Appaṭisaṅkhā’ (Without reflection): Without having reflected.

Evameva khoti ettha idaṃ opammasaṃsandanaṃ – āpānīyakaṃso viya hi loke piyarūpaṃ sātarūpaṃ ārammaṇaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ, ghammābhitattapuriso viya vaṭṭanissito puthujjano, āpānīyakaṃsena nimantanapuriso viya loke piyarūpena sātarūpena ārammaṇena nimantakajano, āpānīyakaṃse sampattiñca ādīnavañca ārocento āpānakamanusso viya ācariyupajjhāyādiko kalyāṇamitto. Yatheva hi tassa purisassa apalokitamanusso āpānīyakaṃse guṇañca ādīnavañca āroceti, evameva ācariyo vā upajjhāyo vā bhikkhuno pañcasu kāmaguṇesu assādañca nissaraṇañca katheti.

‘Evameva kho’ (Just so): Herein, this application of the simile should be understood. An object in the world that is pleasing and agreeable should be seen as like the bowl of liquor mixed with poison. An ordinary person who is dependent on the cycle of existence should be seen as like the man afflicted by heat. A person who invites with a pleasing and agreeable object in the world should be seen as like the man who invites with the bowl of liquor mixed with poison. A good friend, such as a teacher or preceptor, should be seen as like the man at the drinking place who explains the good qualities and the dangers of the bowl of liquor mixed with poison. For just as the man who is consulted explains to that person both the good qualities and the dangers in the bowl of liquor mixed with poison, just so a teacher or preceptor speaks to a monk on the gratification and the escape in the five strands of sensual pleasure.

Tattha yathā āpānīyakaṃsamhi guṇe ca ādīnave ca ārocite so [P 2.0121] puriso piyavaṇṇādisampadāyameva sañjātavego “sace maraṇaṃ bhavissati, pacchā jānissāmī”ti sahasā appaṭisaṅkhāya taṃ pivitvā maraṇaṃ vā maraṇamattaṃ vā dukkhaṃ nigacchati, evameva, bhikkhu, “pañcasu kāmaguṇesu dassanādivasena uppannasomanassamattameva assādo, ādīnavo pana [V 2.0106] diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyiko bahu nānappakāro, appassādā kāmā bahudukkhā bahupāyāsā”ti [M 2.0112] evaṃ ācariyupajjhāyehi ānisaṃsañca ādīnavañca kathetvā – “samaṇapaṭipadaṃ paṭipajja, indriyesu guttadvāro bhava bhojane mattaññū jāgariyaṃ anuyutto”ti evaṃ ovaditopi assādabaddhacittatāya “sace vuttappakāro ādīnavo bhavissati, pacchā jānissāmī”ti ācariyupajjhāye apasādetvā uddesaparipucchādīni ceva vattapaṭipattiñca pahāya lokāmisakathaṃ kathento kāme paribhuñjitukāmatāya sikkhaṃ paccakkhāya hīnāyāvattati. Tato duccaritāni pūrento sandhicchedanādikāle “coro aya”nti gahetvā rañño dassito idheva hatthapādādichedanaṃ patvā samparāye catūsu apāyesu mahādukkhaṃ anubhoti.

Therein, just as when, after the good qualities and the dangers in the bowl of liquor mixed with poison have been explained, that person—in whom a strong impulse has arisen solely due to its perfection of pleasing color and so on—without reflecting, hastily drinks it, thinking, ‘If death is to be, I will know it later,’ and thereby comes to death or to suffering equivalent to death; just so, a monk, although instructed by teachers and preceptors that ‘in the five strands of sensual pleasure, the gratification is merely the joy that has arisen by way of seeing and so on, while the danger, present and future, is manifold and various; sensual pleasures have little gratification, much suffering, much despair,’ and although advised thus: ‘Undertake the practice of a recluse, be one whose sense-doors are guarded, be moderate in eating, be devoted to wakefulness,’ due to his mind being bound to gratification, he thinks, ‘If the danger spoken of is to be, I will know it later.’ Disparaging his teachers and preceptors, abandoning recitation, questioning, and the practice of the duties, he speaks worldly talk and, from a desire to enjoy sensual pleasures, he renounces the training and reverts to the low life. Then, while fulfilling evil deeds, at a time of housebreaking or the like, he is seized as ‘a thief’ and shown to the king. Right here he arrives at the cutting off of hands and feet, and in the next life, he experiences great suffering in the four states of deprivation.

Pānīyena vā vinetunti sītena vārinā harituṃ. Dadhimaṇḍakenāti dadhimaṇḍanamattena. Bhaṭṭhaloṇikāyāti saloṇena sattupānīyena. Loṇasovīrakenāti sabbadhaññaphalakaḷīrādīni pakkhipitvā loṇasovīrakaṃ nāma karonti, tena.

‘Pānīyena vā vinetuṃ’ (Or to dispel it with a drink): To remove it with cool water. ‘Dadhimaṇḍakena’ (With whey): With mere whey. ‘Bhaṭṭhaloṇikāya’ (With salted roasted-flour drink): With a drink of roasted grain-flour with salt. ‘Loṇasovīrakena’ (With salt-sour gruel): They make what is called loṇasovīraka by adding all kinds of grains, fruits, shoots, and so on; with that.

Opammasaṃsandanaṃ panettha – ghammābhitattapuriso viya vaṭṭasannissitakāle yogāvacaro daṭṭhabbo, tassa purisassa paṭisaṅkhā āpānīyakaṃsaṃ pahāya pānīyādīhi pipāsassa vinodanaṃ viya bhikkhuno ācariyupajjhāyānaṃ ovāde ṭhatvā chadvārādīni pariggahetvā anukkamena vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhentassa arahattaphalādhigamo, pānīyādīni cattāri pānāni viya hi cattāro maggā, tesu aññataraṃ pivitvā surāpipāsitaṃ vinodetvā sukhino yena kāmaṃ gamanaṃ viya khīṇāsavassa catumaggapānaṃ pivitvā taṇhaṃ vinodetvā agatapubbaṃ nibbānadisaṃ gamanakālo veditabbo. Chaṭṭhaṃ.

Herein, as for the application of the simile: The practitioner of meditation should be seen as like the man afflicted by heat at the time when he is dependent on the cycle of existence. That man’s reflection—having abandoned the bowl of liquor mixed with poison and dispelled his thirst with drinks such as water—is like the attainment of the fruit of Arahantship by a monk who, abiding in the advice of his teachers and preceptors, has taken control of the six doors and so on, and has gradually developed insight. For the four paths are like the four drinks beginning with water. Just as, having drunk one of them and dispelled the thirst for liquor, being happy, one goes wherever one wishes, so too should be understood the time of going to the previously unreached direction of Nibbāna for one whose taints are destroyed, who has drunk the drink of the four paths and dispelled the thirst which is craving. The sixth is finished.

7. Naḷakalāpīsuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Naḷakalāpī Sutta

67. Sattame [P 2.0122] kinnu kho, āvusoti kasmā pucchati? “Evaṃ puṭṭho kathaṃ nu kho byākareyyā”ti. Therassa ajjhāsayajānanatthaṃ. Apica atīte dve aggasāvakā imaṃ pañhaṃ vinicchayiṃsūti anāgate bhikkhū jānissantītipi pucchati. Idāneva kho mayanti idaṃ thero yassa nāmarūpassa viññāṇaṃ paccayoti vuttaṃ, tadeva nāmarūpaṃ viññāṇassa paccayoti [M 2.0113] vuttattā āha[V 2.0107]. Naḷakalāpiyoti idha pana ayakalāpādivasena upamaṃ anāharitvā viññāṇanāmarūpānaṃ abaladubbalabhāvadassanatthaṃ ayaṃ upamā ābhatā.

67. In the seventh sutta, why does he ask, ‘What indeed, friend?’ It is with the thought, ‘Being asked thus, how indeed would he answer?’ for the purpose of knowing the Elder’s intention. Moreover, he also asks with the thought, ‘In the past, the two chief disciples resolved this question; thus, in the future, the monks will know.’ The Elder said this—‘Just now, indeed, we...’—because it was stated that consciousness is a condition for that name-and-form, and that very name-and-form was stated to be a condition for consciousness. Regarding ‘like a sheaf of reeds,’ here, however, without bringing a simile by way of a bundle of iron or the like, this simile was brought forth to show the powerless and weak state of consciousness and name-and-form.

Nirodho hotīti ettake ṭhāne paccayuppannapañcavokārabhavavasena desanā kathitā. Chattiṃsāya vatthūhīti heṭṭhā vissajjitesu dvādasasu padesu ekekasmiṃ tiṇṇaṃ tiṇṇaṃ vasena chattiṃsāya kāraṇehi. Ettha ca paṭhamo dhammakathikaguṇo, dutiyā paṭipatti, tatiyaṃ paṭipattiphalaṃ. Tattha paṭhamanayena desanāsampatti kathitā, dutiyena sekkhabhūmi, tatiyena asekkhabhūmīti. Sattamaṃ.

‘Cessation occurs’—in this much of the text, the teaching is stated by way of the five-aggregate existence that has arisen from conditions. By ‘thirty-six grounds’ is meant by thirty-six reasons, by way of three rounds each in each of the twelve sections that were explained below. And here, the first is the quality of the Dhamma-preacher, the second is the practice, the third is the fruit of the practice. Therein, by the first method, the accomplishment of the teaching is stated; by the second, the plane of the trainee; by the third, the plane of the non-trainee. The seventh is finished.

8. Kosambisuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Kosambī Sutta

68. Aṭṭhame aññatrevāti ekacco hi parassa saddahitvā yaṃ esa bhaṇati, taṃ bhūtanti gaṇhāti. Aparassa nisīditvā cintentassa yaṃ kāraṇaṃ ruccati, so “atthi eta”nti ruciyā gaṇhāti. Eko “cirakālato paṭṭhāya evaṃ anussavo atthi, bhūtameta”nti anussavena gaṇhāti. Aññassa vitakkayato ekaṃ kāraṇaṃ upaṭṭhāti, so “attheta”nti ākāraparivitakkena gaṇhāti. Aparassa cintayato ekā diṭṭhi uppajjati, yāyassa taṃ kāraṇaṃ nijjhāyantassa khamati, so “attheta”nti diṭṭhinijjhānakkhantiyā gaṇhāti. Thero pana pañcapi etāni kāraṇāni paṭikkhipitvā paccakkhañāṇena paṭividdhabhāvaṃ pucchanto aññatreva, āvuso musila, saddhāyātiādimāha. Tattha aññatrevāti saddhādīni kāraṇāni ṭhapetvā, vinā etehi [P 2.0123] kāraṇehīti attho. Bhavanirodho nibbānanti pañcakkhandhanirodho nibbānaṃ.

8. In the eighth sutta, regarding ‘apart from...’: Indeed, a certain person, having faith in another, accepts what that person says as true. For another, while sitting and thinking, a reason is pleasing, so he accepts it by way of inclination, thinking, ‘This exists.’ One person accepts by way of oral tradition, thinking, ‘From a long time ago, there has been such an oral tradition; this is true.’ For another who is reasoning, a certain reason occurs, so he accepts it by way of reasoned consideration, thinking, ‘This exists.’ For another who is thinking, a certain view arises, which is approved by one who reflects on that reason exhaustively, so he accepts it by way of approval of a view after exhaustive reflection, thinking, ‘This exists.’ But the Elder Paviṭṭha, having rejected these five reasons, wishing to ask about the state of having been penetrated with direct knowledge, said, ‘Apart from faith, friend Musīla…’ and so on. Therein, ‘apart from’ means setting aside reasons such as faith; the meaning is ‘without these reasons.’ ‘The cessation of becoming is Nibbāna’ means the cessation of the five aggregates is Nibbāna.

Tuṇhī ahosīti thero khīṇāsavo, ahaṃ pana khīṇāsavoti vā na vāti vā avatvā tuṇhīyeva ahosi. Āyasmā nārado āyasmantaṃ paviṭṭhaṃ etadavocāti kasmā avoca? So kira cintesi – “bhavanirodho nibbānaṃ nāmāti sekhehipi jānitabbo pañho esa, ayaṃ pana thero imaṃ theraṃ asekhabhūmiyā kāreti, imaṃ ṭhānaṃ jānāpessāmī”ti etaṃ avoca.

68. Regarding ‘he was silent’: The Elder is one whose taints are destroyed; however, without saying, ‘I am one whose taints are destroyed,’ or ‘I am not,’ he was just silent. Regarding ‘Venerable Nārada said this to Venerable Paviṭṭha,’ why did he say it? It is said that he thought: ‘This question—“The cessation of becoming is called Nibbāna”—should be known even by trainees. However, this Elder is placing that Elder on the plane of the non-trainee. I will make him know this point.’ Thinking thus, he said this.

Sammappaññāya [M 2.0114] sudiṭṭhanti saha vipassanāya maggapaññāya suṭṭhu diṭṭhaṃ. Na camhi arahanti anāgāmimagge ṭhitattā arahaṃ na homīti dīpeti. Yaṃ panassa idāni “bhavanirodho nibbāna”nti [V 2.0108] ñāṇaṃ, taṃ ekūnavīsatiyā paccavekkhaṇañāṇehi vimuttaṃ paccavekkhaṇañāṇaṃ. Udapānoti vīsatiṃsahatthagambhīro pānīyakūpo. Udakavārakoti udakaussiñcanavārako. Udakanti hi kho ñāṇaṃ assāti tīre ṭhitassa olokayato evaṃ ñāṇaṃ bhaveyya. Na ca kāyena phusitvāti udakaṃ pana nīharitvā kāyena phusitvā viharituṃ na sakkuṇeyya. Udapāne udakadassanaṃ viya hi anāgāmino nibbānadassanaṃ, ghammābhitattapuriso viya anāgāmī, udakavārako viya arahattamaggo, yathā ghammābhitattapuriso udapāne udakaṃ passati. Evaṃ anāgāmī paccavekkhaṇañāṇena “upari arahattaphalasamayo nāma atthī”ti jānāti. Yathā pana so puriso udakavārakassa natthitāya udakaṃ nīharitvā kāyena phusituṃ na labhati, evaṃ anāgāmī arahattamaggassa natthitāya nibbānaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā arahattaphalasamāpattiṃ appetvā nisīdituṃ na labhati. Aṭṭhamaṃ.

Regarding ‘well seen with right wisdom’: it is well seen with path-wisdom together with insight. By ‘I am not an Arahant,’ he shows: ‘Because of being established in the path of the non-returner, I am not an Arahant.’ But the knowledge he now has that ‘the cessation of becoming is Nibbāna’ is the reviewing knowledge that is distinct from the nineteen reviewing knowledges. ‘A well’ means a drinking-water well twenty or thirty cubits deep. ‘A water-drawing rope’ means a rope for drawing up water. Regarding ‘the knowledge is indeed like water’: for one standing on the bank and looking, such knowledge would arise. Regarding ‘and not having touched it with the body’: but he would not be able to draw out the water and dwell having touched it with the body. Indeed, like seeing water in a well is the non-returner's seeing of Nibbāna; like a man overcome by heat is the non-returner; like the water-drawing rope is the path to Arahantship. Just as the man overcome by heat sees water in the well, so the non-returner knows with reviewing knowledge, ‘Above, there is what is called the attainment of the fruit of Arahantship.’ But just as that man, due to the absence of a water-drawing rope, does not get to draw out the water and touch it with his body, so the non-returner, due to the absence of the path to Arahantship, does not get to make Nibbāna the object and, having generated the attainment of the fruit of Arahantship, to sit. The eighth is finished.

9. Upayantisuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Upayanti Sutta

69. Navame [P 2.0124] upayantoti udakavaḍḍhanasamaye upari gacchanto. Mahānadiyoti gaṅgāyamunādikā mahāsaritāyo. Upayāpetīti upari yāpeti, vaḍḍheti pūretīti attho. Avijjā upayantīti avijjā upari gacchantī saṅkhārānaṃ paccayo bhavituṃ sakkuṇantī. Saṅkhāre upayāpetīti saṅkhāre upari yāpeti vaḍḍheti. Evaṃ sabbapadesu attho veditabbo. Apayantoti apagacchanto osaranto. Avijjā apayantīti avijjā apagacchamānā osaramānā upari saṅkhārānaṃ paccayo bhavituṃ na sakkuṇantīti attho. Saṅkhāre apayāpetīti saṅkhāre apagacchāpeti. Esa nayo sabbapadesu. Navamaṃ.

In the ninth sutta, 'upayanto' means going above during the time of the water's increase. 'Mahānadiyo' means the great rivers, such as the Ganges and Yamuna. 'Upayāpeti' means it causes to go above, it causes to increase, it causes to fill; this is the meaning. 'Avijjā upayantī' means ignorance, going upwards, is able to become a condition for formations. 'Saṅkhāre upayāpeti' means it causes formations to go above and increase. In all terms, the meaning should be understood thus. 'Apayanto' means going away, declining. 'Avijjā apayantī' means ignorance, going away, declining, is not able to become a condition for formations above it; this is the meaning. 'Saṅkhāre apayāpeti' means it causes formations to go away. This is the method in all terms. The ninth is finished.

10. Susimasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Susima Sutta

70. Dasame garukatoti sabbehi devamanussehi pāsāṇacchattaṃ viya cittena garukato. Mānitoti manena piyāyito. Pūjitoti catupaccayapūjāya [M 2.0115] pūjito. Apacitoti nīcavuttikaraṇena apacito. Satthārañhi disvā manussā hatthikkhandhādīhi otaranti maggaṃ denti, aṃsakūṭato sāṭakaṃ apanenti, āsanato vuṭṭhahanti vandanti. Evaṃ so tehi apacito nāma hoti. Susimoti evaṃnāmako vedaṅgesu kusalo paṇḍitaparibbājako. Ehi tvanti tesaṃ kira etadahosi [V 2.0109] – “samaṇo gotamo na jātigottādīni āgamma lābhaggappatto jāto, kaviseṭṭho panesa uttamakavitāya sāvakānaṃ ganthaṃ bandhitvā deti, taṃ te uggaṇhitvā upaṭṭhākānaṃ upanisinnakathampi anumodanampi sarabhaññampīti evamādīni kathenti, te tesaṃ pasannā lābhaṃ upasaṃharanti. Sace mayaṃ yaṃ samaṇo gotamo jānāti, tato thokaṃ jāneyyāma, attano samayaṃ tattha pakkhipitvā [P 2.0125] mayampi upaṭṭhākānaṃ katheyyāma, tato etehi lābhitarā bhaveyyāma. Ko nu kho samaṇassa gotamassa santike pabbajitvā khippameva uggaṇhituṃ sakkhissatī”ti. Te evaṃ cintetvā “susimo paṭibalo”ti disvā taṃ upasaṅkamitvā evamāhaṃsu.

70. In the tenth sutta, 'garukato' means revered in mind by all gods and humans like a stone parasol. 'Mānito' means cherished by the mind. 'Pūjito' means worshipped with the worship of the four requisites. 'Apacito' means revered through the act of humble conduct. For when people see the Teacher, they descend from their elephants' backs and so on, they give way, they remove their upper garments from their shoulders, they rise from their seats, and they pay homage. Thus he is what is called 'revered' by them. 'Susimo' refers to a wise wanderer of this name, skilled in the Vedāṅgas. 'Ehi tvaṃ' (Come, you!)—it is said that this was their deliberation: "The ascetic Gotama has not become one who has attained the pinnacle of gain on account of birth, lineage, and so on. Rather, this foremost of poets composes a text for his disciples by means of supreme poetry and gives it. They learn it and then speak to their supporters with things such as conversations when seated near, rejoicing, and recitation in a pleasing voice. Those supporters, being pleased with them, bring them gain. If we were to know a little of what the ascetic Gotama knows, we could insert our own doctrine into it and we too could teach our supporters. Then we would become greater gainers than these. Who, now, having gone forth in the presence of the ascetic Gotama, will be able to learn quickly?" Having deliberated thus and seeing that Susima was capable, they approached him and spoke thus.

Yenāyasmā ānando tenupasaṅkamīti kasmā upasaṅkami? Evaṃ kirassa ahosi, “kassa nu kho santikaṃ gantvā ahaṃ imaṃ dhammaṃ khippaṃ laddhuṃ sakkhissāmī”ti? Tato cintesi – “samaṇo gotamo garu tejussado niyamamanuyutto, na sakkā akāle upasaṅkamituṃ, aññepi bahū khattiyādayo samaṇaṃ gotamaṃ upasaṅkamanti, tasmimpi samaye na sakkā upasaṅkamituṃ. Sāvakesupissa sāriputto mahāpañño vipassanālakkhaṇamhi etadagge ṭhapito, mahāmoggallāno samādhilakkhaṇasmiṃ etadagge ṭhapito, mahākassapo dhutaṅgadharesu anuruddho dibbacakkhukesu, puṇṇo mantāṇiputto dhammakathikesu, upālitthero vinayadharesu etadagge ṭhapito, ayaṃ pana ānando bahussuto tipiṭakadharo, satthāpissa tattha tattha kathitaṃ dhammaṃ āharitvā katheti, pañcasu ṭhānesu etadagge ṭhapito, aṭṭhannaṃ varānaṃ lābhī, catūhi acchariyabbhutadhammehi samannāgato, tassa samīpaṃ gato khippaṃ dhammaṃ laddhuṃ sakkhissāmī”ti. Tasmā yenāyasmā ānando tenupasaṅkami.

Regarding 'He approached where the venerable Ānanda was': why did he approach? It seems this was his thought: "To whose presence, having gone, will I be able to quickly obtain this Dhamma?" Then he reflected: "The ascetic Gotama is venerable, possessed of great splendor, and devoted to his routine; it is not possible to approach him at an improper time. Also, many others, such as nobles, approach the ascetic Gotama, and at that time too it is not possible to approach. Among his disciples, Sāriputta has great wisdom and is placed foremost in the characteristic of insight; Mahāmoggallāna is placed foremost in the characteristic of concentration; Mahākassapa among those who uphold the ascetic practices; Anuruddha among those with the divine eye; Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta among the Dhamma-speakers; and the elder Upāli is placed foremost among the upholders of the Vinaya. But this Ānanda is of great learning, a bearer of the Tipiṭaka; even the Teacher brings up the Dhamma spoken by him in various places and teaches it. He is placed foremost in five respects, is a recipient of eight boons, and is endowed with four amazing and wondrous qualities. Having gone to his presence, I will be able to quickly obtain the Dhamma." Therefore, he approached where the venerable Ānanda was.

Yena [M 2.0116] bhagavā tenupasaṅkamīti kasmā sayaṃ apabbājetvā upasaṅkami? Evaṃ kirassa ahosi – “ayaṃ titthiyasamaye pāṭiyekko ‘ahaṃ satthā’ti paṭijānanto carati, pabbajitvā sāsanassa alābhāyapi parisakkeyya. Na kho panassāhaṃ ajjhāsayaṃ ājānāmi, satthā jānissatī”ti. Tasmā taṃ ādāya yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami. Tenahānanda, susimaṃ pabbājethāti satthā kira cintesi – “ayaṃ paribbājako titthiyasamaye ‘ahaṃ pāṭiyekko satthā’ti paṭijānamāno carati, ‘idha maggabrahmacariyaṃ carituṃ icchāmī’ti kira vadati. Kiṃ nu kho mayi pasanno, udāhu mayhaṃ sāvakesu, udāhu mayhaṃ vā mama sāvakānaṃ vā dhammakathāya pasanno”ti? Athassa ekaṭṭhānepi pasādābhāvaṃ [P 2.0126] ñatvā, “ayaṃ mama sāsane dhammaṃ thenessāmīti pabbajati. Itissa āgamanaṃ aparisuddhaṃ; nipphatti nu kho kīdisā”ti? Olokento “kiñcāpi [V 2.0110] ‘dhammaṃ thenessāmī’ti pabbajati, katipāheneva pana ghaṭetvā arahattaṃ gaṇhissatī”ti ñatvā “tenahānanda, susimaṃ pabbājethā”ti āha.

Regarding 'He approached where the Blessed One was': why did he approach without ordaining him himself? It seems this was his thought: "This man, in the fold of the sectarians, wanders about declaring, 'I am a separate teacher.' Having gone forth, he might even strive for the non-gain of the Dispensation. I, however, do not know his intention; the Teacher will know." Therefore, taking him along, he approached where the Blessed One was. Regarding 'Therefore, Ānanda, ordain Susima,' it is said the Teacher reflected: "This wanderer, in the fold of the sectarians, wanders about declaring, 'I am a separate teacher.' He says, it seems, 'Here I wish to practice the holy life of the path.' What now? Is he confident in me, or in my disciples, or is he confident in the Dhamma-talk of me or my disciples?" Then, having known his lack of confidence in even a single respect, he thought: "This one is going forth in my Dispensation to steal the Dhamma. Thus his coming is impure. What indeed will be the nature of his attainment?" Observing, he knew: "Although he goes forth to steal the Dhamma, nevertheless, within just a few days, having striven, he will grasp Arahantship." Knowing this, he said: "Therefore, Ānanda, ordain Susima."

Aññā byākatā hotīti te kira bhikkhū satthu santike kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā temāsaṃ vassaṃ vasantā tasmiṃyeva antotemāse ghaṭentā vāyamantā arahattaṃ paṭilabhiṃsu. Te “paṭiladdhaguṇaṃ satthu ārocessāmā”ti pavāritapavāraṇā senāsanaṃ saṃsāmetvā satthu santikaṃ āgantvā attano paṭiladdhaguṇaṃ ārocesuṃ. Taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Aññāti arahattassa nāmaṃ. Byākatāti ārocitā. Assosīti so kira ohitasoto hutvā tesaṃ tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ ṭhitaṭṭhānaṃ gacchati taṃ taṃ kathaṃ suṇitukāmo. Yena te bhikkhū tenupasaṅkamīti kasmā upasaṅkami? Taṃ kirassa pavattiṃ sutvā etadahosi – “aññā nāma imasmiṃ sāsane paramappamāṇaṃ sārabhūtā ācariyamuṭṭhi maññe bhavissati, pucchitvā naṃ jānissāmī”ti. Tasmā upasaṅkami.

Regarding 'Aññā byākatā hoti' (Final knowledge was declared): It is said that those monks, having received a meditation subject from the Teacher, while residing for the three months of the rains-retreat, striving and endeavoring within those very three months, attained Arahantship. Thinking, 'We shall announce the quality we have attained to the Teacher,' having completed the Pavāraṇā invitation, they put their lodgings in order, went to the Teacher's presence, and announced the quality they had attained. Referring to that, this was said. 'Aññā' is a name for Arahantship. 'Byākatā' means it was announced. Regarding 'Assosi' (He heard): It is said that he, having become one with an attentive ear and desiring to hear their various conversations, would go to the place where those monks were. Regarding 'Yena te bhikkhū tenupasaṅkami' (He approached those monks): Why did he approach? It is said that having heard that account, this thought occurred to him: 'What is called "aññā" in this Dispensation seems to be the highest measure, the essential substance, I think it must be the teacher's closed fist. Having asked about it, I shall come to know it.' Therefore, he approached.

Anekavihitanti anekavidhaṃ. Iddhividhanti iddhikoṭṭhāsaṃ. Āvibhāvaṃ tirobhāvanti āvibhāvaṃ gahetvā tirobhāvaṃ, tirobhāvaṃ gahetvā āvibhāvaṃ kātuṃ sakkothāti pucchati. Tirokuṭṭanti parakuṭṭaṃ. Itarapadadvayepi [M 2.0117] eseva nayo. Ummujjanimujjanti ummujjanañca nimujjanañca. Pallaṅkenāti pallaṅkabandhanena. Kamathāti nisīdituṃ vā gantuṃ vā sakkothāti pucchati? Pakkhī sakuṇoti pakkhayutto sakuṇo. Ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthārato pana imassa iddhividhassa, ito paresaṃ dibbasotādīnañca vaṇṇanānayo visuddhimagge vuttanayena veditabboti.

'Anekavihitaṃ' means of many kinds. 'Iddhividhaṃ' means the division of psychic power. Regarding 'āvibhāvaṃ tirobhāvaṃ' (becoming manifest and unmanifest), he asks: 'Are you able to become unmanifest after having been manifest, and to become manifest after having been unmanifest?' 'Tirokuṭṭaṃ' means through the other side of a wall. For the other two terms as well, this is the same method. 'Ummujjanimujjaṃ' means emerging and submerging. 'Pallaṅkena' means by means of the cross-legged posture. Regarding 'kamathā' (you travel), he asks: 'Are you able to sit or to go?' 'Pakkhī sakuṇo' means a bird endowed with wings. This is the summary here. But in detail, the method of explaining this psychic power, and those that follow, such as the divine ear and so on, should be understood according to the method stated in the Visuddhimagga.

Santā vimokkhāti aṅgasantatāya ceva ārammaṇasantatāya ca santā āruppavimokkhā. Kāyena phusitvāti nāmakāyena phusitvā paṭilabhitvā. Paññāvimuttā kho mayaṃ, āvusoti, āvuso, mayaṃ nijjhānakā [P 2.0127] sukkhavipassakā paññāmatteneva vimuttāti dasseti. Ājāneyyāsi vā tvaṃ, āvuso susima, na vā tvaṃ ājāneyyāsīti kasmā evamāhaṃsu? Evaṃ kira nesaṃ ahosi – “mayaṃ imassa ajjhāsayaṃ gahetvā kathetuṃ na sakkhissāma, dasabalaṃ pana pucchitvā nikkaṅkho bhavissatī”ti. Dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇanti vipassanāñāṇaṃ, taṃ paṭhamataraṃ uppajjati. Nibbāne ñāṇanti vipassanāya ciṇṇante pavattamaggañāṇaṃ, taṃ pacchā uppajjati. Tasmā bhagavā evamāha.

'Santā vimokkhā' (the peaceful liberations) means the formless liberations are peaceful due to the peacefulness of the jhāna factors and the peacefulness of the object. 'Kāyena phusitvā' (having touched with the body) means having touched and attained with the mental body. 'Paññāvimuttā kho mayaṃ, āvuso' (We, friend, are liberated by wisdom) shows this: 'Friend, we are without jhāna, dry-insight meditators; we are liberated by wisdom alone.' Why did they speak thus: 'Whether you understand, friend Susīma, or whether you do not understand...'? It is said this thought occurred to them: 'We will not be able to speak by grasping his inclination, but having asked the One of Ten Powers, he will become free from doubt.' 'Dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇaṃ' is insight-knowledge; it arises first. 'Nibbāne ñāṇaṃ' is the path-knowledge that occurs at the culmination of insight practice; it arises later. Therefore, the Blessed One spoke thus.

Ājāneyyāsi vātiādi kasmā vuttaṃ? Vināpi samādhiṃ evaṃ ñāṇuppattidassanatthaṃ. Idañhi [V 2.0111] vuttaṃ hoti – susima, maggo vā phalaṃ vā na samādhinissando, na samādhiānisaṃso, na samādhissa nipphatti, vipassanāya paneso nissando, vipassanāya ānisaṃso, vipassanāya nipphatti, tasmā jāneyyāsi vā tvaṃ, na vā tvaṃ jāneyyāsi, atha kho dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇaṃ pubbe, pacchā nibbāne ñāṇanti.

Why was the statement beginning with 'Ājāneyyāsi vā' spoken? It was spoken to show the arising of knowledge in this way even without concentration. For this is the meaning that was stated: 'Susīma, the path or the fruit is not a consequence of concentration, not a benefit of concentration, not a completion of concentration. Rather, this is a consequence of insight, a benefit of insight, a completion of insight. Therefore, whether you know or you do not know, it is nevertheless the case that first the knowledge of the stability of phenomena arises, and afterwards, the knowledge in Nibbāna arises.'

Idānissa paṭivedhabhabbataṃ ñatvā teparivaṭṭaṃ dhammadesanaṃ desento taṃ kiṃ maññasi, susima? Rūpaṃ niccaṃ vā aniccaṃ vātiādimāha? Te parivaṭṭadesanāvasāne pana thero arahattaṃ patto. Idānissa anuyogaṃ āropento jātipaccayā jarāmaraṇanti, susima, passasītiādimāha. Api pana tvaṃ, susimāti idaṃ kasmā ārabhi? Nijjhānakānaṃ sukkhavipassakabhikkhūnaṃ pākaṭakaraṇatthaṃ. Ayañhettha adhippāyo – na kevalaṃ tvameva nijjhānako sukkhavipassako, etepi bhikkhū evarūpāyevāti. Sesaṃ sabbattha pākaṭamevāti. Dasamaṃ.

Now, having known his capacity for realization, while teaching the Dhamma discourse with its three revolutions, He said: 'What do you think, Susīma? Is form permanent or impermanent?' and so on. At the end of that discourse with three revolutions, the Elder attained Arahantship. Now, establishing him in the practice, He said: 'Susīma, do you see that with birth as a condition, there is aging-and-death?' and so on. Why did He begin with, 'And you, Susīma...'? It was to make manifest the dry-insight monks who are without jhāna. Indeed, this is the intention here: 'It is not only you, Susīma, who are a dry-insight meditator without jhāna; these monks are also of such a nature.' The rest is evident everywhere. The tenth is finished.

Mahāvaggo sattamo.

The Great Chapter, the seventh, is finished.

8. Samaṇabrāhmaṇavaggo

8. The Chapter on Ascetics and Brahmins

1. Jarāmaraṇasuttādivaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Sutta on Aging-and-Death and so on

71-72. Samaṇabrāhmaṇavagge [M 2.0118] jarāmaraṇādīsu ekekapadavasena ekekaṃ katvā ekādasa suttāni vuttāni, tāni uttānatthānevāti.

1. 71-72. In the Chapter on Ascetics and Brahmins, eleven suttas were spoken, with each sutta being formed by way of each single term among those beginning with aging-and-death. They have only an obvious meaning.

Samaṇabrāhmaṇavaggo aṭṭhamo.

The Chapter on Ascetics and Brahmins, the eighth, is finished.

9. Antarapeyyālaṃ

The Intermediate Repetition Section

1. Satthusuttādivaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Sutta on the Teacher, and so on

73. Ito [V 2.0112][P 2.0128] paraṃ “satthā pariyesitabbo”tiādinayappavattā dvādasa antarapeyyālavaggā nāma honti. Te sabbepi tathā tathā bujjhanakānaṃ veneyyapuggalānaṃ ajjhāsayavasena vuttā. Tattha satthāti buddho vā hotu sāvako vā, yaṃ nissāya maggañāṇaṃ labhati, ayaṃ satthā nāma, so pariyesitabbo. Sikkhā karaṇīyāti tividhāpi sikkhā kātabbā. Yogādīsu yogoti payogo. Chandoti kattukamyatākusalacchando. Ussoḷhīti sabbasahaṃ adhimattavīriyaṃ. Appaṭivānīti anivattanā. Ātappanti kilesatāpanavīriyameva. Sātaccanti satatakiriyaṃ. Satīti jarāmaraṇādivasena catusaccapariggāhikā sati. Sampajaññanti tādisameva ñāṇaṃ. Appamādoti saccabhāvanāya appamādo. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

1. From here onward, twelve suttas that proceed by the method beginning with 'the teacher should be sought' are called the Antarapeyyāla Chapter. All these were spoken according to the disposition of trainable persons capable of understanding the truths in various ways. Therein, as for 'teacher': be it the Buddha or a disciple, whomever one relies on to obtain path-knowledge, this one is called a teacher; he should be sought. As for 'training should be done': the threefold training should be undertaken. Among terms beginning with 'striving,' as for 'striving' (yoga): it is application. As for 'desire' (chanda): it is wholesome desire which is the wish to act. As for 'ardor' (ussoḷhī): it is supreme energy that endures all things. As for 'unyielding' (appaṭivāni): it is not turning back. As for 'exertion' (ātappa): it is the very energy that torments the defilements. As for 'persistence' (sātacca): it is continuous action. As for 'mindfulness' (sati): it is mindfulness that comprehends the Four Truths by way of aging-and-death, and so on. As for 'clear comprehension' (sampajañña): it is knowledge of the same kind. As for 'diligence' (appamāda): it is non-negligence in the development of the truths. The remaining meaning in all instances is obvious.

Antarapeyyālo navamo.

73. The Intermediate Repetition Section, the ninth, is finished.

Nidānasaṃyuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Connected Discourses on Causation is finished.

2. Abhisamayasaṃyuttaṃ

The Connected Discourses on Realization

1. Nakhasikhāsuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Nakhasikhā Sutta

74. Abhisamayasaṃyuttassa [V 2.0113][P 2.0129][M 2.0119] paṭhame nakhasikhāyanti maṃsaṭṭhānena vimutte nakhagge. Nakhasikhā ca nāma lokiyānaṃ mahatīpi hoti, satthu pana rattuppalapattakoṭi viya sukhumā. Kathaṃ panettha paṃsu patiṭṭhitoti? Adhiṭṭhānabalena. Bhagavatā hi atthaṃ ñāpetukāmena adhiṭṭhānabalena tattha patiṭṭhāpito. Satimaṃ kalanti mahāpathaviyā paṃsuṃ satakoṭṭhāse katvā tato ekakoṭṭhāsaṃ. Paratopi eseva nayo. Abhisametāvinoti paññāya ariyasaccāni abhisametvā ṭhitassa. Purimaṃ dukkhakkhandhaṃ parikkhīṇaṃ pariyādiṇṇaṃ upanidhāyāti etadeva bahutaraṃ dukkhaṃ, yadidaṃ parikkhīṇanti evaṃ paṭhamaṃ vuttaṃ dukkhakkhandhaṃ upanidhāya, ñāṇena taṃ tassa santike ṭhapetvā upaparikkhiyamāneti attho. Katamaṃ panettha purimadukkhaṃ nāma? Yaṃ parikkhīṇaṃ. Katamaṃ pana parikkhīṇaṃ? Yaṃ paṭhamamaggassa abhāvitattā uppajjeyya. Katamaṃ pana upanidhāya? Yaṃ sattasu attabhāvesu apāye aṭṭhamañca paṭisandhiṃ ādiṃ katvā yattha katthaci uppajjeyya, sabbaṃ taṃ parikkhīṇanti veditabbaṃ. Sattakkhattunti satta vāre, sattasu attabhāvesūti attho. Paramatāti idamassa paraṃ pamāṇanti dasseti. Mahatthiyoti mahato atthassa nipphādako. Paṭhamaṃ.

74. In the first sutta of the Connected Discourses on Realization, as for 'on the tip of the nail': it means at the tip of the nail, which is free from the place of flesh. And that called the tip of the nail, for worldly people, can be large, but for the Teacher, it is as subtle as the tip of a red lotus petal. How then was dust established there? By the power of determination. Indeed, it was established there by the Blessed One, who wished to make the meaning known, through the power of determination. As for 'a hundredth part': it means one part after having divided the dust of the great earth into one hundred parts. This same method applies later on. As for 'one who has realized': it means of a person who stands having penetrated the Noble Truths with wisdom. As for the phrase 'having compared the former mass of suffering that is destroyed and exhausted': the meaning is, by comparing the mass of suffering first mentioned thus, 'This itself is the much greater suffering, that is, what is destroyed,' or, being investigated by placing it near that mass of suffering with knowledge. Herein, what is that called 'former suffering'? That which is destroyed. And what is that which is destroyed? That which would arise because the first path has not been developed. And what is this compared with? That which would arise in seven existences, in the plane of misery, and, beginning with an eighth relinking, anywhere whatsoever—all that should be understood as destroyed. As for 'at most seven times': the meaning is seven times, in seven existences. As for 'at the most': this shows, 'this is his limit.' As for 'of great benefit': it is an accomplisher of great benefit. The first.

2. Pokkharaṇīsuttavaṇṇanā

2. Explanation of the Pokkharaṇī Sutta

75. Dutiye pokkharaṇīti vāpī. Ubbedhenāti gambhīratāya. Samatittikāti mukhavaṭṭisamā. Kākapeyyāti sakkā hoti tīre ṭhitena kākena pakatiyāpi mukhatuṇḍikaṃ otāretvā pātuṃ. Dutiyaṃ.

75. In the second sutta, 'a pond' means a lake. 'In height' means in depth. 'With level banks' means level with the brim. 'Drinkable by a crow' means that it is possible for a crow standing on the bank to naturally dip its beak and drink. The second.

3. Saṃbhejjaudakasuttādivaṇṇanā

3. Explanation of the Saṃbhejjaudaka Sutta and Others

76-77. Tatiye [V 2.0114][P 2.0130] yatthimāti yasmiṃ sambhijjaṭṭhāne imā. Saṃsandantīti samāgantvā sandanti. Samentīti samāgacchanti. Dve vā ti vāti dve vā tīṇi vā. Udakaphusitānīti udakabindūni. Saṃbhejjaudakanti aññāhi nadīhi saddhiṃ sambhinnaṭṭhāne udakaṃ. Catutthaṃ uttānatthameva. Tatiyacatutthāni.

76-77. In the third sutta, 'where these' means in which place of confluence these rivers are. 'They flow together' means having come together, they flow. 'They meet' means they come together. 'Two or three' means two or three. 'Drops of water' means water drops. 'Confluent water' means water in a place where it has merged with other rivers. The fourth sutta is of plain meaning. The third and fourth.

5. Pathavīsuttādivaṇṇanā

5. Explanation of the Pathavī Sutta and Others

78-84. Pañcame [M 2.0120] mahāpathaviyāti cakkavāḷabbhantarāya mahāpathaviyā uddharitvā. Kolaṭṭhimattiyoti padaraṭṭhipamāṇā. Guḷikāti mattikaguḷikā. Upanikkhipeyyāti ekasmiṃ ṭhāne ṭhapeyya. Chaṭṭhādīsu vuttanayeneva attho veditabbo. Pariyosāne pana aññatitthiyasamaṇabrāhmaṇaparibbājakānaṃ adhigamoti bāhirakānaṃ sabbopi guṇādhigamo paṭhamamaggena adhigataguṇānaṃ satabhāgampi sahassabhāgampi satasahassabhāgampi na upagacchatīti. Pañcamādīni.

78-84. In the fifth sutta, 'from the great earth' means having taken from the great earth that is within the Cakkavāḷa. 'The size of a jujube stone' means the size of a jujube seed. 'Pellets' means pellets of fine earth. 'He might place' means one should place in one spot. In the sixth and following suttas, the meaning should be understood in the way already stated. But at the conclusion, 'the attainment of other sectarians, ascetics, brahmins, and wanderers' means that all the attainment of qualities by outsiders does not approach even a hundredth, a thousandth, or a hundred-thousandth part of the qualities attained by the first path. The fifth and following.

Abhisamayasaṃyuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Connected Discourses on Realization is concluded.

3. Dhātusaṃyuttaṃ

3. The Connected Discourses on Elements

1. Nānattavaggo

1. The Chapter on Diversity

1.Dhātunānattasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Explanation of the Discourse on the Diversity of Elements

85. Dhātusaṃyuttassa [V 2.0115][M 2.0121] paṭhame [P 2.0131] nissattaṭṭhasuññataṭṭhasaṅkhātena sabhāvaṭṭhena dhātūti laddhanāmānaṃ dhammānaṃ nānāsabhāvo dhātunānattaṃ. Cakkhudhātūtiādīsu cakkhupasādo cakkhudhātu, rūpārammaṇaṃ rūpadhātu, cakkhupasādavatthukaṃ cittaṃ cakkhuviññāṇadhātu. Sotapasādo sotadhātu, saddārammaṇaṃ saddadhātu, sotapasādavatthukaṃ cittaṃ sotaviññāṇadhātu. Ghānapasādo ghānadhātu, gandhārammaṇaṃ gandhadhātu, ghānapasādavatthukaṃ cittaṃ ghānaviññāṇadhātu. Jivhāpasādo jivhādhātu, rasārammaṇaṃ rasadhātu, jivhāpasādavatthukaṃ cittaṃ jivhāviññāṇadhātu. Kāyapasādo kāyadhātu, phoṭṭhabbārammaṇaṃ phoṭṭhabbadhātu, kāyapasādavatthukaṃ cittaṃ kāyaviññāṇadhātu. Tisso manodhātuyo manodhātu, vedanādayo tayo khandhā sukhumarūpāni nibbānañca dhammadhātu, sabbampi manoviññāṇaṃ manoviññāṇadhātūti. Ettha ca soḷasa dhātuyo kāmāvacarā, avasāne dve catubhūmikāti. Paṭhamaṃ.

85. In the first sutta of the Chapter on Diversity, the meaning should be understood thus: 'diversity of elements' is the diverse intrinsic nature of phenomena that have gained the name 'element' by way of the meaning of their true nature, which is designated as being not a living being and as being void. Among 'the eye-element, etc.': eye-sensitivity is the eye-element; a visible object is the form-element; consciousness based on eye-sensitivity is the eye-consciousness-element. Ear-sensitivity is the ear-element; a sound object is the sound-element; consciousness based on ear-sensitivity is the ear-consciousness-element. Nose-sensitivity is the nose-element; an odor object is the odor-element; consciousness based on nose-sensitivity is the nose-consciousness-element. Tongue-sensitivity is the tongue-element; a taste object is the taste-element; consciousness based on tongue-sensitivity is the tongue-consciousness-element. Body-sensitivity is the body-element; a tangible object is the tangible-element; consciousness based on body-sensitivity is the body-consciousness-element. The three mind-elements are the mind-element. The three aggregates beginning with feeling, subtle material phenomena, and Nibbāna are the mental-object-element. All mind-consciousness is the mind-consciousness-element. Herein, sixteen elements are of the sense-sphere; the two at the end are of the four planes. The first.

2. Phassanānattasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Explanation of the Discourse on the Diversity of Contact

86. Dutiye uppajjati phassanānattanti nānāsabhāvo phasso uppajjati. Tattha cakkhusamphassādayo cakkhuviññāṇādisampayuttā, manosamphasso manodvāre paṭhamajavanasampayutto, tasmā. Manodhātuṃ paṭiccāti manodvārāvajjanaṃ kiriyāmanoviññāṇadhātuṃ paṭicca paṭhamajavanasamphasso uppajjatīti ayamettha attho. Dutiyaṃ.

86. In the second sutta, as for 'diversity of contact arises,' it means contact of diverse nature arises. Therein, eye-contact and so forth are associated with eye-consciousness and so on; mind-contact, at the mind-door, is associated with the first impulsion. Therefore, regarding 'dependent on the mind-element,' this is the meaning here: dependent on the functional mind-consciousness-element which is mind-door adverting, the contact associated with the first impulsion arises. The second.

3. Nophassanānattasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Explanation of the Discourse on the Non-Diversity of Contact

87. Tatiye [V 2.0116][P 2.0132] no manosamphassaṃ paṭicca uppajjati manodhātūti manodvāre paṭhamajavanasampayuttaṃ phassaṃ paṭicca āvajjanakiriyāmanoviññāṇadhātu no uppajjatīti evamattho daṭṭhabbo. Tatiyaṃ.

87. In the third sutta, as for 'the mind-element does not arise dependent on mind-contact,' the meaning should be understood thus: dependent on the contact associated with the first impulsion at the mind-door, the functional mind-consciousness-element which is adverting does not arise. The third.

4. Vedanānānattasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Explanation of the Discourse on the Diversity of Feeling

88. Catutthe [M 2.0122] cakkhusamphassajā vedanāti sampaṭicchanamanodhātuto paṭṭhāya sabbāpi tasmiṃ dvāre vedanā vatteyyuṃ, nibbattiphāsukatthaṃ pana anantaraṃ sampaṭicchanavedanameva gahetuṃ vaṭṭatīti vuttaṃ. Manosamphassaṃ paṭiccāti manodvāre āvajjanasamphassaṃ paṭicca paṭhamajavanavedanā, paṭhamajavanasamphassaṃ paṭicca dutiyajavanavedanāti ayamadhippāyo. Catutthaṃ.

88. In the fourth sutta, as for 'feeling born of eye-contact,' although all feelings at that door, starting from the receiving mind-element, may occur, for the sake of ease in demonstrating the arising, it is said that it is appropriate to take only the feeling associated with receiving which is immediately subsequent. As for 'dependent on mind-contact,' the intended meaning is this: dependent on the adverting-contact at the mind-door, the feeling of the first impulsion arises; and dependent on the contact of the first impulsion, the feeling of the second impulsion arises. The fourth.

5. Dutiyavedanānānattasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Explanation of the Second Discourse on the Diversity of Feeling

89. Pañcame tatiyacatutthesu vuttanayāva ekato katvā desitāti. Iti dutiyādīsu catūsu suttesu manodhātuṃ manodhātūti agahetvā manodvārāvajjanaṃ manodhātūti gahitaṃ. Sabbāni cetāni tathā tathā kathite bujjhanakānaṃ ajjhāsayena desitāni. Ito paresupi eseva nayo. Pañcamaṃ.

89. In the fifth discourse, the teaching is given by combining the methods explained in the third and fourth. Thus, in the four discourses beginning with the second, 'mind-element' is taken to mean mind-door adverting, not the mind-element itself, which comprises five-door adverting and receiving. All these were taught in various ways according to the disposition of those who are to be awakened. This same method applies in the subsequent sections as well. The fifth.

6. Bāhiradhātunānattasuttavaṇṇanā

6. Explanation of the Discourse on the Diversity of External Elements

90. Chaṭṭhe pana pañca dhātuyo kāmāvacarā, dhammadhātu catubhūmikāti. Chaṭṭhaṃ.

90. In the sixth discourse, however, the five elements are of the sense-sphere, and the dhamma-element is of the four planes. The sixth.

7. Saññānānattasuttavaṇṇanā

7. Explanation of the Discourse on the Diversity of Perception

91. Sattame rūpadhātūti āpāthe patitaṃ attano vā parassa vā sāṭakaveṭhanādivatthukaṃ rūpārammaṇaṃ. Rūpasaññāti cakkhuviññāṇasampayuttā saññā. Rūpasaṅkappoti sampaṭicchanādīhi tīhi [V 2.0117] cittehi sampayutto saṅkappo. Rūpacchandoti rūpe chandikataṭṭhena chando. Rūpapariḷāhoti rūpe anuḍahanaṭṭhena [P 2.0133] pariḷāho. Rūpapariyesanāti pariḷāhe uppanne sandiṭṭhasambhatte gahetvā tassa rūpassa paṭilābhatthāya pariyesanā. Ettha ca saññāsaṅkappachandā ekajavanavārepi nānājavanavārepi labbhanti, pariḷāhapariyesanā pana nānājavanavāreyeva labbhantīti. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, dhātunānattanti ettha ca evaṃ rūpādinānāsabhāvaṃ dhātuṃ paṭicca rūpasaññādinānāsabhāvasaññā uppajjatīti iminā nayena attho veditabbo. Sattamaṃ.

91. In the seventh discourse, 'the element of form' means a form-object that has come into range, such as one's own or another's cloth or turban. 'Perception of form' means perception associated with eye-consciousness. 'Thought of form' means thought associated with the three minds beginning with receiving. 'Desire for form' means desire in the sense of an inclination towards form. 'Fever for form' means fever in the sense of burning on account of form. 'Search for form' means, when fever has arisen, taking along friends one has seen and associated with, and searching for the sake of obtaining that form. Herein, perception, thought, and desire are found both in a single impulsion-process and in separate impulsion-processes, but fever and search are found only in separate impulsion-processes. And here, regarding 'Thus, O monks, is the diversity of elements,' the meaning should be understood by this method: thus, dependent on an element of diverse nature such as form, a perception of diverse nature such as perception of form arises. The seventh.

8. Nopariyesanānānattasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Explanation of the Discourse on the Diversity of Non-Searches

92. Aṭṭhame [M 2.0123] no dhammapariyesanaṃ paṭicca uppajjati dhammapariḷāhoti evaṃ āgataṃ paṭisedhamattameva nānaṃ. Aṭṭhamaṃ.

92. In the eighth discourse, regarding the passage that has come thus: 'Fever for the Dhamma does not arise dependent on a search for the Dhamma,' the only difference is the mere negation. The eighth.

9. Bāhiraphassanānattasuttādivaṇṇanā

9. Explanation of the Discourse on the Diversity of External Contacts, and so forth

93-94. Navame uppajjati rūpasaññāti vuttappakāre ārammaṇe uppajjati saññā. Rūpasaṅkappoti tasmiṃyeva ārammaṇe tīhi cittehi sampayuttasaṅkappo. Rūpasamphassoti tadevārammaṇaṃ phusamāno phasso. Vedanāti tadeva ārammaṇaṃ anubhavamānā vedanā. Chandādayo vuttanayāva. Rūpalābhoti pariyesitvā laddhaṃ saha taṇhāya ārammaṇaṃ “rūpalābho”ti vuttaṃ. Ayaṃ tāva sabbasaṅgāhikanayo ekasmiṃ yevārammaṇe sabbadhammānaṃ uppattivasena vutto. Aparo āgantukārammaṇamissako hoti – rūpasaññā rūpasaṅkappo phasso vedanāti ime tāva cattāro dhammā dhuvaparibhoge nibaddhārammaṇe honti. Nibaddhārammaṇañhi iṭṭhaṃ kantaṃ manāpaṃ piyaṃ yaṃkiñci viya upaṭṭhāti, āgantukārammaṇaṃ pana yaṃkiñci samānampi khobhetvā tiṭṭhati.

In the ninth discourse, 'perception of form arises' means that perception arises with regard to an object of the kind previously described. 'Thought about form' means the thought associated with three minds with regard to that same object. 'Contact with form' means the contact that touches that very object. 'Feeling' means the feeling that experiences that same object. Desire and the rest are as previously explained. 'Acquisition of form' means the object obtained by seeking, together with craving; thus it is called 'acquisition of form.' This, then, is the all-inclusive method, stated by way of the arising of all phenomena in relation to a single object. Another method involves the admixture of an adventitious object: perception of form, thought about form, contact, and feeling—these four phenomena occur in a habitual object of constant use. For a habitual object, though it may be desirable, pleasing, agreeable, and dear, presents itself as something of no account; but an adventitious object, though it may be of no account, stands there causing agitation.

Tatridaṃ vatthu – eko kira amaccaputto gāmiyehi parivārito gāmamajjhe ṭhatvā kammaṃ karoti. Tasmiñcassa samaye upāsikā nadiṃ gantvā nhatvā alaṅkatapaṭiyattā dhātigaṇaparivutā gehaṃ gacchati. So dūrato disvā “āgantukamātugāmo bhavissatī”ti saññaṃ uppādetvā “gaccha, bhaṇe jānāhi, kā esā”ti purisaṃ pesesi. So gantvā taṃ disvā paccāgato, “kā esā”ti puṭṭho yathāsabhāvaṃ ārocesi. Evaṃ āgantukārammaṇaṃ [P 2.0134] khobheti[V 2.0118]. Tasmiṃ uppanno chando rūpachando nāma, tadeva ārammaṇaṃ katvā uppanno pariḷāho rūpapariḷāho nāma, sahāye gaṇhitvā tassa pariyesanaṃ rūpapariyesanā nāma, pariyesitvā laddhaṃ saha taṇhāya ārammaṇaṃ rūpalābho nāma.

Here is the story: A certain minister's son, surrounded by villagers, stood in the middle of the village and conducted his business. At that time, his wife, having gone to the river, bathed, adorned herself, and surrounded by a group of attendants, was returning home. Seeing her from a distance, he formed the perception, 'This must be a visiting woman,' and sent a man, saying, 'Go, my good man, find out who she is.' The man went, saw her, and upon returning, when asked, 'Who is she?' reported the actual situation. Thus, the adventitious object causes agitation. The desire that arose in regard to it is called 'desire for form'; taking that very object as its basis, the fever that arose is called 'fever for form'; gathering companions and searching for that object is called 'search for form'; having searched, the object obtained together with craving is called 'the acquisition of form'.

Uruvalliyavāsī cūḷatissatthero panāha – “kiñcāpi bhagavatā phassavedanā pāḷiyā majjhe gahitā, pāḷiṃ pana parivaṭṭetvā vuttappakāre ārammaṇe uppannā saññā rūpasaññā, tasmiṃyeva saṅkappo rūpasaṅkappo tasmiṃ [M 2.0124] chando rūpacchando, tasmiṃ pariḷāho rūpapariḷāho, tasmiṃ pariyesanā rūpapariyesanā, pariyesitvā laddhaṃ saha taṇhāya ārammaṇaṃ rūpalābho. Evaṃ laddhārammaṇe pana phusanaṃ phasso, anubhavanaṃ vedanā. Rūpasamphasso rūpasamphassajā vedanāti idaṃ dvayaṃ labbhatī”ti. Aparampi avibhūtavāraṃ nāma gaṇhanti. Ārammaṇañhi sāṇipākārehi vā parikkhittaṃ tiṇapaṇṇādīhi vā paṭicchannaṃ hoti, taṃ “upaḍḍhaṃ diṭṭhaṃ me ārammaṇaṃ, suṭṭhu naṃ passissāmī”ti olokayato tasmiṃ ārammaṇe uppannā saññā rūpasaññā nāma. Tasmiṃyeva uppannā saṅkappādayo rūpasaṅkappādayo nāmāti veditabbā. Etthāpi ca saññāsaṅkappaphassavedanāchandā ekajavanavārepi nānājavanavārepi labbhanti, pariḷāhapariyesanālābhā nānājavanavāreyevāti. Dasamaṃ uttānamevāti. Navamadasamāni.

The Elder Cūḷatissa of Uruvelā said: 'Although the Blessed One has included contact and feeling in the middle of the Pāli text, by reordering the Pāli, perception that has arisen in an object in the described manner is ‘perception of form’; thought about it is ‘thought of form’; desire for it is ‘desire for form’; fever for it is ‘fever for form’; the search for it is ‘search for form’; having searched, the object obtained along with craving is ‘acquisition of form’. Thus, in the object that has been obtained, touching is contact, and experiencing is feeling. ‘Contact with form’ and ‘feeling born of contact with form’—this pair is obtained.' They also take up what is called the 'unmanifest section.' For the object may be enclosed by curtain-fences or covered by grass, leaves, and so on. For one who looks at it thinking, 'I have seen half of the object; I will see it well,' the perception that has arisen in that object is called 'perception of form'. The thoughts and so on that have arisen in it are to be understood as 'thoughts of form' and so on. Here too, perception, thought, contact, feeling, and desire may be obtained in a single impulsion-process or in different impulsion-processes, while fever, search, and acquisition are obtained only in different impulsion-processes. The tenth is self-evident. Thus ends the ninth and tenth discourses.

Nānattavaggo paṭhamo.

The First Chapter on Diversity.

2. Dutiyavaggo

2. The Second Chapter

1. Sattadhātusuttavaṇṇanā

1. Explanation of the Discourse on the Seven Elements

95. Dutiyavaggassa paṭhame ābhādhātūti ālokadhātu. Ālokassapi ālokakasiṇe parikammaṃ katvā uppannajjhānassāpīti sahārammaṇassa jhānassa etaṃ nāmaṃ. Subhadhātūti subhakasiṇe uppannajjhānavasena sahārammaṇajjhānameva[P 2.0135]. Ākāsānañcāyatanameva ākāsānañcāyatanadhātu. Saññāvedayitanirodhova saññāvedayitanirodhadhātu. Iti bhagavā anusandhikusalassa bhikkhuno tattha nisīditvā pañhaṃ pucchitukāmassa okāsaṃ dento desanaṃ niṭṭhāpesi.

95. In the first discourse of the second chapter, the ‘element of radiance’ is the element of light. This is a name for the jhāna together with its object, referring to the light kasiṇa and also to the jhāna that has arisen after performing the preliminary work on the light kasiṇa. The ‘element of the beautiful’ is precisely the jhāna together with its object, by means of the jhāna that has arisen in relation to the beautiful kasiṇa. The base of infinite space itself is the element of the base of infinite space. The very cessation of perception and feeling is the element of the cessation of perception and feeling. Thus, the Blessed One, wishing to grant an opportunity to a monk skilled in making connections who was sitting there and desired to ask a question, concluded the teaching at the level of a summary exposition.

Andhakāraṃ [V 2.0119] paṭiccāti andhakāro hi ālokena paricchinno, ālokopi andhakārena. Andhakārena hi so pākaṭo hoti. Tasmā “andhakāraṃ paṭicca paññāyatī”ti āha. Asubhaṃ paṭiccāti etthāpi eseva nayo. Asubhañhi subhena, subhañca asubhena paricchinnaṃ, asubhe sati subhaṃ paññāyati, tasmā evamāha. Rūpaṃ paṭiccāti rūpāvacarasamāpattiṃ paṭicca. Rūpāvacarasamāpattiyā hi sati ākāsānañcāyatanasamāpatti nāma [M 2.0125] hoti rūpasamatikkamo vā, tasmā evamāha. Viññāṇañcāyatanadhātuādīsupi eseva nayo. Nirodhaṃ paṭiccāti catunnaṃ khandhānaṃ paṭisaṅkhāappavattiṃ paṭicca. Khandhanirodhañhi paṭicca nirodhasamāpatti nāma paññāyati, na khandhapavattiṃ, tasmā evamāha. Ettha ca catunnaṃ khandhānaṃ nirodhova nirodhasamāpattīti veditabbo.

Regarding ‘dependent on darkness’: for darkness is demarcated by light, and light is also demarcated by darkness. Indeed, by darkness, that light becomes manifest. Therefore, He said, “It is known in dependence on darkness.” Regarding ‘dependent on the unattractive’: here too, this same method applies. For the unattractive is demarcated by the attractive, and the attractive by the unattractive. When the unattractive exists, the attractive is known. Therefore, He spoke thus. Regarding ‘dependent on form’: this means dependent on the form-sphere attainment. For when the form-sphere attainment exists, there is what is called the attainment of the base of infinite space, or there is the transcending of form. Therefore, He spoke thus. This same method also applies to the element of the base of infinite consciousness and so on. Regarding ‘dependent on cessation’: this means dependent on the non-occurrence of the four [mental] aggregates for a delimited period through reflective knowledge. For the attainment of cessation is known in dependence on the cessation of the aggregates, not on their occurrence. Therefore, He spoke thus. And here, the very cessation of the four [mental] aggregates should be understood as the attainment of cessation.

Kathaṃ samāpatti pattabbāti kathaṃ samāpattiyo kīdisā samāpattiyo nāma hutvā pattabbāti? Saññāsamāpatti pattabbāti saññāya atthibhāvena saññāsamāpattiyo saññāsamāpattiyo nāma hutvā pattabbā. Saṅkhārāvasesasamāpatti pattabbāti sukhumasaṅkhārānaṃ avasiṭṭhatāya saṅkhārāvasesasamāpatti nāma hutvā pattabbā. Nirodhasamāpatti pattabbāti nirodhova nirodhasamāpatti nirodhasamāpatti nāma hutvā pattabbāti attho. Paṭhamaṃ.

Regarding ‘How is attainment to be reached?’: This means, what kind of attainments are they, and how are they to be reached? Regarding ‘The attainment of perception is to be reached’: by the existence of perception, the attainments of perception are to be reached by being what are called the attainments of perception. Regarding ‘The attainment with residual formations is to be reached’: by the fact of subtle formations remaining, the attainment with residual formations is to be reached by being what is called the attainment with residual formations. Regarding ‘The attainment of cessation is to be reached’: the very cessation of the four mental aggregates, being what is called the attainment of cessation, is to be reached. This is the meaning. End of the first sutta.

2. Sanidānasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Discourse with a Cause

96. Dutiye sanidānanti bhāvanapuṃsakametaṃ, sanidāno sapaccayo hutvā uppajjatīti attho. Kāmadhātuṃ, bhikkhave, paṭiccāti ettha kāmavitakkopi kāmadhātu [P 2.0136] kāmāvacaradhammāpi, visesato sabbākusalampi. Yathāha –

96. In the second discourse, 'with a cause' (sanidānaṃ) is an abstract neuter noun. The meaning is that it arises having a cause, having a condition. In the phrase 'Dependent on the sense-sphere element, O bhikkhus,' sensual thought is also the sense-sphere element, as are phenomena of the sensual sphere, and especially all that is unwholesome. As it is said:

“Tattha katamā kāmadhātu? Kāmapaṭisaṃyutto takko vitakko saṅkappo appanā byappanā cetaso abhiniropanā micchāsaṅkappo, ayaṃ vuccati kāmadhātu. Heṭṭhato avīcinirayaṃ pariyantaṃ karitvā uparito paranimmitavasavattī deve antokaritvā yaṃ etasmiṃ antare etthāvacarā ettha pariyāpannā khandhadhātuāyatanā rūpā vedanā saññā saṅkhārā viññāṇaṃ, ayaṃ vuccati kāmadhātu. Sabbepi akusalā dhammā kāmadhātū”ti (vibha. 182).

“Herein, what is the sense-sphere element? Reasoning, thought, conception, application, sustained application, directing of the mind, and wrong conception connected with sensual desire—this is called the sense-sphere element. From below, making the Avīci hell the limit, and from above, including the Paranimmitavasavattī devas, whatever aggregates, elements, and sense bases that move about and are included within this interval—form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness—this is called the sense-sphere element. All unwholesome states are the sense-sphere element.”

Ettha [V 2.0120] sabbasaṅgāhikā asambhinnāti dve kathā honti. Kathaṃ? Kāmadhātuggahaṇena hi byāpādadhātuvihiṃsādhātuyo gahitā hontīti ayaṃ sabbasaṅgāhikā.
