Tāsaṃ pana dvinnaṃ dhātūnaṃ visuṃ āgatattā sesadhammā kāmadhātūti ayaṃ asambhinnakathā. Ayamidha gahetabbā imaṃ kāmadhātuṃ ārammaṇavasena vā sampayogavasena vā paṭicca kāmasaññā nāma uppajjati. Kāmasaññaṃ [M 2.0126] paṭiccāti kāmasaññaṃ pana sampayogavasena vā upanissayavasena vā paṭicca kāmasaṅkappo nāma uppajjati. Iminā nayena sabbapadesu attho veditabbo. Tīhi ṭhānehīti tīhi kāraṇehi. Micchā paṭipajjatīti ayāthāvapaṭipadaṃ aniyyānikapaṭipadaṃ paṭipajjati.

Here, there are two kinds of discussion: all-inclusive and unmixed. How so? Because by the taking up of the sense-sphere element, the elements of ill will and harmfulness are also taken up; this is the all-inclusive discussion. But because those two elements are presented separately, the remaining phenomena are the sense-sphere element; this is the unmixed discussion. This latter one should be understood here. Dependent on this sense-sphere element, either by way of object or by way of association, what is called sensual perception arises. In the phrase 'dependent on sensual perception,' it means that dependent on sensual perception, either by way of association or by way of decisive support condition, what is called sensual intention arises. In this way, the meaning should be understood in all passages. 'By three grounds' means by three reasons. 'He practices wrongly' means he practices a path that is not in accordance with reality, a path that does not lead to liberation.

Byāpādadhātuṃ, bhikkhaveti ettha byāpādavitakkopi byāpādadhātu byāpādopi. Yathāha –

In the phrase 'The element of ill will, O bhikkhus,' the thought of ill will is also the element of ill will, as is ill will itself. As it is said:

“Tattha katamā byāpādadhātu? Byāpādapaṭisaṃyutto takko vitakko…pe… ayaṃ vuccati byāpādadhātu. Dasasu āghātavatthūsu cittassa āghāto paṭivirodho kopo pakopo…pe… anattamanatā cittassa, ayaṃ vuccati byāpādadhātū”ti (vibha. 182).

“Herein, what is the element of ill will? Reasoning and thought connected with ill will… this is called the element of ill will. In regard to the ten grounds for resentment, resentment of the mind, opposition, anger, rage… displeasure of the mind—this is called the element of ill will.”

Imaṃ byāpādadhātuṃ sahajātapaccayādivasena paṭicca byāpādasaññā nāma uppajjati. Sesaṃ purimanayeneva veditabbaṃ.

Dependent on this element of ill will, by way of the co-nascence condition and so on, what is called the perception of ill will arises. The rest should be understood in the same way as before.

Vihiṃsādhātuṃ, bhikkhaveti ettha vihiṃsāvitakkopi vihiṃsādhātu vihiṃsāpi. Yathāha –

In the phrase 'The element of harmfulness, O bhikkhus,' the thought of harmfulness is also the element of harmfulness, as is harmfulness itself. As it is said:

“Tattha katamā vihiṃsādhātu? Vihiṃsāpaṭisaṃyutto takko vitakko…pe… ayaṃ vuccati vihiṃsādhātu. Idhekacco pāṇinā vā leḍḍunā [P 2.0137] vā daṇḍena vā satthena vā rajjuyā vā aññataraññatarena vā satte viheṭheti. Yā evarūpā heṭhanā viheṭhanā hiṃsanā vihiṃsanā rosanā parūpaghāto, ayaṃ vuccati vihiṃsādhātū”ti (vibha. 182).

“Herein, what is the element of harmfulness? Reasoning and thought connected with harmfulness... this is called the element of harmfulness. Herein, someone torments beings with their hand, with a clod of earth, with a stick, with a weapon, with a rope, or with some other such thing. Whatever such tormenting, injuring, harming, violence, vexing, or assault on others there is—this is called the element of harmfulness.”

Imaṃ vihiṃsādhātuṃ sahajātapaccayādivasena paṭicca vihiṃsāsaññā nāma uppajjati. Sesamidhāpi purimanayeneva veditabbaṃ.

Dependent on this element of harmfulness, by way of the co-nascence condition and so on, what is called the perception of harmfulness arises. Here too, the rest should be understood in the same way as before.

Tiṇadāyeti [V 2.0121] tiṇagahane araññe. Anayabyasananti avuḍḍhiṃ vināsaṃ. Evameva khoti ettha sukkhatiṇadāyo viya ārammaṇaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ, tiṇukkā viya akusalasaññā, tiṇakaṭṭhanissitā pāṇā viya ime sattā. Yathā sukkhatiṇadāye ṭhapitaṃ tiṇukkaṃ khippaṃ vāyamitvā anibbāpentassa te pāṇā anayabyasanaṃ pāpuṇanti. Evameva ye samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā [M 2.0127] uppannaṃ akusalasaññaṃ vikkhambhanatadaṅgasamucchedappahānehi nappajahanti, te dukkhaṃ viharanti.

‘In a grass thicket’ (tiṇadāye) means in a wilderness that is a thicket of grass. ‘Misfortune and ruin’ (anayabyasanaṃ) means decline and destruction. In the phrase ‘Just so,’ the object should be seen as like a dry grass thicket; the unwholesome perception as like a grass torch; and these beings as like creatures dependent on grass and sticks. Just as when a grass torch placed in a dry grass thicket is not quickly extinguished through effort, those creatures meet with misfortune and ruin, so too, those ascetics or brahmins who do not abandon an arisen unwholesome perception through suppression, temporary cutting off, and complete cutting off, dwell in suffering.

Visamagatanti rāgavisamādīni anugataṃ akusalasaññaṃ. Na khippameva pajahatīti vikkhambhanādivasena sīghaṃ nappajahati. Na vinodetīti na nīharati. Na byantīkarotīti bhaṅgamattampi anavasesento na vigatantaṃ karoti. Na anabhāvaṃ gametīti na anuabhāvaṃ gameti. Evaṃ sabbapadesu na – kāro āharitabbo. Pāṭikaṅkhāti pāṭikaṅkhitabbā icchitabbā.

‘Gone astray’ means an unwholesome perception that follows the unevenness of lust and so on. ‘Does not quickly abandon’ means one does not swiftly abandon it by means of suppression and so on. ‘Does not dispel’ means one does not remove it. ‘Does not make an end of it’ means one does not make it come to an end without leaving even a fragment remaining. ‘Does not bring to non-existence’ means one does not cause it to not arise anew. Thus, in all these passages, the negative particle 'na' should be supplied. ‘Is to be expected’ means it is to be expected, to be desired.

Nekkhammadhātuṃ, bhikkhaveti ettha nekkhammavitakkopi nekkhammadhātu sabbepi kusalā dhammā. Yathāha –

In the phrase 'The element of renunciation, O bhikkhus,' the thought of renunciation is also the element of renunciation, as are all wholesome states. As it is said:

“Tattha katamā nekkhammadhātu? Nekkhammapaṭisaṃyutto takko vitakko…pe… sammāsaṅkappo, ayaṃ vuccati nekkhammadhātū”ti (vibha. 182).

“Herein, what is the element of renunciation? Reasoning and thought connected with renunciation… right intention—this is called the element of renunciation.”

Idhāpi duvidhā kathā. Nekkhammadhātuggahaṇena hi itarāpi dve dhātuyo gahaṇaṃ gacchanti kusaladhammapariyāpannattā, ayaṃ sabbasaṅgāhikā. Tā pana dhātuyo visuṃ dīpetabbāti tā ṭhapetvā sesā sabbakusalā nekkhammadhātūti ayaṃ asambhinnā. Imaṃ nekkhammadhātuṃ sahajātādipaccayavasena paṭicca nekkhammasaññā nāma uppajjati. Saññādīni paṭicca vitakkādayo yathānurūpaṃ.

Here too, the discussion is twofold. By the taking up of the element of renunciation, the other two elements are also taken up because they are included in wholesome states; this is the all-inclusive discussion. But those elements should be explained separately. Therefore, having set them aside, all the remaining wholesome states are the element of renunciation; this is the unmixed discussion. Dependent on this element of renunciation, by way of co-nascent conditions and so on, what is called the perception of renunciation arises. Dependent on perception and so forth, thoughts and so forth arise in accordance with their respective conditions.

Abyāpādadhātuṃ, bhikkhaveti ettha abyāpādavitakkopi abyāpādadhātu abyāpādopi. Yathāha –

In the phrase 'The element of non-ill will, O bhikkhus,' the thought of non-ill will is also the element of non-ill will, as is non-ill will itself. As it is said:

“Tattha katamā abyāpādadhātu[P 2.0138]? Abyāpādapaṭisaṃyutto takko…pe… ayaṃ vuccati [V 2.0122] abyāpādadhātu. Yā sattesu metti mettāyanā mettāyitattaṃ mettācetovimutti, ayaṃ vuccati abyāpādadhātū”ti (vibha. 182).

“Herein, what is the element of non-ill will? Reasoning connected with non-ill will… this is called the element of non-ill will. Whatever loving-kindness towards beings, friendly manner, state of being friendly, and liberation of mind through loving-kindness there is—this is called the element of non-ill will.”

Imaṃ abyāpādadhātuṃ paṭicca vuttanayeneva abyāpādasaññā nāma uppajjati.

Dependent on this element of non-ill will, in the very manner that has been stated, what is called the perception of non-ill will arises.

Avihiṃsādhātuṃ, bhikkhaveti etthāpi avihiṃsāvitakkopi avihiṃsādhātu karuṇāpi. Yathāha –

In the phrase 'The element of non-harming, O bhikkhus,' here too, the thought of non-harming is also the element of non-harming, as is compassion itself. As it is said:

“Tattha [M 2.0128] katamā avihiṃsādhātu? Avihiṃsāpaṭisaṃyutto takko…pe… ayaṃ vuccati avihiṃsādhātu. Yā sattesu karuṇā karuṇāyanā karuṇāyitattaṃ karuṇācetovimutti, ayaṃ vuccati avihiṃsādhātū”ti (vibha. 182).

“Therein, what is the element of non-harming? Thought connected with non-harming… this is called the element of non-harming. That which is compassion for beings, the manner of compassion, the state of being compassionate, the mind-release of compassion—this is called the element of non-harming.”

Imaṃ avihiṃsādhātuṃ paṭicca vuttanayeneva avihiṃsāsaññā nāma uppajjati. Sesaṃ sabbattha vuttānusāreneva veditabbaṃ. Dutiyaṃ.

Dependent on this element of non-harming, in the manner already stated, there arises what is called the perception of non-harming. The rest should be understood everywhere in accordance with what has been said. The Second.

3. Giñjakāvasathasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Giñjakāvasatha Sutta

97. Tatiye dhātuṃ, bhikkhaveti ito paṭṭhāya ajjhāsayaṃ dhātūti dīpeti. Uppajjati saññāti ajjhāsayaṃ paṭicca saññā uppajjati, diṭṭhi uppajjati, vitakko uppajjatīti. Idhāpi “kaccāno pañhaṃ pucchissatī”ti tassa okāsadānatthaṃ ettāvatāva desanaṃ niṭṭhāpesi. Asammāsambuddhesūti chasu satthāresu. Sammāsambuddhāti mayamasma sammāsambuddhāti. Kiṃ paṭicca paññāyatīti kismiṃ sati hotīti? Satthārānaṃ uppannaṃ diṭṭhiṃ pucchati. Asammāsambuddhesu tesu sammāsambuddhā eteti evaṃ uppannaṃ titthiyasāvakānampi diṭṭhiṃ pucchatiyeva.

97. In the third sutta, with the words 'element, bhikkhus,' from this point onwards, he clarifies 'element' as inclination. As for 'perception arises,' this means that dependent on inclination, perception arises, view arises, and thought arises. Here too, thinking, 'Kaccāna will ask a question,' he concluded the discourse at just this point in order to give him the opportunity. 'Regarding the unsammāsambuddhas' refers to the six teachers. As for 'Sammāsambuddhas,' this refers to their claim, 'We are Sammāsambuddhas.' As for 'On what basis is it known?,' this means, 'When what exists, does it occur?' He asks about the view that has arisen in the teachers. Regarding those unsammāsambuddhas, he also asks about the view that has arisen even among the disciples of the sectarians, namely, 'These are Sammāsambuddhas.'

Idāni yasmā tesaṃ avijjādhātuṃ paṭicca sā diṭṭhi hoti, avijjādhātu ca nāma mahatī dhātu, tasmā mahatiṃ dhātuṃ paṭicca tassā uppattiṃ dīpento mahatī kho esātiādimāha. Hīnaṃ, kaccāna, dhātuṃ paṭiccāti hīnaṃ ajjhāsayaṃ paṭicca. Paṇidhīti cittaṭṭhapanaṃ. Sā panesā itthibhāvaṃ vā makkaṭāditiracchānabhāvaṃ vā patthentassa uppajjati. Hīno [V 2.0123][P 2.0139] puggaloti yassete hīnā dhammā uppajjanti, sabbo so puggalopi hīno nāma. Hīnā vācāti yā tassa vācā, sāpi hīnā. Hīnaṃ ācikkhatīti so ācikkhantopi hīnameva ācikkhati, desentopi hīnameva desetīti sabbapadāni yojetabbāni. Upapattīti dve upapattiyo paṭilābho ca nibbatti ca. Nibbatti hīnakulādivasena veditabbā, paṭilābho cittuppādakkhaṇe hīnattikavasena. Kathaṃ? Tassa hi pañcasu nīcakulesu uppajjanato hīnā nibbatti, vessasuddakulesu uppajjanato majjhimā, khattiyabrāhmaṇakulesu uppajjanato paṇītā. Dvādasākusalacittuppādānaṃ pana paṭilābhato [M 2.0129] hīno paṭilābho, tebhūmakadhammānaṃ paṭilābhato majjhimo, navalokuttaradhammānaṃ paṭilābhato paṇīto. Imasmiṃ pana ṭhāne nibbattiyeva adhippetāti. Tatiyaṃ.

Now, because for them that view arises dependent on the element of ignorance, and the element of ignorance is a great element, therefore, showing its arising as dependent on a great element, the Blessed One said the words beginning with, 'This is indeed great….' 'Dependent on a low element, Kaccāna' means dependent on a low inclination. 'Resolution' is the placing of the mind. Moreover, this arises in one who longs for female existence or the existence of animals such as monkeys. 'A low person' means that one in whom these low states arise, that person is indeed called low. 'Low speech' means that whatever speech one has, that too is low. 'He declares what is low' means that even when explaining, he declares only what is low; when teaching, he teaches only what is low. All these terms should be connected accordingly. As for 'arising,' there are two kinds of arising: acquisition and generation. Generation should be understood by way of birth in a low family and so forth, while acquisition should be understood by way of the low triad at the moment of the arising of consciousness. How so? For that person, being born in the five inferior families is low generation; being born in the families of merchants and farmers is middling; being born in the families of nobles and brahmins is excellent. As for acquisition, the acquisition of the twelve unwholesome consciousnesses is low acquisition; the acquisition of the states of the three planes is middling; the acquisition of the nine supramundane states is excellent. However, in this context, only generation is intended. The Third.

4. Hīnādhimuttikasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Discourse on Those of Inferior Inclination

98. Catutthe saṃsandantīti ekato honti. Samentīti samāgacchanti, nirantarā honti. Hīnādhimuttikāti hīnajjhāsayā. Kalyāṇādhimuttikāti kalyāṇajjhāsayā. Catutthaṃ.

98. In the fourth discourse, 'saṃsandanti' means they come together with the same disposition. 'Samenti' means they come together; they are without interval. 'Hīnādhimuttikā' means those of inferior disposition. 'Kalyāṇādhimuttikā' means those of noble disposition. The Fourth.

5. Caṅkamasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Discourse on Walking Meditation

99. Pañcame passatha noti passatha nu. Sabbe kho eteti sāriputtatthero bhagavatā “etadaggaṃ, bhikkhave, mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ mahāpaññānaṃ yadidaṃ sāriputto”ti (a. ni. 1.189) mahāpaññesu etadagge ṭhapito. Iti naṃ “khandhantaraṃ dhātvantaraṃ āyatanantaraṃ satipaṭṭhānabodhipakkhiyadhammantaraṃ tilakkhaṇāhataṃ gambhīraṃ pañhaṃ pucchissāmā”ti mahāpaññāva parivārenti. Sopi tesaṃ pathaviṃ pattharento viya sinerupādato vālikaṃ uddharanto viya cakkavāḷapabbataṃ bhindanto viya sineruṃ ukkhipanto viya ākāsaṃ vitthārento viya candimasūriye uṭṭhāpento viya ca pucchitapucchitaṃ katheti. Tena vuttaṃ “sabbe kho ete, bhikkhave, bhikkhū mahāpaññā”ti.

99. In the fifth discourse, passatha no means passatha nu. Sabbe kho ete (all these): The Venerable Sāriputta was placed by the Blessed One at the foremost position among those of great wisdom, [as stated in the passage,] “Foremost, bhikkhus, among my bhikkhu disciples who are of great wisdom is this Sāriputta.” Therefore, thinking, “We will ask him profound questions, struck by the three characteristics, concerning the analysis of the aggregates, the analysis of the elements, the analysis of the sense bases, and the analysis of the foundations of mindfulness and the factors of enlightenment,” only those of great wisdom surrounded him. And he, like one spreading out the earth, like one extracting sand from the foot of Mount Sineru, like one splitting the Cakkavāḷa mountain, like one lifting Mount Sineru, like one expanding the sky, and like one causing the sun and moon to rise, would answer every question that was asked. For that reason, it was said: “All these bhikkhus, bhikkhus, are of great wisdom.”

Mahāmoggallānopi bhagavatā “etadaggaṃ, bhikkhave, mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ iddhimantānaṃ yadidaṃ mahāmoggallāno”ti [P 2.0140] iddhimantesu etadagge ṭhapito. Iti naṃ “parikammaṃ ānisaṃsaṃ [V 2.0124] adhiṭṭhānaṃ vikubbanaṃ pucchissāmā”ti iddhimantova parivārenti. Sopi tesaṃ vuttanayeneva pucchitapucchitaṃ katheti. Tena vuttaṃ “sabbe kho ete, bhikkhave, bhikkhū mahiddhikā”ti.

The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna was also placed by the Blessed One at the foremost position among those endowed with psychic power, [as stated in the passage,] “Foremost, bhikkhus, among my bhikkhu disciples who are endowed with psychic power is this Mahāmoggallāna.” Therefore, thinking, “We will ask him about the preparatory work, the benefit, the determination, and the transformation,” only those endowed with psychic power surrounded him. And he, in the very manner already described, would answer every question that was asked. For that reason, it was said: “All these bhikkhus, bhikkhus, are of great psychic power.”

Mahākassapopi bhagavatā “etadaggaṃ, bhikkhave, mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ dhutavādānaṃ yadidaṃ mahākassapo”ti dhutavādesu etadagge ṭhapito. Iti naṃ “dhutaṅgaparihāraṃ ānisaṃsaṃ samodhānaṃ adhiṭṭhānaṃ bhedaṃ pucchissāmā”ti dhutavādāva parivārenti. Sopi tesaṃ tatheva pucchitapucchitaṃ byākaroti. Tena vuttaṃ “sabbe kho ete, bhikkhave, bhikkhū dhutavādā”ti.

The Venerable Mahākassapa was also placed by the Blessed One at the foremost position among the advocates of ascetic practices, [as stated in the passage,] “Foremost, bhikkhus, among my bhikkhu disciples who are advocates of ascetic practices is this Mahākassapa.” Therefore, thinking, “We will ask him about the observance of the ascetic practices, their benefits, their combination, their determination, and their distinctions,” only the advocates of ascetic practices surrounded him. And he, in that same way, would explain every question that was asked. For that reason, it was said: “All these bhikkhus, bhikkhus, are advocates of ascetic practices.”

Anuruddhattheropi [M 2.0130] bhagavatā “etadaggaṃ, bhikkhave, mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ dibbacakkhukānaṃ yadidaṃ anuruddho”ti (a. ni. 1.192) dibbacakkhukesu etadagge ṭhapito. Iti naṃ “dibbacakkhussa parikammaṃ ānisaṃsaṃ upakkilesaṃ pucchissāmā”ti dibbacakkhukāva parivārenti. Sopi tesaṃ tatheva pucchitapucchitaṃ katheti. Tena vuttaṃ “sabbe kho ete, bhikkhave, bhikkhū dibbacakkhukā”ti.

The Venerable Anuruddha was also placed by the Blessed One at the foremost position among those who possess the divine eye, [as stated in the passage,] “Foremost, bhikkhus, among my bhikkhu disciples who possess the divine eye is this Anuruddha.” Therefore, thinking, “We will ask him about the preparatory work, the benefit, and the defilements of the divine eye,” only those who possess the divine eye surrounded him. And he, in that same way, would answer every question that was asked. For that reason, it was said: “All these bhikkhus, bhikkhus, possess the divine eye.”

Puṇṇattheropi bhagavatā “etadaggaṃ, bhikkhave, mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ dhammakathikānaṃ yadidaṃ puṇṇo mantāṇiputto”ti (a. ni. 1.196) dhammakathikesu etadagge ṭhapito. Iti naṃ “dhammakathāya saṅkhepavitthāragambhīruttānavicitrakathādīsu taṃ taṃ ākāraṃ pucchissāmā”ti dhammakathikāva parivārenti. Sopi tesaṃ “āvuso, dhammakathikena nāma ādito parisaṃ vaṇṇetuṃ vaṭṭati, majjhe suññataṃ pakāsetuṃ, ante catusaccavasena kūṭaṃ gaṇhitu”nti evaṃ taṃ taṃ dhammakathānayaṃ ācikkhati. Tena vuttaṃ “sabbe kho ete, bhikkhave, bhikkhū dhammakathikā”ti.

The Venerable Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta was also placed by the Blessed One at the foremost position among Dhamma speakers, [as stated in the passage,] “Foremost, bhikkhus, among my bhikkhu disciples who are Dhamma speakers is this Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta.” Therefore, thinking, “We will ask him about this and that aspect of Dhamma teaching, such as being concise, detailed, profound, plain, and varied,” only Dhamma speakers surrounded him. And he would instruct them on this and that method of Dhamma teaching, saying: “Friends, a Dhamma speaker, so-called, should at the beginning praise the assembly, in the middle, he should explain emptiness, and at the end, he should grasp the pinnacle by means of the Four Truths.” For that reason, it was said: “All these bhikkhus, bhikkhus, are Dhamma speakers.”

Upālittheropi bhagavatā “etadaggaṃ, bhikkhave, mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ vinayadharānaṃ yadidaṃ upālī”ti (a. ni. 1.228) vinayadharesu etadagge ṭhapito. Iti naṃ “garukalahukaṃ satekicchaatekicchaṃ āpattānāpattiṃ pucchissāmā”ti vinayadharāva parivārenti. Sopi tesaṃ pucchitapucchitaṃ tatheva [P 2.0141] katheti. Tena vuttaṃ “sabbe kho ete, bhikkhave, bhikkhū vinayadharā”ti.

The Venerable Upāli was also placed by the Blessed One at the foremost position among the upholders of the Vinaya, [as stated in the passage,] “Foremost, bhikkhus, among my bhikkhu disciples who are upholders of the Vinaya is this Upāli.” Therefore, thinking, “We will ask him about grave and light offenses, remediable and irremediable offenses, and what is an offense and what is not an offense,” only the upholders of the Vinaya surrounded him. And he, in that same way, would answer every question that was asked. For that reason, it was said: “All these bhikkhus, bhikkhus, are upholders of the Vinaya.”

Ānandattheropi [V 2.0125] bhagavatā “etadaggaṃ, bhikkhave, mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ bahussutānaṃ yadidaṃ ānando”ti (a. ni. 1.223) bahussutesu etadagge ṭhapito. Iti naṃ “dasavidhaṃ byañjanabuddhiṃ aṭṭhuppattiṃ anusandhiṃ pubbāparaṃ pucchissāmā”ti bahussutāva parivārenti. Sopi tesaṃ “idaṃ evaṃ vattabbaṃ, idaṃ evaṃ gahetabba”nti sabbaṃ katheti. Tena vuttaṃ “sabbe kho ete, bhikkhave, bhikkhū bahussutā”ti.

The Venerable Ānanda was also placed by the Blessed One at the foremost position among the learned, [as stated in the passage,] “Foremost, bhikkhus, among my bhikkhu disciples who are learned is this Ānanda.” Therefore, thinking, “We will ask him about the tenfold verbal intelligence, the occasion of arising of the teachings, the connections, and the sequence of what precedes and follows,” only the learned surrounded him. And he would explain everything, saying, “This should be recited thus; this should be understood thus.” For that reason, it was said: “All these bhikkhus, bhikkhus, are learned.”

Devadatto pana pāpiccho icchāpakato, tena naṃ “kulasaṅgaṇhanaparihāraṃ nānappakārakaṃ kohaññataṃ pucchissāmā”ti pāpicchāva parivārenti. Sopi tesaṃ taṃ taṃ niyāmaṃ ācikkhati. Tena vuttaṃ “sabbe kho ete, bhikkhave, bhikkhū pāpicchā”ti.

Devadatta, however, was of evil desires and overcome by wishes. For that reason, thinking, “We will ask him about the procedure for ingratiating oneself with families and various kinds of deceit,” only those of evil desires surrounded him. And he would explain to them this and that method. For that reason, it was said: “All these bhikkhus, bhikkhus, are of evil desires.”

Kasmā [M 2.0131] panete avidūre caṅkamiṃsūti. “Devadatto satthari paduṭṭhacitto anatthampi kātuṃ upakkameyyā”ti ārakkhaggahaṇatthaṃ. Atha devadatto kasmā caṅkamīti? “Akārako ayaṃ, yadi kārako bhaveyya, na idha āgaccheyyā”ti attano katadosapaṭicchādanatthaṃ. Kiṃ pana devadatto bhagavato anatthaṃ kātuṃ samattho, bhagavato vā ārakkhakiccaṃ atthīti? Natthi. Tena vuttaṃ “aṭṭhānametaṃ, ānanda, anavakāso, yaṃ tathāgato parūpakkamena parinibbāyeyyā”ti (cūḷava. 341). Bhikkhū pana satthari gāravena āgatā. Teneva bhagavā evaṃ vatvā “vissajjehi, ānanda, bhikkhusaṅgha”nti vissajjāpesi. Pañcamaṃ.

But why did these elders walk back and forth nearby? It was for the purpose of taking up guard, thinking, “Devadatta, with a mind corrupted towards the Teacher, might endeavor to do harm.” Then why did Devadatta walk back and forth? It was to conceal the fault he had committed, thinking, “This one is not a perpetrator; if he were a perpetrator, he would not have come here.” But is Devadatta capable of doing harm to the Blessed One, or is there a need for the Blessed One to be guarded? There is not. Therefore, it was said: “It is impossible, Ānanda, it is not a possibility that the Tathāgata should attain final Nibbāna through the endeavor of another.” The bhikkhus, however, had come out of respect for the Teacher. For that very reason, the Blessed One, having spoken thus, had them dismissed, saying, “Dismiss, Ānanda, the community of bhikkhus.” The fifth.

6. Sagāthāsuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Sagātha Sutta

100. Chaṭṭhe gūtho gūthena saṃsandati sametīti samuddantare janapadantare cakkavāḷantare ṭhitopi vaṇṇenapi gandhenapi rasenapi nānattaṃ anupagacchanto saṃsandati sameti, ekasadisova hoti nirantaro. Sesesupi eseva nayo. Ayaṃ pana aniṭṭhaupamā hīnajjhāsayānaṃ hīnaajjhāsayassa sarikkhabhāvadassanatthaṃ āhaṭā, khīrādivisiṭṭhopamā kalyāṇajjhāsayānaṃ ajjhāsayassa sarikkhabhāvadassanatthaṃ.

100. In the sixth sutta, as for ‘excrement merges and unites with excrement’: even if it is on the other side of an ocean, another country, or another world-system, not becoming different in color, smell, or taste, it associates and unites; it becomes exactly the same, without distinction. In the remaining cases, such as urine and spittle, this same method applies. This undesirable simile of excrement and so on was brought forth by the Blessed One to show the state of similarity of the disposition for those with inferior dispositions; the desirable simile of preparations such as ghee was brought forth to show the state of similarity of the disposition for those with noble dispositions.

Saṃsaggāti [P 2.0142] dassanasavanasaṃsaggādivatthukena taṇhāsnehena. Vanatho jātoti kilesavanaṃ jātaṃ[V 2.0126]. Asaṃsaggena chijjatīti ekato ṭhānanisajjādīni akarontassa asaṃsaggena adassanena chijjati. Sādhujīvīti parisuddhajīvitaṃ jīvamāno. Sahāvaseti sahavāsaṃ vaseyya. Chaṭṭhaṃ.

‘Through association’ means: through the adhesive of craving which is based on association through seeing, association through hearing, and so on. ‘The thicket is born’ means: the forest of defilements is born. ‘It is cut off through non-association’ means: for one who does not perform postures such as standing and sitting together, it is cut off through non-association, through not seeing. ‘One who lives well’ means: one who lives a purified livelihood. ‘One should dwell with’ means: one should dwell together. The sixth.

7. Assaddhasaṃsandanasuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Assaddhasaṃsandana Sutta

101. Sattame assaddhā assaddhehītiādīsu buddhe vā dhamme vā saṅghe vā saddhāvirahitā nirojā nirasā puggalā samuddassa orimatīre ṭhitā pārimatīrepi ṭhitehi assaddhehi saddhiṃ tāya assaddhatāya ekasadisā nirantarā honti. Tathā ahirikā bhinnamariyādā alajjipuggalā ahirikehi, anottappino pāpakiriyāya abhāyamānā anottappīhi, appassutā sutavirahitā appassutehi, kusītā ālasiyapuggalā [M 2.0132] kusītehi, muṭṭhassatino bhattanikkhittakākamaṃsanikkhittasiṅgālasadisā muṭṭhassatīhi, duppaññā khandhādiparicchedikāya paññāya abhāvena nippaññā tādiseheva duppaññehi, saddhāsampannā cetiyavandanādikiccapasutā saddhehi, hirimanā lajjipuggalā hirimanehi, ottappino pāpabhīrukā ottappīhi, bahussutā sutadharā āgamadharā tantipālakā vaṃsānurakkhakā bahussutehi, āraddhavīriyā paripuṇṇaparakkamā āraddhavīriyehi, upaṭṭhitassatī sabbakiccapariggāhikāya satiyā samannāgatā upaṭṭhitassatīhi, paññavanto mahāpaññehi vajirūpamañāṇehi paññavantehi saddhiṃ dūre ṭhitāpi tāya paññāsampattiyā saṃsandanti samenti. Sattamaṃ.

101. In the seventh sutta, in passages such as ‘the faithless with the faithless’: persons who are devoid of faith in the Buddha, the Dhamma, or the Saṅgha, who are without the nutritive essence of faith and without the taste of faith, though standing on this shore of the ocean, are, by that very faithlessness, exactly the same as and without distinction from the faithless who stand on the far shore. Likewise, the shameless, who have broken the boundary of moral shame, the unscrupulous persons, are exactly the same as and without distinction from the shameless. Those without fear of wrongdoing, who are not afraid of evil action, are exactly the same as and without distinction from those without fear of wrongdoing. The unlearned, devoid of learning, are exactly the same as and without distinction from the unlearned. The lazy, indolent persons, are exactly the same as and without distinction from the lazy. The unmindful, who are like a crow that has dropped its rice or a jackal that has dropped its meat, are exactly the same as and without distinction from the unmindful. The unwise, who are without wisdom due to the absence of the wisdom that discerns the aggregates and so on, are exactly the same as and without distinction from such unwise persons. Those endowed with faith, who are devoted to duties such as venerating cetiyas, though they may be far away, associate and unite with the faithful through that very accomplishment in faith. Those with a sense of shame, scrupulous persons, associate with those with a sense of shame. Those with fear of wrongdoing, who are afraid of evil, associate and unite with those with fear of wrongdoing. The very learned—who are bearers of the teachings, bearers of the scriptures, guardians of the tradition, and protectors of the noble lineage—associate and unite with the very learned. Those of aroused energy, of perfected effort, associate and unite with those of aroused energy. Those of established mindfulness, endowed with the mindfulness that comprehends all duties, associate and unite with those of established mindfulness. The wise, together with the wise who possess great wisdom and knowledge like a diamond, though they stand far apart, associate and unite through that very accomplishment in wisdom. The seventh.

8-12. Assaddhamūlakasuttādivaṇṇanā

8-12. Commentary on the Discourses Rooted in Lack of Faith, and the Like

102-106. Aṭṭhamādīni teyeva assaddhādidhamme tikavasena katvā desitāni. Tattha aṭṭhame assaddhādimūlakā kaṇhapakkhasukkapakkhavasena pañca tikā vuttā, navame ahirikamūlakā cattāro. Dasame [P 2.0143] anottappamūlakā tayo, ekādasame appassutamūlakā dve, dvādasame kusītamūlako eko tiko vuttoti sabbepi pañcasu suttantesu pannarasa tikā honti. Pannarasa cete suttantātipi vadanti. Ayaṃ tikapeyyālo nāma. Aṭṭhamādīni.

102-106. The eighth and following five suttas were taught by formulating those very same qualities—faithlessness and so on—by way of triads. Therein, in the eighth, five triads rooted in faithlessness and so on are stated by way of the dark side and the bright side. In the ninth, four triads are rooted in shamelessness. In the tenth, three are rooted in lack of moral dread. In the eleventh, two are rooted in little learning. In the twelfth, one triad is rooted in laziness. Thus, in all five suttas, there are fifteen triads. And the teachers also say that these fifteen are suttas. This is called the Peyyāla of Triads. The eighth and following.

Dutiyo vaggo.

The Second Chapter.

3. Kammapathavaggo

3. The Chapter on the Courses of Action

1-2. Asamāhitasuttādivaṇṇanā

1-2. Commentary on the Discourses Beginning with the Unconcentrated

107-108. Ito [V 2.0127] paresu paṭhamaṃ assaddhādipañcakavasena vuttaṃ, tathā dutiyaṃ. Paṭhame pana asamāhitapadaṃ catutthaṃ, dutiye dussīlapadaṃ. Evaṃ vuccamāne bujjhanakapuggalānaṃ ajjhāsayena hi etāni vuttāni. Ettha asamāhitāti upacārappanāsamādhirahitā. Dussīlāti nissīlā. Paṭhamadutiyāni.

107-108. Hereafter, the first sutta is stated by way of the pentad beginning with faithlessness, and likewise the second. But in the first, the fourth term is 'unconcentrated'; in the second, the fourth term is 'immoral'. For these suttas were spoken in this way according to the disposition of persons capable of understanding. Herein, 'unconcentrated' means devoid of access concentration and absorption concentration. 'Immoral' means without morality. The first and second suttas.

3-5. Pañcasikkhāpadasuttādivaṇṇanā

3-5. Commentary on the Discourses Beginning with the Five Precepts

109-111. Tatiyaṃ [M 2.0133] pañcakammapathavasena bujjhanakānaṃ ajjhāsayavasena vuttaṃ, catutthaṃ sattakammapathavasena, pañcamaṃ dasakammapathavasena. Tattha tatiye surāmerayamajjappamādaṭṭhāyinoti surāmerayasaṅkhātaṃ majjaṃ yāya pamādacetanāya pivanti, sā “surāmerayamajjappamādo”ti vuccati, tasmiṃ tiṭṭhantīti surāmerayamajjappamādaṭṭhāyino. Ayaṃ tāvettha asādhāraṇapadassa attho.

109-111. The third sutta was spoken by way of the five courses of action, the fourth by way of the seven courses of action, and the fifth by way of the ten courses of action, according to the disposition of those capable of understanding. Therein, in the third, regarding the term 'one who partakes of surā, meraya, and majja, which are a basis for heedlessness' (surāmerayamajjappamādaṭṭhāyino): the intoxicant known as surā and meraya—with whatever negligent volition one drinks it, that volition is called 'surā-meraya-majja-ppamāda'. Because they stand (tiṭṭhanti) in that, they are called surāmerayamajjappamādaṭṭhāyino. This, for now, is the meaning of the unique term herein.

Pañcame pāṇaṃ atipātentīti pāṇātipātino, pāṇaghātikāti attho. Adinnaṃ ādiyantīti adinnādāyino, parassahārinoti attho. Vatthukāmesu kilesakāmena micchā carantīti kāmesumicchācārino. Musā vadantīti musāvādino[P 2.0144], paresaṃ atthabhañjakaṃ tucchaṃ alikaṃ vācaṃ bhāsitāroti attho. Pisuṇā vācā etesanti pisuṇavācā. Mammacchedikā pharusā vācā etesanti pharusavācā. Samphaṃ niratthakaṃ vacanaṃ palapantīti samphappalāpino. Abhijjhāyantīti abhijjhāluno, parabhaṇḍe lubbhanasīlāti attho. Byāpannaṃ pūtibhūtaṃ cittametesanti byāpannacittā. Micchā pāpikā viññugarahitā etesaṃ diṭṭhīti micchādiṭṭhikā, kammapathapariyāpannāya “natthi dinna”ntiādivatthukāya micchattapariyāpannāya aniyyānikadiṭṭhiyā samannāgatāti attho. Sammā sobhanā viññupasatthā etesaṃ diṭṭhīti sammādiṭṭhikā, kammapathapariyāpannāya “atthi dinna”ntiādikāya kammassakatadiṭṭhiyā sammattapariyāpannāya maggadiṭṭhiyā ca samannāgatāti attho. Idaṃ tāvettha anuttānānaṃ padānaṃ padavaṇṇanāmattaṃ.

In the fifth sutta: because they destroy a living being (pāṇaṃ atipātenti), they are destroyers of life (pāṇātipātino); the meaning is killers of life (pāṇaghātikā). Because they take what is not given (adinnaṃ ādiyanti), they are takers of what is not given (adinnādāyino); the meaning is those who steal another's property (parassahārino). Because they engage wrongly (micchā caranti) in sensual pleasures (vatthukāmesu) with defiled desire (kilesakāmena), they are those who engage in sexual misconduct (kāmesumicchācārino). Because they speak falsely (musā vadanti), they are speakers of falsehood (musāvādino); the meaning is those who speak words that are destructive of others' welfare, empty, and untrue. Because they have divisive speech (pisuṇā vācā etesaṃ), they are called pisuṇavācā. Because they have harsh speech that cuts to the quick (mammacchedikā pharusā vācā etesaṃ), they are called pharusavācā. Because they prattle (palapanti) frivolous (samphaṃ), meaningless speech (niratthakaṃ vacanaṃ), they are idle chatterers (samphappalāpino). Because they covet (abhijjhāyanti), they are covetous (abhijjhāluno); the meaning is that they are by nature greedy for another's property. Because they have a corrupt, putrid mind (byāpannaṃ pūtibhūtaṃ cittam etesaṃ), they are those with a mind of ill will (byāpannacittā). Because their view is wrong, evil, and censured by the wise (micchā pāpikā viññugarahitā etesaṃ diṭṭhi), they are holders of wrong view (micchādiṭṭhikā); the meaning is that they are endowed with a wrong view that does not lead out of saṃsāra, which is included in the state of wrongness, has as its basis 'there is nothing given,' etc., and is included in the courses of action. Because their view is right, beautiful, and praised by the wise (sammā sobhanā viññupasatthā etesaṃ diṭṭhi), they are holders of right view (sammādiṭṭhikā); the meaning is that they are endowed with the view of the ownership of kamma, which has as its basis 'there is what is given,' etc., and is included in the courses of action, and with the path-view, which is included in the state of rightness. This, for now, is merely an explanation of the terms for these unobvious words.

Yo [V 2.0128] pana tesaṃ pāṇātipāto adinnādānaṃ kāmesumicchācāro musāvādo pisuṇavācā pharusavācā samphappalāpo abhijjhā byāpādo micchādiṭṭhīti kaṇhapakkhe dasavidho attho hoti. Tattha pāṇassa atipāto pāṇātipāto, pāṇavadho pāṇaghātoti vuttaṃ hoti. Pāṇoti cettha vohārato satto, paramatthato jīvitindriyaṃ. Tasmiṃ pana pāṇe pāṇasaññino jīvitindriyupacchedakaupakkamasamuṭṭhāpikā kāyavacīdvārānaṃ aññataradvārappavattā vadhakacetanā pāṇātipāto. So guṇavirahitesu tiracchānagatādīsu pāṇesu khuddake pāṇe appasāvajjo, mahāsarīre mahāsāvajjo. Kasmā? Payogamahantatāya[M 2.0134], payogasamattepi vatthumahantatāya. Guṇavantesu manussādīsu appaguṇe appasāvajjo, mahāguṇe mahāsāvajjo. Sarīraguṇānaṃ pana samabhāve sati kilesānaṃ upakkamānañca mudutāya appasāvajjo, tibbatāya mahāsāvajjoti veditabbo.

Now, the meaning of the tenfold dark side is as follows: destroying life, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, idle chatter, covetousness, ill will, and wrong view. Therein, the destruction (atipāto) of a living being (pāṇassa) is destroying life (pāṇātipāto); this is said to mean the killing of a being, the slaying of a being. Herein, 'pāṇa' is conventionally a being; in the ultimate sense, it is the life faculty. With regard to that being, the volition to kill (vadhakacetanā) that arises in one who perceives it as a living being, which instigates the effort that cuts off the life faculty, and which proceeds through one of the two doors of body or speech, is 'destroying life'. That offense, with regard to beings devoid of virtue, such as animals, is of little blame in the case of a small being, and of great blame in the case of a large-bodied being. Why? Because of the greatness of the effort; or, even when the effort is the same, because of the greatness of the object. Among virtuous beings, such as humans, it is of little blame in the case of one of little virtue, and of great blame in the case of one of great virtue. But when the physical and virtuous qualities are equal, it should be understood that it is of little blame due to the mildness of the defilements and the effort, and of great blame due to their intensity.

Tassa pañca sambhārā honti – pāṇo, pāṇasaññitā, vadhakacittaṃ, upakkamo, tena maraṇanti. Cha payogā sāhatthiko, āṇattiko, nissaggiyo, thāvaro, vijjāmayo, iddhimayoti. Imasmiṃ panatthe vitthāriyamāne atippapañco hoti, tasmā taṃ [P 2.0145] na vitthārayāma, aññañca evarūpaṃ. Atthikehi pana samantapāsādikaṃ vinayaṭṭhakathaṃ (pārā. aṭṭha. 172) oloketvā gahetabbo.

Its components are five: a living being, the perception of it as a living being, the intention to kill, the effort, and death as a result of that. The means of execution are six: by one's own hand (sāhatthika), by command (āṇattika), by missile (nissaggiya), by a fixed device (thāvara), by knowledge or spells (vijjāmaya), and by psychic power (iddhimaya). But to elaborate on this matter here would be too much of a proliferation; therefore, we do not elaborate on it, nor on anything else of this kind. However, those who are interested should understand it by consulting the Vinaya commentary, the Samantapāsādikā.

Adinnassa ādānaṃ adinnādānaṃ, parassaharaṇaṃ theyyaṃ corikāti vuttaṃ hoti. Tattha adinnanti parapariggahitaṃ, yattha paro yathākāmakāritaṃ āpajjanto adaṇḍāraho anupavajjo hoti. Tasmiṃ pana parapariggahite parapariggahitasaññino tadādāyakaupakkamasamuṭṭhāpikā theyyacetanā adinnādānaṃ. Taṃ hīne parasantake appasāvajjaṃ, paṇīte mahāsāvajjaṃ. Kasmā? Vatthupaṇītatāya. Vatthusamatte sati guṇādhikānaṃ santake vatthusmiṃ mahāsāvajjaṃ, taṃ taṃ guṇādhikaṃ upādāya tato tato hīnaguṇassa santake vatthusmiṃ appasāvajjaṃ.

The taking (ādānaṃ) of what is not given (adinnassa) is taking what is not given (adinnādāna); it is said to mean the carrying away of another's property, theft, or robbery. Herein, 'what is not given' means what is possessed by another, with regard to which that other person, in acting as they please, is not liable to punishment and is not blameworthy. With regard to such property possessed by another, the volition to steal (theyyacetanā)—which arises in one who perceives it as possessed by another and which initiates the effort to take it—is taking what is not given. That offense is of little blame in the case of another's inferior property, and of great blame in the case of superior property. Why? Because of the superiority of the object. When the objects are of equal value, the offense is of great blame in the case of an object belonging to those of superior virtue; and in relation to those of superior virtue, it is of little blame in the case of an object belonging to one of lesser virtue.

Tassa pañca sambhārā honti – parapariggahitaṃ, parapariggahitasaññitā, theyyacittaṃ, upakkamo, tena haraṇanti. Cha payogā sāhatthikādayova. Te ca kho yathānurūpaṃ theyyāvahāro, pasayhāvahāro, paṭicchannāvahāro, parikappāvahāro, kusāvahāroti imesaṃ avahārānaṃ vasena pavattāti ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthāro pana samantapāsādikāyaṃ (pārā. aṭṭha. 92) vutto.

Of this, there are five components: an object belonging to another, the perception that it belongs to another, the intention to steal, the effort, and taking it away by that effort. There are six methods, which are those beginning with acting with one's own hand. And these, indeed, proceed in accordance with what is appropriate, by way of these types of taking: theft by stealth, theft by force, theft by concealment, theft by planning, and theft by fraud. This is the summary here; the detailed explanation, however, is stated in the Samantapāsādikā.

Kāmesumicchācāroti [V 2.0129] ettha pana kāmesūti methunasamācāresu. Micchācāroti ekantanindito lāmakācāro. Lakkhaṇato pana asaddhammādhippāyena kāyadvārappavattā agamanīyaṭṭhānavītikkamacetanā kāmesumicchācāro. Tattha agamanīyaṭṭhānaṃ nāma purisānaṃ tāva māturakkhitā piturakkhitā mātāpiturakkhitā bhāturakkhitā bhaginirakkhitā ñātirakkhitā [M 2.0135] gottarakkhitā dhammarakkhitā sārakkhā saparidaṇḍāti māturakkhitādayo dasa, dhanakkītā chandavāsinī bhogavāsinī paṭavāsinī odapattakinī obhatacumbaṭā dāsī ca bhariyā ca kammakārī ca bhariyā ca dhajāhaṭā muhuttikāti etā dhanakkītādayo dasāti vīsati itthiyo. Itthīsu pana dvinnaṃ sārakkhasaparidaṇḍānaṃ, dasannañca dhanakkītādīnanti dvādasannaṃ itthīnaṃ aññe purisā. Idaṃ agamanīyaṭṭhānaṃ nāma. So panesa [P 2.0146] micchācāro sīlādiguṇarahite agamanīyaṭṭhāne appasāvajjo, sīlādiguṇasampanne mahāsāvajjo. Tassa cattāro sambhārā – agamanīyavatthu, tasmiṃ sevanacittaṃ, sevanappayogo, maggenamaggapaṭipattiadhivāsananti. Eko payogo sāhatthiko eva.

Now, in the phrase 'sexual misconduct': 'in sensual pleasures' means in sexual intercourse. 'Wrong conduct' means conduct that is utterly blameworthy and base. By characteristic, however, sexual misconduct is the volition, arisen at the body-door with an unrighteous intention, of transgressing in an unapproachable place. Therein, for men, what is called an 'unapproachable place' is, first, twenty types of women: the ten beginning with one protected by her mother—one protected by her mother, one protected by her father, one protected by both mother and father, one protected by her brother, one protected by her sister, one protected by her relatives, one protected by her clan, one protected by the Dhamma, one with a guardian, and one under penalty; and these ten beginning with one bought with wealth—one bought with wealth, one living by consent, one living for possessions, one living for cloth, one ritually married with water, one who has put down her head-pad, a slave who is also a wife, a worker who is also a wife, one captured in war, and a temporary wife. For women, however—for the twelve types of women, that is, the two, the one with a guardian and the one under penalty, and the ten beginning with the one bought with wealth—other men are an unapproachable place. This misconduct is of little blame when the unapproachable place is devoid of virtues such as morality, and of great blame when it is endowed with virtues such as morality. Of this, there are four components: an unapproachable object, the intention to engage with it, the effort of engaging, and the consent to the contact of path with path. The effort is only one: the personal one.

Musāti visaṃvādanapurekkhārassa atthabhañjanako vacīpayogo kāyappayogo vā, visaṃvādanādhippāyena panassa paravisaṃvādanakāyavacīpayogasamuṭṭhāpikā cetanā, musāvādo. Aparo nayo – musāti abhūtaṃ atacchaṃ vatthu. Vādoti tassa bhūtato tacchato viññāpanaṃ. Lakkhaṇato pana atathaṃ vatthuṃ tathato paraṃ viññāpetukāmassa tathāviññattisamuṭṭhāpikā cetanā musāvādo. So yamatthaṃ bhañjati, tassa appatāya appasāvajjo, mahantatāya mahāsāvajjo. Api ca gahaṭṭhānaṃ attano santakaṃ adātukāmatāya natthītiādinayappavatto appasāvajjo, sakkhinā hutvā atthabhañjanatthaṃ vutto mahāsāvajjo. Pabbajitānaṃ appakampi telaṃ vā sappiṃ vā labhitvā hasādhippāyena “ajja gāme telaṃ nadī maññe sandatī”ti pūraṇakathānayena pavatto appasāvajjo, adiṭṭhaṃyeva pana “diṭṭha”ntiādinā nayena vadantānaṃ mahāsāvajjo. Tassa cattāro sambhārā honti – atathaṃ vatthu, visaṃvādanacittaṃ, tajjo vāyāmo, parassa tadatthavijānananti. Eko payogo sāhatthikova. So kāyena vā kāyapaṭibaddhena vā vācāya vā paravisaṃvādakakiriyākaraṇe daṭṭhabbo. Tāya ce kiriyāya paro tamatthaṃ jānāti, ayaṃ kiriyāsamuṭṭhāpikacetanākkhaṇeyeva musāvādakammunā bajjhati.

'Falsehood' is the verbal or bodily effort that destroys the benefit of one who is intent on deceiving. Or, it is the volition of one with the intention to deceive, which gives rise to bodily and verbal efforts that deceive others; this is 'false speech'. Another method: 'falsehood' is an unreal, untrue matter. 'Speech' is making it known as real and true. By characteristic, however, false speech is the volition of one who wishes to make another know an untrue matter as true, which gives rise to such a communication. It is of little fault due to the smallness of the benefit it destroys, and of great fault due to its greatness. Furthermore, for householders, false speech that proceeds from the unwillingness to give one's own possession, such as saying, 'It does not exist,' is of little fault. False speech spoken when acting as a witness in order to destroy the benefit is of great fault. For the ordained, having received even a little oil or ghee, false speech that proceeds by way of exaggeration with the intention to jest, such as, 'Today in the village, I think oil flows like a river,' is of little fault. But for those who speak of what was not seen as 'seen,' by this method, it is of great fault. Of this, there are four components: an untrue matter, the intention to deceive, the corresponding effort, and the other's understanding of that meaning. The effort is only one, the personal one. This is to be understood as the act of deceiving another by body, by what is connected to the body, or by speech. And if by that action the other person understands that meaning, one is bound by the kamma of false speech at the very moment of the volition that gives rise to the action.

Pisuṇavācātiādīsu yāya vācāya, yassa taṃ vācaṃ bhāsati, tassa hadaye attano piyabhāvaṃ, parassa ca suññabhāvaṃ karoti, sā pisuṇavācā[M 2.0136]. Yāya pana attānampi parampi pharusaṃ [V 2.0130] karoti, yā vācā sayampi [P 2.0147] pharusā, neva kaṇṇasukhā na hadayaṅgamā, ayaṃ pharusavācā. Yena pana samphaṃ palapati niratthakaṃ, so samphappalāpo. Tesaṃ mūlabhūtā cetanāpi pisuṇavācādināmameva labhati. Sā eva ca idha adhippetāti.

Regarding 'malicious speech' and so on: The speech by which, when one speaks it to a person, one creates in that person's heart a state of affection for oneself and a state of emptiness toward another—that is malicious speech. The speech, however, that makes both oneself and the other harsh, the speech that is itself harsh, neither pleasant to the ear nor agreeable to the heart—this is harsh speech. That by which one babbles what is flimsy and useless—that is idle chatter. The volition that is the root of these also receives the name 'malicious speech,' and so on. And it is that volition alone that is intended here.

Tattha saṃkiliṭṭhacittassa paresaṃ vā bhedāya, attano piyakamyatāya vā kāyavacīpayogasamuṭṭhāpikā cetanā pisuṇavācā. Sā yassa bhedaṃ karoti, tassa appaguṇatāya appasāvajjā, mahāguṇatāya mahāsāvajjā. Tassā cattāro sambhārā – bhinditabbo paro, iti ime nānā bhavissanti, vinā bhavissantīti bhedapurekkhāratā, iti ahaṃ piyo bhavissāmi vissāsikoti piyakamyatā vā, tajjo vāyāmo, tassa tadatthavijānananti.

Therein, malicious speech is the volition of one with a defiled mind, which gives rise to bodily and verbal efforts, either for the sake of dividing others or for the sake of desiring to be dear. It is of little fault due to the few virtues of the one whom it divides, and of great fault due to their great virtues. Of this, there are four components: another who is to be divided; being intent on division, thinking, 'Thus they will become different, they will become separated,' or the desire to be dear, thinking, 'Thus I will be dear and trusted'; the corresponding effort; and that person's understanding of that meaning.

Parassa mammacchedakakāyavacīpayogasamuṭṭhāpikā ekantapharusacetanā pharusavācā. Tassā āvibhāvatthamidaṃ vatthu – eko kira dārako mātu vacanaṃ anādiyitvā araññaṃ gacchati. Mātā taṃ nivattetuṃ asakkontī, “caṇḍā taṃ mahiṃsī anubandhatū”ti akkosi. Athassa tatheva araññe mahiṃsī uṭṭhāsi. Dārako, “yaṃ mama mātā mukhena kathesi, taṃ mā hotu, yaṃ cittena cintesi, taṃ hotū”ti saccakiriyaṃ akāsi. Mahiṃsī tattheva baddhā viya aṭṭhāsi. Evaṃ mammacchedakopi payogo cittasaṇhatāya pharusavācā na hoti. Mātāpitaro hi kadāci puttake evaṃ vadanti – “corā vo khaṇḍākhaṇḍikaṃ karontū”ti, uppalapattampi ca nesaṃ upari patantaṃ na icchanti. Ācariyupajjhāyā ca kadāci nissitake evaṃ vadanti – “kiṃ ime ahirikā anottappino caranti, niddhamatha ne”ti. Atha ca nesaṃ āgamādhigamasampattiṃ icchanti. Yathā ca cittasaṇhatāya pharusavācā na hoti, evaṃ vacanasaṇhatāya apharusavācāpi na hoti. Na hi mārāpetukāmassa “imaṃ sukhaṃ sayāpethā”ti vacanaṃ apharusavācā hoti. Cittapharusatāya panesā pharusavācāva. Sā yaṃ sandhāya pavattitā, tassa appaguṇatāya appasāvajjā, mahāguṇatāya mahāsāvajjā. Tassā tayo sambhārā – akkositabbo paro, kupitacittaṃ, akkosanāti.

Harsh speech is an entirely harsh volition that gives rise to bodily and verbal actions that cut what is cherished by another. To illustrate this, here is a story: A certain child, disregarding his mother’s words, went into the forest. Unable to make him return, the mother cursed, 'May a fierce buffalo chase you!' And indeed, a buffalo arose for him in the forest. The child then made an act of truth: 'What my mother spoke with her mouth, may that not come to pass; what she intended in her mind, may that happen.' The buffalo stood there as if bound. Thus, even an effort that cuts what is cherished, if the mind is gentle, is not harsh speech. For sometimes parents say to their children, 'May thieves cut you to pieces!' yet they do not even wish a lotus petal to fall upon them. Similarly, teachers and preceptors sometimes say to their dependents, 'Why do these shameless and heedless ones go about? Drive them away!' Yet they still desire their accomplishment in learning and attainment. And just as, due to a gentle mind, it is not harsh speech, so too, due to gentle speech, it is not necessarily non-harsh speech. For the speech of one who wishes to have someone killed, saying, 'Have him lie down comfortably,' is not non-harsh speech. Rather, due to the harshness of mind, this is indeed harsh speech. It is of little fault if it is directed towards one with few virtues, and of great fault if directed towards one with many virtues. It has three components: another to be abused, an angry mind, and the act of abusing.

Anatthaviññāpikā [M 2.0137][P 2.0148] kāyavacīpayogasamuṭṭhāpikā akusalacetanā samphappalāpo. So āsevanamandatāya appasāvajjo, āsevanamahantatāya mahāsāvajjo. Tassa dve sambhārā – bhāratayuddha-sītāharaṇādi-niratthakakathā-purekkhāratā, tathārūpīkathākathanañcāti.

Frivolous talk is an unwholesome volition that gives rise to bodily and verbal actions making known what is unbeneficial. It is of little fault through little indulgence, and of great fault through much indulgence. It has two components: being preoccupied with meaningless tales, such as the war of the Bhāratas and the abduction of Sītā; and the speaking of such talk.

Abhijjhāyatīti [V 2.0131] abhijjhā. Parabhaṇḍābhimukhī hutvā tanninnatāya pavattatīti attho. Sā “aho vatidaṃ mamassā”ti evaṃ parabhaṇḍābhijjhāyanalakkhaṇā adinnādānaṃ viya appasāvajjā mahāsāvajjā ca. Tassā dve sambhārā parabhaṇḍaṃ attano pariṇāmanañca. Parabhaṇḍavatthuke hi lobhe uppannepi na tāva kammapathabhedo hoti, yāva na “aho vatidaṃ mamassā”ti attano pariṇāmetīti.

It covets, thus it is covetousness. The meaning is that it proceeds by being directed towards another's property, with an inclination towards it. It is characterized by coveting another's property with the thought, 'Oh, would that this were mine!' Like taking what is not given, it can be of little fault or great fault. It has two components: another's property and turning it towards oneself. For even when greed arises with respect to another's property, there is no breach of the course of action so long as one does not turn it towards oneself with the thought, 'Oh, would that this were mine!'

Hitasukhaṃ byāpādayatīti, byāpādo. So paravināsāya manopadosalakkhaṇo. Pharusavācā viya appasāvajjo mahāsāvajjo ca. Tassa dve sambhārā parasatto ca, tassa ca vināsacintā. Parasattavatthuke hi kodhe uppannepi na tāva kammapathabhedo hoti, yāva na “aho vatāyaṃ ucchijjeyya vinasseyyā”ti tassa vināsaṃ cinteti.

It destroys welfare and happiness, thus it is ill will. It has the characteristic of mental corruption for the sake of another's destruction. Like harsh speech, it can be of little fault or great fault. It has two components: another being, and the thought of that being's destruction. For even when anger arises with respect to another being, there is no breach of the course of action so long as one does not think of that being's destruction with the thought, 'Oh, may this one be cut off, may they perish!'

Yathābhuccagahaṇābhāvena micchā passatīti micchādiṭṭhi. Sā “natthi dinna”ntiādinā nayena viparītadassanalakkhaṇā samphappalāpo viya appasāvajjā mahāsāvajjā ca. Api ca aniyatā appasāvajjā, niyatā mahāsāvajjā. Tassā dve sambhārā – vatthuno ca gahitākāraviparītatā yathā ca naṃ gaṇhāti, tathābhāvena tassā upaṭṭhānanti.

Because it sees wrongly due to an absence of grasping according to reality, it is wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi). It is characterized by distorted seeing, in the manner of 'there is no result of what is given,' etc. Like frivolous talk, it can be of little fault or of great fault. Moreover, the indeterminate view is of little fault, while the determinate view is of great fault. It has two components: the distortedness of the manner in which the object is grasped, and the presentation of that view because the object is not in fact as it is grasped.

Imesaṃ pana dasannaṃ akusalakammapathānaṃ dhammato koṭṭhāsato ārammaṇato vedanāto mūlatoti pañcahākārehi vinicchayo veditabbo. Tattha dhammatoti etesu hi paṭipāṭiyā satta cetanādhammāva honti, abhijjhādayo tisso cetanāsampayuttā. Koṭṭhāsatoti paṭipāṭiyā satta, micchādiṭṭhi cāti ime aṭṭha kammapathā eva honti, no mūlāni, abhijjhābyāpādā kammapathā ceva mūlāni ca. Abhijjhā hi mūlaṃ patvā [P 2.0149] lobho akusalamūlaṃ hoti, byāpādo doso akusalamūlaṃ.

Now, the analysis of these ten unwholesome courses of action should be understood in five ways: by nature, by division, by object, by feeling, and by root. Herein, by nature: in these, in sequence, seven are volitional states themselves, while the three beginning with covetousness are associated with volition. By division: in sequence, seven, and wrong view—these eight are only courses of action, not roots. Covetousness and ill-will are both courses of action and roots. For covetousness, when it reaches the status of a root, becomes greed, an unwholesome root; ill-will becomes hatred, an unwholesome root.

Ārammaṇatoti pāṇātipāto jīvitindriyārammaṇato saṅkhārārammaṇo hoti, adinnādānaṃ sattārammaṇaṃ vā saṅkhārārammaṇaṃ vā, micchācāro phoṭṭhabbavasena [M 2.0138] saṅkhārārammaṇova, sattārammaṇotipi eke. Musāvādo sattārammaṇo vā saṅkhārārammaṇo vā, tathā pisuṇavācā. Pharusavācā sattārammaṇāva. Samphappalāpo diṭṭhasutamutaviññātavasena sattārammaṇo vā saṅkhārārammaṇo [V 2.0132] vā, tathā abhijjhā. Byāpādo sattārammaṇova. Micchādiṭṭhi tebhūmakadhammavasena saṅkhārārammaṇā.

By object: killing, because its object is the life faculty, has formations as its object. Taking what is not given has a being or formations as its object. Sexual misconduct, by way of the tangible, has only formations as its object, though some say it also has a being as its object. False speech has a being or formations as its object, and similarly divisive speech. Harsh speech has only a being as its object. Frivolous speech, by way of what is seen, heard, sensed, or cognized, has a being or formations as its object; similarly covetousness. Ill-will has only a being as its object. Wrong view, by way of phenomena of the three planes, has formations as its object.

Vedanātoti pāṇātipāto dukkhavedano hoti. Kiñcāpi hi rājāno coraṃ disvā hasamānāpi “gacchatha naṃ ghātethā”ti vadanti, sanniṭṭhāpakacetanā pana nesaṃ dukkhasampayuttāva hoti. Adinnādānaṃ tivedanaṃ, micchācāro sukhamajjhattavasena dvivedano, sanniṭṭhāpakacitte pana majjhattavedano na hoti. Musāvādo tivedano, tathā pisuṇavācā pharusavācā dukkhavedanā, samphappalāpo tivedano, abhijjhā sukhamajjhattavasena dvivedanā, tathā micchādiṭṭhi. Byāpādo dukkhavedano.

By feeling: killing is accompanied by painful feeling. For although kings, seeing a thief, may even be laughing when they say, 'Go, execute him,' their decisive volition is still associated with painful feeling. Taking what is not given is accompanied by threefold feeling. Sexual misconduct is accompanied by twofold feeling, by way of pleasure and equanimity, but in the decisive mind, equanimous feeling does not arise. False speech is accompanied by threefold feeling; similarly divisive speech. Harsh speech is accompanied by painful feeling. Frivolous speech is accompanied by threefold feeling. Covetousness is accompanied by twofold feeling, by way of pleasure and equanimity, as is wrong view. Ill-will is accompanied by painful feeling.

Mūlatoti pāṇātipāto dosamohavasena dvimūlako hoti, adinnādānaṃ dosamohavasena vā lobhamohavasena vā, micchācāro lobhamohavasena. Musāvādo dosamohavasena vā lobhamohavasena vā, tathā pisuṇavācā samphappalāpo ca. Pharusavācā dosamohavasena, abhijjhā mohavasena ekamūlā, tathā byāpādo. Micchādiṭṭhi lobhamohavasena dvimūlāti.

By root: killing is two-rooted, by way of aversion and delusion. Taking what is not given is two-rooted, by way of aversion and delusion, or by way of greed and delusion. Sexual misconduct is two-rooted, by way of greed and delusion. False speech is two-rooted, by way of aversion and delusion, or by way of greed and delusion; likewise are divisive speech and frivolous speech. Harsh speech is two-rooted, by way of aversion and delusion. Covetousness is one-rooted, by way of delusion; likewise is ill-will. Wrong view is two-rooted, by way of greed and delusion.

Pāṇātipātā paṭiviratātiādīsu pāṇātipātādayo vuttatthā eva. Yāya pana viratiyā ete paṭiviratā nāma honti, sā bhedato tividhā hoti sampattavirati samādānavirati samucchedaviratīti. Tattha asamādinnasikkhāpadānaṃ attano jātivayabāhusaccādīni paccavekkhitvā “ayuttaṃ amhākaṃ evarūpaṃ kātu”nti sampattaṃ vatthuṃ avītikkamantānaṃ uppajjamānā [P 2.0150] virati sampattaviratīti veditabbā sīhaḷadīpe cakkanaupāsakassa viya. Tassa kira daharakāleyeva mātu rogo uppajji. Vejjena ca “allasasakamaṃsaṃ laddhuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vuttaṃ. Tato cakkanassa bhātā “gaccha tāta khettaṃ āhiṇḍāhī”ti cakkanaṃ pesesi. So tattha gato. Tasmiñca samaye eko saso taruṇasassaṃ khādituṃ āgato hoti. So taṃ disvā vegena dhāvanto valliyā baddho “kiri kirī”ti saddamakāsi[M 2.0139]. Cakkano tena saddena gantvā taṃ gahetvā cintesi “mātu bhesajjaṃ karomī”ti. Puna cintesi – “na metaṃ patirūpaṃ, yvāhaṃ mātu jīvitakāraṇā paraṃ jīvitā voropeyya”nti. Atha naṃ “gaccha araññe sasehi saddhiṃ tiṇodakaṃ paribhuñjā”ti muñci. Bhātarā ca “kiṃ tāta saso laddho”ti? Pucchito taṃ pavattiṃ ācikkhi. Tato naṃ bhātā paribhāsi. So mātu santikaṃ gantvā, “yatohaṃ jāto[V 2.0133], nābhijānāmi sañcicca pāṇaṃ jīvitā voropetā”ti saccaṃ vatvā aṭṭhāsi, tāvadeva cassa mātā arogā ahosi.

In such phrases as 'one who abstains from killing living beings,' the terms beginning with 'killing' have meanings that have already been stated. However, the abstention by which these persons are called 'abstaining' is, by way of division, of three kinds: abstention on occasion (sampattavirati), abstention by undertaking (samādānavirati), and abstention by cutting off (samucchedavirati). Herein, for those who have not undertaken the training precepts, the abstention that arises in them—who, having reflected on their own birth, age, great learning, and so on, think, 'It is not suitable for us to do such a thing,' and thus do not transgress the object that has come to hand—is to be known as abstention on occasion. This is like the case of the lay devotee Cakkana on the island of Sīhaḷa. It is said that when he was just a youth, his mother fell ill. And a physician said, 'It is proper to get fresh hare's meat.' Then Cakkana's brother sent Cakkana, saying, 'Go, my dear, and wander through the field.' He went there. And at that time, a certain hare had come to eat the young grain. Seeing Cakkana, that hare, while running with speed, was bound by a vine and made the sound, 'kiri kiri.' Hearing that sound, Cakkana went and caught it, and he thought, 'I will make medicine for my mother.' Again he thought: 'It is not proper for me, that I, for the sake of my mother's life, should deprive another of life.' Then he released it, saying, 'Go, and in the forest, together with other hares, enjoy grass and water.' And his brother asked, 'Well, my dear, was a hare caught?' Being asked, he related that event. Then his brother reviled him. He went to his mother's presence and, making a statement of truth, stood there, saying, 'From when I was born, I do not recall having intentionally deprived a living being of life.' And at that very moment, his mother became free from illness.

Samādinnasikkhāpadānaṃ pana sikkhāpadasamādāne ca tatuttari ca attano jīvitaṃ pariccajitvā vatthuṃ avītikkamantānaṃ uppajjamānā virati samādānaviratīti veditabbā, uttaravaḍḍhamānapabbatavāsīupāsakassa viya. So kira ambariyavihāravāsīpiṅgalabuddharakkhitattherassa santike sikkhāpadāni gahetvā khettaṃ kasati. Athassa goṇo naṭṭho, so taṃ gavesanto uttaravaḍḍhamānapabbataṃ āruhi, tatra naṃ mahāsappo aggahesi. So cintesi – “imāya tikhiṇāya vāsiyā sīsaṃ chindāmī”ti. Puna cintesi – “na metaṃ patirūpaṃ, yvāhaṃ bhāvanīyassa garuno santike sikkhāpadaṃ gahetvā bhindeyya”nti. Evaṃ yāvatatiyaṃ cintetvā – “jīvitaṃ pariccajāmi, na sikkhāpada”nti aṃse ṭhapitaṃ tikhiṇadaṇḍavāsiṃ araññe chaḍḍesi. Tāvadeva mahāvāḷo naṃ muñcitvā agamāsīti.

Furthermore, for those who have undertaken the training precepts, the abstention that arises in them—who, having given up even their own lives, do not transgress the object, both at the time of undertaking the precept and thereafter—is to be known as abstention by undertaking. This is like the case of the lay devotee who dwelt at Uttara-Vaḍḍhamāna mountain. It is said that he, having taken the precepts in the presence of the elder Piṅgala-Buddharakkhita, a resident of the Ambariya Monastery, was plowing a field. Then his ox was lost. Searching for it, he ascended Uttara-Vaḍḍhamāna mountain. There a great serpent seized him. He thought: 'With this sharp adze, I will cut off its head.' Again he thought: 'It is not proper for me, that I, having taken the precept in the presence of a venerable teacher, should break it.' Having thought thus up to the third time, he resolved, 'I will give up my life, but I will not give up the precept,' and threw the sharp-handled adze that was placed on his shoulder into the wilderness. At that very moment, the great serpent released him and went away.

Ariyamaggasampayuttā [P 2.0151] pana virati samucchedaviratīti veditabbā, yassā uppattito pabhuti pāṇaṃ ghātessāmīti ariyapuggalānaṃ cittampi na uppajjatīti.

But the abstinence associated with the noble path is to be known as abstinence by cutting off, from the arising of which onwards not even the thought, 'I will kill a living being,' arises for noble persons.

Yathā ca akusalānaṃ, evaṃ imesampi kusalakammapathānaṃ dhammato koṭṭhāsato ārammaṇato vedanāto mūlatoti pañcahākārehi vinicchayo veditabbo. Tattha dhammatoti etesu hi paṭipāṭiyā satta cetanāpi vaṭṭanti viratiyopi, ante tayo cetanāsampayuttāva.

And just as for the unwholesome, so too for these wholesome courses of action, the analysis is to be known in five aspects: by way of nature, by way of component, by way of object, by way of feeling, and by way of root. Therein, as to 'by way of nature': for the seven in sequence, both volition and abstention are applicable; for the last three, only phenomena associated with volition are applicable.

Koṭṭhāsatoti paṭipāṭiyā satta kammapathā eva, na mūlāni, ante tayo kammapathā ceva mūlāni ca. Anabhijjhā hi mūlaṃ patvā alobho [M 2.0140] kusalamūlaṃ hoti, abyāpādo adoso kusalamūlaṃ, sammādiṭṭhi amoho kusalamūlaṃ.

As to 'by way of component': the seven in sequence are only courses of action, not roots; the last three are both courses of action and roots. For non-covetousness, having attained the status of a root, becomes the wholesome root of non-greed; non-ill-will becomes the wholesome root of non-aversion; and right view becomes the wholesome root of non-delusion.

Ārammaṇatoti pāṇātipātādīnaṃ. Ārammaṇāneva etesaṃ ārammaṇāni. Vītikkamitabbavatthutoyeva hi virati nāma hoti. Yathā pana nibbānārammaṇo ariyamaggo kilese pajahati, evaṃ jīvitindriyādiārammaṇāpete kammapathā pāṇātipātādīni dussīlyāni pajahantīti veditabbā.

As to 'by way of object': the very objects of killing living beings, and so on, are the objects of these abstentions. For abstinence is indeed from the very thing that is to be transgressed. And just as the noble path, which has Nibbāna as its object, abandons the defilements, so too it is to be known that these courses of action, which have the life-faculty and so on as their object, abandon the immoralities of killing living beings and so on.

Vedanātoti [V 2.0134] sabbe sukhavedanā vā honti majjhattavedanā vā. Kusalaṃ patvā hi dukkhavedanā nāma natthi.

As to 'by way of feeling': all are accompanied by either pleasant feeling or neutral feeling. For in the wholesome sphere, there is no such thing as painful feeling.

Mūlatoti paṭipāṭiyā satta ñāṇasampayuttacittena viramantassa alobhaadosaamohavasena timūlā honti, ñāṇavippayuttacittena viramantassa dvimūlā. Anabhijjhā ñāṇasampayuttacittena viramantassa dvimūlā hoti, ñāṇavippayuttacittena ekamūlā. Alobho pana attanāva attano mūlaṃ na hoti. Abyāpādepi eseva nayo. Sammādiṭṭhi alobhaadosavasena dvimūlāvāti. Tatiyādīni.

As to 'by way of root': the seven in sequence, for one who abstains with a mind associated with knowledge, are three-rooted, by way of non-greed, non-aversion, and non-delusion; for one who abstains with a mind dissociated from knowledge, they are two-rooted. Non-covetousness, for one who abstains with a mind associated with knowledge, is two-rooted; for one who abstains with a mind dissociated from knowledge, it is one-rooted. However, non-greed is not its own root. For non-ill-will, too, this is the same method. Right view is only two-rooted, by way of non-greed and non-aversion. The third and so on.

6. Aṭṭhaṅgikasuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Aṭṭhaṅgika Sutta

112. Chaṭṭhaṃ aṭṭhamaggaṅgavasena bujjhanakānaṃ ajjhāsayavasena vuttaṃ. Chaṭṭhaṃ.

112. The sixth was spoken by way of the eight factors of the path, in accordance with the disposition of those who are to understand. The sixth.

7. Dasaṅgasuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Dasaṅga Sutta

113. Sattamaṃ dasamicchattasammattavasena. Tattha micchāñāṇinoti micchāpaccavekkhaṇena samannāgatāti attho. Micchāvimuttinoti aniyyānikavimuttino [P 2.0152] kusalavimuttīti gahetvā ṭhitā. Sammāñāṇinoti sammāpaccavekkhaṇā. Sammāvimuttinoti niyyānikāya phalavimuttiyā samannāgatāti. Sattamaṃ.

113. The seventh is in terms of the tenfold wrongness and rightness. Therein, 'one with wrong knowledge' means one endowed with wrong reflection. 'One with wrong liberation' means those who are established in a liberation that does not lead out, having taken it to be a wholesome liberation. 'One with right knowledge' means right reflection. 'One with right liberation' means endowed with the fruition-liberation that does lead out. The seventh.

Kammapathavaggo tatiyo.

The Third Chapter on the Courses of Action is concluded.

4. Catutthavaggo

4. The Fourth Chapter

1. Catudhātusuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Catudhātu Sutta

114. Catutthavaggassa [M 2.0141] paṭhame pathavīdhātūti patiṭṭhādhātu. Āpodhātūti ābandhanadhātu. Tejodhātūti [V 2.0135] paripācanadhātu. Vāyodhātūti vitthambhanadhātu. Ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthārato pana vīsatikoṭṭhāsādivasena etā kathetabbā. Paṭhamaṃ.

114. In the first sutta of the fourth chapter, 'the earth element' means the element of foundation. 'The water element' means the binding element. 'The fire element' means the maturing element. 'The air element' means the upholding element. This is the summary here; in detail, however, these should be discussed in terms of the twenty parts, and so on. The first.

2. Pubbesambodhasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Pubbesambodha Sutta

115. Dutiye ayaṃ pathavīdhātuyā assādoti ayaṃ pathavīdhātunissayo assādo. Svāyaṃ kāyaṃ abbhunnāmetvā udaraṃ pasāretvā, “idha me aṅgulaṃ pavesituṃ vāyamathā”ti vā hatthaṃ pasāretvā, “imaṃ nāmetuṃ vāyamathā”ti vā vadati, evaṃ pavattānaṃ vasena veditabbo. Aniccātiādīsu hutvā abhāvākārena aniccā, paṭipīḷanākārena dukkhā, sabhāvavigamākārena vipariṇāmadhammā. Ayaṃ pathavīdhātuyā ādīnavoti yena ākārena sā aniccā dukkhā vipariṇāmadhammā, ayamākāro pathavīdhātuyā ādīnavoti attho. Chandarāgavinayo chandarāgappahānanti nibbānaṃ āgamma pathavīdhātuyā chandarāgo vinīyati ceva pahīyati ca, tasmā nibbānamassā nissaraṇaṃ.

115. In the second sutta, “This is the gratification in the earth element” means this is the gratification dependent on the earth element. This should be understood by way of those who behave thus: having bent the body forward and extended the belly, they say, “Try to insert a finger here,” or having extended the arm, they say, “Try to bend this.” Regarding “impermanent,” and so on: it is impermanent in the sense of non-existence after having been; it is suffering in the sense of oppression; it has the nature of changing in the sense of the loss of its inherent nature. “This is the danger in the earth element” means that the aspect by which it is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—this aspect is the danger of the earth element. The removal of desire and lust is the abandoning of desire and lust. Through Nibbāna, desire and lust for the earth element are both removed and abandoned; therefore, Nibbāna is its escape.

Ayaṃ āpodhātuyā assādoti ayaṃ āpodhātunissayo assādo. Svāyaṃ aññaṃ āpodhātuyā upaddutaṃ disvā, “kiṃ ayaṃ nipannakālato paṭṭhāya passāvaṭṭhānābhimukho nikkhamati ceva pavisati ca, appamattakampissa kammaṃ karontassa sedatintaṃ vatthaṃ pīḷetabbatākāraṃ pāpuṇāti, anumodanamattampi kathentassa tālavaṇṭaṃ gaṇhitabbaṃ hoti, mayaṃ pana sāyaṃ nipannā pātova uṭṭhahāma, māsapuṇṇaghaṭo [P 2.0153] viya no sarīraṃ, mahākammaṃ karontānaṃ sedamattampi no na uppajjati, asanisaddena viya dhammaṃ kathentānaṃ sarīre usumākāramattampi no natthī”ti evaṃ pavattānaṃ vasena veditabbo.

“This is the gratification in the water element” means this is the gratification dependent on the water element. This should be understood by way of those who, seeing another afflicted by the water element, reflect: 'Why does this person, from the time they lie down, constantly go back and forth to the place of urination? Even when performing a small task, their sweat-soaked clothes reach the point of needing to be wrung out. Even when merely saying words of approval, they have to hold a palm-leaf fan. But we, having lain down in the evening, rise only in the morning; our bodies are like a pot full of water. Even when performing great tasks, not even a drop of sweat arises in us. Even when teaching the Dhamma with a voice like thunder, not the slightest warmth arises in our bodies.' Thus, it should be understood in terms of those behaving in this way.

Ayaṃ [M 2.0142] tejodhātuyā assādoti ayaṃ tejodhātunissayo assādo. Svāyaṃ sītagahaṇike disvā, “kiṃ ime kiñcideva yāgubhattakhajjamattaṃ ajjhoharitvā thaddhakucchino nisīditvā sabbarattiṃ aṅgārakaṭāhaṃ pariyesanti, phusitamattesupi sarīre patitesu aṅgārakaṭāhaṃ ottharitvā pārupitvāva nipajjanti? Mayaṃ pana atithaddhampi maṃsaṃ vā pūvaṃ vā khādāma, kucchipūraṃ bhattaṃ bhuñjāma, tāvadeva no sabbaṃ pheṇapiṇḍo viya vilīyati, sattāhavaddalikāya vattamānāya sarīre sītānudahanamattampi no natthī”ti evaṃ pavattānaṃ vasena veditabbo.

“This is the gratification in the fire element” means this is the gratification dependent on the fire element. This should be understood by way of those who, seeing those with a weak digestion, reflect: 'Why do these people, after consuming just a little gruel, rice, or solid food, sit with stiff bellies all night, searching for a charcoal brazier? Even when just a few drops of rain fall on their bodies, they huddle over the charcoal brazier, cover themselves, and lie down. But we, even when eating very tough meat or cakes, or consuming a bellyful of rice, digest everything in that very moment as easily as a lump of foam dissolves. Even when a seven-day rain is falling, there is not even the slightest feeling of cold on our bodies.' Thus, it should be understood according to those who behave in this way.

Ayaṃ [V 2.0136] vāyodhātuyā assādoti ayaṃ vāyodhātunissayo assādo. Svāyaṃ aññe vātabhīruke disvā, “imesaṃ appamattakampi kammaṃ karontānaṃ anumodanamattampi kathentānaṃ sarīraṃ vāto vijjhati, gāvutamattampi addhānaṃ gatānaṃ hatthapādā sīdanti, piṭṭhi rujjati, kucchivātasīsavātakaṇṇavātādīhi niccupaddutā telaphāṇitādīni vātabhesajjāneva karontā atināmenti, amhākaṃ pana mahākammaṃ karontānampi tiyāmarattiṃ dhammaṃ kathentānampi ekadivaseneva dasa yojanāni gacchantānampi hatthapādasaṃsīdanamattaṃ vā piṭṭhirujjanamattaṃ vā na hotī”ti, evaṃ pavattānaṃ vasena veditabbo. Evaṃ pavattā hi etā dhātuyo assādenti nāma.

“This is the gratification in the air element” means this is the gratification dependent on the air element. This should be understood by way of those who, seeing others who are afraid of the wind, reflect: ‘For these people, even when performing the slightest action or merely uttering words of approval, the wind pierces their bodies. After going just a gāvuta, their hands and feet grow numb, their backs ache. Constantly afflicted by abdominal wind, head-wind, ear-wind, and the like, they spend their time making wind remedies like oil and molasses. But for us, even when performing great tasks, teaching the Dhamma throughout the three watches of the night, or traveling ten yojanas in a single day, there is not even numbness in our hands and feet or pain in our backs.’ It should be understood by way of those who are thus constituted. For those who are thus constituted indeed find gratification in these elements.

Abbhaññāsinti abhivisiṭṭhena ñāṇena aññāsiṃ. Anuttaraṃ sammāsambodhinti uttaravirahitaṃ sabbaseṭṭhaṃ sammā sāmañca bodhiṃ, atha vā pasatthaṃ sundarañca bodhiṃ. Bodhīti rukkhopi maggopi sabbaññutaññāṇampi nibbānampi. “Bodhirukkhamūle paṭhamābhisambuddho”ti (mahāva. 1; udā. 1) ca “antarā ca bodhiṃ antarā ca gaya”nti (mahāva. 11; ma.ni. 1.285) ca āgataṭṭhānesu hi rukkho bodhīti vuccati. “Bodhi vuccati catūsu maggesu ñāṇa”nti (cūḷani. khaggavisāṇasuttaniddesa 121) āgataṭṭhāne [P 2.0154] maggo. “Pappoti bodhiṃ varabhūrimedhaso”ti (dī. ni. 3.217) āgataṭṭhāne sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ. “Patvāna bodhiṃ amataṃ asaṅkhata”nti āgataṭṭhāne nibbānaṃ. Idha pana bhagavato arahattamaggo adhippeto.

“I have directly known” means: I knew with superior knowledge. “The unsurpassed perfect enlightenment” means: the enlightenment that is without superior, the highest of all, perfectly and by oneself; or, the praised and beautiful enlightenment. “Enlightenment” (bodhi) can mean the tree, the path, omniscient knowledge, and also Nibbāna. For in passages such as, “At the foot of the Bodhi tree, he first attained perfect enlightenment” and “between the Bodhi and Gayā,” the tree is called “Bodhi.” In the passage, “Bodhi is said to be the knowledge in the four paths,” it means the path. In the passage, “The one of supreme and vast wisdom attains Bodhi,” it means omniscient knowledge. In the passage, “having attained Bodhi, the deathless, the unconditioned,” it means Nibbāna. Here, however, the Arahant path of the Blessed One is intended.

Sāvakānaṃ [M 2.0143] arahattamaggo anuttarā bodhi hoti, na hotīti? Na hoti. Kasmā? Asabbaguṇadāyakattā. Tesañhi kassaci arahattamaggo arahattaphalameva deti, kassaci tisso vijjā, kassaci cha abhiññā, kassaci catasso paṭisambhidā, kassaci sāvakapāramīñāṇaṃ. Paccekabuddhānampi paccekabodhiñāṇameva deti. Buddhānaṃ pana sabbaguṇasampattiṃ deti abhiseko viya rañño sabbalokissariyabhāvaṃ. Tasmā aññassa kassacipi anuttarā bodhi na hoti.

Is the Arahant path of disciples unsurpassed enlightenment, or is it not? It is not. Why? Because it is not the giver of all qualities. For indeed, for some of those disciples, the Arahant path gives only the fruit of Arahantship; for some, the three knowledges; for some, the six higher knowledges; for some, the four analytical knowledges; and for some, the knowledge of a disciple's perfections. For Paccekabuddhas, too, their Arahant path gives only the knowledge of a Paccekabodhi. But for Buddhas, their Arahant path gives the accomplishment of all qualities, just as the consecration of a king gives sovereignty over the whole world. Therefore, for any other whatsoever, it is not unsurpassed enlightenment.

Abhisambuddhoti paccaññāsinti “abhisambuddho ahaṃ patto paṭivijjhitvā ṭhito”ti evaṃ paṭijāniṃ. Ñāṇañca pana me dassanaṃ udapādīti adhigataguṇadassanasamatthaṃ paccavekkhaṇañāṇañca me udapādi. Akuppā me vimuttīti “ayaṃ mayhaṃ arahattaphalavimutti akuppā”ti evaṃ [V 2.0137] ñāṇaṃ udapādi. Tattha dvīhākārehi akuppatā veditabbā kāraṇato ca ārammaṇato ca. Sā hi catūhi maggehi samucchinnakilesānaṃ puna anivattanatāya kāraṇatopi akuppā, akuppadhammaṃ nibbānaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā pavattatāya ārammaṇatopi akuppā. Antimāti pacchimā. Natthi dāni punabbhavoti idāni puna añño bhavo nāma natthīti.

As for ‘I have fully awakened and understood,’ this means I declared: ‘I am fully awakened, I have attained, I stand having penetrated.’ As for ‘And knowledge and vision arose in me,’ this means the reviewing knowledge, capable of seeing the qualities that have been attained, arose in me. As for ‘My liberation is unshakable,’ this means the knowledge arose: ‘This liberation of mine, which is the fruit of Arahantship, is unshakable.’ Therein, unshakability should be known in two aspects: by way of cause and by way of object. For that liberation is unshakable by way of cause because of the non-return of the defilements utterly cut off by the four paths; and it is unshakable by way of object because it proceeds having made Nibbāna, the unshakable state, its object.
