As for ‘final,’ this means the last birth. As for ‘There is now no renewed existence,’ this means: now there is no other existence called ‘becoming’ again.

Imasmiṃ sutte cattāri saccāni kathitāni. Kathaṃ? Catūsu hi dhātūsu assādo samudayasaccaṃ, ādīnavo dukkhasaccaṃ, nissaraṇaṃ nirodhasaccaṃ, nirodhappajānano maggo maggasaccaṃ. Vitthāravasenapi kathetuṃ vaṭṭatiyeva. Ettha hi yaṃ pathavīdhātuṃ paṭicca uppajjati sukhaṃ somanassaṃ, ayaṃ pathavīdhātuyā assādoti pahānapaṭivedho samudayasaccaṃ. Yā pathavīdhātu aniccā dukkhā vipariṇāmadhammā, ayaṃ pathavīdhātuyā, ādīnavoti pariññāpaṭivedho dukkhasaccaṃ. Yo pathavīdhātuyā chandarāgavinayo chandarāgappahānaṃ, idaṃ pathavīdhātuyā nissaraṇanti sacchikiriyāpaṭivedho nirodhasaccaṃ. Yā imesu tīsu ṭhānesu diṭṭhi saṅkappo vācā kammanto ājīvo vāyāmo sati samādhi, ayaṃ bhāvanāpaṭivedho maggasaccanti. Dutiyaṃ.

In this sutta, the four truths are taught. How? For in the four elements, gratification is the truth of the origin; danger is the truth of suffering; escape is the truth of cessation; and the path that understands cessation is the truth of the path. It is also proper to explain it by way of detailed analysis. For here, whatever pleasure and joy arises in dependence on the earth element, this is the gratification of the earth element—thus, the penetration by way of abandoning is the truth of the origin. That the earth element is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change, this is the danger of the earth element—thus, the penetration by way of full understanding is the truth of suffering. Whatever is the removal of desire and lust, the abandoning of desire and lust, for the earth element, this is the escape from the earth element—thus, the penetration by way of realization is the truth of cessation. Whatever in these three instances is right view, right thought, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration—this penetration by way of development is the truth of the path. The second.

3. Acariṃsuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Acariṃ Sutta

116. Tatiye [P 2.0155] acarinti ñāṇacārena acariṃ, anubhavanacārenāti attho. Yāvatāti yattako. Tatiyaṃ.

116. In the third sutta, as for ‘I wandered,’ it means: I wandered with the conduct of knowledge, that is, with the conduct of experiencing. As for ‘as far as,’ it means ‘however much.’ The third.

4. Nocedaṃsuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Nocedaṃ Sutta

117. Catutthe [M 2.0144] nissaṭātiādīni ādito vuttapaṭisedhena yojetvā “na nissaṭā, na visaṃyuttā, na vippamuttā, na vimariyādikatena cetasā vihariṃsū”ti evaṃ veditabbāni. Dutiyanaye vimariyādikatenāti nimmariyādikatena. Tattha duvidhā mariyādā kilesamariyādā vaṭṭamariyādāti. Tattha ca yassa upaḍḍhā kilesā pahīnā, upaḍḍhā appahīnā, vaṭṭaṃ vā pana upaḍḍhaṃ pahīnaṃ, upaḍḍhaṃ appahīnaṃ, tassa cittaṃ pahīnakilese vā vaṭṭaṃ vā sandhāya vimariyādikataṃ, appahīnakilese vā vaṭṭaṃ vā sandhāya na vimariyādikataṃ. Idha pana ubhayassāpi pahīnattā [V 2.0138] “vimariyādikatena cetasā”ti vuttaṃ, mariyādaṃ akatvā ṭhitena atikkantamariyādena cetasāti attho. Iti tīsupi imesu suttesu catusaccameva kathitaṃ. Catutthaṃ.

117. In the fourth sutta, the words beginning with ‘nissaṭā’ should be understood by connecting them with the negation stated at the beginning, thus: ‘They were not released, not disjoined, not freed; they did not dwell with a mind made without boundaries.’ In the second method, ‘with a mind made without boundaries’ means with a mind without demarcation. Here, a boundary is twofold: the boundary of defilements and the boundary of the round of existence. In this regard, for a person by whom half the defilements are abandoned and half are not abandoned, or half the round of existence is abandoned and half is not abandoned, their mind is considered ‘made without boundaries’ with reference to the abandoned defilements or the abandoned round of existence, and ‘not made without boundaries’ with reference to the unabandoned defilements or the unabandoned round of existence. Here, however, since both have been abandoned, it was said, ‘with a mind made without boundaries.’ The meaning is: with a mind that stands having made no boundary, with a mind that has transcended boundaries. Thus, in all three of these suttas, only the Four Truths were taught. The fourth.

5. Ekantadukkhasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Ekantadukkha Sutta

118. Pañcame ekantadukkhāti atikkamitvā ṭhitassa tattakāro viya ekanteneva dukkhā. Dukkhānupatitāti dukkhena anupatitā. Dukkhāvakkantāti dukkhena okkantā otiṇṇā. Sukhāti sukhavedanāya paccayabhūtā. Evaṃ sabbattha attho veditabbo. Imasmiṃ sutte dukkhalakkhaṇaṃ kathitaṃ. Pañcamaṃ.

118. In the fifth sutta, `ekantadukkhā` (exclusively suffering) means: just as a mass of embers that remains after the flames have subsided is intensely hot, so it is exclusively suffering. `Dukkhānupatitā` (beset by suffering) means constantly fallen into suffering. `Dukkhāvakkantā` (entered into suffering) means descended into, immersed in suffering. `Sukhā` (pleasure) means being a condition for pleasant feeling. Thus the meaning should be understood in all instances. In this sutta, the characteristic of suffering was taught. The fifth.

6-10. Abhinandasuttādivaṇṇanā

6–10. Commentary on the Abhinanda Sutta and others

119-123. Chaṭṭhasattamesu vivaṭṭaṃ, avasāne tīsu catusaccamevāti. Chaṭṭhādīni.

In the sixth and seventh suttas, freedom from the round of existence is taught; in the final three, only the Four Truths are taught. Thus it should be understood. The suttas from the sixth onward are concluded.

Catuttho vaggo.

The Fourth Chapter.

Dhātusaṃyuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Dhātusaṃyutta is concluded.

4. Anamataggasaṃyuttaṃ

4. The Anamatagga Saṃyutta

1. Paṭhamavaggo

1. The First Chapter

1. Tiṇakaṭṭhasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Tiṇakaṭṭha Sutta

124. Anamataggasaṃyuttassa [V 2.0139][P 2.0156][M 2.0145] paṭhame anamataggoti anu amataggo, vassasataṃ vassasahassaṃ ñāṇena anugantvāpi amataggo aviditaggo, nāssa sakkā ito vā etto vā aggaṃ jānituṃ, aparicchinnapubbāparakoṭikoti attho. Saṃsāroti khandhādīnaṃ avicchinnappavattā paṭipāṭi. Pubbā koṭi na paññāyatīti purimamariyādā na dissati. Yadaggena cassa purimā koṭi na paññāyati, pacchimāpi tadaggeneva na paññāyati, vemajjheyeva pana sattā saṃsaranti. Pariyādānaṃ gaccheyyāti idaṃ upamāya khuddakattā vuttaṃ. Bāhirasamayasmiñhi attho paritto hoti, upamā mahatī. “Hatthī viya ayaṃ goṇo, goṇo viya sūkaro, samuddo viya taḷāka”nti hi vutte na tesaṃ tādisaṃ pamāṇaṃ hoti. Buddhasamaye pana upamā parittā, attho mahā. Pāḷiyañhi eko jambudīpo gahito, evarūpānaṃ pana jambudīpānaṃ satepi sahassepi satasahassepi tiṇādīni tena upakkamena pariyādānaṃ gaccheyyuṃ, na tveva purisassa mātu mātaroti. Dukkhaṃ paccanubhūtanti tumhehi dukkhaṃ anubhūtaṃ. Tibbanti tasseva vevacanaṃ. Byasananti ñātibyasanādianekavidhaṃ. Kaṭasīti susānaṃ, pathavīyeva vā. Sā hi punappunaṃ marantehi sarīranikkhepena vaḍḍhitā. Alamevāti yuttameva. Paṭhamaṃ.

124. In the first sutta of the Anamatagga Saṃyutta, the meaning should be understood as follows. `Anamatagga` means ‘a beginning that is not known by tracing back’ (`anu amataggo`); even after tracing back with knowledge for a hundred years or a thousand years, its beginning is not known, its beginning is not apparent. It is not possible to know its beginning from this time or that. The meaning is: having an undemarcated prior and posterior end. `Saṃsāra` is the uninterrupted succession of the aggregates and so on. ‘The prior end is not discerned’ means the prior boundary is not seen. By whatever beginning its prior end is not discerned, by that very same beginning its posterior end is also not discerned; beings, however, wander only in the very middle. The phrase ‘would be exhausted’ is said because of the smallness of the simile. For in external doctrines, the meaning is small, but the simile is great. For when it is said, “This ox is like an elephant, a pig is like an ox, a reservoir is like the ocean,” they do not have such a measure. In the Buddha’s teaching, however, the simile is small, but the meaning is great. For in the Pāli, one Jambudīpa is taken; however, the grass, sticks, and so on in even a hundred, a thousand, or a hundred thousand such Jambudīpas would be exhausted by that effort, but not so the successive mothers of a person. `Dukkhaṃ paccanubhūtaṃ` means ‘suffering has been experienced by you.’ `Tibbaṃ` is a synonym for that very word. `Byasanaṃ` refers to the manifold afflictions such as the loss of relatives. `Kaṭasī` is a charnel ground, or the earth itself. For it has been augmented by the casting off of bodies by those who die again and again. `Alameva` means ‘it is indeed fitting.’ The first.

2. Pathavīsuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Pathavī Sutta

125. Dutiye mahāpathavinti cakkavāḷapariyantaṃ mahāpathaviṃ. Nikkhipeyyāti taṃ pathaviṃ bhinditvā vuttappamāṇaṃ guḷikaṃ karitvā ekamantaṃ ṭhapeyya. Dutiyaṃ.

125. In the second sutta, “the great earth” means the great earth up to the limit of the world-system. “Should set aside” means breaking up that earth, making balls of the size mentioned, and placing them to one side. The second.

3. Assusuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Assu Sutta

126. Tatiye [V 2.0140][P 2.0157][M 2.0146] kandantānanti sasaddaṃ rudamānānaṃ. Passannanti sanditaṃ pavattaṃ. Catūsu mahāsamuddesūti sinerurasmīhi paricchinnesu catūsu mahāsamuddesu. Sinerussa hi pācīnapassaṃ rajatamayaṃ, dakkhiṇapassaṃ maṇimayaṃ, pacchimapassaṃ phalikamayaṃ, uttarapassaṃ suvaṇṇamayaṃ. Pubbadakkhiṇapassehi nikkhantā rajatamaṇirasmiyo ekato hutvā mahāsamuddapiṭṭhena gantvā cakkavāḷapabbataṃ āhacca tiṭṭhanti, dakkhiṇapacchimapassehi nikkhantā maṇiphalikarasmiyo, pacchimuttarapassehi nikkhantā phalikasuvaṇṇarasmiyo, uttarapācīnapassehi nikkhantā suvaṇṇarajatarasmiyo ekato hutvā mahāsamuddapiṭṭhena gantvā cakkavāḷapabbataṃ āhacca tiṭṭhanti. Tāsaṃ rasmīnaṃ antaresu cattāro mahāsamuddā honti. Te sandhāya vuttaṃ “catūsu mahāsamuddesū”ti. Ñātibyasanantiādīsu byasananti viasanaṃ, vināsoti attho. Ñātīnaṃ byasanaṃ ñātibyasanaṃ, bhogānaṃ byasanaṃ bhogabyasanaṃ. Rogo pana sayameva ārogyaṃ viyasati vināsetīti byasanaṃ, rogova byasanaṃ rogabyasanaṃ. Tatiyaṃ.

126. In the third sutta, `kandantānaṃ` means “of those weeping aloud.” `Passannaṃ` means “that which has flowed forth.” “In the four great oceans” refers to the four great oceans bounded by the rays of Mount Sineru. For the eastern side of Sineru is made of silver, the southern side of jewels, the western side of crystal, and the northern side of gold. Rays of silver and jewels emanating from the eastern and southern sides, combining together, travel over the surface of the great ocean, strike against the Cakkavāḷa mountain, and stop. Rays of jewels and crystal emanating from the southern and western sides, rays of crystal and gold emanating from the western and northern sides, and rays of gold and silver emanating from the northern and eastern sides, combining together, travel over the surface of the great ocean, strike against the Cakkavāḷa mountain, and stop. The four great oceans are between these rays. It was in reference to these that “in the four great oceans” was said. In `ñātibyasananti` and so on, `byasananti` means ruin or destruction. `Ñātibyasanaṃ` is the ruin of relatives; `bhogabyasanaṃ` is the ruin of wealth. As for illness, it itself destroys health, thus it is called a destruction (`byasana`); illness itself is a destruction, `rogabyasanaṃ`. The third.

4. Khīrasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Khīra Sutta

127. Catutthe mātuthaññanti ekanāmikāya manussamātu khīraṃ. Imesañhi sattānaṃ gaṇḍuppādakipillikādīsu vā macchakacchapādīsu vā pakkhijātesu vā nibbattakāle mātukhīrameva natthi, ajapasumahiṃsādīsu nibbattakāle khīraṃ atthi, tathā manussesu. Tattha ajādikāle ca manussesu cāpi “devī sumanā tissā”ti evaṃ nānānāmikānaṃ kucchiyaṃ nibbattakāle aggahetvā tissāti ekanāmikāya eva mātu kucchiyaṃ nibbattakāle pītaṃ thaññaṃ catūsu mahāsamuddesu udakato bahutaranti veditabbaṃ. Catutthaṃ.

127. In the fourth sutta, 'mother's milk' (`mātuthaññaṃ`) means the milk of a human mother with a single name. For when these beings are born as worms, ants, and so on; as fish, turtles, and so on; or as birds, there is no mother's milk at the time of birth. But when born as goats, sheep, buffaloes, and so on, or as humans, there is milk. Among these, both in the case of goats etc. and humans, even without taking into account those born in the wombs of mothers with various names such as Devī, Sumanā, or Tissā, it should be understood that the milk drunk at the time of birth from the womb of a mother with a single name such as Tissā is more than the water in the four great oceans. The fourth.

5. Pabbatasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Pabbata Sutta

128. Pañcame sakkā pana, bhanteti so kira bhikkhu cintesi – “satthā anamataggassa saṃsārassa dīghatamattā ‘na sukaraṃ na sukara’nti kathetiyeva[M 2.0147], kathaṃ nacchindati[P 2.0158], sakkā nu kho upamaṃ kārāpetu”nti. Tasmā evamāha. Kāsikenāti tayo kappāsaṃsū ekato gahetvā [V 2.0141] kantitasuttamayena atisukhumavatthena. Tena pana parimaṭṭhe kittakaṃ khīyeyyāti. Sāsapamattaṃ. Pañcamaṃ.

128. In the fifth sutta, regarding 'But is it possible, venerable sir?': it is said that a certain monk thought, 'The Teacher only says, “It is not easy, it is not easy,” on account of the extreme length of beginningless saṃsāra. How is it not cut off? Is it possible to have a simile made?' Therefore, he spoke thus. 'With a Kāsi cloth' means with an extremely fine cloth made from thread spun by taking three cotton fibers together. When one rubs with it, how much would wear away? The amount of a mustard seed. The fifth.

6. Sāsapasuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Sāsapa Sutta

129. Chaṭṭhe āyasaṃ nagaranti āyasena pākārena parikkhittaṃ nagaraṃ, na pana anto āyasehi ekabhūmikādipāsādehi ākiṇṇanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Chaṭṭhaṃ.

129. In the sixth sutta, 'an iron city' means a city surrounded by an iron rampart, but it should be understood as not being crowded inside with iron palaces of one story and so on. The sixth.

7. Sāvakasuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Sāvaka Sutta

130. Sattame anussareyyunti ekena kappasatasahasse anussarite aparo tassa ṭhitaṭṭhānato aññaṃ satasahassaṃ, aññopi aññanti evaṃ cattāropi cattārisatasahassāni anussareyyuṃ. Sattamaṃ.

130. In the seventh sutta, regarding 'they should recollect': when one hundred thousand eons have been recollected by one disciple, another recollects another hundred thousand from the point where that one stopped; and another disciple, yet another hundred thousand. In this way, all four would recollect four hundred thousand eons. The seventh.

8-9. Gaṅgāsuttādivaṇṇanā

8-9. Commentary on the Gaṅgā Sutta and so on

131-132. Aṭṭhame yā etasmiṃ antare vālikāti yā etasmiṃ āyāmato pañcayojanasatike antare vālikā. Navame vattabbaṃ natthi. Aṭṭhamanavamāni.

In the eighth sutta, 'whatever sand is in this interval' means the sand that is in this interval of five hundred yojanas in length. Regarding the ninth, there is nothing to be said. The eighth and ninth suttas.

10. Puggalasuttavaṇṇanā

10. The Commentary on the Puggala Sutta

133. Dasame aṭṭhikaṅkalotiādīni tīṇipi rāsivevacanāneva. Imesaṃ pana sattānaṃ saaṭṭhikālato anaṭṭhikālova bahutaro. Gaṇḍuppādakādipāṇabhūtānañhi etesaṃ aṭṭhimeva natthi, macchakacchapādibhūtānaṃ pana aṭṭhimeva bahutaraṃ, tasmā anaṭṭhikālañca bahuaṭṭhikālañca aggahetvā samaṭṭhikālova gahetabbo. Uttaro [P 2.0159] gijjhakūṭassāti gijjhakūṭassa uttarapasse ṭhito. Magadhānaṃ giribbajeti magadharaṭṭhassa giribbaje, giriparikkhepe ṭhitoti attho. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti. Dasamaṃ.

133. In the tenth sutta, the three terms beginning with 'a skeleton' are all synonyms for 'heap.' But for these beings, the time without bones is much greater than the time with bones. For those beings who have become creatures such as earthworms, there are no bones at all; but for those who have become fish, turtles, and so on, there are very many bones. Therefore, not taking the time without bones and the time with many bones, only the time with a moderate amount of bones should be taken. 'North of Vulture's Peak' means standing on the northern side of Vulture's Peak. 'In Giribbaja of the Magadhans' means standing in Giribbaja of the Magadha country, which is surrounded by mountains; this is the meaning. The rest is clear everywhere. The tenth sutta.

Paṭhamo vaggo.

The First Chapter.

2. Dutiyavaggo

2. The Second Chapter

1. Duggatasuttavaṇṇanā

1. The Commentary on the Duggata Sutta

134. Dutiyavaggassa [V 2.0142][M 2.0148] paṭhame duggatanti daliddaṃ kapaṇaṃ. Durūpetanti dussaṇṭhānehi hatthapādehi upetaṃ. Paṭhamaṃ.

134. In the first sutta of the second chapter, 'wretched' means impoverished and pitiable. 'Ill-formed' means endowed with badly-formed hands and feet. The first sutta.

2. Sukhitasuttavaṇṇanā

2. The Commentary on the Sukhita Sutta

135. Dutiye sukhitanti sukhasamappitaṃ mahaddhanaṃ mahābhogaṃ. Susajjitanti alaṅkatapaṭiyattaṃ hatthikkhandhagataṃ mahāparivāraṃ. Dutiyaṃ.

135. In the second sutta, 'happy' means endowed with happiness, of great wealth, and of great possessions. 'Well-equipped' means adorned and prepared, mounted on an elephant's back, with a great retinue. The second sutta.

3. Tiṃsamattasuttavaṇṇanā

3. The Commentary on the Tiṃsamatta Sutta

136. Tatiye pāveyyakāti pāveyyadesavāsino. Sabbe āraññikātiādīsu dhutaṅgasamādānavasena tesaṃ āraññikādibhāvo veditabbo. Sabbe sasaṃyojanāti sabbe sabandhanā, keci sotāpannā, keci sakadāgāmino, keci anāgāmino. Tesu hi puthujjano vā khīṇāsavo vā natthi. Gunnantiādīsu setakāḷādivaṇṇesu ekekavaṇṇakālova gahetabbo. Pāripanthakāti paripanthe tiṭṭhanakā panthaghātacorā. Pāradārikāti paradāracārittaṃ āpajjanakā. Tatiyaṃ.

136. In the third sutta, ‘Pāveyyakā’ means inhabitants of the Pāveyya country. In ‘all are forest-dwellers’ and so on, their being forest-dwellers etc. should be understood by way of their undertaking of the ascetic practices. ‘All with fetters’ means all have bonds; some are stream-enterers, some are once-returners, and some are non-returners. Indeed, among them there is no worldling or one whose corruptions are destroyed. In ‘of cattle’ and so on, among the colors such as white, black, etc., a time of a single color should be taken. ‘Highwaymen’ means path-destroying thieves who stand on the path. ‘Adulterers’ means those who commit transgression with the wives of others. The third sutta.

4-9. Mātusuttādivaṇṇanā

4–9. The Commentary on the Mātusutta and so on

137-142. Catutthādīsu liṅganiyamena ceva cakkavāḷaniyamena ca attho veditabbo. Purisānañhi mātugāmakālo, mātugāmānañca purisakāloti evamettha liṅganiyamo. Imamhā cakkavāḷā sattā paracakkavāḷaṃ, paracakkavāḷā ca imaṃ cakkavāḷaṃ saṃsaranti. Tesu imasmiṃ cakkavāḷe mātugāmakāle mātubhūtaññeva dassento yo namātābhūtapubboti āha. Yo napitābhūtapubbotiādīsupi eseva nayo. Catutthādīni.

In the fourth sutta and so on, the meaning should be understood by the principle of gender and the principle of the world-system. For there is a time for men to be women, and a time for women to be men; thus, in this context, there is no fixity of gender. Beings from this world-system transmigrate to another world-system, and from another world-system to this one. Among these, in this world-system, the Blessed One, wishing to show that during a time as a woman, one has indeed been a mother, said, 'There is no one who has not previously been a mother.' In 'There is no one who has not previously been a father' and so on, this same method should be understood. The fourth and following suttas.

10. Vepullapabbatasuttavaṇṇanā

10. The Commentary on the Vepullapabbata Sutta

143. Dasame [V 2.0143][P 2.0160][M 2.0149] bhūtapubbanti atītakāle ekaṃ apadānaṃ āharitvā dasseti. Samaññā udapādīti paññatti ahosi. Catūhena ārohantīti idaṃ thāmamajjhime sandhāya vuttaṃ. Agganti uttamaṃ. Bhaddayuganti sundarayugalaṃ. Tīhena ārohantīti ettāvatā kira dvinnaṃ buddhānaṃ antare yojanaṃ pathavī ussannā, so pabbato tiyojanubbedho jāto.

143. In the tenth sutta, by ‘in the past’ He brings forth and shows a story from a past time. ‘A designation arose’ means a concept came to be. ‘They climb with four’—this was said with reference to those of medium strength. ‘Supreme’ means the best. ‘An excellent pair’ means a fine pair of disciples. By ‘They climb with three’, it is meant that, it is said, in the interval between the two Buddhas, the earth rose one yojana, and that mountain became three yojanas in height.

Appaṃ vā bhiyyoti vassasatato uttariṃ appaṃ dasa vā vīsaṃ vā vassāni. Puna vassasatameva jīvanako nāma natthi, uttamakoṭiyā pana saṭṭhi vā asīti vā vassāni jīvanti. Vassasataṃ pana appatvā pañcavassadasavassādikāle mīyamānāva bahukā. Ettha ca kakusandho bhagavā cattālīsavassasahassāyukakāle, koṇāgamano tiṃsavassasahassāyukakāle nibbattoti idaṃ anupubbena parihīnasadisaṃ kataṃ, na pana evaṃ parihīnaṃ, vaḍḍhitvā vaḍḍhitvā parihīnanti veditabbaṃ. Kathaṃ? Kakusandho tāva bhagavā imasmiṃyeva kappe cattālīsavassasahassāyukakāle nibbatto āyuppamāṇaṃ pañca koṭṭhāse katvā cattāro ṭhatvā pañcame vijjamāneyeva parinibbuto. Taṃ āyu parihāyamānaṃ dasavassakālaṃ patvā puna vaḍḍhamānaṃ asaṅkheyyaṃ hutvā tato parihāyamānaṃ tiṃsavassasahassāyukakāle ṭhitaṃ, tadā koṇāgamano nibbatto. Tasmimpi tatheva parinibbute taṃ āyu dasavassakālaṃ patvā puna vaḍḍhamānaṃ asaṅkheyyaṃ hutvā parihāyitvā vīsavassasahassakāle ṭhitaṃ, tadā kassapo bhagavā nibbatto. Tasmimpi tatheva parinibbute taṃ āyu dasavassakālaṃ patvā puna vaḍḍhamānaṃ asaṅkheyyaṃ hutvā parihāyitvā vassasatakālaṃ pattaṃ, atha amhākaṃ sammāsambuddho nibbatto. Evaṃ anupubbena parihāyitvā vaḍḍhitvā vaḍḍhitvā parihīnanti veditabbaṃ. Tattha ca yaṃ āyuparimāṇesu mandesu buddhā nibbattanti, tesampi tadeva āyuparimāṇaṃ hotīti. Dasamaṃ.

‘A little or more’ means a little beyond one hundred years, for ten or twenty years. Again, there is no one, so to speak, who lives for a full hundred years; at the highest limit, they live for sixty or eighty years. But many die without reaching one hundred years, passing away at five, ten, or so years of age. And here, that the Blessed One Kakusandha arose when the lifespan was forty thousand years, and Koṇāgamana when it was thirty thousand years—this is presented as if it were a gradual decline, but it did not decline in this way. It should be understood that it declined after having increased and increased. How so? The Blessed One Kakusandha arose in this very eon when the lifespan was forty thousand years. Having divided the lifespan into five portions and lived for four, he attained parinibbāna while the fifth portion was still present. That lifespan, while decreasing, reached a period of ten years, and then, while increasing again, became incalculable. From there, while decreasing, it stood at a period of a thirty-thousand-year lifespan, and at that time Koṇāgamana arose. When he too attained parinibbāna in the same way, that lifespan reached a period of ten years, and then, while increasing again, became incalculable. Having decreased from the incalculable, it stood at a period of a twenty-thousand-year lifespan, and at that time the Blessed One Kassapa arose. When he too attained parinibbāna in the same way, that lifespan reached a period of ten years, and then, while increasing again, became incalculable. Having decreased from the incalculable, it reached a period of a hundred-year lifespan, and then our Perfectly Enlightened One arose. Thus, it should be understood that having declined in sequence, it declines again after increasing and increasing. And in that context, when Buddhas arise during periods of shorter lifespans, their own lifespan is that very same lifespan. The tenth sutta.

Dutiyo vaggo.

The Second Chapter.

Anamataggasaṃyuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Anamatagga Saṃyutta is concluded.

5. Kassapasaṃyuttaṃ

5. The Kassapa Saṃyutta

1. Santuṭṭhasuttavaṇṇanā

1. The Commentary on the Discourse on Contentment

144. Kassapasaṃyuttassa [V 2.0144][P 2.0161][M 2.0150] paṭhame santuṭṭhāyanti santuṭṭho ayaṃ. Itarītarenāti na thūlasukhumalūkhapaṇītathirajiṇṇānaṃ yena kenaci, atha kho yathāladdhādīnaṃ itarītarena yena kenaci santuṭṭhoti attho. Cīvarasmiñhi tayo santosā yathālābhasantoso yathābalasantoso yathāsāruppasantosoti. Piṇḍapātādīsupi eseva nayo.

144. In the first discourse of the Kassapa Saṃyutta, the meaning is to be understood thus. Santuṭṭhāyaṃ means: 'This Kassapa is content.' By itarītarena is not meant with just any of the coarse, fine, rough, excellent, durable, or worn-out robes; rather, the meaning is being content with whatever is obtained, whether inferior or superior. Indeed, regarding robes, there are three kinds of contentment: contentment with what is obtained, contentment according to one’s strength, and contentment with what is suitable. This same method applies to almsfood and so on.

Tesaṃ ayaṃ pabhedasaṃvaṇṇanā – idha bhikkhu cīvaraṃ labhati sundaraṃ vā asundaraṃ vā, so teneva yāpeti, aññaṃ na pattheti, labhantopi na gaṇhāti. Ayamassa cīvare yathālābhasantoso. Atha pana pakatidubbalo vā hoti ābādhajarābhibhūto vā, garucīvaraṃ pārupanto kilamati, so sabhāgena bhikkhunā saddhiṃ taṃ parivattetvā lahukena yāpentopi santuṭṭhova hoti. Ayamassa cīvare yathābalasantoso. Aparo paṇītapaccayalābhī hoti, so paṭṭacīvarādīnaṃ aññataraṃ mahagghacīvaraṃ bahūni vā cīvarāni labhitvā – “idaṃ therānaṃ cirapabbajitānaṃ, idaṃ bahussutānaṃ anurūpaṃ, idaṃ gilānānaṃ, idaṃ appalābhīnaṃ hotū”ti datvā tesaṃ purāṇacīvaraṃ vā saṅkārakūṭādito vā pana nantakāni uccinitvā tehi saṅghāṭiṃ katvā dhārentopi santuṭṭhova hoti. Ayamassa cīvare yathāsāruppasantoso.

This is the detailed explanation of their divisions. Here, a monk obtains a robe, whether beautiful or not beautiful, and he makes do with just that, not desiring another, nor taking it even if he obtains it. This is his contentment with robes according to what is obtained. Furthermore, a monk may be naturally weak, or overwhelmed by sickness and old age, and becomes weary wearing a heavy robe. He exchanges it with a compatible monk for a lighter one and, making do with that, he is indeed content. This is his contentment with robes according to his strength. Another monk is a recipient of excellent requisites, and having obtained a valuable robe or many robes, he thinks, 'This is for the elders who have long been ordained; this is suitable for the learned, this for the sick, this for those who receive little,' and gives them away. He then picks up their old robes or rags from a refuse heap or similar places, makes a double-layered robe with them, and wears it, remaining indeed content. This is his contentment with robes according to what is suitable.

Idha pana bhikkhu piṇḍapātaṃ labhati lūkhaṃ vā paṇītaṃ vā, so teneva yāpeti, aññaṃ na pattheti, labhantopi na gaṇhāti. Ayamassa piṇḍapāte yathālābha santoso. Yo pana attano pakativiruddhaṃ vā byādhiviruddhaṃ vā piṇḍapātaṃ labhati, yenassa paribhuttena aphāsu hoti, so sabhāgassa bhikkhuno taṃ datvā tassa hatthato sappāyabhojanaṃ bhutvā [P 2.0162] samaṇadhammaṃ karontopi santuṭṭhova hoti. Ayamassa piṇḍapāte yathābalasantoso. Aparo bahuṃ paṇītaṃ piṇḍapātaṃ [V 2.0145] labhati, so taṃ cīvaraṃ viya cirapabbajita-bahussuta-appalābhagilānānaṃ datvā[M 2.0151], tesaṃ vā sesakaṃ piṇḍāya vā caritvā missakāhāraṃ bhuñjantopi santuṭṭhova hoti. Ayamassa piṇḍapāte yathāsāruppasantoso.

Furthermore, here a monk obtains almsfood, whether coarse or excellent, and he makes do with just that, not desiring anything else, nor accepting it even when obtaining it. This is his contentment with almsfood according to what is obtained. But if a monk obtains almsfood contrary to his constitution or contrary to his illness, which when consumed causes him discomfort, he gives it to a compatible monk and, having eaten suitable food from that monk’s hand, remains indeed content even while performing the duties of a recluse. This is his contentment with almsfood according to his strength. Another obtains much excellent almsfood. He gives it away, as he would a robe, to the long-ordained, the learned, those who receive little, and the sick, and either eats their leftovers or goes on almsround and eats a mixed meal, yet he remains indeed content. This is his contentment with almsfood according to what is suitable.

Idha pana bhikkhu senāsanaṃ labhati manāpaṃ vā amanāpaṃ vā, so tena neva somanassaṃ na paṭighaṃ uppādeti, antamaso tiṇasanthārakenāpi yathāladdheneva tussati. Ayamassa senāsane yathālābhasantoso. Yo pana attano pakativiruddhaṃ vā byādhiviruddhaṃ vā senāsanaṃ labhati, yatthassa vasato aphāsu hoti, so taṃ sabhāgassa bhikkhuno datvā tassa santake sappāyasenāsane vasantopi santuṭṭhova hoti. Ayamassa senāsane yathābalasantoso. Aparo mahāpuñño leṇamaṇḍapakūṭāgārādīni bahūni paṇītasenāsanāni labhati, so tāni cīvarādīni viya cirapabbajitabahussutaappalābhagilānānaṃ datvā yattha katthaci vasantopi santuṭṭhova hoti. Ayamassa senāsane yathāsāruppasantoso. Yopi “uttamasenāsanaṃ nāma pamādaṭṭhānaṃ, tattha nisinnassa thinamiddhaṃ okkamati, niddābhibhūtassa paṭibujjhato pāpavitakkā pātubhavantī”ti paṭisañcikkhitvā tādisaṃ senāsanaṃ pattampi na sampaṭicchati, so taṃ paṭikkhipitvā abbhokāsarukkhamūlādīsu vasanto santuṭṭhova hoti. Ayampi senāsane yathāsāruppasantoso.

Furthermore, here a monk obtains a dwelling, whether agreeable or disagreeable, and he generates neither joy nor aversion because of it; at the very least, he is content with whatever he has obtained, even a grass mat. This is his contentment with dwellings according to what is obtained. But if a monk obtains a dwelling that is contrary to his constitution or contrary to his illness, where dwelling causes him discomfort, he gives it to a compatible monk and remains indeed content while dwelling in a suitable dwelling belonging to that monk. This is his contentment with dwellings according to his strength. Another monk, one of great merit, obtains many excellent dwellings such as cave-dwellings, pavilions, gabled houses, and so forth. He gives them away, as he would robes and so forth, to the long-ordained, the learned, those who receive little, and the sick. He remains indeed content wherever he stays. This is his contentment with dwellings according to what is suitable. Yet another monk reflects thus: 'A superior dwelling is a cause for negligence. For one sitting there, sloth and torpor descend. When overcome by sleep, evil thoughts arise upon awakening.' Having considered this, he does not accept such a dwelling even if it is obtained. Rejecting it, he dwells contentedly in the open air, at the foot of trees, and so forth. This too is his contentment with dwellings according to what is suitable.

Idha pana bhikkhu bhesajjaṃ labhati lūkhaṃ vā paṇītaṃ vā, so yaṃ labhati teneva tussati, aññaṃ na pattheti, labhantopi na gaṇhāti. Ayamassa gilānapaccaye yathālābhasantoso. Yo pana telenatthiko phāṇitaṃ labhati, so taṃ sabhāgassa bhikkhuno datvā tassa hatthato telaṃ gahetvā vā aññadeva vā pariyesitvā bhesajjaṃ karontopi santuṭṭhova hoti. Ayamassa gilānapaccaye yathābalasantoso. Aparo mahāpuñño bahuṃ telamadhuphāṇitādipaṇītabhesajjaṃ labhati, so taṃ cīvaraṃ viya cirapabbajita-bahussuta-appalābhagilānānaṃ datvā tesaṃ ābhatena yena kenaci yāpentopi [P 2.0163] santuṭṭhova hoti. Yo pana ekasmiṃ bhājane muttaharītakaṃ ṭhapetvā ekasmiṃ catumadhuraṃ “gaṇha, bhante, yadicchasī”ti vuccamāno sacassa tesu aññatarenapi rogo vūpasammati, atha “muttaharītakaṃ nāma buddhādīhi vaṇṇita”nti catumadhuraṃ paṭikkhipitvā muttaharītakena bhesajjaṃ karonto paramasantuṭṭhova [M 2.0152] hoti. Ayamassa gilānapaccaye yathāsāruppasantoso. Iti ime tayo santose sandhāya “santuṭṭhāyaṃ, bhikkhave, kassapo itarītarena cīvarenā”ti vuttaṃ.

Furthermore, here a monk obtains medicine, whether coarse or excellent. He is content with what he obtains and does not long for anything else; even if he obtains more, he does not take it. This is his contentment with requisites for the sick according to what is obtained. Furthermore, if a monk who needs oil obtains molasses, he gives it to a compatible monk and, taking oil from his hand or seeking out other oil, prepares the medicine and remains indeed content. This is his contentment with requisites for the sick according to his strength. Another, a monk of great merit, obtains much excellent medicine such as oil, honey, and molasses. He gives it away, as he would a robe, to the long-ordained, the learned, those who receive little, and the sick; and, making do with whatever is brought for them, he remains indeed content. Furthermore, if someone places myrobalan steeped in cow's urine in one vessel and the four sweets in another, saying, 'Take, venerable sir, what you wish,' and if his illness would be pacified by either of them, then, thinking, 'Myrobalan steeped in cow's urine is praised by the Buddha and others,' he rejects the four sweets and, preparing the medicine with the myrobalan steeped in cow's urine, is supremely content. This is his contentment with requisites for the sick according to what is suitable. Thus, it was with reference to these three kinds of contentment that the Blessed One said: 'Monks, this Kassapa is content with whatever robe.'

Vaṇṇavādīti [V 2.0146] eko santuṭṭho hoti, santosassa vaṇṇaṃ na katheti. Eko na santuṭṭho hoti, santosassa vaṇṇaṃ katheti. Eko neva santuṭṭho hoti, na santosassa vaṇṇaṃ katheti. Eko santuṭṭho ca hoti, santosassa ca vaṇṇaṃ katheti. Ayaṃ tādisoti dassetuṃ itarītaracīvarasantuṭṭhiyā ca vaṇṇavādīti vuttaṃ. Anesananti dūteyyapahiṇagamanānuyogappabhedaṃ nānappakāraṃ anesanaṃ. Aladdhāti alabhitvā. Yathā ca ekacco “kathaṃ nu kho cīvaraṃ labhissāmī”ti puññavantehi bhikkhūhi saddhiṃ ekato hutvā kohaññaṃ karonto uttasati paritassati, ayaṃ evaṃ aladdhā ca cīvaraṃ na paritassati. Laddhā cāti dhammena samena labhitvā. Agadhitoti vigatalobhagedho. Amucchitoti adhimattataṇhāya mucchaṃ anāpanno. Anajjhāpannoti taṇhāya anotthaṭo apariyonaddho. Ādīnavadassāvīti anesanāpattiyañca gadhitaparibhoge ca ādīnavaṃ passamāno. Nissaraṇapaññoti, “yāvadeva sītassa paṭighātāyā”ti vuttanissaraṇameva jānanto paribhuñjatīti attho. Itarītarena piṇḍapātenātiādīsupi yathāladdhādīnaṃ yena kenaci piṇḍapātena, yena kenaci senāsanena, yena kenaci gilānapaccayabhesajjaparikkhārenāti evamattho daṭṭhabbo.

By 'one who speaks in praise' (vaṇṇavādī) is meant this: one monk is content but does not speak in praise of contentment. Another is not content but speaks in praise of contentment. Another is neither content nor speaks in praise of contentment. Another is both content and speaks in praise of contentment. To show that he is of this last kind, it was said that he is 'content with whatever robe and speaks in praise [of contentment]'. By 'improper seeking' (anesanaṃ) is meant various kinds of improper livelihood, such as the particular practice of engaging in going on errands as a messenger. By 'not having obtained' (aladdhā) is meant 'without having obtained'. Just as a certain person, thinking, 'How shall I obtain robes?' becomes anxious and distressed while associating with meritorious monks and acting deceitfully—this one, not having obtained robes, does not become distressed. By 'having obtained' (laddhā ca) is meant 'having obtained righteously and justly'. By 'without greed' (agadhito) is meant 'devoid of the greed of craving'. By 'not infatuated' (amucchito) is meant 'not fallen into the stupor of excessive craving'. By 'not attached' (anajjhāpanno) is meant 'not overwhelmed or enveloped by craving'. By 'seeing danger' (ādīnavadassāvī) is meant 'seeing the danger in the offense of improper seeking and in greedy consumption'. By 'with wisdom of escape' (nissaraṇapaññoti) is meant: he consumes, knowing only the escape that has been taught, as in the phrase, 'Just for the warding off of cold...' This is the meaning. In the phrases beginning with 'with whatever almsfood' (itarītarena piṇḍapātena), and so on, the meaning should be understood thus: with whatever almsfood, etc., that has been received; with any kind of almsfood, with any kind of lodging, with any kind of requisite of medicine for the sick.

Kassapena vā hi vo, bhikkhave, ovadissāmīti ettha yathā mahākassapatthero catūsu paccayesu tīhi santosehi santuṭṭho, tumhepi tathārūpā bhavathāti ovadanto kassapena ovadati nāma. Yo vā panassa kassapasadisoti etthāpi yo vā panaññopi [P 2.0164] kassapasadiso mahākassapatthero viya catūsu paccayesu tīhi santosehi santuṭṭho bhaveyya, tumhepi tathārūpā bhavathāti ovadanto kassapasadisena ovadati nāma. Tathattāya paṭipajjitabbanti “sammāsambuddhassa imāya imasmiṃ santuṭṭhisutte vuttasallekhācārapaṭipattiyā kathanaṃ nāma bhāro, amhākampi [M 2.0153] imaṃ paṭipattiṃ paripūraṃ katvā pūraṇaṃ bhāroyeva, āgato kho pana bhāro gahetabbo”ti cintetvā yathā mayā kathitaṃ, tathattāya tathābhāvāya tumhehipi paṭipajjitabbanti. Paṭhamaṃ.

Here, regarding the statement 'Monks, I shall advise you with Kassapa,' it means that by advising, 'Just as the Elder Mahākassapa was content with the three kinds of contentment regarding the four requisites, so too should you be of such a kind,' one advises with Kassapa. And here, regarding 'Or if one were similar to Kassapa,' it means that by advising, 'Even if another is similar to Kassapa, just as the Elder Mahākassapa was content with the three kinds of contentment regarding the four requisites, so too should you be of such a kind,' one advises with one similar to Kassapa. By 'one should practice for the sake of that state' (tathattāya paṭipajjitabbaṃ) is meant: thinking, 'For the Perfectly Enlightened One, the teaching of this practice of austere conduct mentioned in this Discourse on Contentment is a burden; for us too, to fulfill this practice completely is also a burden; but a burden that has come must be taken up,' you too should practice for the sake of that state, for becoming so, just as I have taught. The First.

2. Anottappīsuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Anottappī Sutta

145. Dutiye anātāpīti yaṃ vīriyaṃ kilese ātapati, tena rahito. Anottappīti nibbhayo kilesuppattito kusalānuppattito ca bhayarahito. Sambodhāyāti sambujjhanatthāya. Nibbānāyāti [V 2.0147] nibbānasacchikiriyāya. Anuttarassa yogakkhemassāti arahattassa tañhi anuttarañceva catūhi ca yogehi khemaṃ.

145. In the second, ‘without ardour’ (anātāpī) means devoid of the energy that scorches defilements. ‘Without dread’ (anottappī) means fearless, lacking fear of the arising of defilements and of the non-arising of wholesome states. ‘For awakening’ (sambodhāya) means for the purpose of awakening. ‘For Nibbāna’ (nibbānāya) means for the realization of Nibbāna. ‘For the unsurpassed security from bondage’ (anuttarassa yogakkhemassa) refers to arahantship, for that is both unsurpassed and secure from the four bonds.

Anuppannātiādīsu ye pubbe appaṭiladdhapubbaṃ cīvarādiṃ vā paccayaṃ upaṭṭhākasaddhivihārika-antevāsīnaṃ vā aññatarato manuññavatthuṃ paṭilabhitvā taṃ subhaṃ sukhanti ayoniso gaṇhantassa aññataraṃ vā pana ananubhūtapubbaṃ ārammaṇaṃ yathā tathā vā ayoniso āvajjentassa lobhādayo pāpakā akusalā dhammā uppajjanti, te anuppannāti veditabbā. Aññathā hi anamatagge saṃsāre anuppannā nāma pāpakā dhammā natthi. Anubhūtapubbepi ca vatthumhi ārammaṇe vā yassa pakatibuddhiyā vā uddesaparipucchāya vā pariyattinavakammayonisomanasikārānaṃ vā aññataravasena pubbe anuppajjitvā pacchā tādisena paccayena sahasā uppajjanti, imepi “anuppannā uppajjamānā anatthāya saṃvatteyyu”nti veditabbā. Tesuyeva pana vatthārammaṇesu punappunaṃ uppajjamānā nappahīyanti nāma, te “uppannā appahīyamānā anatthāya saṃvatteyyu”nti veditabbā. Ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthārato pana uppannānuppannabhedo ca pahānappahānavidhānañca sabbaṃ visuddhimagge ñāṇadassanavisuddhiniddese kathitaṃ.

In the phrase ‘not yet arisen’ (anuppannā), etc., when one improperly grasps as beautiful and pleasant any previously unacquired requisite such as robes, or any agreeable object obtained from a supporter, a co-resident, or a pupil—or when one improperly attends in any way to any previously unexperienced object—then evil, unwholesome states such as greed arise. These should be understood as ‘not yet arisen’. Otherwise, indeed, in the beginningless cycle of existence, there are no evil states that have not arisen before. Even regarding an object or basis previously experienced, if such states had not arisen before but later suddenly arise due to some condition—whether through natural intelligence, instruction and questioning, or by some means among study, new activity, and wise attention—these too should be understood as ‘not yet arisen, arising to one’s detriment’. Furthermore, when these same states arise repeatedly in relation to the same objects or bases and are not abandoned, they should be understood as ‘arisen and not abandoned, leading to harm’. This is the summary here. The detailed classification of arisen and unarisen states, as well as the methods for abandoning and not abandoning them, is fully explained in the section on ‘Purification by Knowledge and Vision’ in the Visuddhimagga.

Anuppannā [P 2.0165] me kusalā dhammāti appaṭiladdhāpi sīlasamādhimaggaphalasaṅkhātā anavajjadhammā. Uppannāti teyeva paṭiladdhā. Nirujjhamānā anatthāya saṃvatteyyunti te sīlādidhammā parihānivasena puna anuppattiyā nirujjhamānā anatthāya saṃvatteyyunti veditabbā. Ettha ca lokiyā parihāyanti, lokuttarānaṃ parihāni natthīti. “Uppannānaṃ kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ ṭhitiyā”ti imassa [M 2.0154] pana sammappadhānassa vasenāyaṃ desanā katā. Dutiyamaggo vā sīghaṃ anuppajjamāno, paṭhamamaggo nirujjhamāno anatthāya saṃvatteyyāti evampettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Iti imasmiṃ sutte ime cattāro sammappadhānā pubbabhāgavipassanāvasena kathitāti. Dutiyaṃ.

‘Unarisen in me are wholesome states’ (anuppannā me kusalā dhammā) means the blameless states known as virtue, concentration, path, and fruition, which have not yet been attained. ‘Arisen’ (uppannā) means those very states have been attained. ‘Ceasing, they would lead to my harm’ (nirujjhamānā anatthāya saṃvatteyyuṃ) – it should be understood that those states of virtue and so on, ceasing due to decline and non-reappearance, would lead to harm. And here, mundane states decline, but there is no decline for supramundane states. However, this teaching was given by means of this right effort: ‘for the stability of arisen wholesome states’ (uppannānaṃ kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ ṭhitiyā). Alternatively, if the second path does not quickly arise, the first path, having ceased, would lead to harm. Thus, this is how the meaning here should be understood. In this way, in this sutta, these four right efforts are explained in terms of preliminary insight. The Second.

3. Candūpamasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Sutta on the Simile of the Moon

146. Tatiye candūpamāti candasadisā hutvā. Kiṃ parimaṇḍalatāya? No, apica kho yathā cando gaganatalaṃ pakkhandamāno na kenaci saddhiṃ santhavaṃ vā sinehaṃ vā ālayaṃ vā [V 2.0148] nikantiṃ vā patthanaṃ vā pariyuṭṭhānaṃ vā karoti, na ca na hoti mahājanassa piyo manāpo, tumhepi evaṃ kenaci saddhiṃ santhavādīnaṃ akaraṇena bahujanassa piyā manāpā candūpamā hutvā khattiyakulādīni cattāri kulāni upasaṅkamathāti attho. Apica yathā cando andhakāraṃ vidhamati, ālokaṃ pharati, evaṃ kilesandhakāravidhamanena ñāṇālokapharaṇena cāpi candūpamā hutvāti evamādīhipi nayehi ettha attho daṭṭhabbo.

146. In the third sutta, ‘like the moon’ (candūpamā) means being similar to the moon. In what way? Due to its perfect roundness? No. Rather, just as the moon, while moving through the expanse of the sky, does not form any intimacy, affection, attachment, liking, longing, or obsession with anyone, and yet is dear and pleasing to the great multitude, so too should you, by not forming intimacy and so on with anyone, become dear and pleasing to many people, and like the moon, approach the four families, beginning with the Khattiyas. This is the meaning. Furthermore, just as the moon dispels darkness and spreads light, so too, by dispelling the darkness of defilements and spreading the light of knowledge, you become like the moon. The meaning here should be understood through these and similar methods.

Apakasseva kāyaṃ apakassa cittanti teneva santhavādīnaṃ akaraṇena kāyañca cittañca apakassitvā, apanetvāti attho. Yo hi bhikkhu araññepi na vasati, kāmavitakkādayopi vitakketi, ayaṃ neva kāyaṃ apakassati, na cittaṃ. Yo hi araññepi kho viharati, kāmavitakkādayo pana vitakketi, ayaṃ kāyameva apakassati, na cittaṃ. Yo gāmante vasati[P 2.0166], kāmavitakkādayopi kho na ca vitakketi, ayaṃ cittameva apakassati, na kāyaṃ. Yo pana araññe ceva vasati, kāmavitakkādayo ca na vitakketi, ayaṃ ubhayampi apakassati. Evarūpā hutvā kulāni upasaṅkamathāti dīpento “apakasseva kāyaṃ apakassa citta”nti āha.

‘Withdraw the body, withdraw the mind’ (apakasseva kāyaṃ apakassa cittaṃ) means that by this very non-formation of intimacy and so on, one withdraws and removes both body and mind; this is the meaning. For a bhikkhu who does not dwell even in the forest and also thinks thoughts of sensuality and so on, this one withdraws neither the body nor the mind. Indeed, a bhikkhu who dwells even in the forest but thinks thoughts of sensuality and so on, this one withdraws only the body, not the mind. A bhikkhu who lives near a village but does not think thoughts of sensuality and so on, this one withdraws only the mind, not the body. But a bhikkhu who dwells in the forest and does not think thoughts of sensuality and so on, this one withdraws both. To show that one should approach the families having become like this, He said, ‘Withdraw the body, withdraw the mind’.

Niccanavakāti niccaṃ navakāva, āgantukasadisā eva hutvāti attho. Āgantuko hi paṭipāṭiyā sampattagehaṃ pavisitvā sace naṃ gharasāmikā disvā, “amhākaṃ puttabhātaro vippavāsaṃ gatā evaṃ vicariṃsū”ti anukampamānā nisīdāpetvā bhojenti, bhuttamattoyeva “tumhākaṃ bhājanaṃ [M 2.0155] gaṇhathā”ti uṭṭhāya pakkamati, na tehi saddhiṃ santhavaṃ vā karoti, na kiccakaraṇīyāni vā saṃvidahati, evaṃ tumhepi paṭipāṭiyā sampattagharaṃ pavisitvā yaṃ iriyāpathesu pasannā manussā denti, taṃ gahetvā chinnasanthavā, tesaṃ kiccakaraṇīye abyāvaṭā hutvā nikkhamathāti dīpeti.

‘Always like a newcomer’ (niccanavakā) means always being just like a visitor; this is the meaning. For a visitor, upon entering a house in due course, if the householders see him and, feeling compassion, thinking, ‘Our sons and brothers who have gone abroad must be wandering just like this,’ they seat him and offer food. As soon as he has eaten, he rises and leaves, saying, ‘Take your dish,’ without forming intimacy with them or arranging for any duties. Similarly, He indicates: ‘You too, having entered a house in due course, should accept what people, pleased with your deportment, give, then depart, having severed intimacy and remaining uninvolved in their duties.’

Imassa pana niccanavakabhāvassa āvibhāvatthaṃ dvebhātikavatthu kathetabbaṃ – vasāḷanagaragāmato kira dve bhātikā nikkhamitvā pabbajitā, te cūḷanāgatthero ca mahānāgatthero cāti paññāyiṃsu. Te cittalapabbate tiṃsa vassāni vasitvā arahattaṃ pattā “mātaraṃ passissāmā”ti āgantvā vasāḷanagaravihāre vasitvā punadivase mātugāmaṃ piṇḍāya pavisiṃsu. Mātāpi tesaṃ uḷuṅkena yāguṃ nīharitvā ekassa patte ākiri. Tassā taṃ olokayamānāya [V 2.0149] puttasineho uppajji. Atha naṃ āha – “tvaṃ, tāta, mayhaṃ putto mahānāgo”ti. Thero “pacchimaṃ theraṃ puccha upāsike”ti vatvā pakkāmi. Pacchimatherassapi yāguṃ datvā, “tāta, tvaṃ mayhaṃ putto cūḷanāgo”ti pucchi? Thero “kiṃ, upāsike, purimaṃ theraṃ na [P 2.0167] pucchasī”ti? Vatvā pakkāmi. Evaṃ mātarāpi saddhiṃ chinnasanthavo bhikkhu niccanavako nāma hoti.

Furthermore, to make manifest this state of being always like a newcomer, the story of the two brothers should be told. It is said that two brothers from the town-village of Vasāḷa went forth and became monks; they became known as the Elder Cūḷanāga and the Elder Mahānāga. After dwelling on Cittalapabbata mountain for thirty years and attaining Arahantship, they thought, ‘We will see our mother,’ and came to stay at the Vasāḷanagara monastery. The next day, they entered their mother’s village for alms-food. Their mother brought out rice gruel with a ladle and poured it into one elder’s bowl. As she was looking at him, affection for her son arose in her. Then she said to him, ‘Dear one, you are my son, Mahānāga.’ The elder, saying, ‘Laywoman, ask the elder who comes after,’ departed. Having given gruel to the elder who came after as well, she asked, ‘Dear one, are you my son, Cūḷanāga?’ The elder, saying, ‘Why, laywoman, did you not ask the elder who came before?’ departed. In this way, a bhikkhu who has severed intimacy even with his mother is called ‘one who is always like a newcomer’.

Appagabbhāti na pagabbhā, aṭṭhaṭṭhānena kāyapāgabbhiyena, catuṭṭhānena vacīpāgabbhiyena, anekaṭṭhānena manopāgabbhiyena ca virahitāti attho. Aṭṭhaṭṭhānaṃ kāyapāgabbhiyaṃ nāma saṅghagaṇapuggala-bhojanasālā-jantāgharanahānatittha-bhikkhācāramagga-antaragharappavesanesu kāyena appatirūpakaraṇaṃ. Seyyathidaṃ – idhekacco saṅghamajjhe pallatthikāya vā nisīdati pāde pādaṃ ādhāyitvā vāti evamādi (mahāni. 165). Tathā gaṇamajjhe. Gaṇamajjheti catuparisasannipāte vā suttantikagaṇādisannipāte vā. Tathā vuḍḍhatare puggale. Bhojanasālāya pana vuḍḍhānaṃ āsanaṃ na deti, navānaṃ āsanaṃ paṭibāhati. Tathā jantāghare. Vuḍḍhe cettha anāpucchā aggijalanādīni karoti. Nhānatitthe ca yadidaṃ “daharo vuḍḍhoti pamāṇaṃ akatvā āgatapaṭipāṭiyā nhāyitabba”nti vuttaṃ, tampi anādiyanto pacchā āgantvā udakaṃ otaritvā vuḍḍhe ca nave ca bādhati. Bhikkhācāramagge pana aggāsanaaggodakaaggapiṇḍānaṃ [M 2.0156] atthāya purato gacchati bāhāya bāhaṃ paharanto. Antaragharappavesane vuḍḍhehi paṭhamataraṃ pavisati, daharehi saddhiṃ kāyakīḷanakaṃ karotīti evamādi.

‘Not impudent’ (appagabbhā) means not being impudent, that is, being free from the eight kinds of bodily impudence, the four kinds of verbal impudence, and the numerous kinds of mental impudence; this is the meaning. The eight kinds of bodily impudence consist of improper bodily conduct in the midst of the Sangha, a group, an individual, in a dining hall, a steam-bath house, at a bathing place, on the alms-round path, and when entering a house. For instance, a certain person here sits cross-legged in the midst of the Sangha, or sits with one foot placed on the other, and so on. Similarly, in the midst of a group. ‘In the midst of a group’ means in a gathering of the four assemblies or in a gathering of a group of Suttantikas, etc. Likewise, towards a senior person. Furthermore, in the dining hall, one does not give a seat to the elders and obstructs a seat for the junior monks. Similarly, in the steam-bath house. And here, without asking the elders, one does things like lighting the fire. And at the bathing place, not heeding what was said—‘One should bathe in order of arrival, without making a measure of “junior” or “senior”’—one arrives later, enters the water, and obstructs both the elders and the juniors. Furthermore, on the alms-round path, for the sake of the best seat, best water, and best alms-food, one goes in front, striking arm against arm. When entering a house, one enters before the elders; one engages in bodily play with the juniors, and so on.

Catuṭṭhānaṃ vacīpāgabbhiyaṃ nāma saṅghagaṇapuggalaantaragharesu appatirūpavācānicchāraṇaṃ. Seyyathidaṃ – idhekacco saṅghamajjhe anāpucchā dhammaṃ bhāsati. Tathā pubbe vuttappakārassa gaṇassa majjhe puggalassa ca santike, tattheva manussehi pañhaṃ puṭṭho vuḍḍhataraṃ anāpucchā [P 2.0168] vissajjeti. Antaraghare pana “itthannāme kiṃ atthi? Kiṃ yāgu, udāhu khādanīyaṃ bhojanīyaṃ? Kiṃ me dassasi? Kiṃ ajja khādissāma? Kiṃ bhuñjissāma? Kiṃ pivissāmā”tiādīni bhāsati.

The four kinds of verbal impudence consist of uttering improper speech in the midst of the Sangha, a group, an individual, or within a house. For instance, a certain person here teaches the Dhamma in the midst of the Sangha without having asked permission. Similarly, in the midst of a group of the type previously mentioned or in the presence of an individual, when asked a question by laypeople there, one answers without asking a more senior monk. But within a house, one says such things as: ‘Is so-and-so there? Is there gruel, or hard food and soft food? What will you give me? What shall we eat today? What shall we consume? What shall we drink?’ and so on.

Anekaṭṭhānaṃ manopāgabbhiyaṃ nāma tesu tesu ṭhānesu kāyavācāhi ajjhācāraṃ anāpajjitvāpi manasāva kāmavitakkādīnaṃ vitakkanaṃ. Apica dussīlasseva sato “sīlavāti [V 2.0150] maṃ jano jānātū”ti evaṃ pavattā pāpicchatāpi manopāgabbhiyaṃ. Iti sabbesampi imesaṃ pāgabbhiyānaṃ abhāvena appagabbhā hutvā upasaṅkamathāti vadati.

In many respects, what is called mental impudence is the thinking of thoughts of sensual desire and so forth with the mind alone, even without having committed transgression by body or speech in those various situations. Moreover, for one who is unvirtuous, the evil desire that has arisen thus, 'Let people know me as virtuous,' is also mental impudence. Thus, he says: 'Approach without impudence, having become free from all these forms of impudence.'

Jarudapānanti jiṇṇakūpaṃ. Pabbatavisamanti pabbate visamaṃ papātaṭṭhānaṃ. Nadīvidugganti nadiyā viduggaṃ chinnataṭaṭṭhānaṃ. Apakasseva kāyanti tādisāni ṭhānāni yo khiḍḍādipasuto kāyaṃ anapakassa ekatobhāriyaṃ akatvāva vāyupatthambhakaṃ aggāhāpetvā cittampi anapakassa “ettha patito hatthapādabhañjanādīni pāpuṇātī”ti anādīnavadassāvitāya anubbejetvā sampiyāyamāno oloketi, so patitvā hatthapādabhañjanādianatthaṃ pāpuṇāti. Yo pana udakatthiko vā aññena vā kenaci kiccena oloketukāmo kāyaṃ apakassa ekato bhāriyaṃ katvā vāyupatthambhakaṃ gāhāpetvā, cittampi apakassa ādīnavadassanena saṃvejetvā oloketi, so na patati, yathāruciṃ oloketvā sukhī yenakāmaṃ pakkamati.

'Jarudapāna' means an old well. 'Pabbatavisama' means an uneven, precipitous place on a mountain. 'Nadīvidugga' means a place with a broken bank in a river, which is difficult to traverse. Regarding 'without withdrawing the body': Suppose a person given to play and so forth looks at such places. Without withdrawing the body, without making it lean to one side, without making it firm through the air element, and also without withdrawing the mind, not being alarmed due to not seeing the danger—'If I fall here, I will suffer broken hands and feet'—he looks on playfully. That person falls and meets with the misfortune of broken hands and feet, and so on. But one who wishes to look, either because he needs water or for some other reason, withdraws the body, makes it lean to one side, makes it firm through the air element, and also withdraws the mind, becoming alarmed by seeing the danger, and then looks. That person does not fall. Having looked as he wishes, he departs happily wherever he desires.

Evameva [M 2.0157] khoti ettha idaṃ opammasaṃsandanaṃ – jarudapānādayo viya hi cattāri kulāni, olokanapuriso viya bhikkhu. Yathā anapakaṭṭhakāyacitto tāni olokento puriso tattha patati, evaṃ arakkhitehi kāyādīhi kulāni upasaṅkamanto bhikkhu kulesu bajjhati, tato nānappakāraṃ sīlapādabhañjanādianatthaṃ pāpuṇāti. Yathā pana apakaṭṭhakāyacitto puriso tattha na patati, evaṃ rakkhiteneva kāyena rakkhitehi cittehi rakkhitāya vācāya suppaṭṭhitāya satiyā apakaṭṭhakāyacitto hutvā kulāni upasaṅkamanto bhikkhu kulesu na bajjhati. Athassa yathā tattha apatitassa purisassa, na pādā bhañjanti, evaṃ sīlapādo na bhijjati. Yathā hatthā na [P 2.0169] bhañjanti, evaṃ saddhāhattho na bhijjati. Yathā kucchi na bhijjati, evaṃ samādhikucchi na bhijjati. Yathā sīsaṃ na bhijjati, evaṃ ñāṇasīsaṃ na bhijjati, yathā ca taṃ khāṇukaṇṭakādayo na vijjhanti, evamimaṃ rāgakaṇṭakādayo na vijjhanti. Yathā so nirupaddavo yathāruci oloketvā sukhī yenakāmaṃ pakkamati, evaṃ bhikkhu kulāni nissāya cīvarādayo paccaye paṭisevanto kammaṭṭhānaṃ vaḍḍhetvā saṅkhāre sammasanto arahattaṃ patvā lokuttarasukhena sukhito yenakāmaṃ agatapubbaṃ nibbānadisaṃ gacchati.

Regarding 'Just so': Herein, this is the connection of the simile. Indeed, the four families should be seen as being like the old well and so forth; the monk should be seen as being like the person looking. Just as a person with an unwithdrawn body and mind falls there while looking at them, so too a monk who approaches families with an unguarded body and so forth becomes bound in the families. From that, he meets with various misfortunes, beginning with the breaking of the foot of virtue. But just as a person with a withdrawn body and mind does not fall there, so too a monk who approaches families with a guarded body, guarded minds, guarded speech, and well-established mindfulness—having withdrawn his body and mind—does not become bound in the families. Then, for him, just as the feet of the person who did not fall there are not broken, so the foot of virtue is not broken. Just as the hands are not broken, so the hand of faith is not broken. Just as the belly is not broken, so the belly of concentration is not broken. Just as the head is not broken, so the head of wisdom is not broken. And just as stumps, thorns, and so forth do not pierce that person, so the thorns of lust and so forth do not pierce this monk. Just as that person, being unharmed, looks as he wishes and, being happy, departs wherever he desires, so too this monk, relying on families and using the requisites such as robes, develops his meditation subject, contemplates the conditioned phenomena, attains arahantship, and, being happy with supramundane happiness, goes to the direction of Nibbāna, a place not gone to before.

Idāni yo hīnādhimuttiko micchāpaṭipanno evaṃ vadeyya “sammāsambuddho ‘tividhaṃ pāgabbhiyaṃ pahāya niccanavakattena candūpamā kulāni upasaṅkamathā’ti vadanto aṭṭhāne ṭhapeti, asayhaṃ [V 2.0151] bhāraṃ āropeti, yaṃ na sakkā kātuṃ taṃ kāretī”ti, tassa vādapathaṃ pacchinditvā, “sakkā evaṃ kātuṃ, atthi evarūpo bhikkhū”ti dassento kassapo, bhikkhavetiādimāha.

Now, a person of inferior inclination and wrong practice might say thus: 'The Perfectly Enlightened One, in saying, "Having abandoned the threefold impudence, approach families always as a new guest, like the moon," places one in an impossible situation, imposes an unbearable burden, and makes one do what cannot be done.' To cut off this line of argument and to show, 'It is possible to act thus; there is such a monk,' the Blessed One said the words beginning with, 'Kassapa, O monks...'

Ākāse pāṇiṃ cālesīti nīle gaganantare yamakavijjutaṃ cārayamāno viya heṭṭhābhāgaṃ uparibhāgaṃ ubhatopassesu pāṇiṃ sañcāresi. Idañca pana tepiṭake buddhavacane asambhinnapadaṃ nāma. Attamanoti tuṭṭhacitto sakamano, na domanassena pacchinditvā gahitamano. Kassapassa, bhikkhaveti idampi purimanayeneva paravādaṃ pacchinditvā atthi evarūpo bhikkhūti dassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ.

Regarding 'He moved his hand in the sky': As if causing a pair of lightning flashes to move about in the blue expanse of the sky, he moved his hand downwards, upwards, and to both sides. And this, in the word of the Buddha in the Tipiṭaka, is called an uncompounded term. Regarding 'delighted': It means his mind was pleased, his mind was his own, not a mind seized and overcome by displeasure. This statement, 'Regarding Kassapa, O monks...' was also spoken in the same way as before, to cut off the argument of the opponents and to show, 'There is such a monk.'

Pasannākāraṃ [M 2.0158] kareyyunti cīvarādayo paccaye dadeyyuṃ. Tathattāya paṭipajjeyyunti sīlassa āgataṭṭhāne sīlaṃ pūrayamānā, samādhivipassanā maggaphalānaṃ āgataṭṭhāne tāni tāni sampādayamānā tathābhāvāya paṭipajjeyyuṃ. Anudayanti rakkhaṇabhāvaṃ. Anukampanti muducittataṃ. Ubhayañcetaṃ kāruññasseva vevacanaṃ. Kassapo, bhikkhaveti idampi purimanayeneva paravādaṃ pacchinditvā atthi evarūpo bhikkhūti dassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Kassapena vāti ettha candopamādivasena yojanaṃ katvā purimanayeneva attho veditabbo. Tatiyaṃ.

Regarding 'They might show signs of faith': They might give requisites such as robes. Regarding 'They might practice for the state of thusness': Fulfilling virtue where virtue is concerned, and accomplishing concentration, insight, path, and fruition where they are concerned, they should practice for that state of being. 'Anudaya' means the state of wishing to protect. 'Anukampa' means tenderness of mind. Both these terms are synonyms for compassion. This statement, 'Kassapa, O monks...' was also spoken by the Blessed One in the same way as before, to cut off the argument of the opponents and to show, 'There is such a monk.' In the phrase 'Or by Kassapa,' having made the connection by way of the moon simile and so on, the meaning should be understood in the same way as before. The Third Sutta.

4. Kulūpakasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Kulūpaka Sutta

147. Catutthe [P 2.0170] kulūpakoti kulagharānaṃ upagantā. Dentuyeva meti dadantuyeva mayhaṃ. Sandīyatīti aṭṭīyati pīḷiyati. Sesamettha vuttanayānusāreneva veditabbaṃ. Catutthaṃ.

147. In the fourth sutta, 'kulūpaka' means 'a monk who approaches the houses of families'. 'Dentuyeva me' means 'May they indeed give to me'. 'Sandīyati' means 'is wearied, is oppressed'. The rest here should be understood only in accordance with the method already stated. The Fourth.

5. Jiṇṇasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Jiṇṇa Sutta

148. Pañcame jiṇṇoti thero mahallako. Garukānīti taṃ satthu santikā laddhakālato paṭṭhāya chinnabhinnaṭṭhāne suttasaṃsibbanena ceva aggaḷadānena ca anekāni paṭalāni hutvā garukāni jātāni. Nibbasanānīti pubbe bhagavatā nivāsetvā apanītatāya evaṃladdhanāmāni. Tasmāti yasmā tvaṃ jiṇṇo ceva garupaṃsukūlo ca. Gahapatānīti paṃsukūlikaṅgaṃ vissajjetvā gahapatīhi dinnacīvarāni dhārehīti vadati. Nimantanānīti piṇḍapātikaṅgaṃ vissajjetvā salākabhattādīni [V 2.0152] nimantanāni bhuñjāhīti vadati. Mama ca santiketi āraññikaṅgaṃ vissajjetvā gāmantasenāsaneyeva vasāhīti vadati.

148. In the fifth sutta, 'jiṇṇa' means 'the elder is of great age'. 'Garukāni' (heavy) means that from the time he received it from the Teacher, it had become heavy, having become many layers in torn and broken places through stitching with thread and the application of patches. 'Nibbasanāni' (cast-off robes) means they received this name because they were previously worn and then discarded by the Blessed One. 'Tasmā' (therefore) means 'because you are both old and your rag-robe is heavy'. 'Gahapatāni' (householders' robes) means he says, 'Having abandoned the ascetic practice of wearing rag-robes, wear robes given by householders.' 'Nimantanāni' (invitations) means he says, 'Having abandoned the ascetic practice of going for alms-food, partake of invited meals such as token-meals.' 'Mama ca santike' (and near me) means he says, 'Having abandoned the ascetic practice of forest-dwelling, dwell only in a monastery near a village.'

Nanu ca yathā rājā senāpatiṃ senāpatiṭṭhāne ṭhapetvā tassa rājūpaṭṭhānādinā attano kammena ārādhentasseva taṃ ṭhānantaraṃ gahetvā aññassa dadamāno ayuttaṃ nāma karoti, evaṃ satthā mahākassapattherassa paccuggamanatthāya tigāvutaṃ maggaṃ gantvā rājagahassa ca nāḷandāya ca antare bahuputtakarukkhamūle nisinno tīhi ovādehi upasampādetvā tena saddhiṃ attano cīvaraṃ parivattetvā theraṃ jātiāraññikaṅgañceva jātipaṃsukūlikaṅgañca [M 2.0159] akāsi, so tasmiṃ kattukamyatāchandena satthu cittaṃ ārādhentasseva paṃsukūlādīni vissajjāpetvā gahapaticīvarapaṭiggahaṇādīsu niyojento ayuttaṃ nāma karotīti. Na karoti. Kasmā? Attajjhāsayattā. Na hi satthā dhutaṅgāni vissajjāpetukāmo, yathā pana aghaṭṭitā bheriādayo saddaṃ na vissajjenti, evaṃ aghaṭṭitā evarūpā puggalā [P 2.0171] na sīhanādaṃ nadantīti nadāpetukāmo sīhanādajjhāsayena evamāha. Theropi satthu ajjhāsayānurūpeneva “ahaṃ kho, bhante, dīgharattaṃ āraññiko cevā”tiādinā nayena sīhanādaṃ nadati.

Is it not so? Just as a king, having appointed a general to the position of general, does something improper if he takes away that rank and gives it to another while that general is still pleasing him through his service to the king and so on; in the same way, the Teacher went a distance of three gāvutas to meet the Elder Mahākassapa, sat down at the foot of the Bahuputtaka banyan tree between Rājagaha and Nāḷandā, ordained him with three exhortations, exchanged his own robe with him, and established the Elder in the practice of being a natural forest-dweller and a natural rag-robe wearer. If that Teacher, while the Elder was pleasing the Teacher's mind with the desire to do what is to be done, were to make him abandon the rag-robe practice and so on and enjoin him in the acceptance of householders' robes and so on, would he not be doing something improper? He does not do so. Why? Because of his intention for the Elder's welfare. Indeed, the Teacher does not wish to make him abandon the ascetic practices. But just as unstruck drums and so on do not emit a sound, in the same way, such individuals, when unprompted, do not roar a lion's roar. Thus, wishing to make him roar, he spoke thus with the intention of eliciting a lion's roar. The Elder, too, in perfect accordance with the Teacher's intention, roars a lion's roar with the words beginning, 'For a long time, venerable sir, I have been a forest-dweller...'

Diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāranti diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāro nāma āraññikasseva labbhati, no gāmantavāsino. Gāmantasmiñhi vasanto dārakasaddaṃ suṇāti, asappāyarūpāni passati, asappāye sadde suṇāti, tenassa anabhirati uppajjati. Āraññiko pana gāvutaṃ vā aḍḍhayojanaṃ vā atikkamitvā araññaṃ ajjhogāhetvā vasanto dīpibyagghasīhādīnaṃ sadde suṇāti, yesaṃ savanapaccayā amānusikāsavanarati uppajjati. Yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ –

Regarding 'a pleasant abiding in the visible state': what is called 'a pleasant abiding in the visible state' is obtained only by a forest-dweller, not by one who dwells near a village. For one dwelling near a village hears the sound of children, sees unsuitable sights, and hears unsuitable sounds; because of that, non-delight arises in him. But a forest-dweller, having gone past a gāvuta or half a yojana and entered the forest to dwell, hears the sounds of leopards, tigers, lions, and so on. Due to hearing these, a superhuman delight in hearing arises. Regarding this, it was said:

“Suññāgāraṃ paviṭṭhassa, santacittassa bhikkhuno;

Amānusī ratī hoti, sammā dhammaṃ vipassato.

For a monk who has entered a secluded dwelling, whose mind is peaceful, and who rightly sees the Dhamma with insight, a superhuman delight arises.

“Yato yato sammasati, khandhānaṃ udayabbayaṃ;

Labhatī pītipāmojjaṃ, amataṃ taṃ vijānataṃ. (dha. pa. 373-374);

Whenever he reflects upon the arising and passing away of the aggregates, he obtains joy and gladness. For those who know, that is the Deathless.

“Purato [V 2.0153] pacchato vāpi, aparo ce na vijjati;

Tattheva phāsu bhavati, ekassa ramato vane”ti.

If before or behind no other person is found, then indeed, for one delighting alone in the forest, there is comfort.

Tathā piṇḍapātikasseva labbhati, no apiṇḍapātikassa. Apiṇḍapātiko hi akālacārī hoti, turitacāraṃ gacchati, parivatteti, palibuddhova gacchati, tattha ca bahusaṃsayo hoti. Piṇḍapātiko pana na akālacārī hoti, na turitacāraṃ gacchati, na parivatteti, apalibuddhova gacchati, tattha ca na bahusaṃsayo hoti.

Likewise, this is obtained only by one who goes for alms-food, not by one who does not go for alms-food. For one who does not go for alms-food is one who goes at an improper time, he goes hurriedly, he turns back, he goes as if obstructed, and in that there is much doubt. But one who goes for alms-food is not one who goes at an improper time, he does not go hurriedly, he does not turn back, he goes unobstructed, and in that there is not much doubt.

Kathaṃ? Apiṇḍapātiko hi gāmato dūravihāre vasamāno kālasseva “yāguṃ vā pārivāsikabhattaṃ vā lacchāmi, āsanasālāya vā pana [M 2.0160] uddesabhattādīsu kiñcideva mayhaṃ pāpuṇissatī”ti makkaṭakasuttāni chindanto sayitagorūpāni uṭṭhāpento pātova gacchanto akālacārī hoti. Manusse khettakammādīnaṃ atthāya gehā nikkhanteyeva sampāpuṇituṃ [P 2.0172] migaṃ anubandhanto viya vegena gacchanto turitacārī hoti. Antarā kiñcideva disvā “asukaupāsako vā asukaupāsikā vā gehe, no gehe”ti pucchati, “no gehe”ti sutvā “idāni kuto labhissāmī”ti? Aggidaḍḍho viya pavedhati, sayaṃ pacchimadisaṃ gantukāmo pācīnadisāya salākaṃ labhitvā aññaṃ pacchimadisāya laddhasalākaṃ upasaṅkamitvā, “bhante, ahaṃ pacchimadisaṃ gamissāmi, mama salākaṃ tumhe gaṇhatha, tumhākaṃ salākaṃ mayhaṃ dethā”ti salākaṃ parivatteti. Ekaṃ vā pana salākabhattaṃ āharitvā paribhuñjanto “aparassāpi salākabhattassa pattaṃ dethā”ti manussehi vutte, “bhante, tumhākaṃ pattaṃ detha, ahaṃ mayhaṃ patte bhattaṃ pakkhipitvā tumhākaṃ pattaṃ dassāmī”ti aññassa pattaṃ dāpetvā bhatte āhaṭe attano patte pakkhipitvā pattaṃ paṭidento pattaṃ parivatteti nāma. Vihāre rājarājamahāmattādayo mahādānaṃ denti, iminā ca bhiyyo dūragāme salākā laddhā, tattha agacchanto puna sattāhaṃ salākaṃ na labhatīti alābhabhayena gacchati, evaṃ gacchanto palibuddho hutvā gacchati nāma. Yassa cesa salākabhattādino atthāya gacchati, “taṃ dassanti nu kho me, udāhu na dassanti, paṇītaṃ nu kho dassanti, udāhu lūkhaṃ, thokaṃ nu kho, udāhu bahukaṃ, sītalaṃ nu kho, udāhu uṇha”nti evaṃ tattha ca bahusaṃsayo hoti.

How? For a monk who does not observe the alms-food-goer's practice, dwelling in a monastery far from the village, he thinks early in the morning: 'I will receive rice gruel or the meal for those undergoing probation. Or perhaps something will come to me in the dining hall, such as a designated meal or other offerings.' Cutting spiderwebs, rousing sleeping cattle, and going out very early—thus, he is one who goes at an improper time. In order to meet people who have just left their homes for field work and so on, he goes with speed, like one chasing a deer—thus, he is one who moves hastily. Along the way, seeing someone, he asks, 'Is such-and-such a layman or laywoman at home, or not at home?' Hearing, 'Not at home,' he frets, 'Where will I get anything now?' and trembles like one burned by fire. Wishing to go west, he receives a token for alms-food from the east. Then, approaching another monk who has received a token from the west, he says, 'Venerable sir, I am going west. You take my token, and give me your token.' Thus, he exchanges tokens. Or, having brought and eaten a single token-meal, when people say, 'Give the bowl for another token-meal,' he says, 'Venerable sir, give your bowl. I will put the food in my bowl and then give your bowl back to you.' Having had another's bowl given, when the food is brought, he puts it in his own bowl and returns the other bowl—this is called 'exchanging bowls.' When a great offering is being given in the monastery by kings, royal ministers, and others, and this monk has received a token for a more distant village, he goes there out of fear of not receiving, thinking, 'If I do not go there, I will not get a token again for seven days.' Going in this way, he goes obstructed. Furthermore, regarding the token-meal and so on for which he goes, he has many doubts: 'Will they give it to me or not? Will they give fine food or coarse? A little or a lot? Cold or hot?' Thus, in that situation, he has much uncertainty.

Piṇḍapātiko pana kālasseva vuṭṭhāya vattapaṭivattaṃ katvā sarīraṃ paṭijaggitvā vasanaṭṭhānaṃ [V 2.0154] pavisitvā kammaṭṭhānaṃ manasikatvā kālaṃ sallakkhetvā mahājanassa uḷuṅkabhikkhādīni dātuṃ pahonakakāle gacchatīti na akālacārī hoti, ekekaṃ padavāraṃ cha koṭṭhāse katvā vipassanto gacchatīti na turitacārī hoti, attano garubhāvena “asuko gehe, na gehe”ti na pucchati, salākabhattādīniyeva na gaṇhāti. Agaṇhanto kiṃ parivattessati? Na aññassa vasena palibuddhova hoti[M 2.0161], kammaṭṭhānaṃ manasikaronto yathāruci gacchati, itaro viya na bahusaṃsayo hoti. Ekasmiṃ gāme vā vīthiyā vā alabhitvā aññattha carati. Tasmimpi alabhitvā aññattha caranto missakodanaṃ saṅkaḍḍhitvā amataṃ [P 2.0173] viya paribhuñjitvā gacchati.

But an alms-food-goer rises early, attends to his duties, takes care of his body, enters his dwelling, focuses on his meditation subject, discerns the proper time, and goes when the people are able to give offerings like soup, gruel, and alms-food—thus he is not one who goes at an improper time. He walks contemplating insight, dividing each step into six parts—thus he is not one who walks hastily. Due to his dignified nature, he does not ask, 'Is so-and-so at home or not at home?' He does not accept token-meals and the like at all. Not accepting, what would he exchange? He is not obstructed through dependence on another. Focusing on his meditation subject, he goes as he pleases. He is not full of doubts like the other monk. If he does not receive alms in one village or street, he moves on elsewhere. Even if he does not receive alms there, he continues on, gathering mixed rice and consuming it like nectar as he goes.

Paṃsukūlikasseva labbhati, no apaṃsukūlikassa. Apaṃsukūliko hi vassāvāsikaṃ pariyesanto carati, na senāsanasappāyaṃ pariyesati. Paṃsukūliko pana na vassāvāsikaṃ pariyesanto carati, senāsanasappāyameva pariyesati. Tecīvarikasseva labbhati, na itarassa. Atecīvariko hi bahubhaṇḍo bahuparikkhāro hoti, tenassa phāsuvihāro natthi. Appicchādīnañceva labbhati, na itaresanti. Tena vuttaṃ – “attano ca diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāraṃ sampassamāno”ti. Pañcamaṃ.

It is attainable only by one who wears rag-robes, not by one who does not wear rag-robes. For one who does not wear rag-robes wanders seeking a rains-residence robe, not seeking a suitable lodging. But one who wears rag-robes does not wander seeking a rains-residence robe; he seeks only a suitable lodging. It is attainable only by one who keeps to the three robes, not by the other. For one who does not keep to the three robes has many possessions and much equipment; thus for him there is no ease of living. It is attainable only by those with few wishes and so forth, not by others. Therefore it was said: 'and seeing for oneself a pleasant dwelling in this very life.' Fifth.

6. Ovādasuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Ovāda Sutta

149. Chaṭṭhe ahaṃ vāti kasmā āha? Theraṃ attano ṭhāne ṭhapanatthaṃ. Kiṃ sāriputtamoggallānā natthīti? Atthi. Evaṃ panassa ahosi “ime na ciraṃ ṭhassanti, kassapo pana vīsavassasatāyuko, so mayi parinibbute sattapaṇṇiguhāyaṃ nisīditvā dhammavinayasaṅgahaṃ katvā mama sāsanaṃ pañcavassasahassaparimāṇakālapavattanakaṃ karissati, attano taṃ ṭhāne ṭhapemi, evaṃ bhikkhū kassapassa sussūsitabbaṃ maññissantī”ti. Tasmā evamāha. Dubbacāti dukkhena vattabbā. Dovacassakaraṇehīti dubbacabhāvakaraṇehi. Appadakkhiṇaggāhinoti anusāsaniṃ sutvā padakkhiṇaṃ na gaṇhanti yathānusiṭṭhaṃ na paṭipajjanti, appaṭipajjantā vāmagāhino nāma jātāti dasseti. Accāvadanteti atikkamma vadante, sutapariyattiṃ nissāya ativiya vādaṃ karonteti attho. Ko bahutaraṃ bhāsissatīti dhammaṃ kathento ko bahuṃ bhāsissati, kiṃ tvaṃ, udāhu ahanti? Ko sundarataranti, eko bahuṃ bhāsanto asahitaṃ amadhuraṃ bhāsati, eko sahitaṃ [V 2.0155] madhuraṃ, taṃ sandhāyāha “ko sundaratara”nti? Eko pana bahuñca sundarañca kathento ciraṃ na bhāsati, lahuññeva uṭṭhāti, eko addhānaṃ pāpeti, taṃ sandhāyāha “ko ciratara”nti? Chaṭṭhaṃ.

6. In the sixth sutta, why did the Blessed One say, “I...”? To establish the elder in his own position. Are Sāriputta and Moggallāna not present? They are present. But this thought occurred to him: “These two will not remain for long, but Kassapa has a lifespan of one hundred and twenty years. After my final passing, he will sit in the Sattapaṇṇi Cave, compile the Dhamma and Vinaya, and make my teaching last for five thousand years. I will establish him in my position; in this way, the monks will think that Kassapa’s word should be heeded.” Therefore, he spoke thus. “Difficult to admonish” means difficult to speak to. “By making difficult to admonish” means by causes of being difficult to speak to. “Not taking it straightforwardly” means that after hearing an instruction, they do not accept it respectfully and do not practice as instructed; he shows that those who do not practice become what are called 'perverse takers.' “Speaking excessively” means speaking beyond limits, making extreme arguments based on learning the scriptures; that is the meaning. “Who will speak more?” means, while discussing the Dhamma, who will speak much—you or I? “Who speaks more beautifully?”—one speaks much but disjointedly and unpleasantly, another connectedly and sweetly; referring to this, he asks, “Who speaks more beautifully?” Moreover, one speaks much and beautifully but does not speak for long, rising quickly, while another prolongs it; referring to this, he asks, “Who speaks longer?” Sixth.

7. Dutiyaovādasuttavaṇṇanā

149. Commentary on the Second Discourse on Admonition

150. Sattame [M 2.0162][P 2.0174] saddhāti okappanasaddhā. Vīriyanti kāyikacetasikaṃ vīriyaṃ. Paññāti kusaladhammajānanapaññā. Na santi bhikkhū ovādakāti imassa puggalassa ovādakā anusāsakā kalyāṇamittā natthīti idaṃ, bhante, parihānanti dasseti. Sattamaṃ.

150. In the seventh sutta, ‘faith’ means faith based on conviction. ‘Energy’ means bodily and mental energy. ‘Wisdom’ means the wisdom that knows wholesome states. ‘There are no monks to advise’ means: for this person there are no advisors, instructors, or spiritual friends; this, venerable sir, he indicates, is a decline. Seventh.

8. Tatiyaovādasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Third Discourse on Advice

151. Aṭṭhame tathā hi panāti pubbe sovacassatāya, etarahi ca dovacassatāya kāraṇapaṭṭhapane nipāto. Tatrāti tesu theresu. Ko nāmāyaṃ bhikkhūti ko nāmo ayaṃ bhikkhu? Kiṃ tissatthero kiṃ nāgattheroti? Tatrāti tasmiṃ evaṃ sakkāre kayiramāne. Tathattāyāti tathābhāvāya, āraññikādibhāvāyāti attho. Sabrahmacārikāmoti “ime maṃ parivāretvā carantū”ti evaṃ kāmeti icchati patthetīti sabrahmacārikāmo. Tathattāyāti lābhasakkāranibbattanatthāya. Brahmacārupaddavenāti yo sabrahmacārīnaṃ catūsu paccayesu adhimattacchandarāgo upaddavoti vuccati, tena upaddutā. Abhipatthanāti adhimattapatthanā. Brahmacāriabhipatthanenāti brahmacārīnaṃ adhimattapatthanāsaṅkhātena catupaccayabhāvena. Aṭṭhamaṃ.

151. In the eighth sutta, the particle ‘tathā hi pana’ is used in the sense of establishing the reason for formerly being easy to admonish and now being difficult to admonish. ‘Therein’ means among those elders. ‘Who is this monk?’ means what is the name of this monk? Is it Tissa the elder or Nāga the elder? ‘Therein’ means when such honor is being shown to him. ‘For such a state’ means for that state, that is, for the state of being a forest-dweller, etc. ‘Desiring the companionship of fellow practitioners’ means he desires, wishes, and longs, ‘Let these monks surround me and move about.’ ‘For such a state’ means for the purpose of producing gain and honor. ‘By the harm to the holy life’ means: afflicted by that which is called a harm to the fellow practitioners, namely, the excessive desire and lust for the four requisites. ‘Excessive longing’ means intense longing. ‘By the excessive longing of the practitioners of the holy life’ means by the state of the four requisites, which is described as the excessive longing of the practitioners of the holy life. The eighth.

9. Jhānābhiññasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Discourse on Absorption and Direct Knowledge

152. Navame yāvadeva ākaṅkhāmīti yāvadeva icchāmi. Yāni pana ito paraṃ vivicceva kāmehītiādinā nayena cattāri rūpāvacarajjhānāni, sabbaso rūpasaññānaṃ samatikkamātiādinā nayena catasso arūpasamāpattiyo, sabbaso nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ samatikkamma saññāvedayitanirodhanti evaṃ nirodhasamāpatti, anekavihitaṃ [P 2.0175] iddhividhantiādinā nayena pañca lokikābhiññā ca vuttā. Tattha yaṃ vattabbaṃ siyā, taṃ sabbaṃ anupadavaṇṇanāya ceva [V 2.0156] bhāvanāvidhānena ca saddhiṃ visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 1.69) vitthāritameva. Chaḷabhiññāya pana āsavānaṃ khayāti āsavānaṃ khayena. Anāsavanti āsavānaṃ apaccayabhūtaṃ. Cetovimuttinti arahattaphalasamādhiṃ. Paññāvimuttinti arahattaphalapaññaṃ. Navamaṃ.
