152. In the ninth sutta, ‘as far as I wish’ means as far as I desire. Furthermore, what follows from this—by the method beginning with ‘secluded from sensual pleasures,’ the four form-sphere absorptions; by the method beginning with ‘by completely transcending perceptions of form,’ the four formless attainments; the attainment of cessation, as in ‘having completely transcended the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the cessation of perception and feeling’; and by the method beginning with ‘various kinds of psychic power,’ the five mundane direct knowledges—have been taught. Therein, whatever should be said, all of that has been explained in detail by me in the Visuddhimagga, together with the word-by-word explanation and the method of development. However, regarding the six direct knowledges, ‘from the destruction of the taints’ means by the destruction of the taints. ‘Taintless’ means not being a condition for the taints. ‘Liberation of mind’ means the concentration of the fruit of arahantship. ‘Liberation by wisdom’ means the wisdom of the fruit of arahantship. The ninth.

10. Upassayasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Discourse on the Residence

153. Dasame [M 2.0163] āyāma, bhanteti kasmā bhikkhunīupassayagamanaṃ yācati? Na lābhasakkārahetu, kammaṭṭhānatthikā panettha bhikkhuniyo atthi, tā ussukkāpetvā kammaṭṭhānaṃ kathāpessāmīti yācati. Nanu ca so sayampi tepiṭako bahussuto, kiṃ sayaṃ kathetuṃ na sakkotīti? No na sakkoti. Buddhapaṭibhāgassa pana sāvakassa kathaṃ saddhātabbaṃ maññissantīti yācati. Bahukicco tvaṃ bahukaraṇīyoti kiṃ thero navakammādipasuto, yena naṃ evamāhāti? No, satthari pana parinibbute catasso parisā ānandattheraṃ upasaṅkamitvā, “bhante, idāni kassa pattacīvaraṃ gahetvā caratha, kassa pariveṇaṃ sammajjatha, kassa mukhodakaṃ dethā”ti rodanti paridevanti. Thero “aniccā saṅkhārā, vuddhasarīrepi nillajjova maccurājā pahari. Esā saṅkhārānaṃ dhammatā, mā socittha, mā paridevitthā”ti parisaṃ saññāpeti. Idamassa bahukiccaṃ. Taṃ sandhāya thero evamāha. Sandassesīti paṭipattiguṇaṃ dassesi. Samādapesīti gaṇhāpesi. Samuttejesīti samussāhesi. Sampahaṃsesīti paṭiladdhaguṇena modāpesi.

153. In the tenth, regarding 'Venerable sir, may you come,' why does he request a visit to the nuns' residence? Not for the sake of gain and honor; rather, he requests, thinking, 'There are nuns here who desire meditation subjects; having encouraged them, I will have the meditation subject taught.' But is he not himself a bearer of the Tipiṭaka and a man of great learning? Why can he not teach them himself? It is not that he cannot. But he requests, thinking, 'They will consider the word of a disciple who is the counterpart of the Buddha to be credible.' Regarding 'You have many duties, much to do,' was the Elder Ānanda engaged in new construction work and so on, for which reason the Elder Kassapa said this to him? No. But after the Teacher’s final nibbāna, the four assemblies approached the Elder Ānanda, weeping and lamenting, 'Venerable sir, now whose bowl and robes do you carry and go about with? Whose cell do you sweep? For whom do you offer water for washing the face?' The Elder made the assembly understand, saying, 'Conditioned things are impermanent. The shameless king of death struck even the body of the Buddha. This is the nature of conditioned things. Do not grieve, do not lament.' This was his great responsibility. Referring to this, the Elder Kassapa spoke thus. 'He would instruct' means he showed the quality of the practice. 'He would establish' means he made them grasp it. 'He would inspire' means he roused them. 'He would gladden' means he made them rejoice with the quality they had attained.

Thullatissāti sarīrena thūlā, nāmena tissā. Vedehamuninoti paṇḍitamunino. Paṇḍito hi ñāṇasaṅkhātena vedena īhati sabbakiccāni karoti, tasmā “vedeho”ti vuccati. Vedeho ca so muni cāti, vedehamuni. Dhammaṃ [P 2.0176] bhāsitabbaṃ maññatīti tipiṭakadharassa dhammabhaṇḍāgārikassa sammukhe sayaṃ araññavāsī paṃsukūliko samāno “dhammakathiko aha”nti dhammaṃ bhāsitabbaṃ maññati. Idaṃ kiṃ pana, kathaṃ panāti? Avajānamānā bhaṇati. Assosīti aññena āgantvā ārocitavasena assosi. Āgamehi tvaṃ, āvusoti tiṭṭha tvaṃ, āvuso. Mā te saṅgho uttari upaparikkhīti mā bhikkhusaṅgho atirekaokāse taṃ upaparikkhīti. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – “ānandena buddhapaṭibhāgo sāvako vārito, ekā bhikkhunī na vāritā, tāya saddhiṃ santhavo vā sineho vā bhavissatī”ti mā taṃ saṅgho evaṃ amaññīti.

Thullatissā means she was large (thūlā) in body, and her name was Tissā. 'The Vedeha sage' means the wise sage. For a wise person (paṇḍita) strives and accomplishes all duties with wisdom (veda), which is a term for knowledge (ñāṇa); therefore he is called a 'Vedeha.' He is both a Vedeha and a sage (muni); thus he is a Vedehamuni. 'He thinks the Dhamma should be spoken' means: in the presence of the bearer of the Tipiṭaka, the treasurer of the Dhamma, he—being a forest-dweller and a wearer of rag-robes—thinks, 'I am a Dhamma-preacher,' and considers that the Dhamma should be spoken by him. 'What is this? How is this?' she says, speaking with contempt. 'He heard' means he heard it by way of another who came and informed him. 'You should wait, friend' means 'Stay, friend.' 'Lest the Saṅgha investigate you further' means lest the community of monks investigate you on excessive grounds. This is what is meant: 'Let the Saṅgha not think of you thus: "The disciple who is the counterpart of the Buddha was stopped, but a single nun was not stopped; there must be some intimacy or affection with her."'"

Idāni [V 2.0157][M 2.0164] attano buddhapaṭibhāgabhāvaṃ dīpento taṃ kiṃ maññasi, āvusotiādimāha? Sattaratananti sattahatthappamāṇaṃ. Nāganti hatthiṃ. Aḍḍhaṭṭharatanaṃ vāti aḍḍharatanena ūnaaṭṭharatanaṃ, purimapādato paṭṭhāya yāva kumbhā vidatthādhikasattahatthubbedhanti attho. Tālapattikāyāti taruṇatālapaṇṇena. Cavitthāti cutā, na matā vā naṭṭhā vā, buddhapaṭibhāgassa pana sāvakassa upavādaṃ vatvā mahākassapatthere chahi abhiññāhi sīhanādaṃ nadante tassā kāsāvāni kaṇṭakasākhā viya kacchusākhā viya ca sarīraṃ khādituṃ āraddhāni, tāni hāretvā setakāni nivatthakkhaṇeyevassā cittassādo udapādīti. Dasamaṃ.

Now, to reveal his own status as a counterpart of the Buddha, he said, 'What do you think, friend?' and so on. 'Seven-ratana' means seven cubits in measure. 'Nāga' means an elephant. 'Or aḍḍhaṭṭha-ratana' means eight cubits less half a cubit; the meaning is that from its front feet up to its forehead, it was seven cubits and a span in height. 'With a tālapattikā' means with a young palm leaf. 'She fell' means she fell away from the Dispensation; it does not mean she died or was destroyed. But after she had spoken ill of the disciple who is the counterpart of the Buddha, while the Elder Mahākassapa was roaring a lion's roar with the six direct knowledges, her saffron robes, like thorny branches or like an itching sore, began to consume her body. Having removed them and put on white clothes, in that very moment, a pleasant mental feeling arose in her. The tenth.

11. Cīvarasuttavaṇṇanā

11. Commentary on the Discourse on the Robe

154. Ekādasame dakkhiṇāgirisminti rājagahaṃ parivāretvā ṭhitassa girino dakkhiṇabhāge janapado dakkhiṇāgiri nāma, tasmiṃ cārikaṃ caratīti attho. Cārikā ca nāma duvidhā hoti turitacārikā ca aturitacārikā ca. Tattha yaṃ ekacco ekaṃ kāsāvaṃ nivāsetvā ekaṃ pārupitvā pattacīvaraṃ aṃse laggetvā chattaṃ ādāya sarīrato sedehi paggharantehi divasena sattaṭṭhayojanāni gacchati, yaṃ vā pana buddhā kiñcideva [P 2.0177] bodhaneyyasattaṃ disvā yojanasatampi yojanasahassampi khaṇena gacchanti, esā turitacārikā nāma. Devasikaṃ pana gāvutaṃ aḍḍhayojanaṃ tigāvutaṃ yojananti ettakaṃ addhānaṃ ajjatanāya nimantanaṃ adhivāsayato janasaṅgahaṃ karoto gamanaṃ, esā aturitacārikā nāma. Ayaṃ idha adhippetā.

154. In the eleventh sutta: Regarding Dakkhiṇāgiri, it is the name of a district in the southern part of the mountain that stands surrounding Rājagaha. The meaning is that he was journeying on tour in that district. And a tour is of two kinds: a swift tour and an unhurried tour. Therein, when a certain monk, having put on one saffron robe and draped another, having slung his bowl and robe over his shoulder and taken an umbrella, travels seven or eight yojanas in a day with sweat pouring from his body; or when the Buddhas, seeing some being who is to be awakened, travel a hundred or even a thousand yojanas in an instant—this is called a swift tour. On the other hand, the journeying of one who, accepting an invitation for the day, travels daily a distance of a gāvuta, half a yojana, three gāvutas, or a yojana, for the benefit of the people—this is called an unhurried tour. This latter one is intended here.

Nanu ca thero pañcavīsati vassāni chāyā viya dasabalassa pacchato pacchato gacchantova ahosi, “kahaṃ ānando”ti vacanassa okāsameva na adāsi, so kismiṃ kāle bhikkhusaṅghena saddhiṃ cārikaṃ carituṃ okāsaṃ labhatīti? Satthu parinibbānasaṃvacchare. Parinibbute kira satthari mahākassapatthero satthu parinibbāne sannipatitassa bhikkhusaṅghassa majjhe nisīditvā dhammavinayasaṅgāyanatthaṃ pañcasate bhikkhū uccinitvā, “āvuso, mayaṃ rājagahe vassaṃ vasantā dhammavinayaṃ saṅgāyissāma, tumhe pure [M 2.0165] vassūpanāyikāya attano palibodhaṃ ucchinditvā rājagahe sannipatathā”ti vatvā attanā rājagahaṃ gato. Ānandattheropi bhagavato pattacīvaraṃ ādāya mahājanaṃ saññāpento sāvatthiṃ gantvā tato nikkhamma rājagahaṃ gacchanto dakkhiṇāgirismiṃ cārikaṃ cari. Taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ.

But surely, for twenty-five years the Elder followed the Ten-Powered One from behind, like a shadow, and never gave occasion for the words, 'Where is Ānanda?' to be spoken. At what time, then, did he get the opportunity to journey on tour with the Saṅgha of monks? In the year of the Teacher’s final nibbāna. It is said that when the Teacher had finally attained nibbāna, the Elder Mahākassapa, sitting in the midst of the Saṅgha of monks who had assembled at the Teacher's final nibbāna, selected five hundred monks for the purpose of rehearsing the Dhamma and Vinaya. Having selected them, he said: 'Venerable sirs, residing in Rājagaha for the rains retreat, we shall rehearse the Dhamma and Vinaya. Before the rains retreat begins, you should sever your impediments and assemble in Rājagaha.' Having said this, he himself went to Rājagaha. The Elder Ānanda, too, taking the Blessed One’s bowl and robe and informing the great populace, went to Sāvatthī. Then, departing from there and proceeding towards Rājagaha, he journeyed on tour in Dakkhiṇāgiri. It was with reference to this that it was said.

Yebhuyyena [V 2.0158] kumārabhūtāti ye te hīnāyāvattā nāma, te yebhuyyena kumārakā daharā taruṇā ekavassikadvevassikā bhikkhū ceva anupasampannakumārakā ca. Kasmā panete pabbajitā, kasmā hīnāyāvattāti? Tesaṃ kira mātāpitaro cintesuṃ – “ānandatthero satthu vissāsiko aṭṭha vare yācitvā upaṭṭhahati, icchiticchitaṭṭhānaṃ satthāraṃ gahetvā gantuṃ sakkoti, amhākaṃ dārake etassa santike pabbājema, so satthāraṃ gahetvā āgamissati, tasmiṃ āgate mayaṃ mahāsakkāraṃ kātuṃ labhissāmā”ti. Iminā tāva kāraṇena nesaṃ ñātakā te pabbājesuṃ. Satthari pana parinibbute tesaṃ sā patthanā upacchinnā, atha te ekadivaseneva uppabbājesuṃ.

Regarding 'mostly being boys': those who are called 'reverters to the lower life' were for the most part boys—young, youthful, monks of one or two rains, and unordained boys. Now, why had they gone forth? And why did they revert to the lower life? It is said their parents thought: 'The Elder Ānanda is trusted by the Teacher; having requested eight boons, he attends upon him. He is able to take the Teacher and go to any place he wishes. Let us have our sons go forth in his presence. He will bring the Teacher when he comes, and when he has come, we will get to make a great offering.' For this reason, in the first place, their relatives had them go forth. But when the Teacher had finally attained nibbāna, that aspiration of theirs was cut off. Then, their relatives had them disrobe in a single day.

Yathābhirantanti [P 2.0178] yathāruciyā yathāajjhāsayena. Tikabhojanaṃ paññattanti, idaṃ “gaṇabhojane aññatra samayā pācittiya”nti (pāci. 211). Idaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Tattha hi tiṇṇaṃ janānaṃ akappiyanimantanaṃ sādiyitvā ekato paṭiggaṇhantānampi anāpatti, tasmā “tikabhojana”nti vuttaṃ.

Regarding 'according to their pleasure': this means according to their liking, according to their disposition. Regarding 'a meal for three is prescribed': this was said with reference to the training rule, 'In the case of a group meal, except at the proper time, it is an offense of expiation.' For in that case, there is no offense even for three persons who, having consented to an improper invitation, receive it together. Therefore, it is called 'a meal for three'.

Dummaṅkūnaṃ puggalānaṃ niggahāyāti dussīlapuggalānaṃ niggaṇhanatthaṃ. Pesalānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ phāsuvihārāyāti dummaṅkūnaṃ niggaheneva pesalānaṃ uposathapavāraṇā vattanti, samaggavāso hoti, ayaṃ tesaṃ phāsuvihāro hoti, imassa phāsuvihārassa atthāya. Mā pāpicchā pakkhaṃ nissāya saṅghaṃ bhindeyyunti yathā devadatto sapariso kulesu viññāpetvā bhuñjanto pāpicche nissāya saṅghaṃ bhindi, evaṃ aññepi pāpicchā gaṇabandhena kulesu viññāpetvā bhuñjamānā gaṇaṃ vaḍḍhetvā taṃ pakkhaṃ nissāya mā saṅghaṃ bhindeyyunti, iti iminā kāraṇena paññattanti attho. Kulānuddayatāya cāti bhikkhusaṅghe uposathapavāraṇaṃ katvā samaggavāsaṃ vasante [M 2.0166] manussā salākabhattādīni datvā saggaparāyaṇā bhavanti, iti imāya kulānuddayatāya ca paññattanti attho.

Regarding 'for the restraint of unruly persons': for the purpose of restraining immoral persons. Regarding 'for the comfortable living of amiable monks': it is only by the restraining of the unruly that the Uposatha and Pavāraṇā proceed for the amiable monks, and that there is harmonious living. This is their comfortable living; it is for the sake of this comfortable living. Regarding 'lest those of evil desires, relying on a faction, should split the Saṅgha': just as Devadatta with his followers, by making requests to families and eating, relying on those of evil desires, split the Saṅgha, so too other monks of evil desires, by forming a group, making requests to families and eating, increasing their group, and relying on that faction, should not split the Saṅgha. The meaning is that it was prescribed for this reason. And regarding 'out of compassion for families': when the Saṅgha of monks lives in harmony, having performed the Uposatha and Pavāraṇā, people give ticket-food and so on and are destined for heaven. The meaning is that it was also prescribed for this reason of compassion for families.

Sassaghātaṃ maññe carasīti sassaṃ ghātento viya āhiṇḍasi. Kulūpaghātaṃ maññe carasīti kulāni upaghātento viya hananto viya āhiṇḍasi. Olujjatīti visesena palujjati bhijjati. Palujjanti kho te, āvuso, navappāyāti, āvuso, ete tuyhaṃ pāyena yebhuyyena navakā ekavassikaduvassikā daharā ceva sāmaṇerā ca palujjanti bhijjanti. Na vāyaṃ kumārako mattamaññāsīti ayaṃ kumārako attano pamāṇaṃ na jānātīti theraṃ tajjento āha.

Regarding 'I think you wander as a destroyer of crops': you wander about as if destroying the grain. Regarding 'I think you wander as a destroyer of families': you wander about as if harming, as if striking down the families. Regarding 'it dissolves': it especially falls apart, it breaks. Regarding 'Indeed, venerable sir, your new followers are dissolving': venerable sir, these new ones of yours, for the most part—these young monks of one or two rains and these novices—are dissolving and breaking apart. Regarding 'This boy did not know his measure': meaning, 'This boy does not know his own limit,' he spoke, admonishing the Elder.

Kumārakavādā [V 2.0159] na muccāmāti kumārakavādato na muccāma[P 2.0179]. Tathā hi pana tvanti idamassa evaṃ vattabbatāya kāraṇadassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Ayañhettha adhippāyo – yasmā tvaṃ imehi navehi bhikkhūhi indriyasaṃvararahitehi saddhiṃ vicarasi, tasmā kumārakehi saddhiṃ vicaranto kumārakoti vattabbataṃ arahasīti.

Regarding 'we are not free from being called "boy"': we are not free from the accusation of being a 'boy'. Regarding 'For indeed, you...': this was said to show the reason for his being fit to be addressed in that way. And this is the intention here: since you wander together with these new monks who are devoid of sense-restraint, therefore, by wandering together with boys, you are fit to be called a 'boy'.

Aññatitthiyapubbo samānoti idaṃ yasmā therassa imasmiṃ sāsane neva ācariyo na upajjhāyo paññāyati, sayaṃ kāsāyāni gahetvā nikkhanto, tasmā anattamanatāya aññatitthiyapubbataṃ āropayamānā āha.

Regarding 'being one formerly of another sect': because for the Elder, in this Dispensation, neither a teacher nor a preceptor is known—he went forth on his own, having taken up the saffron robes—therefore, out of displeasure, she spoke, imputing to him the state of having formerly been of another sect.

Sahasāti ettha rāgamohacāropi sahasācāro, idaṃ pana dosacāravasena vuttaṃ. Appaṭisaṅkhāti appaccavekkhitvā, idāni attano pabbajjaṃ sodhento yatvāhaṃ, āvusotiādimāha. Tattha aññaṃ satthāraṃ uddisitunti ṭhapetvā bhagavantaṃ aññaṃ mayhaṃ satthāti evaṃ uddisituṃ na jānāmi. Sambādho gharāvāsotiādīsu sacepi saṭṭhihatthe ghare yojanasatantarepi vā dve jāyampatikā vasanti, tathāpi tesaṃ sakiñcanasapalibodhaṭṭhena gharāvāso sambādhoyeva. Rajāpathoti rāgarajādīnaṃ uṭṭhānaṭṭhānanti mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ. “Āgamanapatho”tipi vattuṃ vaṭṭati. Alagganaṭṭhena abbhokāso viyāti abbhokāso. Pabbajito hi kūṭāgāraratanamayapāsādadevavimānādīsu pihitadvāravātapānesu paṭicchannesu vasantopi neva laggati na sajjati na bajjhati, tena vuttaṃ [M 2.0167] “abbhokāso pabbajjā”ti. Apica sambādho gharāvāso kusalakiriyāya okāsābhāvato rajāpatho asaṃvutasaṅkāraṭṭhānaṃ viya rajānaṃ, kilesarajānaṃ sannipātaṭṭhānato, abbhokāso pabbajjā kusalakiriyāya yathā sukhaṃ okāsasabbhāvato.

Herein, regarding the word 'rashly': conduct arising from lust and delusion is also rash conduct, but this was said by way of conduct arising from hatred. 'Without reflection' means without considering. Now, purifying his own going forth, he said, 'Since I, friend...' and so on. Therein, 'to point to another teacher' means: setting aside the Blessed One, I do not know how to point to another, saying, 'He is my teacher.' In such passages as 'Confined is the household life': even if a husband and wife live in a house of sixty cubits, or even a hundred yojanas apart, still, because of the nature of having possessions and impediments, the household life is indeed confined. 'A path of dust': 'It is the place where the dust of passion and so on arises,' is stated in the Great Commentary. It is also acceptable to say it means 'a path of arrival.' 'Like an open space' means it is called 'open space' in the sense of non-clinging. For one who has gone forth, even while dwelling in gabled halls, jeweled palaces, celestial mansions, and so on, which are enclosed and have their doors and windows shut, does not cling, is not attached, and is not bound. Therefore it is said, 'The going forth is an open space.' Furthermore, the household life is 'confined' due to the lack of opportunity for wholesome action; it is a 'path of dust' because, like an unguarded rubbish heap, it is a place for the gathering of dust, that is, the dust of the defilements. The going forth is an 'open space' because there is opportunity for wholesome action as one pleases.

Nayidaṃ sukaraṃ…pe… pabbajeyyanti ettha ayaṃ saṅkhepakathā – yadetaṃ sikkhattayabrahmacariyaṃ ekampi divasaṃ akhaṇḍaṃ katvā carimakacittaṃ pāpetabbatāya ekantaparipuṇṇaṃ [P 2.0180] caritabbaṃ, ekadivasampi ca kilesamalena amalīnaṃ katvā carimakacittaṃ pāpetabbatāya ekantaparisuddhaṃ, saṅkhalikhitaṃ likhitasaṅkhasadisaṃ dhotasaṅkhasappaṭibhāgaṃ caritabbaṃ, idaṃ na sukaraṃ agāraṃ ajjhāvasatā agāramajjhe vasantena ekantaparipuṇṇaṃ…pe… carituṃ, yaṃnūnāhaṃ kesamassuṃ ohāretvā kasāyarasapītatāya kāsāyāni brahmacariyaṃ carantānaṃ anucchavikāni vatthāni acchādetvā paridahitvā agārasmā nikkhamitvā anagāriyaṃ pabbajjeyyanti. Ettha ca yasmā agārassa [V 2.0160] hitaṃ kasivaṇijjādikammaṃ agāriyanti vuccati, taṃ pabbajjāya natthi, tasmā pabbajjā anagāriyāti ñātabbā, taṃ anagāriyaṃ. Pabbajeyyanti paṭipajjeyyaṃ.

Regarding 'This is not easy... I should go forth,' here is the summary: This holy life of the threefold training must be practiced in an utterly complete way, so that it is unbroken for even a single day, for the purpose of reaching the final consciousness. And for even a single day, it must be practiced in an utterly pure way, so that it is unstained by the stain of defilements, for the purpose of reaching the final consciousness; it must be practiced so that it is polished like a conch shell. This is not easy to practice in an utterly complete way... for one living in a home, dwelling in the midst of a household. What if I were to shave off my hair and beard, put on the saffron robes—robes suitable for those practicing the holy life, which are colored by drinking the astringent sap—and having worn and draped them, go forth from the household life into homelessness? And here, since work beneficial to the household, such as agriculture and commerce, is called 'household work,' and that is not present in the going forth, therefore the going forth should be known as 'non-household.' That 'non-household' life, 'I should go forth,' means 'I should undertake.'

Paṭapilotikānanti jiṇṇapilotikānaṃ terasahatthopi hi navasāṭako dasānaṃ chinnakālato paṭṭhāya pilotikāti vuccati. Iti mahārahāni vatthāni chinditvā kataṃ saṅghāṭiṃ sandhāya “paṭapilotikānaṃ saṅghāṭi”nti vuttaṃ. Addhānamaggappaṭipannoti aḍḍhayojanato paṭṭhāya maggo addhānanti vuccati, taṃ addhānamaggaṃ paṭipanno, dīghamaggaṃ paṭipannoti attho.

'Of rags' means of worn-out rags. For even a new cloth, thirteen cubits long, is called a rag from the moment its fringes are cut. Thus, with reference to a saṅghāṭi made by cutting up valuable cloths, it is said 'a saṅghāṭi of rags'. 'One who has set out on a long journey': a road is called a 'long journey' from half a yojana onwards. 'He has set out on that long journey' means he has set out on a long road.

Idāni yathā esa pabbajito, yathā ca addhānamaggaṃ paṭipanno, imassatthassa āvibhāvatthaṃ abhinīhārato paṭṭhāya anupubbikathā kathetabbā – atīte kira kappasatasahassamatthake padumuttaro nāma satthā udapādi, tasmiṃ haṃsavatīnagaraṃ upanissāya kheme migadāye viharante vedeho nāma kuṭumbiko asītikoṭidhanavibhavo pātova subhojanaṃ bhuñjitvā uposathaṅgāni adhiṭṭhāya gandhapupphādīni gahetvā vihāraṃ gantvā satthāraṃ pūjetvā vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Tasmiṃ khaṇe satthā mahānisabhattheraṃ nāma tatiyasāvakaṃ “etadaggaṃ, bhikkhave, mama sāvakānaṃ [M 2.0168] bhikkhūnaṃ dhutavādānaṃ yadidaṃ nisabho”ti etadagge ṭhapesi. Upāsako [P 2.0181] taṃ sutvā pasanno dhammakathāvasāne mahājane uṭṭhāya gate satthāraṃ vanditvā, “bhante, sve mayhaṃ bhikkhaṃ adhivāsethā”ti āha. Mahā kho, upāsaka, bhikkhusaṅghoti. Kittako bhagavāti. Aṭṭhasaṭṭhibhikkhusatasahassanti. Bhante, ekaṃ sāmaṇerampi vihāre asesetvā bhikkhaṃ adhivāsethāti. Satthā adhivāsesi. Upāsako satthu adhivāsanaṃ viditvā gehaṃ gantvā mahādānaṃ sajjetvā punadivase satthu kālaṃ ārocāpesi. Satthā pattacīvaramādāya bhikkhusaṅghaparivuto upāsakassa gharaṃ gantvā paññattāsane nisinno dakkhiṇodakāvasāne yāgubhattādīni sampaṭicchanto bhattavissaggaṃ akāsi. Upāsakopi satthu santike nisīdi.

Now, to make the meaning of how he went forth and how he set out on the long journey clear, a gradual discourse should be told, starting from his aspiration. It is said that in the past, a hundred thousand aeons ago, a Teacher named Padumuttara arose. While he was dwelling near the city of Haṃsavatī in the Khemā deer park, a householder named Vedeha, who possessed wealth and property of eighty crores, ate a fine meal early in the morning, undertook the Uposatha precepts, took perfumes, flowers, and so on, went to the monastery, honored and paid homage to the Teacher, and sat down to one side. At that moment, the Teacher placed his third disciple, the Elder Mahānisabha, in the foremost position, saying: “Monks, among my monk disciples who are proponents of the ascetic practices, Nisabha is the foremost.” Hearing this, the lay follower was pleased. At the end of the Dhamma talk, after the great crowd had risen and left, he paid homage to the Teacher and said, “Venerable sir, may you consent to a meal from me tomorrow.” “The community of monks is large, lay follower.” “How large, Blessed One?” “Six million, eight hundred thousand monks.” “Venerable sir, without leaving even a single novice in the monastery, may you consent to the meal.” The Teacher consented. The lay follower, knowing the Teacher's consent, went home, prepared a great offering, and on the next day, had the time announced to the Teacher. The Teacher, taking his bowl and robe, surrounded by the community of monks, went to the lay follower's house and sat on the prepared seat. At the conclusion of the water dedication, while receiving the gruel, rice, and other items, he performed the meal service. The lay follower also sat near the Teacher.

Tasmiṃ antare mahānisabhatthero piṇḍāya caranto tameva vīthiṃ paṭipajji. Upāsako disvā uṭṭhāya gantvā theraṃ vanditvā “pattaṃ, bhante, no dethā”ti āha. Thero pattaṃ adāsi. Bhante, idheva pavisatha, satthāpi gehe nisinnoti. Na vaṭṭissati upāsakāti. Upāsako therassa pattaṃ gahetvā piṇḍapātassa pūretvā nīharitvā adāsi. Tato theraṃ anugantvā nivatto satthu santike nisīditvā evamāha – “bhante, mahānisabhatthero ‘satthā gehe nisinno’ti vuttepi pavisituṃ [V 2.0161] na icchi, atthi nu kho etassa tumhākaṃ guṇehi atireko guṇo”ti. Buddhānañca vaṇṇamaccheraṃ nāma natthi. Atha satthā evamāha – “upāsaka, mayaṃ bhikkhaṃ āgamayamānā gehe nisīdāma, so bhikkhu na evaṃ nisīditvā bhikkhaṃ udikkhati. Mayaṃ gāmantasenāsane vasāma, so araññasmiṃyeva vasati. Mayaṃ channe vasāma, so abbhokāsamhiyeva vasati. Iti tassa ayañca ayañca guṇo”ti mahāsamuddaṃ pūrayamānova kathesi. Upāsako pakatiyāpi jalamānadīpo telena āsitto viya suṭṭhutaraṃ pasanno hutvā cintesi – “kiṃ mayhaṃ aññāya sampattiyā, anāgate ekassa buddhassa santike dhutavādānaṃ aggabhāvatthāya patthanaṃ karissāmī”ti?

At that time, the elder Mahānisabha, while walking for alms, took that same street. The lay follower saw him, rose, went up to him, and said, “Venerable sir, please give us your bowl.” The elder gave the bowl. The lay follower said, “Venerable sir, please enter here; the Teacher is also seated in the house.” The elder replied, “It is not proper, lay follower.” The lay follower took the elder's bowl, filled it with almsfood, brought it out, and gave it to him. Then, after following the elder a short distance, he turned back, sat near the Teacher, and said this: “Venerable sir, even when told 'the Teacher is seated in the house,' the elder Mahānisabha did not wish to enter. Is there some virtue in him surpassing your virtues?” Now, Buddhas have no jealousy regarding praise. Then the Teacher said: “Lay follower, we sit in houses awaiting alms; that monk does not sit thus expecting alms. We dwell in dwelling places near villages; he dwells only in the forest. We dwell under roofs; he dwells only in the open air. Thus, he has this virtue and that virtue,” and he spoke as if filling the great ocean. The lay follower, like an already burning lamp sprinkled with oil, became even more exceedingly inspired and thought: “What use to me is any other attainment? In the future, in the presence of a Buddha, I will make an aspiration to become the foremost among those who uphold the ascetic practices.”

So [P 2.0182] punapi satthāraṃ nimantetvā teneva niyāmena satta divasāni dānaṃ datvā sattame divase aṭṭhasaṭṭhibhikkhusatasahassassa ticīvarāni datvā satthu pādamūle nipajjitvā evamāha – “yaṃ me, bhante, satta divasāni dānaṃ dentassa [M 2.0169] mettaṃ kāyakammaṃ mettaṃ vacīkammaṃ mettaṃ manokammaṃ, imināhaṃ na aññaṃ devasampattiṃ vā sakkamārabrahmasampattiṃ vā patthemi, idaṃ pana me kammaṃ anāgate ekassa buddhassa santike mahānisabhattherena pattaṭṭhānantaraṃ pāpuṇanatthāya terasadhutaṅgadharānaṃ aggabhāvassa paccayo hotū”ti. Satthā “mahantaṃ ṭhānaṃ iminā patthitaṃ, samijjhissati nu kho”ti olokento samijjhanabhāvaṃ disvā āha – “manāpaṃ te ṭhānaṃ patthitaṃ, anāgate satasahassakappamatthake gotamo nāma buddho uppajjissati, tassa tvaṃ tatiyasāvako mahākassapatthero nāma bhavissasī”ti. Taṃ sutvā upāsako “buddhānaṃ dve kathā nāma natthī”ti punadivase pattabbaṃ viya taṃ sampattiṃ amaññittha. So yāvatāyukaṃ sīlaṃ rakkhitvā tattha kālaṅkato sagge nibbatti.

Then again, having invited the Teacher, he gave alms for seven days in the same manner. On the seventh day, he gave the three robes to six million eight hundred thousand monks, and lying down at the Teacher's feet, he said: “Venerable sir, by whatever bodily action, verbal action, and mental action associated with loving-kindness I have performed while giving alms for seven days—by this I do not aspire to any other divine prosperity or the prosperity of Sakka, Māra, or Brahmā. But may this deed of mine in the future, in the presence of a Buddha, serve as a condition for attaining the foremost position among those who uphold the thirteen ascetic practices, the position attained by the elder Mahānisabha.” The Teacher, considering, “A great position has been aspired to by him. Will it be fulfilled?” saw that it would be fulfilled and said: “A desirable position you have aspired to. In the future, after a hundred thousand aeons, a Buddha named Gotama will arise. You will be his third disciple, named the elder Mahākassapa.” Hearing this, the lay follower, thinking, “There is no such thing as a second word for Buddhas,” regarded that attainment as if it were to be attained the very next day. He protected his virtue for as long as he lived and, having passed away from there, was reborn in heaven.

Tato paṭṭhāya devamanussesu sampattiṃ anubhavanto ito ekanavutikappe vipassimhi sammāsambuddhe bandhumatīnagaraṃ nissāya kheme migadāye viharante devalokā cavitvā aññatarasmiṃ parijiṇṇe brāhmaṇakule nibbatti. Tasmiñca kāle “vipassī bhagavā sattame sattame saṃvacchare dhammaṃ kathetī”ti mahantaṃ kolāhalaṃ hoti. Sakalajambudīpe devatā “satthā dhammaṃ kathessatī”ti ārocenti, brāhmaṇo taṃ sāsanaṃ assosi. Tassa ca nivāsanasāṭako eko hoti, tathā brāhmaṇiyā, pārupanaṃ pana dvinnampi ekameva. Sakalanagare “ekasāṭakabrāhmaṇo”ti paññāyati. Brāhmaṇānaṃ kenacideva kiccena sannipāte sati brāhmaṇiṃ gehe ṭhapetvā sayaṃ gacchati[V 2.0162], brāhmaṇīnaṃ sannipāte sati sayaṃ gehe tiṭṭhati, brāhmaṇī taṃ vatthaṃ pārupitvā gacchati. Tasmiṃ pana [P 2.0183] divase brāhmaṇo brāhmaṇiṃ āha – “bhoti, kiṃ rattiṃ dhammassavanaṃ suṇissasi divā”ti? “Mayaṃ mātugāmajātikā nāma rattiṃ sotuṃ na sakkoma, divā sossāmī”ti brāhmaṇaṃ gehe ṭhapetvā vatthaṃ pārupitvā upāsikāhi saddhiṃ divā gantvā satthāraṃ vanditvā ekamante nisinnā dhammaṃ sutvā upāsikāhiyeva saddhiṃ āgamāsi. Atha brāhmaṇo brāhmaṇiṃ gehe ṭhapetvā vatthaṃ pārupitvā vihāraṃ gato.

From that time onward, enjoying prosperity among gods and humans, in the ninety-first aeon from the present, when Vipassī, the Perfectly Enlightened One, was dwelling in the Khemā Migadāya near the city of Bandhumatī, he passed away from the deva world and was reborn in a certain impoverished brahmin family. And at that time, a great clamor arose: “The Blessed One Vipassī teaches the Dhamma every seventh year.” Throughout all of Jambudīpa, deities proclaimed, “The Teacher will teach the Dhamma!” The brahmin heard that message. He had one lower garment, and the brahmin woman likewise, but for the two of them, there was only one upper garment. Throughout the entire city, he was known as “the one-garment brahmin.” When there was a gathering of brahmins for some business, he would leave the brahmin woman at home and go himself. When there was a gathering of brahmin women, he would stay at home, and the brahmin woman would put on that garment and go. On that day, the brahmin said to the brahmin woman, “Good lady, will you listen to the Dhamma teaching at night or during the day?” “We womenfolk are not able to listen at night; I will listen during the day.” Leaving the brahmin at home, she put on the upper garment and went with the female lay devotees during the day. Having paid homage to the Teacher, she sat to one side, listened to the Dhamma, and returned with the very same female lay devotees. Then the brahmin, leaving the brahmin woman at home, put on the upper garment and went to the monastery.

Tasmiṃ ca samaye satthā parisamajjhe alaṅkatadhammāsane sannisinno cittabījaniṃ ādāya ākāsagaṅgaṃ otārento viya sineruṃ matthaṃ katvā [M 2.0170] sāgaraṃ nimmathento viya dhammakathaṃ katheti. Brāhmaṇassa parisante nisinnassa dhammaṃ suṇantassa paṭhamayāmasmiṃyeva sakalasarīraṃ pūrayamānā pañcavaṇṇā pīti uppajji. So pārutavatthaṃ saṅgharitvā “dasabalassa dassāmī”ti cintesi. Athassa ādīnavasahassaṃ dassayamānaṃ maccheraṃ uppajji, so “brāhmaṇiyā ca mayhañca ekameva vatthaṃ, aññaṃ kiñci pārupanaṃ natthi, apārupitvā ca nāma bahi carituṃ na sakkā”ti sabbathāpi adātukāmo ahosi. Athassa nikkhante paṭhamayāme majjhimayāmepi tatheva pīti uppajji, so tatheva ca cintetvā tatheva adātukāmo ahosi. Athassa majjhimayāme nikkhante pacchimayāmepi tatheva pīti uppajji, so “taraṇaṃ vā hotu maraṇaṃ vā, pacchāpi jānissāmī”ti vatthaṃ saṅgharitvā satthu pādamūle ṭhapesi. Tato vāmahatthaṃ ābhujitvā dakkhiṇena hatthena tikkhattuṃ apphoṭetvā “jitaṃ me jitaṃ me”ti tayo vāre nadi.

At that time, the Teacher, seated gracefully on an adorned Dhamma seat in the midst of the assembly, taking up an ornate fan, delivered a Dhamma discourse as if causing the celestial Ganges to descend, and as if churning the ocean making Mount Sineru the churning rod. For the brahmin, who was sitting at the edge of the assembly listening to the Dhamma, in the very first watch, a five-colored rapture arose, filling his entire body. He folded his upper garment and thought, “I will give it to the One with Ten Powers.” Then stinginess arose in him, showing a thousand dangers, and he thought, “For the brahmin woman and me, there is only one garment; there is no other upper garment whatsoever, and it is not possible to go outside without wearing one.” Thus, he became completely unwilling to give. When the first watch had passed, in the middle watch as well, rapture arose in the same way, and thinking in the same way, he again became unwilling to give. When the middle watch had passed, in the last watch as well, rapture arose in the same way. He thought, “Let there be crossing over or let there be death, I will know later,” and folding the garment, he placed it at the Teacher’s feet. Then, bending his left arm and striking his upper arm three times with his right hand, he cried out three times, “I have conquered! I have conquered!”

Tasmiñca samaye bandhumarājā dhammāsanassa pacchato antosāṇiyaṃ nisinno dhammaṃ suṇāti. Rañño ca nāma “jitaṃ me”ti saddo amanāpo hoti. So purisaṃ pesesi “gaccha etaṃ puccha kiṃ vadesī”ti? So tena gantvā pucchito āha – “avasesā hatthiyānādīni āruyha asicammādīni gahetvā parasenaṃ jinanti, na taṃ acchariyaṃ, ahaṃ pana [P 2.0184] pacchato āgacchantassa kūṭagoṇassa muggarena sīsaṃ bhinditvā taṃ palāpento viya maccheracittaṃ madditvā pārutavatthaṃ dasabalassa adāsiṃ, taṃ me macchariyaṃ jita”nti āha. Puriso gantvā taṃ pavattiṃ rañño ārocesi. Rājā āha – “amhe bhaṇe dasabalassa anurūpaṃ na jānimhā, brāhmaṇo pana jānī”ti vatthayugampi pesesi. Taṃ disvā brāhmaṇo cintesi – “ayaṃ mayhaṃ tuṇhī nisinnassa paṭhamaṃ kiñci adatvā satthu guṇe kathentassa adāsi, satthu guṇe paṭicca uppannena mayhaṃ [V 2.0163] ko attho”ti tampi vatthayugaṃ dasabalasseva adāsi. Rājā “kiṃ brāhmaṇena kata”nti? Pucchitvā, “tampi tena vatthayugaṃ tathāgatasseva dinna”nti sutvā aññāni dve vatthayugāni pesesi. So tānipi adāsi. Rājā aññānipi cattārīti evaṃ yāva dvattiṃsa vatthayugāni pesesi. Atha brāhmaṇo [M 2.0171] “idaṃ vaḍḍhetvā gahaṇaṃ viya hotī”ti attano atthāya ekaṃ brāhmaṇiyā atthāya ekanti dve vatthayugāni gahetvā tiṃsa yugāni tathāgatasseva adāsi. Tato paṭṭhāya ca satthu vissāsiko jāto.

At that time, King Bandhuma was sitting behind the Dhamma seat inside a screen, listening to the Dhamma. Now, for a king, the cry “I have conquered!” is unpleasant. So he sent a man, saying, “Go and ask him what he is saying.” The man went and asked, and the brahmin replied: “Other warriors mount elephants and so on, take up swords and shields, and conquer an enemy army—that is no marvel. But I, just as one might smash the head of a fierce, charging bull coming from behind with a club and make it flee, have crushed my mind of stinginess and given my upper garment to the One with Ten Powers. That stinginess of mine is conquered.” The man went and reported the matter to the king. The king said, “Sirs, we did not know what is appropriate for the One with Ten Powers, but the brahmin knows,” and he sent a pair of garments. Seeing it, the brahmin thought, “This king, who at first gave me nothing while I was sitting silently, gave this only when I spoke of the Teacher's virtues. What use to me is this gain that has arisen on account of the Teacher’s virtues?” and he gave that pair of garments to the One with Ten Powers as well. The king asked, “What did the brahmin do?” and upon hearing, “He gave that pair of garments to the Tathāgata as well,” he sent another two pairs of garments. The brahmin gave those as well. The king sent another four, and so on, up to thirty-two pairs of garments. Then the brahmin thought, “This is becoming like taking by making it increase,” and taking one pair for himself and one pair for the brahmin woman—two pairs of garments in total—he gave the thirty pairs to the Tathāgata. From then on, he became a confidant of the Teacher.

Atha naṃ rājā ekadivasaṃ sītasamaye satthu santike dhammaṃ suṇantaṃ disvā satasahassagghanikaṃ attano pārutaṃ rattakambalaṃ datvā āha – “ito paṭṭhāya idaṃ pārupitvā dhammaṃ suṇāhī”ti. So “kiṃ me iminā kambalena imasmiṃ pūtikāye upanītenā”ti? Cintetvā, antogandhakuṭiyaṃ tathāgatamañcassa upari vitānaṃ katvā agamāsi. Atha ekadivasaṃ rājā pātova vihāraṃ gantvā antogandhakuṭiyaṃ satthu santike nisīdi. Tasmiñca samaye chabbaṇṇā buddharasmiyo kambalaṃ paṭihaññanti, kambalo ativiya virocati. Rājā uddhaṃ olokento sañjānitvā āha – “bhante, amhākaṃ esa kambalo, amhehi ekasāṭakabrāhmaṇassa dinno”ti. Tumhehi, mahārāja, brāhmaṇo pūjito, brāhmaṇena ahaṃ pūjitoti. Rājā “brāhmaṇo yuttakaṃ aññāsi, na maya”nti pasīditvā yaṃ manussānaṃ upakārabhūtaṃ, taṃ [P 2.0185] sabbaṃ aṭṭhaṭṭhakaṃ katvā sabbaṭṭhakaṃ nāma dānaṃ datvā purohitaṭṭhāne ṭhapesi. Sopi “aṭṭhaṭṭhakaṃ nāma catusaṭṭhi hotī”ti catusaṭṭhi salākabhattāni upanibandhāpetvā yāvajīvaṃ dānaṃ datvā sīlaṃ rakkhitvā tato cuto sagge nibbatti.

Then one day, during the cold season, the king saw him listening to the Dhamma near the Teacher and gave him his own red blanket worth a hundred thousand, saying, “From now on, wear this and listen to the Dhamma.” The brahmin thought, “What use is this blanket to me, applied to this putrid body?” and having made a canopy over the Tathāgata’s couch in the inner fragrant chamber, he returned home. Then one day, the king went to the monastery early in the morning and sat near the Teacher inside the inner fragrant chamber. At that time, the Buddha’s rays struck the blanket, and the blanket shone exceedingly. The king looked up, recognized it, and said, “Venerable sir, this is our blanket; it was given by us to the one-garment brahmin.” The Teacher replied, “Great king, you honored the brahmin, and the brahmin honored me.” The king was pleased and thought, “The brahmin understood what is proper, not I,” and making everything that is useful to humans into sets of eight, he gave the gift called the ‘all-eights’ and appointed him to the position of royal chaplain. He too, thinking, “Eight times eight is sixty-four,” established sixty-four ticket-alms, observed the precepts, and when he passed away from that existence, he was reborn in heaven.

Puna tato cuto imasmiṃ kappe koṇāgamanassa ca bhagavato kassapadasabalassa cāti dvinnaṃ buddhānaṃ antare bārāṇasiyaṃ kuṭumbiyaghare nibbatto, so vuddhimanvāya gharāvāsaṃ vasanto ekadivasaṃ araññe jaṅghavihāraṃ carati. Tasmiñca samaye paccekabuddho nadītīre cīvarakammaṃ karonto anuvāte appahonte saṅgharitvā ṭhapetuṃ āraddho. So disvā, “kasmā, bhante, saṅgharitvā ṭhapethā”ti? Āha. Anuvāto nappahotīti. “Iminā, bhante, karothā”ti sāṭakaṃ datvā, “nibbattanibbattaṭṭhāne me kenaci parihāni mā hotū”ti patthanaṃ paṭṭhapesi. Gharepissa bhaginiyā saddhiṃ bhariyāya kalahaṃ karontiyā paccekabuddho piṇḍāya pāvisi.

Again, passing away from there, in this aeon, during the interval between the two Buddhas, the Blessed Koṇāgamana and Kassapa of the Ten Powers, he was reborn in Bārāṇasī in a householder’s family. Having reached maturity and living the household life, one day he was taking a walk in the forest. At that time, a Paccekabuddha was doing robe-work on the riverbank, and as the border-strip was insufficient, he had begun to fold it up to put it away. Seeing this, the man asked, “Venerable sir, why are you folding it up to put it away?” The Paccekabuddha replied, “The border-strip is not sufficient.” “Venerable sir, please make it with this,” he said, giving his outer garment, and he made an aspiration: “In whatever place I am reborn, may I have no deficiency of any kind.” At his home, while his wife was quarreling with his sister, the Paccekabuddha entered for alms-food.

Athassa [V 2.0164][M 2.0172] bhaginī paccekabuddhassa piṇḍapātaṃ datvā tassa bhariyaṃ sandhāya “evarūpaṃ bālaṃ yojanasatena parivajjeyya”nti patthanaṃ paṭṭhapesi. Sā gehadvāre ṭhitā taṃ sutvā, “imāya dinnaṃ bhattaṃ esa mā bhuñjatū”ti pattaṃ gahetvā piṇḍapātaṃ chaḍḍetvā kalalassa pūretvā adāsi. Itarā disvā, “bāle maṃ tāva akkosa vā pahara vā. Evarūpassa pana dve asaṅkheyyāni pūritapāramissa pattato bhattaṃ chaḍḍetvā kalalaṃ dātuṃ na yutta”nti āha. Athassa bhariyāya paṭisaṅkhānaṃ uppajji. Sā “tiṭṭhatha, bhante”ti kalalaṃ chaḍḍetvā pattaṃ dhovitvā gandhacuṇṇena ubbaṭṭetvā pavarassa catumadhurassa pūretvā upari āsittena padumagabbhavaṇṇena sappinā vijjotamānaṃ paccekabuddhassa hatthe ṭhapetvā, “yathā ayaṃ piṇḍapāto obhāsajāto, evaṃ obhāsajātaṃ me sarīraṃ hotū”ti patthanaṃ paṭṭhapesi. Paccekabuddho anumoditvā ākāsaṃ pakkhandi. Tepi jāyampatikā yāvatāyukaṃ kusalaṃ katvā sagge nibbattitvā [P 2.0186] puna tato cavitvā upāsako bārāṇasiyaṃ asītikoṭivibhavassa seṭṭhino putto hutvā nibbatti, itarā tādisasseva dhītā hutvā nibbatti.

Then his sister offered alms-food to the Paccekabuddha and, with reference to his wife, made the aspiration: “May I avoid such a fool by a hundred yojanas.” Standing at the door of the house, the wife heard this and thought, “May this one not eat the food given by this woman.” Snatching the bowl, she threw out the alms-food, filled it with mud, and gave it back. The other woman, seeing this, said: “O foolish one, you may scold me or strike me. But it is not right to throw out the food from the bowl of one who has fulfilled the perfections for two incalculable aeons and to give mud instead.” Then, reflection arose in his wife. She said, “Venerable sir, please wait,” and throwing out the mud, she washed the bowl, rubbed it with fragrant powder, filled it with the finest four sweets, and placed it in the Paccekabuddha’s hands, gleaming with ghee the color of a lotus’s inner pollen which had been poured on top. She then made the aspiration: “Just as this alms-food is luminous, so may my body be luminous.” The Paccekabuddha, having expressed his appreciation, soared into the sky. That husband and wife, having done good deeds for as long as they lived, were reborn in heaven. Passing away from there, the layman was reborn in Bārāṇasī as the son of a merchant possessing eighty crores of wealth, and the other was reborn as the daughter of a similarly wealthy merchant.

Tassa vuddhippattassa tameva seṭṭhidhītaraṃ ānayiṃsu. Tassā pubbe adinnavipākassa tassa kammassa ānubhāvena patikulaṃ paviṭṭhamattāya ummārabbhantare sakalasarīraṃ ugghāṭitavaccakuṭi viya duggandhaṃ jātaṃ. Seṭṭhikumāro “kassāyaṃ gandho”ti pucchitvā “seṭṭhikaññāyā”ti sutvā “nīharatha nīharathā”ti ābhataniyāmeneva kulagharaṃ pesesi. Sā eteneva nīhārena sattasu ṭhānesu paṭinivattitā cintesi – “ahaṃ sattasu ṭhānesu paṭinivattā. Kiṃ me jīvitenā”ti? Attano ābharaṇabhaṇḍaṃ bhañjāpetvā suvaṇṇiṭṭhakaṃ kāresi ratanāyataṃ vidatthivitthataṃ caturaṅgulubbedhaṃ. Tato haritālamanosilāpiṇḍaṃ gahetvā aṭṭha uppalahatthake ādāya kassapadasabalassa cetiyakaraṇaṭṭhānaṃ gatā. Tasmiñca khaṇe ekā iṭṭhakapanti parikkhipitvā āgacchamānā ghaṭaniṭṭhakāya ūnā hoti. Seṭṭhidhītā vaḍḍhakiṃ āha – “imaṃ iṭṭhakaṃ ettha ṭhapethā”ti. Amma, bhaddake kāle āgatāsi, sayameva ṭhapehīti. Sā āruyha telena haritālamanosilaṃ yojetvā tena bandhanena iṭṭhakaṃ patiṭṭhapetvā upari [M 2.0173] aṭṭhahi uppalahatthakehi pūjaṃ katvā vanditvā, “nibbattanibbattaṭṭhāne me kāyato candanagandho vāyatu, mukhato uppalagandho”ti patthanaṃ katvā, cetiyaṃ vanditvā, padakkhiṇaṃ katvā agamāsi.

When he reached maturity, they brought him that very merchant’s daughter. By the power of her past kamma, the result of which had not yet been given, just as she entered her husband's home and was within the threshold, a foul stench arose from her entire body, like an opened latrine. The merchant’s son, asking, “Whose is this stench?” and hearing it was the merchant’s daughter, ordered, “Take her out, take her out!” and had her sent back to her family home in the very manner she was brought. Having been turned away in this manner from seven places, she thought: “I have been turned away from seven places. What use is this life to me?” She had her ornaments broken and made into a golden brick, a ratana in length, a span in width, and four fingers in thickness. Then, taking a lump of yellow orpiment and red arsenic, along with eight handfuls of blue water lilies, she went to the place where the cetiya of the Buddha Kassapa, the Ten-Powered One, was being built. At that moment, a row of bricks being laid around it was lacking the joining brick. The merchant’s daughter said to the chief builder, “Place this brick here.” He replied, “Mother, you have come at a fortunate time. Place it yourself.” She climbed up, mixed the yellow orpiment and red arsenic with oil, and set the brick firmly in place with that mortar. Then, making an offering above it with the eight handfuls of blue water lilies, she paid homage and made this aspiration: “In every place I am reborn, may a sandalwood fragrance emanate from my body, and a blue water lily fragrance from my mouth.” Having paid homage to the cetiya and circumambulated it, she departed.

Atha tasmiṃyeva khaṇe yassa seṭṭhiputtassa paṭhamaṃ gehaṃ nītā, tassa taṃ ārabbha sati udapādi[V 2.0165]. Nagarepi nakkhattaṃ saṃghuṭṭhaṃ hoti. So upaṭṭhāke āha – “tadā idha ānītā seṭṭhidhītā atthi, kahaṃ sā”ti? “Kulagehe sāmī”ti. “Ānetha naṃ, nakkhattaṃ kīḷissāmā”ti. Te gantvā, taṃ vanditvā ṭhitā “kiṃ, tātā, āgatatthā”ti? Tāya puṭṭhā [P 2.0187] taṃ pavattiṃ ācikkhiṃsu. “Tātā, mayā ābharaṇabhaṇḍena cetiyaṃ pūjitaṃ, ābharaṇaṃ me natthī”ti. Te gantvā seṭṭhiputtassa ārocesuṃ. “Ānetha naṃ, piḷandhanaṃ labhissāmā”ti. Te ānayiṃsu. Tassā saha gharappavesena sakalagehaṃ candanagandhañceva nīluppalagandhañca vāyi.

Then at that very moment, a recollection concerning the merchant's daughter, to whose house she had first been taken, arose in that merchant's son. In the city, a festival had also been proclaimed. He said to his attendants, “There was that merchant's daughter who was brought here then—where is she?” “She is in her family's house, master.” “Bring her, we shall enjoy the festival.” They went, paid respects to her, and stood there. She asked, “Why have you come, sirs?” Being asked by her, they explained the matter. “Sirs, I have offered my ornaments to the cetiya; I have no adornments.” They went and reported this to the merchant's son. “Bring her, we will get adornments.” They brought her. Simultaneously with her entry into the house, the entire house was filled with the fragrance of sandalwood and the fragrance of blue water lilies.

Seṭṭhiputto taṃ pucchi – “paṭhamaṃ tava sarīrato duggandho vāyi, idāni pana te sarīrato candanagandho, mukhato uppalagandho vāyati. Kiṃ eta”nti? Sā ādito paṭṭhāya attano katakammaṃ ārocesi. Seṭṭhiputto “niyyānikaṃ vata buddhānaṃ sāsana”nti pasīditvā yojanikaṃ suvaṇṇacetiyaṃ kambalakañcukena parikkhipitvā tattha tattha rathacakkappamāṇehi suvaṇṇapadumehi alaṅkari. Tesaṃ dvādasahatthā olambakā honti. So tattha yāvatāyukaṃ ṭhatvā sagge nibbattitvā tato cuto bārāṇasito yojanamatte ṭhāne aññatarasmiṃ amaccakule nibbatti. Seṭṭhikaññā devalokato cavitvā rājakule jeṭṭhadhītā hutvā nibbatti.

The merchant's son asked her, “At first, a foul odor emanated from your body, but now a sandalwood fragrance emanates from your body, and a blue water lily fragrance from your mouth. What is the reason for this?” She recounted the deed she had done from the very beginning. The merchant's son, gaining faith and thinking, “Truly, the teaching of the Buddhas leads to liberation!” enveloped a golden cetiya one yojana in extent with a woolen cloak and adorned it in various places with golden lotuses the size of chariot wheels. Their pendants were twelve cubits long. He remained there for as long as he lived and was reborn in heaven. Passing away from there, he was reborn in a certain minister's family at a place one yojana from Bārāṇasī. The merchant's daughter, having passed away from the deva world, was reborn as the eldest daughter in a royal family.

Tesu vayappattesu kumārassa vasanagāme nakkhattaṃ saṃghuṭṭhaṃ, so mātaraṃ āha – “sāṭakaṃ me amma dehi, nakkhattaṃ kīḷissāmī”ti. Sā dhotavatthaṃ nīharitvā adāsi. “Amma thūlaṃ ida”nti. Aññaṃ nīharitvā adāsi, tampi paṭikkhipi. Aññaṃ nīharitvā adāsi, tampi paṭikkhipi. Atha naṃ mātā āha – “tāta, yādise gehe mayaṃ jātā, natthi no ito sukhumatarassa paṭilābhāya puñña”nti. “Labhanaṭṭhānaṃ gacchāmi ammā”ti. “Putta ahaṃ ajjeva tuyhaṃ bārāṇasinagare rajjapaṭilābhampi icchāmī”ti. So mātaraṃ vanditvā āha – “gacchāmi ammā”ti. “Gaccha, tātā”ti. Evaṃ kirassā cittaṃ ahosi [M 2.0174] – “kahaṃ gamissati, idha vā ettha vā gehe nisīdissatī”ti? So pana puññaniyāmena nikkhamitvā bārāṇasiṃ gantvā uyyāne maṅgalasilāpaṭṭe sasīsaṃ pārupitvā nipajji. So cā bārāṇasirañño kālaṅkatassa sattamo divaso hoti.

When they had come of age, a festival was proclaimed in the village where the boy lived. He said to his mother, 'Mother, give me a cloth; I will play at the festival.' She brought out a washed cloth and gave it to him. 'Mother, this is coarse,' he said. She brought out another and gave it to him, but he rejected that too. She brought out yet another and gave it to him, but he rejected that as well. Then his mother said to him, 'Dear son, in the kind of family we were born into, we have no merit to obtain anything finer than this.' 'Mother, I will go to a place where one can be obtained.' 'Son, I wish for you to obtain the kingdom in the city of Bārāṇasī this very day.' He paid respects to his mother and said, 'I am going, Mother.' 'Go, dear son,' she replied. It is said that this was her thought: 'Where will he go? He will just sit here or there in the house.' But he, by the fixed consequence of his merit, left and went to Bārāṇasī, where he lay down in the park on the auspicious stone slab, covering himself including his head. And that was the seventh day since the king of Bārāṇasī had passed away.

Amaccā rañño sarīrakiccaṃ katvā rājaṅgaṇe nisīditvā mantayiṃsu – “rañño ekā dhītāva atthi, putto natthi. Arājakaṃ rajjaṃ na tiṭṭhati. Ko rājā hotī”ti mantetvā, “tvaṃ [V 2.0166] hohi, tvaṃ hohī”ti. Purohito [P 2.0188] āha – “bahuṃ oloketuṃ na vaṭṭati, phussarathaṃ vissajjemā”ti. Te kumudavaṇṇe cattāro sindhave yojetvā, pañcavidhaṃ rājakakudhabhaṇḍaṃ setacchattañca rathasmiṃyeva ṭhapetvā rathaṃ vissajjetvā pacchato tūriyāni paggaṇhāpesuṃ. Ratho pācīnadvārena nikkhamitvā uyyānābhimukho ahosi, “paricayena uyyānābhimukho gacchati, nivattemā”ti keci āhaṃsu. Purohito “mā nivattayitthā”ti āha. Ratho kumāraṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā ārohanasajjo hutvā aṭṭhāsi. Purohito pārupanakaṇṇaṃ apanetvā pādatalāni olokento “tiṭṭhatu ayaṃ dīpo, dvisahassadīpaparivāresu catūsu dīpesu esa rajjaṃ kātuṃ yutto”ti vatvā, “punapi tūriyāni paggaṇhātha punapi paggaṇhāthā”ti tikkhattuṃ tūriyāni paggaṇhāpesi.

Having performed the king's funeral rites, the ministers sat in the royal courtyard and deliberated: 'The king has only one daughter; there is no son. A kingdom without a king does not stand. Who shall be king?' Having deliberated thus, they said to one another, 'You be king, you be king.' The royal chaplain said, 'It is not proper to look around much; let us release the auspicious Phussa chariot.' They yoked four Sindhu horses the color of the kumuda lily, placed the five kinds of royal insignia and the white parasol upon the chariot itself, and sent the chariot forth, having musical instruments played behind it. The chariot left through the eastern gate and headed toward the park. Some said, 'It goes toward the park out of familiarity—let us turn it back.' The royal chaplain said, 'Do not turn it back.' The chariot circumambulated the prince and stood ready for mounting. The royal chaplain moved aside the edge of the covering and, looking at the soles of his feet, said, 'Let this island of Jambudīpa be; this one is fit to rule in the four great continents surrounded by two thousand lesser islands.' Then he said, 'Sound the instruments again! Sound them again!' and three times he had the instruments sounded.

Atha kumāro mukhaṃ vivaritvā oloketvā, “kena kammena āgatatthā”ti? Āha. “Deva, tumhākaṃ rajjaṃ pāpuṇātī”ti. “Rājā kaha”nti. “Devattaṃ gato sāmī”ti. “Kati divasā atikkantā”ti? “Ajja sattamo divaso”ti. “Putto vā dhītā vā natthī”ti. “Dhītā atthi deva, putto natthī”ti. “Tena hi karissāmi rajja”nti. Te tāvadeva abhisekamaṇḍapaṃ katvā rājadhītaraṃ sabbālaṅkārehi alaṅkaritvā uyyānaṃ ānetvā kumārassa abhisekaṃ akaṃsu.

Then the prince uncovered his face, looked, and asked, 'For what purpose have you come?' They replied, 'Your Majesty, the kingdom has come to you.' 'Where is the king?' 'Our master has gone to the state of a deva.' 'How many days have passed?' 'Today is the seventh day.' 'Is there no son or daughter?' 'There is a daughter, Your Majesty, but no son.' 'In that case, I shall rule the kingdom.' At that very moment, they prepared the consecration pavilion, adorned the king's daughter with all ornaments, brought her to the park, and performed the prince’s consecration.

Athassa katābhisekassa satasahassagghanikaṃ vatthaṃ upahariṃsu. So “kimidaṃ, tātā”ti? Āha. “Nivāsanavatthaṃ devā”ti. “Nanu, tātā, thūla”nti. “Manussānaṃ paribhogavatthesu ito sukhumataraṃ natthi devā”ti. “Tumhākaṃ rājā evarūpaṃ nivāsesī”ti? “Āma, devā”ti. “Na maññe puññavā tumhākaṃ [M 2.0175] rājā, suvaṇṇabhiṅgāraṃ āharatha, labhissāma vattha”nti. Suvaṇṇabhiṅgāraṃ āhariṃsu. So uṭṭhāya hatthe dhovitvā, mukhaṃ vikkhāletvā, hatthena udakaṃ ādāya, puratthimadisāya abbhukkiri, ghanapathaviṃ [P 2.0189] bhinditvā aṭṭha kapparukkhā uṭṭhahiṃsu. Puna udakaṃ gahetvā dakkhiṇaṃ pacchimaṃ uttaranti evaṃ catasso disā abbhukkiri, sabbadisāsu aṭṭha aṭṭha katvā dvattiṃsa kapparukkhā uṭṭhahiṃsu. So ekaṃ dibbadussaṃ nivāsetvā ekaṃ pārupitvā “nandarañño vijite suttakantikā itthiyo mā suttaṃ kantiṃsūti evaṃ bheriṃ cārāpethā”ti vatvā, chattaṃ ussāpetvā, alaṅkatapaṭiyatto hatthikkhandhavaragato nagaraṃ pavisitvā, pāsādaṃ āruyha mahāsampattiṃ anubhavi.

Then, to him who had been consecrated, they offered a cloth worth a hundred thousand. He asked, 'What is this, my good sirs?' They replied, 'It is a lower garment, Your Majesty.' 'But my good sirs, is it not coarse?' 'Among the garments used by humans, there is nothing finer than this, Your Majesty.' 'Did your king wear such a garment?' 'Yes, Your Majesty.' 'I think your king was not a man of great merit. Bring a golden ewer; we shall obtain a cloth.' They brought a golden ewer. Rising, he washed his hands, rinsed his mouth, took water in his hand, and sprinkled it towards the eastern direction. Splitting the solid earth, eight wish-fulfilling trees arose. Again taking water, he sprinkled it towards the southern, western, and northern directions. In each of the four directions, eight trees arose, making thirty-two wish-fulfilling trees in total. He put on one divine cloth as a lower garment and draped another, then said, 'Have it proclaimed by drumbeat thus: “In King Nanda’s dominion, let women who spin thread not spin thread!”' Having said this, he had the white parasol raised, and, adorned and arrayed, mounted on the back of a splendid elephant, he entered the city, ascended the palace, and experienced great prosperity.

Evaṃ [V 2.0167] kāle gacchante ekadivasaṃ devī rañño sampattiṃ disvā, “aho tapassī”ti kāruññākāraṃ dassesi. “Kimidaṃ devī”ti? Ca puṭṭhā, “atimahatī, deva, sampatti, atīte buddhānaṃ saddahitvā kalyāṇaṃ akattha, idāni anāgatassa paccayaṃ kusalaṃ na karothā”ti? Āha. “Kassa dassāmi? Sīlavanto natthī”ti. “Asuñño, deva, jambudīpo arahantehi, tumhe dānameva sajjetha, ahaṃ arahante lacchāmī”ti āha. Rājā punadivase pācīnadvāre dānaṃ sajjāpesi. Devī pātova uposathaṅgāni adhiṭṭhāya uparipāsāde puratthābhimukhā urena nipajjitvā – “sace etissā disāya arahanto atthi, āgacchantu amhākaṃ bhikkhaṃ gaṇhantū”ti āha. Tassaṃ disāyaṃ arahanto nāhesuṃ. Taṃ sakkāraṃ kapaṇaddhikayācakānaṃ adaṃsu.

As time passed, one day the queen, seeing the king’s prosperity, showed an expression of compassion, thinking, 'Alas, the poor man!' When he asked, 'What is this, queen?' she replied, 'Your Majesty, your prosperity is immense. In the past, having placed faith in the Buddhas, you performed good deeds. But now, you do not perform wholesome deeds as a cause for the future.' 'To whom shall I give? There are no virtuous ones.' 'Your Majesty, Jambudīpa is not empty of arahants. You just prepare the alms, and I will find the arahants.' The next day, the king had alms prepared at the eastern gate. The queen, having undertaken the Uposatha precepts early in the morning, lay down on her chest facing east on the upper story of the palace and made an aspiration: 'If there are arahants in this direction, may they come and accept our almsfood.' There were no arahants in that direction. So they gave those offerings to the destitute, wayfarers, and beggars.

Punadivase dakkhiṇadvāre dānaṃ sajjetvā tatheva akāsi, punadivase pacchimadvāre. Uttaradvāre sajjitadivase pana deviyā tatheva nimantentiyā himavante vasantānaṃ padumavatiyā puttānaṃ pañcasatānaṃ paccekabuddhānaṃ jeṭṭhako mahāpadumapaccekabuddho bhātike āmantesi “mārisā, nandarājā [P 2.0190] tumhe nimanteti, adhivāsetha tassā”ti. Te adhivāsetvā punadivase anotattadahe mukhaṃ dhovitvā ākāsena āgantvā uttaradvāre otariṃsu. Manussā gantvā “pañcasatā, deva, paccekabuddhā āgatā”ti rañño ārocesuṃ. Rājā saddhiṃ deviyā gantvā vanditvā pattaṃ gahetvā paccekabuddhe pāsādaṃ āropetvā tesaṃ dānaṃ datvā bhattakiccāvasāne rājā [M 2.0176] saṅghatherassa, devī saṅghanavakassa pādamūle nipajjitvā, “ayyā paccayehi na kilamissanti, mayaṃ puññena na hāyissāma, amhākaṃ yāvajīvaṃ idha nivāsāya paṭiññaṃ dethā”ti paṭiññaṃ kāretvā uyyāne pañca paṇṇasālāsatāni pañca caṅkamanasatānīti sabbākārena nivāsaṭṭhānaṃ sampādetvā tattha vasāpesuṃ.

On the next day, he prepared alms at the southern gate and did likewise; on the following day, at the western gate. Then, on the day the alms were prepared at the northern gate, as the queen was inviting them in the same way, Mahāpaduma Paccekabuddha, the eldest of the five hundred Paccekabuddhas—the sons of Padumavatī dwelling in the Himavanta—addressed his younger brothers: 'Sirs, King Nanda invites you; please accept his invitation.' They consented, and on the next day, after washing their faces in Lake Anotatta, they came through the sky and descended at the northern gate. Men went and informed the king, 'Sire, five hundred Paccekabuddhas have arrived.' The king, together with the queen, went, paid homage, took their bowls, led the Paccekabuddhas up to the palace, and gave them alms. At the conclusion of the meal, the king prostrated himself at the feet of the Saṅghathera, and the queen at the feet of the Saṅghanavaka. They had them make a promise, saying, 'Venerable sirs, may you not be troubled concerning the requisites, and may we not decline in merit. Please grant us the promise to reside here for the duration of your lives.' Having obtained their promise, they prepared a dwelling place in the park with five hundred leaf-huts and five hundred walking paths, complete in every way, and had them dwell there.

Evaṃ kāle gacchante rañño paccanto kupito. “Ahaṃ paccantaṃ vūpasametuṃ gacchāmi, tvaṃ paccekabuddhesu mā pamajjī”ti deviṃ ovaditvā gato. Tasmiṃ anāgateyeva paccekabuddhānaṃ āyusaṅkhārā khīṇā. Mahāpadumapaccekabuddho tiyāmarattiṃ jhānakīḷaṃ kīḷitvā aruṇuggamane ālambanaphalakaṃ ālambitvā ṭhitakova anupādisesāya nibbānadhātuyā parinibbāyi, etenupāyena sesāpīti sabbepi parinibbutā. Punadivase devī paccekabuddhānaṃ nisīdanaṭṭhānaṃ haritūpalittaṃ kāretvā pupphāni vikiritvā dhūpaṃ datvā tesaṃ āgamanaṃ olokayantī [V 2.0168] nisinnā āgamanaṃ apassantī purisaṃ pesesi – “gaccha, tāta, jānāhi, kiṃ ayyānaṃ kiñci aphāsuka”nti? So gantvā mahāpadumassa paṇṇasālāya dvāraṃ vivaritvā tattha apassanto caṅkamanaṃ gantvā ālambanaphalakaṃ nissāya ṭhitaṃ disvā vanditvā, “kālo, bhante”ti āha. Parinibbutasarīraṃ kiṃ kathessati? So “niddāyati maññe”ti gantvā piṭṭhipāde hatthena parāmasi. Pādānaṃ sītalatāya ceva thaddhatāya ca parinibbutabhāvaṃ ñatvā dutiyassa santikaṃ agamāsi, evaṃ tatiyassāti sabbesaṃ parinibbutabhāvaṃ ñatvā rājakulaṃ gato. “Kahaṃ, tāta, paccekabuddhā”ti? Puṭṭho “parinibbutā, devī”ti āha. Devī kandantī rodantī nikkhamitvā nāgarehi [P 2.0191] saddhiṃ tattha gantvā sādhukīḷitaṃ kāretvā paccekabuddhānaṃ sarīrakiccaṃ katvā dhātuyo gahetvā cetiyaṃ patiṭṭhāpesi.

As time passed, the king’s border region became rebellious. 'I am going to pacify the border region; you must not be heedless regarding the Paccekabuddhas,' he advised the queen and departed. Even before he returned, the life-formations of the Paccekabuddhas were exhausted. The Mahāpaduma Paccekabuddha, after sporting in jhāna for the three watches of the night, leaned on a leaning-board at the rising of the dawn and, just as he was standing, attained Parinibbāna with the Nibbāna-element without residue remaining. By this same method, all the remaining ones also attained Parinibbāna. On the next day, the queen had the Paccekabuddhas’ sitting place smeared with fresh cow-dung, scattered flowers, offered incense, and sat watching for their arrival. Seeing no sign of their coming, she sent a man, saying: 'Go, my good man, and find out if there is any discomfort for the venerable sirs.' He went, opened the door of Mahāpaduma’s leaf-hut, and not seeing him there, went to the walking path. Seeing him standing leaning against the leaning-board, he paid homage and said, 'Venerable sir, it is time.' What would a body that has attained Parinibbāna say? Thinking, 'I suppose he is sleeping,' the man went and touched the top of his feet with his hand. By the coldness and stiffness of the feet, he knew the state of Parinibbāna and went to the second one. In this way, going to the third and so on, he knew the state of Parinibbāna of all of them and went to the royal household. When asked, 'My good man, where are the Paccekabuddhas?' he replied, 'Queen, they have attained Parinibbāna.' The queen, weeping and wailing, went out with the townspeople and went there. She had solemn rites performed, conducted the funeral rites for the Paccekabuddhas, took their relics, and had a cetiya established.

Rājā paccantaṃ vūpasametvā āgato paccuggamanaṃ āgataṃ deviṃ pucchi “kiṃ, bhadde, paccekabuddhesu nappamajji, nirogā ayyā”ti? “Parinibbutā devā”ti. Rājā cintesi – “evarūpānampi paṇḍitānaṃ maraṇaṃ uppajjati, amhākaṃ kuto mokkho”ti? So nagaraṃ agantvā uyyānameva pavisitvā jeṭṭhaputtaṃ pakkosāpetvā tassa rajjaṃ paṭiyādetvā sayaṃ samaṇakapabbajjaṃ pabbaji, devīpi [M 2.0177] “imasmiṃ pabbajite ahaṃ kiṃ karissāmī”ti? Tattheva uyyāne pabbajitā. Dvepi jhānaṃ bhāvetvā tato cutā brahmaloke nibbattiṃsu.

The king, having pacified the border region and returned, asked the queen who had come to greet him, 'My dear, were you not heedless regarding the Paccekabuddhas? Are the venerable sirs free from illness?' 'They have attained Parinibbāna, sire,' she replied. The king reflected, 'Even for such wise ones, death arises. For us, whence could there be liberation?' He did not enter the city but went directly into the park, had his eldest son summoned, handed over the kingdom to him, and himself went forth as an ascetic. The queen, too, thinking, 'Now that he has gone forth, what shall I do?' went forth right there in the park. Both developed meditative absorption and, after passing away from that state, were reborn in the Brahma-world.

Tesu tattheva vasantesu amhākaṃ satthā loke uppajjitvā pavattitavaradhammacakko anupubbena rājagahaṃ pāvisi. Ayaṃ pippalimāṇavo magadharaṭṭhe mahātitthabrāhmaṇagāme kapilabrāhmaṇassa aggamahesiyā kucchimhi nibbatto, ayaṃ bhaddā kāpilānī maddaraṭṭhe sāgalanagare kosiyagottabrāhmaṇassa aggamahesiyā kucchismiṃ nibbattā. Tesaṃ kho anukkamena vaḍḍhamānānaṃ pippalimāṇavassa vīsatime vasse bhaddāya soḷasame vasse sampatte mātāpitaro puttaṃ oloketvā, “tāta, tvaṃ vayappatto, kulavaṃso nāma patiṭṭhapetabbo”ti ativiya nippīḷayiṃsu. Māṇavo āha – “mayhaṃ sotapathe evarūpaṃ kathaṃ mā kathetha. Ahaṃ yāva tumhe dharatha, tāva paṭijaggissāmi, tumhākaṃ pacchato nikkhamitvā pabbajissāmī”ti. Te katipāhaṃ atikkamitvā puna kathayiṃsu, sopi tatheva paṭikkhipi. Puna kathayiṃsu, punapi paṭikkhipi. Tato paṭṭhāya mātā nirantaraṃ kathetiyeva.

While they were dwelling right there, our Teacher arose in the world, set in motion the supreme Wheel of the Dhamma, and in due course entered Rājagaha. This youth Pippali was conceived in the womb of the chief wife of the brahmin Kapila in the brahmin village of Mahātittha in the Magadha country. This Bhaddā Kāpilānī was conceived in the womb of the chief wife of the brahmin of the Kosiya clan in the city of Sāgala in the Madda country. As they were growing up in due course, when the youth Pippali reached his twentieth year and Bhaddā her sixteenth year, his mother and father looked at their son and pressed him exceedingly, saying, 'Dear son, you have reached the proper age; the family lineage must be established.' The youth said: 'Mother and Father, do not speak such words in my hearing. As long as you live, I will look after you. After you are gone, I will leave the household and go forth.' After a few days had passed, they spoke again, and he refused in the same way. They spoke again, and again he refused. From then on, his mother spoke continuously.

Māṇavo [V 2.0169] “mama mātaraṃ saññāpessāmī”ti rattasuvaṇṇassa nikkhasahassaṃ datvā suvaṇṇakārehi ekaṃ itthirūpaṃ kārāpetvā tassa majjanaghaṭṭanādikammapariyosāne taṃ rattavatthaṃ nivāsāpetvā vaṇṇasampannehi pupphehi ceva nānāalaṅkārehi ca alaṅkārāpetvā mātaraṃ pakkosāpetvā āha – “amma evarūpaṃ ārammaṇaṃ labhanto gehe vasāmi, alabhanto [P 2.0192] na vasāmī”ti. Paṇḍitā brāhmaṇī cintesi – “mayhaṃ putto puññavā dinnadāno katābhinīhāro, puññaṃ karonto na ekakova akāsi, addhā etena saha katapuññā suvaṇṇarūpakapaṭibhāgā bhavissatī”ti aṭṭha brāhmaṇe pakkosāpetvā sabbakāmehi santappetvā suvaṇṇarūpakaṃ rathaṃ āropetvā, “gacchatha, tātā, yattha amhākaṃ jātigottabhogehi samānakule evarūpaṃ dārikaṃ passatha, imameva suvaṇṇarūpakaṃ, paṇṇākāraṃ katvā dethā”ti uyyojesi.

The young man, thinking, “I will make my mother understand,” gave a thousand nikkhas of red gold and had the goldsmiths fashion a female figure. When the work of polishing, burnishing, and so on was finished, he had it dressed in a red garment, had it adorned with colorful flowers and various ornaments, had his mother summoned, and said: “Mother, if I obtain such a person, I will remain at home; if I do not, I will not remain.” The wise brahmin woman reflected: “My son is meritorious, has given alms, and has made aspirations. When he performed meritorious deeds, he did not do so alone. Surely, there must be a woman who has performed meritorious deeds together with him and is a counterpart to this golden figure.” She had eight brahmins summoned, satisfied them with all desirable things, placed the golden figure on a chariot, and sent them off, saying: “Go, sirs. Wherever you see a young woman in a family equal to ours in birth, lineage, and wealth who is of such a form, make this very golden figure a gift and give it to her.”

Te “amhākaṃ nāma etaṃ kamma”nti nikkhamitvā, “kattha gamissāmā”ti? Cintetvā, “maddaraṭṭhaṃ nāma itthākaro, maddaraṭṭhaṃ gamissāmā”ti maddaraṭṭhe sāgalanagaraṃ [M 2.0178] agamiṃsu. Tattha taṃ suvaṇṇarūpakaṃ nhānatitthe ṭhapetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu. Atha bhaddāya dhātī bhaddaṃ nhāpetvā alaṅkaritvā sirigabbhe nisīdāpetvā nhāyituṃ āgacchantī taṃ rūpakaṃ disvā, “ayyadhītā me idhāgatā”ti saññāya tajjetvā “dubbinite, kiṃ tvaṃ idhāgatā”ti? Talasattikaṃ uggiritvā, “gaccha sīgha”nti gaṇḍapasse pahari. Hattho pāsāṇe paṭihato viya kampittha. Sā paṭikkamitvā “evaṃ thaddhaṃ nāma mahāgīvaṃ disvā, ‘ayyadhītā me’ti saññaṃ uppādesiṃ, ayyadhītāya hi me ayaṃ nivāsanapaṭiggāhikāpi ayuttā”ti āha. Atha naṃ te manussā parivāretvā “evarūpā te sāmidhītā”ti pucchiṃsu. “Kiṃ esā, imāya sataguṇena sahassaguṇena mayhaṃ ayyā abhirūpatarā, dvādasahatthe gabbhe nisinnāya padīpakiccaṃ natthi, sarīrobhāseneva tamaṃ vidhamatī”ti. “Tena hi āgacchā”ti taṃ khujjaṃ gahetvā suvaṇṇarūpakaṃ rathaṃ āropetvā kosiyagottassa gharadvāre ṭhatvā āgamanaṃ nivedayiṃsu.

Thinking, “This task is ours,” they set out. After considering, “Where shall we go?” they decided, “The Madda country is a mine of beautiful women; we shall go to the Madda country,” and so they went to the city of Sāgala in the Madda country. There, they placed the golden figure at a bathing ford and sat to one side. Now, Bhaddā’s nurse, having bathed and adorned Bhaddā and seated her in the glorious inner chamber, was coming to bathe herself. Seeing the figure, and perceiving, “My noble lady has come here,” she scolded it, saying, “You undisciplined one, why have you come here?” Raising her palm, she struck its cheek, saying, “Go quickly!” Her hand trembled as if it had struck a stone. Stepping back, she said, “Seeing such a stiff, large-necked thing, I formed the perception, ‘It is my noble lady.’ Indeed, this thing is not even fit to be the receiver of my noble lady's discarded garments.” Then those men surrounded her and asked, “Is your master's daughter of such a form?” “What is this figure? My lady is a hundred times, a thousand times more beautiful than this. When she is seated in a twelve-cubit chamber, there is no need for a lamp; she dispels the darkness with the radiance of her body alone.” “In that case, come,” they said. Taking the hunchbacked woman and placing the golden figure onto the chariot, they stood at the door of the house of the Kosiyagotta and announced their arrival.

Brāhmaṇo paṭisanthāraṃ katvā, “kuto āgatatthā”ti? Pucchi. “Magadharaṭṭhe mahātitthagāme kapilabrāhmaṇassa gharato”ti. “Kiṃ [P 2.0193] kāraṇā āgatā”ti. “Iminā nāma kāraṇenā”ti. “Kalyāṇaṃ, tātā, samajātigottavibhavo amhākaṃ brāhmaṇo, dassāmi dārika”nti paṇṇākāraṃ gaṇhi. Te kapilabrāhmaṇassa sāsanaṃ pahiṇiṃsu – “laddhā dārikā, kattabbaṃ karothā”ti. Taṃ sāsanaṃ sutvā pippalimāṇavassa ārocayiṃsu – “laddhā kira dārikā”ti. Māṇavo “ahaṃ na [V 2.0170] labhissāmīti cintesiṃ, ime laddhāti ca vadanti, anatthiko hutvā paṇṇaṃ pesissāmī”ti rahogato paṇṇaṃ likhi, “bhaddā attano jātigottabhogānurūpaṃ gharāvāsaṃ labhatu, ahaṃ nikkhamitvā pabbajissāmi, mā pacchā vippaṭisārinī ahosī”ti. Bhaddāpi “asukassa kira maṃ dātukāmā”ti sutvā rahogatā paṇṇaṃ likhi, “ayyaputto attano jātigottabhogānurūpaṃ gharāvāsaṃ labhatu. Ahaṃ nikkhamitvā pabbajissāmi, mā pacchā vippaṭisārī ahosī”ti. Dvepi paṇṇāni antarāmagge samāgacchiṃsu. “Idaṃ kassa paṇṇa”nti? Pippalimāṇavena bhaddāya pahitanti. “Idaṃ kassa paṇṇa”nti? Bhaddāya pippalimāṇavassa pahitanti ca vutte dvepi vācetvā, “passatha dārakānaṃ kamma”nti phāletvā araññe chaḍḍetvā [M 2.0179] samānapaṇṇaṃ likhitvā ito ca etto ca pesesuṃ. Iti tesaṃ anicchamānānaṃyeva samāgamo ahosi.

The brahmin, after extending a friendly welcome, asked: “From where have you come?” “From the house of the brahmin Kapila in the village of Mahātittha in the Magadha country.” “For what reason have you come?” “For this very reason.” “Excellent, sirs. He is a brahmin equal to us in birth, lineage, and wealth. I will give the young woman.” And he accepted the gift. They sent a message to the brahmin Kapila: “The young woman has been obtained; please make the necessary arrangements.” Hearing that message, they informed the young man Pippali: “It seems the young woman has been obtained.” The young man thought, “I thought I would not get her, but they say she has been obtained.” Being disinclined, he went into seclusion and wrote a letter: “May Bhaddā obtain a household life suitable to her birth, lineage, and wealth. I am going to leave and go forth; may she not later be regretful.” Bhaddā, too, hearing, “It seems they wish to give me to so-and-so,” went into seclusion and wrote a letter: “May the noble son obtain a household life suitable to his birth, lineage, and wealth. I am going to leave and go forth; may he not later be regretful.” The two letters met on the road. When asked, “Whose letter is this?” it was said, “It was sent by the young man Pippali to Bhaddā.” And when asked, “Whose letter is this?” it was said, “It was sent by Bhaddā to the young man Pippali.” Having read both, the messengers said, “Look at what these children are doing!” Tearing them up and discarding them in the wilderness, they wrote a suitable letter and sent it on to each destination. Thus, their union came about even though they were unwilling.

Taṃdivasaṃyeva ca māṇavopi ekaṃ pupphadāmaṃ ganthāpesi, bhaddāpi ekaṃ ganthāpesi. Tāni āsanamajjhe ṭhapetvā bhuttasāyamāsā ubhopi “sayanaṃ āruhissāmā”ti samāgantvā māṇavo dakkhiṇapassena sayanaṃ āruhi. Bhaddā vāmapassena āruhitvā āha – “yassa passe pupphāni milāyanti, tassa rāgacittaṃ uppannanti vijānissāma, imaṃ pupphadāmaṃ na allīyitabba”nti. Te pana aññamaññassa sarīrasamphassabhayena tiyāmarattiṃ niddaṃ anokkamantāva vītināmenti, divā pana hasitamattampi na hoti. Te lokāmisena asaṃsaṭṭhā yāva mātāpitaro dharanti, tāva kuṭumbaṃ avicāretvā [P 2.0194] tesu kālaṅkatesu vicārayiṃsu. Mahatī māṇavassa sampatti, ekadivasaṃ sarīraṃ ubbaṭṭetvā chaḍḍetabbaṃ suvaṇṇacuṇṇameva magadhanāḷiyā dvādasanāḷimattaṃ laddhuṃ vaṭṭati. Yantabaddhāni saṭṭhi mahātaḷākāni, kammanto dvādasayojaniko, anurādhapurappamāṇā cuddasa dāsagāmā, cuddasa hatthānīkā, cuddasa assānīkā, cuddasa rathānīkā.

On that very day, the young man had a flower garland made, and Bhaddā also had one made. Having placed them in the middle of the seat, and after eating the evening meal, they both came together with the thought, “We shall ascend the couch.” The young man ascended the couch on the right side. Bhaddā ascended on the left side and said: “We shall know that a thought of lust has arisen in the one on whose side the flowers wither. This flower garland is not to be touched.” Fearing physical contact with one another, they passed the three watches of the night without falling asleep. During the day, there was not even so much as a smile. Uninvolved with worldly pleasures, they did not manage the household as long as their parents were living; they only managed it after their parents had passed away. The young man's fortune was great: in a single day, the gold dust to be discarded after being rubbed on his body amounted to twelve Magadhan nāḷis. There were sixty great reservoirs fitted with machinery, an estate of twelve yojanas, fourteen slave-villages the size of Anurādhapura, fourteen corps of elephants, fourteen corps of horses, and fourteen corps of chariots.

So ekadivasaṃ alaṅkataṃ assaṃ āruyha mahājanaparivuto kammantaṃ gantvā khettakoṭiyaṃ ṭhito naṅgalehi bhinnaṭṭhānato kākādayo sakuṇe gaṇḍuppādakādipāṇe uddharitvā khādante disvā, “tātā, ime kiṃ khādantī”ti pucchi? “Gaṇḍuppādake ayyā”ti. “Etehi kataṃ pāpaṃ kassa hotī”ti? “Tumhākaṃ, ayyā”ti. So cintesi – “sace etehi kataṃ pāpaṃ mayhaṃ hoti, kiṃ me karissati sattaasītikoṭidhanaṃ? Kiṃ dvādasayojano kammanto, kiṃ yantabaddhāni [V 2.0171] saṭṭhi mahātaḷākāni, kiṃ cuddasa gāmā? Sabbametaṃ bhaddāya kāpilāniyā niyyātetvā nikkhamitvā pabbajissāmī”ti.

One day, riding a decorated horse and surrounded by a great crowd, he went to his place of work. Standing at the edge of the field, he saw birds such as crows picking up and eating creatures such as earthworms from the places broken by the plows. He asked, "Fathers, what are these eating?" "Creatures such as earthworms, lord." "Whose is the evil deed done by these?" "Yours, lord." He thought, "If the evil deed done by these is mine, what use to me is my wealth of eighty-seven crores? What use is the twelve-yojana domain, the sixty great lakes bound by machines, or the fourteen villages? After entrusting all this to Bhaddā Kāpilānī, I will leave home and go forth."

Bhaddāpi kāpilānī tasmiṃ khaṇe abbhantaravatthumhi tayo tilakumbhe pattharāpetvā dhātīhi parivutā nisinnā kāke tilapāṇake khādamāne disvā, “ammā kiṃ ime khādantī”ti? Pucchi. “Pāṇake ayye”ti. “Akusalaṃ kassa hotī”ti? “Tumhākaṃ ayye”ti. Sā cintesi – “mayhaṃ catuhatthavatthaṃ nāḷikodanamattañca laddhuṃ vaṭṭati, yadi ca panetaṃ ettakena janena kataṃ akusalaṃ mayhaṃ hoti, bhavasahassenapi vaṭṭato sīsaṃ ukkhipituṃ na sakkā[M 2.0180], ayyaputte āgatamatteyeva sabbaṃ tassa niyyātetvā nikkhamma pabbajissāmī”ti.

At that moment, Bhaddā Kāpilānī also, having had three large pots of sesame spread out inside the granary and being surrounded by nurses, was seated and saw crows eating sesame insects. She asked, "Mothers, what are these eating?" "Small creatures, madam." "Whose is the unwholesome deed?" "Yours, madam." She thought: "A four-cubit cloth and a nāḷi-measure of cooked rice is sufficient for me, yet if this unwholesome deed done by so many beings becomes mine, it will not be possible to lift my head from the round of existence even in a thousand lifetimes. As soon as the noble son returns, I will hand everything over to him, leave home, and go forth."

Māṇavo āgantvā nhatvā pāsādaṃ āruyha mahārahe pallaṅke nisīdi, athassa cakkavattino anucchavikaṃ bhojanaṃ sajjayiṃsu. Dvepi bhuñjitvā parijane nikkhante rahogatā phāsukaṭṭhāne nisīdiṃsu. Tato māṇavo bhaddaṃ āha – “bhadde, tvaṃ imaṃ gharaṃ āgacchantī kittakaṃ dhanaṃ āharī”ti? “Pañcapaṇṇāsa sakaṭasahassāni ayyā”ti. “Etaṃ sabbaṃ, yā ca imasmiṃ ghare sattaasītikoṭiyo, yantabaddhā saṭṭhitaḷākādibhedā sampatti [P 2.0195] atthi, sabbaṃ tuyhaṃyeva niyyātemī”ti. “Tumhe pana ayyā”ti. “Ahaṃ pabbajissāmī”ti. “Ayyā ahampi tumhākaṃyeva āgamanaṃ olokayamānā nisinnā, ahampi pabbajissāmī”ti. Tesaṃ ādittapaṇṇakuṭi viya tayo bhavā upaṭṭhahiṃsu. Te “pabbajissāmā”ti vatvā antarāpaṇato kasāyarasapītāni vatthāni mattikāpatte ca āharāpetvā aññamaññaṃ kese ohāretvā, “ye loke arahanto, te uddissa amhākaṃ pabbajjā”ti pabbajitvā thavikāsu patte osāpetvā aṃse laggetvā pāsādato otariṃsu. Gehe dāsesu ca kammakāresu ca na koci sañjāni.

The young man arrived, bathed, ascended the palace, and sat on a magnificent couch. Then they prepared food for him suitable for a wheel-turning monarch. After both had eaten and the attendants had left, they went to a secluded place and sat in a comfortable spot. Then the young man said to Bhaddā: "Bhaddā, when you came to this house, how much wealth did you bring?" "Fifty-five thousand cartloads, sir."
