"All of that, and the eighty-seven crores in this house, and whatever wealth there is, such as the sixty lakes bound by machinery—all of it I hand over to you alone." "But what about you, sir?" "I will go forth." "Sir, I too have been sitting, looking for your return. I too will go forth." To them, the three states of existence appeared like a burning leaf-hut. Saying, "We will go forth," they had ocher-colored robes and clay bowls brought from the market, shaved each other's hair, and went forth, declaring, "Our going forth is in dedication to the Arahants in the world." Having placed their bowls into bags and hung them on their shoulders, they descended from the palace. In the house, not one among the servants and workers knew.

Atha ne brāhmaṇagāmato nikkhamma dāsagāmadvārena gacchante ākappakuttavasena dāsagāmavāsino sañjāniṃsu. Te rudantā pādesu nipatitvā “kiṃ amhe anāthe karotha ayyā”ti? Āhaṃsu. “Mayaṃ, bhaṇe ‘ādittapaṇṇasālā viya tayo bhavā’ti pabbajimhā, sace tumhesu ekekaṃ bhujissaṃ karoma, vassasatampi nappahoti, tumheva tumhākaṃ sīsaṃ dhovitvā bhujissā hutvā jīvathā”ti vatvā tesaṃ rodantānaṃyeva pakkamiṃsu. Thero purato gacchanto nivattitvā olokento cintesi – “ayaṃ bhaddā kāpilānī sakalajambudīpagghanikā itthī mayhaṃ [V 2.0172] pacchato āgacchati. Ṭhānaṃ kho panetaṃ vijjati, yaṃ kocideva evaṃ cinteyya ‘ime pabbajitvāpi vinā bhavituṃ na sakkonti, ananucchavikaṃ karontī”ti. “Koci vā pana manaṃ padūsetvā apāyapūrako bhaveyya. Imaṃ pahāya mayā gantuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti cittaṃ uppādesi.

Then, as they were leaving the brahmin village and going through the gate of the servants' village, the inhabitants of the servants' village recognized them by their appearance and demeanor. Weeping, they fell at their feet and said, "Sirs, why do you make us helpless?" They replied, "Friends, we have gone forth because the three states of existence appeared to us like a burning leaf-hut. If we were to make each one of you a free person, even a hundred years would not be enough. You yourselves, take responsibility for yourselves, become free persons, and live." So saying, they departed while they were still weeping. The elder, walking in front, turning and looking back, thought: "This Bhaddā Kāpilānī, a woman worth the whole of Jambudīpa, is coming behind me. This situation exists, where someone might think, 'Even after going forth, they cannot be apart; they are doing something improper.' Or someone, having corrupted their mind, might become one who fills the states of woe. It is proper for me to abandon her and go." Thus, he gave rise to the thought.

So [M 2.0181] purato gacchanto dvedhāpathaṃ disvā tassa matthake aṭṭhāsi. Bhaddāpi āgantvā vanditvā aṭṭhāsi. Atha naṃ āha – “bhadde, tādisiṃ itthiṃ mama pacchato āgacchantiṃ disvā, ‘ime pabbajitvāpi vinā bhavituṃ na sakkontī’ti cintetvā amhesu paduṭṭhacitto mahājano apāyapūrako bhaveyya. Imasmiṃ dvedhāpathe tvaṃ ekaṃ gaṇha, ahaṃ ekena [P 2.0196] gamissāmī”ti. “Āma, ayya, pabbajitānaṃ mātugāmo nāma malaṃ, ‘pabbajitvāpi vinā na bhavantī’ti amhākaṃ dosaṃ passanti, tumhe ekaṃ maggaṃ gaṇhatha, vinā bhavissāmā”ti tikkhattuṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā catūsu ṭhānesu pañcapatiṭṭhitena vanditvā dasanakhasamodhānasamujjalaṃ añjaliṃ paggayha, “satasahassakappappamāṇe addhāne kato mittasanthavo ajja bhijjatī”ti vatvā, “tumhe dakkhiṇajātikā nāma, tumhākaṃ dakkhiṇamaggo vaṭṭati, mayaṃ mātugāmā nāma vāmajātikā, amhākaṃ vāmamaggo vaṭṭatī”ti vanditvā maggaṃ paṭipannā. Tesaṃ dvedhābhūtakāle ayaṃ mahāpathavī “ahaṃ cakkavāḷagirisinerupabbate dhāretuṃ sakkontīpi tumhākaṃ guṇe dhāretuṃ na sakkomī”ti vadantī viya viravamānā akampi, ākāse asanisaddo viya pavatti, cakkavāḷapabbato unnadi.

He, walking in front, saw a fork in the road and stood at its head. Bhaddā also arrived, paid homage, and stood there. Then he said to her: "Bhaddā, seeing such a woman following behind me, the great populace might think, ‘Even after going forth, they cannot be apart,’ and, with minds corrupted towards us, they would become fillers of the states of woe. At this fork in the road, you take one path, and I will go by the other." "Yes, lord. For those who have gone forth, a woman is indeed a stain. They see a fault in us, thinking, ‘Even after going forth, they are not apart.’ You take one path; we shall be apart." Having circumambulated him three times, she paid homage with the five-point prostration at the four cardinal points, raised her joined palms, radiant with the collection of her ten fingernails, and said: "The bond of friendship formed over a period of a hundred thousand kappas is broken today." Then she said: "You are of the right-hand nature; the right-hand path is suitable for you. We women are of the left-hand nature; the left-hand path is suitable for us." Having paid homage, she set out on her path. At the moment of their parting, this great earth, roaring as if to say, "Though I am able to bear the Cakkavāḷa mountains and Mount Sineru, I am not able to bear your virtues," trembled violently. In the sky, a sound like thunder arose, and the Cakkavāḷa mountain range resounded.

Sammāsambuddho veḷuvanamahāvihāre gandhakuṭiyaṃ nisinno pathavīkampanasaddaṃ sutvā, “kassa nu kho pathavī kampatī”ti? Āvajjento “pippalimāṇavo ca bhaddā ca kāpilānī maṃ uddissa appameyyaṃ sampattiṃ pahāya pabbajitā, tesaṃ viyogaṭṭhāne ubhinnampi guṇabalena ayaṃ pathavīkampo jāto, mayāpi etesaṃ saṅgahaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti gandhakuṭito nikkhamma sayameva pattacīvaraṃ ādāya, asītimahātheresu kañci anāmantetvā tigāvutaṃ maggaṃ paccuggamanaṃ katvā rājagahassa ca nāḷandāya ca antare bahuputtakanigrodharukkhamūle pallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvā nisīdi. Nisīdanto pana aññataro paṃsukūliko viya anisīditvā buddhavesaṃ gahetvā asītihatthā ghanabuddharasmiyo vissajjento nisīdi. Iti tasmiṃ khaṇe paṇṇachattasakaṭacakkakūṭāgārādippamāṇā buddharasmiyo ito cito ca vipphandantiyo vidhāvantiyo candimasahassasūriyasahassauggamanakālo viya kurumānā taṃ vanantaraṃ ekobhāsaṃ akaṃsu. Dvattiṃsamahāpurisalakkhaṇānaṃ [V 2.0173] siriyā samujjalitatārāgaṇaṃ viya gaganaṃ, supupphitakamalakuvalayaṃ viya salilaṃ, vanantaraṃ [P 2.0197] virocittha. Nigrodharukkhassa nāma khandho seto [M 2.0182] hoti, pattāni nīlāni pakkāni rattāni. Tasmiṃ pana divase satasākho nigrodharukkho suvaṇṇavaṇṇo ahosi.

The Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, seated in the Fragrant Cottage at the Great Monastery of the Bamboo Grove, heard the sound of the earth quaking and thought, “On whose account, I wonder, is the earth quaking?” Reflecting, he realized, “The young man Pippali and Bhaddā Kāpilānī, having renounced immeasurable prosperity for my sake, have gone forth. Due to the power of their virtues, this earthquake has arisen at the place of their separation. It is fitting for me to assist them.” Rising from the Fragrant Cottage, he took his bowl and robes himself. Without informing any of the eighty great elders, he traveled three gāvutas to meet them. Between Rājagaha and Nāḷandā, beneath the Bahuputtaka banyan tree, he sat down, having folded his legs in the cross-legged posture. As he sat, he did not sit like some ordinary wearer of rag-robes, but assuming the appearance of a Buddha, he sat down emitting dense Buddha-rays eighty cubits in length. At that moment, Buddha-rays the size of leaf-parasols, cart-wheels, and pinnacled mansions flickered and darted to and fro, making that forest tract a single mass of light, like the time of the rising of a thousand moons and a thousand suns. The forest tract shone brilliantly, like the sky blazing with its host of stars illuminated by the splendor of the thirty-two marks of a great man, and like the water gleaming with fully bloomed lotuses and water lilies. The trunk of a banyan tree is white, its leaves are dark green, and its ripe fruits are red. On that day, however, the hundred-branched banyan tree became the color of gold.

Iti yā sā addhānamaggappaṭipannoti padassa atthaṃ vatvā, “idāni yathā esa pabbajito, yathā ca addhānamaggaṃ paṭipanno. Imassa atthassa āvibhāvatthaṃ abhinīhārato paṭṭhāya ayaṃ anupubbikathā kathetabbā”ti vuttā, sā evaṃ veditabbā.

Thus, having explained the meaning of the phrase 'one who has entered upon the long journey,' that which was stated—'Now, as to how he went forth and how he entered upon the long journey, to clarify this matter, this gradual discourse should be related, starting from his original aspiration'—should be understood in this way.

Antarā ca rājagahaṃ antarā ca nāḷandanti rājagahassa ca nāḷandāya ca antare. Satthārañca vatāhaṃ passeyyaṃ bhagavantameva passeyyanti sace ahaṃ satthāraṃ passeyyaṃ, imaṃyeva bhagavantaṃ passeyyaṃ. Na hi me ito aññena satthārā bhavituṃ sakkāti. Sugatañca vatāhaṃ passeyyaṃ bhagavantameva passeyyanti sace ahaṃ sammāpaṭipattiyā suṭṭhu gatattā sugataṃ nāma passeyyaṃ, imaṃyeva bhagavantaṃ passeyyaṃ. Na hi me ito aññena sugatena bhavituṃ sakkāti. Sammāsambuddhañca vatāhaṃ passeyyaṃ bhagavantameva passeyyanti sace ahaṃ sammā sāmañca saccāni buddhattā sammāsambuddhaṃ nāma passeyyaṃ, imaṃyeva bhagavantaṃ passeyyaṃ. Na hi me ito aññena sammāsambuddhena bhavituṃ sakkāti ayamettha adhippāyo. Evaṃ dassaneneva “bhagavati ‘ayaṃ satthā, ayaṃ sugato, ayaṃ sammāsambuddho’ti nikkaṅkho ahaṃ, āvuso, ahosi”nti dīpeti. Satthā me, bhanteti idaṃ kiñcāpi dve vāre āgataṃ, tikkhattuṃ pana vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Iminā hi so “evaṃ tikkhattuṃ sāvakattaṃ sāvesiṃ, āvuso”ti dīpeti.

‘Between Rājagaha and Nāḷandā’ means between Rājagaha and Nāḷandā. ‘If I were to see the Teacher, I would see the Blessed One himself’ means: ‘If I were to see the Teacher, I would see this very Blessed One. For it is not possible for me to have another Teacher besides him.’ ‘If I were to see the Well-Gone One, I would see the Blessed One himself’ means: ‘If I were to see one called the Well-Gone One, who has gone well by right practice, I would see this very Blessed One. For it is not possible for me to have another Well-Gone One besides him.’ ‘If I were to see the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, I would see the Blessed One himself’ means: ‘If I were to see one called the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, who has perfectly awakened to the truths by himself, I would see this very Blessed One. For it is not possible for me to have another Perfectly Self-Enlightened One besides him.’ This is the intended meaning here. Thus, by the very act of seeing, he shows: “Friend, I became free from doubt regarding the Blessed One, thinking: ‘This is the Teacher, this is the Well-Gone One, this is the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One.’” The phrase “You are my Teacher, venerable sir,” although it appears twice, should be understood as having been spoken three times. For by this he shows: “Thus, friend, I announced my discipleship three times.”

Ajānaññevāti ajānamānova. Dutiyapadepi eseva nayo. Muddhāpi tassa vipateyyāti yassa aññassa “ajānaṃyeva jānāmī”ti paṭiññassa bāhirakassa satthuno evaṃ sabbacetasā samannāgato pasannacitto sāvako evarūpaṃ paramanipaccakāraṃ kareyya, tassa vaṇṭachinnatālapakkaṃ viya gīvato muddhāpi vipateyya, sattadhā pana phaleyyāti attho. Kiṃ vā etena, sace mahākassapatthero [P 2.0198] iminā cittappasādena imaṃ paramanipaccakāraṃ mahāsamuddassa kareyya, tattakapāle pakkhittaudakabindu viya vilayaṃ gaccheyya. Sace cakkavāḷassa kareyya, thusamuṭṭhi viya vikireyya. Sace sinerupabbatassa kareyya, kākatuṇḍena pahaṭapiṭṭhamuṭṭhi viya viddhaṃseyya[M 2.0183]. Sace mahāpathaviyā kareyya, vātāhatabhasmapuñjo viya vikireyya. Evarūpopi pana therassa nipaccākāro [V 2.0174] satthu suvaṇṇavaṇṇe pādapiṭṭhe lomamattampi vikopetuṃ nāsakkhi. Tiṭṭhatu ca mahākassapo, mahākassapasadisānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ sahassampi satasahassampi nipaccākāradassanena neva dasabalassa pādapiṭṭhe lomamattampi vikopetuṃ paṃsukūlacīvare vā aṃsumattampi cāletuṃ sakkoti. Evaṃ mahānubhāvo hi satthā.

‘Not knowing, indeed’ means just not knowing. The same method applies to the second phrase. ‘Even his head would split’ means that if any outside teacher, who makes the claim, ‘I know what I do not know,’ were to receive such supreme reverence from a devoted disciple with full faith, his head would fall from his neck like a ripe palm fruit severed from its stalk, and it would shatter into seven pieces; that is the meaning. Or what of this? If the great elder Mahākassapa were to offer this supreme reverence with this heartfelt devotion to the great ocean, it would vanish like a drop of water thrown onto a heated pan. If he were to offer it to the world-sphere, it would scatter like a handful of chaff. If he were to offer it to Mount Sineru, it would be destroyed like a fistful of flour struck by a crow’s beak. If he were to offer it to the great earth, it would disperse like a heap of ashes struck by the wind. Yet, even such reverence from the elder could not disturb even a single hair on the golden-hued insteps of the Teacher. Let Mahākassapa be. Even a thousand or a hundred thousand monks like Mahākassapa, by showing such reverence, could not disturb a single hair on the insteps of the Ten-Powered One, nor move even a thread of his rag-robe. For such is the great power of the Teacher.

Tasmātiha te kassapāti yasmā ahaṃ jānanto eva “jānāmī”ti, passanto eva ca “passāmī”ti vadāmi, tasmā, kassapa, tayā evaṃ sikkhitabbaṃ. Tibbanti bahalaṃ mahantaṃ. Hirottappanti hirī ca ottappañca. Paccupaṭṭhitaṃ bhavissatīti paṭhamatarameva upaṭṭhitaṃ bhavissati. Yo hi therādīsu hirottappaṃ upaṭṭhapetvā upasaṅkamati therādayopi taṃ sahirikā saottappā ca hutvā upasaṅkamantīti ayamettha ānisaṃso. Kusalūpasaṃhitanti kusalasannissitaṃ. Aṭṭhiṃ katvāti attānaṃ tena dhammena aṭṭhikaṃ katvā, taṃ vā dhammaṃ “esa mayhaṃ attho”ti aṭṭhiṃ katvā. Manasi katvāti citte ṭhapetvā. Sabbacetasā samannāharitvāti cittassa thokampi bahi gantuṃ adento sabbena samannāhāracittena samannāharitvā. Ohitasototi ṭhapitasoto, ñāṇasotañca pasādasotañca odahitvā mayā desitaṃ dhammaṃ sakkaccameva suṇissāmīti evañhi te sikkhitabbaṃ. Sātasahagatā ca me kāyagatāsatīti asubhesu ceva ānāpāne ca paṭhamajjhānavasena sukhasampayuttā kāyagatāsati. Yo ca panāyaṃ tividho ovādo, therassa ayameva pabbajjā ca upasampadā ca ahosi.

‘Therefore, Kassapa’ means: ‘Since I, knowing, say “I know,” and seeing, say “I see,” therefore, Kassapa, you should train yourself thus.’ ‘Tibbanti’ means dense, great. ‘Hirottappanti’ means moral shame and moral dread. ‘It will be present’ means it will be present from the very beginning. For one who approaches elders and others with moral shame and dread established, they too approach him possessing moral shame and dread. This is the benefit here. ‘Connected with the wholesome’ means associated with the wholesome. ‘Aṭṭhiṃ katvā’ means making oneself desirous of that Dhamma, or making that Dhamma one's purpose, thinking, ‘This is my aim.’ ‘Manasi katvā’ means having placed it in the mind. ‘Sabbacetasā samannāharitvā’ means not allowing the mind to go outside even a little, bringing it together with a fully concentrated mind. ‘Ohitasoto’ means with ear applied; having opened the ear of knowledge and the ear of faith, thinking, ‘I will listen respectfully to the Dhamma taught by me.’ Thus indeed should you train yourself. ‘And my mindfulness directed to the body, accompanied by pleasure’ means mindfulness directed to the body associated with pleasure by means of the first jhāna regarding both the foul and the in-and-out breath. And this threefold instruction was the elder’s going forth and higher ordination.

Saraṇoti [P 2.0199] sakileso saiṇo hutvā. Raṭṭhapiṇḍaṃ bhuñjinti saddhādeyyaṃ bhuñjiṃ. Cattāro hi paribhogā theyyaparibhogo iṇaparibhogo dāyajjaparibhogo sāmiparibhogoti. Tattha dussīlassa saṅghamajjhe nisīditvā bhuñjantassāpi paribhogo theyyaparibhogo nāma. Kasmā? Catūsu paccayesu anissaratāya. Sīlavato apaccavekkhitaparibhogo iṇaparibhogo nāma. Sattannaṃ sekhānaṃ paribhogo dāyajjaparibhogo nāma. Khīṇāsavassa paribhogo sāmiparibhogo nāma. Iti khīṇāsavova sāmī hutvā anaṇo paribhuñjati. Thero attanā [M 2.0184] puthujjanena hutvā paribhuttaparibhogaṃ iṇaparibhogaṃyeva karonto evamāha. Aṭṭhamiyā aññā udapādīti aṭṭhame divase arahattaphalaṃ uppajji.

‘Saraṇo’ means being with defilements and with debt. ‘I ate the country's almsfood’ means ‘I ate what was given out of faith.’ For there are four kinds of partaking: partaking by theft, partaking as a debt, partaking as an inheritance, and partaking as a master. Among these, the partaking of an immoral person, even while sitting and eating in the midst of the Saṅgha, is called partaking by theft. Why? Because of not being the master of the four requisites. The unreflecting partaking of a virtuous person is called partaking as a debt. The partaking of the seven trainees is called partaking as an inheritance. The partaking of one whose taints are destroyed is called partaking as a master. Thus, one whose taints are destroyed, being a master, partakes without debt. The elder, considering the partaking he had done while he was a worldling to be indeed partaking as a debt, spoke thus. ‘On the eighth day, final knowledge arose’ means on the eighth day, the fruit of arahantship arose.

Atha kho, āvuso, bhagavā maggā okkammāti maggato okkamanaṃ paṭhamataraṃ taṃdivaseyeva [V 2.0175] ahosi, arahattādhigamo pacchā. Desanāvārassa pana evaṃ āgatattā arahattādhigamo paṭhamaṃ dīpito. Kasmā pana bhagavā maggā okkantoti? Evaṃ kirassa ahosi “imaṃ bhikkhuṃ jātiāraññikaṃ jātipaṃsukūlikaṃ jātiekāsanikaṃ karissāmī”ti. Tasmā okkami.

In the phrase, ‘Then, friends, the Blessed One stepped off the path,’ the stepping off the path occurred first, on that very day; the attainment of arahantship came later. However, because it came thus in the sequence of the discourse, the attainment of arahantship is shown first. But why did the Blessed One step off the path? It seems this occurred to him: ‘I will make this monk one who is by nature a forest-dweller, by nature a wearer of rag-robes, and by nature an eater of one meal a day.’ Therefore, he stepped off.

Mudukā kho tyāyanti mudukā kho te ayaṃ. Imañca pana vācaṃ bhagavā taṃ cīvaraṃ padumapupphavaṇṇena pāṇinā antantena parāmasanto āha. Kasmā evamāhāti? Therena saha cīvaraṃ parivattetukāmatāya. Kasmā parivattetukāmo jātoti? Theraṃ attano ṭhāne ṭhapetukāmatāya. Thero pana yasmā cīvarassa vā pattassa vā vaṇṇe kathite “imaṃ tumhākaṃ gaṇhathā”tivacanaṃ cārittameva, tasmā “paṭiggaṇhātu me, bhante, bhagavā”ti āha. Dhāressasi pana me tvaṃ, kassapa, sāṇāni paṃsukūlāni nibbasanānīti, kassapa, tvaṃ imāni paribhogajiṇṇāni paṃsukūlāni pārupituṃ sakkhissasīti vadati. Tañca kho na kāyabalaṃ sandhāya, paṭipattipūraṇaṃ pana sandhāya evamāha. Ayañhettha adhippāyo – ahaṃ imaṃ cīvaraṃ puṇṇaṃ nāma dāsiṃ pārupitvā āmakasusāne chaḍḍitaṃ taṃ susānaṃ pavisitvā tumbamattehi pāṇakehi samparikiṇṇaṃ te pāṇake vidhunitvā mahāariyavaṃse ṭhatvā aggahesiṃ, tassa me imaṃ cīvaraṃ gahitadivase dasasahassacakkavāḷe mahāpathavī mahāviravaṃ [P 2.0200] viravamānā kampittha, ākāso taṭataṭāyi, cakkavāḷadevatā sādhukāramadaṃsu, “imaṃ cīvaraṃ gaṇhantena bhikkhunā jātipaṃsukūlikena jātiāraññikena jātiekāsanikena jātisapadānacārikena bhavituṃ vaṭṭati, tvaṃ imassa cīvarassa anucchavikaṃ kātuṃ sakkhissasī”ti. Theropi attanā pañcannaṃ hatthīnaṃ balaṃ dhāreti, so taṃ atakkayitvā “ahametaṃ paṭipattiṃ pūressāmī”ti ussāhena sugatacīvarassa anucchavikaṃ kātukāmo “dhāressāmahaṃ, bhante”ti āha. Paṭipajjinti paṭipannosmi. Evaṃ pana cīvaraparivattanaṃ katvā ca therena pārutacīvaraṃ bhagavā [M 2.0185] pārupi, satthu cīvaraṃ thero. Tasmiṃ samaye mahāpathavī udakapariyantaṃ katvā unnadantī kampittha.

‘Mudukā kho tyāyan’ti’ means ‘Soft indeed is this of yours.’ The Blessed One spoke this word while stroking that robe by the hem with his hand the color of a lotus flower. Why did he say this? Because of his wish to exchange robes with the elder. Why did he wish to exchange? Because of his wish to establish the elder in his own place. As for the elder, since it is the custom, when the quality of a robe or bowl is praised, to say, “Take this for yourselves,” he therefore said, “Venerable sir, may the Blessed One accept it from me.” ‘But will you, Kassapa, wear my hempen rag-robes, my outer cloak?’ means: ‘Kassapa, will you be able to wear these rag-robes of mine, worn out from use?’ he said. And he said this not with reference to physical strength, but with reference to the fulfillment of the practice. Here is the intended meaning: ‘I, having entered the charnel ground, took up this robe which had been worn by a slave-girl named Puṇṇā and discarded there. It was swarming with worms the size of gourds. Shaking off those worms and standing firm in the great noble lineage, I picked it up. On the day I took this robe, the great earth in the ten-thousand-world-system trembled, roaring a great roar; the sky thundered; and the deities of the world-systems gave their approval, saying: “A monk who takes up this robe should be by nature a wearer of rag-robes, by nature a forest-dweller, by nature an eater of one meal a day, by nature a practitioner of continuous alms-round wandering. Will you be able to do what is befitting this robe?”’ The elder, too, though he possessed the strength of five elephants, did not consider that, but with zeal, wishing to do what was befitting the Sugata’s robe, thought, ‘I will fulfill this practice,’ and said, ‘Venerable sir, I will wear it.’ ‘Paṭipajjiṃ’ means ‘I have undertaken the practice.’ Having thus exchanged robes, the Blessed One wore the robe worn by the elder, and the elder wore the Teacher’s robe. At that moment, the great earth, down to its watery boundary, roared and trembled.

Bhagavato puttotiādīsu thero bhagavantaṃ nissāya ariyāya jātiyā jātoti bhagavato putto. Urena vasitvā mukhato nikkhantaovādavasena pabbajjāya ceva upasampadāya ca patiṭṭhitattā oraso mukhato jāto. Ovādadhammato jātattā ovādadhammena ca nimmitattā dhammajo dhammanimmito. Ovādadhammadāyādaṃ navalokuttaradhammadāyādameva vā arahatīti dhammadāyādo [V 2.0176] . Paṭiggahitāni sāṇāni paṃsukūlānīti satthārā pārutaṃ paṃsukūlacīvaraṃ pārupanatthāya paṭiggahitaṃ.

In such phrases as ‘son of the Blessed One,’ the elder is the Blessed One’s son because, relying on the Blessed One, he was born with the noble birth. Because he was established in both the going forth and the higher ordination by means of the instruction that came from his mouth, having dwelt at his breast, he is a legitimate son, born from his mouth. Because he was born from the Dhamma of instruction and created by the Dhamma of instruction, he is Dhamma-born and Dhamma-created. He is an heir to the Dhamma because he is worthy of the inheritance of the Dhamma of instruction, or of the inheritance of the nine supramundane Dhammas. ‘The hempen rag-robes were accepted’ means the rag-robe worn by the Teacher was accepted for the purpose of wearing.

Sammā vadamāno vadeyyāti yaṃ puggalaṃ “bhagavato putto”tiādīhi guṇehi sammā vadamāno vadeyya, mamaṃ taṃ sammā vadamāno vadeyya, ahaṃ evarūpoti. Ettāvatā therena pabbajjā ca parisodhitā hoti. Ayañhettha adhippāyo – āvuso, yassa na upajjhāyo paññāyati, na ācariyo, kiṃ so anupajjhāyo anācariyo nhāpitamuṇḍako sayaṃgahitakāsāvo “titthiyapakkantako”ti saṅkhaṃ gato evaṃ tigāvutaṃ maggaṃ paccuggamanaṃ labhati, tīhi ovādehi pabbajjaṃ vā upasampadaṃ vā labhati, kāyena kāyaṃ cīvaraparivattanaṃ labhati? Passa yāva dubbhāsitaṃ vacanaṃ thullanandāya bhikkhuniyāti. Evaṃ pabbajjaṃ [P 2.0201] sodhetvā idāni chahi abhiññāhi sīhanādaṃ nadituṃ ahaṃ kho, āvusotiādimāha. Sesaṃ purimanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Ekādasamaṃ.

As for 'Speaking rightly, one should speak': If one, speaking rightly, were to speak of a person with qualities such as 'son of the Blessed One,' one would be speaking rightly of me, for I am of such a nature. By this much, the elder's going forth is thoroughly purified. And here this is the intention: 'Friend, for whom no preceptor is apparent, no teacher is apparent, would such a one—without preceptor, without teacher, a shaven-headed man who has taken the ochre robes by himself, who has come to be reckoned as a sectarian apostate—obtain a welcoming reception for a distance of three gāvutas? Would he obtain the going forth or the higher ordination with three exhortations? Would he obtain the exchange of robes from body to body? See how ill-spoken was the word of the nun Thullanandā!' Having thus purified the going forth, now, in order to roar the lion's roar with the six super-knowledges, he spoke the words beginning with 'I indeed, friend...' The remainder should be understood by the same method as before. The eleventh.

12. Paraṃmaraṇasuttavaṇṇanā

12. Commentary on the Discourse on After Death

155. Dvādasame tathāgatoti satto. Na hetaṃ, āvuso, atthasaṃhitanti, āvuso, etaṃ diṭṭhigataṃ atthasannissitaṃ na hoti. Nādibrahmacariyakanti maggabrahmacariyassa pubbabhāgapaṭipadāpi na hoti. Etañhi, āvuso, atthasaṃhitanti, āvuso, etaṃ catusaccakammaṭṭhānaṃ atthasannissitaṃ. Etaṃ ādibrahmacariyakanti etaṃ maggabrahmacariyassa ādi pubbabhāgapaṭipadā. Dvādasamaṃ.

155. In the twelfth, 'Tathāgata' means a being. 'This, friend, is not connected with the goal' means: friend, this view is not based on the goal. 'It is not the beginning of the holy life' means: it is not even the preliminary practice for the holy life of the path. 'This, friend, is connected with the goal' means: friend, this meditation subject of the Four Truths is based on the goal. 'This is the beginning of the holy life' means: this is the initial, preliminary practice for the holy life of the path. The twelfth.

13. Saddhammappatirūpakasuttavaṇṇanā

13. Commentary on the Discourse on the Counterfeit of the True Dhamma

156. Terasame [M 2.0186] aññāya saṇṭhahiṃsūti arahatte patiṭṭhahiṃsu. Saddhammappatirūpakanti dve saddhammappatirūpakāni adhigamasaddhammappatirūpakañca pariyattisaddhammappatirūpakañca. Tattha –

156. In the thirteenth, 'they were established through direct knowledge' means they were established in Arahantship. As for 'the counterfeit of the true Dhamma,' there are two counterfeits of the true Dhamma: the counterfeit of the true Dhamma of attainment and the counterfeit of the true Dhamma of learning. Therein:

“Obhāse ceva ñāṇe ca, pītiyā ca vikampati;

Passaddhiyā sukhe ceva, yehi cittaṃ pavedhati.

In light and in knowledge, and in joy, the mind wavers; in tranquility and in happiness, by which the mind trembles.

“Adhimokkhe [V 2.0177] ca paggāhe, upaṭṭhāne ca kampati;

Upekkhāvajjanāya ceva, upekkhāya ca nikantiyā.

It trembles in conviction and in sustained effort, and in mindfulness; in adverting to equanimity, in equanimity, and in delight.

“Imāni dasa ṭhānāni, paññā yassa paricitā;

Dhammuddhaccakusalo hoti, na ca sammoha gacchatī”ti. (paṭi. ma. 2.7); –

For one whose wisdom has familiarized these ten grounds, one becomes skilled in restlessness about phenomena and does not fall into delusion.

Idaṃ vipassanāñāṇassa upakkilesajātaṃ adhigamasaddhammappatirūpakaṃ nāma. Tisso pana saṅgītiyo anāruḷhaṃ dhātukathā ārammaṇakathā asubhakathā ñāṇavatthukathā vijjākaraṇḍakoti imehi pañcahi kathāvatthūhi paribāhiraṃ guḷhavinayaṃ guḷhavessantaraṃ guḷhamahosadhaṃ vaṇṇapiṭakaṃ aṅgulimālapiṭakaṃ raṭṭhapālagajjitaṃ āḷavakagajjitaṃ [P 2.0202] vedallapiṭakanti abuddhavacanaṃ pariyattisaddhammappatirūpakaṃ nāma.

This group of corruptions of insight-knowledge is called the counterfeit of the true Dhamma of attainment. Furthermore, that which was not included in the three councils: the Dhātukathā, Ārammaṇakathā, Asubhakathā, Ñāṇavatthukathā, and Vijjākaraṇḍaka; and external to these five topics of discussion: the Gūḷhavinaya, Gūḷhavessantara, Gūḷhamahosadha, Vaṇṇapiṭaka, Aṅgulimālapiṭaka, Raṭṭhapālagajjita, Āḷavakagajjita, and Vedallapiṭaka—this, being non-Buddha-word, is called the counterfeit of the true Dhamma of learning.

Jātarūpappatirūpakanti suvaṇṇarasavidhānaṃ ārakūṭamayaṃ suvaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ ābharaṇajātaṃ. Chaṇakālesu hi manussā “ābharaṇabhaṇḍakaṃ gaṇhissāmā”ti āpaṇaṃ gacchanti. Atha ne āpaṇikā evaṃ vadanti, “sace tumhe ābharaṇatthikā, imāni gaṇhatha. Imāni hi ghanāni ceva vaṇṇavantāni ca appagghāni cā”ti. Te tesaṃ sutvā, “kāraṇaṃ ime vadanti, imāni piḷandhitvā sakkā nakkhattaṃ kīḷituṃ, sobhanti ceva appagghāni cā”ti tāni gahetvā gacchanti. Suvaṇṇabhaṇḍaṃ avikkiyamānaṃ nidahitvā ṭhapetabbaṃ hoti. Evaṃ taṃ jātarūpappatirūpake uppanne antaradhāyati nāma.

As for 'the counterfeit of gold,' this refers to a kind of ornament made with a golden liquid, made of brass, having a color like gold. During festival times, people go to the market thinking, 'We will get some jewelry.' Then the merchants say to them, 'If you want jewelry, take these. For these are solid, beautiful, and inexpensive.' Hearing them, they think, 'They speak reasonably. Wearing these, it is possible to enjoy the festival; they are splendid and cheap.' Taking them, they go. Genuine gold items, being unsold, have to be stored away. Thus, when the counterfeit of gold arises, that genuine gold is said to disappear.

Atha saddhammassa antaradhānaṃ hotīti adhigamasaddhammassa paṭipattisaddhammassa pariyattisaddhammassāti tividhassāpi saddhammassa antaradhānaṃ hoti. Paṭhamabodhiyañhi [M 2.0187] bhikkhū paṭisambhidappattā ahesuṃ. Atha kāle gacchante paṭisambhidā pāpuṇituṃ na sakkhiṃsu, chaḷabhiññā ahesuṃ. Tato cha abhiññā pāpuṇituṃ asakkontā tisso vijjā pāpuṇiṃsu. Idāni kāle gacchante tisso vijjā pāpuṇituṃ asakkontā āsavakkhayamattaṃ pāpuṇissanti. Tampi asakkontā anāgāmiphalaṃ, tampi asakkontā sakadāgāmiphalaṃ, tampi asakkontā sotāpattiphalaṃ. Gacchante kāle sotāpattiphalampi pattuṃ na sakkhissanti. Atha [V 2.0178] nesaṃ yadā vipassanā imehi upakkilesehi upakkiliṭṭhā āraddhamattāva ṭhassati, tadā adhigamasaddhammo antarahito nāma bhavissati.

Then there is the disappearance of the true Dhamma—the disappearance of the true Dhamma of attainment, the true Dhamma of practice, and the true Dhamma of learning—thus the disappearance of the true Dhamma is threefold. Indeed, in the first period of awakening, the bhikkhus were attainers of the analytical knowledges. Then, as time went on, they were unable to attain the analytical knowledges; they became attainers of the six super-knowledges. Then, being unable to attain the six super-knowledges, they attained the three true knowledges. Now, as time goes on, being unable to attain the three true knowledges, they will attain only the destruction of the taints. Being unable to attain even that, they will attain the fruit of non-returning; being unable to attain even that, the fruit of once-returning; being unable to attain even that, the fruit of stream-entry. As time goes on, they will not be able to attain even the fruit of stream-entry. Then, when their insight is corrupted by these corruptions and remains merely at the stage of being initiated, at that time the true Dhamma of attainment will be said to have disappeared.

Paṭhamabodhiyañhi bhikkhū catunnaṃ paṭisambhidānaṃ anucchavikaṃ paṭipattiṃ pūrayiṃsu. Gacchante kāle taṃ asakkontā channaṃ abhiññānaṃ, tampi asakkontā tissannaṃ vijjānaṃ, tampi asakkontā arahattaphalamattassa. Gacchante pana kāle arahattassa anucchavikaṃ paṭipattiṃ pūretuṃ asakkontā anāgāmiphalassa anucchavikaṃ paṭipattiṃ pūressanti[P 2.0203], tampi asakkontā sakadāgāmiphalassa, tampi asakkontā sotāpattiphalassa. Yadā pana sotāpattiphalassapi anucchavikaṃ paṭipadaṃ pūretuṃ asakkontā sīlapārisuddhimatteva ṭhassanti, tadā paṭipattisaddhammo antarahito nāma bhavissati.

Indeed, in the first period of awakening, the bhikkhus fulfilled the practice suitable for the four analytical knowledges. As time went on, being unable to fulfill that, they fulfilled the practice suitable for the six super-knowledges; being unable to do that, for the three true knowledges; being unable to do that, for merely the fruit of Arahantship. Then, as time goes on, being unable to fulfill the practice suitable for Arahantship, they will fulfill the practice suitable for the fruit of non-returning; being unable to do that, for the fruit of once-returning; being unable to do that, for the fruit of stream-entry. But when they are unable to fulfill even the practice suitable for the fruit of stream-entry and will stand only in mere purity of virtue, at that time the true Dhamma of practice will be said to have disappeared.

Yāva pana tepiṭakaṃ buddhavacanaṃ vattati, na tāva sāsanaṃ antarahitanti vattuṃ vaṭṭati. Tiṭṭhantu tīṇi vā, abhidhammapiṭake antarahite itaresu dvīsu tiṭṭhantesupi antarahitanti na vattabbameva. Dvīsu antarahitesu vinayapiṭakamatte ṭhitepi, tatrāpi khandhakaparivāresu antarahitesu ubhatovibhaṅgamatte, mahāvinaye antarahite dvīsu pātimokkhesu vattamānesupi sāsanaṃ anantarahitameva. Yadā pana dve pātimokkhā antaradhāyissanti, atha pariyattisaddhammassa antaradhānaṃ bhavissati. Tasmiṃ antarahite sāsanaṃ antarahitaṃ nāma hoti. Pariyattiyā hi antarahitāya paṭipatti antaradhāyati, paṭipattiyā antarahitāya adhigamo antaradhāyati. Kiṃ kāraṇā? Ayañhi pariyatti paṭipattiyā paccayo hoti, paṭipatti adhigamassa. Iti paṭipattitopi pariyattimeva pamāṇaṃ.

Furthermore, as long as the Tipiṭaka, the word of the Buddha, exists, it is not proper to say that the Dispensation has disappeared. Let the three Piṭakas stand. When the Abhidhamma Piṭaka has disappeared, even while the other two stand, it is certainly not to be said that the Dispensation has disappeared. When two have disappeared and only the Vinaya Piṭaka stands; and even within that, when the Khandhakas and Parivāras have disappeared, and the Mahāvinaya—the two Vibhaṅgas—has disappeared, as long as the two Pātimokkhas are still present, the Dispensation has not yet disappeared. But when the two Pātimokkhas disappear, then the disappearance of the good Dhamma of learning will occur. When that has disappeared, the Dispensation is said to have disappeared. For when learning has disappeared, practice disappears; when practice has disappeared, attainment disappears. For what reason? Because this learning is a condition for practice, and practice is a condition for attainment. Therefore, even more than practice, learning itself is the measure.

Nanu [M 2.0188] ca kassapasammāsambuddhakāle kapilo nāma anārādhakabhikkhu “pātimokkhaṃ uddisissāmī”ti bījaniṃ gahetvā āsane nisinno “atthi imasmiṃ vattantā”ti pucchi, atha tassa bhayena yesampi pātimokkho vattati, tepi “mayaṃ vattāmā”ti avatvā “na vattāmā”ti vadiṃsu, so bījaniṃ ṭhapetvā uṭṭhāyāsanā gato, tadā sammāsambuddhassa sāsanaṃ osakkitanti? Kiñcāpi osakkitaṃ, pariyatti pana ekanteneva pamāṇaṃ. Yathā hi mahato taḷākassa pāḷiyā thirāya udakaṃ na ṭhassatīti na vattabbaṃ, udake sati padumādīni pupphāni na pupphissantīti na vattabbaṃ, evameva mahātaḷākassa thirapāḷisadise tepiṭake buddhavacane [V 2.0179] sati mahātaḷāke udakasadisā paṭipattipūrakā kulaputtā natthīti na vattabbā, tesu sati mahātaḷāke padumādīni pupphāni viya sotāpannādayo ariyapuggalā natthīti [P 2.0204] na vattabbāti evaṃ ekantato pariyattiyeva pamāṇaṃ.

Is it not so? During the time of Kassapa, the Perfectly Enlightened One, a disagreeable bhikkhu named Kapila, intending to recite the Pātimokkha, took a fan, sat on the seat, and asked: 'Are there any herein who are practicing?' Then, out of fear of him, even those for whom the Pātimokkha was in force, instead of saying, 'We are practicing,' said, 'We are not practicing.' He then put down the fan, rose from his seat, and left. At that time, did the Dispensation of the Perfectly Enlightened One decline? Although it did decline, learning is the ultimate measure. For just as it should not be said that water will not stand in a great reservoir with a firm embankment, nor that lotuses and other flowers will not bloom when water is present; even so, as long as the Tipiṭaka, the word of the Buddha—which is like the firm embankment of a great reservoir—exists, it should not be said that there are no sons of good family who fulfill the practice, who are like the water in the great reservoir. And as long as they exist, it should not be said that there are no noble individuals such as stream-enterers and so on, who are like the lotuses and other flowers in the great reservoir. Thus, it is certain that learning itself is the measure.

Pathavīdhātūti dve satasahassāni cattāri ca nahutāni bahalā mahāpathavī. Āpodhātūti pathavito paṭṭhāya yāva subhakiṇhabrahmalokā uggataṃ kappavināsakaṃ udakaṃ. Tejodhātūti pathavito paṭṭhāya yāva ābhassarabrahmalokā uggato kappavināsako aggi. Vāyodhātūti pathavito paṭṭhāya yāva vehapphalabrahmalokā uggato kappavināsako vāyu. Etesu hi ekadhammopi satthu sāsanaṃ antaradhāpetuṃ na sakkoti, tasmā evamāha. Idheva te uppajjantīti lohato lohakhādakaṃ malaṃ viya imasmiṃ mayhaṃyeva sāsane te uppajjanti. Moghapurisāti tucchapurisā.

The earth element is the great earth, two hundred and forty thousand yojanas thick. The water element is the eon-destroying water that rises from the earth up to the Subhakiṇha Brahmā world. The fire element is the eon-destroying fire that rises from the earth up to the Ābhassara Brahmā world. The air element is the eon-destroying wind that rises from the earth up to the Vehapphala Brahmā world. For not even one of these elements is able to make the Teacher’s Dispensation disappear; therefore, he said thus. 'Here they arise' means: just as rust that eats iron arises from the iron itself, so they arise right within this very Dispensation of mine. 'Worthless individuals' means empty individuals.

Ādikeneva opilavatīti ettha ādikenāti ādānena gahaṇena. Opilavatīti nimujjati. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yathā udakacarā nāvā bhaṇḍaṃ gaṇhantī nimujjati, evaṃ pariyattiādīnaṃ pūraṇena saddhammassa antaradhānaṃ na hoti. Pariyattiyā hi hāyamānāya paṭipatti hāyati, paṭipattiyā hāyamānāya adhigamo hāyati. Pariyattiyā pūrayamānāya pariyattidharā puggalā paṭipattiṃ pūrenti, paṭipattipūrakā adhigamaṃ pūrenti. Iti navacando [M 2.0189] viya pariyattiyādīsu vaḍḍhamānāsu mayhaṃ sāsanaṃ vaḍḍhati yevāti dasseti.

Herein, in the phrase `Ādikeneva opilavati`, `ādikena` means by taking, by grasping. `Opilavati` means it sinks. This is what is said: Just as a water-faring boat sinks while taking on cargo, it is not so that the True Dhamma disappears through the fulfillment of learning and so on. For when learning declines, practice declines; when practice declines, attainment declines. When learning is fulfilled, persons who uphold learning fulfill the practice; those who fulfill the practice fulfill attainment. Thus, it is shown that like the waxing moon, as learning and so on grow, my Dispensation indeed grows.

Idāni yehi dhammehi saddhammassa antaradhānañceva ṭhiti ca hoti, te dassento pañca khotiādimāha. Tattha okkamanīyāti avakkamanīyā, heṭṭhāgamanīyāti attho. Satthari agāravātiādīsu agāravāti gāravarahitā. Appatissāti appatissayā anīcavuttikā. Tattha yo cetiyaṅgaṇaṃ ārohanto chattaṃ dhāreti, upāhanaṃ dhāreti, aññato oloketvā kathaṃ kathento gacchati, ayaṃ satthari agāravo nāma.

Now, to show the principles by which the True Dhamma both disappears and endures, he said, 'Five,' and so on. Therein, `okkamanīyā` means `avakkamanīyā`, conducive to decline; the meaning is leading downwards. In 'disrespect towards the Teacher' and so on, `agāravā` means devoid of respect. `Appatissā` means without deference, not having humble conduct. Therein, one who, while ascending to the shrine grounds, holds an umbrella, wears sandals, or walks along looking elsewhere and talking—this person is called disrespectful towards the Teacher.

Yo dhammassavanassa kāle saṅghuṭṭhe daharasāmaṇerehi parivārito nisīdati, aññāni vā navakammādīni karoti, dhammassavanagge nisinno niddāyati, vikkhitto vā aññaṃ kathento nisīdati, ayaṃ dhamme agāravo nāma.

One who, at the time for hearing the Dhamma, when it has been announced, sits surrounded by young novices, or engages in other new works and so on, or, while sitting in the assembly for hearing the Dhamma, is drowsy, or sits distracted talking about other things—this person is called disrespectful towards the Dhamma.

Yo [V 2.0180] therupaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā, avanditvā nisīdati, hatthapallatthikaṃ dussapallatthikaṃ karoti, aññaṃ vā pana hatthapādakukkuccaṃ [P 2.0205] karoti, vuḍḍhānaṃ santike anajjhiṭṭho katheti, ayaṃ saṅghe agāravo nāma.

One who, having gone to attend upon the elders, sits down without paying homage, clasps the knees with the hands or with a cloth, engages in restless movements of the hands or feet, or speaks uninvited in the presence of the senior monks—this person is called disrespectful towards the Saṅgha.

Tisso pana sikkhā apūrentova sikkhāya agāravo nāma hoti. Aṭṭha samāpattiyo anibbattento tāsaṃ vā pana nibbattanatthāya payogaṃ akaronto samādhismiṃ agāravo nāma. Sukkapakkho vuttavipallāseneva veditabboti. Terasamaṃ.

Furthermore, one who does not fulfill the three trainings is called disrespectful towards the training. One who does not bring into being the eight attainments, or else does not make an effort to bring them into being, is called disrespectful towards concentration. The wholesome side should be understood as simply the opposite of what has been stated. The thirteenth sutta is concluded.

Kassapasaṃyuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Kassapa Saṃyutta is concluded.

6. Lābhasakkārasaṃyuttaṃ

6. The Connected Discourses on Gains and Homage

1. Paṭhamavaggo

1. The First Chapter

1. Dāruṇasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Dāruṇa Sutta

157. Lābhasakkārasaṃyuttassa [V 2.0181][P 2.0206][M 2.0190] paṭhame dāruṇoti thaddho. Lābhasakkārasilokoti ettha lābho nāma catupaccayalābho. Sakkāroti tesaṃyeva sukatānaṃ susaṅkhatānaṃ lābho. Silokoti vaṇṇaghoso. Kaṭukoti tikhiṇo. Pharusoti kharo. Antarāyikoti antarāyakaro. Paṭhamaṃ.

157. In the first sutta of the Connected Discourses on Gains and Homage, 'dāruṇa' means stiff. Here, in 'lābhasakkārasiloka': 'lābha' means the gain of the four requisites. 'Sakkāra' means the gain of those very same well-made, well-prepared things. 'Siloka' means the proclamation of praise. 'Kaṭuka' means sharp. 'Pharusa' means coarse. 'Antarāyika' means causing an obstacle. The first sutta is concluded.

2. Baḷisasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Baḷisa Sutta

158. Dutiye bāḷisikoti baḷisaṃ gahetvā caramāno macchaghātako. Āmisagatanti āmisamakkhitaṃ. Āmisacakkhūti āmise cakkhu dassanaṃ assāti āmisacakkhu. Gilabaḷisoti gilitabaḷiso. Anayaṃ āpannoti dukkhaṃ patto. Byasanaṃ āpannoti vināsaṃ patto. Yathākāmakaraṇīyoti yathākāmena yathāruciyā yatheva naṃ bāḷisiko icchati, tathevassa kattabboti attho. Yathākāmakaraṇīyo pāpimatoti yathā kilesamārassa kāmo, evaṃ kattabbo, nirayaṃ vā tiracchānayoniṃ vā pettivisayaṃ vā pāpetabbo. Dutiyaṃ.

158. In the second sutta, 'a fisherman' (bāḷisika) means a fish-killer who goes about carrying a hook. 'Attached to bait' (āmisagata) means smeared with bait. 'Having an eye for bait' (āmisacakkhu) means: for it, there is sight for the bait, hence 'one with an eye for the bait'. 'Having swallowed the hook' (gilabaḷiso) means the hook has been swallowed. 'Having met with misfortune' (anayaṃ āpanno) means having encountered suffering. 'Having met with disaster' (byasanaṃ āpanno) means having encountered destruction. 'To be dealt with as he wishes' (yathākāmakaraṇīyo) means: to be dealt with according to his will, according to his pleasure; just as the fisherman desires, so it is to be done to it; this is the meaning. 'To be dealt with as the Evil One wishes' (yathākāmakaraṇīyo pāpimato) means: to be dealt with according to the will of the defilement-Māra; to be sent to hell, the animal realm, or the realm of ghosts. The second.

3-4. Kummasuttādivaṇṇanā

3-4. Commentary on the Kummāsutta and Others

159-160. Tatiye mahākummakulanti mahantaṃ aṭṭhikacchapakulaṃ. Agamāsīti “ettha addhā kiñci khāditabbaṃ atthi, taṃ maccharāyanto maṃ esa nivāretī”ti saññāya agamāsi. Papatāyāti [P 2.0207] papatā vuccati dīgharajjukabaddho ayakantakosake daṇḍakaṃ pavesetvā gahito [V 2.0182] kaṇṇikasallasaṇṭhāno, ayakaṇṭako, yasmiṃ vegena patitvā kaṭāhe laggamatte daṇḍako nikkhamati, rajjuko ekābaddho gacchateva. So kummoti so [M 2.0191] viddhakummo. Yena so kummoti udakasaddaṃ sutvā sāsaṅkaṭṭhānaṃ bhavissatīti nivattitvā yena so atthakāmo kummo. Na dāni tvaṃ amhākanti idāni tvaṃ amittahatthaṃ gato, na amhākaṃ santakoti attho. Evaṃ sallapantānaṃyeva ca nesaṃ nāvāya ṭhito luddo rajjukaṃ ākaḍḍhitvā kummaṃ gahetvā yathākāmaṃ akāsi. Sesamettha ito anantarasutte ca uttānameva. Tatiyacatutthāni.

159-160. In the third sutta, 'the great turtle family' (mahākummakulaṃ) means a large family of bony-shelled turtles. 'He went' (agamāsi) means he went with the perception, 'Surely there is something edible here, and this one, being stingy, is preventing me.' By 'papatā' is meant an iron barb, shaped like a barbed arrow, tied to a long rope, and held by inserting a stick into its sheath; when it falls swiftly and sticks in the shell, the stick comes out, and the rope, being tied as one, goes on. By 'that turtle' (so kummo) is meant that pierced turtle. By 'where that turtle was' (yena so kummo) is meant that, hearing the sound of water, he turned back, thinking 'this will be a dangerous place,' to where that turtle, desiring his welfare, was. 'Now you are not ours' (na dāni tvaṃ amhākaṃ) means: 'Now you have fallen into the enemy’s hands; you are not our companion'; this is the meaning. While they were conversing thus, the hunter standing in the boat pulled the rope, caught the turtle, and did as he pleased. The rest is clear here and in the immediately following sutta. The third and fourth suttas.

5. Mīḷhakasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Mīḷhakasutta.

161. Pañcame mīḷhakāti gūthapāṇakā. Gūthādīti gūthabhakkhā. Gūthapūrāti anto gūthena bharitā. Puṇṇā gūthassāti idaṃ purimasseva atthadīpanaṃ. Atimaññeyyāti pacchimapāde bhūmiyaṃ ṭhapetvā purimapāde gūthassa upari āropetvā ṭhitā “ahamhi gūthādī”ti bhaṇantī atimaññeyya. Piṇḍapāto cassa pūroti aparopissa pattapūro paṇītapiṇḍapāto bhaveyya. Pañcamaṃ.

161. In the fifth sutta, 'dung-beetles' (mīḷhakā) means dung-creatures. 'Dung-eaters' (gūthādī) means those who eat dung. 'Full of dung' (gūthapūrā) means filled with dung inside. The phrase 'full of dung' (puṇṇā gūthassa) is an explanation of the meaning of the preceding term. 'Would despise' (atimaññeyya) means that placing their hind feet on the ground and raising their front feet onto the dung, they stand proclaiming, 'I am a dung-eater,' and would despise others. 'And his alms-food would be full' (piṇḍapāto cassa pūro) means: for the other one too, his bowl would be full of excellent alms-food. The fifth.

6. Asanisuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Asanisutta.

162. Chaṭṭhe kaṃ, bhikkhave, asanivicakkanti, bhikkhave, kaṃ puggalaṃ matthake patitvā maddamānaṃ sukkāsanicakkaṃ āgacchatu[P 2.0208]. Appattamānasanti anadhigatārahattaṃ. Iti bhagavā na sattānaṃ dukkhakāmatāya, ādīnavaṃ pana dassetuṃ evamāha. Asanicakkañhi matthake patitaṃ ekameva attabhāvaṃ nāseti, lābhasakkārasilokena pariyādiṇṇacitto nirayādīsu anantadukkhaṃ anubhoti. Chaṭṭhaṃ.

162. In the sixth sutta, 'O bhikkhus, upon whom the thunderbolt-wheel' (kaṃ, bhikkhave, asanivicakkaṃ) means: O bhikkhus, upon which person should the dry thunderbolt-wheel come, falling upon the head and crushing it? 'One whose mind has not been attained' (appattamānasaṃ) means one who has not attained Arahantship. The Blessed One did not speak thus out of a desire for the suffering of beings; rather, he spoke thus to show the danger. For a thunderbolt-wheel that has fallen on the head destroys only one existence, but one whose mind is overcome by gain, honor, and praise experiences endless suffering in hell and other such states. The sixth.

7. Diddhasuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Diddhasutta.

163. Sattame diddhagatenāti gatadiddhena. Visallenāti visamakkhitena. Sallenāti sattiyā. Sattamaṃ.

163. In the seventh sutta, 'by a poisoned [arrow]' (diddhagatena) means by that which has been poisoned. 'By a poisoned arrow' (visallena) means by that which is smeared with poison. 'By an arrow' (sallena) means by a spear. The seventh.

8. Siṅgālasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Siṅgālasutta.

164. Aṭṭhame [V 2.0183][M 2.0192] siṅgāloti jarasiṅgālo. Yathā hi suvaṇṇavaṇṇopi kāyo pūtikāyo tveva, taṃkhaṇaṃ gaḷitampi ca muttaṃ pūtimuttantveva vuccati, evaṃ tadahujātopi siṅgālo jarasiṅgālotveva vuccati. Ukkaṇṭakena nāmāti evaṃnāmakena rogena. So kira sītakāle uppajjati. Tasmiṃ uppanne sakalasarīrato lomāni patanti, sakalasarīraṃ nillomaṃ hutvā, samantato phuṭati, vātabbhāhatā vaṇā rujjanti. Yathā ummattakasunakhena daṭṭho puriso anavaṭṭhitova bhamati, evaṃ tasmiṃ uppanne bhamitabbo hoti, asukaṭṭhāne sotthi bhavissatīti na paññāyati. Aṭṭhamaṃ.

164. In the eighth sutta, 'a jackal' (siṅgālo) means an old jackal. For just as a body, even if of golden color, is still called a 'putrid body'; and just as urine, even if just discharged at that moment, is still called 'putrid urine'; so too a jackal, even if born that very day, is still called an 'old jackal'. 'By the name Ukkaṇṭaka' means by a disease of that name. It is said that it arises in the cold season. When it arises, hairs fall from the entire body; the entire body, having become hairless, breaks out all over, and the sores, when struck by the wind, are painful. Just as a man bitten by a mad dog wanders about unstably, so too, when this disease arises, one must wander; it is not apparent that 'in such-and-such a place there will be safety'. The eighth.

9. Verambhasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Verambhasutta.

165. Navame verambhavātāti evaṃnāmakā mahāvātā. Kīdise pana ṭhāne te vātā vāyantīti? Yattha ṭhitassa cattāro [P 2.0209] dīpā uppalinipattamattā hutvā paññāyanti. Yo pakkhī gacchatīti navavuṭṭhe deve viravanto vātasakuṇo tattha gacchati, taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Arakkhiteneva kāyenātiādīsu hatthapāde kīḷāpento khandhaṭṭhiṃ vā nāmento kāyaṃ na rakkhati nāma, nānāvidhaṃ duṭṭhullakathaṃ kathento vācaṃ na rakkhati nāma, kāmavitakkādayo vitakkento cittaṃ na rakkhati nāma. Anupaṭṭhitāya satiyāti kāyagatāsatiṃ anupaṭṭhapetvā. Navamaṃ.

165. In the ninth sutta, 'Verambha winds' (verambhavātā) are great winds of that name. And in what kind of place do those winds blow? A place where, for one standing there, the four great continents appear to be the size of blue water-lily petals. The phrase 'what bird goes' (yo pakkhī gacchati): when the sky has newly rained and is thundering, a wind-bird goes there; this was said in reference to that. In the phrases beginning with 'with an unprotected body' (arakkhiteneva kāyena): one who plays with their hands and feet, or who bends their shoulder-blades, is called one who 'does not protect the body'; one who speaks various kinds of coarse talk is called one who 'does not protect speech'; one who thinks thoughts of sensual desire and so on is called one who 'does not protect the mind'. 'With mindfulness unestablished' (anupaṭṭhitāya satiyā) means not having established mindfulness directed to the body. The ninth.

10. Sagāthakasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Sagāthaka Sutta.

166. Dasame asakkārena cūbhayanti asakkārena ca ubhayena. Samādhīti arahattaphalasamādhi. So hi tena na vikampati. Appamāṇavihārinoti appamāṇena phalasamādhinā viharantassa. Sātatikanti satatakāriṃ. Sukhumaṃdiṭṭhivipassakanti arahattamaggadiṭṭhiyā sukhumadiṭṭhiphalasamāpattiatthāya vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā āgatattā vipassakaṃ. Upādānakkhayārāmanti upādānakkhayasaṅkhāte nibbāne rataṃ. Āhu sappuriso itīti sappurisoti kathentīti. Dasamaṃ.

166. In the tenth sutta, 'by lack of honor and by both' (asakkārena cūbhayaṃ) means: by lack of honor and by both [i.e., sometimes being honored and sometimes not]. 'Concentration' (samādhi) means the concentration of the fruition of Arahantship. Indeed, it is not shaken by that. 'Of one dwelling in the immeasurable' (appamāṇavihārino) means: of one dwelling with the immeasurable fruition-concentration. 'Constant' (sātatikaṃ) means one who acts constantly. 'One who sees the subtle with insight' (sukhumadiṭṭhivipassakaṃ) means: one who practices insight, because, with the vision of the Arahant path, one has established insight for the sake of attaining the fruition-attainment of subtle vision. 'Delighting in the destruction of clinging' (upādānakkhayārāmaṃ) means: delighting in Nibbāna, which is called the destruction of clinging. 'They call him a good person' (āhu sappuriso iti) means: they say, 'a good person.' The tenth.

Paṭhamo vaggo.

The First Chapter.

2. Dutiyavaggo

2. The Second Chapter.

1-2. Suvaṇṇapātisuttādivaṇṇanā

1–2. Commentary on the Suvaṇṇapātisutta and Others.

167-168. Dutiyavaggassa [V 2.0184][M 2.0193] paṭhame sampajānamusā bhāsantanti appamattakenapi kāraṇena sampajānameva musā bhāsantaṃ. “Sīlaṃ pūressāmī”ti saṃvihitabhikkhuṃ sinerumattopi paccayarāsi cāletuṃ na sakkoti. Yadā pana sīlaṃ pahāya sakkāranissito hoti, tadā kuṇḍakamuṭṭhihetupi musā bhāsati, aññaṃ vā akiccaṃ karoti. Dutiyaṃ uttānamevāti. Paṭhamadutiyāni.

167–168. In the first sutta of the second chapter, `sampajānamusā bhāsantaṃ` means intentionally speaking falsely even for a slight reason. A monk who is well-restrained, thinking, “I will fulfill my virtue,” cannot be moved even by a heap of requisites as large as Mount Sineru. But when, having abandoned virtue, he becomes dependent on honor, then he speaks falsely even for the sake of a handful of broken rice, or does some other improper deed. The second sutta is self-explanatory. The first and second suttas.

3-10. Suvaṇṇanikkhasuttādivaṇṇanā

3–10. Commentary on the Suvaṇṇanikkha Sutta and others.

169. Tatiyādīsu [P 2.0210] suvaṇṇanikkhassāti ekassa kañcananikkhassa. Siṅgīnikkhassāti siṅgīsuvaṇṇanikkhassa. Pathaviyāti cakkavāḷabbhantarāya mahāpathaviyā. Āmisakiñcikkhahetūti kassacideva āmisassa hetu antamaso kuṇḍakamuṭṭhinopi. Jīvitahetūti aṭaviyaṃ corehi gahetvā jīvite voropiyamāne tassapi hetu. Janapadakalyāṇiyāti janapade uttamitthiyā. Tatiyādīni.

169. In the third sutta and others, `suvaṇṇanikkhassa` means of a single nikkha of pure gold. `Siṅgīnikkhassa` means of a nikkha of Siṅgī gold. `Pathaviyā` means of the great earth within the Cakkavāḷa, which is filled with gold and silver. `Āmisakiñcikkhahetu` means for the sake of any material gain whatsoever, even as little as a handful of broken rice. `Jīvitahetu` means for the sake of one's life, even when it is about to be taken by robbers in the forest. `Janapadakalyāṇiyā` means of the most excellent woman in the country. The third and following suttas.

Dutiyo vaggo.

The Second Chapter.

3. Tatiyavaggo

3. The Third Chapter.

1-2. Mātugāmasuttādivaṇṇanā

1–2. Commentary on the Mātugāma Sutta and others.

170-171. Tatiyavaggassa paṭhame na tassa, bhikkhave, mātugāmoti na tassa raho ekakassa nisinnassa tena dhammena atthikopi mātugāmo cittaṃ pariyādātuṃ sakkoti, yassa lābhasakkārasiloko [V 2.0185] cittaṃ pariyādātuṃ sakkotīti, attho. Dutiyaṃ uttānamevāti. Paṭhamadutiyāni.

170–171. In the first sutta of the third chapter, the meaning of `na tassa, bhikkhave, mātugāmo` is as follows: A woman, even one desirous of that base practice, cannot captivate the mind of that monk sitting alone in seclusion, whose mind gain, honor, and fame can captivate. The second sutta is self-explanatory. The first and second suttas.

3-6. Ekaputtakasuttādivaṇṇanā

3–6. Commentary on the Ekaputtaka Sutta and others.

172-175. Tatiye saddhāti sotāpannā. Sesamettha uttānameva. Tathā catutthe pañcame chaṭṭhe ca. Tatiyādīni.

172–175. In the third sutta, `saddhā` refers to a female lay disciple who is a stream-enterer. The rest here is self-evident. Likewise in the fourth, fifth, and sixth. The third and following suttas.

7. Tatiyasamaṇabrāhmaṇasuttavaṇṇanā

7. 7. Commentary on the Third Samaṇabrāhmaṇa Sutta.

176. Sattame [M 2.0194] samudayantiādīsu saha pubbakammena attabhāvo kolaputtiyaṃ vaṇṇapokkharatā kalyāṇavākkaraṇatā dhutaguṇāvīkaraṇaṃ cīvaradhāraṇaṃ parivārasampattīti evamādi lābhasakkārassa samudayo nāma, taṃ samudayasaccavasena nappajānāti, nirodho ca paṭipadā ca nirodhasaccamaggasaccavaseneva veditabbā. Sattamaṃ.

176. In the seventh sutta, regarding 'arising' and so forth: individual existence together with past kamma, being of a good family, beauty of complexion, pleasantness of speech, the manifestation of ascetic qualities, the wearing of robes, and the attainment of an entourage—this and so forth is called the cause of the arising of gain and honor. One does not understand this in terms of the truth of the origin. And cessation and the path should be understood solely in terms of the truth of cessation and the truth of the path. The seventh sutta.

8. Chavisuttavaṇṇanā

8. 8. Commentary on the Chavi Sutta.

177. Aṭṭhame [P 2.0211] yasmā lābhasakkārasiloko narakādīsu, nibbattento sakalampi imaṃ attabhāvaṃ nāseti, idhāpi maraṇampi maraṇamattampi dukkhaṃ āvahati, tasmā chaviṃ chindatītiādi vuttaṃ. Aṭṭhamaṃ.

177. In the eighth sutta, because gain, honor, and fame, by causing rebirth in hell and so forth, destroy this entire individual existence, and because even here it brings death and suffering equivalent to death, therefore, it is said, 'cuts the skin,' and so forth. The eighth sutta.

9. Rajjusuttavaṇṇanā

9. 9. Commentary on the Rajju Sutta.

178. Navame vāḷarajjuyāti suttādimayā rajju mudukā hoti vāḷarajju kharā pharusā, tasmā ayameva gahitā. Navamaṃ.

178. In the ninth sutta, regarding `vāḷarajjuyā`: a rope made of thread and so forth is soft, but a rope of horsehair is hard and coarse; therefore, this very one is taken as a simile. The ninth sutta.

10. Bhikkhusuttavaṇṇanā

10. 10. Commentary on the Bhikkhu Sutta.

179. Dasame diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārāti phalasamāpattisukhavihārā. Tesāhamassāti tesaṃ ahaṃ assa[V 2.0186]. Khīṇāsavo hi lābhī puññasampanno yāgukhajjakādīni gahetvā āgatāgatānaṃ anumodanaṃ karonto dhammaṃ desento pañhaṃ vissajjento phalasamāpattiṃ appetvā nisīdituṃ okāsaṃ na labhati, taṃ sandhāya vuttanti. Dasamaṃ.

179. In the tenth sutta, `diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārā` means the happy dwelling of the attainment of fruition. `Tesāhamassāti` is to be parsed as `tesaṃ ahaṃ assa`. I declare that for him (the Arahant), gain, honor, and fame are an obstacle to these (happy dwellings). For an Arahant whose taints are destroyed, a recipient of offerings and endowed with merit, does not get the opportunity to enter into the attainment of fruition and sit down, as he is occupied giving blessings to those who come again and again with rice-gruel, solid food, and so on, teaching the Dhamma, and answering questions. This was said in reference to that. The tenth sutta.

Tatiyo vaggo.

The Third Chapter is finished.

4. Catutthavaggo

4. 4. The Fourth Chapter.

1-4. Bhindisuttādivaṇṇanā

1–4. Commentary on the Bhindi Sutta and others.

180-183. Catutthavaggassa paṭhamaṃ uttānameva. Dutiyādīsu kusalamūlanti alobhāditividhakusaladhammo. Sukko dhammoti tasseva pariyāyadesanā[M 2.0195]. Ayaṃ panettha saṅkhepattho – yassa kusalamūlādisaṅkhātassa anavajjadhammassa asamucchinnattā devadatto sagge vā nibbatteyya, maggaphalāni vā adhigaccheyya, svāssa samucchedamagamā sabbaso samucchinno vinaṭṭho. Paṭhamādīni.

180–183. The first sutta of the fourth chapter is self-evident. In the second and following suttas, `kusalamūlaṃ` refers to the threefold wholesome state of non-greed and so forth. `Sukko dhammo` is a teaching that is a synonym for that same thing. Here, this is the concise meaning: That faultless Dhamma, designated as 'wholesome roots' and so forth, by the non-severance of which Devadatta could have been reborn in heaven or could have attained the paths and fruits, has been utterly cut off for him; it is completely severed and destroyed. The first and following suttas.

5. Acirapakkantasuttavaṇṇanā

5. 5. Commentary on the Acirapakkanta Sutta.

184. Pañcame parābhavāyāti avaḍḍhiyā vināsāya. Assatarīti vaḷavāya kucchismiṃ gadrabhassa jātā. Attavadhāya gabbhaṃ gaṇhātīti taṃ assena saddhiṃ sampayojenti, sā [P 2.0212] gabbhaṃ gaṇhitvā kāle sampatte vijāyituṃ na sakkoti, pādehi bhūmiyaṃ paharantī tiṭṭhati, athassā cattāro pāde catūsu khāṇukesu bandhitvā kucchiṃ phāletvā potaṃ nīharanti, sā tattheva marati. Tenetaṃ vuttaṃ. Pañcamaṃ.

184. In the fifth sutta, `parābhavāya` means for non-growth, for destruction. An `assatarī` is a mule, born from a male donkey in the womb of a mare. `Attavadhāya gabbhaṃ gaṇhāti` means that when they mate a female mule with a horse, she conceives, and when the time comes, she is unable to give birth. She stands striking the ground with her feet. Then, having tied her four legs to four posts, they cut open her womb and pull out the young one. She dies right there. For that reason, this was said. The fifth sutta.

6. Pañcarathasatasuttavaṇṇanā

6. 6. Commentary on the Pañcarathasata Sutta.

185. Chaṭṭhe bhattābhihāroti abhiharitabbaṃ bhattaṃ. Tassa pana pamāṇaṃ dassetuṃ pañca ca thālipākasatānīti [V 2.0187] vuttaṃ. Tattha eko thālipāko dasannaṃ purisānaṃ bhattaṃ gaṇhāti. Nāsāya pittaṃ bhindeyyunti acchapittaṃ vā macchapittaṃ vāssa nāsapuṭe pakkhipeyyaṃ. Chaṭṭhaṃ.

185. In the sixth sutta, `bhattābhihāro` means food that should be brought forward. To show its measure, `pañca ca thālipākasatāni` was said. Therein, one pot of cooked food serves for ten men. `Nāsāya pittaṃ bhindeyyuṃ` means they would place bear bile or fish bile in his nostrils. The sixth sutta.

7-13. Mātusuttādivaṇṇanā

7–13. Commentary on the Mātu Sutta and others.

186-187. Sattame mātupi hetūti “sace musā bhaṇasi, mātaraṃ te vissajjessāma. No ce bhaṇasi, na vissajjessāmā”ti evaṃ corehi aṭaviyaṃ pucchamāno tassā corahatthagatāya mātuyāpi hetu sampajānamusā na bhāseyyāti attho. Ito paresupi eseva nayoti. Sattamādīni.

186–187. In the seventh sutta, `mātupi hetu` means this: when being questioned thus by robbers in the forest, 'If you speak falsely, we will release your mother. If you do not speak falsely, we will not release her,' one should not knowingly speak a lie even for the sake of one's mother who has fallen into the hands of robbers. This is the meaning. This same method applies to the subsequent ones as well. The seventh and following suttas are finished.

Lābhasakkārasaṃyuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Lābhasakkārasaṃyutta is concluded.

7. Rāhulasaṃyuttaṃ

7. The Rāhulasaṃyutta.

1. Paṭhamavaggo

1. The First Chapter.

1-8. Cakkhusuttādivaṇṇanā

1–8. Commentary on the Cakkhu Sutta and others.

188-195. Rāhulasaṃyuttassa [V 2.0188][P 2.0213][M 2.0196] paṭhame ekoti catūsu iriyāpathesu ekavihārī. Vūpakaṭṭhoti vivekaṭṭho nissaddo. Appamattoti satiyā avippavasanto. Ātāpīti vīriyasampanno. Pahitatto vihareyyanti visesādhigamatthāya pesitatto hutvā vihareyyaṃ. Aniccanti hutvā abhāvākārena aniccaṃ. Atha vā uppādavayavantatāya tāvakālikatāya vipariṇāmakoṭiyā niccapaṭikkhepatoti imehipi kāraṇehi aniccaṃ. Dukkhanti catūhi kāraṇehi dukkhaṃ dukkhamanaṭṭhena dukkhavatthukaṭṭhena satatasampīḷanaṭṭhena sukhapaṭikkhepenāti. Kallanti yuttaṃ. Etaṃ mamāti taṇhāgāho. Esohamasmīti mānagāho. Eso me attāti diṭṭhigāho. Taṇhāgāho cettha aṭṭhasatataṇhāvicaritavasena, mānagāho navavidhamānavasena, diṭṭhigāho dvāsaṭṭhidiṭṭhivasena veditabbo. Nibbindaṃ virajjatīti ettha virāgavasena cattāro maggā kathitā, virāgā vimuccatīti ettha vimuttivasena cattāri sāmaññaphalāni.

In the first [sutta] of the Rāhula Saṃyutta, 'one' (eko) means dwelling alone in the four postures. 'Secluded' (vūpakaṭṭho) means solitary, silent. 'Heedful' (appamatto) means not being separated from mindfulness. 'Ardent' (ātāpī) means endowed with energy. 'I should dwell with a resolute mind' (pahitatto vihareyyaṃ) means I should dwell having sent forth my mind for the sake of attaining distinction. 'Impermanent' (aniccaṃ) is so called because, having come to be, its nature is not to be. Alternatively, it is impermanent for these reasons as well: because it possesses arising and passing away, because it is temporary, because it is subject to change, and because it is the opposite of permanent. 'Suffering' (dukkhaṃ) is so called for four reasons: because of its nature of being hard to bear, because it is a basis for suffering, because of its nature of constant oppression, and because it is the opposite of happiness. 'It is proper' (kallaṃ) means it is suitable. 'This is mine' (etaṃ mama) is grasping by way of craving. 'This I am' (esohamasmi) is grasping by way of conceit. 'This is my self' (eso me attā) is grasping by way of wrong view. Herein, grasping by craving should be understood by way of the one hundred and eight applications of craving; grasping by conceit should be understood by way of the nine kinds of conceit; and grasping by wrong view should be understood by way of the sixty-two kinds of wrong views. In the phrase 'becoming disenchanted, one becomes dispassionate' (nibbindaṃ virajjati), the four paths are taught by way of dispassion. In the phrase 'through dispassion, one is liberated' (virāgā vimuccati), the four fruits of recluseship are taught by way of liberation.

Ettha ca pañcasu dvāresu pasādāva gahitā, manoti iminā tebhūmakaṃ sammasanacāracittaṃ. Dutiye [P 2.0214] pañcasu dvāresu ārammaṇameva. Tatiye pañcasu dvāresu pasādavatthukacittameva, manoviññāṇena tebhūmakaṃ sammasanacāracittaṃ gahitaṃ. Evaṃ sabbattha nayo netabbo. Chaṭṭhe tebhūmakadhammā. Aṭṭhame pana taṇhāti tasmiṃ tasmiṃ dvāre javanappattāva labbhati. Paṭhamādīni.

And here, at the five doors, only the sense faculties are taken. By this term 'mind' (mano), the mind which has the function of investigating the phenomena of the three planes is taken. In the second [sutta], at the five doors, only the sense-objects are taken. In the third [sutta], at the five doors, only the consciousness based on the sense faculty is taken; by mind-consciousness, the mind which has the function of investigating the phenomena of the three planes is taken. In this way, the method should be applied everywhere. In the sixth [sutta], the phenomena of the three planes are taken. In the eighth [sutta], however, by the term 'craving' (taṇhā), only that which has reached impulsion at each respective door is obtained. The first [sutta] and so on [are finished].

9. Dhātusuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Discourse on Elements.

196. Navame [V 2.0189] viññāṇadhātuvasena nāmaṃ, sesāhi rūpanti nāmarūpaṃ kathitaṃ. Navamaṃ.

196. In the ninth [discourse], name is taught by way of the consciousness-element, and form by the remaining [elements]—thus name-and-form is taught. The ninth [discourse is finished].

10. Khandhasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Discourse on Aggregates.

197. Dasame [M 2.0197] rūpakkhandho kāmāvacaro, sesā cattāro sabbasaṅgāhikaparicchedena catubhūmakā. Idha pana tebhūmakāti gahetabbā. Dasamaṃ.

197. In the tenth [discourse], the form aggregate is of the sense-sphere; the remaining four, by way of a comprehensive classification, are of the four planes. Here, however, they are to be taken as being of the three planes. The tenth [discourse is finished].

Paṭhamo vaggo.

The First Chapter.

2. Dutiyavaggo

2. The Second Chapter.

1-10. Cakkhusuttādivaṇṇanā

1-10. Commentary on the Discourses beginning with the Cakkhu Sutta.

198-199. Dutiye dasa uttānatthāneva. Paṭhamādīni.

In the second [chapter], the ten [discourses] have an obvious meaning indeed. The first, etc.

11. Anusayasuttavaṇṇanā

11. Commentary on the Discourse on Underlying Tendencies.

200. Ekādasame imasmiñca saviññāṇake kāyeti attano saviññāṇakakāyaṃ dasseti, bahiddhā cāti parassa saviññāṇakaṃ vā aviññāṇakaṃ vā. Purimena vā attano ca parassa ca viññāṇameva [P 2.0215] dasseti, pacchimena bahiddhā anindriyabaddharūpaṃ. Ahaṅkāramamaṅkāramānānusayāti ahaṃkāradiṭṭhi ca mamaṃkārataṇhā ca mānānusayā ca. Na hontīti ete kilesā kathaṃ jānantassa etesu vatthūsu na hontīti pucchati. Sammappaññāya passatīti saha vipassanāya maggapaññāya suṭṭhu passati. Ekādasamaṃ.

200. In the eleventh [discourse], by 'in this conscious body' he indicates his own conscious body; by 'and externally', another's conscious or unconscious body. Alternatively, by the former he indicates only the consciousness of oneself and of another; by the latter, external form not bound to the sense faculties. 'The underlying tendencies of I-making, mine-making, and conceit' means the view of I-making, the craving of mine-making, and the underlying tendencies of conceit. As for 'they do not exist', he asks: 'For one knowing in what way do these defilements not exist in regard to these objects?' 'One sees with right wisdom' means one sees well with the wisdom of the path together with insight. The eleventh [discourse is finished].

12. Apagatasuttavaṇṇanā

12. Commentary on the Discourse on Being Departed.

201. Dvādasame [V 2.0190] ahaṅkāramamaṅkāramānāpagatanti ahaṃkārato ca mamaṃkārato ca mānato ca apagataṃ. Vidhā samatikkantanti mānakoṭṭhāse suṭṭhu atikkantaṃ. Santaṃ suvimuttanti kilesavūpasamena santaṃ, kileseheva suṭṭhu vimuttaṃ. Sesaṃ uttānamevāti. Dvādasamaṃ.

201. In the twelfth [discourse], 'departed from I-making, mine-making, and conceit' means departed from I-making, from mine-making, and from conceit. 'Transcended distinctions' means having well transcended the divisions of conceit. 'Peaceful, well-liberated' means peaceful through the calming of defilements, and well-liberated from the defilements themselves. The rest is obvious. The twelfth [discourse is finished].

Dutiyo vaggo.

The Second Chapter.

Dvīsupi [M 2.0198] asekkhabhūmi kathitā. Paṭhamo panettha āyācantassa desito, dutiyo anāyācantassa. Sakalepi pana rāhulasaṃyutte therassa vimuttiparipācanīyadhammāva kathitāti.

In both [chapters], the plane of the non-trainee is taught. Herein, the first was taught to one who requested it, the second to one who did not. Moreover, in the entire Rāhula Saṃyutta, only the dhammas that lead to the maturing of the Elder's liberation are taught.

Rāhulasaṃyuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Rāhula Saṃyutta is concluded.

8. Lakkhaṇasaṃyuttaṃ

8. The Lakkhaṇa Saṃyutta.

1. Paṭhamavaggo

1. The First Chapter.

1. Aṭṭhisuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Discourse on the Skeleton.

202. Lakkhaṇasaṃyutte [V 2.0191][P 2.0216][M 2.0199] yvāyaṃ āyasmā ca lakkhaṇoti lakkhaṇatthero vutto, esa jaṭilasahassabbhantare ehibhikkhūpasampadāya upasampanno ādittapariyāyāvasāne arahattaṃ patto eko mahāsāvakoti veditabbo. Yasmā panesa lakkhaṇasampannena sabbākāraparipūrena brahmasamena attabhāvena samannāgato, tasmā “lakkhaṇo”ti saṅkhaṃ gato. Mahāmoggallāno pana pabbajitadivasato sattame divase arahattaṃ patto dutiyo aggasāvako.

202. In the Lakkhaṇa Saṃyutta, regarding the one who is called 'the Venerable Lakkhaṇa', that is, the Elder Lakkhaṇa: he is to be understood as one of the great disciples who, among the thousand matted-hair ascetics, was ordained with the 'Come, bhikkhu' ordination and attained Arahantship at the conclusion of the Fire Sermon. And because he was endowed with a physical existence complete with the characteristics [of a great man], perfect in all aspects, and like that of a Brahmā, he came to be known as 'Lakkhaṇa'. Mahāmoggallāna, however, was the second chief disciple, who attained Arahantship on the seventh day from his ordination.

Sitaṃ pātvākāsīti mandahasitaṃ pātuakāsi, pakāsayi dassesīti vuttaṃ hoti. Kiṃ pana disvā thero sitaṃ pātvākāsīti? Upari pāḷiyaṃ āgataṃ aṭṭhikasaṅkhalikaṃ ekaṃ petaloke nibbattaṃ sattaṃ disvā. Tañca kho dibbena cakkhunā, na pasādacakkhunā. Pasādacakkhussa hi ete attabhāvā na āpāthaṃ āgacchanti. Evarūpaṃ pana attabhāvaṃ disvā kāruññe kattabbe kasmā sitaṃ pātvākāsīti? Attano ca buddhañāṇassa ca sampattiṃ samanussaraṇato. Tañhi disvā thero “adiṭṭhasaccena nāma puggalena paṭilabhitabbā evarūpā attabhāvā mutto ahaṃ, lābhā vata me, suladdhaṃ vata me”ti attano ca sampattiṃ anussaritvā – “aho buddhassa bhagavato ñāṇasampatti, ‘yo kammavipāko, bhikkhave, acinteyyo na cintetabbo’ti desesi, paccakkhaṃ vata katvā buddhā desenti, suppaṭividdhā buddhānaṃ dhammadhātū”ti evaṃ buddhañāṇasampattiñca anussaritvā sitaṃ pātvākāsīti.

'He made a smile appear' means he made a gentle smile appear; it is said he revealed it, he showed it. Having seen what did the elder make a smile appear? Having seen a certain being mentioned in the Pāli text above, a chain of bones, reborn in the realm of petas. And he saw this with the divine eye, not with the physical eye, for these forms of existence do not come into the range of the physical eye. But having seen such a form of existence, when compassion should have been shown, why did he make a smile appear? Because of recollecting his own attainment and the attainment of the Buddha's knowledge. For having seen that, the elder, recollecting his own attainment—'Such forms of existence are to be obtained by a person who has not seen the truths—I am freed! A gain for me, indeed! A great gain for me, indeed!'—and recollecting the attainment of the Buddha's knowledge—'Oh, the attainment of the knowledge of the Blessed One, the Buddha! He taught: “The result of kamma, bhikkhus, is inconceivable, not to be pondered.” Indeed, the Buddhas teach having realized it directly! Well-penetrated is the Dhamma-element of the Buddhas!'—made a smile appear.

Atha [P 2.0217] lakkhaṇatthero kasmā na addasa, kimassa dibbacakkhu natthīti? No natthi, mahāmoggallāno [V 2.0192] pana āvajjento addasa, itaro pana anāvajjanena na addasa. Yasmā pana khīṇāsavā nāma na akāraṇā sitaṃ karonti, tasmā taṃ lakkhaṇatthero pucchi ko nu kho, āvuso moggallāna, hetu, ko paccayo sitassa pātukammāyāti? Thero pana [M 2.0200] yasmā yehi ayaṃ upapatti sāmaṃ adiṭṭhā, te dussaddhāpayā honti, tasmā bhagavantaṃ sakkhiṃ katvā byākātukāmatāya akālo kho, āvusotiādimāha. Tato bhagavato santike puṭṭho idhāhaṃ, āvusotiādinā nayena byākāsi.

Now, why did the Elder Lakkhaṇa not see? Does he not have the divine eye? No, it is not that he does not have it. But Mahāmoggallāna saw by adverting, while the other did not see because of not adverting. And since those whose taints are destroyed do not smile without a reason, the Elder Lakkhaṇa asked him: 'What, friend Moggallāna, is the cause, what is the reason for the appearance of a smile?' The elder, however, because those by whom this rebirth has not been seen for themselves are hard to convince, wishing to explain with the Blessed One as a witness, said, 'It is not the time, friend,' and so on. Then, having been asked in the presence of the Blessed One, he explained in the manner beginning, 'Here, friend...'

Tattha aṭṭhikasaṅkhalikanti setaṃ nimmaṃsalohitaṃ aṭṭhisaṅghātaṃ. Gijjhāpi kākāpi kulalāpīti etepi yakkhagijjhā ceva yakkhakākā ca yakkhakulalā ca paccetabbā. Pākatikānaṃ pana gijjhādīnaṃ āpāthampi etaṃ rūpaṃ nāgacchati. Anupatitvā anupatitvāti anubandhitvā anubandhitvā. Vitudentīti asidhārūpamehi tikhiṇehi lohatuṇḍakehi vijjhitvā vijjhitvā ito cito ca caranti gacchanti. Sā sudaṃ aṭṭassaraṃ karotīti ettha sudanti nipāto, sā aṭṭhikasaṅkhalikā aṭṭassaraṃ āturassaraṃ karotīti attho. Akusalavipākānubhavanatthaṃ kira yojanappamāṇāpi tādisā attabhāvā nibbattanti, pasādussadā ca honti pakkagaṇḍasadisā. Tasmā sā aṭṭhikasaṅkhalikā balavavedanāturā tādisaṃ saddamakāsīti.

Therein, 'a chain of bones' means a white, fleshless, bloodless mass of bones. 'Vultures, crows, and hawks'—these too are to be understood as yakkha-vultures, yakkha-crows, and yakkha-hawks. For this form does not even come into the range of ordinary vultures and so on. 'Having followed again and again' means having pursued again and again. 'They peck' means they pierce again and again with sharp, sword-blade-like iron beaks, moving here and there. As for 'She, it seems, makes a cry of distress': here `sudaṃ` is a particle; the meaning is that the chain of bones makes a cry of distress, a cry of the afflicted. It is said that for the sake of experiencing the result of unwholesome kamma, such forms of existence, even a yojana in size, arise; and they are repulsive, like ripe boils. Therefore that chain of bones, afflicted by strong feeling, made such a sound.

Evañca pana vatvā puna āyasmā mahāmoggallāno “vaṭṭagāmisattā nāma evarūpā attabhāvā na muccantī”ti sattesu kāruññaṃ paṭicca uppannaṃ dhammasaṃvegaṃ dassento tassa mayhaṃ, āvuso, etadahosi acchariyaṃ vata bhotiādimāha. Tato bhagavā therassa ānubhāvaṃ pakāsento cakkhubhūtā vata, bhikkhave[P 2.0218], sāvakā viharantītiādimāha. Tattha cakkhu bhūtaṃ jātaṃ uppannaṃ etesanti cakkhubhūtā, bhūtacakkhukā uppannacakkhukā cakkhuṃ uppādetvā viharantīti attho. Dutiyapadepi eseva nayo. Yatra hi nāmāti ettha yatrāti kāraṇavacanaṃ. Tatrāyaṃ atthayojanā – yasmā nāma sāvakopi evarūpaṃ ñassati vā dakkhati vā sakkhiṃ vā karissati, tasmā avocumha – “cakkhubhūtā vata, bhikkhave, sāvakā viharanti, ñāṇabhūtā vata, bhikkhave, sāvakā viharantī”ti. Pubbeva me so, bhikkhave, satto diṭṭhoti bodhimaṇḍe sabbaññutaññāṇapaṭivedhena appamāṇesu cakkavāḷesu appamāṇe sattanikāye bhavagatiyoniṭhitinivāse ca paccakkhaṃ karontena mayā pubbeva so satto diṭṭhoti vadati.

Having said this, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, wishing to show the spiritual urgency that arose from compassion for beings—'Beings who wander in the round of existence are not freed from such a state of being'—again said, 'Friend, it occurred to me: It is truly wonderful,' and so on. Then the Blessed One, wishing to reveal the Elder’s power, said, 'Truly, monks, the disciples dwell having become the eye,' and so on. Here, 'having become the eye' means those for whom the eye has become, been born, and arisen; the meaning is that they dwell having produced the eye, possessing the eye that has become, the eye that has arisen. The same method applies to the second term. In 'where indeed,' the word 'where' expresses a reason. The connection of meaning here is this: Because even a disciple will know, see, or bear witness to such a state, therefore we said, 'Truly, monks, the disciples dwell having become the eye; truly, monks, the disciples dwell having become knowledge.' 'Monks, that being was seen by me even before,' he says, meaning: 'At the seat of enlightenment, through the penetration of the knowledge of omniscience, while I was directly perceiving in immeasurable world-systems the immeasurable hosts of beings, and their planes of existence, destinations, places of rebirth, stations, and abodes, that being was seen by me even before.'

Goghātakoti [V 2.0193][M 2.0201] gāvo vadhitvā aṭṭhito maṃsaṃ mocetvā vikkiṇitvā jīvikaṃ kappanakasatto. Tasseva kammassa vipākāvasesenāti tassa nānācetanāhi āyūhitassa aparāpariyakammassa. Tatra hi yāya cetanāya narake paṭisandhi janitā, tassā vipāke parikkhīṇe avasesakammaṃ vā kammanimittaṃ vā ārammaṇaṃ katvā puna petādīsu paṭisandhi nibbattati, tasmā sā paṭisandhi kammasabhāgatāya ārammaṇasabhāgatāya vā “tasseva kammassa vipākāvaseso”ti vuccati. Ayañca satto evaṃ uppanno. Tenāha – “tasseva kammassa vipākāvasesenā”ti. Tassa kira narakā cavanakāle nimmaṃsakatānaṃ gunnaṃ aṭṭhirāsiyeva nimittaṃ ahosi. So paṭicchannampi taṃ kammaṃ viññūnaṃ pākaṭaṃ viya karonto aṭṭhisaṅkhalikapeto jāto. Paṭhamaṃ.

A 'cattle-killer' is a being who makes a living by killing cows, removing the meat from the bone, and selling it. 'By the remainder of the result of that very kamma' refers to that subsequently effective kamma accumulated with various intentions. For therein, when the result of the intention by which rebirth in hell was generated is exhausted, taking the remaining kamma or the sign of kamma as object, rebirth occurs again among petas and so on. Therefore, that rebirth, due to sharing the nature of the kamma or sharing the nature of the object, is called 'the remainder of the result of that very kamma'. And this being arose in this way. Therefore, the Blessed One said: 'by the remainder of the result of that very kamma.' It is said that for him, at the time of passing away from hell, the sign was a heap of the fleshless bones of cows. As if making that kamma manifest to the wise, though it was concealed, he was born as a skeleton-peta. The first.

2. Pesisuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Pesi Sutta
