203. Maṃsapesivatthusmiṃ goghātakoti gomaṃsapesiyo katvā sukkhāpetvā vallūravikkayena anekāni vassāni jīvikaṃ kappesi, tenassa narakā cavanakāle maṃsapesiyeva nimittaṃ ahosi. So maṃsapesipeto jāto. Dutiyaṃ.

203. In the story of the lump of flesh, the cattle-killer was one who made a living for many years by making lumps of beef, drying them, and selling the dried meat. Therefore, for him, at the time of passing away from hell, a lump of flesh itself became the sign. He was born as a flesh-lump peta. The second.

3. Piṇḍasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Piṇḍa Sutta

204. Maṃsapiṇḍavatthusmiṃ [P 2.0219] sākuṇikoti sakuṇe gahetvā vikkiṇanakāle nippakkhacamme maṃsapiṇḍamatte katvā vikkiṇanto jīvikaṃ kappesi, tenassa narakā cavanakāle maṃsapiṇḍova nimittaṃ ahosi. So maṃsapiṇḍapeto jāto. Tatiyaṃ.

204. In the story of the lump of flesh: a 'fowler' is one who, when selling the birds he had caught, made his living by making them featherless and skinless, into mere lumps of flesh, and selling them. Therefore, for him, at the time of passing away from hell, the very lump of flesh became the karmic sign. He was born as a flesh-lump peta. The third.

4. Nicchavisuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Nicchavi Sutta

205. Nicchavivatthusmiṃ tassa orabbhikassa eḷake vadhitvā vadhitvā niccamme katvā kappitajīvikassa purimanayeneva niccammaṃ eḷakasarīraṃ nimittaṃ ahosi. So nicchavipeto jāto. Catutthaṃ.

205. In the story of the skinless one: For that sheep butcher who made his living by repeatedly slaughtering sheep and making them skinless, in the very same way as before, the skinless body of a sheep became the karmic sign. He was born as a skinless peta. The fourth.

5. Asilomasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Asiloma Sutta

206. Asilomavatthusmiṃ [V 2.0194][M 2.0202] so sūkariko dīgharattaṃ nivāpapuṭṭhe sūkare asinā vadhitvā vadhitvā dīgharattaṃ jīvikaṃ kappesi, tassa ukkhittāsikabhāvova nimittaṃ ahosi. Tasmā asilomapeto jāto. Pañcamaṃ.

206. In the story of the sword-haired one: That pig butcher, for a long time, made his living by repeatedly slaughtering with a sword the pigs that had been fattened with food. For him, the very state of having a raised sword became the karmic sign. Therefore, he was born as a sword-haired peta. The fifth.

6. Sattisuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Satti Sutta

207. Sattilomavatthusmiṃ so māgaviko ekaṃ migañca sattiñca gahetvā vanaṃ gantvā tassa migassa samīpaṃ āgatāgate mige sattiyā vijjhitvā māresi, tassa sattiyā vijjhanakabhāvoyeva nimittaṃ ahosi. Tasmā sattilomapeto jāto. Chaṭṭhaṃ.

207. In the story of the spear-haired one: That hunter, taking a decoy deer and a spear and going into the forest, would kill the animals that repeatedly came near that deer by piercing them with the spear. For him, the very act of piercing with the spear became the karmic sign. Therefore, he was born as a spear-haired peta. The sixth.

7. Usulomasuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Usuloma Sutta

208. Usulomavatthusmiṃ kāraṇikoti rājāparādhike anekāhi kāraṇāhi pīḷetvā avasāne kaṇḍena vijjhitvā māraṇakapuriso. So kira “amukasmiṃ padese viddho maratī”ti ñatvāva vijjhati. Tassevaṃ jīvikaṃ kappetvā narake uppannassa tato pakkāvasesena idhūpapattikāle usunā vijjhanabhāvoyeva nimittaṃ ahosi. Tasmā usulomapeto jāto. Sattamaṃ.

208. In the story of the arrow-haired one: A `kāraṇika` is an executioner who, having oppressed those who committed royal offenses with many kinds of tortures, finally kills them by shooting them with an arrow. It is said he shoots only after knowing, 'If shot in such-and-such a place, he dies.' For him, having made a living in this way and been reborn in hell, at the time of his rebirth here by the remaining result of his ripened kamma, the very state of being shot by an arrow became the karmic sign. Therefore, he was born as an arrow-haired peta. The seventh.

8. Sūcilomasuttavaṇṇanā

8. The Explanation of the Sūciloma Sutta

209. Sūcilomavatthusmiṃ [P 2.0220] sūtoti assadamako. Godamakotipi vadantiyeva. Tassa patodasūciyā vijjhanabhāvoyeva nimittaṃ ahosi. Tasmā sūcilomapeto jāto. Aṭṭhamaṃ.

209. In the story of the needle-haired one: A `sūta` is a horse tamer. They also say he was a cattle tamer. For him, the very act of piercing with a goad-needle became the karmic sign. Therefore, he was born as a needle-haired peta. The eighth.

9. Dutiyasūcilomasuttavaṇṇanā

9. The Explanation of the Second Sūciloma Sutta

210. Dutiye sūcilomavatthusmiṃ sūcakoti pesuññakārako. So kira manusse aññamaññañca bhindi, rājakule ca “imassa imaṃ nāma atthi, iminā idaṃ nāma kata”nti sūcetvā [V 2.0195] sūcetvā anayabyasanaṃ pāpesi. Tasmā yathā tena sūcetvā manussā bhinnā, tathā sūcīhi bhedanadukkhaṃ [M 2.0203] paccanubhotuṃ kammameva nimittaṃ katvā sūcilomapeto jāto. Navamaṃ.

210. In the second story of the needle-haired one: `Sūcaka` means a slanderer. It is said that he would divide people against one another, and in the royal court, by repeatedly reporting, 'This person has such-and-such; this person did such-and-such,' he would lead them to ruin and disaster. Therefore, just as people were divided by his slandering, so too, in order to experience the suffering of being pierced by needles, having made that very kamma his karmic sign, he was born as a needle-haired peta. The ninth.

10. Kumbhaṇḍasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Kumbhaṇḍa Sutta

211. Aṇḍabhārivatthusmiṃ gāmakūṭakoti vinicchayāmacco. Tassa kammasabhāgatāya kumbhamattā mahāghaṭappamāṇā aṇḍā ahesuṃ. So hi yasmā raho paṭicchanne ṭhāne lañjaṃ gahetvā kūṭavinicchayena pākaṭaṃ dosaṃ karonto sāmike assāmike akāsi, tasmāssa rahassaṃ aṅgaṃ pākaṭaṃ nibbattaṃ. Yasmā daṇḍaṃ paṭṭhapento paresaṃ asayhaṃ bhāraṃ āropesi, tasmāssa rahassaṃ aṅgaṃ asayhabhāro hutvā nibbattaṃ. Yasmā yasmiṃ ṭhāne ṭhitena samena bhavitabbaṃ, tasmiṃ ṭhatvā visamo ahosi, tasmāssa rahassaṅge visamā nisajjāva ahosīti. Dasamaṃ.

211. In the story of the peta with heavy testicles, `gāmakūṭa` means a judging minister. Due to the similarity to his kamma, his testicles became the size of pots, as large as great jars. For, because he took bribes in a secret, concealed place and, through corrupt judgment, making the fault manifest, made owners into non-owners, therefore his private part became manifest. Because, when imposing a punishment, he placed an unbearable burden on others, therefore his private part became an unbearable burden. Because, while established in a position where one should have been fair, he was unfair, therefore his very sitting posture became uneven on account of his private parts. The tenth.

Paṭhamo vaggo.

The First Chapter.

2. Dutiyavaggo

2. The Second Chapter

1. Sasīsakasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Sasīsaka Sutta

212. Pāradārikavatthusmiṃ so satto parassa rakkhitagopitaṃ sassāmikaṃ phassaṃ phusanto mīḷhasukhena kāmasukhena cittaṃ ramayitvā kammasabhāgatāya gūthaphassaṃ phusanto dukkhamanubhavituṃ tattha nibbatto. Paṭhamaṃ.

212. In the story of the adulterer, that being—having contacted the touch of another's wife who was guarded, protected, and had a husband, and having delighted his mind with sensual pleasure, which is a pleasure like filth—was born there, due to the similarity to his kamma, to experience suffering while contacting the touch of excrement. The first.

2. Gūthakhādasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Gūthakhāda Sutta

213. Duṭṭhabrāhmaṇavatthu [P 2.0221] pākaṭameva. Dutiyaṃ.

213. The story of the corrupt brahmin is well-known. The second.

3. Nicchavitthisuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Nicchavitthi Sutta

214. Nicchavitthivatthusmiṃ [V 2.0196] yasmā mātugāmo nāma attano phasse anissaro, sā ca taṃ sāmikassa santakaṃ phassaṃ thenetvā paresaṃ abhiratiṃ uppādesi, tasmā kammasabhāgatāya sukhasamphassā vaṭṭitvā dukkhasamphassaṃ anubhavituṃ nicchavitthī hutvā uppannā. Tatiyaṃ.

214. In the story of the skinless woman, because a woman, by nature, has no authority over her own physical contact, and she, having stolen that contact which is the property of her husband, produced delight for others, therefore, due to the similarity to her kamma, having turned away from pleasant contact, she was born as a skinless woman to experience painful contact. The third.

4. Maṅgulitthisuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Maṅgulitthi Sutta

215. Maṅgulitthivatthusmiṃ [M 2.0204] maṅgulinti virūpaṃ duddasikaṃ bībhacchaṃ. Sā kira yakkhadāsikammaṃ karontī “iminā ca iminā ca evaṃ balikamme kate ayaṃ nāma tumhākaṃ vaḍḍhi bhavissatī”ti mahājanassa gandhapupphādīni vañcanāya gahetvā mahājanaṃ duddiṭṭhiṃ micchādiṭṭhiṃ gaṇhāpesi, tasmā tāya kammasabhāgatāya gandhapupphādīnaṃ thenitattā duggandhā, duddassanassa gāhitattā duddasikā virūpā bībhacchā hutvā nibbattā. Catutthaṃ.

215. In the story of the Maṅgulī woman, `maṅgulī` means deformed, unpleasant to see, and repulsive. It is said that she, while working as a female yakkha's servant, took perfumes, flowers, and so on from the people by deception, saying, 'If an offering is made in this way with this and that, such and such prosperity will be yours.' Thus she caused the people to adopt bad views and wrong views. Therefore, due to the similarity to that kamma: because she had stolen perfumes, flowers, and so on, she was foul-smelling; and because she had caused others to adopt a bad view, she was born unpleasant to see, deformed, and repulsive. The fourth.

5. Okilinīsuttavaṇṇanā

5. The Explanation of the Okilinī Sutta

216. Okilinīvatthusmiṃ uppakkaṃ okiliniṃ okirininti sā kira aṅgāracitake nipannā vipphandamānā viparivattamānā paccati, tasmā uppakkā ceva hoti uṇhena agginā pakkasarīrā, okilinī ca kilinnasarīrā, bindūnissā sarīrato paggharanti, okirinī ca aṅgārasamparikiṇṇā. Tassā hi heṭṭhatopi kiṃsukapupphavaṇṇā aṅgārā, ubhayapassesupi, ākāsatopissā upari patanti. Tena vuttaṃ – “uppakkaṃ okiliniṃ [P 2.0222] okirini”nti. Sā issāpakatā sapattiṃ aṅgārakaṭāhena okirīti tassa kira rañño ekā nāṭakinī aṅgārakaṭāhaṃ samīpe ṭhapetvā gattato udakaṃ puñchati, pāṇinā ca sedaṃ karoti. Rājāpi tāya saddhiṃ kathañca karoti, parituṭṭhākārañca dasseti. Aggamahesī taṃ asahamānā issāpakatā hutvā acirapakkantassa rañño taṃ aṅgārakaṭāhaṃ gahetvā tassā upari aṅgāre okiri. Sā taṃ kammaṃ katvā tādisaṃyeva vipākaṃ paccanubhavituṃ petaloke nibbattā. Pañcamaṃ.

216. In the story of the Okilinī woman, regarding 'uppakkaṃ, okiliniṃ, and okiriniṃ': it is said that she, lying on a heap of coals, writhing and rolling over, is cooked. Therefore, she is indeed thoroughly cooked, having a body cooked by the hot fire; she is also defiled, having a body smeared with filth, and drops ooze from her body; and she is covered, being completely strewn with embers. Indeed, below her are embers the color of kiṃsuka flowers; on both sides too; and from the sky, they fall upon her. Therefore, it was said: 'thoroughly cooked, defiled, and covered.' She, overcome by jealousy, poured a brazier of embers over her co-wife. It is said that a certain female dancer of that king, having placed a brazier nearby, was wiping water from her body and removing sweat with her hand. The king also conversed with her and showed a pleased demeanor. The chief queen, unable to bear this, being overcome by jealousy, when the king had not long departed, took that brazier and poured the embers over her. Having done that kamma, she was reborn in the peta-world to experience a result of just such a kind. The fifth.

6. Asīsakasuttavaṇṇanā

6. The Explanation of the Asīsaka Sutta

217. Coraghātavatthusmiṃ [V 2.0197] so rañño āṇāya dīgharattaṃ corānaṃ sīsāni chinditvā petaloke nibbattanto asīsakaṃ kabandhaṃ hutvā nibbatti. Chaṭṭhaṃ.

217. In the story of the executioner of thieves: he, by the king's command, having cut off the heads of thieves for a long time, upon being reborn in the peta-world, was reborn having become a headless trunk. The sixth.

7-11. Pāpabhikkhusuttādivaṇṇanā

7-11. The Explanation of the Pāpabhikkhu Sutta and others

218-222. Bhikkhuvatthusmiṃ [M 2.0205] pāpabhikkhūti lāmakabhikkhu. So kira lokassa saddhādeyye cattāro paccaye paribhuñjitvā kāyavacīdvārehi asaṃyato bhinnājīvo cittakeḷiṃ kīḷanto vicari. Tato ekaṃ buddhantaraṃ niraye paccitvā petaloke nibbattanto bhikkhusadiseneva attabhāvena nibbatti. Bhikkhunīsikkhamānāsāmaṇerasāmaṇerīvatthūsupi ayameva vinicchayo. Sattamādīni.

218-222. In the story of the monk, 'pāpabhikkhu' means a base monk. It is said that he, having consumed the four requisites given in faith by the world, wandered about unrestrained through the doors of body and speech, with a corrupt livelihood, indulging in mental amusements. Thereafter, having been tormented in hell for one whole Buddha-interval, upon being reborn in the peta-world, he was reborn with an individual existence just like that of a monk. In the stories of the nun, the female probationer, the male novice, and the female novice as well, this very same judgment is to be understood. The seventh and following.

Lakkhaṇasaṃyuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Lakkhaṇa Saṃyutta is concluded.

9. Opammasaṃyuttaṃ

9. The Opamma Saṃyutta

1. Kūṭasuttavaṇṇanā

1. The Explanation of the Kūṭa Sutta

223. Opammasaṃyuttassa [V 2.0198][P 2.0223][M 2.0206] paṭhame kūṭaṃ gacchantīti kūṭaṅgamā. Kūṭaṃ samosarantīti kūṭasamosaraṇā. Kūṭasamugghātāti kūṭassa samugghātena. Avijjāsamugghātāti arahattamaggena avijjāya samugghātena. Appamattāti satiyā avippavāse ṭhitā hutvā. Paṭhamaṃ.

223. In the first discourse of the Opamma Saṃyutta: Kūṭaṅgamā means 'they go to the peak.' Kūṭasamosaraṇā means 'they converge on the peak.' Kūṭasamugghāta means 'by the uprooting of the peak.' Avijjāsamugghāta means 'by the uprooting of ignorance through the path of Arahantship.' Appamattā means 'having become established in the non-absence of mindfulness.' The first.

2. Nakhasikhasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Discourse of the Fingernail Tip

224. Dutiye manussesu paccājāyantīti ye manussalokato cutā manussesu jāyanti, te evaṃ appakāti adhippāyo. Aññatra manussehīti ye pana manussalokato cutā ṭhapetvā manussalokaṃ catūsu apāyesu paccājāyanti, te mahāpathaviyaṃ paṃsu viya bahutarā. Imasmiñca sutte devāpi manusseheva saṅgahitā. Tasmā yathā manussesu jāyantā appakā, evaṃ devesupīti veditabbā. Dutiyaṃ.

224. In the second discourse, 'those reborn among humans' means those who, having passed away from the human world, are reborn among humans; the intention is that they are few. 'Apart from humans' means those who, having passed away from the human world, are reborn in the four woeful states, excepting the human world; they are more numerous, like the dust on the great earth. And in this discourse, devas are also included with humans. Therefore, it should be understood that just as those being born among humans are few, so too are those among the devas. The second.

3. Kulasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Discourse on Families

225. Tatiye suppadhaṃsiyānīti suviheṭhiyāni. Kumbhatthenakehīti ye paragharaṃ pavisitvā dīpālokena oloketvā parabhaṇḍaṃ haritukāmā ghaṭe dīpaṃ katvā pavisanti, te kumbhatthenakā nāma, tehi kumbhatthenakehi. Suppadhaṃsiyo hoti amanussehīti mettābhāvanārahitaṃ paṃsupisācakā vidhaṃsayanti, pageva uḷārā amanussā. Bhāvitāti vaḍḍhitā. Bahulīkatāti punappunaṃ katā. Yānīkatāti yuttayānaṃ viya katā. Vatthukatāti patiṭṭhānaṭṭhena [P 2.0224] vatthu viya katā. Anuṭṭhitāti adhiṭṭhitā[V 2.0199]. Paricitāti samantato citā suvaḍḍhitā. Susamāraddhāti cittena suṭṭhu samāraddhā. Tatiyaṃ.

225. In the third discourse, 'easily destroyed' means easily harmed. 'By pot-thieves' refers to those who, desiring to take another's belongings, enter another's house and, having looked around with the light of a lamp, enter having placed a lamp in a pot; they are called pot-thieves. 'Easily destroyed by non-humans' means that dust-goblins destroy one who is devoid of the development of loving-kindness; how much more so eminent non-humans. 'Developed' means increased. 'Made much of' means done again and again. 'Made a vehicle' means made like a yoked chariot. 'Made a foundation' means made like a basis in the sense of a support. 'Established' means determined. 'Familiarized' means accumulated from all around and well-developed. 'Well undertaken' means well undertaken by the mind. The third.

4. Okkhāsuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Discourse on the Cooking Pot

226. Catutthe okkhāsatanti mahāmukhaukkhalīnaṃ sataṃ. Dānaṃ dadeyyāti paṇītabhojanabharitānaṃ mahāukkhalīnaṃ sataṃ dānaṃ dadeyya. “Ukkāsata”ntipi pāṭho[M 2.0207], tassa daṇḍadīpikāsatanti attho. Ekāya pana dīpikāya yattake ṭhāne āloko hoti, tato sataguṇaṃ ṭhānaṃ sattahi ratanehi pūretvā dānaṃ dadeyyāti attho. Gadduhanamattanti goduhanamattaṃ, gāviyā ekavāraṃ aggathanākaḍḍhanamattanti attho. Gandhaūhanamattaṃ vā, dvīhi aṅgulīhi gandhapiṇḍaṃ gahetvā ekavāraṃ ghāyanamattanti attho. Ettakampi hi kālaṃ yo pana gabbhapariveṇavihārūpacāra paricchedena vā cakkavāḷaparicchedena vā aparimāṇāsu lokadhātūsu vā sabbasattesu hitapharaṇaṃ mettacittaṃ bhāvetuṃ sakkoti, idaṃ tato ekadivasaṃ tikkhattuṃ dinnadānato mahapphalataraṃ. Catutthaṃ.

226. In the fourth discourse, 'a hundred cooking pots' means a hundred large-mouthed cooking pots. 'One should give a gift' means one should give a gift of a hundred large-mouthed cooking pots filled with excellent food. There is also the reading 'a hundred torches,' and its meaning is a hundred stick-lamps. The meaning is that one should give a gift by filling with the seven jewels a place a hundred times larger than the area illuminated by a single lamp. 'The duration of milking' means the duration of milking a cow; the meaning is the duration of pulling the tip of a cow's teat once. Or, 'the duration of smelling a fragrance' means the duration of taking a ball of fragrance with two fingers and smelling it once. For if, even for such a short time, someone is able to develop a mind of loving-kindness that pervades with benefit for all beings—whether limited by the confines of an inner chamber, a monastic residence, and a monastery's precincts, or by the confines of a world-system, or throughout immeasurable world-systems—this is of far greater fruit than that gift given three times in one day. The fourth.

5. Sattisuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Discourse on the Spear

227. Pañcame paṭileṇissāmītiādīsu agge paharitvā kappāsavaṭṭiṃ viya nāmento niyyāsavaṭṭiṃ viya ca ekato katvā alliyāpento paṭileṇeti nāma. Majjhe paharitvā nāmetvā dhārāya [P 2.0225] vā paharitvā dvepi dhārā ekato alliyāpento paṭikoṭṭeti nāma. Kappāsavaṭṭanakaraṇīyaṃ viya pavattento cirakālaṃ saṃvellitakilañjaṃ pasāretvā puna saṃvellento viya ca paṭivaṭṭeti nāma. Pañcamaṃ.

227. In the fifth discourse, regarding the passage beginning with paṭileṇissāmi: When one strikes at the tip and bends it like a cotton roll, or makes it into one and causes it to stick together like a resin ball, this is called paṭileṇeti. When one strikes in the middle and bends it, or strikes on the edge and causes both edges to stick together as one, this is called paṭikoṭṭeti. When one rolls it as in the making of a cotton roll, or as when one spreads out a mat that has been rolled up for a long time and then rolls it up again, this is called paṭivaṭṭeti. The fifth.

6. Dhanuggahasuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Discourse on Archers

228. Chaṭṭhe daḷhadhammā dhanuggahāti daḷhadhanuno issāsā. Daḷhadhanu nāma dvisahassathāmaṃ vuccati, dvisahassathāmaṃ nāma yassa āropitassa jiyābaddho lohasīsādīnaṃ bhāro daṇḍe gahetvā yāva kaṇḍappamāṇā ukkhittassa pathavito muccati. Susikkhitāti dasadvādasavassāni ācariyakule [V 2.0200] uggahitasippā. Katahatthāti yo sippameva uggaṇhāti, so katahattho na hoti, ime pana katahatthā ciṇṇavasībhāvā. Katūpāsanāti rājakulādīsu dassitasippā.

228. In the sixth discourse, daḷhadhammā dhanuggahā means archers with strong bows. A daḷhadhanu or strong bow is said to be of two-thousand strength. Dvisahassathāmaṃ or two-thousand strength means a bow such that when it is strung, its tied string, holding a weight of iron, copper, lead, etc., on a crossbar, lifts that weight from the ground when the bow is raised to the height of an arrow. Sikkhitā means those who have learned the art in a teacher's family for ten or twelve years. Katahatthā means: one who merely learns the art is not katahattha; rather, these are katahatthā because of their state of practiced mastery. Katūpāsanā means those who have demonstrated their art in royal families and so on.

Tassa purisassa javoti evarūpo añño puriso nāma na bhūtapubbo, bodhisattasseva pana javanahaṃsakālo nāma āsi. Tadā bodhisatto cattāri [M 2.0208] kaṇḍāni āhari. Tadā kirassa kaniṭṭhabhātaro “mayaṃ, bhātika, sūriyena saddhiṃ javissāmā”ti ārocesuṃ. Bodhisatto āha – “sūriyo sīghajavo, na sakkhissatha tumhe tena saddhiṃ javitu”nti. Te dutiyaṃ tatiyampi tatheva vatvā ekadivasaṃ “gacchāmā”ti yugandharapabbataṃ āruhitvā nisīdiṃsu. Bodhisatto “kahaṃ me bhātaro”ti? Pucchitvā, “sūriyena saddhiṃ javituṃ gatā”ti vutte, “vinassissanti tapassino”ti te anukampamāno sayampi gantvā tesaṃ santike nisīdi. Atha sūriye uggacchante dvepi bhātaro sūriyena saddhiṃyeva ākāsaṃ pakkhantā, bodhisattopi tehi saddhiṃyeva pakkhanto. Tesu ekassa apatteyeva antarabhattasamaye pakkhantaresu [P 2.0226] aggi uṭṭhahi, so bhātaraṃ pakkositvā “na sakkomī”ti āha. Tamenaṃ bodhisatto “mā bhāyī”ti samassāsetvā pakkhapañjarena paliveṭhetvā darathaṃ vinodetvā “gacchā”ti pesesi.

Regarding 'that man's speed': no other man of such a kind, apart from the Bodhisatta, has ever existed before. However, it was indeed the Bodhisatta's time as King Javanahaṃsa (Swift Goose). At that time, the Bodhisatta brought four arrows. Then, it is said, his younger brothers informed him, saying, 'Revered brother, we will race with the sun.' The Bodhisatta said, 'The sun is swift of speed; you will not be able to race with it.' Having said the same a second and a third time, one day they said, 'We shall go,' and having climbed Mount Yugandhara, they sat down. The Bodhisatta asked, 'Where are my brothers?' When it was said, 'They have gone to race with the sun,' thinking, 'These poor fellows will perish,' out of compassion for them, he himself also went and sat near them. Then, as the sun was rising, both brothers flew into the sky along with the sun, and the Bodhisatta also flew along with them. Among them, for one, during the forenoon period, a fire arose within his wings. He called his brother and said, 'I am not able.' The Bodhisatta comforted him, saying, 'Do not be afraid,' and having enclosed him with the cage of his wings and dispelled his distress, he sent him off, saying, 'Go.'

Dutiyo yāva antarabhattā javitvā pakkhantaresu aggimhi uṭṭhahite tathevāha. Tampi so tatheva katvā “gacchā”ti pesesi. Sayaṃ pana yāva majjhanhikā javitvā, “ete bālāti mayāpi bālena na bhavitabba”nti nivattitvā – “adiṭṭhasahāyakaṃ bārāṇasirājaṃ passissāmī”ti bārāṇasiṃ agamāsi. Tasmiṃ nagaramatthake paribbhamante dvādasayojanaṃ nagaraṃ pattakaṭāhena otthaṭapatto viya ahosi. Atha paribbhamantassa paribbhamantassa tattha tattha chiddāni paññāyiṃsu. Sayampi anekahaṃsasahassasadiso paññāyi. So vegaṃ paṭisaṃharitvā rājagehābhimukho ahosi. Rājā oloketvā – “āgato kira me piyasahāyo javanahaṃso”ti vātapānaṃ vivaritvā ratanapīṭhaṃ paññāpetvā olokento aṭṭhāsi. Bodhisatto ratanapīṭhe nisīdi.

The second brother, having raced until the forenoon, said the same when heat arose within his wings. The Bodhisatta did the same for him and sent him off, saying, 'Go.' He himself, however, having raced until noon, thought, 'These are fools; I too should not be a fool,' and turning back, he went to Bārāṇasī, thinking, 'I will see my unseen friend, the king of Bārāṇasī.' As he was circling over the city, the twelve-yojana city became like a bowl covered with a lid. Then, as he circled again and again, gaps appeared here and there. He himself appeared like many thousands of geese. Withdrawing his speed, he faced the royal palace. The king, looking on, thought, 'It seems my dear friend, the Javanahaṃsa, has come,' and opening a window, he had a jeweled seat prepared and stood watching. The Bodhisatta sat upon the jeweled seat.

Athassa rājā sahassapākena telena pakkhantarāni makkhetvā, madhulāje ceva madhurapānakañca adāsi. Tato naṃ kataparibhogaṃ “samma, kahaṃ agamāsī”ti? Pucchi. So taṃ pavattiṃ ārocetvā “athāhaṃ, mahārāja, yāva majjhanhikā javitvā – ‘natthi javitena attho’ti nivatto”ti ācikkhi. Atha rājā āha – “ahaṃ, sāmi, tumhākaṃ sūriyena saddhiṃ javanavegaṃ [M 2.0209] passitukāmo”ti[V 2.0201]. Dukkaraṃ, mahārāja, na sakkā tayā passitunti. Tena hi, sāmi, sarikkhakamattampi dassehīti. Āma, mahārāja, dhanuggahe sannipātehīti. Rājā sannipātesi. Haṃso tato cattāro gahetvā nagaramajjhe toraṇaṃ kāretvā attano gīvāya ghaṇḍaṃ piḷandhāpetvā toraṇassa upari nisīditvā – “cattāro janā toraṇaṃ nissāya catudisābhimukhā ekekaṃ kaṇḍaṃ khipantū”ti vatvā, sayaṃ paṭhamakaṇḍeneva saddhiṃ uppatitvā, taṃ kaṇḍaṃ aggahetvāva, dakkhiṇābhimukhaṃ gatakaṇḍaṃ dhanuto ratanamattāpagataṃ [P 2.0227] gaṇhi. Dutiyaṃ dviratanamattāpagataṃ, tatiyaṃ tiratanamattāpagataṃ, catutthaṃ bhūmiṃ appattameva gaṇhi. Atha naṃ cattāri kaṇḍāni gahetvā toraṇe nisinnakāleyeva addasaṃsu. So rājānaṃ āha – “passa, mahārāja, evaṃsīgho amhākaṃ javo”ti. Evaṃ bodhisatteneva javanahaṃsakāle tāni kaṇḍāni āharitānīti veditabbāni.

Then the king, having anointed the insides of his wings with oil cooked a thousand times, gave him honeyed parched grain and a sweet drink. After he had partaken, the king asked, 'Friend, where did you go?' He related the events and explained, 'Great king, I raced until noon, and then, thinking, "There is no benefit in racing," I returned.' Then the king said, 'Lord, I wish to see the speed of your race with the sun.' 'It is difficult, great king; it cannot be seen by you.' 'In that case, lord, please show me at least a comparable speed.' 'Yes, great king. Assemble the archers.' The king assembled them. The goose then took four renowned archers, had an arched gateway made in the middle of the city, had a bell fastened to his own neck, and, having sat atop the gateway, said, 'Let the four men, relying on the gateway and facing the four directions, each shoot one arrow.' He himself, flying up at the same instant as the first arrow, then caught the arrow that had gone towards the south when it was a cubit's measure away from the bow. He caught the second when it was two cubits' measure away, the third when it was three cubits' measure away, and the fourth before it reached the ground. Then, they saw him only at the moment he was seated on the gateway, holding the four arrows. He said to the king, 'See, great king, so swift is our speed.' Thus, it should be understood that it was the Bodhisatta himself who, during his time as the Javanahaṃsa, brought those arrows.

Purato dhāvantīti aggato javanti. Na panetā sabbakālaṃ puratova honti, kadāci purato, kadāci pacchato honti. Ākāsaṭṭhakavimānesu hi uyyānānipi honti pokkharaṇiyopi, tā tattha nahāyanti, udakakīḷaṃ kīḷamānā pacchatopi honti, vegena pana gantvā puna puratova dhāvanti. Āyusaṅkhārāti rūpajīvitindriyaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Tañhi tato sīghataraṃ khīyati. Arūpadhammānaṃ pana bhedo na sakkā paññāpetuṃ. Chaṭṭhaṃ.

'Running in front' means they race at the very front. But they are not always only in front; sometimes they are in front, sometimes they are behind. Indeed, in the mansions established in the sky, there are parks and ponds. Those devas, while bathing and playing water-games there, are also behind. But having gone with speed, they again run only in front. 'Life-formation' is said in reference to the material life-faculty. Indeed, that is exhausted more swiftly than them. But the breaking up of immaterial phenomena cannot be made known. The sixth.

7. Āṇisuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Āṇi Sutta

229. Sattame dasārahānanti evaṃnāmakānaṃ khattiyānaṃ. Te kira satato dasabhāgaṃ gaṇhiṃsu, tasmā “dasārahā”ti paññāyiṃsu. Ānakoti evaṃladdhanāmo mudiṅgo. Himavante kira mahākuḷīradaho ahosi. Tattha mahanto kuḷīro otiṇṇotiṇṇaṃ hatthiṃ khādati. Atha hatthī upaddutā ekaṃ kareṇuṃ sakkariṃsu “imissā puttaṃ nissāya amhākaṃ sotthi bhavissatī”ti. Sāpi mahesakkhaṃ puttaṃ vijāyi. Te tampi sakkariṃsu. So vuddhippatto mātaraṃ pucchi, “kasmā maṃ ete sakkarontī”ti? Sā taṃ pavattimācikkhi. So “kiṃ mayhaṃ kuḷīro pahoti? Etha gacchāmā”ti mahāhatthiparivāro [M 2.0210] tattha gantvā paṭhamameva otari. Kuḷīro udakasaddeneva āgantvā taṃ aggahesi. Mahanto kuḷīrassa aḷo, so taṃ ito vā etto vā cāletuṃ asakkonto mukhe soṇḍaṃ pakkhipitvā viravi. Hatthino “yaṃnissāya mayaṃ ‘sotthi bhavissatī’ti [P 2.0228] amaññimhā, so paṭhamataraṃ gahito”ti tato tato palāyiṃsu.

229. In the seventh, 'of the Dasārahas' refers to khattiyas of that name. It is said they took a tenth part from a hundred; therefore, they became known as the 'Dasārahas.' 'Ānaka' is a drum that received such a name. It is said that in the Himālaya, there was a great crab-lake. There, a great crab would eat each and every elephant that came down into the water. Then the elephants, being oppressed, honored a female elephant, thinking, 'Relying on her son, our welfare will come to be.' She too gave birth to a son of great power, and they honored him as well. When he reached maturity, he asked his mother, 'Why do they honor me?' She told him of the matter. He said, 'What can a crab do to me? Come, let us go!' Surrounded by a great retinue of elephants, he went there and entered the water first. The crab, coming just by the sound of the water, seized him. The crab's claw was huge. He, being unable to make it move from here or there, put his trunk into its mouth and roared. The elephants, thinking, 'The one on whom we relied, thinking, "Our welfare will come to be," has been seized first of all,' fled from here and there.

Athassa [V 2.0202] mātā avidūre ṭhatvā “mayaṃ thalanāgā, tumhe udakanāgā nāma, nāgehi nāgo na viheṭhetabbo”ti kuḷīraṃ piyavacanena vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

Then his mother, standing nearby, having spoken to the crab with endearing words, saying, 'We are land-nāgas, you are called water-nāgas; a nāga should not be harmed by nāgas,' spoke this verse:

“Ye kuḷīrā samuddasmiṃ, gaṅgāya yamunāya ca;

Tesaṃ tvaṃ vārijo seṭṭho, muñca rodantiyā paja”nti.

“Of the crabs that are in the ocean, and in the Gaṅgā and Yamunā, you, born of water, are the most excellent. Release the child of me who is weeping.”

Mātugāmasaddo nāma purise khobhetvā tiṭṭhati, tasmā so gahaṇaṃ sithilamakāsi. Hatthipoto vegena ubho pāde ukkhipitvā taṃ piṭṭhiyaṃ akkami. Saha akkamanā piṭṭhi mattikabhājanaṃ viya bhijji. Atha naṃ dantehi vijjhitvā ukkhipitvā thale chaḍḍetvā tuṭṭharavaṃ ravi. Atha naṃ hatthī ito cito ca āgantvā maddiṃsu. Tassa eko aḷo paṭikkamitvā pati, taṃ sakko devarājā gahetvā gato.

The sound of a woman, it is said, agitates men and persists; therefore, he made his grip loose. The young elephant quickly lifted both feet and stepped on its back. As soon as he stepped on it, the back broke like an earthen vessel. Then, having pierced it with his tusks, lifted it up, and thrown it on the land, he made a sound of delight. Then the elephants, coming from here and there, trampled it. One of its claws was thrown off and fell; Sakka, king of the devas, took it and went away.

Itaro pana aḷo vātātapena sukkhitvā pakkalākhārasavaṇṇo ahosi, so deve vuṭṭhe udakoghena vuyhanto dasabhātikānaṃ rājūnaṃ uparisote jālaṃ pasārāpetvā gaṅgāya kīḷantānaṃ āgantvā jāle laggi. Te kīḷāpariyosāne jālamhi ukkhipiyamāne taṃ disvā pucchiṃsu “kiṃ eta”nti? “Kuḷīraaḷo sāmī”ti. “Na sakkā esa ābharaṇatthāya upanetuṃ, pariyonandhāpetvā bheriṃ karissāmā”ti? Pariyonandhāpetvā pahariṃsu. Saddo dvādasayojanaṃ nagaraṃ avatthari. Tato āhaṃsu – “na sakkā idaṃ divase divase vādetuṃ, chaṇadivasatthāya maṅgalabherī hotū”ti maṅgalabheriṃ akaṃsu. Tasmiṃ vādite mahājano anhāyitvā apiḷandhitvā hatthiyānādīni āruyha sīghaṃ sannipatanti. Iti mahājanaṃ pakkositvā viya ānetīti ānako tvevassa nāmaṃ ahosi.

But the other claw, having been dried by wind and sun, became the color of boiled lac. When it rained, it was carried by the flood of water and, floating along, it came and got caught in a net that the ten brother-kings, who were playing in the Gaṅgā, had caused to be spread upstream. At the end of their play, as the net was being lifted, they saw it and asked, 'What is this?' 'It is a crab's claw, sirs.' 'This cannot be used for an ornament. Having had it covered with leather, we will make a drum.' Having had it covered with leather, they struck it. The sound covered the city for twelve yojanas. Then they said, 'This cannot be played every day. Let it be an auspicious drum for festival days,' and they made it an auspicious drum. When it was beaten, the great populace, without even bathing or adorning themselves, would mount elephants, conveyances, and so on, and quickly assemble. Thus, because it brings the great populace as if summoning them, its name became 'Ānaka.'

Aññaṃ [M 2.0211] āṇiṃ odahiṃsūti aññaṃ suvaṇṇarajatādimayaṃ āṇiṃ ghaṭayiṃsu. Āṇisaṅghāṭova avasissīti suvaṇṇādimayānaṃ āṇīnaṃ saṅghāṭamattameva avasesaṃ ahosi. Athassa [P 2.0229] dvādasayojanappamāṇo saddo antosālāyampi dukkhena suyyittha.

'They put in another peg' means they fashioned another peg made of gold, silver, and so on. 'Only the collection of pegs remained' means only the mere collection of pegs made of gold and so on was left. Then its sound, which had a range of twelve yojanas, was heard with difficulty even inside the hall.

Gambhīrāti pāḷivasena gambhīrā sallasuttasadisā. Gambhīratthāti atthavasena gambhīrā mahāvedallasuttasadisā (ma. ni. 1.449 ādayo). Lokuttarāti lokuttaraatthadīpakā. Suññatappaṭisaṃyuttāti [V 2.0203] sattasuññatadhammamattameva pakāsakā saṃkhittasaṃyuttasadisā. Uggahetabbaṃ pariyāpuṇitabbanti uggahetabbe ca pariyāpuṇitabbe ca. Kavikatāti kavīhi katā. Itaraṃ tasseva vevacanaṃ. Cittakkharāti vicitraakkharā. Itaraṃ tasseva vevacanaṃ. Bāhirakāti sāsanato bahibhūtā. Sāvakabhāsitāti tesaṃ tesaṃ sāvakehi bhāsitā. Sussūsissantīti akkharacittatāya ceva savanasampattiyā ca attamanā hutvā sāmaṇeradaharabhikkhumātugāmamahāgahapatikādayo “esa dhammakathiko”ti sannipatitvā sotukāmā bhavissanti. Tasmāti yasmā tathāgatabhāsitā suttantā anuggayhamānā antaradhāyanti, tasmā. Sattamaṃ.

'Profound' means profound by way of the Pāli text, like the Salla Sutta. 'Profound in meaning' means profound by way of the meaning, like the Mahāvedalla Sutta. 'Supramundane' means that which illuminates the supramundane meaning. 'Connected with emptiness' means that which reveals only the natural phenomena of being void of a being, like the Saṃkhitta Saṃyutta. 'Should be learned and should be mastered' refers to things that ought to be learned and mastered. 'Poetic compositions' means made by poets; the other word for this, kāpeyya, is a synonym. 'Of ornate letters' means having various letters; the other word for this, cittabyañjana, is a synonym. 'External' means that which is outside the Dispensation. 'Spoken by disciples' means spoken by the disciples of those teachers. 'They will want to hear' means that novices, young monks, women, great householders, and others, being delighted by the ornateness of the letters and by the excellence of the sound, will assemble, thinking, 'This is a Dhamma-preacher,' and will become desirous of hearing. 'Therefore' means: because the suttantas spoken by the Tathāgata, not being upheld, disappear; therefore... The seventh.

8. Kaliṅgarasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Kaliṅgara Sutta

230. Aṭṭhame kaliṅgarūpadhānāti kaliṅgaraghaṭikaṃ sīsūpadhānañceva pādūpadhānañca katvā. Appamattāti sippuggahaṇe appamattā. Ātāpinoti uṭṭhānavīriyātāpena yuttā. Upāsanasminti sippānaṃ abhiyoge ācariyānañca payirupāsane. Te kira tadā pātova uṭṭhāya sippasālaṃ gacchanti, tattha sippaṃ uggahetvā sajjhāyādīhi abhiyogaṃ katvā mukhaṃ dhovitvā yāgupānāya gacchanti. Yāguṃ pivitvā puna sippasālaṃ gantvā sippaṃ gaṇhitvā sajjhāyaṃ karontā pātarāsāya gacchanti. Katapātarāsā samānā “mā pamādena ciraṃ niddokkamanaṃ ahosī”ti khadiraghaṭikāsu sīse ca pāde ca upadahitvā [P 2.0230] thokaṃ nipajjitvā puna sippasālaṃ gantvā sippaṃ gahetvā sajjhāyanti. Sāyaṃ sajjhāyaṃ karontā ca gehaṃ gantvā bhuttasāyamāsā paṭhamayāmaṃ sajjhāyaṃ katvā sayanakāle tatheva kaliṅgaraṃ [M 2.0212] upadhānaṃ katvā sayanti. Evaṃ te akkhaṇavedhino vālavedhino ca ahesuṃ. Idaṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ.

230. In the eighth, 'using a block of kaliṅgara wood as a support' means having made a small block of kaliṅgara wood into both a head-rest and a foot-rest. 'Not heedless' means not heedless in the acquisition of skills. 'Ardent' means endowed with the exertion of striving energy. 'In attendance' means in great exertion regarding skills and in attending upon teachers. It is said that at that time, they would rise early in the morning and go to the hall of arts. There, having learned a skill and made great exertion with recitation and so on, they would wash their mouths and go to drink gruel. Having drunk the gruel, they would go again to the hall of arts, and having taken up a skill and reciting, they would go for the morning meal. Having had their morning meal, thinking, 'Let there not be a long falling into sleep through heedlessness,' they would place small blocks of acacia wood under their heads and feet, lie down for a short while, and then go again to the hall of arts, take up their skill, and recite. In the evening, while reciting, they would go home, and having eaten their evening meal, they would recite during the first watch of the night. At the time of sleeping, they would sleep in the same way, having made a block of kaliṅgara wood into a support. In this way, they became skilled in shooting in a flash and in splitting a hair. It was with reference to this that it was said.

Otāranti vivaraṃ. Ārammaṇanti paccayaṃ. Padhānasminti padhānabhūmiyaṃ vīriyaṃ kurumānā. Paṭhamabodhiyaṃ kira bhikkhū bhattakiccaṃ katvāva kammaṭṭhānaṃ manasi karonti. Tesaṃ manasikarontānaṃyeva sūriyo atthaṃ gacchati. Te nhāyitvā puna caṅkamaṃ otaritvā paṭhamayāmaṃ caṅkamanti. Tato “mā ciraṃ niddāyimhā”ti sarīradarathavinodanatthaṃ nipajjantā kaṭṭhakhaṇḍaṃ upadahitvā nipajjanti, te puna pacchimayāme vuṭṭhāya caṅkamaṃ otaranti. Te sandhāya idaṃ vuttaṃ. Ayampi dīpo tiṇṇaṃ rājūnaṃ kāle ekaghaṇḍinigghoso ekapadhānabhūmi ahosi. Nānāmukhe pahaṭaghaṇḍi pilicchikoḷiyaṃ osarati, kalyāṇiyaṃ pahaṭaghaṇḍi nāgadīpe osarati[V 2.0204]. “Ayaṃ bhikkhu puthujjano, ayaṃ puthujjano”ti aṅguliṃ pasāretvā dassetabbo ahosi. Ekadivasaṃ sabbe arahantova ahesuṃ. Tasmāti yasmā kaliṅgarūpadhānānaṃ māro ārammaṇaṃ na labhati, tasmā. Aṭṭhamaṃ.

'They find an opportunity' means an opening. 'An object' means a condition. 'In striving' means while making an effort in the sphere of striving. It is said that in the first period of the enlightenment, monks, having completed their meal duties, would attend to their meditation subject. While they were thus attending to it, the sun would set. Having bathed, they would again descend to the walking path and walk during the first watch. Then, thinking, 'Let us not sleep for long,' they would lie down to dispel bodily fatigue, placing a piece of wood under their heads. Rising again in the last watch, they would descend to the walking path. It was said with reference to them. This island, too, during the time of three kings, had the sound of a single bell and was a single ground for striving. The bell struck at Nānāmukha resounds at Pilicchikoḷiya; the bell struck at Kalyāṇī resounds at Nāgadīpa. It came to be that one had to point with an outstretched finger, saying, 'This monk is a worldling, this one is a worldling.' One day, all became arahants. 'Therefore' means: because Māra does not get an opportunity with those who use a block of kaliṅgara wood as a support, therefore. The eighth.

9. Nāgasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Nāga Sutta

231. Navame ativelanti atikkantavelaṃ kālaṃ atikkantappamāṇaṃ kālaṃ. Kimaṅgaṃ panāhanti ahaṃ pana kiṃkāraṇā na upasaṅkamissāmi? Bhisamuḷālanti [P 2.0231] bhisañceva muḷālañca. Abbuhetvāti uddharitvā. Bhiṅkacchāpāti hatthipotakā. Te kira abhiṇhaṃ bhiṅkārasaddaṃ karonti, tasmā bhiṅkacchāpāti vuccanti. Pasannākāraṃ karontīti pasannehi kattabbākāraṃ karonti, cattāro paccaye denti. Dhammaṃ bhāsantīti ekaṃ dve jātakāni vā suttante vā uggaṇhitvā asambhinnena sarena dhammaṃ desenti. Pasannākāraṃ karontīti tesaṃ tāya desanāya pasannā gihī paccaye denti. Neva vaṇṇāya hoti na balāyāti neva guṇavaṇṇāya, na ñāṇabalāya hoti, guṇavaṇṇe pana parihāyante sarīravaṇṇopi sarīrabalampi parihāyati, tasmā sarīrassa neva vaṇṇāya na balāya hoti. Navamaṃ.

231. In the ninth, 'too long' means time that has passed the limit, time that has exceeded the measure. 'Why then should I?' means 'For what reason, then, should I not approach?' 'Lotus stalk and root' means both the lotus stalk and the lotus root. 'Having pulled out' means having extracted. 'Bhiṅkacchāpas' means young elephants. It is said they constantly make a 'bhiṅkāra' sound; therefore, they are called 'bhiṅkacchāpas.' 'They act like one who is pleased' means they do the action that should be done by the faithful; they give the four requisites. 'They speak the Dhamma' means having learned one or two Jātakas or Suttantas, they teach the Dhamma with an unbroken voice. 'They act like one who is pleased' means householders, pleased by that teaching of theirs, give requisites. 'It is not for beauty, nor for strength' means it is not for the splendor of virtue, nor for the strength of knowledge. Furthermore, when the splendor of virtue declines, bodily beauty and bodily strength also decline; therefore, it is not for the body's beauty, nor for its strength. The ninth.

10. Biḷārasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Explanation of the Cat Sutta

232. Dasame [M 2.0213] sandhisamalasaṃkaṭīreti ettha sandhīti bhinnagharānaṃ sandhi, samaloti gāmato gūthanikkhamanamaggo, saṃkaṭīranti saṅkāraṭṭhānaṃ. Mudumūsinti mudukaṃ mūsikaṃ. Vuṭṭhānaṃ paññāyatīti desanā paññāyati. Dasamaṃ.

232. In the tenth sutta, regarding the phrase 'sandhisamalasaṅkaṭīre', 'sandhi' means the junction of broken-apart houses; 'samalo' means the path for excrement to exit from the village; 'saṅkaṭīraṃ' means a refuse heap. 'Mudumūsiṃ' means a soft-fleshed mouse. 'Vuṭṭhānaṃ paññāyati' means the confession of an offense becomes apparent. The tenth.

11. Siṅgālasuttavaṇṇanā

11. Explanation of the Jackal Sutta

233. Ekādasame yena yena icchatīti so jarasiṅgālo icchiticchitaṭṭhāne iriyāpathakappanena sītavātūpavāyanena ca antarantarā cittassādampi labhatīti dasseti. Sakyaputtiyapaṭiññoti idaṃ devadattaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. So hi ettakampi cittassādaṃ anāgate attabhāve na labhissatīti. Ekādasamaṃ.

233. In the eleventh sutta, regarding 'yena yena icchati' (wherever he wishes), it is shown that the old jackal, by adopting postures in whatever place he desires and by the blowing of the cool wind, also obtains from time to time a measure of mental satisfaction. The statement 'Sakyaputtiyapaṭiñña' (the claim of being a son of the Sakyans) was spoken with reference to Devadatta. For indeed, he will not obtain even this much mental satisfaction in a future existence. The eleventh.

12. Dutiyasiṅgālasuttavaṇṇanā

12. Explanation of the Second Jackal Sutta

234. Dvādasame [V 2.0205][P 2.0232] kataññutāti katajānanaṃ. Kataveditāti katavisesajānanaṃ. Tatridaṃ jarasiṅgālassa kataññutāya vatthu – satta kira bhātaro khettaṃ kasanti. Tesaṃ sabbakaniṭṭho khettapariyante ṭhatvā gāvo rakkhati. Athekaṃ jarasiṅgālaṃ ajagaro gaṇhi, so taṃ disvā yaṭṭhiyā pothetvā vissajjāpesi. Ajagaro siṅgālaṃ vissajjetvā tameva gaṇhi. Siṅgālo cintesi – “mayhaṃ iminā jīvitaṃ dinnaṃ, ahampi imassa dassāmī”ti yāgughaṭassa upari ṭhapitaṃ vāsiṃ mukhena ḍaṃsitvā tassa santikaṃ agamāsi. Itare bhātaro disvā, “siṅgālo vāsiṃ haratī”ti anubandhiṃsu. So tehi diṭṭhabhāvaṃ ñatvā vāsiṃ tassa santike chaḍḍetvā palāyi. Itare āgantvā kaniṭṭhaṃ ajagarena gahitaṃ disvā vāsiyā ajagaraṃ chinditvā taṃ gahetvā agamaṃsu. Evaṃ jarasiṅgāle siyā yā kāci kataññutā kataveditā. Sakyaputtiyapaṭiññeti idampi devadattassa ācārameva sandhāya vuttanti. Dvādasamaṃ.

234. In the twelfth sutta, 'kataññutā' (gratitude) means knowing a favor done. 'Kataveditā' means knowing a favor in a special way. In this regard, this is a story concerning the gratitude of an old jackal: It is said that seven brothers were plowing a field. Among them, the very youngest stood at the edge of the field and guarded the cattle. Then a python seized an old jackal. Seeing this, he struck it with a stick and made it release the jackal. The python released the jackal and seized him instead. The jackal thought: 'My life was given by him; I too will give my life for him.' Gripping with its mouth an adze that was placed on top of a porridge pot, it went near him. The other brothers saw this and, thinking, 'The jackal is taking the adze!' they chased after it. It, knowing that it had been seen by them, dropped the adze near him and fled. The others came and, seeing their youngest brother seized by the python, cut the python with the adze, took him, and went away. Thus, even in an old jackal, there can be some gratitude and making known of a favor done. This statement, 'Sakyaputtiyapaṭiñña' (the claim of being a son of the Sakyans), was also spoken with reference only to the conduct of Devadatta. The twelfth.

Opammasaṃyuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Connected Discourses on Similes is concluded.

10. Bhikkhusaṃyuttaṃ

10. The Connected Discourses on Bhikkhus

1. Kolitasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Explanation of the Kolita Sutta

235. Bhikkhusaṃyuttassa [V 2.0206][P 2.0233][M 2.0214] paṭhame, āvusoti sāvakānaṃ ālāpo. Buddhā hi bhagavanto sāvake ālapantā, “bhikkhave”ti ālapanti, sāvakā pana “buddhehi sadisā mā homā”ti, “āvuso”ti paṭhamaṃ vatvā pacchā, “bhikkhave”ti bhaṇanti. Buddhehi ca ālapite bhikkhusaṅgho, “bhante”ti paṭivacanaṃ deti sāvakehi, “āvuso”ti. Ayaṃ vuccatīti yasmā dutiyajjhāne vitakkavicārā nirujjhanti, yesaṃ nirodhā saddāyatanaṃ appavattiṃ gacchati, tasmā yadetaṃ dutiyaṃ jhānaṃ nāma, ayaṃ vuccati “ariyānaṃ tuṇhībhāvo”ti. Ayamettha yojanā. “Dhammī vā kathā ariyo vā tuṇhībhāvo”ti ettha pana kammaṭṭhānamanasikāropi paṭhamajjhānādīnipi ariyo tuṇhībhāvotveva saṅkhaṃ gatāni.

235. In the first sutta of the Bhikkhusaṃyutta, 'āvuso' is the mode of address for disciples. Indeed, the Blessed Ones, the Buddhas, when addressing disciples, address them as 'bhikkhave'. But the disciples, thinking, 'May we not be like the Buddhas,' first say 'āvuso' and afterwards say 'bhikkhave'. And when addressed by the Buddhas, the community of bhikkhus gives the response 'bhante'; when addressed by disciples, they give the response 'āvuso'. As for 'this is called': because in the second jhāna initial and sustained thought cease, and due to their cessation the sound-base reaches non-arising, therefore this which is called the second jhāna is called 'the noble ones' silence'. This is the application here. However, in the context of 'Dhamma talk or noble silence', attending to the meditation subject and also the first jhāna and so on are also reckoned as 'noble silence'.

Vitakkasahagatāti vitakkārammaṇā. Saññāmanasikārāti saññā ca manasikāro ca. Samudācarantīti pavattanti. Therassa kira dutiyajjhānaṃ na paguṇaṃ. Athassa tato vuṭṭhitassa vitakkavicārā na santato upaṭṭhahiṃsu. Iccassa dutiyajjhānampi saññāmanasikārāpi hānabhāgiyāva ahesuṃ, taṃ dassento evamāha. Saṇṭhapehīti sammā ṭhapehi. Ekodibhāvaṃ karohīti ekaggaṃ karohi. Samādahāti sammā ādaha āropehi. Mahābhiññatanti chaḷabhiññataṃ. Satthā kira iminā upāyena satta divase therassa hānabhāgiyaṃ samādhiṃ vaḍḍhetvā theraṃ chaḷabhiññataṃ pāpesi. Paṭhamaṃ.

'Vitakkasahagatā' means having thought as its object. 'Saññāmanasikārā' means both perception and attention. 'Samudācaranti' means they occur. It is said that the Elder was not skilled in the second jhāna. Then, for him who had arisen from it, initial and sustained thought did not arise continuously. Thus, for him, both the second jhāna and perception-and-attention were factors of decline. To show this, he spoke thus: 'Saṇṭhapehi' means properly establish. 'Ekodibhāvaṃ karohi' means make one-pointed. 'Samādaha' means properly place or fix. 'Mahābhiññataṃ' refers to the state of the sixfold direct knowledge. It is said that the Teacher, by this method, over seven days, developed the Elder's concentration, which was a factor of decline, and caused the Elder to attain the state of the sixfold direct knowledge. The first.

2. Upatissasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Upatissa Sutta.

236. Dutiye [P 2.0234] atthi nu kho taṃ kiñci lokasminti idaṃ atiuḷārampi sattaṃ vā saṅkhāraṃ [V 2.0207] vā sandhāya vuttaṃ. Satthupi khoti idaṃ yasmā ānandattherassa satthari adhimatto chando ca pemañca, tasmā “kiṃ nu kho imassa therassa satthu vipariṇāmenapi sokādayo nuppajjeyyu”nti jānanatthaṃ pucchati? Dīgharattanti sūkarakhataleṇadvāre dīghanakhaparibbājakassa vedanāpariggahasuttantaṃ desitadivasato paṭṭhāya atikkantakālaṃ sandhāyāha. Tasmiñhi [M 2.0215] divase therassa ime vaṭṭānugatakilesā samūhatāti. Dutiyaṃ.

236. In the second sutta, the statement, 'Is there anything in the world?' was made referring to even a most excellent being or formation. As for the statement, 'Even regarding the Teacher,' because the Venerable Elder Ānanda had excessive fondness and affection for the Teacher, he therefore asked in order to know, 'What now? For this elder, would sorrow and the like not arise even with the Teacher's change and passing away?' As for 'For a long time,' he spoke referring to the time that had passed, starting from the day the Vedanāpariggaha Suttanta was taught to the wanderer Dīghanakha at the gate of the Sūkarakhata cave. For on that day, these defilements that follow along the round of existence were eradicated in the elder. The second.

3. Ghaṭasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Ghaṭa Sutta.

237. Tatiye ekavihāreti ekasmiṃ gabbhe. Tadā kira bahū āgantukā bhikkhū sannipatiṃsu. Tasmiṃ pariveṇaggena vā vihāraggena vā senāsanesu apāpuṇantesu dvinnaṃ therānaṃ eko gabbho sampatto. Te divā pāṭiyekkesu ṭhānesu nisīdanti, rattiṃ pana nesaṃ antare cīvarasāṇiṃ pasārenti. Te attano attano pattapattaṭṭhāneyeva nisīdanti. Tena vuttaṃ “ekavihāre”ti. Oḷārikenāti idaṃ oḷārikārammaṇataṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Dibbacakkhudibbasotadhātuvihārena hi so vihāsi, tesañca rūpāyatanasaddāyatanasaṅkhātaṃ oḷārikaṃ ārammaṇaṃ. Iti dibbacakkhunā rūpassa diṭṭhattā dibbāya ca sotadhātuyā saddassa sutattā so vihāro oḷāriko nāma jāto. Dibbacakkhu visujjhīti bhagavato rūpadassanatthāya visuddhaṃ ahosi. Dibbā ca sotadhātūti sāpi bhagavato saddasuṇanatthaṃ visujjhi[P 2.0235]. Bhagavatopi therassa rūpadassanatthañceva saddasuṇanatthañca tadubhayaṃ visujjhi. Tadā kira thero “kathaṃ nu kho etarahi satthā viharatī”ti ālokaṃ vaḍḍhetvā dibbena cakkhunā satthāraṃ jetavane vihāre gandhakuṭiyaṃ nisinnaṃ disvā tassa dibbāya sotadhātuyā saddaṃ suṇi. Satthāpi tatheva akāsi. Evaṃ te aññamaññaṃ passiṃsu ceva, saddañca assosuṃ.

237. In the third sutta, ekavihāre ('in one dwelling') means in a single chamber. It is said that at that time, many visiting monks had gathered. When lodgings, either by way of the surrounding cells or by way of the monastery, were insufficient, one chamber was obtained for the two elders. During the day, they would sit in separate places, but at night, they would spread a robe-curtain between them. They would stay, each in the place they had obtained. Therefore, it is said, 'in one dwelling.' As for oḷārikena, this was stated with reference to having a coarse object. For he dwelt by means of the abiding in the divine eye and the divine ear element, and their object, which is coarse, is what is called the form-base and the sound-base. Thus, because form was seen with the divine eye and sound was heard with the divine ear element, that abiding came to be called 'coarse.' Dibbacakkhu visujjhi ('the divine eye was purified') means it became pure for seeing the form of the Blessed One. And dibbā ca sotadhātu ('and the divine ear element') means that too became pure for hearing the voice of the Blessed One. For the Blessed One as well, both of those faculties became pure for seeing the elder's form and for hearing his voice. It is said that at that time, the elder, thinking, 'How indeed is the Teacher dwelling now?' having developed the light, saw the Teacher seated in the perfumed chamber in the Jetavana monastery with the divine eye and heard his voice with the divine ear element. The Teacher also did likewise. Thus, they saw each other and heard each other's voice.

Āraddhavīriyoti paripuṇṇavīriyo paggahitavīriyo. Yāvadeva upanikkhepanamattāyāti tiyojanasahassavitthārassa himavato santike ṭhapitā sāsapamattā pāsāṇasakkharā “himavā nu kho mahā, ayaṃ nu kho pāsāṇasakkharā”ti evaṃ yāva upanikkhepanamattasseva atthāya bhaveyyāti vuttaṃ hoti. Paratopi eseva nayo. Kappanti āyukappaṃ. Loṇaghaṭāyāti cakkavāḷamukhavaṭṭiyā ādhārakaṃ katvā mukhavaṭṭiyā brahmalokaṃ āhacca ṭhitāya loṇacāṭiyāti dasseti.

Āraddhavīriyo ('one with aroused energy') means one with complete energy, one with exerted energy. As for yāvadeva upanikkhepanamattāya ('just for the sake of placing it nearby'), it is said that if a mustard seed-sized stone-gravel were placed near the Himālaya, which extends for three thousand yojanas, it would be for the purpose of merely placing them near each other, as if to ask, 'Is the Himālaya great, or is this stone-gravel great?' This same method applies to the later instance as well. As for kappaṃ ('an aeon'), this refers to a life-aeon. As for loṇaghaṭāya ('of a salt jar'), this indicates a large salt pot that stands making the rim of the Cakkavāḷa its base, and with its opening rim touching the Brahma world.

Ime [V 2.0208][M 2.0216] pana therā upamaṃ āharantā sarikkhakeneva ca vijjamānaguṇena ca āhariṃsu. Kathaṃ? Ayañhi iddhi nāma accuggataṭṭhena ceva vipulaṭṭhena ca himavantasadisā, paññā catubhūmakadhamme anupavisitvā ṭhitaṭṭhena sabbabyañjanesu anupaviṭṭhaloṇarasasadisā. Evaṃ tāva sarikkhakaṭṭhena āhariṃsu. Samādhilakkhaṇaṃ pana mahāmoggallānattherassa vibhūtaṃ pākaṭaṃ. Kiñcāpi sāriputtattherassa avijjamānaiddhi nāma natthi, bhagavatā pana “etadaggaṃ, bhikkhave, mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ iddhimantānaṃ yadidaṃ mahāmoggallāno”ti ayameva etadagge ṭhapito. Vipassanālakkhaṇaṃ pana sāriputtattherassa vibhūtaṃ pākaṭaṃ. Kiñcāpi mahāmoggallānattherassāpi paññā atthi, bhagavatā pana “etadaggaṃ, bhikkhave, mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ mahāpaññānaṃ yadidaṃ sāriputto”ti (a. ni. 1.189) ayameva etadagge ṭhapito. Tasmā yathā ete aññamaññassa dhuraṃ na pāpuṇanti, evaṃ vijjamānaguṇena āhariṃsu. Samādhilakkhaṇasmiñhi mahāmoggallāno nipphattiṃ gato, vipassanālakkhaṇe sāriputtatthero, dvīsupi etesu sammāsambuddhoti. Tatiyaṃ.

Furthermore, these elders, in presenting the simile, did so based on both similarity and existing qualities. How so? This psychic power, by its nature of being extremely lofty and vast, is like the Himālaya. Wisdom, by its nature of having penetrated and being established in the dhammas of the four planes, is like the taste of salt that has permeated all curries. Thus, firstly, they presented it based on similarity. The characteristic of concentration, moreover, was manifest and clear in the Elder Mahāmoggallāna. Although it is not that the Elder Sāriputta lacked psychic power, the Blessed One declared, 'Monks, among my disciples who are monks possessing psychic powers, Mahāmoggallāna is foremost.' Thus, he alone was placed in that foremost position. The characteristic of insight, moreover, was manifest and clear in the Elder Sāriputta. Although the Elder Mahāmoggallāna also possessed wisdom, the Blessed One declared, 'Monks, among my disciples who are monks of great wisdom, Sāriputta is foremost.' Thus, he alone was placed in that foremost position. Therefore, just as these two did not reach the primary role of the other, so they presented the simile based on existing qualities. For in the characteristic of concentration, Mahāmoggallāna attained perfection; in the characteristic of insight, the Elder Sāriputta attained perfection; and in both of these, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One attained perfection. The third.

4. Navasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Nava Sutta

238. Catutthe [P 2.0236] appossukkoti nirussukko. Saṅkasāyatīti viharati. Veyyāvaccanti cīvare kattabbakiccaṃ. Ābhicetasikānanti abhicittaṃ uttamacittaṃ nissitānaṃ. Nikāmalābhīti icchiticchitakkhaṇe samāpajjanasamatthatāya nikāmalābhī. Akicchalābhīti jhānapāripanthike sukhena vikkhambhetvā samāpajjanasamatthatāya adukkhalābhī. Akasiralābhīti yathāparicchedena vuṭṭhānasamatthatāya vipulalābhī, paguṇajjhānoti attho. Sithilamārabbhāti sithilavīriyaṃ pavattetvā. Catutthaṃ.

238. In the fourth, appossukko ('unconcerned') means free from agitation. Saṅkasāyati means 'he dwells.' Veyyāvaccaṃ ('service') refers to duties to be performed regarding robes. Ābhicetasikānaṃ ('of those devoted to the higher mind') refers to those who rely on the higher, supreme mind. Nikāmalābhī ('one who obtains at will') means one who obtains at will due to being capable of attaining it at any moment wished. Akicchalābhī ('one who obtains without difficulty') means one who obtains without hardship, being capable of attaining it by easily suppressing the obstacles to jhāna. Akasiralābhī ('one who obtains without trouble') means one who obtains abundantly, being capable of rising from it according to a set determination; the meaning is one skilled in jhāna. Sithilamārabbha ('having started slackly') means having exerted slack energy. The fourth.

5. Sujātasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Sujāta Sutta

239. Pañcame abhirūpoti aññāni rūpāni atikkantarūpo. Dassanīyoti daṭṭhabbayutto. Pāsādikoti dassanena cittaṃ pasādetuṃ samattho. Vaṇṇapokkharatāyāti chavivaṇṇasundaratāya. Pañcamaṃ.

239. In the fifth, abhirūpo ('handsome') means one whose form surpasses other forms. Dassanīyo ('pleasing to see') means fit to be seen. Pāsādiko ('inspiring confidence') means capable of gladdening the mind by being seen. Vaṇṇapokkharatāya ('by the beauty of complexion') means by the loveliness of the skin's color. The fifth.

6. Lakuṇḍakabhaddiyasuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Lakuṇḍakabhaddiya Sutta

240. Chaṭṭhe [V 2.0209][M 2.0217] dubbaṇṇanti virūpasarīravaṇṇaṃ. Okoṭimakanti rassaṃ. Paribhūtarūpanti pamāṇavasena paribhūtajātikaṃ. Taṃ kira chabbaggiyā bhikkhū, “āvuso bhaddiya, āvuso, bhaddiyā”ti tattha tattha parāmasitvā nānappakāraṃ kīḷanti ākaḍḍhanti parikaḍḍhanti. Tena vuttaṃ “paribhūtarūpa”nti. Kasmā panesa evarūpo jāto? Ayaṃ kira atīte eko mahārājā ahosi, tassa mahallakā ca mahallakitthiyo ca paṭikūlā honti. So sace mahallake passati, tesaṃ [P 2.0237] cūḷaṃ ṭhapāpetvā kacchaṃ bandhāpetvā yathāruci kīḷāpeti. Mahallakitthiyopi disvā tāsampi icchiticchitaṃ vippakāraṃ katvā yathāruci kīḷāpeti. Tesaṃ puttadhītādīnaṃ santike mahāsārajjaṃ uppajjati. Tassa pāpakiriyā pathavito paṭṭhāya chadevaloke ekakolāhalaṃ akāsi.

240. In the sixth, dubbaṇṇaṃ ('ugly') means having an unattractive body and complexion. Okoṭimakaṃ ('dwarfish') means short. Paribhūtarūpaṃ ('of despised form') means of a nature to be despised on account of his size. It is said that the group-of-six monks, calling out, 'Friend Bhaddiya, friend Bhaddiya,' would touch him here and there and play in various ways, pulling him towards them and dragging him about. For that reason, it was said 'of despised form.' But why was he born with such a form? It is said that in a past life, this one was a great king to whom old men and old women were repulsive. If he saw old men, he would have their topknots tied up, have them wear a loincloth, and make them play as he pleased. Seeing old women, too, he would do various improper things to them as he wished and make them play as he pleased. Great shame arose in them in the presence of their sons, daughters, and others. His evil action caused a single great uproar extending from the earth up to the six deva realms.

Atha sakko cintesi – “ayaṃ andhabālo mahājanaṃ viheṭheti, karissāmissa niggaha”nti. So mahallakagāmiyavaṇṇaṃ katvā yānake ekaṃ takkacāṭiṃ āropetvā yānaṃ pesento nagaraṃ pavisati. Rājāpi hatthiṃ āruyha nagarato nikkhanto taṃ disvā – “ayaṃ mahallako takkayānakena amhākaṃ abhimukho āgacchati, vāretha vārethā”ti āha. Manussā ito cito ca pakkhandantāpi na passanti. Sakko hi “rājāva maṃ passatu, mā aññe”ti evaṃ adhiṭṭhahi. Atha tesu manussesu “kahaṃ, deva, kahaṃ devā”ti vadantesu eva rājā saha hatthinā vaccho viya dhenuyā yānassa heṭṭhā pāvisi. Sakko takkacāṭiṃ bhindi.

Then Sakka thought, 'This blind fool is harassing the people; I will inflict punishment on him.' Assuming the appearance of an old villager, he placed a single pot of buttermilk on a small cart and, driving the cart, entered the city. The king, having mounted an elephant, had left the city when he saw him and said, 'This old man is coming toward us with a buttermilk cart. Stop him, stop him!' The people rushed here and there but could not see him. For Sakka had resolved, 'Only the king shall see me, no one else.' Then, as the people were saying, 'Where, O king? Where, O king?' the king, along with his elephant, went beneath the cart like a calf beneath a cow. Sakka broke the pot of buttermilk.

Rājā sīsato paṭṭhāya takkena kilinnasarīro ahosi. So sarīraṃ ubbaṭṭāpetvā uyyānapokkharaṇiyaṃ nhatvā alaṅkatasarīro nagaraṃ pavisanto puna taṃ addasa. Disvā “ayaṃ so amhehi diṭṭhamahallako puna dissati. Vāretha vāretha na”nti āha. Manussā “kahaṃ, deva, kahaṃ, devā”ti ito cito ca vidhāviṃsu. So paṭhamavippakārameva puna pāpuṇi. Tasmiṃ khaṇe sakko goṇe ca yānañca antaradhāpetvā ākāse [M 2.0218] ṭhatvā āha, “andhabāla, tvaṃ mayi takkavāṇijako eso”ti saññaṃ karosi, sakkohaṃ devarājā, “tavetaṃ pāpakiriyaṃ nivāressāmī”ti āgato, “mā puna evarūpaṃ akāsī”ti santajjetvā agamāsi. Iminā kammena so dubbaṇṇo ahosi.

The king, from his head down, was drenched with buttermilk. After having his body rubbed down, he bathed in the royal garden pond and, adorned, was entering the city when he again saw that man. Seeing him, he said, 'This is that same old man we saw before; he is seen again. Stop him, stop him!' The people, saying, 'Where, O king? Where, O king?' ran here and there. He again met with the same mistreatment as before. At that moment, Sakka made the oxen and the cart disappear and, standing in the sky, said, 'Foolish blind man, you perceive me as a seller of buttermilk. I am Sakka, king of the gods. I have come to prevent this evil deed of yours. Do not do such a thing again!' Having thus threatened him, he departed. Because of this deed, he became ill-favored.

Vipassīsammāsambuddhakāle [V 2.0210] panesa cittapattakokilo nāma hutvā kheme migadāye vasanto ekadivasaṃ himavantaṃ gantvā madhuraṃ ambaphalaṃ tuṇḍena gahetvā āgacchanto bhikkhusaṅghaparivāraṃ satthāraṃ disvā cintesi – “ahaṃ aññesu divasesu rittako tathāgataṃ passāmi. Ajja pana me imaṃ ambapakkaṃ atthi, dasabalassa taṃ dassāmī”ti otaritvā ākāse carati. Satthā tassa cittaṃ ñatvā upaṭṭhākaṃ [P 2.0238] olokesi. So pattaṃ nīharitvā dasabalaṃ vanditvā satthu hatthe ṭhapesi. Kokilo dasabalassa patte ambapakkaṃ patiṭṭhāpesi. Satthā tattheva nisīditvā taṃ paribhuñji. Kokilo pasannacitto punappunaṃ dasabalassa guṇe āvajjetvā dasabalaṃ vanditvā attano kulāvakaṃ gantvā sattāhaṃ pītisukheneva vītināmesi. Iminā kammena saro madhuro ahosi.

Furthermore, during the time of the Perfectly Enlightened Buddha Vipassī, this one had become a cuckoo with variegated wings and was living in the Khemā deer park. One day, having gone to the Himālaya, he took a sweet, ripe mango in his beak and was returning when he saw the Teacher surrounded by the community of monks. He thought: 'On other days, I see the Tathāgata empty-handed. But today I have this ripe mango. I will give it to the One of Ten Powers.' Descending, he moved through the sky. The Teacher, knowing his thought, looked at his attendant. The attendant brought out the bowl, paid homage to the One of Ten Powers, and placed it in the Teacher's hand. The cuckoo placed the ripe mango in the bowl of the One of Ten Powers. The Teacher sat right there and partook of it. The cuckoo, with a confident mind, repeatedly reflected on the qualities of the One of Ten Powers, paid homage to the One of Ten Powers, went to his own nest, and passed seven days in bliss and happiness alone. Through this deed, his voice became sweet.

Kassapasammāsambuddhakāle pana cetiye āraddhe “kiṃpamāṇaṃ karoma? Sattayojanappamāṇaṃ. Atimahantaṃ etaṃ, chayojanappamāṇaṃ karoma. Idampi atimahantaṃ, pañcayojanaṃ karoma, catuyojanaṃ, tiyojanaṃ, dviyojana”nti. Ayaṃ tadā jeṭṭhakavaḍḍhakī hutvā, “evaṃ, bho, anāgate sukhapaṭijaggitaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vatvā rajjuṃ ādāya parikkhipanto gāvutamattake ṭhatvā, “ekekaṃ mukhaṃ gāvutaṃ hotu, cetiyaṃ yojanāvaṭṭaṃ yojanubbedhaṃ bhavissatī”ti āha. Te tassa vacane aṭṭhaṃsu. Cetiyaṃ sattadivasasattamāsādhikehi sattahi saṃvaccharehi niṭṭhitaṃ. Iti appamāṇassa buddhassa pamāṇaṃ akāsīti. Tena kammena okoṭimako jāto.

Furthermore, during the time of Kassapa, the Perfectly Enlightened One, when a cetiya was being started, they discussed, 'What size shall we make it? Seven yojanas. That is too large. Let us make it six yojanas. This too is too large. Let us make it five yojanas, four yojanas, three yojanas, two yojanas.' At that time, this one, being the chief carpenter, said, 'Sirs, it is proper to make it easy to maintain in the future.' And taking a measuring rope, he marked out the measure of a gāvuta and said, 'Let each face be a gāvuta; the cetiya will be a yojana in circumference and a yojana in height.' They abided by his words. The cetiya was completed in seven years, seven months, and seven days. Thus, he set a measure for the immeasurable Buddha. Because of that deed, he was born a dwarf.

Hatthayo pasadā migāti hatthino ca pasadamigā ca. Natthi kāyasmiṃ tulyatāti kāyasmiṃ pamāṇaṃ nāma natthi, akāraṇaṃ kāyapamāṇanti attho. Chaṭṭhaṃ.

'Elephants and pasada deer' means elephants and pasada deer. 'There is no equality in the body' means there is no such thing as a standard measure in the body; the measure of the body is not a cause. This is the meaning. The Sixth.

7. Visākhasuttavaṇṇanā

7. The Commentary on the Visākha Sutta

241. Sattame [M 2.0219] poriyā vācāyāti puravāsīnaṃ nagaramanussānaṃ vācāsadisāya aparihīnakkharapadāya madhuravācāya. Vissaṭṭhāyāti asandiddhāya apalibuddhāya, pittasemhehi [P 2.0239] anupahatāyāti attho. Anelagalāyāti yathā dandhamanussā mukhena kheḷaṃ gaḷantena vācaṃ bhāsanti, na evarūpāya, atha kho niddosāya visadavācāya. Pariyāpannāyāti catusaccapariyāpannāya [V 2.0211] cattāri saccāni amuñcitvā pavattāya. Anissitāyāti vaṭṭanissitaṃ katvā akathitāya. Dhammo hi isinaṃ dhajoti navavidhalokuttaradhammo isīnaṃ dhajo nāmāti. Sattamaṃ.

241. In the seventh, 'by urbane speech' means by sweet speech, similar to the speech of city-dwellers, with undiminished letters and words. 'Clear' means unambiguous, unconfused; that is, unaffected by bile and phlegm—this is the meaning. 'Without slurring' means not like the way slow-witted people speak with saliva dripping from their mouths, but rather with faultless, clear speech. 'Included' means included in the four truths, proceeding without abandoning the four truths. 'Unattached' means not spoken by making it dependent on the round of existence. 'For the Dhamma is the banner of the seers' means the ninefold supramundane Dhamma is called the banner of the seers. The Seventh.

8. Nandasuttavaṇṇanā

8. The Commentary on the Nanda Sutta

242. Aṭṭhame ākoṭitapaccākoṭitānīti ekasmiṃ passe pāṇinā vā muggarena vā ākoṭanena ākoṭitāni, parivattetvā ākoṭanena paccākoṭitāni. Añjetvāti añjanena pūretvā. Acchaṃ pattanti vippasannavaṇṇaṃ mattikāpattaṃ. Kasmā pana thero evamakāsīti? Satthu ajjhāsayajānanatthaṃ. Evaṃ kirassa ahosi “sace satthā ‘sobhati vata me ayaṃ kaniṭṭhabhātiko’ti vakkhati, yāvajīvaṃ iminā vākārena carissāmi. Sace ettha dosaṃ dassati, imaṃ ākāraṃ pahāya saṅkāracoḷaṃ gahetvā cīvaraṃ katvā dhārento pariyantasenāsane vasanto carissāmī”ti. Assasīti bhavissasi.

242. In the eighth, 'beaten and beaten again' means beaten on one side with the hand or a mallet, and then turned over and beaten again. 'Having anointed' means having filled with unguent. 'A clear bowl' means a clay bowl with an especially clear color. But why did the elder act in this way? To know the Teacher's intention. It is said he thought thus: 'If the Teacher says, "How splendid is this younger brother of mine!", I will conduct myself in this manner for as long as I live. If he points out a fault in this, I will abandon this manner, take a rag from a rubbish heap, make it into a robe, and wearing it, I will conduct myself while living in a remote dwelling.'

Aññātuñchenāti abhilakkhitesu issarajanagehesu kaṭukabhaṇḍasambhāraṃ sugandhaṃ bhojanaṃ pariyesantassa uñcho ñātuñcho nāma. Gharapaṭipāṭiyā pana dvāre ṭhitena laddhaṃ missakabhojanaṃ aññātuñcho nāma. Ayamidha adhippeto. Kāmesu anapekkhinanti vatthukāmakilesakāmesu nirapekkhaṃ. Āraññiko cātiādi sabbaṃ samādānavaseneva vuttaṃ. Kāmesu ca anapekkhoti idaṃ suttaṃ devaloke accharāyo dassetvā āgatena aparabhāge kathitaṃ. Imassa kathitadivasato paṭṭhāya thero ghaṭento vāyamanto katipāheneva arahatte patiṭṭhāya sadevake loke aggadakkhiṇeyyo jāto. Aṭṭhamaṃ.

`Aññātuñchena` (by unknown alms-gathering): The alms-gathering of one who seeks fragrant food prepared with an assortment of pungent items in the distinguished houses of powerful people is called `ñātuñcho` (known alms-gathering). However, the alms-gathering of one who seeks mixed food obtained by standing at the door while going from house to house in order is called `aññātuñcho` (unknown alms-gathering). This latter one is intended here. `Kāmesu anapekkhinaṃ` (indifferent to sensual pleasures) means indifferent to sensual pleasures of the object-kind and sensual pleasures of the defilement-kind. All of this, beginning with `Āraññiko ca` (and a forest-dweller), was said only by way of undertaking the ascetic practices. This sutta, `Kāmesu ca anapekkho` (And indifferent to sensual pleasures), was taught in a later part by the Blessed One after he had returned from showing the celestial nymphs in the deva world. Starting from the day this was taught, the elder, striving and making an effort, in just a few days was established in arahantship and became the foremost of those worthy of offerings in the world with its devas. Eighth.

9. Tissasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Tissa Sutta

243. Navame [M 2.0220][P 2.0240] dummanoti uppannadomanasso. Kasmā panāyaṃ evaṃ dukkhī dummano jātoti? Khattiyapabbajito hesa, tena naṃ pabbājetvā dupaṭṭasāṭakaṃ nivāsāpetvā varacīvaraṃ pārupetvā akkhīni añjetvā manosilātelena sīsaṃ makkhesuṃ. So bhikkhūsu rattiṭṭhānadivāṭṭhānaṃ gatesu “bhikkhunā nāma vivittokāse nisīditabba”nti ajānanto bhojanasālaṃ gantvā mahāpīṭhaṃ āruhitvā nisīdi. Disāvacarā āgantukā paṃsukūlikā bhikkhū āgantvā, “imināva [V 2.0212] nīhārena rajokiṇṇehi gattehi na sakkā dasabalaṃ passituṃ. Bhaṇḍakaṃ tāva ṭhapessāmā”ti bhojanasālaṃ agamaṃsu. So tesu mahātheresu āgacchantesu niccalo nisīdiyeva. Aññe bhikkhū “pādavattaṃ karoma, tālavaṇṭena bījāmā”ti āpucchanti. Ayaṃ pana nisinnakova “kativassatthā”ti? Pucchitvā, “mayaṃ avassikā. Tumhe pana kativassatthā”ti? Vutte, “mayaṃ ajja pabbajitā”ti āha. Atha naṃ bhikkhū, “āvuso, adhunā chinnacūḷosi, ajjāpi te sīsamūle ūkāgandho vāyatiyeva, tvaṃ nāma ettakesu vuḍḍhataresu vattaṃ āpucchantesu nissaddo niccalo nisinno, apacitimattampi te natthi, kassa sāsane pabbajitosī”ti? Parivāretvā taṃ vācāsattīhi paharantā “kiṃ tvaṃ iṇaṭṭo vā bhayaṭṭo vā jīvituṃ asakkonto pabbajito”ti? Āhaṃsu. So ekampi theraṃ olokesi, tena “kiṃ maṃ olokesi mahallakā”ti? Vutte aññaṃ olokesi, tenapi tatheva vutte athassa “ime maṃ parivāretvā vācāsattīhi vijjhantī”ti khattiyamāno uppajji. Akkhīsu maṇivaṇṇāni assūni sañcariṃsu. Tato ne āha – “kassa santikaṃ āgatatthā”ti. Te “kiṃ pana tvaṃ ‘mayhaṃ santikaṃ āgatā’ti? Amhe maññasi gihibyañjanabhaṭṭhakā”ti vatvā, “sadevake loke aggapuggalassa satthu santikaṃ āgatamhā”ti āhaṃsu. So “mayhaṃ bhātu santike āgatā tumhe, yadi evaṃ idāni vo āgatamaggeneva gamanaṃ [P 2.0241] karissāmī”ti kujjhitvā nikkhanto antarāmagge cintesi – “mayi imināva nīhārena gate satthā ete na nīharāpessatī”ti dukkhī dummano assūni pavattayamāno agamāsi. Iminā kāraṇena esa evaṃ jātoti.

243. In the ninth, 'dummano' (distressed) means one with an arisen displeasure of the heart. Why then did this one become so miserable and distressed? Because he was one who had gone forth from the royal caste. Therefore, having ordained him, they had him wear a double-layered lower garment, had him put on a superior robe, applied collyrium to his eyes, and anointed his head with realgar oil. When the monks had gone to their places for the night and for the day, he, not knowing that 'a monk should sit in a secluded place,' went to the dining hall, ascended a large seat, and sat down. Visiting rag-robe-wearing monks, who had come from other regions, arrived and thinking, 'It is not possible to see the One with Ten Powers with our bodies covered in dust in this very condition. Let us first put down our requisites,' they went to the dining hall. When those great elders were approaching, he remained seated without moving. Other monks asked, 'Shall we perform the duty of washing the feet? Shall we fan with a palm-leaf fan?' But this one, remaining seated, asked, 'How many rains-retreats do you have?' When they replied, 'We do not yet have a rains-retreat. But you, how many rains-retreats do you have?' he said, 'We were ordained today.' Then the monks said to him, 'Friend, you are with a freshly shorn top-knot; even now the smell of lice wafts from the base of your head. While so many more senior monks are asking to perform their duties, you sit silent and unmoving. You have not even a particle of respect. In whose dispensation have you gone forth?' Surrounding him and striking him with verbal spears, they said, 'Have you gone forth because you were oppressed by debt, or oppressed by fear, or unable to make a living?' He looked at one elder. When that one said, 'Why do you look at me, old man?' he looked at another. When that one also said the same thing, the thought arose in him, 'These monks have surrounded me and are piercing me with verbal spears,' and his royal pride arose. Tears the color of gems circulated in his eyes. Then he said to them, 'To whose presence have you come?' They replied, 'What, do you think we have come to your presence, you who have merely shed the appearance of a layman? We have come to the presence of the Teacher, the foremost person in the world with its gods.' He, becoming angry, said, 'You have come to my brother's presence. If so, I will now make you go back by the very path you came.' Having departed, he thought on the way, 'If I go in this manner, the Teacher will not have these monks expelled.' Miserable and distressed, letting tears flow, he went on. For this reason, he became thus.

Vācāsannitodakenāti [M 2.0221] vacanapatodena. Sañjambharimakaṃsūti sañjambharitaṃ nirantaraṃ phuṭaṃ akaṃsu, upari vijjhiṃsūti vuttaṃ hoti. Vattāti pare yadicchakaṃ vadatiyeva. No ca vacanakkhamoti paresaṃ vacanaṃ khamituṃ na sakkoti. Idāni tāva tvaṃ iminā kopena iminā vuttavācāsannitodakena viddho. Atīte pana raṭṭhato ca pabbājitoti. Evaṃ vutte, “katarasmiṃ kāle bhagavā”ti? Bhikkhū bhagavantaṃ yāciṃsu.

By `vācāsannitodakena` is meant by the goad that is speech. As for `sañjambharimakaṃsu`, it means they made continuous contact, they pierced from above; thus it is said. As for `vattā` (a speaker), it means others speak whatever they wish. As for `no ca vacanakkhamo`, it means one is not able to endure the speech of others. Now you are pierced by this anger, by this aforementioned goad of speech. But in the past, you were banished from the country. When this was said, the monks requested of the Blessed One, 'At what time, Blessed One?'

Satthā āha – atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ bārāṇasirājā rajjaṃ kāresi. Atheko jātimā, eko mātaṅgoti dve isayo bārāṇasiṃ agamaṃsu. Tesu jātimā puretaraṃ gantvā kumbhakārasālāyaṃ nisīdi. Mātaṅgo tāpaso pacchā gantvā tattha okāsaṃ yāci kumbhakāro “atthettha paṭhamataraṃ [V 2.0213] paviṭṭho pabbajito, taṃ pucchā”ti āha. So attano parikkhāraṃ gahetvā sālāya dvāramūle ṭhatvā, “amhākampi ācariya ekarattivāsāya okāsaṃ dethā”ti āha. “Pavisa, bho”ti. Pavisitvā nisinnaṃ, “bho, kiṃ gottosī”ti? Pucchi. “Caṇḍālagottomhī”ti. “Na sakkā tayā saddhiṃ ekaṭṭhāne nisīdituṃ, ekamantaṃ gacchā”ti. So ca tattheva tiṇasanthārakaṃ pattharitvā nipajji, jātimā dvāraṃ nissāya nipajji. Itaro passāvatthāya nikkhamanto taṃ urasmiṃ akkami. “Ko eso”ti ca vutte? “Ahaṃ ācariyā”ti āha. “Re caṇḍāla, kiṃ aññato maggaṃ na passasi? Atha me āgantvā akkamasī”ti. “Ācariya, adisvā me akkantosi, khama mayha”nti. So mahāpurise bahi nikkhante cintesi – “ayaṃ paccāgacchantopi itova āgamissatī”ti parivattetvā nipajji. Mahāpurisopi “ācariyo ito sīsaṃ katvā nipanno, pādasamīpena gamissāmī”ti pavisanto puna urasmiṃyeva akkami. “Ko [P 2.0242] eso”ti ca vutte? “Ahaṃ ācariyā”ti āha. “Paṭhamaṃ tāva te ajānantena kataṃ, idāni maṃ ghaṭentova akāsi, sūriye te uggacchante sattadhā muddhā phalatū”ti sapi. Mahāpuriso kiñci avatvā purearuṇeyeva sūriyaṃ gaṇhi, nāssa uggantuṃ adāsi. Manussā ca hatthiassādayo ca pabujjhiṃsu.

The Teacher said: In the past, in Bārāṇasī, the king of Bārāṇasī was ruling the kingdom. Then two ascetics, one of high birth named Jātimā and one named Mātaṅga, went to Bārāṇasī. Of the two, Jātimā went first and sat down in a potter's hall. The ascetic Mātaṅga, arriving later, asked for a space there. The potter said, 'There is a renunciant who entered here first; ask him.' So he took his own requisites, stood at the door of the hall, and said, 'Teacher, please give me also space to stay for one night.' 'Enter, sir.' After he had entered and was seated, Jātimā asked, 'Sir, what is your clan?' 'I am of the Caṇḍāla clan.' 'It is not possible to sit in the same place with you. Go to one side.' And so Mātaṅga spread out a grass mat right there and lay down. Jātimā lay down near the door. The other one, Mātaṅga, while going out to urinate, stepped on Jātimā's chest. When Jātimā said, 'Who is that?' Mātaṅga replied, 'It is I, teacher.' 'Hey, Caṇḍāla, do you not see another way? And yet you come and step on me.' 'Teacher, I stepped on you without seeing; please forgive me.' When the Great Being had gone outside, Jātimā thought, 'When this one returns, he will come from this very direction,' and so he turned around and lay down. The Great Being, thinking, 'The teacher is lying with his head in this direction; I will go by way of his feet,' entered and again stepped on his chest. When Jātimā said, 'Who is that?' Mātaṅga replied, 'It is I, teacher.' 'The first time, you did it unknowingly, but now you have done it while vexing me! When the sun rises, may your head split into seven pieces!' he cursed. The Great Being said nothing, but just before dawn, he seized the sun and did not allow it to rise. The people, and the elephants, horses, and other animals, awoke.

Manussā [M 2.0222] rājakulaṃ gantvā, “deva, sakalanagare appabuddho nāma natthi, na ca aruṇuggaṃ paññāyati, kinnu kho eta”nti? Tena hi nagaraṃ parivīmaṃsathāti. Te parivīmaṃsantā kumbhakārasālāyaṃ dve tāpase disvā, “imesaṃ etaṃ kammaṃ bhavissatī”ti gantvā rañño ārocesuṃ. Raññā ca “pucchatha ne”ti vuttā āgantvā jātimantaṃ pucchiṃsu – “tumhehi andhakāraṃ kata”nti. “Na mayā kataṃ, esa pana kūṭajaṭilo chavo anantamāyo, taṃ pucchathā”ti. Te āgantvā mahāpurisaṃ pucchiṃsu – “tumhehi, bhante, andhakāraṃ kata”nti. “Āma ayaṃ ācariyo maṃ abhisapi, tasmā mayā kata”nti. Te gantvā rañño ārocesuṃ. Rājāpi āgantvā mahāpurisaṃ “tumhehi kataṃ, bhante”ti? Pucchi. “Āma, mahārājā”ti. “Kasmā bhante”ti? “Iminā abhisapitomhi, sace maṃ eso khamāpessati, sūriyaṃ vissajjessāmī”ti. Rājā “khamāpetha, bhante, eta”nti āha. Itaro “mādiso jātimā kiṃ evarūpaṃ caṇḍālaṃ khamāpessati? Na khamāpemī”ti.
