The people went to the royal court and said, 'Your Majesty, in the entire city, there is no one who is not awake, and the dawn is not apparent. What could this be?' 'In that case, investigate the city.' While investigating, they saw two ascetics in the potter's hall and thought, 'This must be their doing.' They went and reported to the king. And having been told by the king, 'Question them,' they came and asked Jātimanta, 'Was the darkness made by you?' 'It was not made by me. But this deceitful, matted-haired ascetic is a vile person of infinite trickery. Ask him.' They came and asked the Great Being, 'Venerable Sir, was the darkness made by you?' 'Yes. This teacher cursed me; therefore, it was made by me.' They went and reported to the king. The king also came and asked the Great Being, 'Venerable Sir, was this made by you?' 'Yes, Great King.' 'For what reason, Venerable Sir?' 'I was cursed by this one. If he asks for my forgiveness, I will release the sun.' The king said, 'Venerable Sir, ask forgiveness of him.' The other said, 'How could one like me, a man of high birth, ask forgiveness of such a caṇḍāla? I will not ask for forgiveness.'

Atha naṃ manussā “na kiṃ tvaṃ attano ruciyā khamāpessasī”ti? Vatvā hatthesu ca pādesu [V 2.0214] ca gahetvā pādamūle nipajjāpetvā “khamāpehī”ti āhaṃsu. So nissaddo nipajji. Punapi naṃ “khamāpehī”ti āhaṃsu. Tato “khama mayhaṃ, ācariyā”ti āha. Mahāpuriso “ahaṃ tāva tuyhaṃ khamitvā sūriyaṃ vissajjessāmi, sūriye pana uggate tava sīsaṃ sattadhā phalissatī”ti vatvā, “imassa sīsappamāṇaṃ mattikāpiṇḍaṃ matthake ṭhapetvā etaṃ nadiyā galappamāṇe udake ṭhapethā”ti āha. Manussā tathā akaṃsu. Ettāvatā saraṭṭhakaṃ rājabalaṃ sannipati. Mahāpuriso sūriyaṃ muñci. Sūriyarasmi āgantvā mattikāpiṇḍaṃ pahari. So sattadhā bhijji. Tāvadeva so nimujjitvā ekena titthena uttaritvā palāyi. Satthā [P 2.0243] imaṃ vatthuṃ āharitvā, “idāni tāva tvaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ santike paribhāsaṃ labhasi, pubbepi imaṃ kodhaṃ nissāya raṭṭhato pabbājito”ti anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā atha naṃ ovadanto na kho te taṃ tissa patirūpantiādimāha. Navamaṃ.

Then the people said to him, 'Will you not ask for forgiveness of your own accord?' Having said this, they seized him by the hands and feet, made him lie down at the Great Being's feet, and said, 'Ask for forgiveness!' He lay there silent. Again they said to him, 'Ask for forgiveness!' Then he said, 'Forgive me, teacher.' The Great Being said, 'First, I will forgive you and release the sun; but when the sun rises, your head will split into seven pieces.' Having said this, he instructed, 'Place a lump of clay the size of his head on his head, and then place him in the river in water up to his neck.' The people did so. At that point, the royal army from the entire country had gathered. The Great Being released the sun. A ray of the sun came and struck the lump of clay, and it shattered into seven pieces. At that very moment, that ascetic dived under the water, emerged at a landing place, and fled. The Teacher, having related this story and made the connection, said: 'Now, you receive censure in the presence of the monks; in a past life too, on account of this anger, you were banished from the country.' Then, admonishing him, he spoke the words beginning with, 'This is not fitting for you, Tissa...' The ninth.

10. Theranāmakasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Theranāmaka Sutta

244. Dasame vaṇṇavādīti ānisaṃsavādī. Yaṃ atītaṃ taṃ pahīnanti atīte khandhapañcake chandarāgappahānena taṃ pahīnaṃ nāma hoti. Anāgatanti anāgatampi khandhapañcakaṃ tattha chandarāgapaṭinissaggena paṭinissaṭṭhaṃ nāma hoti[M 2.0223]. Sabbābhibhunti sabbā khandhāyatanadhātuyo ca tayo bhave ca abhibhavitvā ṭhitaṃ. Sabbavidunti taṃ vuttappakāraṃ sabbaṃ viditaṃ pākaṭaṃ katvā ṭhitaṃ. Sabbesu dhammesūti tesveva dhammesu taṇhādiṭṭhilepehi anupalittaṃ. Sabbañjahanti tadeva sabbaṃ tattha chandarāgappahānena jahitvā ṭhitaṃ. Taṇhakkhaye vimuttanti taṇhakkhayasaṅkhāte nibbāne tadārammaṇāya vimuttiyā vimuttaṃ. Dasamaṃ.

244. In the tenth, 'one who speaks praise' means one who speaks of benefits. 'What is past is abandoned' means the past five aggregates are called 'abandoned' by the abandonment of desire and lust in regard to them. 'The future' means the future five aggregates are also called 'relinquished' by the relinquishment of desire and lust in regard to them. 'The conqueror of all' means one who stands having overcome all aggregates, sense bases, elements, and the three kinds of existence. 'The all-knower' means one who stands having made all that has been described known and manifest. 'In all phenomena' means unsmeared by the stains of craving and views in those very phenomena. 'Having abandoned all' means one who stands having abandoned all that by the abandonment of desire and lust in regard to it. 'Liberated in the destruction of craving' means liberated by the liberation that has Nibbāna, which is known as 'the destruction of craving,' as its object. The tenth.

11. Mahākappinasuttavaṇṇanā

11. Commentary on the Mahākappina Sutta

245. Ekādasame mahākappinoti evaṃnāmako abhiññābalappatto asītimahāsāvakānaṃ abbhantaro mahāthero. So kira gihikāle kukkuṭavatīnagare tiyojanasatikaṃ rajjaṃ akāsi. Pacchimabhavikattā pana tathārūpaṃ sāsanaṃ sotuṃ ohitasoto vicarati. Athekadivasaṃ amaccasahassaparivuto uyyānakīḷikaṃ agamāsi. Tadā ca majjhimadesato jaṅghavāṇijā taṃ nagaraṃ gantvā, bhaṇḍaṃ paṭisāmetvā, “rājānaṃ passissāmā”ti paṇṇākārahatthā rājakuladvāraṃ gantvā, “rājā [V 2.0215] uyyānaṃ gato”ti sutvā, uyyānaṃ gantvā, dvāre ṭhitā, paṭihārassa ārocayiṃsu. Atha rañño nivedite rājā pakkosāpetvā niyyātitapaṇṇākāre vanditvā ṭhite, “tātā, kuto [P 2.0244] āgatatthā”ti? Pucchi. “Sāvatthito devā”ti. “Kacci vo raṭṭhaṃ subhikkhaṃ, dhammiko rājā”ti? “Āma, devā”ti. “Atthi pana tumhākaṃ dese kiñci sāsana”nti? “Atthi, deva, na pana sakkā ucchiṭṭhamukhehi kathetu”nti. Rājā suvaṇṇabhiṅgārena udakaṃ dāpesi. Te mukhaṃ vikkhāletvā dasabalābhimukhā añjaliṃ paggaṇhitvā, “deva, amhākaṃ dese buddharatanaṃ nāma uppanna”nti āhaṃsu. Rañño “buddho”ti vacane sutamatte sakalasarīraṃ pharamānā pīti uppajji. Tato “buddhoti, tātā, vadathā”ti? Āha. “Buddhoti deva vadāmā”ti. Evaṃ tikkhattuṃ vadāpetvā, “buddhoti padaṃ aparimāṇaṃ, nāssa sakkā parimāṇaṃ kātu”nti tasmiṃyeva pasanno satasahassaṃ datvā puna “aññaṃ kiṃ sāsana”nti? Pucchi. “Deva dhammaratanaṃ nāma uppanna”nti. Tampi sutvā tatheva tikkhattuṃ paṭiññaṃ gahetvā aparampi satasahassaṃ datvā puna “aññaṃ kiṃ sāsana”nti? Pucchi. “Saṅgharatanaṃ deva uppanna”nti. Tampi sutvā tatheva tikkhattuṃ paṭiññaṃ gahetvā aparampi satasahassaṃ [M 2.0224] datvā dinnabhāvaṃ paṇṇe likhitvā, “tātā, deviyā santikaṃ gacchathā”ti pesesi. Tesu gatesu amacce pucchi, “tātā, buddho loke uppanno, tumhe kiṃ karissathā”ti? “Deva tumhe kiṃ kattukāmā”ti? “Ahaṃ pabbajissāmī”ti. “Mayampi pabbajissāmā”ti. Te sabbepi gharaṃ vā kuṭumbaṃ vā anapaloketvā ye asse āruyha gatā, teheva nikkhamiṃsu.

245. In the eleventh discourse, Mahākappina is a great elder among the eighty great disciples, one who has attained the power of higher knowledge and has such a name. It is said that during his time as a householder, he ruled a kingdom of three hundred yojanas in the city of Kukkuṭavatī. But because he was in his last existence, he went about with an attentive ear to hear such a message. Then one day, surrounded by a thousand ministers, he went to the park for amusement. At that time, merchants traveling on foot from the Middle Country, having come to that city and stored their goods, thought, “We will see the king.” With gifts in hand, they went to the palace gate, and hearing, “The king has gone to the park,” they went to the park, stood at the gate, and announced themselves to the gatekeeper. Then, when it was reported to the king, the king had them summoned. When they, having presented their gifts, stood paying homage, he asked, “Sirs, from where have you come?” “From Sāvatthī, Your Majesty.” “Is your country prosperous, and is the king righteous?” “Yes, Your Majesty.” “Is there any news in your country?” “There is, Your Majesty, but it cannot be spoken with mouths that have eaten.” The king had water given in a golden pitcher. They, having rinsed their mouths, raised their folded hands facing the Ten-Powered One and said, “Your Majesty, in our country the Buddha-jewel has arisen.” For the king, at the mere hearing of the word “Buddha,” joy arose, pervading his entire body. Then he said, “Sirs, do you say ‘Buddha’?” “We say ‘Buddha,’ Your Majesty.” Having had them say it three times, and thinking, “The word ‘Buddha’ is immeasurable; it is not possible to determine its measure,” he was pleased right then and there and gave a hundred thousand. He then asked, “What other news is there?” “Your Majesty, the Dhamma-jewel has arisen.” Hearing that too, he took an affirmation three times in the same way and gave another hundred thousand. He then asked, “What other news is there?” “The Saṅgha-jewel has arisen, Your Majesty.” Hearing that too, he took an affirmation three times in the same way and gave another hundred thousand. Having written on a leaf the fact of the gift, he sent them off, saying, “Sirs, go to the queen’s presence.” When they had gone, he asked his ministers, “Sirs, the Buddha has arisen in the world. What will you do?” “Your Majesty, what do you intend to do?” “I will go forth.” “We too will go forth.” All of them, without taking leave of their homes or wealth, departed on the very horses they had ridden there.

Vāṇijā anojādeviyā santikaṃ gantvā paṇṇaṃ dassesuṃ. Sā vācetvā “raññā tumhākaṃ bahū kahāpaṇā dinnā, kiṃ tumhehi kataṃ, tātā”ti? Pucchi. “Piyasāsanaṃ devi ānīta”nti. “Amhepi sakkā, tātā, suṇāpetu”nti. “Sakkā devi, ucchiṭṭhamukhehi pana vattuṃ na sakkā”ti. Sā suvaṇṇabhiṅgārena udakaṃ dāpesi. Te mukhaṃ vikkhāletvā rañño ārocitanayeneva ārocesuṃ. Sāpi sutvā uppannapāmojjā teneva nayena ekekasmiṃ pade tikkhattuṃ paṭiññaṃ gahetvā paṭiññāgaṇanāya tīṇi tīṇi katvā navasatasahassāni adāsi. Vāṇijā sabbānipi dvādasasatasahassāni labhiṃsu. Atha ne “rājā kahaṃ, tātā”ti, pucchi. “Pabbajissāmīti [P 2.0245] nikkhanto devī”ti. “Tena hi, tātā, tumhe gacchathā”ti te uyyojetvā raññā saddhiṃ gatānaṃ amaccānaṃ mātugāme pakkosāpetvā, “tumhe attano sāmikānaṃ gataṭṭhānaṃ jānātha ammā”ti pucchi. “Jānāma ayye, raññā saddhiṃ uyyānakīḷikaṃ [V 2.0216] gatā”ti. Āma gatā, tattha pana gantvā, “buddho uppanno, dhammo uppanno, saṅgho uppanno”ti sutvā, “dasabalassa santike pabbajissāmā”ti gatā. “Tumhe kiṃ karissathā”ti? “Tumhe pana ayye kiṃ kattukāmā”ti? “Ahaṃ pabbajissāmi, na tehi vantavamanaṃ jivhagge ṭhapeyya”nti. “Yadi evaṃ, mayampi pabbajissāmā”ti sabbā rathe yojāpetvā nikkhamiṃsu.

The merchants went to Queen Anojā and presented the letter. She had it read and asked, “Sirs, the king has given you many coins. What have you done?” “Your Majesty, we have brought a pleasing message.” “Sirs, is it possible for us to hear it too?” “It is possible, Your Majesty, but it cannot be spoken with mouths that have eaten.” She had water given in a golden pitcher. They rinsed their mouths and reported in the same way they had reported to the king. She too, upon hearing it, was filled with joy and, in the same way, for each term she took an affirmation three times, and making the gift for each three times that of the king, she gave nine hundred thousand. The merchants received twelve hundred thousand in all. Then she asked them, “Sirs, where is the king?” “Your Majesty, he has departed, saying, ‘I will go forth.’” “In that case, sirs, you may go.” Having dismissed them, she had the wives of the ministers who had gone with the king summoned and asked, “Mothers, do you know where your husbands have gone?” “We know, my lady. They went with the king for amusement in the park.” “Yes, they went, but having gone there and heard, ‘The Buddha has arisen, the Dhamma has arisen, the Saṅgha has arisen,’ they have gone to go forth in the presence of the Ten-Powered One. What will you do?” “But what do you intend to do, my lady?” “I will go forth. I would not place on the tip of my tongue the vomit spewed by them.” “If so, we too will go forth.” All of them had chariots yoked and departed.

Rājāpi amaccasahassena saddhiṃ gaṅgāya tīraṃ pāpuṇi. Tasmiñca samaye gaṅgā pūrā hoti. Atha naṃ disvā, “ayaṃ gaṅgā pūrā caṇḍamacchākiṇṇā, amhehi saddhiṃ āgatā dāsā vā manussā vā natthi, ye no nāvaṃ vā uḷumpaṃ vā katvā dadeyyuṃ, etassa pana satthu guṇā nāma heṭṭhā avīcito upari yāva bhavaggā patthaṭā, sace esa satthā sammāsambuddho, imesaṃ assānaṃ khurapiṭṭhāni mā tementū”ti udakapiṭṭhena asse pakkhandāpesuṃ[M 2.0225]. Ekaassassāpi khurapiṭṭhamattaṃ na temi, rājamaggena gacchantā viya paratīraṃ patvā purato aññaṃ mahānadiṃ pāpuṇiṃsu. Tattha aññā saccakiriyā natthi, tāya eva saccakiriyāya tampi aḍḍhayojanavitthāraṃ nadiṃ atikkamiṃsu. Atha tatiyaṃ candabhāgaṃ nāma mahānadiṃ patvā tampi tāya eva saccakiriyāya atikkamiṃsu.

The king, together with a thousand ministers, reached the bank of the Ganges. At that time, the Ganges was full. Then, seeing it, he thought, “This Ganges is full and teeming with fierce fish. There are no servants or men who came with us who might make a boat or a raft and give it to us. However, the virtues of this Teacher are spread from Avīci below up to the peak of existence above. If this Teacher is a Perfectly Enlightened One, may the hooves of these horses not get wet.” They urged the horses onto the surface of the water. Not even so much as the hoof of a single horse got wet. As if traveling on a royal road, they reached the far shore and came upon another great river ahead. There was no other act of truth; by that very same act of truth they crossed that river too, which was half a yojana wide. Then they came to a third great river named Candabhāga and crossed that too by that very same act of truth.

Satthāpi taṃdivasaṃ paccūsasamaye mahākaruṇāsamāpattito vuṭṭhāya lokaṃ olokento “ajja mahākappino tiyojanasatikaṃ rajjaṃ pahāya amaccasahassaparivāro mama santike pabbajituṃ āgacchatī”ti disvā, “mayā tesaṃ paccuggamanaṃ kātuṃ yutta”nti pātova sarīrapaṭijagganaṃ katvā, bhikkhusaṅghaparivāro sāvatthiyaṃ piṇḍāya caritvā, pacchābhattaṃ [P 2.0246] piṇḍapātapaṭikkanto sayameva pattacīvaraṃ gahetvā, ākāse uppatitvā candabhāgāya nadiyā tīre tesaṃ uttaraṇatitthassa abhimukhe ṭhāne mahānigrodharukkho atthi, tattha pallaṅkena nisīditvā parimukhaṃ satiṃ upaṭṭhapetvā chabbaṇṇabuddharasmiyo vissajjesi. Te tena titthena uttarantā ca chabbaṇṇabuddharasmiyo ito cito ca vidhāvantiyo olokentā dasabalassa puṇṇacandasassirikaṃ mukhaṃ disvā, “yaṃ satthāraṃ uddissa mayaṃ pabbajitā, addhā so eso”ti dassaneneva niṭṭhaṃ gantvā diṭṭhaṭṭhānato paṭṭhāya onatā vandamānā āgamma satthāraṃ vandiṃsu. Rājā gopphakesu gahetvā satthāraṃ vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi saddhiṃ amaccasahassena. Satthā tesaṃ dhammaṃ kathesi. Desanāpariyosāne sabbe arahatte patiṭṭhāya satthāraṃ pabbajjaṃ yāciṃsu. Satthā “pubbe ime cīvaradānassa [V 2.0217] dinnattā attano cīvarāni gahetvāva āgatā”ti suvaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ hatthaṃ pasāretvā, “etha bhikkhavo svākkhāto dhammo, caratha brahmacariyaṃ sammā dukkhassa antakiriyāyā”ti āha. Sāva tesaṃ āyasmantānaṃ pabbajjā ca upasampadā ca ahosi, vassasaṭṭhikattherā viya satthāraṃ parivārayiṃsu.

On that day, the Teacher, rising from the attainment of great compassion at dawn and surveying the world, saw: 'Today, Mahākappina, having abandoned his kingdom of three hundred yojanas, surrounded by a thousand ministers, is coming to my presence to go forth.' Seeing this, he thought, 'It is proper for me to go out to meet them.' Early in the morning, after attending to his bodily needs, surrounded by the community of monks, he walked for alms in Sāvatthī. After the meal, having returned from the alms-round, he alone took his bowl and robe, rose into the sky, and on the bank of the Candabhāgā River, at a place opposite their landing ford, there was a great banyan tree. There, having sat down cross-legged and established mindfulness before him, he emitted the six-colored Buddha-rays. As they were crossing by that ford, they saw the six-colored Buddha-rays flashing here and there. Looking, they saw the face of the Ten-Powered One, glorious like the full moon, and thought: 'For the sake of which Teacher we have gone forth, surely this is he.' Having reached this conclusion by the mere sight of him, from the very place they saw him, they bowed down, paying homage as they approached, and paid homage to the Teacher. The king, taking hold of the Teacher's ankles, paid homage and sat to one side together with the thousand ministers. The Teacher taught them the Dhamma. At the conclusion of the discourse, all were established in Arahantship and requested the going-forth from the Teacher. The Teacher, knowing, 'Because in a previous existence these ones gave the gift of robes, they have come having brought their own robes,' extended his golden-colored hand and said: 'Come, monks. The Dhamma is well-proclaimed. Live the holy life for the complete ending of suffering.' That itself was the going-forth and higher ordination for those venerable ones. Like elders of sixty rains, they surrounded the Teacher.

Anojāpi devī rathasahassaparivārā gaṅgātīraṃ patvā rañño atthāya ābhataṃ nāvaṃ vā uḷumpaṃ vā adisvā attano byattatāya cintesi – “rājā saccakiriyaṃ katvā gato bhavissati, so pana satthā na kevalaṃ tesaṃyeva [M 2.0226] atthāya nibbatto, sace so satthā sammāsambuddho, amhākaṃ rathā mā udake nimujjiṃsū”ti udakapiṭṭhe rathe pakkhandāpesi. Rathānaṃ nemivaṭṭimattampi na temi. Dutiyatatiyanadīpi teneva saccakārena uttaramānāyeva nigrodharukkhamūle satthāraṃ addasa. Satthā “imāsaṃ attano sāmike passantīnaṃ chandarāgo uppajjitvā maggaphalānaṃ antarāyaṃ kareyya, so evaṃ kātuṃ na sakkhissatī”ti yathā aññamaññe na passanti, tathā akāsi. Tā sabbāpi titthato uttaritvā dasabalaṃ vanditvā nisīdiṃsu. Satthā tāsaṃ dhammaṃ kathesi, desanāpariyosāne [P 2.0247] sabbāpi sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhāya aññamaññe passiṃsu. Satthā “uppalavaṇṇā āgacchatū”ti cintesi. Therī āgantvā sabbā pabbājetvā ādāya bhikkhunīnaṃ upassayaṃ gatā. Satthā bhikkhusahassaṃ gahetvā ākāsena jetavanaṃ agamāsi. Imaṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ – “mahākappinoti evaṃ nāmako abhiññābalappatto asītimahāsāvakānaṃ abbhantaro mahāthero”ti.

Queen Anojā, surrounded by a thousand chariots, reached the bank of the Ganges. Not seeing any boat or raft brought for the king, she thought with her own intelligence: 'The king must have gone after performing an act of truth. But that Teacher was not born solely for their sake. If that Teacher is indeed a Perfectly Enlightened One, may our chariots not sink in the water.' She had the chariots enter upon the surface of the water. Not even the felloe of the wheels got wet. Crossing the second and third rivers by means of that same act of truth, she saw the Teacher at the foot of the banyan tree. The Teacher thought: 'If these women see their husbands, lustful desire might arise in them and create an obstacle to the paths and fruits, and thus they would not be able to succeed.' Therefore, he made it so that they did not see one another. All of them, having crossed at the ford, paid homage to the Ten-Powered One and sat down. The Teacher taught them the Dhamma. At the conclusion of the discourse, all were established in the fruit of stream-entry and saw one another. The Teacher thought: 'Let Uppalavaṇṇā come.' The elder nun arrived, gave the going-forth to them all, and taking them, went to the nuns' quarters. The Teacher, taking the thousand monks, went through the sky to Jetavana. Regarding this, it is said: 'Mahākappina'—so named, who has attained the power of super-knowledge, a great elder among the eighty great disciples.

Janetasminti janite pajāyāti attho. Ye gottapaṭisārinoti ye “mayaṃ vāseṭṭhā gotamā”ti gottaṃ paṭisaranti paṭijānanti, tesaṃ khattiyo seṭṭhoti attho. Vijjācaraṇasampannoti aṭṭhahi vijjāhi ceva pannarasadhammabhedena caraṇena ca samannāgato. Tapatīti virocati. Jhāyī tapati brāhmaṇoti khīṇāsavabrāhmaṇo duvidhena jhānena jhāyamāno tapati virocati. Tasmiṃ pana khaṇe kāludāyitthero duvidhena jhānena jhāyamāno avidūre nisinno hoti. Buddho tapatīti sabbaññubuddho virocati. Sabbamaṅgalagāthā kiresā. Bhātikarājā kira ekaṃ pūjaṃ kāretvā ācariyakaṃ āha – “tīhi ratanehi amuttaṃ ekaṃ jayamaṅgalaṃ vadathā”ti. So tepiṭakaṃ buddhavacanaṃ sammasitvā imaṃ gāthaṃ vadanto “divā tapati ādicco”ti vatvā atthaṅgamentassa sūriyassa añjaliṃ paggaṇhi. “Rattimābhāti candimā”ti, uṭṭhahantassa candassa añjaliṃ [V 2.0218] paggaṇhi. “Sannaddho khattiyo tapatī”ti rañño añjaliṃ paggaṇhi. “Jhāyī tapati brāhmaṇo”ti bhikkhusaṅghassa añjaliṃ paggaṇhi. “Buddho tapati tejasā”ti vatvā pana mahācetiyassa añjaliṃ paggaṇhi. Atha naṃ rājā “mā hatthaṃ otārehī”ti ukkhittasmiṃyeva hatthe sahassaṃ ṭhapesi. Ekādasamaṃ.

The meaning of 'in this people' is 'among the people in which one is born.' 'Those who resort to lineage' means those who resort to and profess their lineage, saying, 'We are Vāseṭṭhas, Gotamas.' Among them, the khattiya is best; this is the meaning. 'Endowed with knowledge and conduct' means endowed with the eight kinds of knowledge and with the conduct divided into fifteen factors. 'Shines' means radiates. 'The meditating brahmin shines' means the brahmin who has destroyed the taints, meditating with the two kinds of meditation, shines and radiates. At that moment, the Elder Kāludāyi was seated not far away, meditating with the two kinds of meditation. 'The Buddha shines' means the All-Knowing Buddha radiates. This, it is said, is the All-Auspicious Verse. It is said that King Bhātika, having arranged an offering, said to his teacher: 'Recite a verse of victory and blessing that is apart from the Three Jewels.' He, having reflected on the Buddha's word in the Tipiṭaka, recited this verse. Saying 'The sun shines by day,' he raised his hands in homage to the setting sun. Saying 'The moon is radiant by night,' he raised his hands in homage to the rising moon. Saying 'The khattiya shines when armed,' he raised his hands in homage to the king. Saying 'The meditating brahmin shines,' he raised his hands in homage to the Saṅgha of monks. But saying 'The Buddha shines with majesty,' he raised his hands in homage to the Great Stupa. Then the king, saying 'Do not lower your hand,' placed a thousand on his raised hand. The eleventh.

12. Sahāyakasuttavaṇṇanā

12. The Commentary on the Sahāyaka Sutta.

246. Dvādasame [M 2.0227] cirarattaṃsametikāti dīgharattaṃ saṃsanditvā sametvā ṭhitaladdhino. Te kira pañcajātisatāni ekatova vicariṃsu. Sameti nesaṃ saddhammoti idāni imesaṃ ayaṃ sāsanadhammo [P 2.0248] saṃsandati sameti. Dhamme buddhappavediteti buddhena pavedite dhamme etesaṃ sāsanadhammo sobhatīti attho. Suvinītā kappinenāti attano upajjhāyena ariyappavedite dhamme suṭṭhu vinītā. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti. Dvādasamaṃ.

246. In the twelfth: 'Having come together for a long time' means having associated and come together for a long time, they have stood in their attainment. It is said that they wandered together for five hundred lifetimes. 'Their true Dhamma comes together' means now this teaching Dhamma connects and comes together for them. 'In the Dhamma proclaimed by the Buddha' means their teaching Dhamma shines in the Dhamma proclaimed by the Buddha; this is the meaning. 'Well-trained by Kappina' means well-trained by their own preceptor in the Dhamma proclaimed by the Noble One. The rest is clear throughout. The twelfth.

Bhikkhusaṃyuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Bhikkhu Saṃyutta is concluded.

Iti sāratthappakāsiniyā saṃyuttanikāya-aṭṭhakathāya

Thus, in the Sāratthappakāsinī, the Commentary on the Saṃyutta Nikāya,

Nidānavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

the explanation of the Nidāna Vagga is concluded.
